I indeed exhorted the people, saying, House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. But because the Lord has cast off the people of Jacob, and has cast them off because they either did or suffered the things which we have expounded above, therefore I foretell to you the evils that are to come, and I exhort you to enter the rocks and hide in the caves from the face of the Babylonian or the Roman army, when all things will be laid waste, according to what we read in the Gospel: Then they will say to the mountains, Fall upon us; and to the rocks, Hide us (Luke 23:30). But according to the anagogy we are commanded, before the face of the Lord's majesty, to take on the strength of the rock, of which it is said: The rock is a refuge for the hares (Ps 103 [104]:18); and, On a rock you have exalted me (Ps 26 [27]:6). Moses too is set in a cleft of the rock to see the back parts of God (Exod 33). And, The people drank from the spiritual rock that followed them (1 Cor 10:4). And he hides himself in the rock who enters his chamber and, having shut the door, adores the Father, so that, though placed in an earthly body, he does not feel the passing storm of the world.

2:11

The lofty eyes of man are humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down; but the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. When the enemies have come, and the Babylonian or Roman sword has laid waste the whole province, and the columns of warriors have besieged Jerusalem, then neither riches nor nobility of birth nor the power of offices will be able to defend anyone; but there will be one captivity for all, and God alone will be exalted, whose wrath no one will be able to avoid. Many understand these things of the day of judgment: that every creature, in comparison with the divine glory, will be humbled and bowed down, and will feel itself to be nothing.

2:12

For the day of the Lord of hosts is upon everyone proud and lofty, and upon everyone arrogant. These things too are joined to the former. In that day, he says, in which the Lord alone will be exalted, that is, in the day of the Lord's vengeance, all the lofty and the arrogant and the high will be subjected to captivity and the sword. Μεταφορικῶς the word is about the great and the princes: that the more they have been proud, the more they are brought low. For the Lord resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5). Those who understand it of the day of judgment think that the devil is called proud and lofty and high and arrogant; who in his pride says: I will set my seat above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the lofty mountain, above all the lofty mountains, toward the North; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High (Isa 14:13, 14): when out of the mouth of infants and sucklings praise will be perfected, that the enemy and the avenger may be destroyed (Ps 8:3).

2:13

And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan. In Psalm 28 (29) too it is sung: The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and will crush them like the calf of Lebanon (Ps 28 [29]:5, 6). And in Psalm 36 (37): I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:35, 36). The oaks of Bashan too, which Aquila translated δρύας, Symmachus and Theodotion βαλάνους, we know to be acorn-bearing trees, which, even if they bear fruit, are food for swine, not for men. Bashan is a region of Arabia, over which Og ruled, who was called king of Bashan; and it means αἰσχύνη, that is, ignominy; and if we chose to translate it confusion, that would rather signify σύγχυσιν, that is, Babylon, than Bashan. Upon all, then, who are lifted up in pride, and do works of ignominy, and wallow in the mire of lusts, the vengeance of the Lord will rise. But if the prudent reader should ask why cedar wood was set in the temple of the Lord, and why in Psalm 103 (104), according to the Hebrew truth, we read, The trees of the Lord shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which you have planted; there the sparrows will build their nests (Ps 103 [104]:16, 17); and why among the other trees the cedars too are summoned to the praises of the Lord; and why at the coming of the Savior, when all the trees and the wood of the field will clap with their branches, it is written: I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box, and the cypress and the pine (Isa 41:19 LXX); and now the prophetic word threatens the day of the Lord upon the cedars of Lebanon? it must be said that out of the same kind of men some are raised up to the kingdom, others dragged down to punishment; and the cedars of Lebanon, which will be broken because of their pride, are chosen when they are of good odor and have said with the Apostle: We are the good odor of Christ (2 Cor 2:15).

2:14

And upon all the lofty mountains, and upon all the hills that are lifted up. Just as in a good sense, according to the variety of virtues, men are called mountains and hills, so among the impious, according to the diversity of vices, and above all of pride, some are mountains, others hills, upon which the day of the Lord will be; of whom it is written in Ezekiel: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the mountains and the hills: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and your high places shall be scattered, and your altars shall be broken, and the rest (Ezek 6:3).

2:15

And upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall. Those who refer these things to the times of Vespasian and Hadrian say that what is written was fulfilled bodily: that no lofty tower, no strongest wall, no multitude of ships and industry of trade could prevail against the might of the Roman army; but that the inhabitants of Judea came into such terror that they, with their wives and children, buried themselves in pits of the earth with the gold and silver which they thought would be a help to them, and sought out the deepest caves. For if the belly is the god of the gluttonous and the luxurious, why should not gold and silver be called the god of the avaricious? Others refer these things to Babylonian times. So I will run through each point according to the laws of tropology. A tower is built either for the defense of a city or for a lookout, so that the enemy may be seen coming from afar. Each of us, then, ought to build a tower, having first reckoned the cost, lest, according to the parable of the Gospel (Luke 14), he be laughed at when he cannot finish the work. This tower, well built, stands firm. But if, raised up in pride, it has no firm foundations, it will fall upon him by whom it was built, like that one in Siloam which killed eighteen men. Hence the Lord too says to his hearers: And unless you repent, you will likewise perish (Luke 13:3). In what follows too we shall read that the Lord built a tower in his vineyard, and made a winepress, and put a wall around it, but that all these things were destroyed and laid waste because they swelled with the vain brow of pride (Isa 5). Lofty walls too are built so that the city may not be quickly destroyed, so that it may not lie open to enemies: for the Churches are surrounded with the wisest men and fortified with every reason, lest any perverse doctrine prevail against the truth. Of such walls God speaks to Jerusalem: Behold, upon my hands I have painted your walls, and they are always in my sight (below, Isa 49:16 LXX). But if those who before had attacked the Church, having come to know the truth, pass over to the faith and fight for that which they had before attacked, then this will be fulfilled: You shall quickly be built by those by whom you had been destroyed (ibid., 17). In Leviticus too we read that a house which is in walled cities, if it has not been redeemed within the year, is confirmed to the buyer as a perpetual possession; but if it is in country places and villages which have no walls, it can always be redeemed, and the buyer's price remains unsettled (Lev 25).

2:16

And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all that is beautiful to see. For Tarshish, which all translated alike, the Seventy alone translated sea. The Hebrews think that in their own tongue the sea is properly called THARSIS (תרסים), and that when it is called IAM (ים), it is called so not in the Hebrew tongue but in the Syriac. Jehoshaphat too had ships which he sent to Tarshish (1 Kgs 22:49), but they were broken at Ezion-geber. Solomon too had ships which went to Tarshish (1 Kgs 10:22) and returned after three years and brought the king silver and gold, ivory and apes. But because both kings had sinned, the one given to pleasure and a lover of women of foreign nations, the other joining himself with the king of Samaria, both of which things are referred to the pagans and the heretics, in whom there is nothing but the glitter of eloquence, and a sense built up by diabolical art, and dead speech, which is interpreted in the ivory teeth, and a likeness of human reason, which is perceived in the apes; therefore we read in the Psalms, With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish (Ps 47 [48]:8). And of these ships the same Isaiah speaks: Woe to the wings of the ships which are beyond Ethiopia (below, Isa 18:1 LXX). But there are on the contrary good ships too, of which it is said in the same psalms: Those who go down to the sea in ships and do business in many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep (Ps 106 [107]:23). For those who are not idle in the waves of this world, but work, and carry the Lord's merchandise, and hasten to come to the harbor of rest, they see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep, when they have come to deep knowledge and, searching all things, that is, even the deep things of God, have beheld his wonders. Josephus thinks Tarshish is Tarsus, a city of Cilicia; others think it a region of India, and that by this name too one of the twelve gems is called, the stone which among us is called chrysolite, from the likeness of its color to the sea. But it is better to take Tarshish absolutely as either the sea or the open main. For Jonah, sailing from Joppa, could not reach India, to which one cannot sail by that sea; but simply go out to the open sea and make for whatever islands. And what follows, And upon all that is beautiful to see, or, as the Seventy translated, And upon every sight of the beauty of ships, is to be taken in the same sense: that whatever seems beautiful in words and is built up by human reason will be destroyed by the day of the Lord, if it lifts itself up against the knowledge of God.

2:18

And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the height of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day, and the idols shall be utterly broken. Human speech seems to have reason so long as it has not been compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood draws near to the truth, like stubble to fire, it is quickly devoured and perishes, and all the doctrines of falsehood, which are now called idols because they are feigned and fabricated, will be utterly broken.

2:19

In that day man shall cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he had made for himself, to worship moles and bats; and he shall go into the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth. We have often said that silver and gold are taken for speech and sense; and though these were given by God to men so that they might either speak of God or perceive God and praise their creator, they abuse this gift for the fashioning of idols; according to what is written: I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal of my silver and gold (Hos 2:8). When, then, someone, terrified by the fear of the Lord, has first hidden his idols in the cave of his breast and concealed them in the abysses of the earth, not daring to bring out what he had wickedly fashioned, the second advance is that he cast away what he had first concealed and not suffer it to be in him. For moles, as we have translated, the Seventy have vain things, Aquila ὀρυκτὰ, Symmachus unfruitful things; Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, PHARPHAROTH (פרפרות). It is an animal without eyes, which always digs the earth and throws out the soil, and, eating the roots underneath, is harmful to crops; the Greeks call it ἀσπάλακα. The bat, a bird of the night, which received from them the fitting name νυκτερὶς because it flits about in the night, is a small animal, like a mouse, sounding not so much with voice and song as with squeaking; and though it is seen to fly, it shuns the light and cannot bear to see the sun. To such animals are compared the idols, which, blind and dark, are worshiped by the blind, and all doctrines contrary to the truth. And when these have been abandoned in the day of the Lord, those who have cast them away will enter the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones, so as to dwell not in the dust of the earth and in vile mud but in firm reason, and find for themselves the various openings of the virtues, through which they may be able to come to the truth. These things, according to the anagogy, I have touched on as I could in brief words; the Hebrews refer them to Babylonian times and the overthrow of Jerusalem, when the Lord rose to strike the land of the Jews.

2:20

Cease, therefore, from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he himself is reckoned lofty. The Seventy omitted this, and in the Greek copies it was added by Origen under asterisks from the edition of Aquila; in the Hebrew it reads thus: HEDALU LACHEM MEN AADAM ASER NASAMA BAAPHPHO CHI BAMA NESAB HU. Where we have said, he himself is reckoned lofty, Aquila translated, in what is this one reckoned. The Hebrew word BAMA (במה) means either ὕψωμα, that is, a high place, which we read both in the books of Kingdoms and in Ezekiel, or else in what, and it is written with the same letters, BETH, MEM, HE; and according to the character of the passages, if we wish to read in what, we say BAMMA; but if high place or lofty, we read BAMA. The Jews, then, understanding that the prophecy is about Christ, interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that they might seem not to praise Christ but to count him as nothing. For what consequence of words is there, and what order of reason and sense, that we should say: Since these things are so, and the day of the Lord is to come, in which the whole state of Judea is to be overthrown and all things broken, I warn and command you to cease from the man who breathes and lives as we men do, because he is to be reckoned as nothing? Would any man so praise someone as to say: Beware of offending him who is altogether nothing? Therefore it must be understood the other way: Since all these things are to come upon you, and are foretold by the prophetic spirit, I warn and command you to cease from him who according to the flesh is indeed a man, and has a soul, and so breathes and draws breath through his nostrils as we men breathe and live, but who according to the divine majesty both is lofty and is reckoned and believed so. Turning it over silently in my mind, I cannot find the reason why the Seventy would not translate into Greek so clear a prophecy about Christ. For as to the others, who did translate it but dragged the ambiguous word to an impious sense, it is no wonder why they translated badly and would not say anything glorious about Christ, in whom they did not believe: being, namely, Jews or half-Jews, that is, Ebionites. And that Christ is lofty or most high, which among the Hebrews is called by another word, ELION (עליון), we read in Psalm 86 (87): Shall not a man say to Zion, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her (Ps 86 [87]:5)? And in the Gospel: And you, child, shall be called the Prophet of the Most High (Luke 1:76). And not to draw out a long rope (for in the exposition of the holy Scriptures we ought to follow the truth, not contention), in this place BAMA among the Hebrews means not lofty but a high place, that is, loftiness itself and sublimity: as if we were to say of someone, he is not divine but divination, not a stream but a fountain, not a man but humanity itself. Origen interpreted this passage thus: Because it is said in the singular of one man, it can be referred also to the Lord Savior, the Prophet commanding them to cease from him who is reckoned as something great, although at present he appears as a man and to have breath in his nostrils, as other men too breathe.

Book Two

Having finished the first volume on Isaiah, which I dictated in hasty speech as I could, not as I would, seeking out the sense of the Scriptures rather than the words of a composed discourse, I shall now pass on to the second; and whatever strength is in me, and whatever will inclined toward the Lord, I shall offer to him who spoke through the Prophet: I have multiplied visions, and in the hands of the Prophets I have been likened (Hos 12:10). Wherefore I beseech you, virgin of Christ Eustochium, that while we contend in the explanation of the Scriptures, you with Moses may lift up your hands to the Lord, so that we who, going out of Egypt, have crossed the Red Sea may conquer Amalek, which means devouring and licking up; and that we may be able to say with you: Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle, and my fingers for war (Ps 143 [144]:1).

3:1

For behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and the strong: all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water. Up to this point they think it is spoken of the judgment. What follows concerns the captivity to come, which some refer to the Babylonians, others to the Romans. But it is better, as we said above, for everything to be referred to the Lord's passion. For after he was slain, all graces and gifts were taken away from the Jews, according to what is written in the Gospel: The Law and the Prophets until John the Baptist (Matt 11:13). And the order is this: Because you would not cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, who has been reckoned exalted, but on the contrary you shed the blood of the righteous one and devised the worst counsel, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is useless to us (Wis 2:12), therefore you shall eat the fruit of your own devices. Among the Jews after the Passion of the Lord nothing is strong, nothing is mighty, but all things are weak and languid. Nor can anyone among them say: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil 4:13), Christ Jesus our Lord. And since according to the Seventy we read the mighty man and the mighty woman, to the mighty man we can fit this: Until we all meet in the perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph 4:13). And further, of the mighty woman: I wish, he says, to present you all as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor 11:2). Now the strength of bread and the strength of water is taken for all food and drink. We read that Moses was on Mount Sinai, and for forty days did not eat bread and did not drink water (Exod 34). That too which is said to Adam: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken (Gen 3:19), is to be heard in the same way. So also what is said by the Savior: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that goes forth through the mouth of God (Matt 4:4). The strength of bread, then, will be taken away from them: he who says, I am the living bread, who came down from heaven (John 6:51). And the strength of water, of which the same Lord spoke: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:13). Of such loaves we read in Proverbs as well: Open your eyes, and be filled with loaves (Prov 20:13). The Jews have bread, but without strength; they have waters, but without vigor. For they read the Scriptures, but do not understand them; they hold the parchments, and have lost Christ, who is written in the parchments (1 Cor 3). For they are fed on milk, like little children, and not on solid food. And because they have lost their strength and are weak, therefore they eat vegetables. But the food of athletes is solid, which both sustains human life and furnishes strength to the living (Rom 14). Of such bread and water, that they are to be taken away from the Jews, another Prophet too bears witness, saying: Behold, the day will come, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord (Amos 8:11).

3:2

The strong man and the man of war, the judge and the Prophet, and the soothsayer, and the old man. For strong man, which alone is in the Hebrew, the Seventy translated two words together, giant and strong man, meaning the same man to be the giant who is the strong man. Of the strong man we have spoken above. Now a giant in the good sense, that is, of the Lord and Savior, we read in the eighteenth psalm: He has exulted as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit even to its height (Ps 18 [19]:8). But if we read of Nimrod the giant (Gen 10), who was a hunter before the Lord, and of the giants (Gen 6) on whose account the flood came upon the earth, they are to be taken in the contrary sense. The man of war, too, we understand according to the history in this way: that they have been taken captive, and to this day are in servitude, and have not laid aside the yoke of slavery; that they do not even have judges of their own, but are subject to Roman judges, so much so that Roman rulers judge those of their princes who seem to be of standing among the people. But this too must be said: that there is no man of war among them in the Law, having the knowledge of judging, but all things are vain and perishable and full of folly. As for the Prophet, that he has ceased to exist among them no one doubts. We ask, according to the Hebrew, how we are to interpret soothsayer, whom all have translated diviner, except the Seventy, who for this translated conjecturer. And it must be said that future things are often told even through soothsayers, as we read of the diviner Balaam, and of the diviners of the five cities of the Philistines, Gaza and Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron and Ashdod, who give counsel how the ark of the Lord is to be sent back (1 Sam 6). And the sense is: both true things and false will alike be taken away from the Jews. The old man too, whom the Seventy translated elder, he understands to be taken away from the Jews, he who would know that in the holy Scriptures elders are chosen for merit and wisdom, not for age. For old men have not ceased to exist among the Jews; we often see them reach a decrepit old age. And we read in the beginning of Daniel, according to Theodotion, of two elders grown old in evil days (Dan 13). For Moses too is commanded to choose elders whom he knows to be elders (Exod 18). And the apostle Paul writes most fully to Timothy what kind of elder ought to be chosen (1 Tim 5). Hence it is said in Proverbs as well: The glory of old men is gray hair (Prov 20:29). What is this gray hair? Doubtless wisdom, of which it is written: Prudence is the gray hair of men (Wis 4:8). And though we read that from Adam to Abraham men lived nine hundred years and more (Gen 24), no one before was called an elder, that is, an old man, except Abraham, who is shown to have lived far fewer years. Hence John too, after the children and the young men, writes also to the old, saying: I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning (1 John 2:13). And Rehoboam the son of Solomon lost the kingdom for this reason, that he would not listen to the elders (1 Kgs 12).

3:3

The captain of fifty. Συνεκδοχικῶς, the whole from a part. For just as those who command a hundred soldiers are called Centurions, and those who command a thousand Chiliarchs, whom we call Tribunes, from the fact that they command a tribe: so in the army of Israel those who were at the head of fifty soldiers were called captains of fifty. Hence too we call Decurions those who command ten men. Nor is it a wonder if among the Jews every rank of warriors has perished, since they have no power to serve under the sword and to bear arms. But since the number fifty is always referred to penitence, and Christ is the prince of penitence and the head of those who are saved through penitence, let us briefly lay open the mysteries of this number. In Genesis we read, when Abraham speaks to the Lord, that he said first that the city should be saved for fifty righteous, if they were found in it. And in Numbers there is the most celebrated festival of the seven weeks, that is, of Pentecost. The Jubilee too, that is, the year of remission, which is woven of seven weeks of years, that is, of forty-nine years, in which the trumpets sound and the ancient possession returns to everyone, contains this mystery. Hence David too writes the Psalm of penitence at the fiftieth number. We read also in the same book of Numbers that of the booty and spoils the priests were to receive the fiftieth head, of men as well as of beasts, and the Levites who guard the doors of the tabernacle the fiftieth. That parable of the Gospel as well (Luke 7 and 16), in which two debtors are spoken of, one who owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty, refers to this understanding. Hence the Apostle too, among the Ephesians, to whom he had unfolded every mystical thing, wishes to remain until Pentecost, until they should be perfectly converted to the Lord, saying: For a great and evident door has been opened to me, but there are many adversaries (1 Cor 16:9). But the devil also imitates the army of Israel, concerning which Jethro had given counsel to his son-in-law Moses, that he should set over the people tribunes and centurions and captains of fifty (Exod 18). Hence the impious king (2 Kgs 1) sends two captains of fifty with the soldiers under them to bring Elijah: they were consumed by divine fire. But the third of them is saved, who, having turned to prayers, had come to know the mysteries of penitence. Hence the Jews too, unwilling that the Lord should be perfect or the captain of fifty, say to him: You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham? (John 8:57). And he, knowing himself to be the prince not only of the penitent but also of the righteous, answered: Before Abraham was, I am (ibid., 58). And that the Lord is the Captain of Fifty we can understand from a single festival, of which he says: The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt 12:8). If of the Sabbath, then of the Kalends too. If of the Kalends, then of the Pasch, that is, of the Unleavened Bread. If of the Pasch, then of the Jubilee. If of the Jubilee, then of Tabernacles. If of Tabernacles, then of Pentecost, which is referred to the fiftieth number.

And the honorable in countenance, and the counselor. For two, that is, honorable in countenance, and counselor, the Seventy translated one, wonderful man counselor. Among the other graces the Lord will take this too away from Judea, that they have no counselor, but do everything without counsel. And there is that praiseworthy and admirable saying of a Greek poet: "He is first in happiness who is wise of himself; second, he who listens to the wise." But he who lacks both is useless, both to himself and to all. Hence we read this too in our books: Let your friends be very many, but your counselor one of a thousand (Sir 6:6). And again: Do all things with counsel (Prov 13:10); and prudence will give you a wonderful counselor. Decrees of the Senate too are called consulta, and the chief men of Rome were once called consuls, either from consulting for the citizens or from ruling all things by counsel. And we in the Church have our senate, the assembly of elders. Since, then, among other things Judea has lost even its old men, how will it be able to have counsel, which properly belongs to the elders?

And the wise architect. For which Aquila translated the wisest of craftsmen, to show that they once had many craftsmen: such as was that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, whom God filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge, so that in every work he was a most accomplished workman, not only in gold and silver but also in bronze and the other things that Moses enumerates, he who built the Tabernacle of God (Exod 31). Since, then, they have lost their architects, all the grace of building has been transferred to the Church. Hence the apostle Paul says: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation (1 Cor 3:10). Jeremiah too was an architect, who not only rooted up and dug under and destroyed, but also built (Jer 18). Hence the same Apostle says: We are God's husbandry, God's building (1 Cor 3:9). Our Lord too is called the builder of walls (Eph 2). And in the Gospel he who made all things is taunted as the son of a carpenter (Matt 13). In the volume of Kings too we read that king Solomon sent and took Hiram the Tyrian, the son of a widow woman, who was of the tribe of Naphtali and had a Tyrian father, a worker in bronze. And he came in to the king and did all the works for king Solomon: in him there is a type of the Church to be built, which was begotten not only of the tribe of Judah but also of Naphtali, and of a Tyrian father, he who had a widowed mother, because she had lost her former husband (1 Kgs 7). And many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa 54). But in the book of Chronicles too we read of the valley of craftsmen: And Seraiah begot Joab, the father of the valley of craftsmen: for craftsmen were there (1 Chr 4:14). They are said to dwell in a valley for this reason, that knowledge did not puff them up, but they followed the humble and meek Jesus, and could say with the Apostle: For I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an Apostle (1 Cor 15:9). And elsewhere: We know in part, and we prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor 13:9).

And the one prudent in mystic speech. For which the Seventy translated the prudent hearer; Theodotion, the prudent enchanter; Aquila, the prudent whisperer; Symmachus, the one prudent in mystic speech, whom we too have followed in this place. First it must be said, according to the Seventy, that among the other spiritual graces a prudent hearer too is necessary in the Church. For to one is given prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits (1 Cor 12:10). Hence there were also established among the people of the Jews priestly ranks, to discern prophets and false prophets, that is, to understand who spoke from the Spirit of God and who from the contrary spirit. Let us read Jeremiah. But the prudent one in mystic speech (Jer 14), or the whisperer, and, as Theodotion would have it, the enchanter, seems to me to be a man learned and practiced both in the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel and the Apostles, who can heal each disturbance of the soul by his teaching and bring it back to a settled state of mind: while the fornicator recovers chastity, and the glutton frugality, and the man once greedy gives alms. Sift through all the synagogues of the Jews, and you will be able to find no teacher who enjoins holy things and, despising riches, teaches that poverty is to be pursued. Of such enchanters against serpents and asps, that is, against sinners who have abandoned the righteousness of God, David spoke in the Psalm: Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly, they have spoken falsehoods. Their fury is after the likeness of a serpent: like the deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the enchanters, nor of the sorcerer who charms wisely (Ps 57 [58]:4ff.). Every word of the Apostle is an enchantment against serpents and asps, which sinners and heretics do not hear, because they shut their ears so as not to hear the truth.

3:4

And I will give children to be their princes. If it is said in the person of the Prophet: For behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty man and the mighty woman: all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water, and the rest, how does the same prophet now say: I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them? Therefore, according to prophetic custom, while the Prophet is speaking, God suddenly speaks through the Prophet in his own person, and says: I will give children to be their princes: for having removed the things I had given before, and having taken away good things as though in anger, now on the contrary I will give evil things. I took away the old man and the captain of fifty, and the wonderful counselor, and the wise architect, and the prudent hearer, and so on. In their place I will give children as princes. For those who have lost the elder, such as the discourse above has shown, such as Abraham too was who was first called an elder, rightly receive young men as princes (Gen 7). Of these we read in Ecclesiastes too: Woe to you, O city, whose king is a youth, and your princes eat in the morning. Blessed is the land whose king is a son of the freeborn (Eccl 10:16). Such a young king was Rehoboam the son of Solomon, who followed the counsels of the young men (1 Kgs 12): not that he was young in age, but in wisdom. Otherwise, he is related to have received the kingdom at forty years and more. And on the contrary, Solomon was twelve years old when he took up the rule, and because he had wisdom, he was therefore not called a youth. For there was in him breadth of heart and amplitude of wisdom as great as the sand on the shores of the sea. Hence the Apostle too writes to Timothy: Let no one despise your youth (1 Tim 4:12). For he who is young in age is an old man in maturity. And Daniel, according to Theodotion, was called a boy before he judged (Dan 13); but after God stirred up his spirit in him and he judged the elders, he received the dignity of the eldership. To Jeremiah too, who had said to the Lord who was sending him, You who are ruler, O Lord: Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a youth (Jer 1:6), the Lord answered: Do not say, I am a youth; for before you were formed in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from your mother's womb I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet among the nations. For this reason, I think, the young widows too are commanded by the Apostle (1 Tim 5) to take husbands and be mothers of families and bring up their children, because many have gone back after Satan; and when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation, because they have made void their first faith. Nor is a widow supported on the Church's provisions unless she is sixty years old and has maturity of character as well as of age. One might think that what the Apostle forbids (1 Tim 3), that a neophyte be made a bishop, pertains to this, because he is a little one in faith, lest, puffed up into pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. And the judgment of the devil is nothing else but pride, on account of which he fell from heaven. Hence the Savior too says: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18).

And the effeminate shall rule over them. For which in the Hebrew is written THALULIM (תעלולים), whom the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted as mockers, Aquila ἐναλλάκτας, those who change themselves and take turns in shameful acts, such as we read of in the book of Judges concerning the Levite's concubine in Gibeah (Judg 19). Let us consider the Patriarchs of the Jews, and the young men or boys, effeminate and abounding in luxuries, and we shall see that the prophecy has been fulfilled. We may also call mockers the teachers of the people of Israel, who devour the people of God like a morsel of bread, and interpret the holy Scriptures perversely, and make sport of the folly of their disciples.

3:5

And the people shall rush, man upon man, each one upon his neighbor: the boy shall riot against the old man, and the base against the noble. When the princes are young men, and mockers of the Lord, such as the prophetic discourse describes, then no order will be kept, whether of dignity or of age or of knowledge; but boys will rebel against old men, and the base against the noble, and they will fall upon one another. And that saying of the Apostle will be fulfilled: Biting one another, you have been consumed by one another (Gal 5:15). That these things befell the people of the Jews under Titus the son of Vespasian, Josephus writes (Jewish War, Book 5): and that, when they were being besieged by the Romans, Jerusalem was divided by sedition into three parts, and some held the citadel and the Temple, others the lower, others the upper part of the city.

3:6

For a man shall take hold of his brother, of the household of his father: You have a garment, be our prince; and let this ruin be under your hand. For ruin, Symmachus and Theodotion translated weakness; the Seventy, food. It signifies the scarcity of men, and above all the want of all things, so that whoever has food and clothing is believed to be powerful and rich and illustrious. And what it says according to the Hebrew, And let this ruin be under your hand, has this sense: Let our misery and calamity be sustained and protected by your help. And this must be considered, that each man chooses for himself his own prince, and that there is sedition in the choosing of princes, while some think some men worthy of rule and others others. Nor do they say to them, Your possessions and riches and revenues will be able to sustain us; but, This weakness, or my food, will be healed by your judgment and will hang upon it.

3:7

And he will answer in that day, saying, I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor garment; do not appoint me prince of the people. For physician, Symmachus and the Seventy translated prince; Theodotion, ἐπιδεσμεύοντα, one who binds up wounds and provides for health. He will answer is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added from the Seventy. For in the Hebrew it is joined to what is written above: In that day he will say, I am not a physician, and the rest. And he will say it who has been chosen prince. And just as the people desires to have as prince the one whom it perceives to be richer in comparison with itself, so the one who is chosen, considering his poverty and his weakness, testifies that he is unworthy of the honor conferred and cannot heal vices, that is, cure the sick, give food to the hungry, clothe the naked, since he himself is scarcely able to sustain himself. Let us not, then, at once acquiesce in the judgment of the multitude; but when chosen for leadership, let us know our measure and be humbled under the mighty hand of God, because God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5). How many, having neither bread nor clothing, though they themselves are hungry and naked, and have no spiritual food and have not kept the tunic of Christ whole, promise others both nourishment and clothing, and, full of wounds, boast that they are physicians; nor do they keep that saying of Moses: Provide another whom you may send, and that other command: Seek not to be made a judge, lest perhaps you be unable to take away iniquities (Sir 7:6). Jesus alone heals all sicknesses and infirmities, of whom it is written: Who heals the broken in heart, and binds up their bruises (Ps 146 [147]:3).

3:8-9

For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed: because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty. The recognition of their countenance has answered them: and they have proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and have not hidden it. It is the Prophet who says this, not, as many think, the one who had been chosen prince. And he says that no one is willing to be set over a sinful people for this reason, that both Judah and Jerusalem, both the city and the province of Judea, or the tribe of Judah, have fallen alike. And he gives the causes of their impiety: that they blasphemed against the Lord and said, Away, away, crucify such a one; we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15, 16), and by the fury of their tongue provoked the most merciful Lord to bitterness. The recognition of their countenance will answer them: that is, they have received back their own sins; or, as the Seventy translated, the confusion of their countenance has stood against them: that is, they have always had their own offenses before their eyes. And just as the Sodomites, sinning with all license and having not even any shame in their crime, said to Lot, Bring the men out, that we may lie with them (Gen 19:5): so these too, crying out publicly, proclaimed their sin and had no modesty in blaspheming. For to hide one's impiety is the second plank after shipwreck and a consolation of miseries. Hence they are also called princes of Sodom, because they had the sins of Sodom.

3:10-11

Woe to their soul, because evils have been repaid to them. Say to the righteous that it is well, because they have eaten the fruit of their own devices. Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be done to him. According to the Hebrew and the other Translators it has this sense: Woe to them, because they have received back their crimes. Therefore you who hear, or who read the book of the Prophet, praise the righteousness of God, because he has done well: because the wicked have eaten the labors of their own hands. And woe to the wicked people unto evil: for it has received what it deserved. And he who handed over his prince to the Roman power himself lies subject to Roman servitude. But according to the Seventy Translators, who said: Woe to their soul, because they have devised the worst counsel against themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, because he is useless to us; therefore they shall eat the fruits of their works, it is clearly said of the passion of Christ, that they entered upon the worst counsel, not so much against the righteous one as against themselves and their own soul; and now they eat the fruits of their works. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap (Gal 6:5-8), and each one will bear his own burden.

3:12

My people, their exactors have despoiled them, and women have ruled over them. For women, whom Symmachus alone translated so, and who in Hebrew are called NASIM (נשים), Aquila and the Seventy translated ἀπαιτοῦντας, which means exactors; Theodotion δανειστὰς, that is, usurers. Now the prophetic discourse speaks against the Scribes and Pharisees, who for the sake of base gain, to receive tithes and first-fruits, denied the Son of God. And he does not call them masters, scribes and teachers, but exactors (Luke 20), who think that piety is a means of gain, and devour, not, as in the Apostle, only the houses of widows, but the whole people; and, accusing their luxury and their shameful way of life, he calls them not only exactors, as men seen to exact money from the unwilling, but women, because they do everything for lust's sake and are given over to pleasures. Let us too, then, beware that we be not exactors among the people; that, as the impious Porphyry says, matrons and women be not our senate, ruling in the Churches, and that the favor of women judge not of the priestly rank.

3:13

My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you, and scatter the way of your steps, or throw it into confusion. He had called the Scribes and Pharisees exactors, not masters; and above, mockers, who because of gifts, which blind the eyes even of the wise, not only did not rebuke the sinners among the people, but for the sake of riches and profits extolled them with praises, calling them blessed, and pillars of the house of God, and the other things flatterers are wont to say. He, then, is the churchman teacher who moves tears, not laughter, who rebukes sinners, who calls no one blessed, no one happy, and does not anticipate the sentence of his judge, since holy Scripture says (Sir 11:30): Call no man blessed before death. But in another place too we read (Prov 27:14): He who blesses his friend in the morning with a loud voice differs in nothing from one who curses. Therefore, despising the judgments of men, let us neither be lifted up by their praises nor saddened by their disparagements; but let us enter upon the right way and the paths trodden by the holy prophets, and let us hear the prophet Jeremiah saying: Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the everlasting paths of the Lord, which is the good way, and walk in it (Jer 6:16). And if ever we go astray and, being men, proceed by a perverse road, let us await the promises of the Lord, who says through Ezekiel: I will give them another way, and another heart (Ezek 36). But the exactors have perverted and troubled the way of the Lord, so that, having the key of knowledge, they neither entered themselves nor suffered the people to enter, but made them lose the way of the truth, which says in the Gospel: I am the way, and the life, and the truth (John 14:6).

3:13-14

The Lord stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples. The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people, and with its princes. The people, which was deceived through simplicity and inexperience, is still called the people of God, and is therefore judged that it may be saved. Nor does the Lord sit in the attire of one judging, as we read in Daniel: Thrones were set, and books were opened (Dan 7:9); but he stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples, wishing those to stand whose way had been scattered. But against the princes and elders of his people he comes to judgment, not to judge but to be judged alike with them, giving them room for defense, if they can have anything to answer, according to what is said in the fiftieth psalm: That you may be justified in your words, and may overcome when you are judged (Verse 6). In the prophet Micah too we read something of the kind (Mic 6), which we have interpreted in its place. This present passage, then, is taken against the Pharisees and the Δευτερωτὰς. And between the old men and the princes there was, I think, in the old people what there is now between the elders and the bishops.

For you have grazed down my vineyard: the plunder of the poor is in your house. Why do you wear down my people, and grind the faces of the poor?, or crush them, and as the Seventy interpreted, put them to confusion. He keeps the prophetic custom of suddenly changing the persons: for above the Lord himself had said, My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you; and afterwards the Prophet had added, The Lord stands to judge: the Lord will come to judgment. Therefore after the prophet, the Lord himself, who had come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes, speaks to them and rebukes the offenders: Why do you graze down my vineyard?, of which it is written: You have brought a vine out of Egypt (Ps 79 [80]:9). And in this same prophet: The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:7). This vineyard the Lord in the Gospel too let out to most wicked husbandmen, who killed the son of the householder sent to them (Matt 21). The plunder of the poor, he says, is in your houses. Take the poor man either simply, as one who needs alms, or rather as the poor in spirit, of whom it is written: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And the apostle Paul: Only, he says, that we should be mindful of the poor (Gal 2:10). And what follows, Why do you wear down my people, and grind the faces of the poor?, or put them to confusion, is plainly said to the princes of the Jews. But it can also be referred to our own princes, if they wear down the common people subject to them, and publicly reprove and confound the poor when they offend, but do not dare even to say mu to the rich who sin worse. And the plunder of the poor is in their houses when they fill their treasuries and abuse the wealth of the Church for their luxuries, and either keep for themselves or distribute to their relatives the public offerings given for the support of the poor, and make the want of others into the riches of themselves and their own.

3:15

And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion are lifted up, and have walked with outstretched neck, and went with nods of the eyes, and clapped, and walked, and stepped with their feet in measured gait. Above, both the prophet and the Lord had rebuked both the people and the princes; now the prophetic discourse turns to the women of whom he had said before, And women have ruled over them, lest they should think themselves strangers to the crime, they on account of whose luxuries and wantonness the exactors grazed down the Lord's vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in their houses, and they wore down his people and put to confusion the faces of the poor. Some think these are truly the women of the Jews; others judge that it is said metaphorically of the cities of Judea, which are called daughters of Zion: the lesser towns, that is, villages and townships. Hence in the book of Joshua too the names of the cities are set down tribe by tribe (Josh 15), and afterwards the villages and fortresses are described and are called daughters. Others, according to tropology, take the women to be souls, which, if they walk with outstretched neck and raise themselves up in pride, and pursue not manly hardness but the softness of women, are rebuked by the prophetic discourse and lose all the ornaments of the virtues, which are described under the crescents and necklaces and jewels and bracelets, the headbands and hair-ornaments and the rest of this kind. This testimony is to be turned also against the women of the Church who walk with outstretched neck and speak with nods of the eyes and clap with their hands as well as their feet, and who, to step in measured gait, do not follow nature as their guide, but hire actors as their teachers.

3:16

The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and will lay bare their hair, and instead of adornment there will be disgrace. This will befall us too whose sins are concealed, when that which is written has been fulfilled: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Luke 8:17). For so long as we are covered by the hair and garment of ignorance, and men think us, who are within full of dead men's bones, to be whitened sepulchers (Matt 23), we seem to have some cleanness. But when what is hidden has been laid open, all the hair will be taken away, and a foul baldness will appear to all.

3:17

In that day the Lord will take away the adornment of the shoes. In what day? The Jews think, that of the Babylonian captivity. We prove that it is more truly when they were taken by the Romans and lost all the ornaments of clothing and gems, of gold and jewels, and their various furnishings. Or else, through the metaphor of the women, all the adornment of the cities is related to have been destroyed. Understand the ornaments of the cities to be in the streets and porticoes, the forum and the gymnasia and the public walls. If we refer these to the state of souls, let us recall that we have read of the shod feet of him who is to eat the flesh of the lamb and celebrate the Pasch, and that neither the garments nor the shoes of those passing through the wilderness were worn out. What are these shoes? Those of which the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: Your feet shod in preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph 6:15). These shoes souls will lose when they walk with outstretched neck and drag their garments with their feet, and instead of matronly cleanness sweep up the filth of the ground.

3:18, 21

And the crescents, and the necklaces, and the jewels, and the bracelets, and the headbands, and the hair-ornaments, and the anklets, and the little chains, and the scent-boxes, and the earrings, and the rings, and the gems hanging on the forehead. He describes the jewels of the women, and through them the insignia of the cities; or, according to the anagogy, the ornaments of the various virtues. Women have little bosses hanging down in the likeness of the moon, which we transfer to the ornaments of the Church, which is illumined by the sun of righteousness. Necklaces too, hanging down as far as the breast, show the understanding and the ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) of the mind in the heart. And jewels, which in a single word signify all ornaments; and the good works of bracelets, such as Rebecca received at her betrothal (Gen 24); and headbands, the ornaments of the head; hair-ornaments, that it may have judgment of each thing; and anklets, by which our step is adorned, that we may hear: Your foot will not stumble (Ps 90 [91]); and: He will rescue my feet from falling (Ps 55 [56]); and little chains, which are woven of rods of gold and silver, that is, of the sense and the words of the Scriptures; and scent-boxes, that we may be the good odor of Christ (2 Cor 2:15); and earrings, that we may not hear the judgment of blood, but the words of the Lord who says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8); and rings, with which we are sealed for the service of the Lord, whom God the Father has sealed. Hence it is said to the prince of Tyre: You are the seal of likeness (Ezek 28:12). The prodigal son too received a ring with the robe (Luke 15), and shoes; and gems hanging on the forehead, by which our faces are adorned. Of the adornment of this head we read in the psalm as well: Like ointment on the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron (Ps 132 [133]:1). Although the Seventy Translators, Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translate all these in different ways, we have woven them together as we could, either from the Hebrew or from their translation; nor do we wish to linger longer on each, lest the exposition become trifling and produce weariness in the prudent reader.

3:22

And the changes of raiment, and the mantles, and the linen cloths. For linen cloths the Seventy interpreted transparent Laconian garments, wishing to signify the very fine garments with which the bodies of the Lacedaemonians were covered, who were most ready for war and of a rather austere life; although neither the Hebrew nor any other of the translators has Laconian. Changes of raiment and mantles, which Symmachus translated more expressively ἀναβολαια, are ornaments of women's clothing, by which the shoulders and breasts are covered. Changes of raiment, according to the anagogy, are those of which it is said: They will go from strength to strength (Ps 83 [84]:8); and linen cloths, that, washed in the Lord, we may enjoy delights, according to what is written in the Psalms: You will give them to drink of the torrent of your pleasure (Ps 35 [36]:9). But all these things the daughters of Zion lost, because they walked with outstretched neck and with nods of the eyes made a show of pride, thinking that what they had was of their own power and not of the grace of the Lord.

3:23

And the pins, and the mirrors, and the fine linens, and the fillets, and the summer veils. Women have pins, by which the arrangement of the dressed hair is held together, so that it may not flow too loosely and be scattered into straggling locks. They have mirrors too, in which they look at their face, and if they see anything lacking, they add to their adornment. They have fine linens, which are called wraps; and fillets, with which the hair is bound, which they call ταινίας. They have summer veils too, which we can call mantles, with which Rebecca also was covered; and today too the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia are veiled with them. In Hebrew they are called ARDIDIM, in Greek θέριστρα, from the fact that in θέρει, that is, in summer and the heat, they protect the bodies of women. The daughters of Zion, therefore, because of their pride lost the pins by which the rule of all the precepts was held fast. They lost the mirrors which the women staying at the doors of the tabernacle offered in Exodus for making the laver of the Lord (Exod 38); of which the apostle Paul too spoke: But now we see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor 13:12). They lost the fine linens and the fillets, with which they covered their shoulders and bound fast the mind that flowed this way and that; and the summer veils, with which they were covered as by a most safe shade in the heats. We say these things lest we seem altogether to shun the tropology of this place. But it is a very great labor to linger on each item and to seek a broad explanation.

3:24

And instead of a sweet odor there will be a stench, and instead of a girdle, a cord. The penitent says that sins stink: My wounds have putrefied and are corrupted because of my folly (Ps 37 [38]:6). The Apostle commanded the loins to be girded with a girdle, saying: Stand, having your loins girded in truth (Eph 6:14). And of the sinner we read: Each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22). Therefore, instead of the good odor of the virtues, the daughters of Zion will have the rottenness of sins; and instead of the girdle of truth they will be bound with the cords of falsehood, such as those had upon their heads who with rags and filth begged their life from the king of Syria.

And instead of a breast-band, haircloth. For breast-band, as Symmachus interpreted it, the Seventy translated a tunic μεσοπορφύραν, that is, striped with purple, which Aquila expressed as girdle of exultation. Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, PHTHIGIL (פתיגיל), which is a kind of women's ornament. The band covers the breast, and holds that place in women which the Rational holds in the High Priests. Of this breast-band Jeremiah too spoke in mystical speech: If a bride can forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band, I too will forget you, says the Lord (Jer 2:32). The virgin, such as the Apostle desires to present us to Christ (2 Cor 11), so long as she is not corrupted in Egypt and her breasts, which are bound with the breast-band, are not broken, is joined to the bridegroom; and though daily she bears sons of the virtues, she by no means ceases to be a virgin. But if at some time she has spread her feet to every passer-by and followed her lovers, and, according to the prophecy of Hosea, the Lord has hedged in her ways and shut off her paths, she will return to her former husband and will hear: Put off the garments of mourning, and put on the garments of your glory (Hos 2).

3:25

Your most beautiful men too shall fall by the sword, and your strong ones in battle. For most beautiful men the Seventy interpreted, and your most beautiful son, whom you love, shall fall by the sword. If we understand this of the state of a soul which has sinned after the virtues, let us take her most beautiful son to be good works, which have fallen by the enemy's sword; and the strong too to have perished in battle, because the righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in whatever day he has gone astray (Ezek 33:12). But if we follow the history, we shall be taught by these words that the prophet's discourse is not about women whose husbands fell in battle, but about the cities of Judea, which he called daughters of Zion, and whose warriors fell in the conflict. Lastly, the following verse speaks of the same Zion.

3:26

And her gates shall lament and mourn, and the city itself, desolate, shall sit upon the ground. This we see with our eyes to this day. According to tropology the interpretation is easy: that whoever has given place to the devil and has not kept his heart with all watchfulness, his gates mourn; and, the bridegroom being absent, he is ever in mourning, and, falling from the heights, sits in the dust of the earth.

4:1

And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be covered with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us: take away our reproach. When the most beautiful men of the city of Jerusalem have fallen by the sword, and the strong have perished in battle, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has been made desolate through the very great scarcity of men, the warriors having been slain, seven women will take hold of one man, desiring to have seed in Zion and a household in Jerusalem, saying that they have food and clothing, only so that they may not be seen to be without a husband and lie under that curse which is written: Cursed is the barren woman, and she who does not make seed in Israel (Deut 7). Zechariah too agrees with this sense: In those days ten men out of all the tongues of the nations shall take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (Zech 8:23). The numbers seven and ten are familiar to the Jews on account of the sabbath and the ten precepts of the Law, and therefore they make frequent use of them; although, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, in which they interpret the word SABA (שבע) now as seven, now as many, now as oath, it may in this place signify not seven but many. This is according to the letter. But at the coming of the Lord and Savior, seven women, that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, of which the same Prophet is going to speak in what follows: There shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root; and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him (Isa 11:1, 2), will take hold of Jesus, whom they had long desired, because they had been able to find no other in whom they might rest in an everlasting abode. Hence John the Baptist too relates in the Gospel: And he who sent me said to me himself: He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is (John 1:33). In Zechariah too we read of seven eyes upon one stone, and on one golden lampstand seven lamps and seven pipes, and two olive trees on either side of the lamp, founded with a firm root (Zech 3). And that the grace of the Holy Spirit possesses all things needs no exposition. But because among men it always suffered reproach, no one living as the gifts of the Holy Spirit demanded, therefore they desire the name of Jesus to be called upon them, so that what was imperfect in the Law may be completed in the Gospel.

4:2-3

In that day the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence and in glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted, and exultation for those who shall have been saved of Israel. And it shall be that everyone who is left in Zion, and remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, everyone who is written in life in Jerusalem. When the daughters of Zion have lost all adornment because of their pride, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has fallen desolate, and all her warriors have perished in battle, so much so that many women can scarcely have one husband, then the bud of the Christian name will spring up, and the earth will give its fruit; and there will be exultation for those who have been saved of Israel, of whom it was said above as well: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9). And note that not all Israel is saved, but the remnant of the people of Zion, and he who remains in Jerusalem: everyone who is written in life in Jerusalem, to whom the Lord too spoke: Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). It signifies the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles.

4:4

When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have washed the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning. Then the remnant of Israel will be saved, when in the baptism of the Savior their sins have been forgiven them, and that blood has been washed away which the erring people invoked upon itself: His blood be upon us, and upon our children (Matt 27:25). Hence we read above: When you stretch out your hands, I will not hear you: for your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15, 16). And afterwards, calling them to penitence, he adds: Wash yourselves, be clean. And note that he washed the filth of the daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment, but the blood of Jerusalem by the spirit of burning. For what is light is washed; what is heavier is burned out. Of this spirit of judgment and spirit of burning John the Baptist spoke in the Gospel: I baptize you in water, but he who comes after me will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and in fire (Matt 3:11). From which we learn that man gives only water, but God gives the Holy Spirit, by whom both filth is washed away and the sins of blood are purged.

4:5

And the Lord will create over every place of mount Zion, and where he has been called upon, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night. For in Christ there is a new creation, of which we read elsewhere: The old things have passed away: behold, all things have been made new (2 Cor 5:17). For which the Seventy translated: And he will come, and it will be; every place of mount Zion, and all things that are round about it, a cloud will overshadow by day, and the light of flaming fire by night. And who will come, if not he of whom it is written: There will come out of Zion one who will deliver (Isa 59:20 LXX)? And of whom another prophet makes mention: Yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come, and will not delay (Hab 2:3). When he has come, the former happiness will be restored to the people, which they once had in the wilderness, when the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exod 13), so that they may never be troubled either in prosperity or in adversity. This is said in the psalm as well: The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6). And smoke in this place signifies not error and ignorance but glory, according to what, in the opinion of some, we shall read in this same prophet (below, Isa 6): And the house was filled with smoke. And in Joel it is said of the grace of the Holy Spirit which descended upon the apostles: I will pour out of my spirit, and they shall prophesy (Joel 2). And: I will give wonders in the heaven above, and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and vapor of smoke (Acts 2:17). The same thing, I think, is signified also by that in the Psalms: Who touches the mountains, and they shall smoke (Ps 103 [104]:32).

4:6

And over all the glory a protection. And there shall be a tabernacle for a shade by day from the heat, and for security, and for a hiding place from the whirlwind and from the rain. This place the Jews refer to Antichrist, who they judge is signified by the whirlwind and the storm, when the Lord is to defend them from a most powerful adversary. But let us refer everything to the first coming of Christ, of which we read in the psalms as well: He has protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle: upon a rock he has exalted me (Ps 26 [27]:5); upon which the Church, being founded, is shaken by no storm, overthrown by no whirlwind and winds. Very many of the Jews understand both these things and all those with which they are joined of the Babylonian captivity and the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Ezra and Nehemiah.

5:1

I will sing now to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard. The prophet sings a lamentable song to the people of Israel, which he composed of whom it is written in the Gospel: But when he had seen it (doubtless Jerusalem) he wept over it, and said: If you too had known the things that are for your peace, for the days will come upon you, and your enemies will throw up ramparts around you, and will hem you in, and will lay you low, and your children (Luke 19:41ff.). And again: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate (Matt 23:37, 38): to which this is like, which is now said in this song: I will abandon my vineyard. And that Christ is called the beloved and dearest one, whom Aquila interpreted πατράδελφον, uncle, or cousin, the title of the forty-fourth psalm teaches us: A song for the beloved. And the voice of God the Father in the Gospel: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17). And in the sixty-seventh psalm we read: The Lord will give the word to those who preach the good news with great power. The King of powers of the beloved (Ps 67 [68]:12, 13). This beloved, then, made a mournful song for his vineyard, which I will sing to my beloved and pitiable people. Or certainly it is to be understood thus: I will sing to Almighty God the Father the song of Christ, who is my cousin, that is, born of the same nation as I. And that the people of Israel is called the vineyard of God we read also at the end of this song: The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah his praiseworthy shoot. And in the seventy-ninth psalm (Verse 9): You have brought a vine out of Egypt, you have cast out the nations, and planted it. In the Gospel too, in almost the same words in which the Prophet now speaks, the Lord weaves a parable: There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard, and set a wall around it, and dug a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, etc. (Matt 21:33). And in Jeremiah we read: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true: how have you been turned into bitterness, a strange vine? (Jer 2:21). And so Jerusalem, as we have said, is lamented, and her ruin is sung in prophetic speech. But for the Church, and the people once of the nations, another song has been put forth, of which we read in the psalms: Sing to the Lord, all the earth; announce his salvation from day to day. Announce his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples (Ps 95 [96]:2, 3). And again: Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonders. The Lord has made known his salvation, in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness (Ps 97 [98]:1, 2).

My beloved had a vineyard on a horn, the son of oil. Theodotion and Aquila translated this according to the Hebrew; but Symmachus, in his manner, more plainly: My beloved had a vineyard on a horn in the midst of olive trees. The Seventy, moreover, interpreted the sense rather than the word: My beloved had a vineyard on a horn, in a fat place, or a fertile one, for πίων signifies both. And indeed nothing is fatter than the land of Promise, if you consider not the mountainous and desert parts but its whole breadth, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates toward the East, and on the northern side as far as Mount Taurus and Zephyrium of Cilicia, which overhangs the sea. And we often read that horn signifies kingdom and power, as in that saying in the Gospel: He has raised up a horn of our salvation in the house of David his servant (Luke 1:69). And: In you we will toss our enemies with the horn (Ps 43 [44]:6). And in Zechariah four horns denote four most powerful kingdoms (Zech 1). The Hebrews expound this place thus: A vineyard was planted for Christ on a horn, that is, in a strong and lofty place, which is called the son of oil, either because it stands in need of God's mercy and is sustained by his help, or because it has furnished the clear light of the knowledge of God to all nations.

5:2

And he fenced it, and chose out the stones from it, and planted the vine Sorec, and built a tower in its midst, and set up a winepress in it. Through the metaphor of the vineyard, as we said before, he describes the people of the Jews, which he fenced with the help of the Angels. And he chose out the stones from it, either idols or all things that could hinder the worship of God. And he planted it with the vine Sorec, which Symmachus alone interpreted as choice, expressing, as it seems to me, not word for word but the sense contained in the word. For the Hebrews say that Sorec is a kind of excellent vine, because it produces abundant and lasting fruit. Lastly, Sorec is interpreted by some as καλλίκαρπος, which we can render as of most beautiful fruit. He also built a tower in its midst, that is, the temple in the midst of the city; and set up a winepress in it, by which some think the altar is signified. For just as all the grapes are carried to the winepress and trodden, so that wine may be pressed out of them, so the altar receives the fruits of all the people and devours the victims offered, according to what we read of Benjamin, in whose tribe the temple and the altar were: Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will eat, and at evening he will give food (Gen 49:27). All that is said of the vineyard can also be referred to the state of the human soul, which, planted by God for good, has brought forth not grapes but wild grapes, and has afterwards been handed over to the beasts to be trampled, and has not received the divine rain of teachings, because it despised the former gifts.

And I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes. For wild grapes, as we have rendered it, in the Hebrew is written BUSIM (באשים), which Aquila interpreted σαπρίας, that is, most worthless fruits; Symmachus ἀτελῆ, that is, imperfect; the Seventy and Theodotion thorns, with which the Jews crowned the Lord. For while he waited for them to bring grapes to the winepresses at vintage time, for which the eighth, the eightieth and the eighty-third psalms have their titles, they, sinking themselves in the cares and vices of the world, which in the Gospel (Mark 4) are interpreted as thorns, offered the goads of blasphemies. But I think it better that Busim be understood as wild grapes rather than thorns, so that the likeness of the metaphor begun may be kept. Hence the Savior too says in the Gospel: Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? (Matt 7:16).

5:3-4

Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard: what is there that I ought to have done further for my vineyard and have not done for it? Or is it that I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes? I have done, he says, all that I ought: I planted the vineyard in a most fertile place, I set a wall around it, I chose out the stones, and I propped up its shoots with stakes and reeds; the vine itself too was not one of many, but choice and καλλίκαρπος. I built a very strong tower, in which to store the crops and from which to watch the beasts that lie in wait for the crops. I set up a winepress, so that the grapes might be pressed above all in that same place and pour out wine. Since, then, I have done the things I ought to have done, let the inhabitants of Jerusalem and of Judah answer me; nay rather, let them judge between me and my vineyard, what is there that I ought to have done and have not done? And as they keep silent, he answers himself: Unless perhaps I erred in this, that for my labor I waited for it to make grapes, not wild grapes, which an untilled and deserted vineyard is wont to bring forth. Something of the kind the Prophet Nathan, sent to David, says too (2 Sam 12), and he questions him through a parable, so that while judging of another he may pronounce sentence on himself. So here too the people is questioned as though about a vineyard, so that it may answer against itself. This place the Savior carries out more fully in the Gospel (Matt 21), and what is passed over here, he puts as a question to the Scribes and Pharisees. For in Isaiah nothing is said of the husbandmen, nor is it indicated what they are to suffer, but the discourse is only of the vineyard; there, however, as though the vineyard were one thing and the husbandmen another, he speaks of the people and of the teachers in such a way that he destroys the wicked wickedly and lets out the vineyard to other husbandmen, signifying the apostles and those who were to succeed the apostles. Nor is there a ταυτολογία, as many think, in his saying: Or is it that I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes? For above he speaks silently within himself, but here he asks others what he had been thinking.

5:5-6

And now I will show you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; I will break down its wall, and it shall be for trampling. And I will make it desolate; it shall not be pruned, and it shall not be dug: and briers and thorns shall come up over it. I challenged you above, he says, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of the tribe of Judah, to judge between me and my vineyard, and I asked you to say what I ought to have done that I have not done. And since, according to the Gospel parable, you will not answer what I ask, I myself will answer for you, showing what I am going to do: Since I have done for my vineyard all that I ought, and instead of grapes it has brought forth wild grapes, I will take away all that I had given. I will take away the help of the angels, of whom it is written in the psalms: The Angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and will deliver them (Ps 33 [34]:8); and it will be plundered by its adversaries. I will destroy the walls, and it will lie subject to hostile nations, and it will be desolate and will not be pruned for ever, nor dug, so that it may be reduced to briers; and thorns will come up in it. These things are said, under the metaphor of the vineyard, of the desolation of Jerusalem and Judea, which most of the Jews think took place under the Babylonians: and we cannot deny that this was in part fulfilled. But since there follows, And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it, this cannot be understood of that captivity. For Jeremiah too prophesied among the people when the city had already been taken; and Ezekiel, Daniel too and the three boys, are related either to have prophesied or to have done wonderful signs even in the captivity; and afterwards Haggai and Zechariah foretold the future for the consolation of the people in servitude. And the help of God is taken away from those who are unworthy, so that, since they had not perceived God through his benefits, they may perceive him through punishments. Or else he threatens certain harsh and rough things for this reason, that, having turned to penitence, they may avoid the impending torments. The Hebrew word SAITH (שית) all have interpreted by a similar word as thorns. If, then, Saith in the present place is called thorns according to Aquila and Theodotion and the Seventy, let them answer how above they translated Busim not as wild grapes but as thorns.

And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it. These are the clouds which the Lord brought out from the end of the earth, of which we read in the psalm as well: Your truth reaches to the clouds (Ps 35 [36]:6).
