These clouds, since under Elijah all were idolaters, did not rain upon the land of Israel for three years and six months (1 Kgs 18). This indeed we can understand not only of the prophets but of the apostles: that after the passion of the Lord the Jews had neither prophets nor apostles, lest instead of grapes they should bring forth thorns, but that they might pray, for their barrenness and dryness, to him who can supply the rains of the virtues. Hence in Leviticus too he says to them: I will make the heaven of iron for you, and the earth of bronze (Lev 26:19). And in Deuteronomy: The heaven over your head shall be of bronze, and the earth beneath you of iron (Deut 28:23, 24). And again: The Lord will give rain to your land. And: Ashes shall come down from heaven upon you, until it uproots you and destroys you; because land which receives the rain that often comes upon it, and produces not a crop but thorns and thistles, is reprobate and near to a curse, whose end is burning.

5:7

But the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his delightful shoot. That is, of God; or, as the Seventy translated, a most beloved young planting. Israel and Judah differ from each other in this: that the whole people was at first called Israel, and afterwards, when David reigned over the tribe of Judah, and Rehoboam the son of Solomon over two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, those who were in Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, were called Israel; and those over whom men of David's line reigned were called Judah. And since calves were worshiped by Israel in Dan and in Bethel, Samaria was therefore taken first by the Assyrians; and a long time afterwards Judah was led away by the Chaldeans into Babylon, because they had sinned less. Hence in Ezekiel too, for purging the sins of both peoples, there are set on the left side for Israel, according to the Seventy, one hundred and ninety days, or, as is more truly contained in the Hebrew, three hundred and ninety, but for Judah forty days (Ezek 4, according to the Seventy and according to the Hebrew). I say this to show that, in comparison with Israel, that is, the ten tribes, Judah was lovable and beloved, in which were the priests and the Levites, and in which the worship of God was carried on at the time when the prophet Isaiah was speaking to the people. And beautifully Israel, that is, the whole people, is the house; but Judah, which sprang up afterwards when the tribes were separated, is called the delightful young plant. And this too is to be noted, that, according to prophetic custom, what was first said through a metaphor or through a parable is afterwards explained more plainly: that the vineyard and the young planting are Israel and Judah.

And I waited for it to do judgment, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, a cry, or, as the Seventy translated, I waited for it to do judgment, and it did iniquity, and not righteousness, but a cry. We wish to convey to Latin ears what we have learned from the Hebrews. Judgment among them is called MESPHAT (משפט); iniquity, or scattering, as Aquila interpreted, MESPHAA (משפה). Again, righteousness is called SADACA (צדקה), and cry is called SAACA (צעקה). So, by either adding or changing one letter, he so tempered the likeness of the words as to set MESPHAA for MESPHAT and SAACA for SADACA, and to render an elegant structure and sound of words according to the Hebrew tongue. Now God waited for the people of the Jews to do judgment, that is, grapes; and it did iniquity, that is, wild grapes. And he waited for righteousness, that it should receive the bestower of such great gifts sent from the Father; and it made a cry, with which it shouted against the Lord, and cried out, saying: Away, away, crucify such a one (John 19:15). Hence the apostle Paul too writes: Let all anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice (Eph 4:31). Or else, since they had shed the blood of the righteous one, the blood of the Lord's passion cried out to the Lord; therefore they rendered a cry instead of righteousness, according to what we read in Genesis: The voice of the blood of your brother Abel cries to me (Gen 4:10).

5:8

Woe to you who join house to house, and link field to field, as far as the limit of the place: will you alone dwell upon the earth? For what we have said, as far as the limit of the place, the Seventy translated, that you may take something from your neighbor; Symmachus and Theodotion, until place fails, or there is none, so that, though the land fails, greed is by no means sated. This I think is said both generally against all for whom nothing is enough, and specially against the vineyard of the Lord, which instead of grapes made wild grapes, that is, instead of judgment iniquity, and instead of righteousness a cry. For what madness it is, when houses and fields ought to be had to keep off the rains and to sow crops, to desire to have those in all of which you cannot dwell and which you are not able to till, and to make another's need your pleasure! According to tropology some think this said against the heretics, who, moving their feet from the East, come into the plain of Shinar, which means shaking out of teeth, and build the city of confusion and the tower of pride, and hear in other words: Hear these things, leaders of the house of Jacob, and you remnant of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert all that is right, who build Zion in blood and Jerusalem in iniquity (Mic 3:9, 10). These join houses to houses, that is, doctrines to doctrines; to whom it is said through Micah, Do not build a mockery in the house (Mic 3), lest upon the foundation of Christ, which the apostle Paul laid (1 Cor 3), and on which they ought to have built gold, silver, precious stones, they on the contrary build wood, hay, stubble, whose end is burning. Of such houses the Savior speaks in the Gospel: Everyone who hears my words and does not do them shall be likened to a foolish man who built his house upon the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew and beat upon that house, and it fell: and great was the ruin of that house (Matt 7:26, 27). And the heretics go on seeking to join new things to old, and to change the same for more recent ones, until both human sense and speech fail.

5:9

These things of the Lord of hosts are in my ears: Unless many houses are made desolate, great and beautiful, without an inhabitant. For what we have rendered according to the Hebrew, These things of the Lord of hosts are in my ears, that is, the words which the Lord spoke still resound in my ears, the Seventy translated, These things have been heard in the ears of the Lord Sabaoth: not that the Prophet heard the words of the Lord, but that the things the Prophet was going to say were heard in the ears of the Lord; whereas it is more consistent to understand that the Prophet heard what the Lord spoke. And the Lord spoke this: that after the captivity great and most beautiful houses would be desolate, having no inhabitant.

5:10

For ten acres of vineyards shall make one little flask, and thirty measures of seed shall make three measures. For little flask, which the Seventy alone translated, all the others interpreted bath, which in Hebrew is called BETH (בת). And for thirty measures, which we have set down for a cor, which in Hebrew is called OMER (תמר), the Seventy rendered six artabas, which is an Egyptian measure and makes twenty measures. In the excessive barrenness, then, which follows the captivity, ten acres of vineyards will make a bath, that is, three amphorae; and thirty measures of seed, that is, a cor, will make an ephi, which the Seventy interpreted as three measures, that is, three modii. Now bath is said of liquid kinds, and ephi or epha, of the same measure, of dry ones. As we read in Ezekiel according to the Hebrew: You shall have a just ephi, and a just bath. The ephi and the bath shall be equal and of one measure, so that the bath holds the tenth part of a cor, and the ephi the tenth part of a cor: their balance shall be equal according to the measure of the cor (Ezek 45:10, 11). We ask, according to the anagogy, how the houses of the heretics are great and beautiful, which, when the time of judgment has come, have no inhabitant. For all the pomp and structure of words and the arguments of dialectic will be reduced to nothing. And since, according to the apostle Paul (1 Cor 3), we are not only God's building but also his husbandry, which the heretics imitate and are dug under and rooted up by Jeremiah: therefore where ten acres of vineyards, or where ten yoke of oxen are at work, they will make one bath, and thirty measures of seed will make an ephi (Jer 18), so that from the number ten, which in the holy Scriptures is mystical and perfect, and from thirty, at which Ezekiel prophesied (Ezek 1) and the Lord was baptized (Luke 3), they are reduced to an ephi, which, in comparison with a manifold number, is confined to unity. And that building and husbandry are referred to spiritual understanding the apostle Paul teaches in another place too (Eph 4), testifying that believers are founded and rooted in love. Hence Ecclesiastes too (Eccl 2) not only built himself houses but planted vineyards, and made gardens and orchards, and set out every fruit-bearing tree, and constructed pools to water the woodland. But the heretics, having only the image and shadow of the virtues and not the truth itself, without the fruit of works, promise the leaves of words. Of their trees the Lord says: Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt 15:13). For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and their offshoot from Gomorrah: their grape is a grape of gall, and theirs is a cluster of bitterness; their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps (Deut 32:32ff.).

5:11-12

Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so as to be inflamed with wine. Harp and lyre, timbrel and pipe, and wine are in your feasts; and you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands. For drunkenness, as Aquila and Symmachus interpreted it, the Seventy set down the Hebrew word itself, SICERAM (שכר), which signifies every drink that can intoxicate and overturn the settled state of the mind. And, following the sequence of the explanation begun, he rebukes the husbandmen of the vineyard, who, with barrenness impending and the burning near at hand by which the briers and thorns are to be consumed, gave themselves over to luxury and pleasures, not only in eating and drinking but also in the delight of the ears and in the various kinds of the art of music. While they do these things, they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider what is to come. Let us turn this testimony against the princes of the Church, who rise in the morning to pursue strong drink, and to drink until evening; of whom it is said in another place: Woe to you, O city, whose king is a youth, and your princes eat in the morning (Eccl 10:16). Occupied with delights, they do not understand the Creator from the creatures, nor consider the works of his hands, of which we read: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the breath of his mouth (Ps 32 [33]:6). According to a higher understanding, every disturbance of the soul can be called drunkenness, which is conceived from the wine of the fury of dragons and from the incurable venom of asps, which some drink from youth to old age, that is, from morning until evening (Deut 32). Others are roused from the banquet at the third, sixth, or ninth, and the eleventh hour, and it is said to them: Awake, you who are drunk with wine. Upon this wine and upon such grapes and vineyards the Lord rains sulfur and fire from the Lord; and whoever drinks of their wine is inflamed and burned up. He seeks the harp and the psaltery, whose inventor is Jubal, born of the stock of Cain (Gen 4), and does not hear the Lord saying to Aaron: You and your sons shall not drink wine and strong drink when you enter into the tabernacle of testimony, or approach the altar (Lev 10:8). These harps and lyres and timbrel and pipes the Babylonian king had, at whose sounding together the peoples of all nations prostrated themselves on the ground and worshiped the golden statue (Dan 3). And that the first time of human wisdom, when we leave childhood and come to the age of reason, is understood as morning in the Scriptures, many testimonies can teach us; of which, by way of example, a few are to be set down: In the morning I sent the Prophets; and: In the morning you will hear my prayer. In the morning I will stand before you, and will see (Ps 5:4, 5); and: From the night my spirit will rise early (Isa 26:9 LXX); and: O God, my God, to you I watch from the dawn (Ps 62 [63]:1); and: In the mornings I put to death all the sinners of the land, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity (Ps 100 [101]:8); and in another place: Weeping will tarry until evening, and gladness until the morning, and other things like these. And we rise in the morning when we leave our vices behind in childhood, and can say: Remember not the sins of my youth and of my ignorance (Ps 24 [25]:7). And when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, the darkness is put to flight, and at once we put to death all the thoughts that provoke us to sins, and we destroy from the city of our mind those sinners of whom the Savior speaks: Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies (Matt 15:19), and the rest. But most unhappy are those who, occupied from morning until evening with drunkenness, gluttony and divers pleasures, do not understand the works of the Lord in themselves, nor consider why they were created.

5:13

Therefore my people has been led away captive, because it had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished with hunger, and its multitude is dried up with thirst. That these things befell the people of the Jews according to the letter under Vespasian and Titus, the Roman emperors, both Greek and Latin history relates. And this indeed they suffer spiritually today too, enduring not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God; because they neither regarded the work of the Lord nor considered the works of his hands, nor had knowledge of him who has always spoken through the Prophets (Amos 8). Hence in the Psalms too it is said of them: They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city (Ps 58 [59]:16). And that every word of teaching is called bread and water, that saying of the Gospel teaches: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that goes forth from the mouth of God (Luke 4:4); and: Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever (John 4:13). And in the psalm it is said: He has brought me up beside the waters of refreshment (Ps 22 [23]:2). Hence the Lord too will not send away the hungry in the wilderness, lest they grow weary and collapse and be killed by hunger (Matt 15). And of the righteous man it is said: I have been young, and have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread (Ps 36 [37]:25). Some wish to interpret what is said, My people has been led away captive, because it had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished with hunger, and its multitude is dried up with thirst, generally of the underworld and of Gehenna, in which everyone will be punished who has not had knowledge of God.

5:14-15

Therefore the underworld has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit, and its strong ones and its people, and its exalted and glorious ones, shall go down into it. And man shall be bowed down, and the man of rank shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be brought low. Those who rose in the morning to pursue strong drink, and continued in drunkenness until evening, and, occupied with pleasure and delights, would not regard the work of the Lord nor contemplate the works of his hands, were therefore led into captivity, because they had no knowledge of the Son of God, who himself says to them, You know neither me nor him who sent me (John 8:19); and in the captivity itself they perished with hunger and were dried up with thirst. Hence the underworld and death enlarged its soul and opened its mouth, and without any number or satiety devoured those who are to be punished for ever: so that the princes and the people, and the exalted and glorious ones of the land of Judah, went down into it, and all pride was humbled, and the eyes of the lofty were brought low, as they understood that they were mortal; and all that the Lord had announced through the Prophets as to come was fulfilled in fact. Now the underworld is said to have a soul, not because it is a living creature, according to the error of some, but because in words of human usage we express the condition of insensible things: that it is insatiable and is never filled by the multitude of the dead. Just as death too is said to be in the hand of the tongue (Prov 18), and Almighty God says that his soul hates the Sabbaths and New Moons of the Jews (Isa 1). Whatever we have said of the people of the Jews can be referred tropologically to those who, occupied with the delights of the world and not regarding the works of God, are led captive into sin and have no knowledge of God; and therefore they perish with hunger and thirst for good works and virtues, and will be dragged down into Gehenna, and there, consigned to eternal torments, they will see their power and pride changed into misery and humility.

5:16

And the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and the holy God shall be sanctified in righteousness. When the people has been led away captive because it had no knowledge, and has perished with hunger and been dried up with thirst, and the underworld has enlarged its soul, and the strong and the exalted and glorious have gone down into the depth, and man has been bowed down and the man of rank humbled, and all have received according to their deserts: then the Lord will be exalted in judgment, whose judgment before seemed to be unjust, and the holy God will be sanctified by all in righteousness, so that what is said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name (Matt 6:9); and: Righteous Father, the world has not known you (John 17:25). Hence we must beware lest we anticipate the judgment of God, whose judgments are great and unspeakable, and of which the Apostle speaks: His judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable (Rom 11:33), until he lights up the hidden things of darkness and lays open the thoughts of hearts (1 Cor 4:5), he who says in the Gospel: Judge not, that you be not judged (Matt 7:1). In agreement with this sentence the apostle Paul commanded: Who are you that judge another's servant? To his own Lord he stands or falls. But he will stand: for God is able to make him stand (Rom 14:4).

5:17

And the lambs shall feed according to their order, and strangers shall eat the deserts turned into fruitfulness. For the lambs feeding according to their order, which is taken in the good sense, the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated, those that are plundered shall feed like bulls, understanding bulls in place of lambs, and again interpreting lambs in place of strangers. But when the Lord has been exalted in judgment, and the holy one sanctified in his righteousness, so that the wicked husbandmen perish wickedly and the lofty cedar is cut down by the axe of the Lord, then those who are of the number of the lambs, not of the goats, will feed in the meadows of the Church and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing (Ps 22 [23]:1); and what the Jews have deserted, turned into fruitfulness, the people of the nations will eat. This is according to tropology. But to complete the order of the history, the same thing is said in other words of which we read above: Strangers devour your land in your sight, and it is deserted and overthrown by foreign peoples (Isa 1:7). For a multitude of the nations, gathered from the whole world, dwells in Judea; and, the former peoples having been cast out, blindness has therefore come in part upon the house of Israel, that the fullness of the nations might come in (Rom 11). And beautifully, according to the Seventy, those were plundered and laid waste and led into captivity like bulls of whom the Lord had said, Fat bulls have beset me, so that lambs might occupy the places of the bulls.

5:18-19

Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with the rope of a cart. Who say: Let his work make haste and come quickly, that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, and we know it. For the rope of a cart the Seventy translated the strap of the yoke of a heifer, or of a cow. That sins are called bonds we read quite often; among them is this: Each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22). And the Lord, rebuking the offending people, which had joined sins to sins, made a scourge of cords, showing them how they had made the house of God a den of robbers (John 2), and had turned the seat of prayer into a house of trade (Matt 21). The guest too at the Lord's supper, not having a wedding garment, is bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness (Matt 22). And the Lord came to say to those who were in bonds, Come out (Isa 49:9); and to those who were in darkness, Be revealed (Ps 145 [146]:8). For he himself looses the fettered and enlightens the blind, whom Jeremiah calls the prisoners of the earth. Nor does he lament over those who have begun to sin and have at once ceased; for there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin at some time (Eccl 7:21); but over those who have drawn out their sins with a long cord. Hence we read in Numbers too (chapter 19) that the red heifer, whose ashes are the expiation of the people, is not sacrificed and offered at the altar of the Lord unless it has done no earthly works and has not drawn the yoke, nor been bound with the bonds of the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar. And in this same prophet, instead of the girdle of truth, the daughters of Zion are girded with a cord. Ahithophel too and Judas [one of whom betrayed David, the other the Lord], drawing their sins with a very long rope, perished by hanging, thinking that the evil of conscience would be ended by present death, and that there is nothing after death. And that according to the Hebrew and all the other translators they are called cords of vanity signifies this: that for those who commit it sin is easily woven, and is as empty and easy as the threads of spiders are woven; but when we wish to get out of it, we are tied with the most solid bonds. And the cart full and laden with sins they understand more easily who remember that it is written in Zechariah that impiety sits upon a talent of lead (Zech 5), and that the Egyptians, who were weighed down by the heavy burden of their sins, were sunk like lead in the Red Sea (Exod 15). And in another place the sinner says: My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me (Ps 37 [38]:5). These things are said to the princes of the Jews, who were rebuked above for avarice and luxury: that, called by the Lord to penitence, and afterwards by his Apostles, they persevere to this day in blasphemies, and three times every day in all the synagogues, under the name of the Nazarenes, they anathematize the Christian name. And the sense is: Woe to you who think that the day of judgment will not be, or that the captivity which the prophetic discourse foretells will not come; who say to the Prophet: How long will you threaten us with the wrath of God? We wish to know it; let it come now. And they say this in irony, because they think it will not come, but is feigned by the Prophet.

5:20

Woe to you who call evil good, and good evil, putting darkness for light, and light for darkness, putting bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter. It is a crime of the same kind to call good, light and sweet by contrary names as to call evil, darkness and bitter by the names of virtues. This is against those who do not think it a sin if they disparage the good, and do not judge it an offense if they praise the evil. And the Jews put good as evil, and light as darkness, and sweet as bitter, when they took up Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, and crucified Jesus, who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to save what had perished. In Barabbas let us understand the devil, who, though he is night and darkness, transforms himself into an Angel of light (Matt 27). Hence the Apostle too says: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor 6:14, 15). For neither is the lamp to be taken away and put under the bushel or under the bed, but upon the lampstand, that it may give light to all. Nor is a tree bearing evil fruits to be called by the name of a good tree (Matt 5). Hence in Genesis too it is related in mystical speech that God divided between the light and the darkness, which in the beginning were borne over the abyss (Gen 1). And that the Savior is called good, he himself says in the Gospel: The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John 10:11). He says too that he is the light: I am the light of the world (John 8:12); and daily, filled with the heavenly bread, we say: Taste and see how sweet the Lord is (Ps 33 [34]:9). On the contrary, when we say, Deliver us from evil (Matt 6:13), and, The world is set in the evil one (1 John 5:19), we desire to be delivered from the snares of the devil. And that he himself is signified by the names of darkness and bitterness we read quite often. But we can say this too, that all doctrines contrary to the truth are bitter, and the truth alone is sweet. Hence we must beware lest we follow falsehood instead of truth, darkness instead of light. For there are many ways that seem right to men, and their ends reach to the depth of the underworld. There is also the righteous man perishing in his righteousness, to whom it is said: Be not overly righteous (Eccl 7:17). For which reasons Israel promises that he will walk by the king's way and will turn aside neither to the left nor to the right (Deut 5). And to say what I feel: with difficulty can anyone be free of this curse, since we often flatter the wicked for their power and despise the good for their poverty. Hence Aquila interpreted more expressively: Woe to him who says to the evil man, You are good, and to the good man, You are evil (Prov 17:15). And with this sense agrees what Solomon says in Proverbs: He who judges the righteous unrighteous, and the unrighteous righteous, both are abominable with God. The Scribes and Pharisees too, receiving not the words of the Savior but the traditions of men and old wives' fables, made good evil and evil good.

5:21

Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight. You who seem to yourselves, he says, to be wise, who follow the prudence not of God but of men: and though you do not receive the power of God and the wisdom of God, you think yourselves wise (1 Cor 1). Between wisdom and prudence the Stoics say there is this difference: that wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, but prudence only of mortal things. And these things are said consistently against the Scribes and Pharisees, who, having the key of knowledge, neither enter in to Christ themselves nor allow others to enter (Luke 11).

5:22

Woe to you who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men to mix strong drink, that is, drunkenness. Of those to whom he had said above, Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so as to be inflamed with wine, he speaks now too: who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men to mix strong drink (Deut 32). Drunk with the wine of the dragon and the incurable venom of asps, they slandered the power of the Lord. And being drunk themselves, they made the peoples drunk, so that, raving with a like fury, they cried out together against the Lord. According to tropology we have already said before that the priests who are to enter the Tabernacle of God ought not to drink wine and strong drink (Lev 10). To which we now add that it was commanded the Nazirites too, who sanctify themselves to the Lord, that they should neither drink nor eat wine and strong drink and anything that comes from grapes, not even a raisin, nor vinegar made from wine (Num 6). But in Proverbs too it is commanded: Let the mighty who are wrathful not drink wine, lest when they have drunk they forget wisdom. Between wine and strong drink, according to the anagogy, I judge the difference to be this: that wine is one disturbance out of many, for example, of lust, of avarice, of gluttony, and of envy; but strong drink, that is, drunkenness, contains in itself all the passions of the vices, which in the Latin tongue we can more rightly call disturbances, because they overturn the settled state of the mind and make the drunken not know what they do. Those, then, who are set over others ought above all to be free of vices, and most of all of anger, which is nearest to madness, lest the more they can, the more they harm those subject to them. He mixes strong drink who, though full of drunkenness, pretends, in order to deceive men, to have certain shadows and images of the virtues.

5:23

You who justify the wicked for gifts, and take away from the righteous man his righteousness. This too is part of the vices of the vineyard which instead of grapes made wild grapes, and, when the Lord waited for it to do judgment, did iniquity, justifying the wicked for gifts, and considering not the cases but the presents, which blind even the eyes of the wise. Hence we must beware lest we be drunk with wine, in which is luxury (Deut 16:19; Eph 5), and the thighs of our shame be laid bare (Gen 9), and lest we flatter the wicked for gifts and despise the righteousness of the righteous man for his poverty. This is commanded in the Epistle of James as well: that we not become judges of iniquity by honoring the wicked rich and despising the holy poor.

5:24

Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and the heat of the flame burns it up, so their root shall be as ashes, and their bud shall go up as dust. For they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, and have blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. For the causes given above, of pride and drunkenness and avarice, because instead of grapes they brought forth thorns, and hay, wood, stubble, and briers that are to burn, therefore the root of their malice will be reduced to ashes, and every flower and beauty of riches and of the body will be compared to dust (1 Cor 3). For they did not only do these things, but by these steps they came to blasphemy, so that they did not receive the law of the Lord and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel; of which we read above: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa 2:3). The root can be taken as evil thoughts, and the fruit and bud as evil works and words, so that what lies hidden in the root is shown in the bud; and both will be devoured by the Lord's burning. Hence the Apostle too (Heb 12:15) speaks of the root of the bitterness of evils springing up.

5:25

Therefore the fury of the Lord is angered against his people, and he has stretched out his hand over it and struck it, and the mountains are troubled, and their carcasses have become like dung in the midst of the streets. For all this his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Because they cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, which the Lord promises through Jeremiah that he will give, saying: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the pact which I made with your fathers in the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt (Jer 31:31, 32). And they blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel, saying: He has a demon, and is a Samaritan (John 8:48); and: Is not this the son of the carpenter? (Matt 13:55). Therefore the fury of the Lord is angered against his people, that fury which before had been angered against the princes and the mighty, who were wise in their own eyes and justified the wicked for gifts, and the tongue of fire had devoured them like stubble, and the heat of the flame had burned them up, so that the mighty might mightily suffer torments. And he stretched out his hand against it, which he calls his people because it was the portion of his inheritance and the cord of his possession (Deut 32). And he stretches out his hand to strike, and his fury is angered, of which we read in another place too: O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath (Ps 6:1). And Jeremiah: Correct us, he says, O Lord, but in judgment, and not in fury (Jer 10:24). And the Lord is said to rage, not because he is subject to human disturbances, but because we who offend do not fear the Lord unless we have heard him angry. Hence the Apostle too writes (Rom 2) that the goodness and patience of God call us to penitence, but we, according to our hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up wrath for ourselves in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. And what the hand is that is stretched out or lifted up over the sinful people Job says more plainly: For the hand of the Lord has touched me (Job 19:21). Hence the devil too, knowing the mighty hand of the Lord and the arm that has been revealed to all the nations, says to the Lord: Put forth your hand and touch all that he has: and see if he will not bless you to your face (Job 2:5). And that what is to come is spoken of as past follows prophetic custom, in which the things foretold as to come are so certain that they are thought to be past. This is sung in the Psalms too: They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink (Ps 68 [69]:22). And again: They divided my garments among them, and upon my vesture they cast lots (Ps 21 [22]:19). And as for what follows, And he struck it, that is, his people, and the mountains are troubled: some think the mountains are the contrary powers, or those spirits which are in the ministry of God and to whom sinners are handed over to be punished. But we think it is said hyperbolically: that because of the greatness of the impending evils even the mountains are moved, and all the streets of the cities are filled with the corpses of the dead. That this befell the Jews after the passion of the Lord under Vespasian and Hadrian no one doubts. And though these things have been done, his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, or lifted high, which shows the bearing of one who is angry and strikes. And it is to be noted in all these things that he does not reproach them with idolatry, nor with other sins by which they offended God, but because they cast away the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the word of the Lord.

5:26ff.

And he will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth; and behold, he will come swiftly in haste. There shall be none faint nor laboring among them; he shall not slumber nor sleep, nor shall the girdle of his loins be loosed, nor the latchet of his shoe be broken. His arrows are sharp, and all his bows bent; the hoofs of his horses are like flint, and his wheels like the rush of a tempest. His roaring is like a lion's; he shall roar like the lion's whelps, and gnash his teeth, and seize the prey, and embrace it, and there shall be none to rescue it. And he shall resound over it in that day like the sound of the sea: we shall look upon the land, and behold, the darkness of tribulation, and the light is darkened by its gloom. The Hebrews understand this place to be prophesied of the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar, that by the will of God he was brought into Judea and Jerusalem and overthrew the temple. But we, following the order and joining what follows to what precedes, say that the signal was lifted up among the nations far off, and that the Lord whistled for them or drew them from the ends of the earth, for this reason: because they cast away the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the holy word. For if the discourse were about the Babylonians, according to prophetic custom he would have said: I will call him who is from the North, because, relative to the position of Judea, the Assyrians and Chaldeans are in the northern region. Or certainly he would have described the Babylonians and Assyrians more openly. But now, by saying, He will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth, he signifies nations set far off and dwelling at the ends of the earth: doubtless the Romans and all the peoples of Italy, Gaul and Spain, who under Vespasian and Hadrian lay subject to the Roman empire. Hence Italy too, from the fact that Hesperus sets there, was once called Hesperia. And at his coming it was struck, and all the mountains of Judea were troubled, as Theodotion and Symmachus interpreted, or were moved, as Aquila set down, or were embittered, as the Seventy translated, so that by the onslaught of the enemies all the streets were filled with the corpses of the dead. The divine discourse, then, describes the swiftness of the army that comes, which came not by its own will but by the Lord's, nay rather was drawn and summoned by his whistle: that it did not faint nor grow weary on so long a march, and in its greed for plunder did not admit sleep to its eyes, and its shoes too were not worn out; the multitude of archers, the squadrons of horsemen, the heat of the chariots and four-horse teams; that like a lion it came not so much to fight as to plunder and devour; and the howling of the victorious army is compared to the waves of the sea. From this it is to be noted what the sound of the sea signifies wherever it is named in the Scriptures. When, then, the Roman army has come and seized the prey, and there has been no one to rescue it, the Prophet, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, joins himself to the people and says: We shall look upon the land, and behold, the darkness of tribulation. For we shall not dare to look upon heaven, whose dweller we have offended; and our light, which we always had in God, has been darkened by the gloom of tribulations. I have read in someone's Commentaries that what is said, He will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth, ought to be understood of the calling of the nations: that, when the signal of the Cross was lifted up and the burdens of sins laid down, they came swiftly and believed. But I do not know how what follows can agree with this sense.

Book Three

The sheer size of the volumes being woven in the explanation of the prophet Isaiah is enough for me, where to pass anything over is a loss to the understanding. Therefore in the individual books, which signify only their number and order, I have set brief little prefaces. And you, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, I beg to help me with your prayers in the exposition of a most difficult vision: in which God almighty is seen in his majesty; and two Seraphim standing round about him and crying: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory; and the threshold of the temple moved and shaken, and the Jewish house filled with the darkness of error. And the Prophet, in comparison with the divine glory, saying that he has unclean lips and dwells in the midst of a blaspheming people, who cried out with the concordant voice of impiety: Crucify, crucify such a one; and, We have no king but Caesar (John 19:6 and 15). And one of the Seraphim sent to Isaiah, who, having taken a coal from the altar with tongs, was to cleanse the prophet's lips, while the people remained unclean. This, then, is the opening of the third book on Isaiah.

6:1

In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. That Isaiah prophesied under four kings, over Judah and Jerusalem, was shown by the title of the first vision; that is, under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. So when Uzziah was dead, under whom all the things we have expounded above were spoken, his son Jotham succeeded him, who reigned sixteen years, and did what was right in the sight of the Lord, and built the high gate of the temple. While he was ruling, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, so as to show the bearing of one who reigns.

And the things that were under him filled the Temple, or, as Theodotion and Symmachus translated: And the things that were under his feet filled the Temple. For which the Seventy translated: And the house was full of his glory. On this vision, about thirty years ago, when I was at Constantinople and was being trained in the study of the holy Scriptures under that most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of the same city, I know that I dictated a brief and hasty treatise, both to make trial of my little talent and to obey friends who bade me. To that little book, then, I send the reader, and I pray that he be content with the brief exposition of the present time. That Uzziah was struck with leprosy because he claimed for himself a priesthood not permitted to him, the sacred history relates; and when he was dead, the Lord is seen in the Temple which he had polluted (2 Chr 26). From this we perceive that while a leprous king reigns in us, we cannot see the Lord reigning in his majesty, nor know the mysteries of the holy Trinity. Hence also in Exodus, after Pharaoh was dead, who oppressed Israel with clay and straw and bricks, the people, who while he lived could not cry out, cried to the Lord. And Ezekiel, when Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, a most wicked prince, was dead, falls upon his face and cries with a loud voice to the Lord. And beautifully, according to the Hebrew, it is not the Lord himself who filled the Temple, whose throne is heaven and the earth the footstool of his feet, and of whom we read in another place: The Lord is in his holy Temple, the Lord's seat is in heaven (Ps 10 [11]:5); but the things that were under his feet filled the Temple (Isa 66). But who this Lord is who is seen, we learn more fully in the evangelist John and in the Acts of the Apostles. Of whom John says: These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory, and spoke of him (John 12:41), meaning without doubt Christ. Again Paul in the Acts of the Apostles, where at Rome he speaks to the Jews: Well, he says, did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: With the ear you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive; for the heart of this people has been made gross, and with their ears they have heard heavily; and they have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them (Acts 28:26-27). Now the Son was seen in the bearing of one who reigns, and the Holy Spirit spoke, on account of the fellowship of majesty and the unity of substance. Someone may ask how the Prophet now says that he has seen the Lord, and not simply the Lord but the Lord Sabaoth, as he himself testifies in what follows; when the evangelist John has said: No one has ever seen God (John 1:18). And God speaks to Moses: You cannot see my face; for man shall not see my face and live (Exod 33:20). To which we shall answer that not only the divinity of the Father, but not even that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, since in the Trinity there is one nature, can the eyes of the flesh behold; but the eyes of the mind, of which the Savior himself says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). We read that the Lord was seen by Abraham in the figure of a man; and that he who was God wrestled with Jacob as a man. Hence that very place was called Phanuel, that is, the face of God: For I have seen, he says, the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved (Gen 32). Ezekiel too saw the Lord in the form of a man sitting upon the Cherubim; from his loins and downward there was as it were fire, and the upper parts had the appearance of electrum (Ezek 1). The nature of God, then, is not discerned, but he is seen by men as he wills.

6:2

Seraphim stood above it; six wings to the one, and six wings to the other: with two they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another, and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. What we, following the other Translators and the Hebrew truth, in which is written MEMMALLO ממעללו, that is, ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, which in Latin is said above it, have rendered, the Seventy translated round about him, so that the Seraphim are described as standing not above the Temple but round about the Lord. Again, where we said that one of the Seraphim covered his face and feet, by which is understood God's: in the Hebrew is written PHANAU פניו and REGLAU (רגליו), which can be interpreted both as his and as its own: so that, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew speech, the Seraphim may be said to cover both the face and feet of God and their own face and feet. In the seventy-ninth psalm we read: You who sit upon the Cherubim, shine forth (Ps 79 [80]:3): who in our language are interpreted multitude of knowledge. Hence the Lord is plainly shown to sit upon the Cherubim in the manner of a charioteer. But the Seraphim, apart from this place, I do not know that I have read anywhere else in the canonical Scriptures, who are said to stand above the Temple, or round about the Lord. Therefore those err who are accustomed to say in their prayers: You who sit upon the Cherubim and Seraphim, which Scripture has not taught. Now Seraphim is interpreted ἐμπρησταὶ, which we can say as kindling or burning, according to what we read elsewhere: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire (Ps 103 [104]:5). Hence also the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which Latin custom does not receive: Are they not all, he says, ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb 1:14)? Daniel too, when he had described the Lord in the bearing of one who reigns, added: Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him. (Dan 7:10). In the Cherubim, then, the Lord is shown; in the Seraphim he is in part shown, in part hidden. For they cover his face and feet, because we can know neither the things past before the world nor the things to come after the world; but we contemplate only the middle things, which were made in the six days. Nor is it strange to believe this of the Seraphim, since the apostles too open the Savior to believers and hide him from unbelievers; and there was a veil before the Ark of the Testament (Exod 40). They are said also to have wings, on account of their swiftness and their running to and fro in all things; or because they always dwell in higher places. For neither does that which is said of the winds, Who walks upon the wings of the winds (Ps 103 [104]:4), testify that the winds truly have wings, after the fables of the poets and the licence of painters; but rather their swift running to and fro in all things. And each has six wings, because we know only of the making of the world and of the present age. And in that they cry one to another, or, according to the Hebrews, this one to that one, that is, one to one, they exhort one another to the praises of the Lord, and say: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord of hosts, so as to show the mystery of the Trinity in one Godhead; and to testify that no longer the Temple of the Jews, as before, but the whole earth is full of the glory of him who for our salvation deigned to take a human body and to come down to the earth. Indeed, when Moses too was praying the Lord, after the calf had been worshipped, to spare the sinful people, the Lord answered: I will be propitious to them. But as I live, and as my name lives: for the whole earth shall be filled with my glory (Num 14:20-21). And the seventy-first psalm sings: The whole earth shall be filled with his glory (Ps 71 [72]:19). Hence also the Angels cried to the shepherds: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will (Luke 2:14). Impiously, therefore, a certain one understands the two Seraphim as the Son and the Holy Spirit: since, according to the evangelist John and the apostle Paul, we teach that the Son of God was seen in the majesty of one who reigns, and that the Holy Spirit spoke. Some of the Latins understand the two Seraphim as the old and the new Instrument, which speak only of the present age. Hence they are said to have six wings, and to cover the face and feet of God, and to bring forth in rivalry the testimony of the truth, and in all that they cry to show forth the mysteries of the Trinity. And to marvel together that the Lord Sabaoth, being set in the form of God the Father, took the form of a servant and humbled himself even unto death, and the death of the cross (Phil 2), and that no longer, as before, do heavenly things alone know him, but earthly things also.

6:4

And the lintels of the hinges were moved at the voice of him who cried, and the house was filled with smoke. When the Seraphim cried and proclaimed the mystery of the Trinity in all the earth, when the whole earth came to know the passion of the Lord and Savior, at once the threshold of the Temple was moved, or taken away, and all its hinges fell down, the Savior's threat being fulfilled, when he said: Your house shall be left to you desolate (Matt 23:38). And how beautiful is the order of the words! After the earth was filled with the glory of the Lord Sabaoth, the Temple of the Jews was filled with the darkness of ignorance, and with gloom, and with smoke, which is harmful to the eyes. Or certainly by the smoke of the Temple a burning is signified. For first the Gospel of the Savior was preached in the whole world, and forty-two years after the Lord's passion Jerusalem was taken and the Temple burned. The Jews think that the Temple filled with smoke signifies thymiama, that is, incense, and through this the coming of the divine majesty.

6:5

And I said: Woe is me, because I was silent, because I am a man polluted in lips, and I shall dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips, and I have seen with my eyes the king, the Lord of hosts. Abraham too, after he saw the Lord and heard his voice, says that he is earth and ashes (Gen 18); and Isaiah, according to the Seventy Translators, testifies that he is pierced with compunction, not for other crimes, but because he had unclean lips. Happy the conscience that has sinned only in speech, and that not by its own fault, but by fellowship with a people having polluted lips, with whom he was very often compelled to speak. From this it is shown that it is harmful to live with sinners: For he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it (Sir 13:1). But since in the Hebrew we read: Woe is me, because I was silent, the Prophet bewails himself because he was not worthy to praise the Lord Sabaoth with the Seraphim, whom we understand as the Angelic powers. And he did not dare to praise the Lord because he had unclean lips. And he had unclean lips for this reason, because he lived among a sinful people. Or certainly it is to be understood thus: Because I was silent, and did not boldly rebuke Uzziah the impious king, therefore my lips are unclean, and I do not dare to sing the praises of the Lord with the Angels, lest it be said to me: Why do you declare my righteousnesses, and take my covenant in your mouth (Ps 49 [50]:16)? For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sir 15:9). And we say this, not as teaching that Isaiah was such a man, but that he himself, out of humility, and only because of unclean lips, confesses himself unworthy of the praise of God.

6:6

And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand a pebble, which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth, and said: Behold, I have touched your lips with this, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed. One of the Seraphim, which is interpreted kindling, flew, or was sent, to cleanse the Prophet's unclean lips, and to purge them with the live coal, or pebble, which he had taken from the altar. Many, however, think that there are two Seraphim, because one cried to another, although among many too individuals can cry to individuals; and the edition of the Seventy rather signifies very many, who translated, Seraphim stood round about him. For if it were said of two, they would have said not round about, but on either side. And this fits the multitude of Angels, which is made ready for the ministry of God. And they are called Seraphim in the plural number, and Seraph in the singular: just as Cherubim and Cherub. And that an altar, under which are the souls of the martyrs, is seen in heaven, John too speaks in the Apocalypse (Rev 6); and this pebble, which by the Seventy alone was translated ἄνθραξ, that is, carbuncle, may signify not a coal or a live ember, as most think, but ἄνθρακα, that is, the carbuncle stone, which is called fiery because of the likeness of its flame-like color. From this we understand that the altar of God is full of carbuncles, that is, of fiery pebbles and live coals, which purge sins. Hence we read it written of God: Coals were kindled by him (Ps 17 [18]:9). And of the Lord himself it is said that he is a consuming fire. And the Savior in the Gospel: I came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12:49): that he might baptize in the Holy Spirit and in fire. For the fire will prove of what sort each one's work is (1 Cor 3). And he who is to be saved will be saved thus, as if he had passed through fire. And this is to be noted, that to Jeremiah, to whom it was said: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and in your mother's womb I sanctified you (Jer 1:5), because he did not have unclean lips but had only said: I do not know how to speak, for I am a youth, the Lord himself stretched out his hand and touched his mouth and said: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. But to Isaiah, who had said: I am a man polluted in lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips, the hand of God is not stretched out, but a Seraph is sent by God, or flies of his own will, because he has been bound over to this office. And in his hand he holds the pebble, which, according to the Seventy and Theodotion, he took with tongs (in the singular), according to Aquila and Symmachus, who followed the Hebrew, with tongs (in the plural), that is, MALCAIM (מלקחים), so as to touch his mouth and purge his former offenses. And the hand is sent both by God and by the Seraph, so that the Prophet, seeing a member of his own body, may not be terrified by an outward touch. Some of our people think that the tongs, by which the pebble is grasped, are the two Testaments, which are joined to one another by the union of the Holy Spirit. And since the Lord is introduced sitting, and sitting in the Temple, and the house was filled with smoke, of thymiama, as the Jews think, consequently tongs too are set down, which we also read of in the priestly ministry (Exod 37).

6:8

And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Here am I, send me. In place of what both we and all the other translators rendered for us, which in Hebrew is said LANU (לנו), the Seventy, wishing I know not what, set down to this people, which is not found in the Hebrew at all. Now when for us is said in the person of God, it is to be taken in the sense in which we also read in Genesis: Let us make man to our image and likeness (Gen 1:26), so as to indicate the mystery of the Trinity. For just as we read in the Gospel, where the Lord says: I and the Father are one (John 10:30); and one we refer to the nature, are to the distinction of persons: so, when the Lord commands, the Trinity gives the order. And the Lord does not say whom he orders to go, but sets the choice before those who hear, so that the will may obtain the reward. And the Prophet promises that he will go not out of the rashness and arrogance of his own conscience, but out of confidence: since his lips have been cleansed, and his iniquity taken away, and his sin cleansed. So Moses too, to whom the Lord had said: Come, I will send you to Pharaoh king of Egypt (Exod 3:10), and he said: I beseech you, Lord, I am not worthy; provide another whom you may send, or as is read in the Hebrew, Send whom you are going to send (Exod 4:13), answered not out of contempt but out of humility, because he who had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians had heard nothing about his lips being cleansed. And Isaiah, not by his own merit but by the grace of the Lord, by which he was cleansed, offers himself for the ministry. Others, however, think that Isaiah offered himself for this reason, because he supposed that prosperous things were to be announced to the people: but because he heard: Go, say to this people: With your ears you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not know (Isa 6:9), for that reason, in what follows, when the voice of the Lord says to him: Cry, he does not cry at once, but asks, what shall I cry? And Jeremiah, to whom it had been said: Take the cup, and you shall give drink to all the nations to whom I shall send you (Jer 25:15), gladly accepting the cup of punishments to pledge it to the hostile nations, that they might drink and vomit and fall, after he heard, go, and first you shall give drink to Jerusalem, answered: You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived (Jer 20:7). This is an observation of the Hebrews. For our part, however, we say that it was not of rashness but of obedience that he offered himself to the Lord to be sent.

6:9ff.

And he said: Go, and you shall say to this people: Hear with hearing, and do not understand, and see with sight, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, and shut its eyes, lest perhaps it see with its eyes, and hear with its ears, and understand with its heart, and be converted, and be healed. The Seventy translated this place as the evangelist Luke set it down in the Acts of the Apostles: And when they did not agree among themselves, without doubt the Jews, they departed, Paul having said one word: Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: go to this people and say: With the ear you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive; for the heart of this people has been made gross, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them (Acts 28:25ff.). And at what time this prophecy was fulfilled, the Apostle Paul himself says in what follows: Let it be known to you, therefore, that this salvation of God has been sent to the nations, and they will hear (Acts 28:28). Hence too we read in the same Acts of the Apostles that Paul and Barnabas, when the Jews would not believe, said: It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you have thrust it away and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46-47). For thus the Lord has commanded us: I have set you for a light to the nations, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth (Isa 49:6). So according to the Seventy the interpretation is easy: that Isaiah the prophet, at the Lord's command, foretells what the people is going to do. In the Hebrew there is a difficulty: how God himself commands the people to hear with hearing and not understand, and seeing to see and not recognize, and afterward the prophet is introduced speaking, and he entreats the Lord and says: Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, and shut its eyes, lest perhaps it see with its eyes, and hear with its ears, and understand with its heart, and be converted, and be healed (Isa 6:10). And first we must resolve the question that can be put to us: why did the apostle Paul, disputing with Hebrews, speak not according to the Hebrew, which he knew to be correct, but according to the Seventy? The ancient expositors of the Church relate that the evangelist Luke was most learned in the art of medicine, and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Hence his speech too, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, that is, in both volumes, is more polished and has the scent of secular eloquence, and he uses Greek testimonies more than Hebrew. But Matthew and John, of whom the one wove his Gospel in the Hebrew tongue, the other in Greek, bring forward testimonies from the Hebrew, such as this: Out of Egypt I have called my son (Hos 11:1). And: For he shall be called a Nazarene (Matt 2:23). And: Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly (John 7:38). And: They shall look on him whom they pierced (Zech 12:10; John 19:37), and other things like these. The Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews too is gainsaid for this reason, that in writing to Hebrews he uses testimonies that are not found in the Hebrew volumes. But if anyone should say that the Hebrew books were afterward falsified by the Jews, let him hear what Origen answers to this little question in the eighth volume of his Explanations of Isaiah: that the Lord and the Apostles, who rebuke the other crimes in the Scribes and Pharisees, would never have kept silent about this crime, which was the greatest. But if they should say that the Hebrew books were falsified after the coming of the Lord and Savior and the preaching of the Apostles, I shall not be able to hold back my laughter, that the Savior and the Evangelists and the Apostles should have brought forward testimonies in such a way as the Jews were afterward going to falsify them. But of the present place this must be said: that we take refuge in the translation of the Seventy in vain, lest what is said according to the Hebrew should seem blasphemous: Hear with hearing, and do not understand: and see the vision, and do not know, since we find testimonies of this kind in the Seventy Translators too, such as that in Exodus which is said to Pharaoh: For this reason I have raised you up, to show my power in you (Exod 9:16). But if he himself raised him up and hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he should not believe; and of others it is said: God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear (Rom 11:8); and in the Psalms: Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense: let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bend their backs always (Ps 68 [69]:23-24): then those who do not see are not at fault, but he who gave them eyes for not seeing. So even apart from this testimony which we are now trying to expound, the same question remains in the Churches, and either the others will be resolved along with this one, or this one too will be insoluble along with the others. The blessed apostle Paul explains this place more fully to the Romans, and we should be doing something superfluous if we wished to comprise in a brief discourse what he pursued through almost the whole epistle. For he says, after many things: God has shut up all things in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all (Rom 11:32). And marveling at the mysteries of the Lord he added: O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways. And again, disputing about the unbelief of the Jews, he says: Have they so sinned that they should fall? God forbid; but by their offense salvation came to the Gentiles, to provoke them to emulation (Rom 11:11). And a little after: For if their casting away is the reconciliation of the world, what will their taking up be? Is it not life from the dead? And again: For I would not have you ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves, that blindness has come in part upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and then all Israel should be saved. And a little after (Rom 11:25): As concerning the Gospel they are enemies for your sakes, but as concerning the election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers: for the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance. For as you, he says, once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief: so these too have now not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. For God has shut up all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all. It is therefore not the cruelty of God but his mercy that one nation should perish so that all may be saved; that a part of the Jews should not see, so that the whole world may behold. Hence the Lord himself too in the Gospel turns the mystery of the man blind from birth, who had received his eyes, to Tropology, and says: For judgment I came into this world, that those who see may not see, and those who do not see may see (John 9:39). And in another place Simeon speaks: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising again of many (Luke 2:34). So while they do not see, we see; while they fall, we rise again. Understanding this, the Prophet in a certain manner says in other words: O Lord, you command me to speak to the people of the Jews, that they may hear and not understand the Savior, and see him and not recognize him. If you will that your command be fulfilled and the whole world be saved, which I too desire to come about, then blind the heart of this people and make its ears heavy and shut its eyes, that they may not understand, may not hear, may not see. For if they see, and are converted, and understand, and are healed, the whole world will not receive healing. From this we perceive that, however grave the sin, if anyone is converted he can be healed. And at the same time this too is to be understood: that for the greatness of their crime they were judged unworthy even of repentance, as the Lord himself says to Jerusalem: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt 23:37).

6:11, 13

And I said: How long, Lord? And he said: Until the cities are made desolate without inhabitant, and the houses without men, and the land is left deserted. And the Lord will remove men far away, and she that had been forsaken in the midst of the land shall be multiplied. And yet in it there shall be a tithing, and again it shall be for a plundering, like a terebinth, and like an oak that has cast its fruits: the seed that shall have stood in it shall be holy. The Lord says: Go, and tell this people that it hears and does not hear, sees and does not see. And for this reason it neither hears nor sees: because it is not going to understand the words of the Lord nor to recognize his works, and because it has grown fat and broad and has forgotten its Creator (Deut 32). The Prophet answers, and asks anxiously about his people: How long, Lord, will this sentence remain, that hearing it should not hear, and seeing should not see? To whom the Lord answered: So long will it not hear and not see, and have its heart blinded, until the cities of Judea, when Vespasian and Titus make war, are utterly overthrown, so much so that not even their former name remains, and the houses, if any remain, are without inhabitant, and the land is reduced to a wilderness; and the Jewish people is scattered over the whole world, either by flight or by captivity; and the people of the Jews is multiplied no longer in Judea, as before, but among all the nations. And though I say that it is multiplied, so great will be the misfortune of the remnant of the people that, in comparison with its former multitude, scarcely a tenth part remains. And when there is a wilderness in the land itself also (for this place can be understood in two ways: that scarcely a tenth part remains even in the whole world, and that in Judea itself scarcely a small part of the people is preserved), again those very remnants will be for a plundering, when, after about fifty years, Hadrian comes and has utterly plundered the land of Judea, so much so that it is compared to a terebinth and to an oak that has lost its acorns. Finally, after the last devastation, public laws were even posted, and the Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been cast out. But if anyone believes in Christ, and that is fulfilled which we read above: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9): when, according to the Apostle (Rom 9), the remnant will be saved; this seed will be holy, and from the shoot of the Apostles all the Churches will sprout. What we have said, the seed that shall have stood in it shall be holy, or according to Aquila, its shoot shall be a holy seed, is not found in the Seventy Translators, but was added by Origen from the Hebrew and the edition of Theodotion; it is carried in the copies of the Church, so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel may be saved; and that in this too the word of the Lord may be fulfilled, who says: I will kill, and I will make alive, and I will strike, and I will heal (Deut 32:39).

7:1-2

And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah: Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, the king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight against it, and they could not subdue it. And they told the house of David, saying: Syria has come to an agreement with Ephraim; and his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the woods are moved before the wind. Uzziah, who is also Azariah, king of Judah, reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years (2 Kgs 15). At the very end of his time Isaiah saw the things which the preceding discourse has set out. When he was dead and Jotham his son, a most righteous king, was reigning in his place, the prophet at once saw the Lord and Savior reigning in his majesty, and announcing the blindness of the Jewish people, and the overthrow of Jerusalem and of the other cities under Vespasian and Hadrian; and how in the Apostles a remnant was to be saved. As third king, the son of Jotham, Ahaz succeeds, a most impious man (2 Kgs 16; 2 Chr 28), who shut the doors of the temple, and in the valley of Ben-hinnom worshipped the Baals, and consecrated his son to idols; so that he even took away the bronze altar that Solomon had made, and placed in the Temple of God an altar of the idols, whose pattern he had received from Damascus. Justly, therefore, was he forsaken by the help of the Lord, and Rezin the king of Syria, that is, Aram, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel in Samaria, rose up together against him, and came to Jerusalem to storm it (ibid.). We read in the book of Chronicles that Rezin the king of Damascus, having conquered Ahaz, carried many from Judea off to Damascus; and that Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes, which were called Israel, who reigned in Samaria, struck down in one day a hundred and twenty thousand fighting men of Judah, and led captive into Samaria two hundred thousand women, boys and girls, with boundless plunder. Of that contest the prophet has now kept silent, but relates the second battle, when, having had proof of their strength and victory, and lured by the greatness of the plunder, they come again to Judea and desire to subdue Jerusalem, and could not, because the Lord helped it, so that, on the occasion of the mercy by which he was freeing the besieged people, he might announce that his Son would be born of a Virgin. When the house of David, that is, the royal house, heard that Syria and Ephraim, that is, Rezin and Pekah, were coming with joined army, it was terrified and greatly afraid, and both king and people trembled so that you would think the leaves of trees were being tossed by the blasts of the winds. According to the anagogy the interpretation is easy: that while Ahaz the impious king is reigning, the king of Aram, which is interpreted lofty and sublime, so as to indicate the arrogance of secular wisdom, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, who himself too, according to the prophet Hosea, was of the tribe of Ephraim, from which Jeroboam the son of Nebat had set up the golden calves in Bethel and Dan (1 Kgs 12) and had separated the people of God from David, are referred to the heretics, who agree together to storm the Church. And when the house of David hears this, David whom we read in Ezekiel is to be raised up as the good shepherd (Ezek 34), and his people believing simply in the Lord, it trembles greatly. And it trembles for this reason, because it is compared not to fruit-bearing trees but to an unfruitful forest. And that these same heretics and the gentiles fight against the house of David with the swords of arguments and of the dialectical art, no one doubts: so that those who are at variance among themselves agree in attacking the Church; according to that instance in which Herod and Pilate, who were at discord with each other, were bound together in friendship at the Lord's passion.

7:3-4ff.

And the Lord said to Isaiah: Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Jasub your son who is left, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field. And you shall say to him: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and let not your heart be afraid of the two tails of these smoking firebrands, in the wrath of the fury of Rezin and of Syria and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah have taken most evil counsel against you, saying: Let us go up to Judah, and rouse it up, and tear it away to ourselves, and set a king in the midst of it, the son of Tabeel. Thus says the Lord God: It shall not stand, and this shall not be; but the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin, and yet sixty-five years, and Ephraim shall cease to be a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria the son of Remaliah. If you do not believe, you shall not remain. Jasub the son of Isaiah, which is interpreted left over and returning, as a type of the people of Judah, which was to be freed from the hands of two kings, is ordered to go out with his father and to meet Ahaz king of Judah at the place of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field, where we shall read later that under Hezekiah king of Judah Rabshakeh stood and, at the command of Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, blasphemed the people of God. To which place there went out, sent by Hezekiah, the princes of the city whom we read of in the volume of Kings. And Ahaz (2 Kgs 18), though an impious king, is commanded, on account of the mercy of the Lord, to keep silence and not to be terrified, nor let his heart be afraid, thinking that he will suffer things like those he had endured before. And he calls Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Samaria two tails of firebrands, that is, of smoking brands, because in them the kingdom of Syria, that is, of Damascus, was ended, and the kingdom of Samaria, that is, of the ten tribes, which by another name were called Ephraim. For it is written (2 Kgs 16) that Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, under king Ahaz, went up against Damascus and laid it waste, and carried its inhabitants off to Kir, and killed Rezin; and that Hoshea the son of Elah laid an ambush for Pekah the son of Remaliah, and struck him and killed him, and reigned in his place in Israel nine years; and that Shalmaneser king of Assyria came and besieged Samaria, which is now called Sebaste, for three years, and in the ninth year of the reign of Hoshea took it, and sent Hoshea bound into prison, and carried Israel off to the Assyrians, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river Gozan, in the cities, or, as the Seventy translated, in the mountains of the Medes (2 Kgs 17). For although these two most evil kings took counsel to go up to Judah, whose region is set in the mountains, and to rouse it up while it was at rest and in a manner sleeping, and to subjugate it to their own rule, and to set over it as king the son of Tabeel, which is interpreted good God, so as to indicate either a man of this name or an idol; nevertheless thus says the Lord God: This counsel shall not stand, but for the meantime only Damascus shall be the head of the cities of Syria, and in Damascus itself, the metropolis, Rezin shall rule. Further, in Ephraim, on account of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who first reigned from Ephraim, Samaria shall be the head, that is, the royal house in the city of Samaria, and the head of Samaria shall be the son of Remaliah, that is, Pekah; but the kingdom of the ten tribes, that is, of the people of Ephraim, will cease to exist after sixty-five years. Which, unless we attend more carefully, cannot stand. For in the twelfth year of Ahaz the son of Jotham in the tribe of Judah, Hoshea reigned over Samaria, and in the ninth year of his rule he was taken (2 Kgs 17). And Ahaz reigned over Judah sixteen years (2 Kgs 16), and in the seventh year of Hoshea's rule after Ahaz's death Hoshea was taken, and Samaria destroyed, and the whole people carried over into Media: so that if we choose to put sixteen years of Ahaz and seven of Hoshea, the result is twenty-three years, or at most twenty-four; and where will the sixty-five years be, within which the kingdom of Israel is said to be ended? The Hebrews therefore set out this place thus: that Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, when Isaiah too had the beginning of his prophecy, was the first to prophesy against Israel, saying: But Israel shall be led captive out of his land (Amos 7:11, 17). And that the title of his prophecy is against Samaria; and that he began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah king of Judah two years before the earthquake, which they hold to have occurred at the time when Uzziah, entering the Temple of God, claimed the priesthood for himself, and the earth was struck, and the ashes of the altar were poured out, and the king himself was struck with leprosy (2 Chr 26). And they hold that it was the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah when these things happened, whose remaining years are twenty-seven. For Uzziah reigned fifty-two years (2 Kgs 15); after him reigned Jotham his son for sixteen years, and his son Ahaz for another sixteen years; after whom reigned Hezekiah, in the sixth year of whose rule Samaria was taken; and thus sixty-five years are made up together (2 Kgs 16). When the Lord foretold these things through the prophet, both Ahaz and the people did not believe that they would come to pass.
