Hence also at the wrath of the Lord the earth trembled, and the people became fodder for the fire, because there was such cruelty in it that it did not spare even the dearest name of brotherhood, but, deserting and despising the right, it was sated with the things that were on the left, while it hungers for pleasures and evils, and always longs to join worse things to evil ones. Manasseh and Ephraim too, who were born of one womb and begotten of the same parent, broke out into such madness that they were at odds with one another in hostile hatred. Let us read the volumes of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find the civil wars of Samaria among themselves, while some fight for one king and others for another, and how, when their own kings had been killed, they agree on attacking Judah. According to tropology, the Lord will take away head and tail, the greater and the lesser alike. By naming the tail, he shows that the heretics are not men but beasts of burden, which use this member to cover their dung and to keep off small creatures. And after the head he adds the tail bending and perverting, because they overturn the precepts of the law and pervert the right way. He will also destroy the aged man, because he is the head, and the false prophet, who is set in the tail, both teachers and disciples alike: the one sort who for gifts praise sinners, the other who, being praised, do not perceive their own evils nor do penance. Therefore the Lord will not rejoice in their young men: For woe to the city whose king is a youth (Eccl 10:16). And those who have lost God as Father, or the true Lord, will not obtain mercy. For every heretic is a hypocrite, doing one thing and pretending another, and whatever he says, though it may seem to be wisdom, is nevertheless folly. For these things he stretches out his hand to punish, and the devouring flame will consume all their impieties like thorns. And words without virtues, which are compared to an unfruitful forest, will be wrapped in the pride of smoke. At their punishment all the ground will tremble, and the deceived peoples will be handed over to everlasting burnings, because for the sake of shameful gain they do not spare even their own, but vie with one another in taking plunder from the peoples they have deceived, leaving good things and lingering in the worst. And though they always find what is on the left, yet they are never sated with their errors, devouring the flesh of their own arm, and fighting against the Church with equal zeal. On account of luxury and pleasures and gains from the peoples they have discord among themselves, so that from one heresy two arise, and these in turn are divided into parts, so that they may lead away flocks of their own and devour the houses of widows and of sinful women, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3). In all these things the fury of the Lord will not be turned away, consuming and overthrowing vices; but the more they advance in sinning, the more he stretches out his hand for punishment.

10:1ff.

Woe to those who make unjust laws, and who in writing have written injustice, to oppress the poor in judgment, and to do violence to the cause of the humble of my people, that widows might be their prey, and that they might plunder the orphans. What will you do in the day of visitation, and of the calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee? And where will you leave your glory? that you may not be bowed down under the chain, and fall with the slain. For all these his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Most think that these things too are still said against the ten tribes which dwelt in Samaria, because they joined these as well to their former crimes. To us, however, it seems that the prophetic word cries out against the judges of the tribe of Judah and of Jerusalem, namely the scribes and the δευτερωτὰς, because they wrote unjust laws against the law of God, and by their traditions overturned the truth of judgment. For when God says: Honor your father and mother (Exod 20:12), they on the contrary taught sons to say to their parents: Whatever gift comes from me will profit you, so that they do not honor father and mother (Matt 15:5-6; Mark 7:11), and other things like these. And they wrote these most evil laws for this purpose, to oppress the poor and the humble of the people, to make plunder of widows and to despoil orphans. They are asked what they will do when the day either of captivity or of judgment has come, and of the calamity coming from afar, which was foretold long before. To whose help, he says, will you flee, when you have offended God, who is the true helper, and where will you leave your glory? For riches will not profit in the day of wrath, to keep the Assyrian from leading you in chains into the enemy's land, to keep you from falling in battle (Prov 11:4). And finally, just as in the preceding passages he had often said against Samaria: For all these his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, he speaks so against Judah too, because the final captivity is not the end of their evil, but even in the enemy's land the sword of the Lord will pursue them. According to the anagogy, every heretic writes iniquity in order to deceive the poor and humble of the people and to despoil widows and orphans. For the rich man, of whom we read: A man's own riches are the redemption of his soul (Prov 13:8), does not endure threats, is not quickly caught by them. But the poor man, and he who is humble and small among the peoples, is quickly made to stumble by them. The widow too, who has lost God her husband, and the orphan who has lost his father the Creator, of whom it is written: You have forsaken God who begot you, and have forgotten God your nourisher (Deut 32:18), are easily tripped up. What then will they do in the day of judgment, when they have deceived so many, and of the calamity coming from afar? For just as it is said to the righteous man: The word is near, in your mouth and in your heart (Rom 10:8); and in another place: The kingdom of God is within you (Luke 17:21); so the calamity of the heretics will come from afar, prepared for them over a long time. To whom will they flee for refuge, when the God they have is a fiction? To whom will they hand over their glory, when everything is feigned? Nor will they be able to escape the chain with which they have bound very many. Hence also in the vision of the valley of Zion, which, forsaking the height of God, has been deceived by heretical lowliness, it is said of the teachers of knowledge falsely so called: All your princes have fled, and those who were captured were harshly bound (Isa 22:3); and that they fall with the slain one by one, and perish themselves in the slaughter of others, and though they suffer many things, and the day of visitation has come, their destruction is not their end: but they are ever to tremble at the hand of the Lord hanging over them. Up to this point is God's threat against the ten and the two tribes, that is, against Samaria and Jerusalem, which began among the people while Ahaz was still reigning: of these, two and a half tribes were taken captive under him, and the rest under Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz in the kingdom (2 Kgs 16:17). The following prophecy is written against the Assyrians.

10:5ff.

Woe to Assur, the rod of my fury, and he is the staff; in their hand is my indignation. Against a deceitful nation I will send him, and against the people of my fury I will give him charge, to take spoils and to seize prey, and to make it a thing trodden down like the mire of the streets. But he does not think so, and his heart does not reckon so, but his heart will be set on crushing, and on the slaughter of very many nations. For he says: Are not my princes all of them kings? Is it not: as Carchemish, so Chalanno and as Arpad, so Hamath? Is it not: as Damascus, so Samaria? As my hand found the kingdoms of the idol, so also their images from Jerusalem and from Samaria. Shall I not, as I did to Samaria and to her idols, so do to Jerusalem and to her images? Let us set down in this place the translation of the Seventy, which disagrees with the Hebrew in very many things. LXX: Woe to the Assyrians: the rod of my fury is he, in their hands; my wrath I will send against a lawless nation, and to my people I will give command to make spoils and prey, and to trample the cities, and to lay them in the dust: but he did not so think, and did not so reckon; but his mind is to crush, and to destroy very many nations. And if they say to him: You alone are prince, he will answer: I have not taken the region which is above Babylon, and Chalane, where the tower was built. But I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria: as I have taken these, so I will take all kingdoms. Howl, you carved images in Jerusalem and Samaria; for as I did to Samaria and to her idols, so I will do to Jerusalem and to her images. First it must be known that in the Hebrew it does not have Chalane, but CHALANNO (כלנו). For the last letter of this name is not IOD, as they supposed, but VAU, letters which differ from each other only in size. Now the tower was built in the plain of Shinar, in which were Erech, Accad, and Chalanne, and Babylon, which received its name from the confusion of tongues (Gen 11). Arabia, moreover, is not found in the Hebrew, but Hamath, which the Syrians to this day call Epiphania. Howl too, you carved images in Jerusalem, they added of their own. And what is written above: If they say to him, You alone are prince, he will answer, I have not taken the region this one and that one, but I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria, suggests this sense: When, he says, those who have been taken captive say to the Assyrian, You are prince of all, he, still feeling himself to be weak, will answer: How do you call me prince, when I have taken only Arabia and Damascus and Samaria, and have not yet brought under my power the nations set far off beyond Babylon? But as I took Arabia, Damascus and Samaria, so I will lay all kingdoms beneath me. Let us pass to the Hebrew, and briefly note what seems right to us. Woe to the Assyrian, that is, Sennacherib, because he is the rod and the staff of my fury, for in his hand is my indignation, and through him I will strike a most deceitful nation, which has always limped between me and the idols, which lied that it would do my precepts; and against the people of my fury I will command him to despoil it and plunder it, and to reduce it to dust, and to trample it like the mire of the streets, that is, to strike it and not kill it, to wound it and not take away its life. But he went beyond the measure of my anger, and raged not only against Israel, against which he had been directed, but against very many nations, so as to crush all the kingdoms round about, and his sword raged even to the slaughter of very many nations. For, lifted up into pride, he dared to say this: My captains are kings of other nations, and, being subject to me, they will rule all nations. As I took Carchemish, so I took Chalanno too; as Arpad, so I gained Hamath too; as Damascus, so I subjected Samaria to myself too. As I have put under my feet the other kingdoms which served the worship of idols, so I will subject to my power Jerusalem too, and Samaria, in which are the same idols. As I took Samaria with its idols, so I will take Jerusalem too, because it worships the same gods. For Carchemish, however, the Seventy, adding of their own, translated the region beyond Babylon, and Chalane where the tower was built, leaving out Arpad altogether. But according to their translation, and with the freedom of tropology, provided it is pious, from what he says, and I will give command to my people to make spoils and prey, and to trample the cities, and to lay them in the dust, we can say this too: that the Lord daily commands his people to reduce to dust the cities of the adversaries, which are raised up against the knowledge of God and have been built by the heretics with enormous labor, and to show that they are nothing. And he, understanding the weakness of the human heart, and that, surrounded as he is with mortal flesh, he cannot have a perfect victory of the virtues nor take all the nations, though others admire him and say: You alone are prince, will answer them: There are many things that I ought to destroy, and have not yet been able to destroy: I know that I do not know. And although I have overcome many arguments of the adversaries, yet there are very many which are still to be overcome. And at the same time, in hope of what is to come, from those which he has overcome he promises himself the victory over the rest as well. Now the images of Jerusalem and of Samaria are bidden to howl: not the things themselves which were fashioned, but those who fashioned them: μετωνυμικῶς, those who made them, by the things that were made: so that not only those who have fabricated idols in the heresies, but those who in the Church through ignorance defend a lie for the truth, may testify by howling and penitence that they have erred.

10:12, 14

And it shall be, when the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I will visit upon the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assur, and upon the glory of the haughtiness of his eyes. For he said: By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood, and I have removed the bounds of the peoples, and I have plundered their princes, and like a mighty one I have pulled down those who sat on high; and my hand has found the strength of the peoples as a nest; and as eggs are gathered which have been left, so I have gathered all the earth, and there was none who moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. For fruit the Seventy translated sense, or great mind. After the captivity of Samaria, and the victory of the Assyrians, and the threat against Jerusalem, that, because it had imitated the images of Samaria, it must be struck with a like sentence, the Prophet now speaks against the Assyrian himself, who was lifted up into pride and thought that what he conquered was the work of his own strength. For the Assyrian, boasting in the swelling of his heart, said that by the strength of his hand he had conquered all the nations, and by incredible wisdom had taken possession of the bounds of all. And according to the Seventy he was of such power that he overthrew from their foundations the cities of warlike men, and seized the whole world like a nest, and made it his prey like eggs abandoned by their mothers. And because he had once taken a metaphor from birds, from the nest and the eggs, he kept it in the rest, so as to say: There was none who moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. So great, he says, was the terror of my strength and victory, that the conquered did not freely utter even weeping and groaning. There are those who think these things are said generally against the kingdom of the Assyrians: that after the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that is, after Jerusalem has been overthrown, the empire of the Assyrians is destroyed. To me, however, from what follows, the threat seems to be properly against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. And what he says: After the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, signifies not the overthrow of the city but its siege, when Rabshakeh, Sennacherib's general, came and did the things which the same Prophet records in later chapters (Isa 37:17). According to tropology, when Samaria and Jerusalem have borne the wrath of the Lord, and have perceived that they erred in fabricating idols, then will the great mind be destroyed, the Assyrian, who was puffed up into such pride against the Lord that he reckoned that all things would yield to his wisdom, and that any lofty doctrines, even those fortified by the art of dialectic, were to be shaken and utterly destroyed: so much so that, like the chicks of birds, they would not be able to rise up on high, and, not yet quickened, would be without sense and torpid, which the example of the eggs shows; and that he would not hear anyone so much as mutter or move his tongue against the reason and strength of his discourse.

10:15

Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or shall the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn? As if a rod should lift itself against him who lifts it, and a staff should exalt itself, which is but wood. Against Sennacherib, or, as many think, Nebuchadnezzar, boasting and saying: By the strength of my hand I have done it, by my wisdom I have understood, and the rest, the holy Prophet answered: O most foolish of mortals, do you think the wrath of God to be your own wisdom, and do you ascribe his command to your own strength? It is as if an axe should boast against him who holds the axe, and a saw against him by whom it is drawn, and they should say that all the works done by axe and saw were accomplished by their own skill. And if someone should lift a rod, and raise a staff to strike whom he will, and the rod and the staff themselves should boast and say that he who was struck was struck by them: so you too, though you have been the instrument of God's will, are lifted up into pride, and boast that all that is done belongs to your own power. Whatever is said to the Assyrian can also be referred both to the pride of the heretics and to the devil, who is called in the Scriptures axe and saw and rod, because through him unfruitful trees are cut down and cleft, and the hardness of unbelievers is sawn, and those who do not receive discipline are struck with the rod. The heretics too are those whose mouth is set against heaven, and their tongue passes through the earth, and who abuse the sense which they received from God for good, turning it to the contrary and the perverse, so as to speak against him by whom they were made, and to turn into blasphemy the ministry of the tongue, by which the Lord should be praised (Ps 72 [73]).

10:16ff.

Therefore the Sovereign Lord of hosts will send leanness among his fat ones, and beneath his glory a burning shall be kindled and burn like the burning of fire. And the light of Israel shall be in fire, and his Holy One in flame: and his thorn and his briers shall be kindled and devoured in one day. And the glory of his forest and of his Carmel shall be consumed from the soul even to the flesh, and he shall be a fugitive for terror, and the remnants of the wood of his forest shall be numbered for their fewness, and a child shall write them down. Because you have done these things, and spoken what I related above, therefore the Lord will send his Angel, and in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand of your army will die: so that all the most powerful, whom he calls fat, are reduced to leanness and to nothing; and, as the Hebrews relate, while the garments of the Assyrians were unharmed, their bodies were burned with a hidden fire: then the light of Israel and his holy one, that is, the angel, will be in fire and in flame, and all the thorns and briers of the Assyrians, that is, their malice, will be consumed, not over a long time, but in one day and moment. And as a forest and Carmel, which is a mountain in Galilee planted with woods, is quickly burned up when fire is set beneath it, so from the soul even to the flesh all the glory of the Assyrian will be consumed. Then the despoiled army will flee, as the same Prophet attests in what follows, and of so innumerable a multitude, which was compared to Carmel and a forest, it will come to such fewness that a little child could number them and write them down. For the Hebrews relate that only ten of his army remained; some of ours will have it that this king is a type of the adverse power. And as in Daniel (ch. 10) we read of the princes of the kingdom of the Persians, and of the kingdom of the Medes, and of the kingdom of the Greeks, so there is also a prince of the Assyrians, who because of his pride is called the great mind, and in the day of judgment will be handed over to the burnings of Gehenna, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. And that the light of Israel and the holy one, that is, the Lord himself, kindles the briers and thorns of the Assyrian, and that all his power and his innumerable peoples are to be brought to nothing. That then he, terrified with fear, like a crooked and fleeing serpent, wishes to escape the punishments hanging over him. And that those who have been able to escape from his forest and confusion and from the wood doomed to perish are worthy to be numbered and written down by the child whose government is upon his shoulders. This same thing can also be referred to the heretics: that after the Church's teaching has shone forth, and all their snares have been laid open, then they come to such desolation that, of the forest and the unfruitful trees and their innumerable multitude, which they had deceived by heretical fraud, scarcely a few remain to follow their error. Where we have rendered, the Lord will send leanness among his fat ones, the Seventy translated, the Lord will send dishonor upon your honor. And where we said: and his Holy One in flame, they rendered: and he will sanctify him in fire: by which some would have it understood that punishments and torments are applied to sinners for this purpose, that they may be purged by divine fire. And where we said: And the glory of his forest and of his Carmel, they translated: The mountains and the hills and the forests shall be quenched, whereby all the brightness and pride and multitude of the Assyrians is quenched and humbled.

10:20ff.

And it shall be in that day, the remnant of Israel, and those who have been saved of the house of Jacob, shall no more lean upon him who strikes them, but shall lean upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. The remnants shall be converted, the remnants, I say, of Jacob, to the mighty Lord. For if your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of it shall be converted. The consummation cut short shall overflow with righteousness. For the Lord God of hosts will make a consummation and a cutting short in the midst of all the earth. Where in the Greek it says: The remnants of Jacob shall be converted to the mighty God, for mighty God there is written in the Hebrew EL GIBBOR (אל גבור), two names of the six names by which, as we read above, the little child and son who is given to us was called. And where it is written: The remnants shall be converted, in place of that it is said in the Hebrew in the singular number, what is left shall be converted, that is, τὸ ὑπόλειμμα ἐπιστρέψει; in the Hebrew it is written SAR JASUB (שאר ישוב). And from the occasion of this expression they think that Jasub son of Isaiah went before as a sign of the people that was to be saved out of Israel. So when the light of Israel and the holy one has consumed the forests and briers of Carmel, and the Assyrian king has fled with a few, then the remnant of Israel, who with Hezekiah as their prince, when the other cities of Judea had been taken, were besieged in Jerusalem, will in no way trust in the Assyrian, as they do now under king Ahaz, who sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians, saying: I am your servant; come up and free me from the hand of the king of Syria, and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen up against me (2 Kgs 16:7); when he took the gold and silver that was found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the king's house, and sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians, and the Assyrian king hearkened to him, and came to Damascus, and took it, and carried it away, and killed Rezin; but, freed from that very Assyrian, the smiter, who had first been a friend and afterwards proved an enemy, they will lean and rely upon the Lord the Holy One of Israel, not falsely, as they had done under the former kings, but in truth. This we read was done under Hezekiah, so that, forsaking their idols, they were converted to the worship of God. And because he had said that a remnant would be saved, he passes to later times, and says that the full salvation will come under Christ. Understanding this, the apostle Paul too writes to the Romans: But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved. For he is finishing the word and cutting it short in equity, because a shortened word will the Lord make upon the earth (Rom 9:27). And as Isaiah said: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become as Sodom, and would have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9). Where, then, the authority of so great a man goes before, let every other interpretation cease. And indeed, if we read Josephus (bk. 10, ch. 2), and how great a multitude of men there was in Jerusalem and in Judea when the Lord suffered, we understand that scarcely a few of the Jews were saved, among the Apostles and apostolic men. Now the shortened and perfect word is the word of the Gospel, which in place of all the ceremonies of the long-winded Law gave a very brief precept of love and faith: that what we would not have done to ourselves, we should not do to another. Hence the Lord too in the Gospel: On these two commandments, he says, hangs all the Law and the Prophets (Matt 22:40). Some refer this chapter to those times when under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, and Ezra, and Nehemiah, a part of the people returned to Judea. To them we shall answer that they do not keep the order of the history, especially since the things that follow are said not against the Babylonians, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar, but against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.

10:24ff.

Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts: Do not fear, my people, dweller in Zion, because of Assur: he will strike you with the rod, and will lift up his staff over you in the way of Egypt. For yet a little while, and a very little, and my indignation will be ended, and my fury upon their crime. And the Lord of hosts will raise up a scourge against him, like the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb, and his rod over the sea, and he will lift it up in the way of Egypt. And it shall be in that day: his burden shall be taken from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck, and the yoke shall rot away before the oil. For rock, which Aquila translated according to the Hebrew, Symmachus and Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, SUR OREB (צור עורב). In place of which the Seventy translated place of tribulation: of which we shall speak in its own place. It seems hard to you, he says, O dweller in Zion, that when all the nations round about have been subjugated by the Assyrian, you alone should be freed from his hands. Listen to what I say: do not fear, my people, that you will be taken when Assur conquers. For although in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18) Sennacherib king of Assyria is to go up against all the fortified cities of Judah, to take them, and to send Rabshakeh to terrify the people besieged in Jerusalem, yet you must know this, that he will strike you not with the sword but with the rod, and, marching against Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, and against the Egyptians and the Red Sea by the way of Egypt, he will only lift his staff against you, and will not be able to strike. For yet a little while, and when he has returned from Egypt with an infinite multitude of his army, and wishes to besiege you, he will at once be struck by my indignation, and by that scourge which I once raised up against the Midianites under Gideon (Judg 7), who by another name was called Jerubbaal: when Oreb and Zebah, princes of the Midianites, were slain upon a very hard rock, that is, flint, which in Hebrew is called SUR (צור), so that the place received the name rock of Oreb from the rock and from the king who was slain upon it. So he will lift his rod over the Red Sea when he marches against the Ethiopians, and will lift it when he returns to you by the way of Egypt: but as soon as he has come from Egypt, the burden will be taken from your shoulders, and the yoke of his rule, and you will cease to serve. And this yoke, that is, the power of the Assyrian, will rot away before the oil, that is, the mercy of God. But we can also understand what he said: He will strike you with the rod, and will lift up his staff over you in the way of Egypt; and again: And his rod over the sea, and he will lift it up in the way of Egypt, in this way too: that he struck very many of the tribe of Judah, and took the cities round about the kingdom of Jerusalem, for this reason, because they had their trust not in God but in the Egyptians. Hence Rabshakeh too reproaches them, saying: Behold, you trust upon a broken staff of reed, upon Egypt. If a man lean upon it, it will go into his hand and pierce it (2 Kgs 18:22): so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. The history of the Midianites is written in the book of Judges (Judg 7), and we read it also in the Psalm: Make their princes like Oreb, and Zeeb, and Zebah, and Zalmunna (Ps 82 [83]:12). They err, therefore, who think that the time is signified when in the book of Numbers (ch. 25) the Midianites are reported to have been slain by Israel from the desert of Sur to Oreb, the mountain of God: for these are written among the Hebrews with other letters, and at that time they were not at mount Oreb, but in the wilderness of Shittim. According to the anagogy, the people that dwells in the Church is commanded not to fear the adversaries, who are always ready to fight and have overturned souls by their much disputation. For they receive a little power against the people of God, and strike not so much with the sword as with the rod, that is, not to kill but to threaten, for this reason, because the people have walked in the way of Egypt and have not trusted in the Lord. But when they have returned to God and have left the road of Egypt, then the scourge of God is to be raised up by his judgment against the adversaries. For Midian means from judgment: so that by the spirit of his mouth and by the oil of mercy the yoke of the enemies may rot away.

10:28ff.

He will come into Aioth, he will pass into Magron: at Machmas he will deposit his baggage. They have passed over in haste; Gabee is our lodging (or, as we have found it written elsewhere: they have lodged a lodging); Rama was astonished, Gaba of Saul fled. Neigh with your voice, daughter of Gallim; give heed, Laisa, poor little Anathoth: Medemena has departed: inhabitants of Gebim, take courage. There is still day enough for a halt at Nob: he will shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. LXX: For he will come into the city of Aggai, and will pass into Mageddo: and at Machmas he will set down his baggage: and he will pass through the valley, and will come into Aggai. Fear will seize Rama, the city of Saul: the daughter of Gallim will flee: give heed, Laisa: it will be heard in Anathot: Medemena was astonished, and the inhabitants of Gebim. Be comforted today in the way, so that he may remain: comfort the mount of the daughter of Zion, and the hill of Jerusalem. In this place the Seventy differ much from the Hebrew: for this reason we have set down both editions, so that, with Christ inspiring us, if we have deserved it, we may say what seems right to us on each point. The prophetic word describes the march and the pomp of the Assyrian as he returns from Egypt to Jerusalem, and with how great a din and how great speed he will come to attack it. And first, he says, he will come into Aioth, where, in his excessive haste, unwilling to stay, he will pass into Magron, and he will have such confidence of taking the city that he will leave his packs at Machmas, as one who will soon return when the city has been overthrown: having laid them down, he will pass it in haste; and in Gabee he will have his lodging: and while he halts there a little, to refresh his weary army, Rama, a neighboring city, will be terrified: Gaba, once the city of Saul, will flee. Then the daughter of Gallim too, which in Hebrew is called BETH GALLIM (בת גלים), will wail so that you would think it the neighing of horses. Therefore, O Laisa, and you, poor, or obedient, or humble Anathoth (for it can be interpreted in three ways), take careful heed, and turn aside from the onrush of the runner, if you can: for the city of Medemena has already departed from its seats. But you who dwell in the hills, which is what Gebim means, safe in the height of your places, take courage, that is, seize your arms. There still remained so much of the day that, standing in the little town of Nob, and looking at the city of Jerusalem from afar, he shook his hand and brandished it over mount Zion, either looking down on it and despising it, or insulting and threatening it, and marveling that, when the whole East had been subjected to him, so small a city should dare to resist his power. These things according to the Hebrews, as they were handed down to us by them, we have touched on in brief discourse. Now let us add what the churchmen think about this place according to the edition of the Seventy. When the yoke of the Assyrian, or, as some wrongly think, of the Babylonian, has been taken from your shoulders and broken, the Assyrian Sennacherib, fleeing with a few survivors, will come into Aggai, which is not found in the Hebrew. And so great will be the panic of the fugitive that he will not dare to remain there, but will pass into Mageddo, which the Scripture itself does not contain either. And because, hampered by his packs, he will not be able to flee more swiftly, he will lay down his baggage in Machmas, and with hurried step will pass through the valley, which the Hebrew text does not have either: and he will come again into Aggai, which is set twice in this place and is not found in the Hebrew. At the sound of his flight Rama, the city of Saul, will tremble: which is plainly false. For the city of Saul is called Gaba, as is contained in the Hebrew. Then he will come into Gallim: Laisa will hear, Anathoth will hear, Medemena will tremble. But the inhabitants of Gebim, and the hills which are in Jerusalem, that is, all the lofty men, are called upon to console Jerusalem: not after a long time, but at the present moment, and on the same day, while the Assyrian is on the way; so that they may remain in their places, and, though disturbed by fear, may in no way flee. This according to the letter. But a certain writer in this place, since he could not find the ἐτυμολογίας of the false names according to the Seventy, and testifies that he could not find them in the book of Hebrew Names, sends us off into uncertainty, so as to say that at the last time of the world, and at the consummation of this age, when punishments are imminent, the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, will flee, and through various places and by varied journeys will desire to flee from the wrath of God. And when he has fled, the inhabitants of Gebim, that is, all the lofty powers, are called upon by the prophetic word to console the fugitive, and to teach him not to flee but to remain on the way and wait for the mercy of God; and not only to console the fugitive, but by good works to call back the daughter of Zion from mourning and to summon her to the salvation of penitence; and that these are the hills in Jerusalem of which we read in the latter part of this prophet: Comfort, comfort my people, O priests: speak to the heart of Jerusalem (Isa 40:1). This he said because, constrained by the truth of the matter, he had nothing else to say.

Behold, the Sovereign Lord of hosts will break the little flask in terror, and the lofty of stature will be cut down, and the high will be humbled, and the thickets of the forest will be overturned with iron, and Lebanon with its lofty ones will fall. Some think that this passage is still said of the Assyrian: that when he has been crushed, all the nations round about which lay under his dominion are cut down and humbled, and the densest forest is overturned; by which they would have it that μεταφορικῶς the people and the princes are understood. And that Lebanon too falls with its lofty ones, so that no power at all is left to Assyria. Others, however, would have it that from this place begins the passage concerning Christ: especially since both we and the Circumcision confess that what follows also is written of him. He had told above the name of the child to be born of the Virgin, that he would be called Emmanuel; and afterwards, that the conception of the prophetess's womb would be called hasten, strip the spoils, make haste to plunder (Isa 8:3), and that he himself would be a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to both houses of Israel: that his government would be upon his shoulder, and he would be called by six names: wonderful, and counselor, and God, and mighty, and father of the age to come, and prince of peace: and that his empire would be multiplied, and of peace there would be no end. Now, in the prologue of his coming, before it is said that he will be born of the stock of Jesse and David, his passion is shown by the figure of the broken flask: that, by God's will, his flesh was handed over to death for this reason, that the loftiness of the Jews might be destroyed, and those once lofty might fall to the earth; and that Lebanon might be cut down with its cedars, of which we read in Zechariah: Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars: howl, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, because the magnificent have been laid waste (Zech 11:1-2). And that he is said to have been crushed and struck by the Father, this too is evidence: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zech 13:7). And another testimony: For they persecuted him whom you struck (Ps 68 [69]:27). The Hebrew word (פארה) PHURA, which Aquila translated κεραμεῖον, Theodotion and Symmachus rendered ληνὸν, that is, winepress, which itself too, according to the title of three psalms, signifies the Lord's passion, as he himself says in Isaiah: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me (Isa 63:3). But the Seventy, bringing in a new sense, translated glorious ones for winepress.

11:1-2

And there shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root: and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and godliness: and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him. Up to the beginning of the Vision, or burden, of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amos saw, all this prophecy is about Christ, and we wish to explain it part by part, lest, being set forth and discussed all at once, it confuse the reader's memory. The Jews interpret the rod and the flower from the root of Jesse as the Lord himself: namely, that in the rod the power of one who reigns is shown, in the flower his beauty. But let us understand the rod from the root of Jesse as the holy Virgin Mary, who had no shoot clinging to her; of whom we also read above: Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Isa 7:14). And the flower as the Lord Savior, who says in the Song of Songs: I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys (Song 2:1). For root, which the Seventy alone translated, in the Hebrew there is written (גזע) GEZA, which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion interpreted as κορμὸν, that is, trunk. And for flower, which in Hebrew is called (נצר) NESER, they translated sprout, to show that long after the time of the Babylonian captivity, when no one of David's stock possessed the glory of the ancient kingdom, Mary arose as if from a trunk, and Christ from Mary. That saying in the Gospel of Matthew of which all churchmen seek, and do not find, where it is written, For he shall be called a Nazarene (Matt 2:23), the learned among the Hebrews think was taken from this place. But it must be known that this NESER is written with the letter SADE, whose peculiar quality and sound, between z and s, the Latin tongue does not express. For it is a hissing sound, and is uttered with clenched teeth, barely, by the pressure of the tongue: and with it the city Zion too is written. Further, Nazirites, whom the Seventy translated sanctified, Symmachus separated, are always written with the letter ZAIN (ז). Upon this flower, then, which will suddenly rise up from the trunk and the root of Jesse through the Virgin Mary, the spirit of the Lord will rest, because in him it pleased all the fullness of the divinity to dwell bodily: not in part, as in the other saints; but, according to the Gospel written in the Hebrew tongue which the Nazarenes read: The whole fountain of the Holy Spirit shall descend upon him. Now the Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty (2 Cor 3:17). In the same volume of Matthew we read that the words written in what follows: Behold my servant whom I have chosen: my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the nations (Matt 12:18), are referred to the understanding of the Savior, upon whom the Spirit of the Lord rested, that is, remained in everlasting habitation: not so as to fly away and descend upon him again; but, according to the testimony of John the Baptist, so as to remain continually; for he says: I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and remaining on him, and I did not know him: but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: He on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining on him, he it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit (John 1:32-33). Further, in the Gospel which we mentioned above, we find these things written: And it came to pass, when the Lord had come up from the water, the whole fountain of the Holy Spirit descended and rested upon him, and said to him: My Son, in all the prophets I was awaiting you, that you might come and I might rest in you. For you are my rest, you are my firstborn son, who reigns for ever. This Spirit is called the Spirit of the Lord and the Spirit of wisdom; for all things were made through him; and without him nothing was made that was made (John 1:3). And in the Psalms it is sung: How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom (Ps 103 [104]:24). And the Apostle writes: Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1). And in Proverbs it is read: God by his wisdom founded the earth, and prepared the heavens by prudence (Prov 3:19). And as the same Word of God is called light, and life, and resurrection, so he is named the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and of counsel and fortitude, and of knowledge, and of godliness, and of the fear of the Lord: not that he is different according to the differences of the names, but that he is one and the same fountain and principle of all virtues. Without Christ, therefore, no one can be wise, nor understanding, nor a counselor, nor strong, nor learned, nor godly, nor full of the fear of God. And this is to be noted, that the Spirit of the Lord, of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, and of knowledge, and of godliness, and of the fear of the Lord, that is, the sevenfold number, which in Zechariah (ch. 3) are called seven eyes on one stone, rests upon the rod and the flower which rose up from Jesse, and so from the stock of David. But especially the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him, for the sake of those who have need of the fear of the Lord, because they are little ones; the fear which perfect love casts out. For he who fears has punishment, and is not perfect (1 John 4:18). Hence the Apostle too says to believers: For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear: but you have received the Spirit of adoption, in which we cry Abba, Father (Rom 8:15). And in Malachi we read: If I am a father, where is my glory? and if I am Lord, where is my fear (Mal 1:6)? of which fear it is sung in the Psalm: Come, children, hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord (Ps 33 [34]:12).

11:3ff.

He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears: but he shall judge the poor in righteousness, and shall reprove with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth, and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked. And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faith the belt of his reins. We refer these things to the first coming of the Savior: the Jews contend that they will come to pass at the end of the world. Further, the Seventy translated: He shall not judge according to glory, nor reprove according to speech: but he shall judge with a lowly judgment, and shall reprove the lowly of the earth. For he accepts no one's person in judgment; but to the scribes and Pharisees and rulers he says: Woe to you, hypocrites: and, The kingdom of God will be taken from you, and will be given to a nation that brings forth its fruits (Matt 23:13; 21:43). Nor did he rebuke according to speech and the hearing of the ears. For when they said: Master, we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in truth, and you care for no one: for you do not look at the faces of men (Matt 22:16), knowing their malice he answered: Why do you test me, hypocrites? and other things like these. But he judged in righteousness the poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of God; and he reproved with equity the meek and humble of the earth, saying to the Apostles: Are you also still without understanding? And again: Do you not yet know nor understand? And to Peter in particular: O you of little faith, why did you doubt (Mark 8:17)? Or certainly, on behalf of the humble and meek he reproved others, who were trying to oppress them (Matt 14:31). He also struck all earthly works with the rod, or, as the Seventy translated, with the word of his mouth, saying in the Gospel: Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth: for I have not come to send peace, but a sword. And with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked (Matt 10:34; Luke 12:51): of whom we read in Psalm 9: You have rebuked the nations, and the wicked has perished: you have blotted out their name for ever and for ever and ever (Ps 9:6). And Paul the Apostle writes: Whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the spirit of his mouth (2 Thess 2:8; Eph 6). And when the wicked has been struck, the Lord is girded with righteousness and truth and faith. For he himself was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1), he who also says in the Gospel: I am the light, and the way, and the truth (John 8:12; 14:6). And of the Psalms it is said: Truth has sprung from the earth: and righteousness has looked down from heaven (Ps 84 [85]:12). Hence the Apostle too exhorts the Ephesians: Stand, therefore, having your loins girded about with truth, and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness (Eph 6:14). But if faith is read in place of truth, this must be said: that the girdle of the Lord, with which Jeremiah was girded (Jer 13), is the faith of believers.

11:6ff.

The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; the calf and the lion and the sheep shall abide together, and a little child shall drive them. The calf and the bear shall feed: their young ones shall rest together, and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. And the infant at the breast shall delight over the hole of the asp; and he that has been weaned shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk. They shall not hurt, and they shall not kill in all my holy mountain, for the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters of the sea that cover it. These things too the Jews, and our judaizers, contend will come to pass according to the letter: that in the glory of Christ, who they think will come at the end of the world, all beasts will be brought back to gentleness, and, laying aside their former fierceness, the wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the rest with the rest, which we now see to be opposed to one another. We must ask them whether, if everything in the present place is taken just as it is written, and nothing is referred to a spiritual understanding, according to the saying of the Apostle: Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ (Eph 1:3), then the root and the rod and the flower too are not to be referred to a sense; and the earth struck by the word of God, and the wicked slain by the spirit of his lips, are to be understood just as they are written; and whether they will be forced to teach how the reins of the Lord are girded with incorporeal things, righteousness and truth? But let us ask them this too: what is worthy of the majesty of the Lord in the wolf and the lamb feeding together, and the leopard lying down with the kid, and the lion eating straw, and a little child putting his hand into the hole of asps? Unless perhaps, according to the fables of the poets, they will restore to us the golden age of Saturn, in which wolves and lambs will feed together, and rivers will run full of honeyed wine, and the sweetest honey will drip from the leaves of the trees, and all things will be filled with fountains of milk. But if they answer that these things will come about for the blessedness of the times, so that men may enjoy all good things without harm to anyone, let them hear from us that nothing is good except virtue, and nothing evil except vice, as the Psalmist says: Who is the man who wills life, and loves to see good days? Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak guile. Turn aside from evil, and do good (Ps 33 [34]:14; 30 [31]:27). Riches, moreover, and health of body, and abundance of all things, and their opposites, poverty, sickness, and want, are reckoned even among the philosophers of the world neither among goods nor among evils, but are called indifferent. Hence the Stoics too, who agree with our doctrine in very many points, call nothing good but honor and virtue alone, and nothing evil but baseness. We have said these things briefly to convict our judaizers of snoring in the heaviest sleep. But according to the life-giving spirit, the understanding is easy. For the wolf, Paul, who at first persecuted and tore the Church, of whom it was said: Benjamin a ravening wolf, dwelt with the lamb, either with Ananias, by whom he was baptized (Gen 49:27; Acts 8), or with the apostle Peter, to whom it was said: Feed my lambs (John 21). And the leopard, who formerly did not change his spots, washed in the fountain of the Lord, lay down with the kid, not the one which is on the left, but the one which is sacrificed in the Lord's pasch. And this is to be noted, that it is not the lamb and the kid that dwell and lie down with the wolf and the leopard, but the wolf and the leopard that imitate the innocence of the lamb and the kid. The lion too, formerly most ferocious, and the sheep, and the calf, will abide together. This we see daily in the Church: rich and poor, powerful and lowly, kings and private men abiding together, and being ruled in the Church by little children, whom we understand as the Apostles and apostolic men, unskilled in speech but not in knowledge. And when they have been bound together by the discipline of the Lord, so that their households too are joined, then will be fulfilled: Their young ones shall rest together. The lion too will eat not flesh but straw, namely, he will feed on simple food. And here it must be observed that it is not the ox that eats flesh, but the lion that eats straw. By straw I think the simple words in the holy Scriptures are understood; and by the wheat and the inner marrow, the sense which is found within the letter: and it often happens that men of the world, ignorant of mystical things, are fed on the simple reading of the Scriptures. The infant too, who is a little one in malice, puts his hand into the hole of the asp, and drives demons out of the possessed bodies of men. But he who has been weaned is no longer nourished on the milk of infancy, but now feeds on solid food. He puts his hand into the den of the basilisk, that is, into the dwelling of Satan himself, and drags him out from there. Hence power was given to the Apostles too to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the strength of the enemy (Luke 10). And the animals that were once venomous will in no way be able to hurt and kill those who dwell on the holy mountain of God, which means the Church, of which it is said in the Gospel: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden (Matt 5:14). And lest we think that this is said of mount Zion, according to the error of the Hebrews, in the following verse the mysteries of the Gospel preaching are shown: For the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord: this is what was said more obscurely above: The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and according to their custom the prophetic words are laid open at the end: Like the waters, he says, of the sea that cover. As the waters of the sea cover the depths of the sea, that is, the earth which is covered by the waves, so the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord. This joining together of those who were formerly of diverse ways the blessed apostle Peter too testifies that he saw in the linen vessel (Acts 10) which was let down from heaven, having four corners, which we understand as the four quarters of the world, so that we may recognize the earth filled with the knowledge of God: in which vessel there were four-footed beasts, and serpents, and wild beasts, and birds of heaven, so that what the Ark did in the flood, the Church may do in the world.

In that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign of the peoples: him the nations shall beseech, and his sepulcher shall be glorious. LXX: And there shall be in that day the root of Jesse, and he who shall rise up to be prince of the nations; in him the nations shall hope, and his rest shall be honor. For his rest, there is set in the Hebrew MNUATHO (מנחתו), which all translated alike. For honor too there is read in the Hebrew CHABOD (כבוד), which plainly means glory. And the sense is: his death shall be glorious, so that what the Savior prays in the Gospel may be fulfilled: Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was (John 17:5). It has been said of his birth, it has been said of the other mysteries in between: he comes to death, which, not by the customary name used of mortals, but because in Christ there was everlasting life, is called rest. But we, to make the sense plain to the reader, for sleep and rest translated sepulcher, another word but the same sense. At that time, then, when the Gospel of Christ has flashed forth in the whole world, and all the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters of the sea covering the earth, there shall be the root of Jesse, and he who shall ascend from its stock as a sign of all the peoples, so that the peoples may see the sign of the Son of man in heaven (Matt 24). He will have horns in his hands, in which his strength will be hidden, so that, being lifted up, he may draw all things to himself (Hab 3). Or, as the Seventy translated, he will rise again from the dead, to be prince of all the nations, and all the nations will hope in him. This Jacob too (Gen 49:10) attests in mystical speech concerning the tribe of Judah: A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up, and he shall be the expectation of the nations. And it shall be in that day, the Lord will set his hand a second time to possess the remnant of his people, which shall be left from the Assyrians, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Ethiopia, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. And he will lift up a sign to the nations, and will gather the fugitives of Israel, and will collect the dispersed of Judah from the four quarters of the earth: and the jealousy of Ephraim shall be taken away, and the enemies of Judah shall perish. Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not fight against Ephraim. And they shall fly upon the shoulder of the Philistines by the sea, together they shall plunder the sons of the East: Edom and Moab shall be the command of their hand, and the sons of Ammon shall be obedient. In that day, that is, at that time, of which it was said above too, when the root of Jesse has risen as a sign of the peoples, or to rule over the nations, the Lord will set his hand a second time; so that it is not, as our judaizers hold, at the end of the world, when the fullness of the nations has come in, that all Israel will then be saved (Rom 11); but let us understand all these things of the first coming. For we cannot, since one day is spoken of both now and above, refer that one to the first coming and this one to the second: lest through these things which follow, those too which went before should have to be referred to that Christ whom the Jews contend has not yet come but is to come. After the calling of the nations, then, which were once reckoned as the tail, Israel will be reckoned as the tail (above, Isa 10): so that the Lord may set his hand a second time and possess the remnant of his people, concerning which we read above too that not all Israel, but a remnant is to be saved, which shall be left from the Assyrians and from Egypt and from the various nations round about. For first the twelve Apostles, and the seventy, and the hundred and twenty souls, and the five hundred to whom the Lord appeared when they were gathered together, then three thousand and five thousand of the Jews believed in the Lord. James too speaks to the apostle Paul, who was himself also of the remnant: You see, brother, how many thousands of the Jews there are who believe? all these are zealous for the law (Acts 21:20). And in the same volume we read: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation that is under heaven, who all marveled and said: Are not these Galileans, and how have we heard each one his own tongue, in which we were born? Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those who dwell in Mesopotamia and Syria, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, and Egypt and Libya, and Cyrene, and sojourners from Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs, we have heard them speaking in our tongues the great works of God (Acts 2:5ff.). From all these nations, then, the remnant of Israel will be saved through the Apostles. The histories of the Church relate that the Apostles, dispersed through the whole world, preached the Gospel: so that some penetrated to the Persians and the Indians, and Ethiopia stretched out her hands to God, and from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia gifts were brought from there to Christ. And lest he seem to signify only the eastern peoples, he adds the rest too: And from the islands of the sea. By the islands of the sea he signifies the western region, which is enclosed by the circuit of the Ocean. He will lift up, then, the sign of the Cross over all nations, and will first gather the people of Israel from the synagogues of the Jews, so that the Apostles might fulfill the command of the Savior, who had said: Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:6). Finally Paul too speaks to the unbelievers among the Jews: It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you have rejected it, and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations, as the Lord commanded us (Acts 13:46-47). By the four quarters he signifies east and west, south and north, so that through these the calling of the world may be shown. At that time, says Isaiah, Ephraim and Judah, who now, while I prophesy, are at odds with each other in hostile hatred, will in no way be enemies, but according to the prophecy of Ezekiel the two rods will be joined into one rod, and those who were formerly separated will be united in the Church of Christ (Ezek 37), so that they toil with common labor among the nations, and fly upon the shoulder of the Philistines by the sea, that is, first preach to the Palestinians of the coast, and then go by sea with winged course to the other nations. Or, according to the Seventy translators: they will fly in the ships of foreigners, together they will plunder the sea: which we may understand from the example of the one apostle Paul, who through Pamphylia, and Asia, and Macedonia, and Achaia, and various islands and provinces, to Italy too (Acts 28), and, as he himself writes, to Spain, was carried in the ships of foreigners (Rom 15). So Ephraim and Judah, that is, those of the twelve tribes from among the Jews who believed in Christ, will together plunder the East, and will stretch out their hands into Edom and Moab, according to what Christ speaks mystically in the person of David: Into Edom I will stretch out my shoe: foreigners will serve me (Ps 59 [60]:10). For these nations, at the time when Isaiah prophesied, were adversaries of the people of the Jews, and therefore he now says that after the root of Jesse has risen to reign among the nations, and the standard of the Cross has been raised for the salvation of the whole world, then Edom too and Moab and the sons of Ammon, that is, the whole breadth of Arabia, give their hands to the Apostles, and in the places of idolatry churches of Christ are raised up.

And the Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt, and shall lift his hand over the river in the strength of his spirit, and shall strike it in seven streams, so that men may cross it shod. And there shall be a way for the remnant of my people that shall be left from the Assyrians, as there was for Israel in the day when it came up from the land of Egypt. As Edom and Moab and the sons of Ammon will give their hands to the Apostles, to obey the Gospel preaching, so the Lord himself, who accomplished those things in his Apostles, will lay waste, not the sea, as according to the Seventy, but, according to the Hebrews, the tongue of the sea of Egypt, which formerly blasphemed against the Lord and presided over the Egyptian superstition. Hence also in the Psalms we read: This great and wide sea, there are creeping things without number (Ps 103 [104]:25-26). To which is added: This dragon which you have formed to mock him. He will lay waste, then, or slay, that is, ἀναθεματίσει, as Theodotion, Aquila and Symmachus translated, the tongue of the sea of Egypt, and will lift his hand over the rivers of Egypt in the strength of his spirit, or with a most violent wind, by which we understand the kingdom of the Romans. For in the reign of Caesar Augustus (Luke 2), when the flower ascended from the root of Jesse, and the first enrollment was made in the Roman world, the kingdom of the Egyptians, formerly most powerful, which had endured for many ages, was destroyed by the death of Cleopatra, and the river of Egypt was struck in seven streams, or in seven valleys. For the Nile of many waters, which formerly flowed in one channel and was impassable, was divided and cut up into seven very low valleys and streams, so that it might be crossed with shod feet. And this signifies tropologically that the nation of the Egyptians, so given over to idolatry and the vainest superstition as to consecrate hawks, owls, dogs, and goats, and asses with a divine name, he distributed from the boundless power of a kingdom among the several judges of the Roman empire, so that Thebes has one judge, Libya another, Pentapolis another, Egypt another, Alexandria another, and so the various regions which the Egyptians call νόμους. And for this reason, under the metaphor, the Nile has been divided into parts and split into streams, so that the Gospel word might run about without any impediment and reach the farthest peoples of Egypt. And as in the times of Moses the Red Sea was dried up so that the people might flee out of Egypt, so on the contrary the rivers of Egypt will be dried up, so that the remnant of the people of God, which will be saved from the Assyrians and from various nations, may cross into Egypt, in no way fleeing it, but taking it and treading it under their foot. Let the prudent and Christian reader hold this rule for the prophetic promises: that what the Jews and ours, or rather not ours but the judaizers, contend will come to pass carnally, we teach to have been already accomplished spiritually, lest on the occasion of fables of this kind and of inextricable questions, according to the Apostle (2 Tim 2), we be forced to judaize.

12:1-2

And you will say in that day: I will confess to you, O Lord, for you were angry with me: your fury is turned away, and you have comforted me. Behold, God is my Savior; I will act confidently and will not fear, for my strength and my praise is the Lord God, and he has become my salvation. You who had formerly said in the wilderness, when you came up from the land of Egypt and the Red Sea was dried up: Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously magnified is he (Exod 15:1), and the rest: now that the tongue of the sea of Egypt has been struck, and its river dried up and cut off and humbled, glorify the Lord and say: I will confess to you, O Lord: because I who deserved your wrath and fury have obtained mercy; for you are my Savior, that is, Jesus, and I have no confidence at all in idols, nor will I fear what is not to be feared; but you are my strength and my praise, who have become my salvation. Let the most wicked heresy hear that the Lord was made so for those who are being saved, and whose Lord he formerly was not, so that we may understand creation and making in the holy Scriptures to mean not always the bringing into being of things which were not, but sometimes the grace toward those who have deserved that God should become theirs.

12:3

You will draw waters in joy from the fountains of the Savior. He whom above he had called Emmanuel, then, Strip the spoils, make haste to plunder, and by the other names, now, lest he seem to be another besides him whom Gabriel announced to the Virgin, saying: And you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people (Matt 1:21), he calls Savior, and proclaims that waters are to be drawn from his fountains, in no way from the waters of the river of Egypt, which have been struck, nor from the waters of the river of Rezin, but from the fountains of Jesus, for so Savior is expressed in the tongue of the Hebrews. Hence he himself also cried out in the Gospel: He who thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says: Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. This, says the Evangelist, he said of the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive. And in another place of the Gospel he himself says: He who drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever: but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 7:37-39; 4:13-14). By the fountains of the Savior let us understand the teaching of the Gospel, of which we read in Psalm 67 (68): In the churches bless God the Lord from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27).

12:4-5

And you will say in that day: Confess to the Lord and call upon his name: make known among the peoples his devices: remember that his name is exalted. Sing to the Lord, for he has done magnificently: proclaim this in all the earth. These things are commanded by the Apostles and the remnant of Israel to those of the nations who have believed: that they confess to the Lord alone, and, forsaking idols, call upon his name, and proclaim all his works to unbelievers; that they may know that he alone is exalted: to whom they must sing that he has done magnificently, and that his mercy may be proclaimed in all the world.

12:6

Exult and praise, O dwelling of Zion: for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel. First it must be said according to the letter: O dwelling of Zion, exult and praise your God, because he who was formerly seen as your God, and was shut within the narrow bounds of the land of Judea, has now filled all the earth with his knowledge, and, rising from death, reigns among the nations, and the nations beseech and adore him; only so, however, that he sets his hand a second time to possess what is left of his people, and to gather the fugitives of Israel, and to collect the dispersed of Judah from the four quarters of the earth: because the seed-bed of the Gospel went forth from the fountains of Israel through the Apostles, who were of the Jews. But it is better that we interpret Zion, that is, a watchtower set on the heights, as the Church, of which Psalm 50 (51) too sings: Deal kindly, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built (Ps 50 [51]:20); so that in her the sacrifice of righteousness may become acceptable to God, oblations and holocausts, and the calf which the most merciful father sacrificed for his penitent son (Luke 15).

Book Five

Many years ago I was asked by Amabilis, a bishop of holy memory, to write on the ten Visions of Isaiah, and because of the constraints of that time I touched in brief discourse on what seemed right to me in each one, setting out only the history, which was what he asked for. Now, φιλοπονωτάτη Eustochium, I am compelled to write Commentaries for you on the whole prophet, and meanwhile, through your prayers, I have come as far as Babylon, which is the first of the ten visions about which I have already spoken before. But it seemed superfluous to me either to repeat the same things again or to put forth differing opinions in a single work. Hence this will be the fifth book on Isaiah, the one which was once published on its own; and when it has been completed to the very end, we shall take up the beginning of the sixth volume according to tropology, and, with you likewise praying to the Lord, we shall pursue the heights of spiritual understanding.

"Up to now, Pope Amabilis, pillar and very name of charity, and to me the most loving of all whom the earth has brought forth, you have been demanding by letter that I discuss for you, in a historical exposition, the ten visions which are the most obscure in Isaiah, and that, leaving aside the Commentaries of our writers, who, following various opinions, have composed many volumes, I lay open the Hebrew truth; and as I hung back and put off this most troublesome kind of explanation to another time, you reminded me again and again. But this year you sent our son Heraclius the deacon, to lay hands on me and summon me into court, and to demand the promise at every moment. What, then, am I to do? Shall I take up a work over which most learned men have toiled, I mean Origen and Eusebius Pamphili, of whom the one roams through the free spaces of allegory and, by interpreting the names of individuals, makes his own ingenuity into the mysteries of the Church, while the other, promising a historical exposition in his title, sometimes forgets his purpose and goes over to the tenets of Origen? Or shall I keep silent, and say openly that I do not know an exposition of this kind? And when will I be able to persuade you that I was unable rather than unwilling, the one being a mark of weakness, the other of pride? Driven by these reasons, I have preferred that you should call my ability rather than my willingness into question; and I will briefly note down what I have learned, laying the foundations of the Scriptures. For the rest, if either you wish it, or there is time, and Christ assents to our will, a spiritual building must be raised on top, so that, with the roof set upon it, we may display the finished ornaments of the Church. You have set before me from Isaiah the Vision of Babylon, and of the Philistines, of Moab, and of Damascus, and of Egypt, and of the desert of the sea, and of Edom, and of Arabia, and of the Valley of vision, and of Tyre: if I strive to expound these more broadly, there will be need of many books, and the voyage of my collector will be put off to another year. So, as you wish, I will fit brief little comments to the individual texts, so that I do not so much expound what I think as leave to you, in few words, what you are to think. We are dictating these things, not writing them: the speech runs as the hand of the secretaries runs. For we do not want our own words to be praised, but the Prophet's sayings to be understood; nor do we vaunt eloquence, but we seek the knowledge of the Scriptures. Let us begin, then, with Babylon."

13:1

The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amos saw. The Hebrew word MESSA (משא) can be understood either as burden or as weight. And wherever it is placed at the head, the things that are said are full of threats. Hence I wonder that the Seventy translators chose to put vision in so grim a matter; but of this elsewhere. Now let us carry through what we have begun. Babylon was the metropolis of the Chaldeans, whose king Nebuchadnezzar, having overcome all the nations as far as Ethiopia, laid waste Judea too among the rest, and in the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah took Jerusalem after a long siege; and he led Zedekiah himself captive to Antioch, which was then called Riblah, and there, after his sons had been killed before their father's eyes, he ordered Zedekiah's eyes to be put out, and sent him, blinded, into a cage, and dragged him to Babylon like a wild beast; so was fulfilled the prophecy of Jeremiah, which sang: You shall enter Babylon, and you shall not see it (Jer 34; 39; 52). For the consolation of the people of the Jews, therefore, the ruin of Babylon is foretold: that just as Nineveh, the metropolis of the Assyrians, whose kings Pul and Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser and Sennacherib had captured the ten tribes, was overthrown when the Chaldean laid it waste, so this city too, which had grown proud against God, should be overthrown by the onslaught of the Medes and Persians.

13:2

Upon a misty mountain lift up a signal, raise the voice, lift up the hand. The misty, or dark, mountain, which in Hebrew is called NESPHE (נשפה), understand as Babylon, on account of its pride. These are the dark mountains, bearing gloom and mist before them, of which Jeremiah says: Give glory to the Lord your God, before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains (Jer 13:16). And a command is given either to the angels or to any ministers whatever, that at God's bidding, and with the hand of the messengers raised, the captivity coming upon Babylon should be proclaimed.

13:3-4

And let the leaders enter the gates: I have commanded my sanctified ones, and have called my mighty ones in my wrath, exulting in my glory. The princes and giants of the Seventy translators Eusebius interprets as angelic powers and the worst demons, who were sent to overthrow Babylon. But we, following the order of the history, say that they are the Medes. Of them Scripture testifies more openly in what follows, saying: Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who will not seek silver, nor want gold. Nor is it surprising if he calls the Medes sanctified for the overthrow of Babylon, since through Jeremiah he called Nebuchadnezzar himself his servant and his dove, because in destroying transgressing Jerusalem he was serving His command. Further, when he says: My mighty ones, and those exulting in my glory, he shows that it was not by their own strength but by the wrath of God that they overthrew the power of so lofty a kingdom.

13:4-5

The sound of a multitude on the mountains, as of many peoples: the sound of the din of the kings of nations gathered together. The Lord of hosts has given command to the army of war, to those coming from a land far off, from the summit of heaven. The Lord and the vessels of his fury, to destroy the whole earth. The onslaught of the Medes and Persians is described: that, having gathered many auxiliaries with them, with their Lord going before the army, they come to lay Babylon waste, to destroy the whole earth; not that they laid waste the whole world, but the whole land of Babylon and of the Chaldeans. For it is an idiom of Holy Scripture that by the whole earth it signifies the whole of that province about which it is speaking; and some, not understanding this, drag the passage to the overthrow of all lands.

13:6

Howl, for the day of the Lord is near: like a devastation it will come from the Lord. An apostrophe is made to the people of the Chaldeans, that they should make the coming evils resound with their weeping, and not doubt the ruin of their city, since the Lord is coming as its devastator.

13:7-8

Therefore all hands will be loosened, and every heart of man will waste away and be crushed. Gripings and pains will seize them: they will be in pain like a woman in labor: each will be astounded at his neighbor: their countenances are scorched faces. This needs no exposition; but it is briefly indicated that so great a weight of evils will press upon them that the hand of Babylon's fighting men will be loosened, and the heart will languish with fear, and pain will wring their bowels after the manner of women in labor, and each will seek the help of another, carrying about a face sallow with pallor; for it is natural that, when evils are imminent, we think others wiser than ourselves.

13:9

Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, and of wrath and of fury, to make the land a wilderness, and to crush its sinners out of it. He calls the day cruel, not by its own desert, but by that of the people. For he is not cruel who cuts the throats of the cruel; but he seems cruel to those who suffer. For even the robber hanging on the gibbet thinks the judge cruel. And at the same time the desolation and devastation of the Babylonian land is announced, and the cause of the devastation is set forth: that all these things come about because of its inhabitants.

13:10

For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread out their light: the sun has been darkened in its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light. The Hebrew word CHISILE (כסילי) the Seventy translated as ὠρίωνα. The Hebrew whom I used as my teacher interpreted it as Arcturus. We, following Symmachus, have used the general word star. And the sense is this: when the cruel day of the Lord has come and his fury has laid all things waste, through the greatness of their fear everything grows dark for mortals, and the sun itself and the moon and the glowing stars seem to deny their brightness. Hence also heaven is clothed in sackcloth, namely because darkness covers all things, and, under the pressure of evils, men perceive nothing else but what the mind compels them to see.

13:11

And I will visit evils upon the world, and against the wicked their iniquity: and I will make the pride of the unbelievers cease, and will humble the arrogance of the mighty.
