From this place and from the one above, where it is written that the sun is darkened in its rising, and the moon is filled with gloom, and the stars withdraw their brightness, and the iniquity of the whole world is visited, some think that what is foretold is not the ruin of Babylon but the consummation of the world; whereas, surely, in keeping with what precedes, by the world as well, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל), and in Greek οἰκουμένη, Babylon is to be understood. For οἰκουμένη in our language means inhabited; and Babylon is called inhabited because of the vast multitude of its people: so that where there had formerly been a countless throng of peoples, there should be desolation and a dwelling of beasts.

13:12

A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold. The cause is plain why God visits the οἰκουμένην, that is, the evils of Babylon: so that, deserted by its inhabitants, it may be reduced to a wilderness. Now, everything that is rare is called precious; just as above, too, according to the history, we read that because of the scarcity of men seven women take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach (Isa 4:1). And in the volume of Samuel it is contained: The word of the Lord was precious in those days (1 Sam 3:1), that is, rare. Note that in the Hebrew PHAZ (פז) is written for gold in general, and OPHIR (אופיר) for fine gold.

13:13

Upon this I will trouble heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place, because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts, and because of the day of the wrath of his fury. Either take it in the sense in which we expounded above concerning the stars, and the sun, and the moon, and the world; or ὑπερβολικῶς, that because of the indignation of God both heaven is sad and the earth is moved, and all the elements too acknowledge the wrath of the Creator.

13:14

And it will be like a little doe fleeing, and like a sheep, and there will be none to gather them. He means the Babylonian and Chaldean people: that at the irruption of the Medes and Persians it will flee as fearfully as a little doe and a sheep at the roaring of a lion and the howling of a wolf; and it has no defender or prince whose command it may follow.

Each will turn to his own people, and every one will flee to his own land. After Babylon has been taken and the enemy army has entered through its gates, all the auxiliaries and the troops of the various nations by which the city had formerly been defended will go back to their own provinces.

13:15

Everyone who is found will be slain: and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword. He who has not fled will be struck down by the blade; and he who has chosen either to resist or to come back will be of so little use to the captured city that he too will shed his own blood.

13:16

Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes: their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be violated. This is what David prophesies in the spirit: Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you your recompense, which you have paid out to us. Blessed is he who will take and dash your little ones against the rock (Ps 136 [137]:8). So great will be the devastation of the city and the savagery of the victors that not even innocent age will be spared, that all the wealth of the houses will be plundered, and the chastity of wives will be violated before their husbands' eyes.

13:17

Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who will not seek silver, nor want gold. What lay hidden has been made plain: that the mighty ones and the giants are by no means to be understood as angels and demons, but as the nation of the Medes, whose prince Darius was the first to destroy the empire of the Babylonians, having slain Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, who was the son of Evil-merodach (Dan 5). And he describes the savagery of the Medes and Persians as so great that, in their ardor to shed blood, they despise gold and silver and count the riches offered to them as mud.

13:18

But with arrows they will kill the little ones, and they will have no pity on the sucklings of the womb, and their eye will not spare the sons. The little ones will be killed, whose wounds will be no smaller than their bodies; and the wombs of pregnant women will be cut open, and the infants dashed out, and the cruel victor will kill the sons pressed to the breasts.

13:19

And Babylon, that glorious one among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah: it will not be inhabited unto the end, and it will not be founded unto generation and generation. We have heard of the Medes, we have heard of Babylon, we have heard of her who is renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans: and we refuse to understand what was, and seek to hear what was not. And we say this, not because we condemn the tropological understanding, but because the spiritual interpretation ought to follow the order of the history; and many, ignorant of this, wander about in the Scriptures in a frenzied error. To this present day, then, the prophecy concerning Babylon is being fulfilled: and just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, so this city too, once overthrown, will not be inhabited forever. For in its place they made Seleucia and Ctesiphon the renowned cities of the Persians.

13:20, 22

Nor will the Arab pitch his tents there; nor will shepherds rest there: but beasts will be there, their houses will be filled with dragons, and ostriches will dwell there, and hairy ones will dance there. And owls will answer in its buildings, and Sirens in the shrines of pleasure. Babylon will be so devastated and deserted that it will not be useful even for the pasturing of herds and flocks. For the Arab and the Saracen will not pitch their tents there, nor will shepherds, weary with toil after the tracks of their flocks, rest there; but among the broken walls and the narrow places of the ancient ruins SIIM (ציים) will dwell: which the Seventy alone translated as beasts; the others kept the very name that is written among the Hebrews, wishing kinds of demons or phantoms to be understood. And their houses, he says, will be filled, as we have said, with dragons; as Aquila translated, with typhoons; as Symmachus, OHIM (אחים), expressing the Hebrew word itself; but the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted it as cries or sounds. And as for what follows: Hairy ones will dance there, they understand either incubi, or satyrs, or certain wild men of the woods, whom some call the fig-tree Fauns, or kinds of demons. For owls, too, all kept the Hebrew word itself, IIM (איים); the Seventy alone translated onocentaurs. And the Sirens are called THENNIM (תנים), which we shall interpret either as demons, or as certain monsters, or at any rate as great dragons, which are crested and fly. By all these things the signs of devastation and solitude are shown: that the depopulation of the once most mighty city is so great that, because of the multitude of demons and beasts, none of the shepherds, that is, of those who seek out the desert, dares to enter it. We have learned from a certain brother, an Elamite, who came out of those regions and now lives the life of the monks at Jerusalem, that there are royal hunting grounds in Babylon, and that beasts of every kind are kept enclosed merely by the circuit of its walls.

14:1

Its time is near to come, and its days will not be prolonged. He says that the time is at hand when it is to be taken by its enemies. For after the captivity of Jerusalem, with no long time in between, it too was laid waste by the Medes and Persians.

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose from Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil. Of this Zephaniah speaks more fully: Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Israel; be glad and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem: for the Lord has taken away your judgment: he has turned away your enemies (Zeph 3:14-15). And it signifies the time when Cyrus king of the Persians permitted the captive people to return to Jerusalem. Read the book of Ezra (Ezra 1), Haggai (Hag 1) and Zechariah (Zech 1): when, under Zerubbabel, and Joshua the high priest, and Ezra, and Nehemiah, the altar, the Temple, and the walls of the city were built.

14:2

The stranger will be joined to them, and will cleave to the house of Jacob, and peoples will take them, and bring them into their own place, and the house of Israel will possess them upon the land of the Lord as menservants and maidservants: and they will take captive those who had taken them captive, and they will subdue their taskmasters. We conjecture that many from various nations came to Jerusalem with the people of the Jews, believing in the God of Israel and abandoning the idols of their errors. And that they were brought back by the king's letters, and received gifts and the expenses of the Temple, there is no doubt. The understanding seems to be hemmed in only on this point: how Israel possessed, in the land of the Lord, those who had once been its conquerors, and subdued its taskmasters, and held them as menservants and maidservants. Unless perhaps synecdochically we understand the whole from the part: that they afterwards enjoyed such prosperity that they acquired for themselves households of menservants and maidservants from the various nations round about as well. It can also be understood of the times of Ahasuerus (Esth 9; Jdt 13), when, after Holofernes had been killed, the enemy army was cut down by Israel. That I cling to the letter and, in the manner of the serpent, eat earth, is your will, who have wished to hear only the historical interpretation.

14:3

And it will come to pass in that day, when the Lord has given you rest from your labor, and from your turmoil, and from your hard servitude, because you served before: you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and you will say. The discourse is directed to Israel: that after it has returned to Jerusalem and shaken off the yoke of servitude, it should recall the former power of Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian summit, and lament him with a pitiful voice, because he has come to such calamity that he seems worthy of pity even to his enemies.

14:4, 7

How has the taskmaster ceased, the tribute come to rest? The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers, that struck the peoples in indignation, that subdued the nations in fury with an incurable blow, that persecuted cruelly: it has come to rest and fallen silent: the whole earth has rejoiced and exulted. This is the voice of Israel lamenting and pitying: how one who was once a lord and conqueror of the lands, despoiling everything with tributes, has been crushed and brought to nothing. He, I say, who was the staff of the wicked, who as sceptre and royal rod struck all in his fury, whose blow could not be endured, who cruelly pursued even those who fled: how he has come to rest and been humbled, and at his ruin the whole earth has fallen silent, uttering only the voice of exultant joy!

14:8

The fir trees too have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon: Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down. By the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon understand the princes of the nations, who were cut down when Nebuchadnezzar struck them; and they too, breaking out into a voice of joy, say: Since you were led down to the underworld, no one else could be found to cut down the great and the mighty.

14:9

The underworld beneath you was thrown into confusion, at the meeting of your coming it roused up giants for you: all the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones: all the princes of the nations, every one, will answer and say to you. These things are to be read emphatically and in the manner of a stage scene; not because they happened, but because they could have happened; unless perhaps we believe that the souls of the kings whom he had killed came to meet the Babylonian king, mocking him. For it is a solace in evils when men see their enemies suffer the same things:

14:10-11

And you too have been wounded as we were, you have become like us: your pride has been dragged down to the underworld: there has fallen your corpse; beneath you the moth will be spread, and worms will be your covering. The speech of the mighty ones and princes of the earth, whom he had called cedars and fir trees above, is addressed to the Babylonian king, now placed in the underworld. We no longer grieve that we were cut down, since you too have fallen by the same axe. All your power, and your pride lifted up to heaven, has been dragged down to the earth. So will your corpse too feed the moth, and a multitude of swarming worms cover it? Through death you will feel the worthlessness of man, you who displayed the power of God in yourself.

14:12, 14

How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning: you have crashed to the earth, you who wounded the nations: who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the North; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. In place of what we have translated, for ease of understanding, How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning, in the Hebrew, to render it word for word, one reads: How you have fallen from heaven, howl, son of the dawn. Now in other words Lucifer is meant; and he is told that he ought to weep and mourn, he who was once so glorious that he was compared to the brightness of the morning star. Just as, he says, the morning star, scattering the darkness, shines forth burning and ruddy, so your progress too among the peoples and in public seemed like a bright star; but you have fallen to the earth, you wounder of nations, who in your pride said: I have attained such power that heaven remains for me, and the stars, so that the things on high must lie beneath my feet. The Jews, however, would have heaven and the stars of God understood of themselves, on the strength of what follows: I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, that is, in the Temple, where the ordinances of God are laid up, and in the sides of the North, that is, in Jerusalem. For it is written: The mountains of Zion, the sides of the North (Ps 47 [48]:3). Nor had it been enough for his pride to desire heavenly things, unless he had burst out into such madness as to claim for himself the likeness of God.

14:15

But you will be dragged down to the underworld, into the depth of the pit. He who in his pride had said: I will ascend into heaven, I will be like the Most High, is dragged down not only to the underworld but to the lowest underworld. For this is what the depth of the pit signifies, in place of which we read in the Gospel of the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Luke 13:28).

14:16-17

Those who see you will bend down toward you and gaze at you (understand: saying): Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities; who did not open the prison to his captives? This too is the voice of those who mock and marvel, how the devastator of all has himself been devastated. And when he says: Who did not open the prison to his captives?, the greatness of his cruelty and impiety is expressed: that he kept even men in chains in prison, and chains were not enough for the wretches unless the horror of darkness also shut them in.

14:18-19

All the kings of the nations, every one, have slept in glory, each man in his own house. But you have been cast out of your tomb like a useless shoot, defiled and wrapped up with those who were slain by the sword, and went down to the foundations of the pit; like a rotting corpse you will have no fellowship, not even with them in burial. The Hebrews tell a fable of this kind. Evil-merodach, who had reigned earlier while his father Nebuchadnezzar lived for seven years among the beasts, was kept in chains together with Jehoiachin king of Judah, after his father had been restored to his kingdom, until his father's death; and when his father died and he succeeded to the kingdom again, and was not accepted by the princes, who feared that the man said to be dead might be alive, then, to give proof that his father was dead, he opened the tomb and dragged out his corpse with a hook and ropes. And the sense is: While all who were killed by you are buried, you alone will lie unburied. Others, however, interpret this place thus: All souls in the underworld will receive some rest; you alone will be bound fast in the outermost darkness. For you will be covered with the blood of all, and the gore of everyone will weigh upon you, as one wrapped in the putrid matter of the dead. Symmachus translated this place thus: Not even with those who are slain in war will you deserve to share in burial. And for what we have said, like a useless shoot, where in the Hebrew one reads CHANESER NETHAB (כנצר נתעב), Aquila translated like defiled putrid matter. Now NESER (נצר) properly denotes a sucker that springs up at the roots of trees and is cut off by farmers as useless; we can understand this very thing as putrid matter and corruption. And at the same time we learn that the underworld is beneath the earth, since Scripture says: To the foundations of the pit.

14:20

For you have destroyed your own land, you have slain your own people. According to the Seventy interpreters, who said: Because you have destroyed my land, and slain my people, there is no doubt what they mean. For Nebuchadnezzar slew and destroyed the land of Judea and its people Israel. According to the Hebrew the understanding is difficult: how he destroyed his own land and slew his own people; unless perhaps it is to be taken in this sense: those whom God had given you for chastening, you have utterly destroyed. Or otherwise: the ancient kingdom of the Assyrians, through your great pride and your lifting up your neck against God, has been utterly destroyed. For had you behaved humbly and known your own measure, the Assyrian and the Babylonian would be reigning to this day. Or in this way: you were so cruel toward foreigners that in your fury you oppressed even the peoples subject to you.

14:21

The seed of the most wicked will not be named forever. Prepare his sons for slaughter in the iniquity of their fathers: they will not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. All the histories agree that, after Belshazzar the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar was slain and Darius succeeded to the kingdom of the Chaldeans, no one of Nebuchadnezzar's stock reigned thereafter. This, then, is what Scripture foretells: that Babylon will come to such devastation that not even of the royal seed will anyone remain, but on account of the father's impiety all his offspring will be wiped out. And for what we translated in the last part of the sentence, nor fill the face of the world with cities, there is written in the Hebrew, for cities, ARIM (ערים), which we can also translate as adversaries; so that the sense is: no one of your seed will be raised up as an adversary who desires to restore the kingdom. According to the Seventy interpreters, who said: Most wicked seed, prepare your sons for slaughter because of the sins of your father, what sense it has I am unable to know.

14:22-23

And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts: and I will destroy the name of Babylon, and the remnant, and the offshoot, and the progeny, says the Lord. And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with a broom, grinding it away, says the Lord of hosts. That Babylon was most mighty, and that, set foursquare on the plains, it extended sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner of the wall, that is, sixty-four thousand in all around its circuit, is reported by Herodotus and many others who have written Greek histories. And its citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, is the tower which was built after the flood, and is said to reach four thousand paces in height, narrowing little by little from broad to narrow, so that the overhanging weight may be borne more easily by the broader parts. They describe marble temples there, golden statues, streets gleaming with stones and gold, and many other things that seem almost incredible. We have recounted all this to show that before the wrath of God all power is dust, and is to be compared to embers and ashes. If it were permitted to go into the barbarian nations and see the last traces of so great a city, we would see the possession of the hedgehog and the pools of water, and that what is now sung by the voice of Isaiah has truly been fulfilled: I will sweep it with a broom, grinding it away; for apart from the walls of baked brick, which are repaired after very many years in order to shut in the beasts, the whole space in between is a wilderness.

14:24-25

The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: If it is not so, that as I have thought, so it will be, and as I have pondered in my mind, so it will come to pass, that I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and tread him down upon my mountains: and his yoke will be taken from them, and his burden will be removed from their shoulder. He returns to the present, that is, to Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, who laid waste Samaria and Judea and, Jerusalem excepted, destroyed everything round about; and he joins things near at hand to things that are to come long afterward, so that the fear hanging over them may be removed: because those who heard could say: We are enduring a siege now, and this man promises things that will come many ages later. This, then, is the order of the prophecy: although Babylon is to be destroyed after very many years, and the whole seedbed of the stock of the Assyrians and of Chaldea is to be utterly destroyed, nevertheless, so that you may not fear the captivity close at hand, the Lord swears (who is to be believed even when he does not swear) that his judgment is not mistaken, and that what he has conceived in his mind will not be made void. And he speaks this with human feeling, namely that he who cannot be deceived is not deceived: I will crush, he says, the Assyrian in my land, and upon my mountains I will tread him down. For in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the army of the Assyrians were destroyed, the Angel laying them waste (2 Kgs 19). And from those who were besieged in Jerusalem his yoke will be taken away, and the heavy dominion that hung over all, and the weight by which they were pressed down, will rather be thrust back upon himself. For when the king of the Assyrians fled into his own land, Hezekiah went out free with the remnant of the people.

14:26-27

This is the counsel that I have devised upon the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out upon all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who will be able to weaken it? And his hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? In this place some think that the prophecy is general, against the whole world, and that the devastation of Babylon and of the Assyrian city is a type of the consummation of the world. We by no means contradict them, so long as we know that here the whole land of the Assyrians is properly signified, and that all the nations allied with the Assyrian king are pointed out. Whatever has been decreed by the Lord is prevented by no one's power. And his hand, stretched out and ready to strike, no one will be able to hold back.

14:28

In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came. We read that four kings of Judea are placed at the head of the Prophet's title: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, each succeeding the other in order and by descent; of whom we read above that Uzziah had died, as Isaiah relates: In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. From this we understand that both the Vision of the Lord seated and the things enjoined upon the Prophet, up to the place where it is written (Isa 6): Like a terebinth and like an oak that spreads out its branches: the holy seed will be its shoot, were prophesied under King Jotham (ibid., 7). The third to succeed is Ahaz, son of Jotham, son of Uzziah king of Judah, under whom Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, and the rest that Scripture records. We know, therefore, that all that is placed in between, up to the present place which we are now striving to expound, was prophesied under Ahaz; and when he died, the fourth, that is, the last, Hezekiah, succeeded, under whom the whole book is woven to the end.

14:29

Do not rejoice, all you Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken: for out of the root of the serpent will come forth a regulus, and its seed swallowing the bird. What we say is natural: when the king of a hostile nation dies, his enemies always rejoice, expecting from the new state of things civil wars and seditions and inexperience in ruling. When Ahaz the sinner died, therefore, who had walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and had been joined to them by kinship, we understand that the Philistines, from close by, rejoiced and mocked Israel, because, having lost a king of mature years, they were subject to the young Hezekiah. Now by Philistines, as we said above, he means the Palestinians, whom the common edition writes as foreigners, although this is the term not for one nation but for all foreign nations. Do not, he says, rejoice, O Philistia, do not mock my people because the rod of Ahaz who struck you has been broken; because the staff which used to strike you seems crushed by death; because the serpent has been slain. For in his place a more harmful one will be born, Hezekiah the regulus, which the Greeks call the basilisk, who will kill you with his gaze and slay you with the breath of his mouth. For just as no bird can pass the gaze of the regulus unharmed, but, however far off it may be, is sucked into its mouth, so you too will perish wholly at the sight of King Hezekiah. And he has kept the metaphor beautifully: for since he had named a serpent and a regulus, he says that birds are devoured by its mouth and breath. And that none of the kings of Judah struck the Philistines as Hezekiah ravaged them, hear the book of Kings: He struck the Philistines as far as Gaza, and as far as its borders: from the tower of the watchmen to the fortified cities (2 Kgs 18:8). And for what we have translated swallowing the bird, where in the Hebrew is written SARAPH MOPHETH (שרף מעופת), it can be interpreted a flying serpent: so that the sense is: from the root of the serpent a regulus will be born, and its fruit, that is, the regulus's, a flying serpent, so that you understand a flying dragon.

14:30

And the firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will rest in confidence. When the regulus has struck you, and the flying dragon has laid waste your borders, you will by no means lie in wait for Judah, nor terrify my poor little people with your treachery; but, hard pressed by your own straits, you will weep over your calamity. And the humble and the poor, who trusted not in riches and in power but in my name, will rest in secure peace, and will dread the onslaught of no enemy.

And I will make your root perish by famine, and I will slay your remnant. He speaks entirely in figures. And the sense is that, while the people of God rest in confidence, the root of the Philistines is dried up, and all its remnant will be consumed.

14:31

Howl, O gate, cry out, O city, all Philistia is laid low: for smoke will come from the north, and there is none who escapes its column. He says the gate for those who are in the gate, and the city for the inhabitants of the city. And he directs his speech to the cities of the Palestinians, that they should wail and mourn as Sennacherib comes and lays everything waste like a torrent. For under King Hezekiah the Assyrian came, and among the other nations laid waste the Philistines. To them Jeremiah speaks: Behold, waters will rise up from the north, and they will be like an overflowing torrent: and they will cover the land and all that fills it, the city and its inhabitants (Jer 47:2). For from the north came the Assyrian, and those who went forth from its heat, subjugating Nineveh and the other nations. At the time when these things were being sung, the smoke was rising on high, that is, a rumor was spreading among the peoples, through the whole range of the nations, that the Phoenicians too and the Palestinians were to be laid waste.

14:32

What will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in her the poor of his people will hope. Because he had said, There is none who escapes its column, Judah too seemed to be included in the general statement. If, he says, the messengers of the Assyrian nation ask why Judah alone has escaped, answer them that the Lord has founded Zion, and has himself protected the humble people by his power. For messengers (מלאכי) the Seventy translated kings (מלכי), misled by an error over a single letter, ALEPH.

15:1

The burden of Moab: because in the night Ar was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent: because in the night the wall was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. Let it suffice to have spoken once about burden and weight. I give only this brief reminder: that sad things always follow a burden, whereas a vision is followed either by glad things at once, or by glad things at the end after the sad. Moab is a province of the Arabs, in which was Balak son of Beor (Num 22), who hired the soothsayer Balaam from Mesopotamia to curse Israel; where also the people were initiated into Baal-peor (ibid., 25). Its metropolis is the city AR (ער), which today is called Areopolis, a name compounded from the Hebrew and the Greek tongue; not, as many suppose, because it is the city of ἄρεος, that is, of Mars. And Ar also means ἀντίδικος, that is, adversary. How great its power was, Jeremiah testifies (Jer 48:2, 7ff.), saying: There is no more exultation in Moab. And again: You have trusted in your fortifications and in your treasures. And again: Moab has been fruitful from his youth, and has rested on his lees, and has not been poured from vessel to vessel, and has not gone into exile; and therefore his taste has remained in him, and his scent has not been changed. And in another place (ibid., 17): How has the strong rod been broken, the glorious staff? And a little later: We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud. His loftiness, and arrogance, and pride, and the haughtiness of his heart I know, says the Lord, and his boasting. Just as, therefore, the Prophet prophesied against Babylon and the Philistines because they had oppressed the people of the Jews, so now the devastation of the Moabites, that is, of Arabia, by the Assyrians and the Babylonians is foretold. For they were laid waste by both nations, at the time when Sennacherib led Israel captive, and when Nebuchadnezzar overthrew Jerusalem (2 Kgs 17 and 25). For at the coming of each enemy he had mocked Ephraim and Judah, as Jeremiah says: Moab will strike his hand in his vomit, and he too will become a derision. For Israel was a derision to you, as though you had found him among thieves (Jer 48:26-27). Because of your words, therefore, which you have spoken against him, you will be led captive. And when he says: In the night AR was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent, it is a fitting beginning for the invective, that he who was conceived at night from his father's incest should be laid waste in darkness. Unless perhaps we take night for the greatness of the terror; and it is to be believed that, because the city trusted in its walls, it was overcome by stratagems and mines. I have heard a certain man of Areopolis say, and indeed the whole city is witness to it, that in a great earthquake in my infancy, when the seas passed over the shores of the whole world, the walls of this city collapsed on that same night.

15:2

The house has gone up, and Dibon, to the high places to lament over Nebo, and over Medeba Moab will howl. Do not let it be irksome to you that I walk along the road of the history; for you yourself wished me to do this. Now what is understood is the royal house; and the city of Dibon goes up to the idols set on the heights: over Nebo and over Medeba, noble cities, the whole province will howl. For in Nebo was consecrated the idol Chemosh, which by another name is called Baal-peor.

On all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. Among the ancients the shaving of the beard and the head was a sign of mourning. By these things, therefore, the greatness of the grief is shown, as Jeremiah cries out the same things against Moab: Every head baldness, and every beard will be shaved, and on all hands a binding, and on every back haircloth (Jer 48:37).

15:3

In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; on its roofs and in its streets all howling will go down into weeping. The tears will not be private; public laments will resound for a public grief; neither matrons nor virgins, nor the tender age of children, nor the broken steps of old men will be kept within doors: the extremity of captivity will know neither shame nor weakness.

15:4

Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out. These are names of cities of the province of Moab, of which Heshbon was once the city of the king of the Amorites, about which the same Jeremiah says: Fire has gone forth from Heshbon, and flame from the midst of Sihon. Now Heshbon means thought, and so Jeremiah, alluding to the name: Against Heshbon, he says, they have thought evil things (Jer 48:2).

Even to Jahaz their voice has been heard. The city of Jahaz overlooks the Dead Sea, where the border of the province of the Moabites lies. This, then, indicates that the howling of the province will resound to its farthest borders. Hence Jeremiah too says: From the cry of Heshbon, up to Elealeh and Jahaz they have uttered their voice (Jer 48:34).

Over this the lightly armed of Moab will howl, its soul will howl for itself. The Hebrew word ELUSE (חלוצי), for which Aquila translated ἐξώμους, that is, lightly armed and with shoulders bared, and Symmachus girded, some think is to be understood not of men but as the name of a city, which today is called Eluza and is situated in the region of Moabitis. But we can also say this: that the whole strength of the fighting men has collapsed, and the whole land has resounded with their weeping for one another. If, however, ELUSE is understood, as Aquila would have it, as with shoulders bared, this sense is suggested to us: that all have bared their breasts to beat them in mourning.

15:5

My heart will cry out to Moab. The Prophet speaks with the feeling of one who grieves, either because the enemies too, upon whom so many evils come, are God's creatures, or because they were to be crushed by such great calamities that they become pitiable even to their enemies. Jeremiah says the very same: Therefore my heart will sound for Moab like a flute.

Its bars, as far as Segor, a heifer of three years. And Jeremiah: From Segor, he says, as far as Horonaim, a heifer of three years. Of this city we have spoken in the books of Hebrew Questions as well, and now we note briefly that it is the fifth city after Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which, being small, was preserved at the prayers of Lot. And it is called Bala, that is, swallowed up, the Hebrews relating that it was overthrown by a third earthquake. It is the city which today in the Syrian tongue is called Zoora, in the Hebrew Segor: in both, the little one. We can take the heifer of three years as signifying full age. For as the thirtieth year is the strongest in men, so the third is in cattle and beasts of burden. Understand the bars, too, as borders and strength, because Segor is situated at the borders of the Moabites, dividing the land of the Philistines from them.

For by the ascent of Luhith he will go up weeping. And Jeremiah: By the ascent of Luhith, weeping, he will go up in tears. We understand it to be the slope of the road that leads to the Assyrians, and by this captivity is signified.

And on the road to Horonaim they will raise a cry of crushing. Again Jeremiah: The voice of a cry from Horonaim, devastation and great crushing. It would take long if I wished to speak about each one, since it is plain that these are the names either of cities in Moab or of places which those who are carried away into exile are leaving.

15:6

For the waters of Nimrim will be deserted. This town lies above the Dead Sea, with salt waters, and barren for that very reason. And either he has alluded to the name, or what had not been so before came about after the devastation: that even the waters were turned to bitterness.

For the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. It is not, as some think, that all the grass truly dried up because of the barren waters of Nimrim; rather, Scripture is speaking by metaphor. And the sense is: in all Moab there will be the salt and bitter waters of Nimrim; as no grass springs up there, so drought will overtake the whole province, that is, from Segor to Horonaim, from border to border. Jeremiah says the very same: The waters of Nimrim will be very bad (Jer 48:34).

15:7

According to the greatness of the work, so also their visitation: they will lead them to the torrent of the willows. For willows we read in the Hebrew ARABIM (ערבים), which can also be understood as Arabs, and can be read ORBIM (עורבים), that is, a village situated on their borders, whose inhabitants are said by many to have provided food for Elijah on Mount Horeb: a name which, because of its ambiguity, is also translated as ravens, and as the West, and as level places. And the sense is: the visitation will be according to the greatness of the disease. Take visitation here not as a remedy but as a blow. I will visit, he says, their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with stripes (Ps 88 [89]:33). The torrent of the willows understand as the rivers of Babylonia, of which David says: On the willows in the midst of it we hung up our instruments (Ps 136 [137]:2); or else as the valley of Arabia through which one passes to the Assyrians.

15:8

For the cry will go round the border of Moab, its howling as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim. Jeremiah too writes almost all the same things. And these are cities and places of the Moabites, in which the crying and wailing of the captive people is described.

15:9

For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood. Where formerly there was luxuriance because of the watered fields and the ever-flowing springs, there, because of the multitude of the slain, streams of blood will flow.

For I will set additions upon Dibon: for those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land. Lest anyone think it a fault of the scribe and, in wishing to correct an error, make one, the one city is written both with the letter M and with the letter B: of these, Dimon is interpreted as silence, Dibon as flowing. Both names having been given it because of the waters that flow silently, to this day this little town is called indifferently both Dimon and Dibon. And as for his saying: I will set additions upon Dibon, since it seemed to raise the question what these might be, he showed it in the following line, saying: For those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land: so that even those who have slipped away in flight are consumed by beasts. Although by metaphor we can also understand the lion as the king of the enemies, so that no one can escape his power, as though it were a roaring.

16:1

Send forth the Lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. What we are interpreting is not history but prophecy. And every prophecy is wrapped in enigmas, and with abrupt sentences passes, while speaking of one thing, to another: lest, if Scripture kept to order, it should be not prophecy but narrative. And the sense is: O Moab, upon whom the lion is about to rage, and from whom not even a remnant will be able to be saved, have this consolation: from you will go forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who will rule over the whole world. From the rock of the desert, that is, from Ruth, who, widowed by the death of her husband, bore Obed by Boaz, and from Obed came Jesse, and from Jesse David, and from David Christ. And the mountain of the daughter of Zion we shall interpret either as the city of Jerusalem itself, or, according to the sacred understanding, as the Church, which is set upon the summit of the virtues.

16:2

And it will be: as a bird fleeing, and young ones flying away from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. He returns to the order he had begun: When I have set, he says, a most savage lion upon those who flee from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land, to break their limbs and bones, then they will fly away in terror, and all the daughters, that is, the villages and cities of the province of Moab, will migrate at the crossing of the Arnon, which is the border of the Amorites and the Moabites. And by putting crossing here too, he signifies captivity.

16:3-4

Take counsel, call a council: make your shade like night at midday, hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My refugees will dwell with you: Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator; for the dust is at an end, the wretched one is finished, he who trampled the land has failed. For wretched one in the Hebrew one reads SOD (סד), which can also be understood as devastator. And he speaks to Moab, that it should find counsel for its safety, and, gathering its elders, convene a council for its salvation. Do you wish, he says, to be saved and to merit the mercy of God? In the clear light and the open flight of my people, be like night and shade; take in the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. And why he said this he adds at once: My refugees will dwell with you. For when Jerusalem has been laid waste, and all Judea, which borders on the Moabites, my people will migrate to you. Be therefore their hiding place, and do not fear the onslaught of the devastator, because he will quickly pass like dust; and the despoiler of the whole land, who trampled it and subjected it under his feet, will perish as a breeze blows. Some wrongly interpret this place of the Antichrist, so as to suppose that at that time the saints will cross over to the Arabs because of their nearness to the city of Jerusalem, and that the Arabs are now commanded not to betray those who flee to them.

16:5

And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. The Hebrews interpret this place thus: When the Assyrian has been put to flight, Hezekiah, a righteous man, will reign over Judah and will hold the throne of David, judging in truth the people of God subject to him. Others understand it of Christ: when the dust of the Antichrist is at an end, and the devastator who trampled the whole earth has been taken away, Christ the king will come, who will sit in the tabernacle of David, and in the day of judgment will render to all according to their works. Nor is there any doubt that this passage prophesies of Christ. But we can understand the same thing of his first coming, and show it in the tabernacle of the Church: that throughout the whole land of Moab the trophies of the Churches as they rise bear witness to the dominion of Christ.

16:6-7

We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is exceedingly proud: his pride, and his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of it will howl: to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick, tell of its wounds. Again he returns to the present, and accuses Moab of pride, because it was lifted up far more than its strength warranted; and because of this pride Moab will howl to Moab, that is, the people to the city, or the metropolis to the province, and the whole land will resound with howling over the walls of baked brick, of which Jeremiah too says: Therefore I will wail over Moab, and to all Moab I will cry out, to the men of the earthen wall, lamenting (Jer 48:31). And by these things he shows both the power of its former prosperity and the wounds of its sudden overthrow.

16:8

For the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted: the vine of Sibmah. Between Heshbon and Sibmah there are scarcely five hundred paces; and by the metaphor of the vine he signifies the devastation of the whole province.

The lords of the nations have cut down its shoots. He keeps the metaphor he had begun, showing that the kings of the nations who had laid Moab waste ravaged all its hamlets and fortresses.

They have reached as far as Jazer: they have wandered in the desert: its offshoots have been left behind: they have crossed the sea. Understand the shoots and offshoots as its people and its fugitives; and the crossing of the sea as the captivity into Babylon, about which we shall read later: The burden of the desert of the sea.

16:9

Therefore I will lament with the weeping of Jazer, the vine of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh. This is the voice of the Prophet lamenting, and attesting the greatness of the devastation by the greatness of his tears, and weeping for the vine of Jazer and of Sibmah, and for Heshbon and Elealeh, cities once most strong, cut down as the Assyrian pruned them.

For upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. Understand the treaders of the grapes, gathering in the joy of the vintage, as the armies of the enemies; and that in the very season of joy the season of captivity has come.

16:10

And joy and exultation will be taken away from Carmel. It is an idiom of the Scriptures always to liken Carmel, a rich and wooded mountain which overlooks Ptolemais and on which Elijah prayed, to fertility and abundance; and by this it signifies that all joy and fertility are to be taken away from cities once most fruitful.

And in the vineyards he will not exult, nor shout for joy. What is understood is the former vintager, that is, the husbandman of the province of Moabitis. Accordingly he immediately added:

He who used to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. By no means will the joyful vintager sing the vintage shout at the vintage; but everywhere hostile devastation and the clamor of the victors will arise.

16:11

Therefore my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inmost parts for the wall of baked brick. Lest anyone should think the Prophet's lament a sign of exultation, by which he rejoiced that the enemies of the people of Israel were captives, he says that it is out of affection, and out of the inmost grief of his heart, that he mourns the overthrow of a city once most mighty.

16:12

And it will come to pass, when it has become apparent that Moab has labored over its high places, it will enter its sanctuaries to pray, and it will not prevail. It is the last misery not to have help even in those whom it has always worshiped. Deserted, he says, by your own strength, and with all your defenders slain, you will go to the idols, you will venerate the shrines, and you will find no help in those upon whom the devastation will come together with you.

16:13

This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. From what time, do you suppose? Clearly from the time when Moab was created. And the Lord says: The Moabites and the Ammonites shall not enter into the Church of God (Deut 23:3). Or we may understand from that time as of ancient time: that these things were decreed long ago by the divine sentence; not that the foreknowledge of God brought about the cause of the devastation, but that the future devastation was known beforehand to the majesty of God.

16:14

And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away, above all its great people, and it will be left small and slight, by no means many. This prophecy, as we said above, is directed against the Moabites after the death of Ahaz, in the reign of Hezekiah, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity by Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. So, just as a hireling waits for the setting of the sun, and day and night looks for the end of his work so as to receive his fixed wage, so too after three years Moab will be destroyed when the Assyrian comes, and scarcely a few will be left in the land to inhabit the overthrown cities and to till the deserted fields. It can also be a prediction about the Babylonian captivity: that after Jerusalem had been taken and three years had passed, Moab was to be laid waste by the Chaldeans; or else that within the space of three years no rest was to be given them.

17:1

The burden of Damascus: Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city, and it will be like a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks, and they will rest there, and there will be none to frighten them. And help will cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. After Babylon and the Philistines and Moab, the discourse turns to Damascus, that is, Aram, which itself was once a royal city too, and held the primacy in all Syria: Antioch and Laodicea and Apamea were not yet flourishing, cities which we know to have grown after Alexander and the empire of the Macedonians. Because, then, it always gave help to the ten tribes against Judah, as the history of Kings and Chronicles relates, he signifies that devastation by the Assyrians is drawing near to them too, as the king of the Assyrians says: I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria. For as I have taken them, and all kingdoms, I will take you too. And in the volume of Kings we read: The king of the Assyrians went up to Damascus, and took it, and carried it away to Cyrene (2 Kgs 16:9). He also slew Rezin, who was king of Damascus: all of which it suffered while Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem. Behold, he says, Damascus will cease to be a city: already captivity is near, already the Assyrian has set his army in motion. And it will be like a heap of stones in ruin, so that only broken walls and traces of its former power are to be seen in the vastness of the ruins. The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks. Aroer means tamarisk, which is properly a tree that grows in the wilderness and in salty soil; and by this the devastation is shown. They will rest there: the flocks is understood; and there will be none to frighten them. For the solitude will be so great that not even a robber lying in wait is to be feared. And help will cease from Ephraim: by no means will the ten tribes have help in it against Judah. And the kingdom from Damascus: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [from the common or popular edition] will cease is understood. But when he says that the kingdom ceases and rests, he does not signify a perpetual devastation, but takes away for the present the power by which it formerly reigned in all Syria. And the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As, he says, the ten tribes were destroyed when the Assyrian ravaged them, and all their glory was led into captivity, so the few who remain in Damascus will imitate them, and will have the glory of their allied nation. Take glory as said by irony, for ignominy. And all this will happen because the Lord has spoken, whose words cannot be made void. Some think that this prophecy is the same as the one we read in Jeremiah: Damascus is dissolved, it has turned to flight, trembling has seized it, anguish and pains have held it like a woman in labor (Jer 49:24, 27). And again: I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it will devour the ramparts of Ben-hadad. But it must be known that Jeremiah describes the Babylonian captivity of the city of Damascus, that is, of the few whom the king of the Assyrians had left in it; whereas Isaiah announces the captivity by the Assyrians that is close at hand. Others suppose that the Roman captivity is foretold, since the people of the Jews too was taken captive, and Damascus, over which Aretas ruled, endured a like servitude: so that all that is written about it is to be transferred to the time of Christ and to the mysteries of the Apostles.

17:4

And it will come to pass in that day, the glory of Jacob will be made thin, and the fat of his flesh will waste away. When, he says, Damascus has been taken and has ceased to be a city, and such glory has crowned it as crowned Israel, that is, the ten tribes, then all the defense, and the fattest flesh, and the refuge of Jacob will waste away: for by no means will he have allies to join with him in laying Jerusalem waste. We have read above that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, and that it was announced to the house of David: Syria has rested upon Ephraim; of whom the Prophet speaks to Ahaz: Do not fear, and let not your heart be afraid of these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the wrath of the fury of Rezin king of Syria and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah have taken most evil counsel against you.

17:5-6

And it will be like one gathering in the harvest what has remained, and his arm will gather the ears: and it will be like one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there will be left in it as it were a cluster, and as at the shaking of an olive tree two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five on its topmost boughs, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. Those who understand the present devastation of Damascus as under the Roman empire maintain that these words signify the Apostles: that just as a few ears and olives are wont to remain in the field or on the trees, so the remnant of Israel is saved; especially since there follows: In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, that is, to Christ. The two olives, and three, and four, and five they interpret as fourteen Apostles: that is, the twelve who were chosen, and a thirteenth, James, who is called the brother of the Lord, and also Paul the Apostle, the vessel of election (Acts 9:15). But those who think that what was said was fulfilled in the times of the Assyrians would have it understood thus: that under the Assyrian captivity Damascus was not entirely destroyed, but, when some had been carried away to Cyrene, another part of the tillers of the land was left behind, which itself was afterwards destroyed when the Babylonian laid it waste; until under the Macedonians and the Ptolemies it was restored again, and at the coming of Christ it was indeed a city, but not of such power as it had been before. And the sense is: as few will remain in Damascus as the few ears that commonly remain after the reapers, which the poor are wont to glean in the very broad and very rich valley of Rephaim; or the few olives on the olive tree that have escaped the diligence of the gatherer.

17:7-8

In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. And he will not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought: and they will not look to the groves and the shrines. They think that this was fulfilled in the times of Christ, when, the kingdom of Damascus having been destroyed, the everlasting empire of the Savior succeeded, and the error of idolatry was diminished. The intention of these interpreters is indeed pious, but it does not keep the order of the history. We, however, say that, when Damascus had been overthrown and the ten tribes had been led away to the Assyrians, those who were left of the tribes that belonged to Israel turned, at Hezekiah's letters, to the worship of God, and came to the temple at Jerusalem, as the history of Chronicles relates (2 Chr 30). When Damascus has been destroyed, therefore, men will turn to their maker, that is, to him who created them, and their eyes will look by no means to the idols which they had made in Bethel and in Dan, but to God, despising the shrines and altars which their fingers had wrought.

17:9

In that day the cities of its strength will be abandoned like ploughs, and the crops that were abandoned before the face of the sons of Israel, and it will be deserted. He does not say this against Damascus, but against the ten tribes, which were called Israel: that just as, at the coming of the people of God out of Egypt, all the nations that inhabited the land of promise, struck with sudden terror, abandoned their ploughs and the heaps of grain and their work half done, seeking safety in their feet, so the land of Israel too should remain desolate for a long time. Hence I wonder that for ploughs and heaps of grain Aquila chose to translate potsherd and Emir; Symmachus, forest and Amir; the Seventy, the Amorites and the Hivites. Theodotion alone set down the Hebrew word, ARS ET EMIR: which among them is read more correctly HORES (חרש) ET AMIR (והאמיר), that is, ploughshares and heaps of crops.

17:10

Because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. These things, he says, you will suffer, O Israel, because you have abandoned God your Savior, who freed you from Egypt, who subjected hostile nations to you: and you have not remembered your helper.

Therefore you will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot. This is to be read more pointedly and as irony. Because, he says, you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper: will you on that account have to plant a faithful planting, and not rather sow a foreign shoot, for the enemy to snatch away? Or certainly thus: my sons, who were begotten from the stock of my people, you have established in the land for this purpose, that you might make them foreign and most wicked.

17:11

In the day of your planting, wild grapes, and in the morning your seed will flower. The harvest has been taken away in the day of inheritance, and it will grieve grievously. These, he says, are the fruits of your works that you will reap: your vine of Sorek will degenerate into wild grapes, your seed will hold out hope in the blade; but when ripeness has come, it will be reaped by another. And then you will grieve grievously, when you lose what you hoped for and almost already held.

17:12, 14

Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the multitude of the roaring sea: and the tumult of crowds, like the sound of many waters: the peoples will roar like the sound of flooding waters: and he will rebuke him, and he will flee far off: and he will be snatched away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the storm. At eventide: and behold, confusion in the morning, and he will not endure. This is the portion of those who have laid us waste, and the lot of those who plunder us. Those who suppose that the earlier captivity of Damascus was brought on by the Romans refer this also that is written: Man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, to the times of Christ and of the Apostles. And what follows as well: You will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot: in the day of your planting, wild grapes, and the rest, they take to concern the unbelief of the Jews. And this passage which we have now set out they interpret of the heathen, who persecute the Church. What follows too, He will rebuke him, and he will flee far off, they take of the devil, showing by a tropological interpretation the devastation of the persecutors and of the demons. But we follow the order we have begun, and cover historical foundations with a historical roof. Woe, he says, to all the nations that have made war against my people, whose onslaught was so great that it must be likened to the waves of the sea. But when they have come raging and have flooded my land, then their prince Sennacherib will flee from him, rebuked; and as dust is scattered when the wind snatches it, and a whirlwind is rolled on high in a storm, so he will indeed approach Jerusalem, besieging it, but he will be struck by the Angel; he will come in the morning, and will see the army of his power destroyed. And this will be the portion of those who have laid us waste. The Prophet says this either in the person of the people, or joining himself to his nation (2 Kgs 19:35-36). Afterwards we read: The Angel of the Lord went out, and struck in the camp of the Assyrians one hundred and eighty-five thousand: and they arose in the morning, and behold, all were the corpses of the dead. And Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went out, and departed, and returned, and dwelt in Nineveh.

18:1

Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. The Hebrew word SELSEL (צלצל), which Symmachus interpreted as sound and Theodotion as birds, we have rendered as cymbal. Aquila translated double shadow. But it must be known that a shadow is called SEL (צל), and here the syllable itself is doubled. From this we can understand the saying thus: Woe to the land that promises help in the shadow of its wings. And whereas Scripture says: He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven (Ps 90 [91]:1), for which in the Hebrew is written, He will abide in the shadow of the Almighty, this land, boasting that it has the very likeness of God, promises, though itself set in dangers, to give support to others. And it signifies either No, the city of Egypt which is now called Alexandria, or Egypt, on which Jerusalem always leaned as on a shaken reed, which, when it breaks, pierces the hand of the one who leans on it. And here the order is most beautiful: that just as in the former Vision the prophetic word threatened Damascus, because the ten tribes had help in it, asking God's mercy, so now too devastation is foretold to Egypt, for the sake of whose help the invocation of God was neglected. For this is the land which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, that is, beyond the streams of the river Nile, which no one doubts flows from Ethiopia into Egypt. Egypt can be called the cymbal of wings because of the swiftness of its crops: for the swift and rapid flight of birds gives back the sound of a cymbal. Some, from what follows: Who sends envoys by sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters, understand the Roman empire, and refer the whole history to the times of Vespasian and Titus, by whom Jerusalem was overthrown. But it does not accord with our faith that the Lord should threaten the Roman empire for having overthrown an impious nation, and then say that gifts are to be brought to Mount Zion; unless perhaps we take these things too spiritually, of the Church.

18:2

Who sends envoys by sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters. Go, swift messengers, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a terrible people, after whom there is no other, to a nation waiting and trampled down, whose land the rivers have plundered. Among the Hebrews Egypt, and the Egyptian, and the Egyptians are all called by one word, MESRAIM (מצרים). Let this be said lest anyone stick at the word when he finds the masculine in place of the feminine, that is, the man in place of the land; for now too it is said: Who sends envoys by sea, that is, Mesraim herself, the Egyptian himself: because from Alexandria, which was then, as we have said, called No, envoys were sent to Jerusalem, and, in vessels of papyrus, that is, in letters, or else in ships, promising them their help, they said: Go swiftly to the Jews' convulsed nation, torn by the attack of the Assyrians: to a people once terrible, which enjoyed the command of God, to whose power no other is to be compared: to a nation which always waited for the help of God, and nevertheless is trampled down by men: whose land the rivers, that is, various kings, have ravaged. Others, however, think that the apostrophe is directed to the Lord, and that the sense is: O God, who send the Prophets into the sea of this world, and, admonishing the people through letters as if by men under sail, command your messengers: Go swiftly to my nation, torn and convulsed, to a most mighty people, which was once a terror to all the nations round about, which always waited for the help of God, and, because of the greatness of its sins, does not deserve to receive what it hopes for: whose land the kings of various nations have laid waste, and the rest that follows. Eusebius of Caesarea, promising a historical interpretation in his title, wanders off into various senses; and when I read his books, I found something very different from what he promised in the heading. For wherever the history fails him, he passes over to allegory, and joins together things so far apart that I marvel at his combining stone and iron into one body by a new architecture of speech. I have given this brief warning lest anyone think that we have borrowed what we say from his springs; for in the present passage too he says that the prophecy is directed against the Jews and Jerusalem, because at the beginning of the Christian faith they sent letters to all the nations that they should not accept the passion of Christ, and sent them as far as Ethiopia and the Western region, and filled the whole world with the spreading of this blasphemy.

18:3

All you inhabitants of the world who dwell on the earth, when the signal has been raised on the mountains, you will see, and you will hear the blast of the trumpet. All you nations round about, he says, when you hear my command like a signal raised on the mountains, and my order like the blast of a trumpet resounding on high, then you will see what I have commanded.

18:4

For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will consider in my place. What is it that the Lord spoke to the Prophet? What follows: until the things I have commanded come about, I will rest in my seat: as the Jews think, in the Temple; as we think, in the heavens. And I will consider, he says, what end of things is coming.

As the noonday light is clear, and as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest. Just as in the whole day nothing is clearer than noon, when the sun glows from mid-heaven and lights up the whole world alike; and just as in the heat and scorching warmth, when the naked reaper is baked and his panting attests the greatness of his labor, the coolness of the dew is most welcome, if the morning moisture makes the dry stalks easy to cut: so my word, which I will consider in my place, will come welcome to all who believe in me.

18:5-6

For before the harvest it has wholly blossomed, and an unripe perfection has budded, and its little branches will be cut off with pruning hooks, and what is left will be cut away and shaken off. And they will be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth, and the birds will be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts of the earth will winter upon it. Because he had spoken of noon, and had mentioned beforehand a cloud of dew in summer and harvest, and had taken his metaphor from husbandry, he keeps it in the rest, describing the pride of Egypt and the devastation of its people, and the corpses throughout the whole province which are to be devoured by birds. For as crops that burst forth before ripeness quickly perish, and, budding before the fullness of their time comes, are useless, so, he says, the peoples of Egypt will be cut off with pruning hooks like useless branches, and all the offshoots will be stripped bare. And lest you should think he speaks of a vine and not of men, he turns the metaphor into the truth of history: And they will be left, he says, together to the birds of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth. For birds and beasts devour not the cut branches of trees, but corpses. Let us read Ezekiel more fully, where he prophesies against Pharaoh and against Egypt, and we shall find all these things written most plainly (Ezek 29). And when he says: The birds will be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts will winter upon it, he either truly signifies the multitude of the slain, or shows through the same metaphor that it is to be laid waste by all the nations.

18:7

At that time a gift will be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn away and torn apart, from a terrible people, after whom there has been no other: from a nation waiting, waiting and trampled down, whose land the rivers have plundered, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion. After the devastation of Egypt and the destruction of its empire, Israel will by no means trust in the vanity of its shadow, but will return to the Lord, and will bring its gifts to Mount Zion, that is, to his temple, entreating him alone, whose protection is true and eternal. And we understand this to have been done under Zerubbabel and Joshua, and Ezra and Nehemiah. The Seventy, for what we have said, waiting, waiting, where in the Hebrew is written hoping, hoping, translated to the contrary ἀνέλπιστον, that is, not hoping. And for this reason they gave Eusebius occasion to think that this is to be understood of the nations, which have neither hope, nor the Testament of God, nor the Prophets, rather than of the Jews: that gifts were afterwards to be sent by them to the Church, which is set upon a watchtower, and spiritual victims offered.

19:1

The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the images of Egypt will be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt will waste away in its midst. It is the custom of the Scriptures to append plain things to obscure ones, and to bring out in open speech what they had first said in enigmas. Hence in the present place too, because he had threatened Egypt: Woe to the land that overshadows with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and the rest that the prophetic discourse wove together, he now makes the understanding plainer, and speaks with threats to Egypt itself: that not through angels but the Lord himself comes upon a light cloud, that is, a swift one, and enters Egypt, and the idols of Egypt tremble, and the heart of the strong wastes away, and the prophecy of Ezekiel is fulfilled: I will destroy the images, and I will make the idols cease from Memphis (Ezek 30:13). Some refer this whole prophecy to the times of the Savior, when he entered upon a light cloud, that is, the human body which he had taken from the Virgin, weighed down by no seed of human intercourse; or that he was carried by a light cloud, that is, by the virginal body, and at his entry all the demons trembled, and then came the first ruin of the idols, unable to bear the presence of the Lord.

19:2

And I will make Egyptians rush against Egyptians, and a man will fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. When the Lord has entered Egypt and destroys a most powerful nation by his presence, the first victory will be that Egyptians fall out with Egyptians and fight one another with rebellious hatred: which, it is clear, came about in the times of the Assyrians and of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, some sitting still and others resisting. And that he foretells these things of the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah is witness, saying: Egypt is a choice and beautiful heifer; a goader will come to her from the North. And again: The daughter of Egypt has been put to shame, and delivered into the hand of the people of the North (Jer 46:20, 24). Ezekiel too, agreeing with equal authority of prophecy: And I will make the multitude of Egypt cease, he says, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. And again: I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I will put my sword into his hand, and I will break the arms of Pharaoh. And they will know that I am the Lord, when I have put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he has stretched it out over the land of Egypt, and I will scatter Egypt among the nations (Ezek 30:10, 24ff.). But if we refer these things to the times of the Savior, let us take this example from the Gospel: Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth: I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his neighbor, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies will be those of his own household (Matt 10:34ff.). And again in another place: Two will be divided against three, and three against two: father against son, and mother against daughter, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law (Luke 12:52-53).

19:3

And the spirit of Egypt will be broken in its inward parts, and I will cast down its counsel: and they will consult their images and their diviners, and those with pythonic spirits, and the soothsayers. When sedition has arisen in Egypt, some desiring to serve the Babylonian, others unwilling to submit their necks to his yoke; or else some believing in Christ, and others resisting, the spirit of Egypt will be broken and torn apart, since not all wish the same things, and all their counsel will be brought to nothing. Then they will go to their images; and they will ask the diviners, and the soothsayers, and the seers, and those schooled in the magic arts, why these things have happened.

19:4

And I will deliver Egypt into the hand of cruel masters, and a mighty king will rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts. We follow a twofold understanding: either of the Chaldean times, when Egypt was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar; or of the Roman empire, when, after Antony and Cleopatra had been overcome, Augustus Caesar subjugated Egypt. That the Babylonians were cruel all Scripture testifies: they did not spare little ones, and wounded them with their darts, and had no pity on pregnant women. And that the Roman kingdom was most mighty the Scripture of Daniel also testifies (Dan 7), setting forth the fourth beast, which has teeth and claws of iron.

19:5, 7

And the water will dry up from the sea, and the river will be desolated and dried up, and the streams will fail; the channels of the embankments will be diminished and dried up. The reed and the rush will wither, the bed of the stream will be laid bare from its source, and every watered sowing will be dried up, will wither, and will be no more. It is natural that, when captivity has come through the wrath of God, pestilence should follow upon his indignation, and all the elements together should rage against those who have offended God. Hence it is written in another Prophet (Jer 12) that both the birds in the air and the fish in the waters fail, so that all things are withdrawn from human use. This we say if we choose to take it simply of a drought of the river Nile and its streams. But if by metaphor: in the river we understand the kingdom, and in the streams its leaders; and in the greenery, the rush and the papyrus the whole abundance of Egypt, so that through these things the riches of Egypt are described, in which Egypt is most fertile. Let us read Ezekiel, where King Pharaoh is described as a great dragon dwelling in the rivers, and he says: The river is mine, and I made myself. And he hears: I will put a bridle in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers stick to your scales, and I will draw you out of the midst of your rivers, and all your fish will cling to your scales, and I will cast you into the desert (Ezek 29:3-4). At the coming of Christ, however, all these things are to be understood τροπικῶς, in keeping with what we read above: The Lord will make the sea of Egypt desert. And again: The Lord will lay his hand upon the violent river of Egypt, and will strike it in seven valleys, so that one may pass over it with shod feet: namely, that all the error of the Egyptian waters, and the evil arts by which they deluded the peoples subject to them, are dried up at the coming of Christ. And as for his saying: The water will dry up from the sea, we can also take it historically: that what is signified is not the great sea, but Lake Mareotis, because Scripture calls all gatherings of waters seas. These things can also be understood as said hyperbolically. And what follows: The bed of the stream will be laid bare from its source, describes the stream and the source drying up together.

19:8, 10

And the fishermen will mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river will lament, and those who spread a net upon the face of the water will waste away. And those who work flax will be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine things: and its watered places will be withered: all who made pools for catching fish. Take this too in two ways: that when Egypt has been laid waste and the whole province dried up with drought, the fishermen mourn, and those who used to cast a hook into the river lament, and those who worked nets and dragnets and wove little vessels of various kinds out of rush, that is, the princes and those of royal stock, and the rulers; and that at the coming of Christ all the fishermen of a perverse kind, who, contrary to the apostolic discipline, caught men for perdition, and with a foolish wisdom wove nets and dragnets in which to ensnare the lost, were confounded, and that there is no such fisherman, or a rare one, in the land of Egypt. We see this fulfilled in fact, in that the trophies of the Churches are rising, and throughout Egypt the idols have fallen.

19:11, 13

The princes of Tanis are foolish; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel: how will you say to Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where now are your wise men? Let them announce to you and show what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools, the princes of Memphis have withered: they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples. That Tanis was the metropolis of Egypt the Psalmist also declares, because Moses worked there the many signs which are described in Exodus: He set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis (Ps 77 [78]:43). That Memphis too was given over to the magic arts, the traces of its old error show to the present time. And this is briefly indicated: that when the Babylonian devastation came, all the counsels of the Magi and of those who promised knowledge of the future were convicted of folly; and that at the coming of Christ all were brought to nothing, since the seers of Egypt could find no counsel how to suppress the Christian doctrine. It is an idiom of the Scriptures to put corner for kingdom, because it holds the peoples together, and is, as it were, the strongest part of the whole house. Hence Christ too, who holds together the walls of the two peoples, is called the corner stone (Eph 2).
