And his adding: How will you say to Pharaoh, I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings, signifies that the Egyptians feign heroes and gods as the founders of their race: Horus, and Isis, and Osiris, and Typhon.

19:14-15

The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of giddiness: and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man errs and vomits: and Egypt will have no work to do, head and tail, bending and bridling. Let us speak first of the translation, and afterwards we shall discuss what is written. For spirit of giddiness one can also translate spirit of error. In what we have translated, bending and bridling, we can also say bent and wanton, so that we understand the old man and the boy. For we, while translating what is written in haste, misled by its ambiguity, rendered the Hebrew word AGMON (אגמון) as bridling, which Aquila translated more expressively στρεβλοῦντα, that is, one who does nothing rightly but everything perversely, so as to signify a boy. The sense, then, is: The princes of Tanis have become fools, and the wise counselors have given Pharaoh foolish counsel, and the princes of Memphis have withered, and they have deceived Egypt, the corner of the peoples, because the Lord has mingled in them a spirit of error and giddiness, so that they do not know what they are saying, and make Egypt err. And as a drunken man, vomiting, brings up what he had taken in, and does not know where he is, but lies out of his mind: so Egypt will have no work or counsel that has either a head or an end, or that suits either the old or the young, of whom the former, through excess of age, are foolish and rave, and the latter, through wantonness and infancy, do not know what they are doing. And whether you wish to take this of the Babylonian devastation or of the coming of Christ, both according to the letter and according to the spiritual understanding, it will hold together.

19:16-17

In that day Egypt will be like women, and they will be astonished and afraid before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he will shake over it. And the land of Judah will be a festival to Egypt: everyone who remembers it will tremble before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has devised against it. I think it better even to censure one's own error than, while blushing to confess one's inexperience, to persist in error. In what I translated, And the land of Judah will be a festival to Egypt, for festival one reads in the Hebrew AGGA (חגה), which can be interpreted both as festival (whence Haggai too is rendered festive) and as fear; this Aquila translated more expressively γύρωσιν, as when someone, afraid and trembling, casts his eyes about and dreads the approaching enemy. If, then, we choose to take it in a good sense, that the remembrance of Judah is a joy to Egypt, it is rightly called a festival. But if, as I judge, festival is turned into fear, let us understand dread or terror: that when Nebuchadnezzar has come, and all the hands of the brave men have been loosened like those of women, even the name of Judah is a terror to Egypt, because, in wishing to bring it help, it has suffered such great evils. Concerning our own times no one doubts that, in comparison with the Christians, all the heathen are like women, holding feeble opinions, and that whatever they say is turned into folly, while they are astonished at so great a conversion of the nation, and marvel at and understand the hand of the Lord; and whoever of the Gentiles remembers the Christian name confesses with fear the weakness of idolatry.

19:18

In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan, and swearing by the Lord of hosts: one will be called the city of the sun. For city of the sun the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated asedec, which one of our writers interprets as city of righteousness; and, led astray by error, because according to the Hebrew ARES (חרס) is written, he thinks it means earth, which is written with other letters. Symmachus, then, translated better: one will be called the city of the sun; for ARES, an ambiguous word, means both potsherd and sun, because both are parched and dry. Onias, not understanding this place, built a temple in Egypt in the town of Ἡλιοπόλεως. Read the Histories of Josephus (Josephus, book 12, chapter 9). Others would have Ares, that is, ὄστρακον, that is, potsherd, understood as the city of Ostracine, and the other cities near Rhinocorura and Casium, which, it is clear, speak to this day in Egypt the Canaanite tongue, that is, Syriac; and they think that Syrians and Arabs from the neighborhood were transported into that land by Nebuchadnezzar. Further, those who expound the prophecy of the coming of Christ and of the Roman empire take the five cities either as the law of the Lord, which was first translated in Alexandria, or as the five orders of the Church: bishops, presbyters, deacons, the faithful, catechumens; or certainly as the spiritual understanding of the law, of which the Apostle too says: I would speak five words in the Churches with my understanding, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue (1 Cor 14); and they take it that one of the five cities is called the city of the sun, namely of righteousness, in whose wings is healing.

19:19, 21

In that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and an inscription to the Lord at its border. And it will be for a sign and for a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they will cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior and a defender to free them. And the Lord will be known by Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day, and will worship him with victims and gifts, and will vow vows to the Lord and pay them. From this place to the end of the Egyptian Vision, or Burden, both the Jews and our writers would have it understood of the coming of Christ; but they put off their hopes into the future, while we hold them as already accomplished. Take day for time: although Josephus maintains that these things were done under Onias, who, fleeing into Egypt with a very great crowd of Jews, built a temple and an altar, and with vain rashness tried to fulfill the prophecy of Christ. But one altar is spoken of in the way that there is one faith, and one baptism, and one Church. And an inscription to the Lord at its border: there is no doubt that this signifies the Gospel and the writings of the Apostles. For just as above, according to the tropological understanding, the land of Judah, fearful or festal to Egypt, is understood as the Old Testament, so too the inscription at the borders of Egypt is shown to be the history of the Gospels. Next he adds: And it will be for a sign and for a testimony, namely of the Lord's passion. Then those who have believed, when Egyptians rush against Egyptians, and a man fights against his brother, and city battles against city, when the time of persecution has broken upon them, will implore the mercy of the Lord, and at once the Savior will come, that is, Jesus, for that is what it means in our language. And the Lord will be known by the Egyptians, and they will know him, whether the persecutors who have been overcome, or the believers set free by his present help. And they will worship him with victims and gifts, and will vow vows to the Lord and pay them. Let the Jews answer: It is commanded in the Law that no altar be made except in the one place which the Lord God has chosen, and that victims be sacrificed only by priests of the Levitical race (Deut 26). Behold, Isaiah teaches openly that the Egyptians know the Lord and worship him, and offer victims and gifts, and vow vows and pay them. If the Egyptians have a priesthood, the testimony of Paul is fulfilled in them as well, who says: When the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law (Heb 7:12).

19:22

And the Lord will strike Egypt with a blow, and will heal it: and they will turn to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them, and will heal them. For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. Persecution serves not for the denial of believers, but for their proving and their crown.

19:23

In that day there will be a road from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian will enter Egypt, and the Egyptian the Assyrians: and the Egyptians will serve Assyria. Before the coming of Christ each nation had its own king, and no one could go from one nation to another; but in the Roman empire all things have been made one. Let the learned reader turn over the ancient histories, and he will find that the whole region from the Euphrates to the Tigris, and all between, belonged to the Assyrians. Those, therefore, whom the ancients called Assyrians we now call Syrians, naming the whole from the part. And when it is said: The Egyptians will serve the Syrians, it is to be taken either thus: that Roman legions furnished with Syrian soldiers guard Egypt; or that the two nations trade with each other, and the cities of Syria receive the abundance of Egypt, just as, conversely, Egypt is watered with the goods of Palestine and Phoenicia. Some of our writers wrongly refer these things to the thousand years, and in the Jewish manner declare that they will come to pass at the consummation of the world, when the Antichrist, coming from the Assyrians, has taken possession of Egypt and Ethiopia.

19:24-25

In that day Israel will be the third with the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands to the Assyrian: but my inheritance is Israel. By no means will Israel be crushed in the middle between Egypt and the Assyrian, now with the Antiochi and Demetrii dragging the kingdom of Judah to themselves, now with the Ptolemies claiming its possession for themselves; but it too, established under the Roman empire, and through this under the empire of Christ, will be of the same condition as Egypt and the Assyrians, and will be blessed in all the earth. For out of Zion will go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. Then it will be said by the Lord: Blessed is my people of Egypt: when, led not by Moses but by Christ the Lord, countless thousands of men have filled the deserts and, with Pharaoh drowned, have said in the desert: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified: horse and rider he has cast into the sea (Exod 15:1). Then also the work of the hands of the Lord will be among the Assyrians; for these nations above all, Egypt and Mesopotamia, flourish with swarms of monks, and vie with one another in equal piety. And the inheritance of Christ is Israel, that is, the places of his nativity, and of his cross, and of his resurrection and ascension, to which men flock from the whole world.

20:1

In the year in which Tartan came into Azotus, when Sargon king of the Assyrians had sent him, and he had fought against Azotus and taken it. At that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah son of Amos, saying: Go and loose the sackcloth from your loins, and take your shoes from your feet: and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. And the Lord said: As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, a sign and portent of three years will be upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia. So will the king of the Assyrians drive off the captivity of Egypt and the exile of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. And they will be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their hope, and of Egypt their glory. And the inhabitant of this island will say in that day: Behold, this was our hope, those to whom we fled for help, to free us from the face of the king of the Assyrians; and how shall we be able to escape? We have set down the whole content of this passage so that we may discuss each point part by part. Azotus, which in Hebrew is called ESDOD (אשדוד), was a most powerful city of Palestine, one of the five cities: Sargon king of the Assyrians, who is called by seven names, sent the commander of his army, whose name was Tartan, and took it and held it. At the time, then, when the neighboring city was taken, Isaiah is commanded to lay aside his tunic of sackcloth (for this was the garb of the prophet lamenting the sins of the people), and the shoes from his feet, which the Seventy call caligae, and to go about naked and barefoot, presenting a type of the captivity of the Egyptians and of the Ethiopians, who had been a help to the Egyptians: that just as Isaiah walked naked and displayed his unsightliness to the onlookers with bare buttocks, so all Egypt and Ethiopia, when the Assyrian ravaged them, should become naked, and nothing at all should remain in the land. And let no one think this contrary to the prosperity promised above to the Egyptians: for there, after the evils, future blessedness is foretold; whereas here the present captivity is narrated, in which, having destroyed Israel and Damascus and the Philistines, he went straight on to Egypt, and overcame them and the Ethiopians alike. And lest this seem doubtful to anyone, let us set down the testimony of Isaiah himself: And Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah: for he had heard that he had set out from Lachish: and he heard men saying of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia: He has come out to fight against you (2 Kgs 19:8-9). And at the same time we learn the obedience of the prophets: that a man of noble birth (for the Hebrews relate that Isaiah was the father-in-law of Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah) did not blush to go about naked, but, judging nothing more honorable than the commands of God, laid aside the sackcloth, and when it was thrown off he was naked, having had before only one tunic, and that of haircloth. And when it is said: A sign and portent of three years will be upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia, this signifies that Egypt and Ethiopia were to be laid waste by the Assyrians for three years. Then, he says, the inhabitant of this island will say, that is, Jerusalem, which is beaten by the waves of the neighboring nations: Was this our hope? And did we flee to these to give us help, who could not rescue themselves from the evil of captivity? This, then, is the order of the providence of God, who disposes the whole race of men by his ineffable judgment. Against the wrath of God Israel hoped in Damascus: let the city be destroyed which, against his will, gives help to the impious. Judah hoped in the Egyptians: let Egypt too be destroyed. The Egyptians trusted in the Ethiopians: let the Ethiopians too be conquered by the Assyrians. The Assyrians grew proud, thinking the victory to be not God's but their own strength's: let them too be conquered by the Babylonians. Babylon lifted up its head against God: let it too be overcome by the Medes and Persians. The Persians and Medes in part persecuted the people of God, and the most savage ram tossed all the peoples toward the East and the West: let the he-goat Alexander come and trample him under his feet. And let him who was lifted up beyond measure perish by poison, and his kingdom be divided into parts; and when it has long been dashed against itself, let it be ravaged as the Roman conquers. The Roman himself has torn the flesh of the saints with iron teeth and claws and with bloody mouth: let a stone be cut from the mountain without hands, and let it crush like potsherds the kingdom that was first most mighty and of iron, and then brittle and weak (Dan 2).

21:1

The burden of the desert of the sea. If I did not read in what follows in this chapter: Babylon, my beloved, has become a wonder to me; and again: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground; and above: Go up, Elam, and besiege, O Mede, I would be in doubt what this Burden is that is laid upon the desert of the sea. It is plain, therefore, that Babylon is called the desert of the sea, as Jeremiah says in the person of God: And I will make her sea desert, and I will dry up her land, and Babylon will become heaps of sand (Jer 51:36-37). And it is called sea because of the multitude of its inhabitants. Hence above, too, the multitude of Egypt was compared to the sea: The Lord will make the sea of Egypt desert. And that the Medes and Persians fought against Babylon and overthrew it, we read in the aforesaid Jeremiah: Sharpen the arrows, fill the quivers. The Lord will rouse the spirit of the kings of the Medes, and his mind is against Babylon, to destroy it, for it is the vengeance of the Lord, the vengeance of his Temple. Upon the walls of Babylon lift up a signal, strengthen the watch, set up watchmen, prepare ambushes: for the Lord has purposed, and has done all that he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon. And again: Lift up a signal in the land, sound the trumpet among the nations, sanctify the nations against her, proclaim against her to the kings of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, number Tapsar against her, bring up the horse like the stinging locust. Sanctify the nations against her, the kings of Media, its leaders and all its magistrates, and all the land of its dominion. And the land will be shaken and troubled, because the thought of the Lord has kept watch against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon desert and uninhabitable (Jer 51:11ff.).

21:1-2

As whirlwinds come from the southwest, it comes from the desert, from a terrible land. A hard vision has been announced to me. The voice of the Babylonian people in fear is brought in, or of Babylon itself, because it hears that the Medes and Elamites are preparing an army against it and are coming from the wilderness; and it sets forth an example by way of comparison. As, it says, a violent storm usually comes from the southwest wind, so devastation comes upon me from the wilderness, from a terrible land, whose very name I cannot hear without dread. A hard vision has been announced to me: for what is harder than captivity at hand?

He who is unbelieving acts faithlessly: and he who is a despoiler lays waste. In the Hebrew it can be read thus: You who slay, slay; and you who lay waste, lay waste, so that the prophetic utterance is directed to the Elamite and the Mede himself, urging him to accomplish what he has begun, to go up fearlessly, to besiege the most mighty city. But if it is read as we have translated, as though spoken of a third person, he who is unbelieving acts faithlessly: and he who is a despoiler lays waste, it is to be joined with what precedes, in which Babylon declares that a hard vision has been announced to it.

Go up, Elam, besiege, O Mede: I have made all its groaning cease. Do not fear, he says, O Persian and Mede, the multitude of Babylon; do not dread its past power: I have made to cease all its groaning and the weight with which it used to oppress you before; either because no one now groans and grieves, oppressed by the power of Babylon; or because Babylon itself is oppressed by such great evils that it does not even have freedom to groan.

21:3-4

Therefore my loins are filled with pain: anguish has possessed me, like the anguish of a woman giving birth: I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw. My heart has withered, darkness has stupefied me. Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me. The Prophets are obscure for this reason, that the persons in them change very often. So now too the voice of Isaiah is brought in, lamenting Babylon in the prophetic spirit: that such great evils are to come upon it that he who tells of them, overcome by fear, cannot burst out into words, seeing the blood of so great a multitude shed; and, moved by the feeling of pity (for he is a man speaking of men), he grieves no less than a woman is wont to howl in childbirth; but, troubled and trembling, and falling to the ground, with his eyes darkened, he does not know what he is saying. And for what we have rendered: Babylon, my beloved, in the Hebrew one reads NESEPH ESCI (נשף השקי); and it is the very word which we set down at the beginning of the Babylonian Burden, upon a misty mountain: for there Neseph is written for misty or dark. And this city is properly so called because of its height and the summit of its pride raised up to heaven.

21:5

Set the table, watch in the watchtower those eating and drinking: arise, princes, seize the shield. This place is taken in two ways. O Medes and Elamites, to whom I said above: Go up, Elam, besiege, O Mede, take food, prepare yourselves for the coming battle, lest, when the time of fighting has come, weariness hold you back. And when you have eaten and drunk, arise, seize your arms, vanquish the Babylonian. And his saying, watch in the watchtower, is read in this sense: look out diligently for what is to come. It can also be understood thus: O Babylon, prepare a table and a banquet for Belshazzar your king, son of Evil-merodach, grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and see what happens after the meal, at which he will drink toasts to harlots and concubines from the vessels of the Lord. O princes, who recline at table with the king (and he means the Medes and Persians), arise and seize your arms to kill the king. We learn this more fully in the volume of Daniel (Dan 5).

21:6ff.

For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and let him announce whatever he sees. And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel. And he gazed diligently with much attention, and the lion cried out: Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day, and upon my watch I stand whole nights. Behold, there comes this rider, a man of the two-horsed chariot; and he answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground. My threshing, and son of my threshing floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you. He gives the reasons for the fear above: why anguish possessed him like a woman in labor, and he fell down on hearing, and was terrified and surrounded with dark horror. Thus, he says, the Lord said to me: Go and appoint a watchman, to foretell the future to you in the prophetic spirit; and when I had set him in the watchtower, he saw a two-horse chariot coming, and a charioteer upon it, and an ass and a camel drawing the chariot. And he signifies Cyrus king of the Persians and of the Medes, coming with a small and a great empire. For before Cyrus the Persians were obscure, and were held of no account among the nations; the Medes were always most mighty. This one rider, then, supported by the army of two nations, comes against Babylon: and that watchman who had been set to look out for what was to come cried out like a lion; or else the prophet himself is called a lion. And because there was doubt about the person of the watchman who had seen Cyrus coming up, he himself explains it more plainly, and says: Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day, declaring himself to be the watchman of the Lord, who, always set in the prophetic office, and obeying the command of the Lord by day and by night, speaks whatever he commands. What, then, did the lion cry out? Behold, there comes this rider, a man of the two-horsed chariot: there is no doubt that Cyrus is indicated. And the lion himself, who had cried out above, answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground. For when the rider of the two-horse chariot laid it waste, Babylon was destroyed forever, and the temple of Bel and all the idols were leveled to the ground. And in what follows: My threshing, and son of my threshing floor, he makes an apostrophe to Jerusalem, and to the Temple which stands on the threshing floor of Ornan, and says to her: O Jerusalem, and you people, son of my Temple, let not what I have said seem incredible to you: for they are not my words but the Lord's, and it is his words that have resounded through my mouth. Some think, but wrongly, that this is said not to Jerusalem but to Babylon, of which he said above as well: Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me; and that the sense is: You who have crushed me will yourself be crushed too, not by my word, but by the power of the Lord, which foretells to you that these things will come. But what the Seventy interpreters meant in this place, in translating uriam for lion, which in Hebrew is called ARIA (אריה), I do not well understand, especially since the aforementioned priest Urias, who is called to bear witness, is written with other letters.

21:11-12

The burden of Duma. He calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? And the watchman said: The morning comes, and the night: if you seek, seek; turn, come. For Duma the Seventy put Idumaea. But Duma is not the whole province of Edom, but a certain region of it which lies toward the south, and is twenty miles distant from the city of Palestine which today is called Eleutheropolis: near it are the mountains of Seir, which took their name from their founder; for Seir means shaggy and hairy, which Esau was. In the prophet Obadiah we have discussed this nation more fully: there it was necessary to go over the ancient history, and to draw in as testimony the same Visions of Ezekiel and Jeremiah, and especially the prophecy against Mount Seir (Ezek 25 and 35; Jer 49); and that saying from the Psalms: Into Edom I will stretch out my shoe; and elsewhere: The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek (Ps 59 [60]:10; Ps 82 [83]:7-8). Amos also says: For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he pursued his brother with the sword, and violated his mercy (Amos 1:11), or, as Symmachus translated, his bowels: because he dared to fight against kindred peoples, and to be at variance with them in hostile hatred. Now the region of Esau was in the region of Duma, that is, in the mountains of Seir. We believe that this, as a metropolis, in keeping with the order of the preceding Visions, was conquered by the Assyrians or by Nebuchadnezzar, and that, mindful of its former stock, since it was begotten of the line of Abraham and Isaac, it implored the help of God, and under the compulsion of necessity begged for his clemency. Now, therefore, the Lord recounts: He who is besieged in Seir and surrounded by enemies implores my help, and says: O watchman of Israel, who guard your people with an everlasting watch, and, as it were in the night, keep vigil while they sleep, lest the enemy break in, why do you not protect us also, who are of his seed, with like clemency? To them I reply, the watchman and keeper of whom it is written: He who guards Israel will not slumber nor sleep (Ps 120 [121]:4). Morning comes for my people, and night for the nation of the Edomites; to them I will give light, you I will leave in darkness. Or certainly thus: the light has come, the night being past; if you call upon my help, and are of the stock of my servant Abraham, do not seek me only in your necessities, but turn to me with your whole mind. Come, and I will receive you as penitents. Let this be said according to the history. For the rest, because of the similarity of the letter, and because RES and DALETH differ little from each other, some of the Hebrews read Roma for Duma, wishing the prophecy to be directed against the Roman empire, by the frivolous persuasion by which they always think that the Romans are pointed out under the name of Edom: but Duma means silence.

21:13ff.

The burden in Arabia. In the forest at evening you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. Meeting the thirsty, bring water: you who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of the swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the bent bow, from the face of grievous battle. For thus says the Lord to me: Yet in one year, as in the year of a hireling: and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the sons of Kedar will be diminished: for the Lord God of Israel has spoken. As I sought, and long turned over with deliberation, what Arabia this was to which the prophetic word is directed, whether the Moabites, or the Ammonites and Edomites, and all the other regions which are now called Arabia, what follows in this same Vision gave me occasion to see that the Ishmaelites must be understood: All the glory of Kedar will be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the sons of Kedar will be diminished (Isa 21:16-17). The book of Genesis teaches that from Ishmael were born Kedar and the Hagarenes, who by a perverted name are called Saracens. These dwell throughout the whole wilderness; of them, I think, the poet too speaks: And the Barcaei, roaming far and wide (Virgil, Aeneid 4); and the aforesaid volume: He will dwell over against the face of all his brothers (Gen 16:12): because a very broad desert stretches from India as far as Mauretania and the Atlantic Ocean. This, I think, is what the title in Jeremiah expresses: To Kedar and to the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck (Jer 49:28); and at once there follows: Thus says the Lord: Arise and go up to Kedar, and lay waste the sons of the East: they will take their tents and their flocks; they will carry off for themselves their skins and all their vessels and their camels (ibid., 29); and again: For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has taken counsel against you, he has devised plans against you. Arise and go up against a nation at ease, dwelling confidently, says the Lord: no doors, no bars for them: they dwell alone. And their camels will be for plunder, and the multitude of their cattle for a prey. And I will scatter to every wind those who have the hair of their head cut round: and from all their borders I will bring destruction upon them, says the Lord: and Hazor will be a dwelling of dragons, deserted forever; no man will remain there, nor will a son of man inhabit it (ibid., 30ff.). I have set down the whole testimony of the prophecy from Jeremiah, so that you may understand without doubt what Kedar is. And consider how he has described exactly the nation of the Ishmaelites, that is, of the Saracens: because they dwell in tents; they hold whatever abodes the night drives them to; they have herds, and flocks, and droves of camels; they have neither doors nor bars, for they do not live in cities but dwell in the wilderness. These too, then, were destroyed by the Babylonians, in that they overthrew to the ground the city of Hazor, which was the metropolis of that nation in the desert; and yet, though their droves of camels and sheep were taken, and their skins and tents divided by lot, the destruction of that whole nation is not signified, because on dromedary camels they are wont to flee a hundred miles and more in a single day through the vast wilderness. All the glory of Kedar, he says, will be taken away; and when the number of the archers has been diminished, since they excel above all in that art of fighting, the rest who have fled will remain. Since we have understood what Kedar is, and what Arabia, and what Hazor, let us see what the prophet Isaiah says: In the forest at evening you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. The word ARAB (ערב), as we have often said already, is used for evening, and Arabia, and raven, and plain, and the West. And for what we, following the Seventy, have translated you will sleep, one can render you will stay or you will dwell, that is, αὐλιθήσεσθε, which in Hebrew is THALINU (תלנו). DODANIM (דדנים) too is rendered as kinsmen and relatives. So it is now foretold to the Jews who have been able to escape the Babylonian siege, and to cross from the devastation of the whole province to the neighboring desert, that they will dwell in the wilderness of Arabia, on the road that leads to their brothers. And again the discourse turns to the Ishmaelites, and urges them to mercy: Run, and go to meet your brothers, weary and in peril from burning thirst, and bring them water: for so great is the heat of the sun that, unless you come to their aid, they will perish in the wilderness; and bring not only water but bread too to the fugitives, so that your clemency may relieve those whom the siege has worn out. And at the same time he gives the reason why he commands this to be done, saying: They have fled the Babylonian sword, they have fled the bows of the Elamites, they have fled the threatening battle. And do not despise the wretched: your captivity too will come quickly. For as the hireling's year is swift, and he thinks all labor short until he reaches the wage he longs for, so all the glory of the sons of Kedar will be taken from you, and your arrows will be broken, and a small number of fighters will remain. Some, from the words yet in one year, and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away, would have it that what is foretold is not the Babylonian captivity, of which Jeremiah too speaks, but that of the Assyrians, who, one year after the devastation of Judea, pursued the Saracens far and wide. Moreover, that place in which we have translated: You who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread, and have read it in the imperative mood, as if in the person of the Lord, they affirm can be read in the Hebrew thus: Those who dwell in the land of the south met the fugitive with bread; so that, when God had said to them, Meeting the thirsty, bring water, they with hostile mind brought bread without water, to increase their thirst with food.

22:1

The burden of the valley of Vision. The Seventy, although it is not found in the Hebrew, translated more plainly, the word of the valley of Zion. For this city is the seedbed of the prophets, in which the Temple was built and the Visions of the Lord were multiplied. Because, then, it is placed among the other nations and reckoned as one of many, it is by no means called a mountain, according to that prophetic saying: Its foundations are on the holy mountains: the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:1); but a valley, because it has been humbled. Jeremiah says this very thing in other words, when he receives the cup full of wine and gives it to all the nations, and last of all holds it out to Jerusalem, that it may drink and vomit and fall and go mad: signifying that it too was to be laid waste by the Babylonians (Jer 25). The history of Kings and of Jeremiah tells this more fully. From this we understand that God is equally the creator of all, and disposes all things by the same judgment, according to what he himself says through Amos: Are you not to me as the sons of the Ethiopians, O sons of Israel? says the Lord. Did I not bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt, and the Palestinians from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene? Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom (Amos 9:7). Lest the Jews should think that they had a privilege of merit because they had been led out of Egypt, he says that the other nations too had been transferred to other lands by his command.

What is it with you too, that you also have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops, full of clamor, a crowded city, an exultant town? A Hebrew used to tell me that the present Vision does not belong to the time when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and led Zedekiah, bound and deprived of his eyes, to Babylon, but to the times of Sennacherib, when Shebna the high priest betrayed a great part of the city, and only Zion, that is, the citadel and the Temple, and the nobles remained, after the example of the city of Rome, which, when the Gauls burst in, preserved its patricians and the flower of its youth in the citadel. But we can also speak of it as of the Babylonian captivity; although Eusebius refers everything to the coming of Christ, and thinks it was fulfilled in the times of Vespasian and Titus. Let us then pick out each point, touching briefly on the threefold exposition. What is it with you too? What do you have, he says, O Zion, that you too have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops? When he says, you too, he shows that the others had gone up before. Have you also been reckoned among the nations, that you are besieged by enemies and climb onto the housetops, full of the howling and lamentation of wretched women, you who were once a royal city?

22:3

Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in war. All your princes have fled together, and have been harshly bound. All who were found have been bound together: they have fled far away. If you refer it to the times of Sennacherib, when the city was partly taken, they are rightly said not to have been conquered by the sword nor slain in war, but by treachery, some fleeing from the city, and others, whom the enemy overpowered, bound in chains. But if to the Babylonian captivity, which is also the truer view, we shall say that they were overcome not by battle but by siege. And if you wish to understand it tropologically, with Eusebius, of the coming of Christ, you will say that they were slain not by the sword but by unbelief, and that all their princes withdrew from God and were bound with the cords of sins, and that there was none of the Pharisees who was not bound in the nets of the devil.

22:4

Therefore I said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: do not press to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. If at the devastation of Babylon the Prophet weeps with the feeling of a mourner, and says: Anguish has possessed me, like the anguish of a woman giving birth: I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw, my heart has withered, darkness has stupefied me: Babylon my beloved has been made a wonder to me, how much more now, at the ruin of his own city, can he accept no consolation, giving himself wholly to lamentation!

22:5

For it is a day of slaughter, and of trampling, and of weeping, for the Lord God of hosts in the Valley of vision. He gives the reasons, according to the threefold understanding, why he said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: because Zion has been trampled down, once the mountain of visions and now the valley of weeping.

22:6

Searching the wall, and magnificent upon the mountain: and Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a horseman, and the shield laid bare the wall. The army of Babylon is described entering the city, occupying the temple, and proudly driving through the streets in four-horse chariots. And that the shield, which is wont to cover other things, laid bare the gilded doorposts and the walls clad with marble facing, sounds elegantly in the Hebrew, and the sense is most beautiful: that the shield protected no one, but laid bare, since all the riches were torn out by the strength of the soldiers. If, however, the Elamites are set in the battle, Elam being a city of the Assyrians, it cannot be referred to the times of the Roman overthrow, unless perhaps we interpret everything allegorically.

22:7, 9

And your choice valleys will be full of chariots, and the horsemen will set their seats at the gate. And the covering of Judah will be uncovered, and you will see in that day the armory of the house of the forest, and you will see the breaches of the city of David, that they have been multiplied. He plainly describes the captivity which took place in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, of which Jeremiah too speaks: Behold, I will call together all the families of the kingdoms of the North, says the Lord, and they will come, and each will set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its walls round about (Jer 1:15). And lest we should think this foretold in word and not fulfilled in deed, the same Jeremiah says: In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, the city was opened, and all the princes of the king of Babylon entered, and sat in the middle gate (Jer 39:2). Then, therefore, a countless army was poured out round about the city of Jerusalem, and the Holy of holies was opened, and the armory, which was planted with a grove, was thrown open by the enemy's ravaging, and, the walls having been breached, the enemy entered through all parts of the city.

22:10-11

And you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and you numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and you destroyed houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool: and you did not look up to him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar. He relates how they prepared the city for the siege: they transferred the waters of the lower pool, which could be captured, to the upper fortification; they destroyed houses and built walls; family by family they reckoned up how much water each house should receive; they made a cistern between the two walls, and restored the old pool to store the waters; and they did not rather call upon the help of God, who is the founder of the city and the Lord of the pool; as if he had said in other words: You have placed your trust in man, and not in God, who is the maker of man. Some, according to mystical senses, understand the old pool as the shadow of the Law, and the reservoir built between two walls, namely the New and the Old Testament, as built by the traditions and commandments of the Pharisees, one that cannot hold water: and that they did not look to the Son of God, nor believe in the presence of him whom they had not seen of old, because they had always been unbelieving toward the precepts of God.

22:12, 14

And the Lord God of hosts will call in that day to weeping, and to lamentation, and to baldness, and to the girding of sackcloth. And behold, joy and gladness, slaying calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it has been revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: If this iniquity will be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts. When the captivity was at hand and Jerusalem besieged, while sword, famine and thirst pressed hard upon the city, Jeremiah called the people to repentance (Jer 34); and on the contrary the kings and princes, and the wretched multitude, with the despair of men perishing, gave themselves over to feasting. But nothing so offends God as a stiff neck after sins, and contempt born of despair. This he says through Amos too: For three and for four impieties I will not turn him back: because he both devised it and did it, and did not repent, and moreover taught evil. Hence now too it is said: If this iniquity will be forgiven you until you die (Amos 1:4). The allegorical interpreters think this was foretold of the passion of Christ: that God called the unhappy people to repentance even after the cross of the Lord Savior, and nevertheless they gave themselves over to despair and pleasure. For the beginning of this vision, where he says: Full of clamor, a crowded city, an exultant town, they refer to that time when the people, stirred up by the Pharisees, resounded with one voice against Jesus: Crucify, crucify such a one: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:6, 7). The Apostle too made use of the example of this testimony, writing to the Corinthians about the resurrection: If the dead do not rise, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die (1 Cor 15:32).

22:15ff.

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, who is over the Temple, and you will say to him: What are you doing here? or as whom are you here, that you have hewn out a tomb for yourself here? You have hewn out a monument on high, a tabernacle for yourself carefully in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away, as a cock is carried away, and he will lift you up like a cloak. Crowning, he will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will throw you into a broad and spacious land: there you will die, and there will be the chariots of your glory, the shame of the house of your Lord. And I will drive you out from your station, and depose you from your ministry. And it will come to pass in that day, I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah. And I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and I will give your power into his hand: and he will be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. And I will lay the key of the house of David upon his shoulder, and he will open, and there will be none to shut: and he will shut, and there will be none to open. And I will fix him as a peg in a sure place, and he will be for a throne of glory to his father's house. And they will hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, vessels of various kinds: every small vessel, from the vessels of bowls even to every vessel of the musicians. In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken. We said above that Shebna was the high priest who betrayed the city to the Assyrians. But since this belongs to Hebrew tradition, and Scripture does not say it, let us understand him as proud, swollen and given to pleasure, trampling the peoples under his feet; and that, because he had done all the things the Prophet describes, his priesthood was transferred to Eliakim son of Hilkiah, so that, with him cast out, a new high priest might be made. From this we understand that pride, which offends God, is to be shunned with all zeal, and that it cannot be safe even with the privilege of the high priesthood. This is the Shebna (as some think) and the Eliakim of whom the same Prophet wrote further on: The king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a heavy force: and he stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field; and there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder (Isa 36:2ff.). The Prophet, then, is commanded to go in to the high priest, who dwelt, according to the Seventy, in the pastophorium; according to Aquila, in the tabernacle; for which Theodotion, following the Hebrew truth, says: Go in to this Socen, which can be interpreted fair and upright (so that, namely, κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν, unjust and crooked is to be understood), to the high priest of the temple, and you will say to him: You who dwell in the house of God, whose crimes run riot through the whole city, why are you secure in your works, as though you did not fear captivity? Have you hewn yourself a tomb in the rock, and built so proudly that your ambition should follow you even in death? Hear what the Lord's sentence upon you is: as a cock is carried off on the shoulder of the one carrying it, and men each lift their cloak onto the shoulder, so your removal into captivity will be easy. You will have a crown, not of the golden plate and of the sanctification of the Lord, but of tribulation and anguish. For as a ball, if it is thrown down a slope, cannot stand still but rolls on in swift course, so you too will be led away to a most broad land, which we may understand as either Egypt or the plains of Babylonia, and there you will die; and there will be the chariots of your glory, all the powers and riches on which you now lean as you go about. There you will feel the shame of the house of your Lord: because you will suffer these things on account of your evil works and the violation of the Temple of your God. I will drag you down from your rank and cast you out of the office of high priest, and in your place I will clothe Eliakim my servant, son of Hilkiah, with your garments, and adorn him with your girdle, just as Eleazar was clothed with the garments of his father Aaron. To him I will give the authority of the Temple, so that he may have the people, not subject to him as a slave, but loving him as a son. He will receive the key of my house, and carry it on his shoulder; he will have authority over all the ceremonies. And as, when a peg is fixed in the wall of the Temple and set in a very firm place, all the vessels of the priests and Levites are hung upon it, both those needed in the sacrifices and those of the musicians of every kind, so the whole people will hang upon the authority of Eliakim my servant. And as for his saying: In that day the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken, many refer it to Shebna: that when Eliakim had been fixed as a peg, the former peg, which had been fixed, collapsed. But since there follows: And what had hung upon it will perish, which by no means happened when Shebna was cast down, we understand this to be said: that when Shebna was deposed, Eliakim received the high priesthood, the dignity of whose priesthood the final captivity overthrew. Those who take everything according to ἀναγωγὴν would have the priesthood of the Jews fall in the high priesthood of Shebna, and the mysteries of the Gospel worship shown in the succession of Eliakim, which means God rising again: so that what follows: In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, pertains to the ruin of the former people. And no one doubts, both according to the history and according to the allegory, that, because he had said peg, the metaphor is kept in the hanging up of vessels of different kinds; and that when the former have been broken, others are hung up.

23:1

The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of the sea, for the house is laid waste from which they were wont to come: from the land of Cethim it has been revealed to them. Be silent, you who dwell in the island, the merchandise of Sidon. The prophet Ezekiel sets forth more plainly and more fully both the overthrow of Tyre and the causes of the overthrow, saying: Son of man, because Tyre has said of Jerusalem: Aha, the gates of the peoples are broken, she has turned to me, I shall be filled, she is deserted. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and I will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea comes up in waves, and I will scatter the walls of Tyre, and destroy its towers, and I will scrape its dust from it (Ezek 26:2ff.). And who these many nations are, which will flood over Tyre like the surging sea, he teaches by name in what follows: Behold, I will bring upon Tyre Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the North, a king of kings, with horses and chariots and horsemen, and a great company and people. Your daughters that are in the field he will slay with the sword; and he will surround you with siegeworks, and will heap up a mound round about, and will raise the shield against you, and will set mantlets and battering rams against your walls, and will destroy your towers with his weapons, and the rest that follows to the end of the vision. For in another prophecy too, which is seen to be against the Egyptians, the same Scripture weaves in: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made his army serve a great service against Tyre: every head made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, and no wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29). By this he signifies that a mound was heaped up over a long time by the army of Babylon, so that he tried beforehand to do what Alexander did afterwards, joining the island to the mainland (Quintus Curtius, book 4). Just as, therefore, we have read above God's threats against Babylon and the Philistines, and Moab, and Egypt, and the Edomites and Ishmaelites, because they mocked the captivity of his people, so now too a prophecy is woven against Tyre, hostile and mocking at the overthrow of Jerusalem: that it too is to be destroyed by the same enemy. We have read the histories of the Greeks, and especially of those who describe the wars of the Assyrian nation; and there we find that after the captivity of Jerusalem the Palestinians, and the Arabs, and the Damascenes, and after them the Egyptians were overthrown. And that these nations, and Tyre above all, always attacked Israel and rejoiced at its overthrow, the prophet Amos explains at the opening of his volume (Amos 1), and the Psalmist, briefly singing praises to God, declares: O God, who will be like you? Do not keep silent, nor be restrained, O God. For behold, your enemies have made a noise: and those who hate you have lifted up the head. They have devised malicious counsel against your people, and have plotted against your holy ones. They have said: Come, and let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more. For they have plotted with one mind, together they have made a covenant against you: the tents of the Edomites, and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre (Ps 82 [83]:1ff.). From all these we learn that the weight of God's wrath came upon Tyre the harlot, who is described here under the figure of a prostitute, and in Ezekiel under the metaphor of a ship (Ezek 27). Howl, he says, you ships of the sea. For this we read in the Seventy of Carthage; and in the Hebrew there is THARSIS (תרשיש), about which I have argued both on the prophet Jonah and in a certain letter. And because Carthage is a colony of the Tyrians, we can in the present place take Tharsis not only as the sea in general but also as Carthage: that ships no longer come to Tyre from Africa, nor from the land of Cethim, which some interpret as Cyprus: for to this day there is among them the city of Citium, from which came Zeno too, the heresiarch of the Stoic sect; although many of our writers, and especially the beginning of Maccabees, consider Cethim to be the islands of Italy and Macedonia. For Scripture records this, that Alexander king of the Macedonians went out from the land of Cethim. And in naming it an island he does not lie: for afterwards it was made part of the mainland by Nebuchadnezzar or by Alexander, when many mounds were heaped up in the narrow strait for its capture. He also calls it the merchandise of Sidon, in keeping with the following line, in which he says: Be ashamed, O Sidon. For the histories relate that Tyre is a colony of Sidon.

23:3

Those crossing the sea have filled you; in many waters the seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river is its produce. That Tyre delights in trade and is the emporium of the whole world, both present times prove and Ezekiel describes at length. And that merchants cross the seas in carrying their goods, there is no one who doubts; nor does the city itself have such great wealth from the land of its own region, which is very narrow and hemmed in by the borders of Galilee and of Damascus, as it has from the shipping of goods. The whole Nile and the fertility of Egypt pour into Tyre from close at hand. For Nile, which we read among the Hebrews as SIOR (שיחר), the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted merchants; this word means turbid, and by this signifies the waters of the Nile, as Jeremiah testifies: What have you to do with Egypt, that you should drink the waters of Geon? (Jer 2:18): for which in the Hebrew there is Sior, that is, turbid.

23:4

Be ashamed, O Sidon: for the sea has spoken, the strength of the sea, saying: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth, and I have not nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. I said above that Tyre is a colony of the Sidonians. Hear, then, O mother, all the seas crying out together against your daughter, and in a manner uttering a voice, though by nature they cannot speak: In vain have I brought riches together; to no purpose have I gathered wealth from the whole world into Tyre: she that was rich, she that was luxurious, and once rejoiced in a multitude of peoples, in which a throng of mortals was born, a troop of children, swarms of youth, whose streets rang with the games of virgins and infants, of young men and girls, has now been reduced to solitude. It is customary to make προσωποποιΐας out of mute things.

23:5

When it has been heard in Egypt, they will grieve when they hear of Tyre. This is plain: that the Egyptians, after they have heard that a most mighty and neighboring nation has been destroyed by a long siege, know that destruction is drawing near to them too.

23:6

Cross the seas, howl, you who dwell in the island. Again, for sea and Tharsis the Seventy translated Carthage. We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, when they saw no hope of escape, embarked on ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Hence too it is said in Ezekiel: No wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29): because all the wealth of the city had been carried away, and all the nobles had left it empty.

23:7

Is not this yours, which gloried from the days of old in its antiquity? He convicts Tyre of pride, because it gloried in the antiquity of its founding and did not look to God, but, recalling the names of its fathers, thought itself eternal.

Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad. He means those who had remained in the city and were led captive to Babylon.

23:8

Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned? Read Ezekiel again (Ezek 27), and you will learn from the lament over its prince how great the glory of Tyre was. He calls it crowned because, as a king among a great multitude of men raises his head adorned with a diadem, so Tyre, gleaming and lofty in riches, and shining with gold and gems and silk and purple, was esteemed a queen among all nations.

Whose merchants are princes, its traders the renowned of the earth. We marvel that the envoy of Pyrrhus once said of the city of Rome: I have seen a city of kings. Behold, long before those times the merchants and traders of Tyre are described as princes and renowned men: so that by this the greatness of its opulence is shown, since a merchant of Tyre could be a king in the other's words.

23:9

The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory, and to bring into ignominy all the renowned of the earth. Because above, in the manner of one asking, he had said: Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned?, now he himself answers: It is not that the threads of the fates have been spun thus, as fools think; it is not that the wheel of fortune has run; but it has been accomplished by the judgment of God and by his will, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4); and he reminds the arrogant of their condition, so that through misery they may learn the power of him whose clemency they had refused to feel through his benefits.

23:10

Pass through your land like a river, daughter of the sea: there is no girdle for you any more. As, he says, a river, or, as the Hebrew has it more expressively, a stream, for it is called IOR (יאר), is easily crossed on foot, so you too, led into captivity, will pass through your land, O daughter of the sea, either because you are an island, or because it was written of you above: The sea has spoken, the strength of the sea: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth. And what sense his next words have, there is no girdle for you any more, Symmachus teaches more openly: you will no longer be able to resist, that is, you will not have the strength, nor your loins girded for fighting, so as to be able to go out against your adversaries.

23:11

He has stretched out his hand over the sea, he has troubled kingdoms. Who stretched out his hand? From the very tenor of the discourse there is no doubt that it is God, of whom he said above: The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory. He stretched out his hand, then, over all the seas, signifying the world and the earth, and troubled all the nations, among which you too, O Tyre, were troubled; or else over the sea, in which you are properly situated.

23:12

The Lord has given command against Canaan, to crush its strong ones. He shows what the sea is over which the Lord stretched out his hand, saying: He has given command against Canaan. For Tyre was founded in the land of Canaan. Read the Scriptures, and especially the Gospel (Mark 7), where the Syrophoenician woman, pleading for her daughter, comes out of the land of Canaan, and is called a Canaanite woman. And at the same time, because he had said: He has stretched out his hand, lest you should believe that the Lord works with limbs and by bodily function, he added, he has given command, so that for God to have done is to have commanded.

23:12

And he said: You will no more glory, suffering calumny, O virgin daughter of Sidon; rise, cross over to Cethim: there too there will be no rest for you. God, who devised to pull down the pride of all glory, who gave command against Canaan to crush its strong ones, himself says: You will by no means glory any longer, nor trust in your own power. O virgin daughter of Sidon, that is, colony of the Sidonians, you will indeed flee in ships to the islands of the West, or to Cyprus, and the other lands of Macedonia and Greece; but there too, with God against you, you will not be able to find rest. Besides, everyone who is a wanderer and a stranger in the world, and of uncertain abode, is always in straits, continually in grief.

23:13-14

Behold the land of the Chaldeans, such a people there was not: Assyria founded it for captivity; they carried away its mighty men, they undermined its houses, they made it a ruin. Howl, you ships of the sea, for your strength has been laid waste. Because he had said above: Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad; and again, Pass through your land like a river; and because the people of Tyre was twofold, those who had fled and crossed over to Cethim, and those who had remained in the city, he speaks to both. Of those who had fled he said above: Rise, cross over to Cethim, there too there will be no rest for you. Of those who had remained and were led into captivity: Behold, he says, the inhabitants of the land of the Chaldeans, whose power no peoples had before, and which was founded by the Assyrian, have carried away the mighty men of Tyre. They undermined not only the walls but all the dwellings of the city, and made it a ruin. Since, then, some have fled and others have been captured, howl, you ships, whether of the sea or of Carthage; for your mart and your colony has been destroyed. And at the same time consider how he has praised the Chaldeans. He did not say, such a people will not be hereafter: for the kingdom of the Romans is more powerful and harsher; but, there was not before. He who denied what went before conceded what follows.

23:15

And it will come to pass in that day, you will be in oblivion, O Tyre, for seventy years, like the days of one king. From this place to the end of this prophecy prosperous things are announced to Tyre: that it ought to repent; that it is to be built again; that the overthrow of Tyre is to last only seventy years, the years during which the temple of God too was desolate: so that the city that mocked at the ruins of another should also match the time of that one's ruins. The seventy years of one king many think to be said of Nebuchadnezzar, the years during which the kingdom of the Assyrian nation continued in Jerusalem. Others think it is said in general: that he who has had a long time of reigning cannot go beyond seventy years.

23:16

But after seventy years it will be for Tyre like the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about the city, harlot given over to oblivion; sing well, repeat the song, that you may be remembered. Because you have committed fornication with very many nations, and your former lovers have despised you, desolate and naked and filthy with the squalor of captivity, take up the harp now, redouble your songs, go about the city, lament your former brothel, and wash away with tears the traces of your old error, so that you may call forth the mercy of God upon you.

23:17

And it will come to pass after seventy years, the Lord will visit Tyre, and will bring it back to its wages, and again it will commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth. That all these things were fulfilled according to the history is shown by the concordant writings of the Greeks and Phoenicians: that after seventy years it was restored and returned to its former power, and became the mart of all the nations; and these, I think, are called fornications: so that, as he who commits fornication enters the brothel and pays the wage of debauchery, so the trader, flocking in from the whole world, has filled up the beauty of the city as of a harlot.

23:18

And its merchandise and its wages will be sanctified to the Lord: they will not be hidden away nor laid up. For its merchandise will be for those who dwell before the Lord, that they may eat to the full and be clothed even to old age. We find that these things have not yet been done according to the history; unless perhaps it is to be thought that after the building of Jerusalem and the restoration of Tyre the cities were friendly to each other, and Tyre often sent gifts to the temple of God: as we read in Ezra too (Neh 13:16), that he drove off the Tyrians who were selling fish on the sabbath, and did not allow them to enter the city: and from this one item of trade one must judge of the rest as well. The Jews put off their vain hopes into the future, declaring that these things are to be fulfilled after the Antichrist, in the thousand years. Nor is it surprising if those invent such things who, having spurned the truth of Christ, are to receive the Antichrist, the instrument of the devil, since even judaizing Christians contend that these things were said of the blessedness of the thousand years. But I, just as in the vision of Babylon I understand the time of the consummation under the type of its overthrow, and in Egypt refer to the time of Christ the altar of the Lord set up when the idols were destroyed, and in the vision of Moab recognize the throne of the Savior set up in its land, and in the visions of Damascus and all the others have no doubt that they are mysteries of our own times, so also in the vision of Tyre, which is the last, I interpret it of the time of Christian felicity: that after it was built and recovered its former state, and every merchant entered its harbor according to the old custom, their merchandise and their labor too are dedicated to the Lord. Let us behold the Churches of Christ built in Tyre; let us consider the wealth of all, that it is not laid up nor treasured, but given to those who dwell before the Lord, who, serving the altar, partake of the altar (1 Cor 9). And the Tyrians minister, not for riches, nor for heaping up the wealth of the priests, but for supplying the necessities of life: so that, according to the Apostle, having food and clothing, we may be content with these (1 Tim 6). And note that he did not say that the merchandise and wages of Tyre sanctified to the Lord are to be given to those who dwell in Jerusalem, as the Jews think, but to those who are before the Lord, who serve him. For so too the Lord has ordained, that those who preach the Gospel should live by the Gospel (1 Cor 9). And to serve the Lord and to dwell before him is a matter not of place but of merit. Thus far we have discussed, by a historical interpretation, the visions of Isaiah, or the burdens which he laid upon certain nations, as you bade and as we were able, pressing only on the footsteps of the Hebrew truth. What follows pertains to all the nations, and in general to the consummation of the whole world. About this neither did you ask me to write, nor did I have the leisure to dictate superfluously what was not asked, I who have scarcely written what was asked.

Book Six

What I promised in the preceding volume, namely that upon the foundations of the history, if Christ should assent to our wish, I would raise a spiritual building and, with the roof set in place, display the ornaments of the perfected Church, this I shall try to do in the following two books, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, by your prayers and the mercy of the Lord, so that with the same labor with which the fifth book embraced the history, the sixth and seventh may touch upon the anagogy: not discussing everything, lest the volumes become many, but briefly indicating what churchmen before us have thought.

13:1

The burden or vision against Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amos saw. He saw, not with the eyes of the flesh but with those of the mind, how great and heavy a weight was to be laid upon Babylon. And since Babylon, which in Hebrew is called BABEL (בבל), means confusion, because there the speech of those building the tower was confounded, spiritually this world is understood, which is set in wickedness and confounds not only the tongues but also the works and the minds of each person. The king of this Babylon is the true Nebuchadnezzar, who grows proud against the Lord and says in his heart: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the North; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High. He it is who showed the Lord all the kingdoms of the world and said to him: All these have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matt 4:9). Accordingly, in what follows the threat is in no way against Babylon, but against the whole world. The Lord Sabaoth commanded a most warlike nation to come from a distant land, from the height of heaven, to destroy the whole world. And again: Behold, the day comes of incurable fury and wrath, to make the whole world a desert and to destroy sinners out of it. And then: I will command evils for the whole world, and for the ungodly their sins. From these it is proved that everything said against Babylon pertains to the confusion and destruction of this world.

13:2

Upon a misty mountain, or a level one, lift up a sign. It is commanded to the Apostles, and to apostolic men and teachers of the Churches, that when they are about to fight against Babylon they should raise the sign of the Lord's cross, not in a low place and in sunken valleys, but on a misty or level mountain. Of these, the one signifies the hidden mysteries of the Church, to see which, and to hear the voice of God, Moses entered into the darkness and the mist. For God made darkness his hiding place, and cloud and mist round about him (Ps 17 [18]). The other teaches that we ought so to climb to the heights of the Church's doctrines as to be humbled, according to the Apostle Paul, and to say: I who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor 15:9). He too raised the sign upon a level mountain when, with the humility implanted in him, he said: For I judged myself to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And this sign, in the passages above as well, was raised by him who arose from the root of Jesse among the nations, to gather the lost of Israel.

Exalt the voice, lift up the hand. For which the Seventy translated: Comfort with the hand. He exalts his voice who speaks of lofty things and despises present things as brief and transitory. He who hears from the same Isaiah: Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice in strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem, lifts up his hand, he who can say with David: The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice (Ps 140 [141]:2); and who in every place lifts up holy hands, so that he not only lifts up his hands but also comforts with his hand: so that he does not say to the poor man, Come tomorrow and receive; but rather comforts his poverty and need with present mercy.

And let the leaders enter the gates. LXX: Open, you princes. The leaders of the Church enter the gates of the mysteries of God and know the mysteries of the Scriptures, having the key of knowledge, so as to open them to the peoples entrusted to them. Hence it is commanded that the teachers should open and the disciples should enter.

13:3

I have commanded my sanctified ones. For which the LXX: I will command, and I will lead them. For he himself sanctifies his ministers, so that both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified may all be of one. He who in another place also says to believers: Be holy, because I also am holy, himself commands and will lead his princes, so that they may do what has been commanded (Lev 19:2).

And I have called my mighty ones in my wrath, exulting in my glory. LXX: Giants come to fulfill my fury, rejoicing together and doing outrage. According to the Hebrew, what is said clings to what precedes: that he who had given command to his sanctified ones himself called his mighty ones, exulting in his glory. But according to the Seventy, the giants who come to fulfill the fury of the Lord, rejoicing and glad at another's injury, are to be taken as the left-hand and hostile powers, of which we also read in the psalms: He sent upon them the fury of his wrath, fury and wrath and tribulation, a sending by evil angels (Ps 77 [78]:49). Of these is also the destroyer in Egypt, who does not dare to enter the doorposts smeared with the blood of the lamb (Exod 12), and that spirit who went out and stood in the sight of the Lord and said: I will deceive Ahab. And the Lord said to him: You will deceive him and you will prevail; go forth and do so (1 Kgs 22:21, 22). Hence in the same volume of Kings Micaiah said: I saw the Lord of Israel sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven stood about him on the right and on the left (ibid., 19). The right-hand powers are those of the angels who are sent for good things; the left-hand, those of the angels to whom we are handed over for punishment. Hence the Apostle too says: Whom I have delivered, he says, to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1:20). Now the name of the giants, for which in the Hebrew GEBORIM (גברים), that is, of the mighty, is set down, the Seventy and Theodotion turned into the likeness of the fables of the Gentiles, just as they also name the Sirens and the Titans and Arcturus, the Hyades and Orion, which among the Hebrews are called by other names. But if the giants are rebels against God, and all heresies, being contrary to the truth, rebel against God, all heretics are giants, who rejoice in their error and glory most of all when they have done outrage to the Church.

13:5

The voice of a multitude on the mountains, as of crowded peoples; the voice of the sound of kings of nations gathered together. This passage is taken in three ways. First, that when the sign has been raised on the level mountain, the multitude of the nations comes, itself also set upon the mountains, and it is divided into two, namely into peoples and into kings, into disciples and teachers, of whom the Savior spoke in the Gospel: Many will come from the East and from the West, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt 8:11). And it is called one voice, and harmonious, for this reason: that the Apostle's saying may be proved: That you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfect in the same mind and in the same judgment (1 Cor 1:10). Secondly, the pride of the heretics is described, who, believing themselves to be on the mountains, are lifted up against the knowledge of God, and speak iniquity on high, and set their mouth against heaven; they too have peoples, they have kings, who devour the deceived people. The third interpretation is this: since he had said above, giants come to fulfill my fury, rejoicing together and doing outrage, he describes the arrogance of the giants themselves, and their agreement, in the evil sense, in punishing those who have been handed over to them.

The Lord of hosts has commanded the army of war, coming from a far land, from the height of heaven: the Lord and the vessels of his fury, to destroy the whole earth. LXX: The Lord Sabaoth commanded a most warlike nation to come from a distant land, from the highest ÷ foundation ⁚ of heaven, the Lord and his warriors, to destroy the whole world. Foundation is to be marked beforehand with an obelus. In the volume of Kings and of Chronicles we read (2 Sam 24; 1 Chr 21) that the wrath of God was kindled against Israel when David numbered the people and offended the Lord. In the Psalms too it is written: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chasten me in your wrath, and other things like these, for which I have read in the Commentaries of a certain writer [he means Basil] that the wrath of God can be understood as a hostile power to which we are handed over for punishment, of which it is also sung in the eighth psalm: That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger (Ps 8:3). Those who come from a far land and from the height of heaven can be called warriors, namely also the ministering angels, who are to be sent at the consummation of the world to make bundles of the tares and, separated from the wheat, to prepare them for everlasting burning (Matt 13). The whole earth, too, is destroyed when earthly works are overthrown. There are also other warriors of the Lord, equipped with the armor of the Apostle, who daily in the Church, which is understood as the οἰκουμένη, that is, the world and the inhabited land, destroy and slay those who are lifted up against the knowledge of God.

13:6-7

Howl, for the day of the Lord is near; it will come like devastation from the Lord. Therefore all hands will be loosened, and every heart of man will melt and be crushed. Since the warriors of the Lord are to come to destroy the whole earth, howl and do penance, you for whom punishment is coming. For the day of the Lord is near, either of the consummation of the whole world and of the judgment, or of each one's departure from life. For there comes from the Lord a plundering, which we have called devastation in order to keep the metaphor, since he had spoken first of warriors. When the day of judgment or of falling asleep has come, all hands will be loosened, to which it is said in another place: Be strengthened, you loosened hands. And the hands will be loosened because no work worthy of the righteousness of God will be found: And no living person will be justified in his sight (Ps 142 [143]:2). Hence the Prophet says in the psalms: If you mark iniquities, O Lord, who will endure (Ps 129 [130]:3)? Every heart too, or soul of man, will melt, and will tremble at the consciousness of its sin. This is the fearful and terrible day of which Zephaniah also speaks: Fear before the face of the Lord, for the day of the Lord is near (Zeph 1:14). And again: Near is the great day of the Lord: near, and very swift. And Amos: Woe, he says, to those who desire the day of the Lord: why would you have the day of the Lord, which is darkness and not light (Amos 5:18)?
