For, O Moab, my fugitives who had forsaken me, who had gone out of the Church and, abandoning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, were following their own sense; or those who had dwelt with you, when the destroyer, the devil, begins to persecute them, do you, turned with your whole mind to the fear of the Lord, offer them hiding places: and know that after the coming of the Lamb, who arose from the rock of the desert as ruler of the whole earth and came to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, all the power of the devil, which is compared to dust, is at an end. And the wretch is consumed who made many wretched: and he has failed who trampled the whole earth, namely those who were earthly. And when he has been consumed and brought to nothing and has utterly failed, a throne and an everlasting kingdom will be prepared. First in mercy (for we are all (Rom 3) under sin, and need the grace of God); and he will sit in the tabernacle of David, which had fallen and has been raised up, who after mercy will judge, and seek righteousness, and render to each according to his works. Let us consider from the beginning of the Burden, or of the word, of Moab, in which it is said: By night Ar of Moab has been laid waste, and the rest up to this place; and we shall see how by steps and in the order of penance Israelites are made from Moabites, and flee like birds and fly away like young ones from the nest, so as to cross over by the Arnon and dwell on the mountain of the daughter of Zion: and, all the power of the devil or of the Antichrist having been crushed, Christ reigns in them and sets his throne among those who have been saved by mercy and righteousness. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5).

16:6ff.

We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. His pride and his arrogance and his indignation are more than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of him will howl: to those who rejoice over the wall of baked brick, speak of his wounds: for the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted, the vineyard of Sibmah. LXX: We have heard of the insolence of Moab: he is exceedingly insolent: his pride and his insolence and his fury are not like your divination: not so will Moab howl: for in Moab all will howl: but for the inhabitants of Deseth you will meditate, and you will not be confounded: the plains of Heshbon will mourn the vineyard of Sibmah. In how many obscurities this passage is wrapped according to the Seventy translators is evident from the fact that it can scarcely be read. Let us speak, therefore, according to the Hebrew. It is the custom of the Scriptures, after they have relieved the despair of the human mind with glad tidings, to deter again by threats the negligent and those unwilling to do penance, lest the goodness of God harden our heart. Of this let us set down only one example. In the hundred and forty-fourth psalm we read: The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works (Ps 144 [145]:9). And a little after: The Lord upholds all who fall, and raises up all who are dashed down. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food in due season. And when he had said first, The Lord keeps all who love him, lest he make the hearer negligent, he added: And all sinners he will destroy. Since, then, he prophesied that when the Antichrist and his parent the devil, who trampled the whole earth, have been consumed, a throne is to be prepared in mercy, and he who is to sit in the tabernacle of David, the prophet speaks in the person of the saints who have been saved from Moab and have learned his pride by their own experience: We have heard of the pride of Moab, or the insolence, as the Seventy translated. For which of the heretics is not proud? who, despising the simplicity of the Church, regards the men of the Church as brute animals, and is lifted up by such a swelling of pride and insolence that he arms his mouth against the Creator himself, disparaging his prophets as though on the authority of the testimony of the Gospel, in which the Savior says: All who came before me were thieves and robbers (John 10:8): so much so that he even calls Moses, the servant of God, a murderer, and disparages Joshua the son of Nun as a bloodthirsty man, who was of such holiness that at the command of his word the sun and moon stood still: and calls David, of whose seed Christ was born (Matt 1), a murderer and an adulterer, not regarding his penance and his meekness, by which the clemency of God is obtained. But although he is proud and arrogant, and exults in his fury, yet he dares more than his strength allows. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, that is, one to another: namely, all the varieties of the heretics and of worldly wisdom will bellow against one another when they are in torments (1 Kgs 6). For this reason, to those who have walls not built of squared stones, of which the Temple was built, and so polished that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of God, O you teachers of the Church, or you who have been saved from the error of Moab, announce their wounds, with which they have been wounded by the darts of the heretics. For all their thoughts, which is what Heshbon signifies, do not belong to the dwelling of the Lord's city, of which it is written: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5); but they are suburbs, so that they may be believed to belong to the city of the Lord: and these suburbs are deserted by the protection of God, or burnt by the divine fire, especially the vineyard of Sibmah, which means lifting up height, because it raises itself on high and tries to build the tower of its pride up to heaven. And what is set down in the Seventy, for the inhabitants of Deseth, is not found in the Hebrew; but in its place is read ARES (חרש), which signifies potsherd, or baked brick.

16:9-10

The lords of the nations have cut down its branches: they have reached as far as Jazer. They have wandered in the desert: its shoots have been left: they have crossed the sea. For this I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vineyard of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh: for upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. And gladness and exultation will be taken away from Carmel: and in the vineyards he will not exult nor shout for joy: he who was accustomed to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. The suburbs of Heshbon, of which we spoke above, are deserted, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which can be interpreted not only as lifting up height but also as some conversion: because in the region of Moab it seems in some part to wish to be converted to the service of the Lord. Of this vineyard of Sibmah, therefore, the lords of the nations, the Apostles and apostolic men, have utterly cut off the branches and shoots, lest from some heresies other heresies should be born and an infinite multitude of the straying should come to be. And they not only cut off the shoots of Sibmah, but reached as far as Jazer, which means their strength: that is, to all the strongest doctrines of the heretics, built by the art of dialectic, in which they seemed to have the strength of their error; and their sword raged so far that at last they wandered in the wilderness and had no one to slay. And though they cut off its branches, yet, through the fault of the most evil root, some shoots remained. But the lords of the nations crossed the sea, that is, the temptations of this world, of which we read in the psalm: I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest swallowed me (Ps 68 [69]:3); and in another place: Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters: they have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep (Ps 106 [107]:23). These, then, crossed the sea, so as to behold the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep of temptations, while they are delivered from them. And so the prophetic word laments the strength of the heretics, that is, Jazer, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God. And I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon, namely their thoughts, and Elealeh, by which they climb to the heights. And why does he lament Jazer and the vineyard of Sibmah, and drench Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears? So that, while he himself weeps, he may teach them also to weep. For, he says, upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. For the vineyard of the Moabites, because of the nearness of the place, is such as is the vineyard of the Sodomites too, of which it is said: For their vine is of the vineyard of the Sodomites, and their shoot of Gomorrah (Deut 32:31). And in Psalm 77 (78) we read of the Egyptian vine which God struck with hail. The harvests of Moab too grow in the valleys which are called Rephaim: and its false vintage is of the vineyard of which it is said above: The lords of the nations have cut down its branches. For these crush the most bitter grapes and tread them with their feet, lest the poisons of the dragon be pressed out of them and all who drink be killed. The gladness and exultation of the heretics, in which they had formerly been accustomed to rejoice, will also be taken away: so that, after they have done penance, they may deserve to hear: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). And what he added, from Carmel, signifies this: not that the heretics truly have Carmel, that is, the knowledge of the spiritual circumcision, but that they falsely boast of having it. And when the vineyards have been cut down, and gladness and exultation taken away from the knowledge falsely so called, then there will be none of the former treaders to tread the grapes which he had trodden before: and their voice will be struck dumb in eternal silence.

16:11ff.

For this my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick. And it will be, when it has appeared that Moab has labored on his high places, he will enter into his holy places to entreat, and he will not prevail. This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. When the error of Moab has been destroyed, or rather its false gladness changed into mourning and tears, my belly, the prophet's, which is composed with musical art like a harp, and which, conceiving from the fear of God, has begotten many children, so that there is no string that does not give back its sound, will resound with the mourning of Moab doing penance: and all my inward parts for the wall of baked brick: for which Theodotion translated for the scattered wall. For all the defenses of the adversaries, in which they formerly trusted, will be destroyed and will fall. And these are the inward parts and the inner things of the prophet, of which David too spoke in the Psalm: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my inner parts his holy name (Ps 102 [103]:1). For just as a harp does not give forth a tuneful and well-composed sound if even one string is broken, so the spiritual belly of the prophet, if one string of the virtues is lacking in it, will not be able to sound forth a sweet melody, nor to cry out with all its inward parts to the brick wall. It is also the opinion of the philosophers that the virtues cleave to one another; and of the Apostle James, that he who lacks one lacks all the virtues. And when Moab has understood that he has labored in vain at the doctrines which he formerly thought lofty, he will enter into his holy places, not those which are holy of themselves, but those which in his error he thought holy, and he will not be able to find help. Or surely, having abandoned the error of falsehood, he will try to enter into the holy places of the Church, to make them his own, and to pray and entreat, but he will not prevail. For we cannot take hold of perfect virtue as soon as we wish. And what he adds: This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time, let us know that an epilogue has been given back to the proem in which he had said, the word against Moab, or the burden, so that what he had begun there he has completed here. And from that time is to be understood as from when he began to speak to him, so that all that he said is one word of God, that is, one sentence. Moreover, according to the Seventy, who translated: The inner parts of the prophet, like a wall renewed by God, and that he is put to shame, that is, Moab, and enters to the altars and to the things that are made by hand, we can discuss it thus, saying that the inward parts of the prophet are always renewed and made stronger by God, so that the adversaries are confounded, and understand the things which have been fabricated by human hand to be empty and of no profit for salvation.

16:14

And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, and he will be left small and slight, by no means many. The three years in which the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, or great riches, as the Seventy translated, are to be understood mystically. For just as the mercy of the Lord is in weights and measure, so torments and punishments too have their measure, so that after three years have passed, in which he will be left small and slight and by no means many, he may then cease to be without glory. And this is to be noted, that according to the prophecy of Ezekiel, when days are counted for years to Israel (Ezek 4), that is, to the ten tribes, which had sinned more grievously, three hundred and ninety years are reckoned in punishments, as it is contained in the Hebrew, not a hundred and ninety, as the common edition has: and to Judah, in which was the Temple of God, forty years. For he who is small deserves mercy: but the mighty will suffer torments mightily (Wis 6). And the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12). Moab, therefore, because he was an outsider and not of the people of God, but was converted after leaving his error, will be left small and slight and without glory, not for many years, but for three only. These are the years of which we read elsewhere too: Remember the days of the age (Isa 46), and again: I thought upon the days of old, and I had the eternal years in mind (Ps 76 [77]:6). For if Israel according to the flesh served the shadow and the patterns, and every solemnity of theirs was a type of things to come, why should not the years of the present time also prefigure the times to come? of which we read in another place too: What will you do in the days of the assembly, and in the days of the festival of the Lord? And what is joined to it, Like the years of a hireling (Hos 9:5), shows this: that false doctrine does everything for gain and profit. For every hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, when he sees the wolf coming, flees, because he is a hireling and the sheep do not belong to him (John 10). For this reason I think that the stranger and the hireling do not eat of the holy things, nor are servants partakers of the holy things. For it is not for love of the Lord but for wages that they do all things, who devour the houses of widows and lead off flocks of their own, to be clothed with their wool and to milk their milk (Matt 23). What we have said of hireling doctrine, let us refer to the rest as well. If I give alms in order to be glorified by men, I have received my reward and am to be called a hireling. If I pretend to be chaste, and there is something else in my conscience, I have not the glory of a hireling but the punishments of a sinner. And in the comparison of two evils, it is a lighter evil to sin openly than to feign and counterfeit holiness. But in this too Moab has made progress: that he who formerly had many companions in his error is afterward reduced to a few; or he who formerly was great in the riches of sins is, after penance, small and poor in malice.

Book Seven

The seventh book is likewise the second according to the anagogy, or rather the last; for in it the tropological explanation of the ten visions comes to an end. When, with your prayers, Eustochium, and with the help of Christ, I have completed it, I shall come to the eighth, and shall unfold both explanations together, as in the earlier books up to the fourth.

17:1

The burden of Damascus. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Damascus; the LXX: The word against Damascus, adding something of their own, as they did at the beginning of Moab. We first read the name Damascus in Genesis: he was Abraham's home-born servant before Isaac, and was thought to be his heir, had not the son of Sarah been begotten by promise (Gen 15). Now it means either kiss of blood, or drinking blood, or blood of sackcloth, all of which suit the people of the heathen, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty, and did works worthy of lamentation and of sackcloth. In the book of Days (2 Chr 24) the history relates that when the year was completed the army of Syria went up against Joash king of Judah, and came into Jerusalem, and slew all the princes of the people, and sent all the spoil to the king of Damascus; it had come with few men, and God had delivered into their hand a very great multitude, because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers. This must be considered according to the anagogy and as a type of things to come, whether we may refer it to the time of the Lord's advent. For after the end of the acceptable year, in which the Gospel was preached by the Savior, the army of the nations went up from Damascus with few men against Judah and Jerusalem, who had forsaken the Lord; and they carried off all their riches of the Law and the Prophets, and sent them to the king of Damascus: namely, churchmen and men of the Gospel teaching, who, in comparison with the whole world, still unbelieving at that time, and with the Jews scattered through the whole earth, were few; and yet the Lord delivered Jerusalem into their hands, because they had forsaken the Son of God, who had been foretold beforehand through the prophets (Acts 9). Therefore I think that for this reason Saul too, who afterwards received the name of Paul from his virtue, went to Damascus because he was a zealot of the Law, and wished to fight against the believers from the nations; and that, overcome there, he followed those who lived in Damascus, so that from there he might go up again to Jerusalem to do battle with the Jews. Nor should it seem contradictory to anyone if in the book of Paralipomenon glad things are foretold of Damascus, and now in Isaiah sad things; for of Israel itself, which is surely the portion of God, now adverse things, now prosperous things are announced. And as it is said to Israel according to the flesh and to the nations: You nations according to the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh; so, on the contrary, there is an Israel according to the spirit, and there are nations according to the spirit, and among the other nations there is a Damascus according to the spirit, lest we rest content with Jewish fables alone.

17:1ff.

Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city, and shall be as a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer shall be left for flocks, and they shall rest there, and there shall be none to make them afraid; and help shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As was shown in the title, by Damascus is signified the calling of the nations, which loved or drank blood; and once they have believed in Christ, they will cease to be cities of their former way of life, and will be as a heap of stones in ruin. For as heaps of stones that are scattered over the fields are carried together into one mound, so out of all the nations a heap of believers has been gathered at the ruin of the people of the Jews, they falling and we rising. The forsaken cities of AROER (ערוער), that is, of the tamarisk, shall also be for the flocks of the Church, so that we may inhabit those which the Jews forsook; or else, idolatry being destroyed, the Gospel shall be built up. This too we see fulfilled in our own times: the Serapeum at Alexandria and the temple of Marnas at Gaza have risen up as churches of the Lord, and the cities of Aroer have been made ready for the flocks of the Gospel. Aroer, that is, tamarisks, grow in desert places, according to what is written in the curse of the man who trusts in man, and whose heart departs from the Lord: He shall be, it says, like the tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see good when it comes; but he shall dwell in dryness, in the desert, in a land of salt and uninhabitable (Jer 17:6). Others again say that from this tree, by the arts of sorcerers, μίστρα, that is, hatreds, are stirred up. Therefore those who were formerly in the desert of the Gentiles, and in hatred of the Christian name, shall serve the flocks of Christ, which shall rest in them, and there shall be none to make them afraid, because the Lord shall dwell among them, and with the Shepherd present they will not be able to fear the wolf. Then the help of God shall cease from Ephraim, by whom in this place are understood the Scribes and Pharisees, according to the prophecy of Hosea, who names Ephraim those who are opposed to the people of God (Hos 5 and 8). And the kingdom shall cease from Damascus, so that sin, and the prince of sin, the devil, may no longer reign in Damascus, which formerly loved blood; but the remnant of Syria, that is, those from the nations who have believed, are to be as the children of Israel formerly were, the kingdom of God having been taken from them and given to the nations which bring forth its fruit, as the Lord God of hosts has spoken through all his prophets.

17:4, 6

And it shall come to pass in that day that the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh shall waste away. And it shall be as one gathering in the harvest what remains, and his arm shall glean the ears, and it shall be as one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there shall be left in it as a cluster of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five at its summits, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. After the remnant of Syria has become as the glory of the children of Israel once was, and through their trespass salvation has been given to the nations, then all the glory of the Jews, by which they were glorious in the whole world, shall be made thin, and the fatness of their flesh shall waste away, since they have no prophets, no signs and mighty works, no present help of God, no dignity of the priesthood; but the whole body of their nation shall wither and be brought to nothing. And since it is said of the calling of the nations: The harvest is great, but the labourers are few (Matt 9), those poor ones shall glean the remnants of the harvest, which were saved through the Apostles, and the scantiest ears, not from the mountains and lofty places, but in the valley of Rephaim, that is, in the lowliness of the letter. And consider that Rephaim, which means giants, signifies the Pharisees and Scribes, as Ephraim did above. Indeed, for the valley of Rephaim the Seventy translated the hard valley, to express the hardness of the Jewish heart. Out of their lowliness those who shall be saved are chosen like ears among the stubble and like clusters at the vintage; and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives, or four or five. For when the smiting of the people of the Jews came, that olive tree of the people of Israel, which under Moses had six hundred thousand armed men (Num 26), and under David, when Joab numbered them, a countless people (2 Sam 24), could scarcely offer a few fruits to the Lord the Savior: two olives, Paul and Barnabas; and three olives, Peter and James and John (Acts 13), who both beheld the Lord transfigured on the mountain and were found worthy to go with the Lord to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Matt 17). The four and five olives make up the remaining nine Apostles, among whom Matthias took the place of Judas the betrayer; and these, according to a diversity of graces unknown to us, are divided into four and five olives, so that they might show in themselves the number of the Gospels and the volumes of the Law, as preachers of both Testaments (Acts 1).

17:7-8

In that day man shall bow down to his maker, and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel. And he shall not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought; they shall not look to the groves and the shrines. At that time, when from the people of Israel, to whom it was formerly said, The Lord your God has called you a fruitful olive tree (Jer 11:16), and of whom we read in the Psalms, Your children like young olive plants round about your table (Ps 127 [128]:3), the Lord in his hunger shall scarcely have found, for the drought of spiritual grace, two olives, and three, or four, or five, the fullness of the nations shall come in, and shall bow down not to idols made with hands but to its God, and looking to the Holy One of Israel they shall despise altars and groves and shrines, knowing what is written: Every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt 15:13).

17:9-10

In that day the cities of his strength shall be forsaken like ploughs and standing corn, which were forsaken before the face of the children of Israel. And it shall be desolate, because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. LXX: In that day your cities shall be forsaken, as the Amorites and the Hivites forsook them before the face of the children of Israel. And they shall be desolate, because you have forsaken God your Savior, and have not remembered the Lord your helper. As under Moses and Joshua the son of Nun the Amorites and the Hivites, and the other nations that dwelt in the land of promise, forsook their ploughshares and standing corn and the heaps in the fields and fled, lest they be seized by their enemies, so the land of Judea and all its strongest cities were forsaken by their inhabitants when the Romans laid Judea waste and besieged Jerusalem. And an apostrophe is made to the land of Judea itself, that is, to those who dwelt in it: You have suffered all these things because you have forgotten God your Savior, which means Jesus, whose coming to you the Law and the Prophets continually announced; and you have not remembered your strong helper, who was always your succour. The cause, then, of the desolate cities of Judea is forgetfulness of the Savior, who had said at the beginning of this Prophet: Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood.

17:11

Therefore you shall plant a faithful plantation, and shall sow a strange seed. In the day of your planting wild grapes, and in the morning your seed shall flower: the harvest is taken away in the day of inheritance, and he shall grieve grievously. LXX: Therefore you shall plant an unfaithful plantation and an unfaithful seed, and in the day on which you plant you shall go astray. But if you sow in the morning, it shall flower for harvest in the day of inheritance, when, as the father of a man, he gives an inheritance to his sons. Where we, following Aquila and Symmachus and the Seventy, have translated in the day of inheritance, which in Hebrew is BIOM NEHELA (ביום נחלה), one can read in the Hebrew in the worst day. And where Aquila and Theodotion translated and man shall grieve, we, taught by the Hebrews, instead of man, which in their tongue is ENOS, have rendered ANUS (אנוש), that is, grievously. Of the ambiguity of this word we shall treat more fully, if the span of this life allows, in Jeremiah, where according to the Seventy it is said: And he is a man, and who shall know him? Let me say, then, what I set out to say. Because you have forgotten, land of Judea, God your Savior, and have not remembered him who always gave you strength, therefore you shall indeed plant a faithful plantation, or as Aquila and Theodotion translated, a beautiful one, or as Symmachus, a good one, preaching one God; but you shall sow a strange seed, not receiving the Father because you do not receive the Son. For whoever believes in the Father believes also in the Son. And because you have sown the strange seed of blasphemy against Jesus in the synagogues of Satan, therefore you shall not gather the grape at the vintage, but the wild grape. And when your seed shall seem to flower, and to have some shadow of piety, while you draw men away from idols, yet when you come to gather the fruits in the day of inheritance you shall grieve grievously, seeing the people of the nations preferred to you. Whence the Apostle also says: I have great sorrow and unceasing grief in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption of sons, and the giving of the law, and the glory, and the covenant, and the promises; whose are the fathers and so on (Rom 9:2ff.). This not only Paul but every saint says, wishing that, together with the branches of the wild olive, the root too may be saved. Now that inheritance is the one we obtain from the Lord, of which the Apostle says: Now there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all in all. Someone may wonder why, where Aquila and Theodotion and Symmachus translated beautiful and good plantations, we have said a faithful plantation. The Hebrew word NEEMANIM (נאמנים), if it is written with the letter ALEPH, sounds πιστοὺς, that is, faithful; but if with AIN, and pronounced NEAMENIM נעמנים, it signifies beautiful. Hence Naomi too, whose name is written with this letter, says in Ruth (Ruth 1:20): Do not call me NOEMI (נעמי), that is, beautiful, but call me bitter.

17:12ff.

Woe to the multitude of many peoples; like the multitude of the roaring sea, and the tumult of the crowds, like the sound of many waters, they shall roar. The peoples shall roar like the multitude of overflowing waters; and he shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far off, and he shall be carried away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the tempest. At eventide, behold, trouble; in the morning, and he shall not stand. This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. Above, under the name of Damascus, we read of the calling of the nations, and the casting off of the Jews, and, through the Apostles and in the Apostles, the election of the few of the Jews who believed. And since, in comparison with the whole world and all the nations, only a small part believed of the Christian people, of whom it was said above: And the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel (for many (Matt 22:14) are called, but few are chosen); and: Not all have faith (2 Thess 3:2): now there follows in due order, not a lament, but a woe to those nations which had refused to believe and persecuted the Christian people. And they are compared to the masses of the waves and to the raging sea, which, as far as in it lies, longs to overwhelm and seize everything. For the peoples shall roar in the spectacles of theatrical licence, and in the cruelty of the amphitheatre, and in the frenzies of the circus, like the sound of overflowing waters, when with a voice concordant in impiety they blaspheme and cry that the Christians be thrown to the lions and the beasts, and other things of the kind. But while they rage like the sea, the Lord shall rebuke the author of their sedition and drive him away from his people. And as dust stirred up on the mountains is carried off the more violently the higher it is, and as a whirlwind that rises from the earth is borne aloft by a sudden tempest, so he too shall be carried off and separated from the people of God and shall flee, lest he be banished to the abyss. And when the day of consummation comes, which is what evening means, then there shall be trouble for him as he recognizes his own sins. And at morning time, that is, on the day of the resurrection, he shall not stand, which the Seventy translated shall not be. But if he shall not be, what will they answer who grant the devil repentance and, as far as in them lies, promise him the summit of an archangel? This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. These words are spoken either by the Christian people, or by the prophet in the person of the believing people: that their persecutors, who oppressed the saints of God with exiles, prisons and confiscations of goods, shall have eternal destruction and shall possess everlasting punishments.

18:1ff.

Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by the sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters: go, swift Angels, to a nation torn away and rent asunder, to a terrible people, after which there is no other, to a nation waiting, waiting and trodden down, whose land the rivers have plundered. All you inhabitants of the world, who dwell on the earth, when the sign has been lifted up on the mountains you shall see, and you shall hear the blast of the trumpet. LXX: Woe to the land of the wings of ships beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, you who send hostages by the sea, and letters of papyrus upon the water. For swift messengers shall go to a lofty nation, and to a foreign and most wicked people, which is beyond it: a nation without hope, and trodden down; now the rivers of the whole earth as a region that is inhabited: their region shall be inhabited, as if a sign were lifted up from the mountain, and the voice of the trumpet were heard. I have set down both editions in a most obscure prophecy, so that nothing may seem to be lacking to those who wish to understand what is written. And at the same time I greatly marvel at those who think that our faith and Christian hope are content with simplicity, because it is written: The commandment of God is clear, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9), and that we ought to seek nothing more than that what is commanded be done; whereas the whole of Scripture, and the Prophets especially, are wrapped in the mysteries of things to come precisely in order to rouse us to understanding, and to what is said in the Gospel: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. Since, then, I have expounded it in the fifth book according to the history and what is contained in the Hebrew, I shall now set out what seems to me according to the anagogy. A prudent reader may perhaps ask what is meant, in the Vision or Burden of Damascus, by the cymbal of wings and the other things that follow. After it had been said of the calling of the nations, of the casting off of the Jews, and of the election of those who believed through the Apostles, and afterwards of the multitude of the nations and the persecutors, who were compared to the waves of the sea, it followed that the prophetic word should also announce the heresies which have troubled the Church and lay it waste to this day, which, while the householder slept, oversowed tares in the field of the Church (Matt 13). And they are called a cymbal, as not having the love of God, according to that saying of the Apostle: If I speak with the tongues of men and of Angels, but have not love, I have become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal (1 Cor 13:1). And they are called not only a cymbal clashing with a harsh sound, but, because of the lightness of heretical speech running off in different directions, a cymbal of wings, or according to the Seventy, wings of ships, since, promising great merchandise, they sail on the waves of this world. By the wings of ships understand the sails by which they are lifted and drawn along. And he fittingly said wings of ships, for every heretic promises lofty things, and though he boasts that he has wings, he nevertheless sticks fast in the salt waves, and does not go far from land, and in mid-course suddenly suffers shipwreck. Hence Aquila translated, instead of cymbal, shadow of wings, for they do not have wings, but a likeness of wings. And what he adds, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, signifies that the heretics surpass all in their impiety. For example: Epicurus says that there is no providence, and that pleasure is the highest good. In comparison with him Marcion is more wicked, and all the heretics who tear the Old Testament to pieces. For while they admit providence, they accuse the Creator, and assert that he erred in very many of his works and did not make them as he ought to have made them: for to what benefit of men, they ask, do serpents, scorpions, crocodiles, and fleas, bugs and gnats belong? These, then, are beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and they send ambassadors on the sea of this world, that is, their disciples, who, carrying their volumes, are rightly said to carry vessels of papyrus, that is, of paper, upon the waters, which are quickly blotted out. For as books by water and damp are soon dimmed, blotted out and perish, so their speech and teaching, though at the beginning it seemed to possess some strength, passes away and slips by. And so it is said to them ironically: O Angels of the heretics, go swiftly. These the blessed apostle Paul calls false apostles, deceitful workers, who transform themselves into Apostles of Christ (2 Cor 11). And go to a nation torn away and rent asunder: torn away from God and mangled by the bites of the heretics. To a terrible people; for nothing is more terrible than blasphemy, which sets its mouth on high. After which there is no other people: for every sin, compared with blasphemy, is lighter. A nation waiting, waiting and trodden down. For all the heretics promise themselves heavenly things and pledge great things, and yet they are trodden down by demons. Whose land the rivers have plundered, rivers which have their waters not from heaven but from the earth. For what corner is there, what remotest wilderness of the earth, which the turbid speech of the heretics does not reach? And so all who inhabit and dwell in the world lift up their eyes to the sign of the heretics, which is lifted up as it were on the mountains, and hear the blast of the trumpet, that is, of their teaching. So much according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy the wings of the heretics are bewailed, which flit like ships over the sea of this world and surpass the impiety of the heathen, whom the Scripture now calls Ethiopians; and it is said to their teaching and speech: You who send books on the sea of this world, the hostages of your perversity, and letters to deceive those who will read them. Swift messengers go to a lofty nation, and to a foreign and most wicked people. For none of the churchmen has as much zeal for good as the heretics have for evil, and they think they gain a profit if they deceive others, and, being lost themselves, destroy the rest. Now the nation is called lofty on account of its pride, and foreign and most wicked because it is estranged from God. Truly a nation without hope, and trodden down, whose rivers throughout the whole earth imitate the dwelling of the Church, so that they may find themselves a lodging and a region in which to lift up the sign of their teaching, in which to sound the trumpet of the Scriptures.

18:4ff.

For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will consider in my place, as the noonday light is clear, and as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest. For before the harvest it has all blossomed, and an unripe perfection shall bud, and its twigs shall be cut off with sickles; and what is left shall be cut away and shaken off. And they shall be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth, and the birds shall be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon it. At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn away and rent asunder, from a terrible people, after which there was no other, from a nation waiting, waiting and trodden down, whose land the rivers have plundered, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion. God rests and contemplates in his place, or according to Aquila, in his firmament, that is, in the Church, of which the apostle Paul says: The pillar and firmament of truth (1 Tim 3:15). And he contemplates the things that are done in the Church, and as the noonday light is clear, so he surveys all things, according to what is said in the eighteenth Psalm, according to the anagogy, of the sun of righteousness: Nor is there anyone who can hide himself from its heat (Ps 18 [19]:7). And as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest and in the burning summer is most welcome, so the Lord refreshes the dwellers of his Church, and in his presence all things flourish. And before the time of the consummation comes, since now we know in part and prophesy in part, many will be found perfect, of whom the Apostle says: Let as many of us as are perfect be of this mind (1 Cor 13; Phil 3:15). But the twigs that are useless shall be cut off with sickles, as the Savior says in the Gospel: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take it away; and every one that bears fruit he will prune, that it may bear more fruit (John 15:2). And those that have been cut off shall be left to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth: to the birds which ravage what is sown by the wayside, and to the beasts to which the soul that does not confess God is delivered; so that whoever has been cut off and cast away by the Lord, and separated from his body, which is the Church, becomes, in summer as in winter, that is, in prosperity and adversity, the dwelling of birds and beasts. But as those who are useless and unfruitful in the Church are cut off and cast out, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump, so on the contrary it may come about that those who had been deceived by heretical error, torn away from the Lord and rent, terrible on account of blasphemy, vainly awaiting lies, trodden down by demons, and scattered by the rivers in various directions, when they remember their God and forsake their most wicked masters, may offer a gift to the Lord of hosts nowhere else but on Mount Zion, and in the watchtower, which is interpreted as the Church. We speak more briefly because we have already said much in the book of the historical explanation.

19:1

The burden of Egypt. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Egypt. LXX: The vision of Egypt. Where in the Hebrew is written MASSA MESRAIM (משא מצרים), which we have translated The burden or weight of Egypt, for which Aquila rendered ἄρμα Αἰγύπτου, we may say that because the prophet takes up and carries the yoke of the Lord, he proved worthy to behold, or to bear, the prophecy of Egypt. Hence I marvel that the Seventy, both in Babylon translated Vision for Weight, and in Philistia and Moab and Damascus Word, and now in Egypt Vision, when in the Hebrew in all these places what is set down is not Word and Vision but MASSA (משא), that is, Burden and weight. And as for Symmachus and Theodotion always translating λῆμμα, that is, a taking up, we ought to know that the prophet received spiritual grace from the Lord to know the mysteries of Egypt, or to behold them with the eyes of the mind, as the Seventy translated. But this Egypt is not the one the Jews suppose, as Josephus thought, who relates in the books of the Antiquities that the priest Onias fulfilled the oracle of Isaiah by building in the district of Heliopolis, which the Egyptians call a νομὸν, a temple after the likeness of the Temple of God, and an altar. For suppose we grant that these things were said of Onias and the altar he built in Egypt: what will be the five cities in Egypt that speak the Canaanite tongue, of which one according to the Seventy is called ἀσεδὲκ, and according to the other translators the city ARS or ARES, or the city of the sun? And who will be this savior who was sent to the Egyptians to save them, so that the Egyptians might know the Lord? When did they worship him with sacrifices and gifts, and pay their vows? When did the Lord strike Egypt and heal it? At what time shall we be able to show it happened that there was a way from Egypt to the Assyrians, and that the Assyrians entered Egypt, and the Egyptians the Assyrians, and that the Egyptians served Assur? When was Israel the third in Egypt, and among the Assyrians as a blessing in the midst of the earth, so that the Lord should say: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands the Assyrian? It is plain that these things do not belong to that Egypt which the Jews suppose. And so this place which we inhabit, and the world which lies in the evil one, we may call Egypt, especially because MESRAIM (מצרים), which is called Egypt, means ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, afflicting, or reducing to straits. Yet we must know that many things of the Burden, or Vision, of Egypt belong to the province of Egypt, which is inhabited and seen to this day. But both in this and in other places of the Scriptures very many things are set down which could not stand according to the history, so that by the necessity of the matter we are compelled to seek a higher understanding.

19:1ff.

Behold, the Lord shall go up upon a light cloud, and shall enter into Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it. And I will make the Egyptians clash against the Egyptians, and a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, kingdom against kingdom. And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken in its bowels, and I will cast down its counsel; and they shall consult their idols and their diviners, and those with familiar spirits, and the soothsayers. And I will deliver Egypt into the hands of cruel lords, and a strong king shall rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts. Most of the prophecy of Egypt, which Isaiah took up or saw, I touched upon in the historical explanation; so now, according to tropology, only the chief points are to be gathered. The Lord went up upon a light cloud, the body of the holy Virgin Mary, which was weighed down by no burden of human seed; or certainly his own body, which was conceived of the Holy Spirit. And he entered into the Egypt of this world, and at once all the idols of Egypt were moved, so that divinations and the whole fraud of idolatry, which held possession of a deceived world, felt itself broken; so much so that the magi from the East, taught by the demons, or understanding from the prophecy of Balaam (Num 24) that the Son of God was born who would destroy all the power of their art, came to Bethlehem, and, the star showing the way, worshipped the child (Matt 2). Then the whole heart of Egypt melted, and Egyptians rose against Egyptians, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth; I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (Matt 10:34ff.). At that time this too was fulfilled: A man's enemies are those of his own household (Mic 7:6). And a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend. For in one house they were divided, two against three and three against two, and father was divided against Son and son against father, city against city and kingdom against kingdom: those who did not believe against those who believed, or else those who believed, longing to save their neighbours. And the spirit of Egypt was broken in its bowels, so that they were no longer of one mind; but, separated against themselves by the spiritual sword, they came to know that all their counsel had been cast down; and nonetheless, remaining in their former error, those who had refused to receive the truth of the faith consulted their idols and their diviners, and those with familiar spirits, and the soothsayers. And when they had done this, the Lord delivered them into the hand of cruel lords, according to that saying of the Apostle: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1:20), so that, oppressed by that hardest servitude, they may return to the most merciful Lord. And fittingly he calls the demons cruel lords, for nothing is crueller than they. The strong king also, who is their lord, is plainly understood as the devil, whom the Lord in the Gospel too calls the strong man; and when he is bound and overpowered, the vessels of his house and the spoil are plundered.

19:5ff.

And the water shall dry up from the sea, and the river shall be laid waste and dried up, and the rivers shall fail; the streams of the embankments shall be diminished and dried up. The reed and the rush shall wither; the bed of the stream shall be laid bare from its source, and every watered sowing shall be dried up; it shall wither and shall not be. And the fishers shall mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river shall lament, and those who spread a net upon the face of the water, and they shall wither away. And those who work flax shall be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine things, and its watered places shall be drooping, all who made pools to catch fish. Foolish are the princes of Tanis; the wise counsellors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel. When the strong king, the harsh one, has ruled in Egypt, all the learning and beauty of worldly eloquence shall dry up, and the devil himself, the source of all the rivers, from whom all lies spring, shall be laid waste, so that the other rivers and streams, which used to be filled from the turbid waters of the Nile, shall fail. The reed and the rush too shall wither from excessive drought. For rush the Seventy translated papyrus, from which paper is made, adding of their own green achi, which is not found in the Hebrew. And when I asked learned men what this word signified, I heard that the Egyptians in their own tongue call by this name everything green that grows in a marsh. Now the reed, according to tropology, is empty speech, having nothing solid in itself; and the papyrus is that which seems indeed to have pith and is not empty, and yet is fragile and quickly withers. All the streams too, once the head of the streams has dried up, shall be dried up, and whatever was formerly watered by the Egyptian waters shall be dried up and shall not be; so that the fishers of Egypt shall mourn, who are utterly opposed to the fishers of the Lord, and those shall lament who used to cast a hook into the river and spread a net upon the face of the water. Those who deceive people one at a time cast a hook into the turbid waters; but those who deceive many at once, speaking publicly in the synagogues of Satan and leading away whole flocks of the peoples, cast a net upon the Egyptian waters. Those too shall be confounded who used to work flax to make the vestments of the priests, plaiting it and weaving fine things, which belongs properly to the art of the dialecticians. For fine things the Seventy translated byssus, which itself also is woven into the vestments of the priests. And what follows, And its watered places shall be drooping, all who made pools to catch fish, signifies that all the snares of the fishers of Egypt shall be destroyed and perish. Where we, following the sense, have translated pools made to catch fish, both in the Hebrew and in all the translators souls are set in place of fish, so that we may be drawn from the history to tropology: namely, that these fishers who made pools and pits made them for this purpose, to ensnare souls in them. It should be noted that for pools the Seventy translated ζύθον, which is a kind of drink made from grain and water, and is commonly called sabaium in the provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia, in the heathen and barbarian speech. The Egyptians use this most of all, so that they give those who drink not pure waters but turbid ones, like dregs mixed in; so that by a drink of this kind is shown the teaching of heretical depravity. Then the princes of Tanis shall be foolish, which means a lowly command. For all the heretics teach a lowliness contrary to loftiness, and drag men down to the underworld, and are princes of a lowly and abject command. The counsellors too of Pharaoh, who is the king of Egypt, and is rightly rendered scatterer and divided, and separated into various parts, shall be convicted of having given foolish counsel, when the Lord destroys the wisdom of the wise and rejects the understanding of the prudent (1 Cor 1).

19:12ff.

How do you say to Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you, and declare what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools, the princes of Memphis have withered; they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples. The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of giddiness, and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man errs and vomits. And there shall be no work for Egypt which may make the head and the tail, bending and curbing. The heretics are accustomed to say to their king, or Pharaoh: We are sons of the wise, who handed down the Apostolic teaching to us from the beginning; we are sons of ancient kings, who are called the kings of the philosophers, and we have the knowledge of the Scriptures joined to worldly wisdom. These he now asks, or the very king of the heretics, where are his wise men who despised the simplicity of the Church; and he compels them to answer what the Lord Sabaoth has purposed concerning the Egypt of this world, and what he will do at the consummation. The princes of Tanis, who held the lowly command of the heretics, are proved to be fools. All the princes of Memphis have withered, who were tainted with the boasting of eloquence and of the mouth. For Memphis means mouth or from the mouth, and μεταφορικῶς signifies speech. And what follows: They have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples, or according to the Seventy: they shall deceive Egypt by tribes, signifies that the kingdom of worldly wisdom is shown to be foolish, and the princes of the several doctrines, who are interpreted as the tribes, are convicted of having had foolish teachers. For the Lord has mingled for them a spirit of giddiness, or of errors, according to what is written: And as they did not see fit to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate mind (Rom 1:28). And as he who is holy can say with Isaiah, We shall make the spirit of your salvation upon the earth, so he who is a sinner will make a spirit of error, that is, a spirit of wickedness, according to what we read also in Jeremiah: Your own transgression shall reprove you, and your wickedness shall rebuke you (Jer 2:19). But if the heretic who does not receive the Old Testament is scandalized that the Lord is said to mingle a spirit of error or of giddiness, let him hear what is written in the Apostle, that is, in the New Testament: God delivered them up in the desires of their heart to uncleanness (Rom 1:24). And again: For this reason God delivered them up to passions of ignominy. And again: God delivered them up to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting. Now they are delivered up in the desires of their heart because they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things. This we read not only in the Epistle to the Romans, but also in that to the Thessalonians concerning Antichrist: Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, God shall send them the working of error, that they may believe a lie, and that all may be judged who did not believe the truth, but took pleasure in the lie (2 Thess 2:10); which I think the apostle Paul took from the present reading of Isaiah, in which he says: The Lord has mingled for them a spirit of error, and they have made Egypt err in all its works, as, he says, a drunken man errs and vomits, one who is drunk with vices. Of such drunkards Joel speaks: Woe to those who are drunk without wine. And not only drunk, but also vomiting the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps; so that, after they have vomited up wine of this kind, they may understand their drunkenness, and recognize that as long as they were drunk they had neither beginning nor end, that is, neither head nor tail, but were an animal maimed at both ends. For beginning and end, as both Symmachus and the Seventy translated, Theodotion, after his custom, set down the Hebrew words themselves, CHAPHPHE (כפה) and AGMON (אגמון), which Aquila translated bent and perverse: wishing old men to be understood by bent, and by perverse wanton boys, who do everything perversely; and hence the sense is that in Egypt not only head and tail are lacking, but also old men and boys, that is, both beginning and end.

19:16-17

In that day Egypt shall be like women, and shall be amazed, and shall fear before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he shall shake over it. And the land of Judah shall be a festival to Egypt; everyone who remembers it shall tremble before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has purposed concerning it. At that time (for that, as we have often said, is what day signifies), when the Lord has mingled a spirit of error and giddiness, so that Egypt vomits up the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, understanding its error and its former drunkenness, Egypt shall fear like a woman: not with the chance fear that is wont to befall men, whom Egypt does not love but strangles and kills, but with the fear of women, whom alone Pharaoh wishes to live. And it shall fear the shaking, or lifting up, of the hand of the Lord, by which punishments are signified, which he will shake and lift up to strike Egypt. Then the land of Judah, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, the Law and the Prophets, the Gospels and the epistles of the Apostles, shall be a festival to Egypt, if it comes to know them; or a fear, if by comparison with their teaching and truth it understands that it has held a lie. Everyone who remembers this land shall tremble with that trembling which leads to life: For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Prov 9:10). And we can take this not only of the consummation of the world, but of the present time as well: that every heretic fears a churchman learned in heavenly teachings, and is terrified at the remembrance of him. And he shall fear and tremble at the counsel of the Lord, which he has purposed concerning the Egypt of this world. We run through each point briefly, so as to pass on to the rest.

19:18

In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue, and swearing by the Lord of hosts: one shall be called the city of the sun. The hand of the Lord lifted up or shaken over Egypt is of great profit, so that the land of Judah becomes a fear to it, and everyone who remembers it trembles. At that time five cities in the land of Egypt shall speak the tongue of Canaan, which most of our writers understand as the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. When we look on a woman to lust after her, our sight speaks the Egyptian tongue. When we hear a judgment of blood, though the Lord says, You shall not receive a vain report (Exod 23:1, LXX), our hearing speaks the Egyptian tongue. When, according to the prophet, we live in delights, and lie upon beds of ivory, and are anointed with the chief ointments, our smell speaks the Egyptian tongue. When our belly is our god (Phil 3), our taste speaks the Egyptian tongue. If we do not hear what the Apostle says, It is good for a man not to touch a woman (1 Cor 7), but on the contrary are joined to a harlot, our touch speaks the Egyptian tongue. But if, on the contrary, we lift up our eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvest, and are no longer bent toward the earth, but, like the woman in the Gospel who for eighteen years could not look up at heaven (Luke 13), lift up our eyes and say, To you have I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens (Ps 122 [123]:1), our eye and sight speaks the Canaanite tongue. If we circumcise our ears and hear the Lord saying, He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8), our hearing speaks the Canaanite tongue. Whoever can say to the bridegroom, We run after you in the fragrance of your ointments (Song 1:3), and, We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place (2 Cor 2:15), his smell speaks the Canaanite tongue. Taste too is taken in a good sense, of him who eats the bread that comes down from heaven, the living bread and not the dead, and who hears that saying, Taste and see how sweet the Lord is (Ps 33 [34]:9): at once it speaks the Canaanite tongue. And there is a spiritual touch also, of which the apostle John says, Our hands have handled of the Word of life (1 John 1:1); and he has it who touches Jesus by faith, so that the Savior can say of him, Someone has touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me (Luke 8:46). We have learned how great the good things are which the uplifted hand of the Lord bestows; let us ask why the five cities of Egypt speak not the Hebrew tongue but the Canaanite tongue. To this we shall try to answer thus. Hebrew sounds περάτην, that is, one who passes over, who passes from place to place. Therefore we too, though we be saints, as long as we are in Egypt and live in the darkness of this world, cannot speak the Hebrew tongue, but the Canaanite tongue, which is midway between the Egyptian and the Hebrew, and for the most part borders on the Hebrew. Canaan means as it were a moving, or as it were answering. When, therefore, we withdraw from Egypt and wish to go out from the power of Pharaoh, so that our land and our confession are fearsome to Egypt, then we are moved and as it were answer to the will of the Lord; and yet, because we are still in the present world, we cannot yet speak the Hebrew tongue. And what follows, five cities swear by the Lord of hosts, signifies that even while placed here we call to mind not demons but almighty God. Of these five cities, the names of the other four being passed over in silence, one is called the city of the sun, which seems to me to refer to sight. For as a city needs the sun and the moon in order to be seen, so we need the sun of righteousness in order that our eyes may be enlightened.

19:19, 21

In that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar of the Lord at its border. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he shall send them a Savior and a defender to deliver them; and the Lord shall be known by Egypt. In sequence to what he had said above, In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue, and swearing by the Lord of hosts, there now follows: There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, which Onias, according to Josephus (Antiquities, book 13, ch. 6), misunderstanding it, tried to fulfil. And the title of the Lord containing his passion, on which was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters, Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews (John 19), for a sign of the Cross, and for a witness to all the nations, which are now called Egypt. And when persecution has grown at the hands of those who afflict the Christian name, then they shall cry in their hearts: Abba, Father (Rom 8). And the Lord of hosts shall send a Savior, that is, Jesus, and a Judge, or defender, to deliver them, so that, delivered, they may know the Lord, and themselves be known by the Lord; and where sin abounded, grace may abound the more (Rom 5). Now one altar of Egypt, that is, of this world, is spoken of, so that we may know that all the altars which are raised up against the altar of the Church are not the Lord's. In the book of the Historical Explanation we said that, up to the end of the vision of Egypt, since the prophecy was manifest, all things are to be referred to Christ.

19:20

And the Egyptians shall know the Lord in that day, and shall worship him with sacrifices and gifts, and they shall vow vows to the Lord and pay them. And the Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague, and shall heal it; and they shall return to the Lord, and he shall be appeased toward them, and shall heal them. After the Egyptians have come to know the Lord, they shall worship him with spiritual sacrifices and gifts; and they shall vow vows to the Lord and pay them, and shall say with David: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit (Ps 50 [51]:19), and: The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice (Ps 140 [141]:2); when, believing in the Nazarene, they themselves have become Nazirites, drinking neither wine nor strong drink (John 19), nor the vinegar which was offered to the Lord to drink, nor whatever is made from the grape of Sodom. And when they have paid their vows with Abel, and God has had regard to them, the elder brother Cain, that is, the people of the Circumcision, will envy, and will shed Christian blood, which shall cry out to the Lord (Gen 4); and therefore he shall go out from the face of God, saying of the Savior: Crucify, crucify him (Luke 23:21), and: We have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). He who is holy in body and spirit offers a vow and pays it to the Lord. Zacchaeus too offered a vow, who promised half of his substance to the poor (Luke 19). It is asked: if a savior and defender was sent to the Egyptians to deliver them from their straits, how is it now said, The Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague? But let us consider what follows: And he shall heal it. For whom the Lord loves he chastens (Heb 12). And the Savior himself in Psalm 68 (69) says to the Father: For they have persecuted him whom you struck, and they have added to the pain of my wounds (Ps 68 [69]:27). If, then, he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us, that by his bruise and wounds we might be healed (Rom 8), the Lord delivered up the martyrs too to suffering, but he will heal them again in the resurrection, so that by their wounds the faith of believers may be confirmed. Hence it is said also to Job: Do you think that I spoke to you otherwise than that you might appear righteous? For he himself causes pain and restores to former health; and he visits his servants with the rod, so as not to take away his mercy from them. Hence the daughters and daughters-in-law who have sinned greatly, and have spread their feet to everyone who passed by, are not visited or chastened, for the Lord says: I will not visit your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery (Hos 4:14). The Lord, then, strikes the Egyptians, not with fire, not with the sword, but with the rod. For what son is there whom his father does not train? So that, after they have been healed, they may return to the Lord, and he may be appeased toward them, and heal them once more. For we always need the mercy of God, and there is no end to his clemency.

19:23

In that day there shall be a way from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian shall enter into Egypt, and the Egyptian into the Assyrians; and the Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians. As we have shown that the other things which go before befell the Egyptians in a good sense, namely, five cities in their land speaking the Canaanite tongue and swearing by the Lord, and the altar of the Lord set in the midst of the land of Egypt, and the pillar, and the witness, and the sign, and the savior who should deliver them; and that the Lord should be known by the Egyptians, and they themselves should know him; and that they should offer sacrifices and gifts, and pay their vows, and, being struck, be healed, and return to the Lord, and he be appeased toward them, and they be healed again: so this too which follows, that the Egyptians serve the Assyrians, is to be taken in a good sense. For the Apostle too serves believers, that he may gain them (1 Cor 9). And Esau is made subject to his brother Jacob (Gen 33), that he may become a sharer in his blessings. Therefore those from the nations who are saved first, and have the altar of the Lord within them, will by their service save those who persist in hardness; and by mingling and fellowship with them they will themselves go to the Assyrians, in order to lead the Assyrians to Egypt, and so that afterwards they may be able to reach the people of Israel. For this reason, I think, the believing wife too serves the unbelieving husband, so that little by little she may draw him from Egypt and from the Assyrians to Judea.

19:25-26

In that day Israel shall be the third to the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands the Assyrian; but my inheritance is Israel. Israel shall be the third in Egypt and among the Assyrians, that he may mingle the whole lump with the leaven of his blessing, and that those who formerly were at hostile variance with one another may be joined together by this clasp of blessing; and that Egypt may be the people of God, and the Assyrian the work of his hands, but Israel his inheritance. The Egyptian is blessed by the Lord, because he is blessed through fellowship with Israel. And the Assyrian is the work of his hands, because in him he has shown his clemency. But Israel alone can say: The Lord is my portion (Lam 3:24), he who beholds God with the mind, and is called his inheritance.

20:1ff.

In the year that Tartan came into Ashdod, when Sargon the king of the Assyrians had sent him, and he had fought against Ashdod and had taken it, at that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying: Go, and loose the sackcloth from your loins, and take your shoes off your feet. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot. And the Lord said: As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent of three years upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia. So shall the king of the Assyrians lead away the captivity of Egypt and the exile of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their hope, and of Egypt their glory. And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day: Was this our hope, to whom we fled for help, that they might deliver us from the face of the king of the Assyrians? And how shall we be able to escape? For Tartan the Seventy translated Thanatan, and for Sargon, Arna: what these mean we cannot know. For we cannot invent false etymologies for false names. Now these are not Hebrew names but Assyrian, and of them we have learned that they sound thus: Tartan, he gave a tower, or superfluous, or putting far off; and Sargon prince of the garden. This king of Assyria, whom we read of above as the great mind, has very many generals, of whom one is Tartan, lifted up in pride, and going far in wickedness, and greater than the rest; and he is sent to attack Ashdod, which in Hebrew is called ASDOD (אשדוד), and means fire of generation; and the general of the king of Assyria overcomes those who serve generation and lust. And the king of the Assyrians, Sargon, prince of gardens, is fittingly said to be given over to pleasure and luxury. Indeed Ahab king of Israel too desired to turn the vineyard of Naboth into a garden (1 Kgs 21); and Naboth, understanding this according to the laws of tropology, chose to die rather than do it, lest his father's inheritance and ancient possession be turned into the delights of an impious king. Now the Prophet is commanded to lay aside the sackcloth and the shoes and walk naked and barefoot, and to be a sign and portent to the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, who persecuted the people of God and were made low on account of their pride. For Egypt means persecuting or afflicting; Ethiopians, lowly and cast down; for everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled (Luke 14:11). These are to be led into captivity and to suffer torments of three years (Exod 12), of which years we read in the Psalms: I thought upon the days of old, and I had the eternal years in mind (Ps 76 [77]:6). Let us not think these are small punishments, but punishments drawn out over long ages. And in that very captivity and exile of Egypt shall go the young and the old, who have been hardened in wickedness and have come to the vices of full age: naked, so that all their crimes may be laid bare (for nothing (Luke 8:17) is hidden that shall not be revealed), and barefoot, because they will not be able to eat the Passover of the Lord; for whoever eats it has his loins girded, and holds a staff in his hand, and stands with shod feet, lest, passing through the wilderness of this world, he be bitten by serpents (Exod 12). Then their buttocks, through which dung is voided, shall be uncovered, and all the shame of Egypt shall be shown, so that those shall be confounded who had their hope in Egypt and in Ethiopia, and shall see their glory changed into confusion; so much so that the inhabitant of this isle, that is, of the world, who is not a stranger and a sojourner, but longed to have a perpetual possession of the world, shall say in his confusion: Is this Egypt, and is this Ethiopia, whose help we hoped for, that they might deliver us from the prince of this world? How then shall we be able to escape, when those in whom we had our hope are taken captive? And this is to be noted, that before Ashdod is taken the Prophet is clothed in sackcloth and has his feet shod, so that he may indeed lament those who have been wounded by the fiery darts of the devil and serve lust, but may nonetheless himself go shod, so as to be able to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and walk safely through the desert of this world, in which there are serpents and scorpions and thirst for good things. But after Ashdod has been taken, as a type of the captivity of Egypt and the exile of Ethiopia, he walks barefoot and naked. For in the holy Land, to which he hastens to go, he could neither stand nor walk clothed in sackcloth and with his feet covered with skin, for the Lord says: Loose the shoe from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground (Exod 3:5).

21:1ff.

The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds come from the south-west, it comes from the desert, from a terrible land. A hard vision has been told to me: he who is unbelieving deals faithlessly, and he who is a spoiler lays waste. Go up, Elam; besiege, O Mede: I have made all its groaning to cease. Therefore my loins are filled with pain; anguish has taken hold of me, like the anguish of a woman in labour. LXX: The vision of the desert of the sea. As a tempest passes through from the desert, coming from the desert. From a terrible land a hard vision has been announced to me: the transgressor transgresses, and the wicked man does wickedly. Against me come the Elamites and the ambassadors of the Persians: now I shall groan, and comfort myself; therefore my loins are filled with anguish, pains have seized me, as a woman in labour. What we think according to the History we have said briefly; now let us gather the chief points of tropology. The vision, or weight, is seen against the sea of this world; and it is seen by the Prophet with how many temptations this world is filled. That the world is called the sea (to pass over many things), I am content with a single testimony of the Psalm: They who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters, these have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep (Ps 106 [107]:23). For those who do the work of God in this world, and say with the Prophet, I have come into the depth of the sea, see his wonders in the deep; and, delivered from temptations and straits, they say that they have heard a terrible and hard vision. Now this very tempest comes from the desert, in which the Lord too was tempted (Matt 4), and Israel lay open to the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions (Num 21). And when it has come, it passes through and goes by; and then he who endures it understands that none transgresses but the transgressor, and none does wickedly but the wicked. That we are overwhelmed, then, by the waves of the sea, and that a savage tempest overpowers us, is our own fault, who were transgressors and wicked before the tempest. And what he says, Against me come the Elamites and the ambassadors of the Persians, has this sense: Elamites means despisers; Persians, tempters. Let those come, then, who are wont to despise, to scorn and to tempt: but I shall groan, and my groaning will be my consolation. But my loins too are filled with anguish, and pains have taken hold of me as of a woman in labour, so that from the fear of the Lord I may conceive and bring forth, and make the spirit of his salvation upon the earth. And rightly, according to the Hebrew, whirlwinds and tempests come from the desert and from a terrible land, where God is not the inhabitant, and where all things are earthly; and whoever is unbelieving does a thing in keeping with his faithlessness, and he who is a spoiler lays waste. Hence he speaks boldly against his adversaries: Go up, Elam; besiege, O Mede: I have made all the groaning of the desert of the sea, and of the terrible land, and of the hardest vision that has been told, to cease. For my loins, doing penance, are full no longer of pleasure, as before, but of pain; and I shall no longer say: My loins are filled with illusions (Ps 37 [38]:7). For anguish and tribulation have taken hold of me, as it is wont to hold a woman in labour. The common edition and the Hebrew differ greatly from each other in this place; therefore we shall touch briefly on both, lest we leave the φιλεγκλημῶσιν some little occasion of carping at us.

21:4-5

I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw; my heart withered, darkness stupefied me; Babylon my beloved has been made a wonder to me. Set the table, behold in the watchtower those who eat and drink: rise up, princes, seize the shield. LXX: I did wickedly so as not to hear, I hastened so as not to see; my heart goes astray, iniquity has overflowed upon me; my soul stands fast in fear. Prepare the table, watch the watchtower: eat, drink; rise up, princes, prepare the shields. At the hearing and at the hardest vision which the Prophet saw coming from the desert of the sea, he says that he fell down and was troubled, and that with his eyes almost darkened and his mind stupefied he did not know what he was seeing.
