For that Babylon (for which Aquila and Theodotion translated darkness, to signify this world, which lies in the evil one (1 John 5), and whose princes, according to the apostle Paul (Eph 6), are the rulers of this darkness), which was once dear either to the Prophet or to God, has become a wonder in its overthrow. Hence the Prophet is commanded, eating at the table of the Lord and filled with his food, to contemplate more carefully what is to come upon the world; and through him it is said to all believers that, eating and drinking the body and blood of the Lord, they should be turned into princes of the Church, and hear with the Apostles, Rise up, and seize the shield of faith from the armour of the apostle Paul (Eph 6), with which they may quench the fiery darts of the devil. This according to the Hebrew and the interpretation begun concerning the world. Let us pass on to the edition of the Seventy, which differs greatly from the foregoing. The Prophet reproves himself, or rather in his own person confesses the error of others, who, following the letter that kills, despise the spirit that gives life; and he says that he did wickedly so as not to hear the law spiritually, but on the contrary hastened not to see the mysteries of God, and did not say with David: Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law (Ps 118 [119]:18). Therefore his heart goes astray, and, filled with Jewish superstition, stands fast not in the love of God but in fear, so that he has the spirit of bondage in fear, and by no means the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8). Hence he is commanded to come to the table of spiritual food, and that all who follow his example should eat and drink at it; and that, having scorned the old error, those who lay in the letter should rise up in the spirit and become princes, and say with the Prophet: Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will (Ps 5:13).

21:6-7

For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and let him declare whatever he sees. And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; and he gazed diligently with much attention, and a lion cried out. LXX: For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set for yourself a watchman, and whatever you see, declare it. And I saw two horsemen riding, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; I heard much hearing, and I called Uriah to the watchtower. The Prophet is bidden to set a watchman in his heart, and to gaze more carefully at what is to come upon the world; and he saw two horsemen, a rider on an ass and a rider on a camel. These someone has interpreted so as to call the rider on the ass, according to the Gospel reading (Matt 21) and the prophecy of Zechariah (Zech 9), Christ; and on the contrary the rider on the camel the opposing power, on account of the foulness of that crooked animal. Others again refer the two riders, of the letter and of the spirit, to the two Testaments. And for what is said in the Hebrew, ARIE (אריה), for which Aquila and Symmachus translated lion and lioness, the Seventy, meaning I know not what, set down οὐρίαν, which a certain man thinks is to be interpreted light of the Lord, though light of the Lord, which is not found here, is written with other letters, and lion, which is read here, with others. And he would have this watchman, whom the Prophet is bidden to set in his heart, be called Uriah, and by the interpretation of the name he refers it to the understanding of Christ, so that, with him dwelling in us, we may be able to see what is to come. This indeed could also be fitted to the lion, since Jacob (Gen 49) and Balaam (Num 23 and 2) name the lion under the mystery of Christ.

21:8, 10

I am upon the watchtower of the Lord, standing continually by day, and I am upon my guard, standing whole nights. Behold, this man comes, the rider of a chariot of horsemen, and he answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken to the ground. My threshing, and the sons of my floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you. LXX: The Lord said: I stood all day, and upon the camp I stood all night; and behold, he comes, the rider of a chariot, and answering he said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all her idols and the things made with hands are broken to the ground. Hear, you who are left and are grieving; hear what I have heard from the Lord Sabaoth; the God of Israel has declared it to us. The Prophet stands on the watchtower of the Lord, and, set in his light, looks forward to what is to come. And this is the guard he keeps, this the office entrusted to him: to see, in the darkness of this world, what is to come. Behold, he says, this man comes, signifying by what follows that he saw the Lord the Savior coming, seated on a chariot of two, and yoking to one car two horses, or rather two animals, the ass and the camel. And this rider of the chariot answered the Prophet, who longed and desired to hear his words, and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, the confusion of the whole world; it fell at my coming, when I took a human body, and it will utterly collapse at the consummation of the world. And all her graven images are broken to the ground. For which the Seventy translated idols and things made with hands, signifying the scripture of the heretics and the various errors of heresies, who are makers of idols and worship what they have fashioned out of their own heart. And what follows, in the person of the Prophet saying, My threshing, and the sons of my floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you, has this sense according to the Hebrew: O people, who are to be stored in my granaries, whom I have therefore threshed in various straits, that I might shake the chaff from you, and the purest wheat might be stored in my granaries: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, is to come upon the whole world, this I have declared to all of you who are in the world. Others again say that the person is still the earlier one, namely the Lord the Savior, and that he himself speaks to the Apostles: What I have heard from the Father I have declared to you (John 15:15). And since in place of this the Seventy read, hear, you who are left and are grieving, this seems to me the sense according to their translation: O Apostles, of whom Isaiah writes, Unless the Lord had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9), whose remnant the Apostle too, writing to the Romans, teaches has been saved (Rom 9): you who were left of the people of the Jews that you might be saved, and grieve over the perdition of your nation, of which we read elsewhere also, There is sorrow in my heart, and continual grief for my brethren, who are Israelites according to the flesh (Rom 9:2, 3): these things which I have heard from God the Father I declare to you, which the God of Israel foretells to you as things to come.

21:11-12

The burden of Dumah: he calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said: The morning comes, and the night. If you seek, seek; turn, and come. LXX: The vision of Idumea: he calls to me out of Seir: Guard the ramparts; I keep guard morning and night; if you seek, seek, and dwell with me. The Hebrew word ELAI (אלי), which all have translated to me, if you choose to read it ELI, means my God or my strong one. And what we have rendered he calls or he summons, that is, καλεῖ, may, by the ambiguity of the Hebrew and the Greek speech, be read call! or summon!; and the sense is: God, who is my watchman, calls me day and night to repentance, so that, leaving Seir, which means shaggy and hairy, I may return and dwell with him. Dumah sounds either likeness or silence; but Idumea is rendered earthly. The Lord therefore speaks to the choir of the Apostles and commands it: Call to me those who are of Seir, so that the multitude of the nations may serve me, which, after the likeness of Esau, has nothing in itself soft and smooth and sleek, but is shaggy, wild, intractable. And you, O Apostles, after you have called the nations to me out of Seir, guard the ramparts of the Church, lest the enemy break in easily; lest the lion, roaring and going about, seeking an entrance by which he may get in, tear and scatter the flock shut up in the Church. And the multitude of the Church answered: Not only in prosperity but in adversity, that is, both by day and by night, I will keep your commandments, O God. To her God says: If you truly seek me, show by your works that you seek me; and let it not suffice you to have sought once, but seek always him whom you have found; and to hold him more perfectly, forget your people and your father's house, and, having forsaken the error of the Gentiles, abide with me in the Church. This we would say according to the Seventy, who put in the title the vision of Idumea, that is, of the earthly, to show that those are called who formerly served earthly works. Further, according to Aquila, who set down Dumah, that is, silence, or likeness, we can understand it thus: that the multitude of the nations is roused to the likeness of the people of Israel, and that where formerly there was silence of the law of God, there the cry of confession should be, and the wild olive be grafted into the good olive. We read also in the parable of the Gospel that servants were sent to call good and bad, and to fill the householder's banquet with whomsoever they found, because the first guests refused to come (Matt 22). The Church too can relate that the Lord cries aloud to her out of Seir, that is, out of earthly places, and calls her forth to salvation; and she may say to the Lord himself: O watchman, why, rising by night, do you dwell in darkness? Why are you, without sin, in the flesh of sin? For what reason did you will to take a human body? The watchman answered, that is, the Samaritan, who in the Gospel carried the wounded man on his shoulders to the inn (Luke 10): The morning comes, and the night. And the sense is: For the multitude of the nations the sun of righteousness has risen, and for the Jews darkness has come; according to what is said by the Lord: For the judgment of this world I have come, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9:39). And the watchman himself, who had said, The morning comes, and the night, speaks to the multitude of the nations: If you seek me, seek more earnestly. Turn to me, you returning sons, and I will heal your bruises; and come to me. The passages are difficult, and since according to the history they are by no means plain, we are compelled to follow various opinions according to the ἀναγωγὴν.

21:13

The burden in Arabia. This is not found in the edition of the Seventy Translators; but what follows, In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the paths of Dodanim, is joined to the preceding vision, so that it reads, if you seek, seek, and dwell with me in the forest. Arabia in our tongue sounds evening, which is the beginning of night and of darkness; and everyone who has the beginning of sins dwells in the evening. But he who comes to the height of them stands in the middle of the night. Hence in Egypt too the firstborn are slain at midnight (Exod 12). And the apostle Peter denied the Lord three times before the cock crew, which is understood as midnight (Matt 26); but after the night was far spent and the day began to draw near, when the darkness of midnight had been overcome and the cock, herald of the light, sounded, he wept bitterly and understood his sin, and at that time he could say: In the evening weeping shall linger, and in the morning gladness (Ps 29 [30]:6). So much meanwhile on the present place. But the name of Arabia, that is, of evening and of the West, receives different meanings in other places of the Scriptures.

In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. LXX: In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the way of Dedan. Those who have begun to be in wickedness, and are entering on the way of sins, do not sleep or linger in sown fields and fallow lands, nor in meadows and cornfields, which the Savior teaches are white for harvest, nor among fruit-bearing trees, but in fruitless forests, where there are brambles and thorns and where beasts dwell. Of such a forest we read also in the volume of Kings, that the wood or forest devoured more than were slain by the sword, when Absalom rose up as a rebel against his father (2 Sam 18). And rightly, since evening is the beginning of evils, they are said to dwell in the way and in the paths, and in the way of Dedan, which means judgments. For as many kinds of sins as they have, so many sentences of judgment do they deserve. But Dedan can also be interpreted great judgment.

21:14-15

Coming to meet the thirsty, bring water, you who inhabit the land of the South; meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of the swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the bent bow, from the face of the grievous battle. LXX: To meet the thirsty bring water, you who dwell in the region of Teman; meet those who flee with bread, because of the multitude of the slain, because of the throng of those who go astray, because of the multitude of the sword, and because of the multitude of the bent bows, and because of the multitude of those who fall in war. You who are in Teman, which means South and perfection, and who dwell in that place of which it is written, God shall come from the South (Hab 3:3), and who are consummated and perfect, and have within you the light of the knowledge of the Scriptures: meet those who flee from Arabia and from the forest with water and bread, and do not wait until they come to you, but imitate that father of the Gospel parable who ran to meet his returning son. And he indeed gave the robe and offered the ring (Luke 15); but you, offer water and bread to those who flee, so that those who were weary and spent may be sustained by your mercy and pass the more quickly to your dwellings. For they have fled the swords of the heretics, the teaching of the Gentiles, the blasphemies of the Jews. And because they have seen many slain by their darts, and very many fallen in battle, they themselves long to be delivered by your help. This place may properly be understood as directed against those who, giving themselves to leisure and sloth, are content with their own salvation and do not stretch out a hand to the penitent and converted.

21:16-17

For thus says the Lord to me: Yet within one year, as in the year of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar shall be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the children of Kedar shall be diminished. For the Lord God of Israel has spoken. I tell you to meet with water and bread those who flee from the forest and from Arabia because the Lord has promised that these things shall be. As the year of a hireling passes quickly, who every day looks for nothing but the wage of his labour, or certainly is always at work and toil in order to receive the wage of his labour, so all the glory of Kedar, which means darkness, of which we read in the Psalm too, I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar (Ps 119 [120]:5), shall swiftly be taken away; and the whole number of the archers, that is, of the various doctrines, which used to wound those placed in the forest of Arabia, shall be brought to nothing, once those fleeing from the forest have been delivered, and have received the water of saving baptism, and have eaten the heavenly bread. For the Lord of all, and properly the God of Israel, that is, of those who behold God with the mind, has spoken that these things shall be.

22:1

The burden of the valley of vision. LXX: The word of the valley of Zion. In the book of Hebrew Names we have set down that Zion means watchtower, which, set on high places, beholds from afar the things that are coming. Since, then, Zion, according to the laws of tropology, is referred to the Church, as in that saying of the second Psalm in the person of the Lord the Savior, But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain (Ps 2:6); and, Those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion (Ps 124 [125]:1); and, The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:2); and more plainly the Apostle: You have come, he says, to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22): we ask why in the present vision it is called the valley of Zion. And by the very sequence of the words we are drawn to a spiritual understanding: that we should know that all the princes of perverse doctrines, who have fallen from the loftiness of the sense of the holy Scriptures and have rolled down to low things, dwell in the valley of Zion. Something of this kind I think Solomon too says in the Proverbs: The eye that mocks its father and despises the old age of its mother, let the ravens of the valleys dig it out, and the young eagles eat it (Prov 30:17). For as soon as the mind of the heretics has mocked the Creator, the Father, and despised the old age of the Church, its mother, it is dug out by foul and unclean birds, which are referred to the opposing powers. Nor can such men say, I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me (Ps 120 [121]:1); but, like brute beasts, they are bowed down to earthly things.

What is the matter with you also, that you too have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops? LXX: What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up onto vain housetops? That which, according to the Seventy translators, is asked in the volume of Kings, what is meant when Elisha says (2 Kgs 2:14), Where is the God of Elijah APHPHO (אפא), is set down more plainly in the present place: where the Seventy translated now, the Hebrew has APHPHO, which we have translated now also; and Aquila, wishing to preserve the Hebrew idiom, set down καίπερτοι, a conjunction which the Latin tongue cannot render. And when he says, What is the matter with you also?, he asks why she too goes up among the others, and, with the reputation of lofty things, abides in low ones. And the sense is: Since the Philosophers are puffed up, and all worldly wisdom, disputing about lofty things, despises the simplicity of the Church, why do you too pursue high things? These the Seventy, σημαντικώτερον, translated δώματα μάταια, that is, vain housetops, to show that there is also another housetop, from which the Savior forbids us to come down (Matt 24), which is not, however, a vain housetop. Indeed the apostle Peter too went up onto the housetop at the sixth hour of prayer (Acts 10). But now, to show the great variety of heresies, he has named not one housetop but very many housetops.

22:2

Full of clamour, a crowded city, an exulting town. LXX: The city is filled with those who cry out, an exulting city. The teaching of the heretics consists not in sense but in much speaking and clamour. Hence, on account of the multitude of those deceived, it is called a crowded city, and exulting on account of its pride. For being puffed up they swell, and boast that they have found holier things.

Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in battle. LXX: Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead dead in battle. The greatest part is overthrown by the deceptions of the heretics without any struggle or debate, and this is a very great crowd. The slain, then, or as the Seventy translated, the wounded of the valley of Zion are not slain and wounded by the sword, but have gone over to the heretics of their own will; and in comparison with those who are overcome after battle, he is the more unhappily wounded and slain who has surrendered of his own accord. Just as in martyrdom too, he who yielded after torments is liable to a lighter penalty than he who denied Christ without any necessity and without the pain of tortures.

22:3

All your princes have fled together, and have been harshly bound. In this place we have followed the translation of the Seventy, because in sense it is not far from the Hebrew. But to translate word for word from the Hebrew, it reads thus among them: All your chief men have departed together, they have been bound by the bow; and the other translators also followed this edition. For all the princes of the heretics have departed from the Church of Christ to the synagogue of Satan, and have gone over together, discordant in faithlessness, concordant in desertion; and they have been bound by the bow, of which it is written in the Psalm: Behold, the sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart (Ps 10 [11]:2), and to send the fiery darts of the devil, which both wound and bind. And therefore they have been harshly bound, because they have stopped their ears like deaf asps, and stopping their ears, which will not hear the voices of the charmers, nor of the sorcerer charming wisely. For this reason the apostle Paul too commands that a heretic be left to his perversity after one admonition (Titus 3), because he is perverted and condemned by his own judgment. For they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us (1 John 2:19). Of these fugitive princes the prince is he whom the same Isaiah calls the fleeing dragon, the crooked serpent, who, when he has sent deadly words into the ears of the deceived, binds them harshly and does not suffer them to escape from his bonds. Delivered from these, the saint rejoiced in the Psalm: My soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers (Ps 123 [124]:7). And in another place, rejoicing that he has escaped, he says: You are my upholder and my refuge. My God, I will hope in him. For he has delivered me from the snare of the fowlers, and from the harsh word (Ps 90 [91]:2-3), or the turbulent word, which properly signifies the teaching of the heretics.

All who were found in you are bound together; they have fled far off. LXX: And the strong in you have fled far away. The Prophet's speech is still against the valley of Zion, whose inhabitants have gone up onto vain housetops and have cried out with a confused clamour, and have been wounded without battle; all of whose princes have fled and been harshly bound, and those who were strong among them have fled further away. For the more prudent a man is in heretical perversity, the further he withdraws from the Lord. And as for what he says according to the Hebrew, All were found in you, we ought to note this: that the heretics too say they have found those whom they have deceived; but their finding is perdition. Accordingly they are bound together and flee far off. Nor am I pleased with that exposition which holds that, according to the diversity of the heresies, the distances of those who flee are also diverse, since the holy Scripture says (Luke 11:23) that all who have been found by the heretics are bound together and have fled very far, the Lord saying: He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters. Hence it is said of Moses (Exod 24): Moses alone drew near to God, but the rest did not draw near. For to his saints God is a God who draws near, and not from afar, says the Lord.

22:4, 6

Therefore I said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly; do not press to comfort me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. For it is a day of slaughter and of trampling and of weeping from the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, searching the wall, and magnificent upon the mountain. LXX: Therefore I said: Let me alone, I will weep bitterly; do not strive to comfort me over the breaking of the daughter of my race; for it is a day of tumult and of perdition and of trampling, and error from the Lord God Sabaoth in the valley of Zion; they err from the least to the greatest, they err upon the mountains. Samuel too mourned for Saul (1 Sam 15), and the Lord and Savior wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19; 2 Cor 12:21); and the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: Lest, when I come to you again, God humble me, and I mourn for many who sinned before and have not done penance. Hence, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, he says to others also: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn? (2 Cor 11:29). So the Prophet too, seeing the people that was once of vision climbing the vain housetops and living in clamour, and all its princes fled and bound with the chains of sins, bursts into tears, and drives away those who would console him, and testifies that he weeps with most bitter weeping, not over the sons but over the daughter of his people, which has lost the dignity of manhood. For the day of judgment and slaughter and trampling will by no means be Jerusalem, which means vision of peace, but of its ancient name Jebus, which means trampling; a day of weeping too, or of error, as the Seventy translated, from the Lord Sabaoth: not that weeping and error come from the Lord, but through the occasion of the holy Scriptures, which the Lord gave to be read, an occasion of error arises for those who can say: Why have you made us err from your way? (Isa 63:17). And in another place: The Lord has mingled for them a spirit of error (ibid. 29:10): so that they should stand not on the mountain of Vision but in the valley of Zion. And this very day, which arises from the Lord of hosts in the valley of Vision to show the works of each, searches the wall of the heretics, which they have built against the Church like a most solid rampart; and it searches the magnificent and glorious one, that is, their teachers, who boast that they stand upon Christ the mountain, of which we read elsewhere: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare to us his way (Isa 2:3). Further, as for what the Seventy translated, they err from the least to the greatest, they err upon the mountains, we ought to understand this: that those who are greater are in greater wickedness, and yet that all err from the least to the greatest, and err upon the mountains: Moses, Jeremiah and the other Prophets, the Evangelists and the Apostles. And though they dwell in the valley, they err in a wondrous way upon the mountains.

22:7, 9

And Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a man, a horseman, and the shield laid bare the wall. And your choice valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set their seats in the gate. And the covering of Judah shall be uncovered, and you shall see in that day the armoury of the house of the forest; and you shall see the breaches of the city of David, that they are multiplied. LXX: But the Elamites took quivers, riders, men upon horses, and a gathering of fighters; and your choice valleys shall be filled with chariots, and horsemen shall throng your gates; and they shall uncover the gates of Judah, and they shall look on that day into the choice houses of the city; and they shall uncover the hidden things of the houses of the citadel of David, and they shall see that they are many. Elam, which means their ascent, or the Elamites, as the Seventy translated, whom we render despisers, took up the quiver to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart; they are horsemen of men in a chariot, to lay bare with their shield and their assault the wall of Zion and the strongholds of the Church. And your choice valleys, he says, and your lowly doctrines, O valley of Zion, shall be full of chariots, those which the Lord sank with Pharaoh, whose horsemen and riders shall set their seats in your gates, so as not to let those besieged and shut up in you go out. Then almighty God, through churchmen, shall uncover the coverings of Judah and all the secrets of those who stand in the confession of the faith; and then, O valley of Zion, in that day and in the clear light of truth, you shall see the whole armour of the Apostle, and of the house of the forest, in which the throng of the nations stands; as it is sung also in Psalm 131 (132): Behold, we have heard of it in Ephrathah; we have found it in the fields of the forest (Ps 131 [132]:6). And when the covering and secret of Judah, which formerly was hidden on account of the mystery, has been uncovered, and you have seen the armour of the Church, then you will understand the schisms of the city of David, which you have multiplied in order to gather to yourself deceived peoples. These Elamites, according to the edition of the Seventy, have not one quiver but several; and they are riders of men, on whose souls they ride; and there is a very great multitude preparing itself for battle against the Church, so that all its valleys are filled; and the horsemen stop up their senses, and by their combat challenge to the contest the churchman, who is interpreted Judah; and when he brings forward the testimonies of the Scriptures and refutes all lies, the heretics will see the houses of the city of David, and will come to know all the things formerly secret: how in the citadel of David, which means strong of hand, that is, of Christ, are all the doctrines of truth. The places are obscure, not only according to the history but according to the ἀναγωγὴν. Those, then, whom our views displease ought to bring forward their own, so that we may acquiesce in their explanation, if it is true.

22:10-11

And you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and you numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and you pulled down houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool; and you did not look to him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar. LXX: And they turned the water of the ancient pool into the city, and they pulled down the houses of Jerusalem to strengthen the walls of the city; and you made yourselves water between the two walls within the ancient pool; and you did not look to him who made it from the beginning, and you did not see its creator. You who will see, or do see, the breaches of the city of David, that is, of the Church, which have been multiplied throughout the whole world; who have gathered the waters of your pool and teaching, not the upper but the lower, and have numbered, or pulled down, the houses of Jerusalem in order to fortify your wall: you have not dug wells which might have living and eternal waters, but broken cisterns, which cannot hold water. And you have made them between the two walls of the New and the Old Testament, and have neglected the water of the old pool, and have not considered God the giver of the law, and have utterly neglected the maker of the world. This according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy, the heretics considered that they were many, and trusting in this multitude they turned the teaching of the Old Testament away from the city of God, which is the Church, and pulled down the houses of Jerusalem in order to build assemblies of the wicked; and while they reject the Old Testament, they have not followed the New either, because the New is strengthened by the testimonies of the Old Testament. Therefore between the two walls, the old and the new, they have made themselves new waters, which they think are more inward and contain greater mysteries than are contained in the Old Testament; and they did not look to God, who is the founder of the Old Testament, and would not see its maker even from afar.

22:12ff.

And in that day the Lord God of hosts shall call to weeping and to mourning, to baldness and to the girding of sackcloth; and behold joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts. Daily the Lord God of hosts calls to repentance the heretics, who, despising the water of the old pool between the two walls, have dug themselves a reservoir and gathered the water of the lower pool, which has its waters not from heaven but from the earth; and he calls them to weeping, for blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh (Matt 5:5); and to mourning, lest afterwards they hear: We have lamented to you, and you have not mourned (ibid. 11:17); and to baldness, that they may shave off all the works of death, and remove from their body whatever does not live in the body; and to the girding of sackcloth, lest afterwards, according to Jerusalem, they be girded with a rope instead of a girdle. But they, on the contrary, instead of weeping and mourning, baldness and haircloth, had joy and gladness, and, as if all things ended with death, killing calves and slaughtering rams, to eat flesh and drink wine, they spoke the words of blasphemers: While we are in the present world, let us abound in delights; for tomorrow, that is, the time to come, will be without sensation. While they were saying these things, the Lord heard the words of blasphemy, and threatened that he would not forgive this iniquity until they either die to sin and vices, or are dragged down to the underworld with their offences. This indeed can be understood not only of the heretics but of every sinner who, neglecting his sins, becomes worse through despair, and, ensnared by pleasures, joins blasphemy to sin, so as to think that all the sensation of the living ends with death, saying that saying of Epicurus: "After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing."

22:15-16ff.

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna who is over the temple, and you shall say to him: What are you doing here, or as whom are you here? For you have hewn yourself a tomb here; you have hewn a memorial on high carefully, a tabernacle for yourself in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away as a cock is carried away, and he will lift you up like a garment. Crowning, he will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will cast you into a land wide and spacious: there you shall die, and there shall be the chariot of your glory, the shame of the house of your Lord. And I will drive you from your station, and depose you from your ministry. And it shall come to pass in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and I will give your power into his hand; and he shall be as a father to those who dwell in Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. And I will lay the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; and he shall open, and there shall be none to shut; and he shall shut, and there shall be none to open. And I will fasten him as a peg in a sure place, and he shall be for a throne of the house of his father. And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, divers kinds of vessels, every small vessel, from the vessels of bowls even to every vessel of the musicians. In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that was fastened in the sure place shall be taken away, and shall be broken and fall; and what hung upon it shall perish, for the Lord has spoken. LXX: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: Go to the pastophorion, to Somnas the treasurer, and you shall say to him: What are you here? Or what have you here? For you have hewn yourself a tomb, and have made yourself a memorial on high, and have marked out for yourself a tabernacle in the earth? Behold, the Lord Sabaoth will cast out and crush a man, and will take away your robe and your glorious crown, and will cast you into a great land, and without measure, and there you shall die; and he will set your excellent chariot in shame, and the house of your prince for trampling. And you shall be removed from your stewardship and from your rank. And it shall come to pass in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe, and will give him your crown with strength, and will give your stewardship into his hands; and he shall be as a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and of Judah, and I will give him the glory of the house of David, and he shall rule, and there shall be none to gainsay. And I will lay the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; and he shall open, and there shall be none to shut; and he shall shut, and there shall be none to open. And I will establish him as a prince in a sure place, and for a throne of glory of his father's house; and every glorious one in his father's house shall trust in him, from the least to the greatest. Every small vessel, from the vessels aganoth; and they shall hang upon him. In that day thus says the Lord Sabaoth: The man who was established in a sure place shall be moved, and shall be taken away and shall fall, and the glory that was upon him shall perish, for the Lord has spoken. The prophet Isaiah is commanded to go in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, which in Hebrew is called SOCHEN (סכן), to Shebna who is over the temple, or as the Seventy translated, ταμίαν, that is, the treasurer and steward of the treasures of the house of God. Now Sochen is interpreted either tabernacle or pastophorion, that is, the chamber in which the one set over the temple dwells. And who else is it that dwelt in the tabernacle of the Jews, and in what was once the house of God, but the word and reasoning of the Jewish law, which was occupied with the reading of the Old Testament? To this tradition and teaching, then, it is said: What are you doing here? Why do you wish to build yourself a house in the letter that kills, and to fix your tabernacle, which has no foundation, in the firmness of the rock, which ought to be called not so much a tabernacle and a house as a tomb and a memorial? And I tell you this because you ought not to toil at hewing a tomb, since the Lord will carry away your priesthood, as GEBER (גבר) is wont to be carried, which all have translated man. But the Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament rendered it cock. As a cock, he says, is carried from one place to another on the shoulder of a porter, so the Lord will lightly carry you away from your place. And you who once had the crown of the high priest, and the sanctification on the plate of gold on which the name of God was written (Exod 28), shall be crowned with tribulation and distress. And as a ball, if it is thrown down a sloping and spacious place, cannot stand still but rolls on without end, so all your people shall be scattered to the ends of the world. And there you shall die with your letter, and all your glory, and the chariots in which you were formerly borne in renown; and the splendour of the house of God shall be turned into shame. For the Lord shall take you away from your station and from your ministry, that is, from the ceremonies of the victims, so that what is written to the Hebrews may be fulfilled: For when the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law also (Heb 7:12). And when you have been cast out of your ministry, I will call my servant Eliakim, to whom I have said in another place also: It is a great thing for you to be called my servant (Isa 49:6, LXX). Eliakim means God rising again, or the resurrection of God. This God rising again, then, who is the son of Hilkiah, that is, of the portion of the Lord, shall receive your place, and shall be clothed with your robe and strengthened with your girdle, so that what you had in the letter he may possess in the spirit; and he shall be the father of those who dwell in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, which is interpreted as the Church, and to the house of Judah, where the true confession of faith is. Hence he himself says to the Apostles: Little children, yet a little while I am with you (John 13:33). And to another: Son, your sins are forgiven you (Matt 9:2). And to another woman: Daughter, your faith has made you whole (Luke 7:50). I will give him, he says, the key of the house of David, he who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev 3). And this very key shall be upon his shoulder, that is, in his passion, according to what is written in another place: Whose government is upon his shoulder (Isa 9:6). For what he has unlocked by his passion cannot be shut; and what he has shut in the ceremonies of the Jews shall be opened by no one else. For I will fasten him as a peg in a sure place, where the assembly of the Faithful is; hence too those who believe in Christ are called the faithful. And he shall be for a throne of glory of his father's house, that is, of the Church; and they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house. Hence it is written in the Gospel also: All the people hung upon him (Luke 19). And this indeed was done not only at that time, but is fulfilled to this day, so that there hang upon him, as it were, divers vessels of God: wisdom and righteousness and all the things by which Christ is called. Divers kinds of vessels: for these Aquila translated SASAIM (צאצאים) and SEPHOTH (הצפעית), which Symmachus rendered grandsons and mixed ones, so that the Apostles and all believers, that is, the sons of sons, and those mixed from all the nations, may hang upon him. From the vessels of bowls, for which Theodotion set down AGANOTH (אגנות): for both small and great shall believe in the Lord. And I think the bowls are the Apostles, full of living waters, of whom it is said: Bless God from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27), in which bowls wisdom has mingled her wine. And every vessel, he says, of the musicians, of those who at all times resound in the praises of God. What follows seems contrary to our sense: how this peg, which had been fastened in a sure place, is taken away and broken, and what had hung upon it falls and perishes, and this happens because the Lord has spoken. This can be resolved thus, if we read that saying of the Gospel, that in the last days the love of many shall grow cold (Matt 24), and the Lord himself says: Do you think the Son of man, when he comes, will find faith upon the earth? (Luke 18:8). It is not, then, the peg that will be broken and fall and perish, which it is impious to say; but the peg will be taken away from the sure place, that is, from the Church, through the impiety that daily grows up, and those who before hung upon him by faith will afterwards through unbelief be broken and fall and perish. And this shall happen in the last days, because the Lord has spoken. For peg, which in Hebrew is called JATHED (יתד), and is rendered alike by all, the Seventy alone translated above prince, and here man. And what almost escaped us in the haste of dictation: Shebna means turn now, or conversion. It is said, therefore, to the prince of the Jews, that he should turn from the Law to the Gospel, and, forsaking the images of the victims, pass over to the truth of the spiritual sacrifice.

23:1

The word of Tyre. What we thought about the burden, or word and taking up, of Tyre according to the Hebrews, we have said above in the book of the historical explanation of the ten Visions. Now we shall run briefly through the whole prophecy against Tyre according to the ἀναγωγὴν and the edition of the Seventy. Tyre is called SOR (צר) in the Hebrew tongue, and is rendered into our speech as distress. Every soul, then, that is taken up with vices and evil thoughts can be called sor.

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for they have perished, and shall come no more. From the land of the Kittim she has been led captive. To whom are the inhabitants of the isle become like? The merchants of Phoenicia, crossing the sea in many waters, the seed of merchants like harvests brought in, the merchants of the nations. For Carthage, in the Hebrew is written THARSIS (תרשיש), which all have translated alike. And Tharsis means contemplation or searching out of joy. Kittim too, which in Hebrew is called CHETIM (כתים), means sea congealing; and for Phoenicia, Sidon is read among them. Those, then, are rebuked whom a throng of evil thoughts surrounds, and who, wishing, as the Apostle says, to become rich, fall into temptations and snares of the devil, and many harmful desires, which drag men down into the deep (1 Tim 6). And they are told that they must howl, knowing that all the trading of this world will perish, and the contemplation of joy and gladness be turned into mourning and tears. For this sea can be sailed no longer, but all things will freeze; and the colonies of the Tyrians will be led captive to punishment. For those who dwell in this isle are like no others than merchants, or carriers, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and pass from one vice to another. And we dwell in an isle as long as we are beaten by the temptations of this world, and on every side our isle and little boat is struck by the waves of the sea. Now the merchants of this isle are from Sidon, which means huntress, and in which dwell very many hunters, of whom it is written: He will deliver you from the snare of the hunters (Ps 90 [91]:3). And in another place the saint rejoices that he has been delivered from their snares, saying: Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (Ps 123 [124]:7). And all the merchants of the nations are compared to crops which quickly wither, or to the harvests of the river, which have their rain not from heaven but from the earth; and therefore they will perish with the nations. Where we read the seed of merchants, in the Hebrew is written the seed of sior, by which the Nile is understood, because it has turbid waters with which the crops of Egypt are watered.

23:4-5

Be ashamed, O Sidon, said the sea; and the strength of the sea said: I have not travailed, nor brought forth, nor nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. And when it is heard in Egypt, pain shall seize them over Tyre. The sea of this world, in which dwell small animals with great, and the dragon which God formed to be mocked, seeing that those who had formerly been taken by the demons have been taken by the hunters of Christ, who hunt from every mountain and hill, speaks to the opposing power of the hunters, which Sidon means, and says to it: Be ashamed, O Sidon; for I have not travailed nor brought forth, nor nourished the young men taken by you, nor brought up the virgins whose folly is condemned in the Gospel (Matt 25). For my travail and childbearing, and my nourishing and bringing up of virgins, have been blotted out by the travail of the Apostles of Christ, one of whom said: My little children, of whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). And: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor 3:2). And again: I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor 11). When Egypt hears this, which in Hebrew is called MESRAIM (מצרים), which means ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, afflicting and constraining, it too will be terrified, understanding that it too will suffer the same things that Tyre has suffered. And while this is referred to all vices, it can also be perceived in the diversity of the heresies, when, one heresy being taken, another trembles, and in the confusion of one the other perceives that it is to be taken. And as it is said of Sodom: For if the signs had been done in them which were done in Capernaum, they would have remained until this day; and it is added: But it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in the day of judgment than for you: so we learn of Tyre and Sidon, the Savior saying: But it shall be lighter for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for that city (Matt 11:21ff.). Hence too the Canaanite woman, who understood that her daughter, that is, her soul, was grievously vexed by a demon, is said to have come out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon to pray to Christ. For she could not otherwise have gone to meet the Savior, unless she had left the borders of Tyre and Sidon.

23:6-7

Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in this isle. Is not this your disgrace from the beginning, before she was delivered up? Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn. What follows, Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn, has been added from the Hebrew, and is marked beforehand with an asterisk, that is, with shining stars. O Tyrians, you who dwell in distress and abide in an isle, exposed on every side to the waves of temptations, depart from it, and go to Carthage, that is, Tharsis, and hasten to true joy, mourning your old sins and the ancient disgrace which you either inflicted on others or suffered from them. And I command this because you see Tyre, your city, about to move from its seats and purpose to other borders, when, having laid aside their old error, they have bowed their necks to the Gospel of the Savior; so that those who formerly dwelt in distress may depart far off and become sojourners and dwellers in the teaching of the Lord the Savior.

23:8-9

Who has purposed these things against Tyre? Is she less, or does she not prevail? Her merchants are princes of Canaan, the renowned of the earth. The Lord Sabaoth has purposed to dissolve all the insolence of those who glory, and to dishonour all that is renowned upon the earth. The word Canaan has been added from the edition of Theodotion; for it Aquila translated merchants. The Holy Spirit therefore asks, or rather by the question affirms, that the Lord has purposed these things against the princes of Tyre, whose whole industry is to seek wealth by trading. And as in the Gospel we read of dealers in pearls (Matt 13), who, having sold all, long to buy one pearl, and who surely are to be called renowned merchants, not of earth but of heaven, so, on the contrary, the merchants of Tyre, that is, of tribulation and distress, are to be called the renowned of the earth, because whatever they do looks to the earth; and princes of Canaan, which means tossed about and shaken. For they do not set their feet upon the rock, nor can it be said of them, The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs (Ps 39 [40]; 103 [104]:18), or for the hares; but rather they endure what the righteous man almost suffered: But my feet were almost moved, my steps had well nigh slipped (Ps 72 [73]:2). The Lord of hosts, then, purposed this counsel: to dissolve the most wicked bonds of the merchants, or rather to scatter the compacted injury through which all who are subject to Tyre grow proud. And as for what he added, and to dishonour all that is glorious upon the earth, the Lord is not the author of dishonour, but shows to be shameful what lies open to shame of itself. This indeed we read in Leviticus also concerning the Priests: With defilement he has defiled him (Lev 21), the priest, no doubt: not that he is the author of the defilement, but that he shows him to be defiled who formerly seemed clean to very many.

23:10-11

Work your land; for ships no longer come from Carthage, and your hand no longer prevails, which provokes kings on the sea. The edition of the Seventy differs greatly in this place from the other translators and from the Hebrew itself; but let us pursue our purpose. Above he had said: Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in the isle. Now he says the opposite: since ships no longer come from Carthage, work your land. For it profited Tyre that the foreign ships perished, so that she is compelled to work her own land, of which it is said in the Proverbs: He who works his land shall be filled with bread (Prov 12:11): so that she may live not from the uncertain hazard of the waves and of shipwrecks, but from the fruits of her own work, of which it is sung in the psalms to the righteous man: You shall eat the labours of your hands (Ps 127 [128]:2). It is written in Hosea that the ways of the harlot were hedged by the Lord with thorns, so that she could not follow her lovers, in order that, driven by this necessity, she might return to her first husband. And this we often observe in the affairs of the world too: many who, through prosperity and abundance of all things, could not perceive the Lord, come to understand him through want, and are converted to the works of righteousness, after their hand no longer prevails to enjoy the felicity of this world, the hand which formerly provoked kings on the sea, or according to Symmachus, troubled them; kings whose heart is in the hand of God. And would that we too, scorning the trade of this sea, might work our land, and by no means wait for the ships of Carthage, or the ships of Tyre which used to go to Carthage, lest we be made subject to the power of the dragon who rules in the sea! But let us fix a steady step upon the land, or rather, hastening to heavenly things, let us work our land, so that, sowing here, we may reap there. Our hand too, which formerly was busied with the affairs of the world, and through power and felicity could move even kings, that is, the saints, from their standing, let it become feeble in the affairs of the sea, so that it may be strong in the work of its own land.

23:12

The Lord Sabaoth has commanded concerning Canaan to destroy its strength, and they shall say: You shall no more do injury and iniquity to the virgin daughter of Sidon. That Tyre and Sidon are in the land of Canaan we have shown above also, setting forth the testimony of the Gospel, in which we read that the Canaanite woman, or Syrophoenician, came out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon and met the Lord the Savior. Now every soul that is set amid the waves of the world and is carried about by every wind of doctrine is to be called Canaan, which means as it were a tossing or a shaking. Hence it is said also to the adulterous old man: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you (Dan 13). It profits Tyre and its distresses, then, that the Canaanite strength should perish, so that it may be said to its inhabitants that they can no longer do injuries and oppress by iniquity the virgin daughter of Sidon. Whoever is taken by the devil in the turmoil of various vices, and is delivered over to the outrages of shame, so as to pollute the body with pleasures and foulness, he is the son or daughter of Sidon. And this is to be known: that Sabaoth is not found in the Hebrew, and on the contrary virgin has been added from the Hebrew.

23:13

If you go to the Kittim, not even there shall there be rest for you; and if to the land of the Chaldeans, it too has been laid waste by the Assyrians. Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts, they raised its tower: its wall has fallen. What follows has been added from the edition of Theodotion under asterisks: Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts; they raised its tower; and joined without asterisks: its wall has fallen. The Kittim are interpreted a stroke consummated or perfect; the Chaldeans in this place, as it were breasts; the Assyrians, reproving. The etymology of Siim we too have not been able to find, and the other translators rendered it by the very name with which it is written among the Hebrews. It is said, therefore, to Tyre, that although she strive to go to the Kittim and avoid the stroke of her distresses, she cannot find perfect rest even there. And again, if she desires to go to the Chaldeans and enjoy their fertility and the abundance of all things, she will find them too desolate, the Assyrians reproving their barrenness; just as the Apostle also delivered sinners to Satan (1 Tim 1), that they might learn not to blaspheme: they are delivered to the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. And Siim laid the foundations of the Chaldeans, by whom I understand the most wicked demons, who raised both the ramparts and the proudest towers of the Chaldean city against the knowledge of the Lord. But all their building has fallen into ruins; for there follows, its wall has fallen. For unless the Lord builds the house, they have laboured in vain who build it (Ps 126 [127]:1). We often see in the world some men pass from one pursuit to another: for example, those who have fared badly in soldiering pass over to trade; and again advocates take up the arms of warriors. They change their occupation in order to change their misfortune; and nonetheless, by the dispensation of God, for those whom he deigns to save everything turns out contrary to their striving, so that through want and miseries they are compelled to have confidence not in themselves but in their Creator.

23:14

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for your strength has perished. The ships of Carthage, that is, of Tharsis, are bidden to howl; for they have not, as above, perished or shall not come, but their strength has perished. For Tharsis, according to another interpretation, is rendered into our tongue consummation of six, or of gladness. Now we read that this world was made in six days, and according to the traditions of the Church it will afterwards be consummated. All the goods of this world, then, and the whole labour of mortals, are compared to the uncertain course of ships, because they will quickly perish, and all the strength of those who sail will be dissolved. Hence it is written in Solomon also: The wise man has gone up to strong cities, and has destroyed their fortifications (Prov 21:22). For whatever is composed by the art of the heretics, of worldly wisdom, and of opposing doctrines, the churchman destroys, and teaches that it is subject to his feet.

23:15ff.

And it shall come to pass in that day that Tyre shall be forsaken seventy years, as the time of one king, as the time of a man. And after seventy years Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about, harlot city given over to forgetfulness. Play well on the harp, sing much, that you may be remembered. And after seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she shall be restored again to her former state; and her trade shall be with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. And her trade and her hire shall be holy to the Lord; but it shall not be gathered for themselves, but for those who dwell before the Lord. All her trade, to eat and drink and be filled in common store, a memorial before the Lord. What is said, a memorial before the Lord, and upon the face of the earth, and as the time of a man, is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added in the Greek. Now Tyre, once straitened, is let go for seventy years, so that, the time of desolation fulfilled, she may turn her once harlot's song into the praises of God, and, taking up the harp, may have all its strings sounding in concord; so that, after she has played well in concord and sung much, there may be a remembrance before God of her who on account of fornication had been given over to forgetfulness; and that she may be restored to her former state, and have the riches of the kingdoms of the whole world, and that the wages of her labour may by no means be gathered for the Tyrians, but for those who dwell in the sight of the Lord, and that they may eat and drink and be filled with all the good things which have been brought together by the labour of all for the gladness of the banquet. The divine word exhorts Sidon and Tyre to repentance, and promises that her labours and wages are to be sanctified to the Lord. Who among sinners would not have hope of salvation, if only he sings well, and all the strings of the virtues, which once had been slackened, are tuned to the praises of the Lord? We read in Psalm 44 (45), which pertains especially to the union of the bridegroom and the bride, that is, to God the Savior and to the mysteries of the Church, that it is said among other things: The daughters of Tyre with gifts, the rich among the people shall entreat your face (Ps 44 [45]:13). And the bridegroom himself speaks again to the Tyrian bride: Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father's house, for the king shall desire your beauty (ibid. 11, 12). Hence in the description of her beauty too it is added: The queen stood at your right hand, in a vesture of gold, surrounded with variety (ibid. 10). And again: All the glory of the king's daughter is within (ibid. 14). And if the king desired the beauty of the penitent Tyrian woman, who has the ornaments of various virtues, how much more shall her hire and her trade belong not to those who remain in Tyre but to those who dwell in the sight of the Lord! These, after they have done penance, shall hear from the Lord the Savior: Eat, my friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved (Song 5:1). And what it is to eat and drink and be filled with the common store of all the virtues, the faithful reader understands. That the temple was desolate for seventy years Jeremiah (Jer 29), Daniel (Dan 9) and Zechariah (Zech 7) teach. And in Ezekiel (Ezek 16) we read of Sodom that it shall be restored to its former state, and of Egypt that, after the desolation of the land of Egypt and the drying up of the seven rivers, it shall recover its old fertility. Now the number seven and seventy, which is made up either of single days or of seven decades, signifies a perfect and consummated repentance; so that Tyre rightly, the time of repentance fulfilled, returns to her former state. Of this harlot, I think, that saying too in the Proverbs of Solomon is signified in mystical speech: Do not heed a most wicked woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman, which for a short while fattens your throat, but afterwards you will find her more bitter than gall (Prov 5:2-4). For she looks out through the window of her house into the streets (Matt 7), because wide and spacious is the way that leads to death; and whatever foolish young man she sees (for the wise she does not dare to tempt) passing by the corners, those who have lost the straight line, she speaks to him in the darkness and in the gloom, and under the appearance of pleasures leads him like a victim to death. If she is converted, and sings well, and fulfils the time of years of perfect repentance, she shall eat and drink and be filled. Let Novatian hear this, and be silent.

Book Eight

The sixth and seventh books above contain the allegory of the fifth volume, which I formerly dictated as a historical explanation. The present work, that is, the eighth book, returns to the interpretation we had begun, so as to discuss both the history and the tropology according to both editions alike. If it seems long to you, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, do not impute it to me, but to the difficulty of Holy Scripture, and especially of the prophet Isaiah, who is wrapped in such great obscurities that, because of the magnitude of the matter, I think an explanation brief which is in itself long. Certainly we write for the studious and for those who desire to know Holy Scripture, not for the fastidious, who are nauseated at every single point. If they desire a river of eloquence and polished declamations, let them read Tully, Quintilian, Gallio, Gabinianus, and, to come to our own, Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Arnobius, Lactantius, Hilary. Our purpose is that Isaiah be understood through us, and by no means that our own words be praised on the occasion of Isaiah.

24:1ff.

Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth, and will lay it bare, and will afflict its face, and will disperse its inhabitants; and as the people is, so will the priest be; and as the servant, so his master; as the handmaid, so her mistress; as the buyer, so he who sells; as the lender, so he who receives the loan; as he who demands repayment, so he who owes. With scattering the earth will be scattered, and with plundering it will be despoiled: for the Lord has spoken this word. After the particular rebuke of the individual nations, Judea, Babylon, the Philistines, Moab, Damascus, Israel, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Edom and Arabia, the valley of vision, and at the last Tyre, in the explanation of which we have said what we could, the prophetic discourse now describes what the whole world is going to suffer at the consummation, and the prophecy is by no means about the individual nations, but about all of them alike. And first, what torments the impious are going to suffer; and how, according to the Gospel and the Apostle, heaven and earth and the fashion of this world pass away (Matt 24; 1 Cor 7), and sinners are led down into hell (Ps 30 [31]), of whom it is written: They shall go into the lowest parts of the earth, they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be the portions of foxes (Ps 62 [63]:10). Then, because according to the quality of their merits there are many mansions with the Father, it is told how the saints are caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and are to be with him always (John 14; 1 Thess 4). For the earth scattered, the Seventy translated the world corrupted; and for its face afflicted, that is, the earth's, the same translated, and he will uncover its face, so that the dead may come forth from their tombs; or he will lay it bare, so that all its works may be brought out into public view, and its inhabitants be dispersed into different places, destined for rewards or for punishments. Then there will be no difference between noble and base, priest and layman, servant and master, handmaid and mistress, rich and poor, the lender and him who is pressed by debt, buyer and seller. For all will stand on equal terms before the judgment seat of Christ, and there will be no respect of persons with God (Rom 14; Col 3). Of this Job too speaks in almost the same words: The small and the great are there, and the servant who does not fear his master (Job 3:19). And the Savior in the Gospel, to whom all judgment has been committed, bears witness in full discourse. The earth, therefore, will be scattered, and all earthly works will be reduced to nothing, so that, the image of the χοϊκοῦ having been abolished, the image of the heavenly may remain. For the first man was from the earth, earthly, and the second from heaven, heavenly: as is the earthly, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly; so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear also the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:47-49). Hence the same Apostle says: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God (ibid., 50). Not that, as the heretics say, the nature of bodies perishes, but that this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality. And all these things will come to pass, because what is to come the Lord has spoken through the prophets.

24:4-5

The earth has mourned and has wasted away, and has been weakened; the world has wasted away, the height of the people of the earth has been weakened, and the earth has been slain by its inhabitants. LXX: The earth has mourned, the world has been corrupted, the lofty of the earth have mourned, but the earth has acted impiously because of its inhabitants. God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Hence the first sentence is against those who are lofty on the earth, that all things which are now strong may be weakened because of those who have mingled blood with blood, and, in the manner of the blood of Abel, have made the gore of the slain cry out to God (Gen 4).

24:6

Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the ordinance, they have broken the everlasting covenant. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, and its inhabitants will sin; therefore its tillers will go mad, and few men will be left. LXX: Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the precepts, the eternal testament. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, because its inhabitants have sinned; therefore the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, and few men will be left. Let the Jews hear, who boast that they alone have received the law of the Lord, that first all the nations and the whole world received the natural law, and that the law was given afterwards through Moses for this reason, because the first law had been broken. Of it the Apostle speaks: For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves: who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom 2:14). Those, then, who have kept these laws will obtain rewards; but those who have neglected them will endure what the prophetic discourse now threatens. And as in the beginning God blessed every creature that he had made (Gen 1), so at the consummation of the world he will curse those who are earthly, and who were not sojourners but inhabitants of the earth, and sinned in it; who, forgetting their condition, have raged against one another in mutual fury. And few will remain who have the heavenly image; or, according to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, because they have lost their spiritual riches.

24:7ff.

The vintage has mourned, the vine has been weakened, all who were glad of heart have groaned. The joy of the timbrels has ceased, the sound of those who rejoice has been stilled, the sweetness of the harp has fallen silent; they shall not drink wine with song, the drink will be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity has been crushed, every house has been shut, with no one entering. There will be an outcry over wine in the streets; all gladness has been forsaken, the joy of the earth has been carried away. And desolation has been left in the city, and calamity will overwhelm the gates: for these things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples. At the consummation of the world, the remembrance of past delights will be the matter of torments. Hence also that rich man clothed in purple at his banquet, who had received his good things in his life, lifting up his eyes from hell, sees Lazarus at rest (Luke 16). And the Lord, rebuking the rich, the luxurious and those who laugh, says in the Gospel: Woe to you rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are now filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall mourn and weep (ibid., 24, 25). When, therefore, the resurrection of the dead has come, and the day of judgment has arrived, then will mourn the wine and the vintage of which Moses speaks: Their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and their shoot of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster is one of bitterness. Their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps (Deut 32:33). Then every drink, or, as it is said in Hebrew, sicera, that is, drunkenness, which overturns the state of the mind and does not allow men to keep watch, will be changed into bitterness: it counterfeits honey for a time to those who use it, and in the end is found more bitter than gall. Then all the sweetness of those who rejoice, and the sound of timbrels and harp, will be turned into lamentation and groaning. Let us press this testimony upon those who at banquets are wanton not only with gluttony and drunkenness but also with their ears, so that through all the senses the strength of the soul grows soft. The city of vanity will be crushed, or every city, or the spiritual Babylon, which sits clothed in purple upon seven hills, whose punishments we read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 18). And he did well to say the city of vanity. For if it is said of heaven and earth and of all things that are earthly: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2), how much more must this be said of one city, which is a small part of the whole world! Then the houses whose ceilings are now gilded, and whose walls, while the poor die of cold without roof or hut, are clothed with veneers of marble and shine with the gleam of sawn ivory, will remain empty. There will be an outcry in the streets over wine, not in the strait and narrow way that leads to life, but in the broad and spacious one that leads to death (Matt 7): over the wine and drunkenness of the error of those who have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands (Ps 75 [76]). For the joy of the earth has been carried away into heaven, and desolation has been left in the once most crowded city, and the calamity of its inhabitants will overwhelm the gates of the busy streets, through which the throngs of the peoples used to stream in. And that we might know plainly that the destruction of the whole world is being announced, he added: These things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the nations, or of the peoples.

24:13, 15

As if a few olives that are left were shaken from the olive tree, and the grape clusters when the vintage is finished. These will lift up their voice and give praise; when the Lord has been glorified, they will neigh from the sea: therefore glorify the Lord in teachings, in the islands of the sea the name of the Lord God of Israel. How far the translation of the Seventy differs in this place from the Hebrew truth, the following words will show. LXX: As if someone were to shake an olive tree, so they will shake them; and if the vintage ceases, these will cry out with clamor. But those who have been left upon the earth will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord; the water of the sea will be troubled; therefore the glory of the Lord will be in the islands of the sea, the name of the Lord will be glorious, of the Lord God of Israel. When few men have been left, when the curse has devoured the earth, and there is desolation in the city, and all these things have happened in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples and nations, so great will be the fewness of the saints, of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Many are called, but few chosen (Matt 20:16); and so violent the oppression of the righteous, that even the elect of God, if it were possible, would be tempted; and their fewness is compared to the very rare berries of olives, of which, when they have been shaken down and gathered, scarcely a few remain at the tops of the branches; and to the way that, when the vintage is finished, the poor, driven by need, are accustomed to go round the empty vines and gather a few grapes. These, then, who remain, and after the vintage and the pressing of the world have been able to escape the hands of the persecuting Antichrist, or the burning of the impending punishment, will lift up their voices on high and will praise God. When the Lord comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels, and they see him reigning in majesty, then they will neigh in the likeness of horses, exulting in the greatness of their joy, and they will neigh from the sea of this world. Therefore you who are now instructed in the Holy Scriptures, and know that such great joy and such great rewards are reserved for you, glorify the Lord in teachings, hearing that which is written: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord (2 Cor 10:17). Not at all in the land of Judea, but in the islands, that is, in the Churches of this sea and world, in which is blessed and praised the name of the Lord God of him who was once Israel, or, of the man who sees God. According to the Seventy, all that we have understood of the saints can be referred to the impious: that when the vintage is finished, then they cry out, set in punishments. But those who have escaped the number of the impious rejoice in the glory of the Lord, and the waters of the peoples of this world are troubled.

24:16

From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the Righteous One; and I said: My secret is mine, my secret is mine: woe is me. LXX: From the wings of the earth we have heard portents: hope for the righteous; and they will say ※ my mystery is mine ⁚. This, which is said, my mystery is mine, is not found in the Seventy, but has been added in the Greek from the translation of Theodotion. Again, for what they put as woe, so as to join it to the following verse, in the Hebrew is said OI LI (אוי לי), which properly means woe is me. Also for ends, which we have set down for the sake of explaining the sense more openly, the Hebrew has MECCHENAPH (מכנף), which means wing, not end. These, then, of whom it was said above: They will lift up their voice and give praise, when they have neighed from the sea, and have glorified the Lord in teachings, and have seen the name of the Lord God of Israel praised in the islands of the sea, then will sing with harmonious voice and say: From the wings of the earth, that is, from the prophets and from the saints of the Lord, who, having taken the wings of a dove, hasten to the kingdoms of the heavens, we have heard his praises proclaimed; and that the glory or hope of the Righteous One is not vain, but all things are fulfilled in deed. So, while the saints say these things, and neigh from the sea, and lift up their voice and give praise, the Prophet speaks to himself: When, he says, I had heard these things, and perceived that the prophecy of the Prophets was to be fulfilled in the overthrow of the world, I said to myself with the inward feeling of my heart: I cannot tell all that I see. My tongue cleaves to my throat, my voice is shut in by grief. Woe is me, what a train of punishments passes before my eyes! I see as present the things that are to come. But those err who think this must be understood as spoken in the person of God, not following the order of the matter. And I wonder in what sense, for psalms and praises, which in the Hebrew reads ZEMROTH (זמרות), the Seventy translated portents, unless perhaps it is a sign and a portent that, the people of the Jews being shut out, the once unbelieving multitude of the nations is saved.

24:17-18

The transgressors have transgressed, and with the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed. Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, who are an inhabitant of the earth; and it shall be that he who flees from the voice of terror shall fall into the pit, and he who extricates himself from the pit shall be held by the snare. LXX: Woe to the transgressors who transgress the law. Fear and the pit and the snare are upon you who inhabit the earth. And it shall be that he who flees fear shall fall into the pit, and he who comes out of the pit shall be caught by the snare. This is the cause of my mourning and groaning, on account of which I said a second time, my secret is mine, my secret is mine: because all have transgressed the law of God, and the Lord's punishment is by no means put off, nor is it foretold as future, but it is imminent, and holds the inhabitants of the earth captive. And when they think they have escaped, they will fall from one thing into another, and wherever they turn they will not evade the impending wrath of the Lord.

24:19-20

For the floodgates from on high have been opened, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. With breaking the earth will be broken, with crushing the earth will be crushed, with shaking the earth will be shaken. With tossing the earth will be tossed like a drunken man, and it will be removed like a tent of one night, and its iniquity will weigh it down, and it will fall, and will not add to rise again. Therefore no one will escape the terror and the snare and the pit of the Lord, because the floodgates from on high, or, as the Seventy translated more plainly, the windows of heaven have been opened, so that the Lord might look down upon all the sins of men, which before, because he did not punish them, he seemed to sinners not to know.
