But after he has seen all the works of mortals through the opened windows, the foundations of the earth have been shaken, according to what is written in another place of the gaze of God: Who looks upon the earth, and will make it tremble (Ps 103 [104]:32). Then the earth will be broken and crushed, and shaken and tossed in the likeness of a drunken man: not that the earth itself is reduced to dust and to nothing, but that all earthly things pass away, and another manner of life succeeds. And as a drunken man does not know what he is doing, but, his sinews growing dull with drunkenness, neither foot nor mind stands to its duty: so the whole earth, that is, all men who dwell on the earth, will be drunk with the greatness of the evils and the punishments, and will be stupefied at all that they see. And as a tent or pavilion of one night is moved from place to place, and the place of the former tent is abandoned by the traveler, so that no trace remains of the past lodging: so the fashion of this world will pass away, and the earth will be deserted which has been weighed down by its iniquity, whose weight and most grievous burden is described in Zechariah: Who sat upon a talent of lead (Zech 5:7). And it will fall, he says, and will not add to rise again. Not that the resurrection of men and of all who dwelt on the earth is denied, but that there will by no means be an earthly manner of life and the state of the former life, since human bodies rise again for this purpose, that souls may be clothed with the same bodies that they had laid aside before, and may receive from God either the good or the evil that they did upon the earth.

24:21ff.

And it will be in that day: the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven on high, and upon the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. And they will be gathered together in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited. And the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of his elders. For what we have translated, and the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, the Seventy translated, the brick will melt, and the wall will fall; what the cause of the error is, the following words will show. The sun in the Hebrew language is called by three names: SEMES (שמש), and HAMMA (המה), which means heat, and HERES (חרס), which signifies ὄστρακον, that is, potsherd or dryness. MAOR (מאר), however, which in Greek is called φωστήρ and in Latin luminary, is common to the sun and the moon. Again, the moon is called JAREE (ירה), which in Greek is called μήνη, because it makes a month by a circuit of thirty days, and LABANA (לבנה), that is, white or bright. In the present place, then, for LABANA, that is, moon, the Seventy translated brick, which in Hebrew is called LEBENA, deceived by the ambiguity of the word. Again, for HAMMA, that is, heat, by which is understood the sun, they put wall, which in Hebrew is called HOMA (הומה). And this is the sense of the whole passage: The windows of heaven have been opened, so that, as the Lord looked out upon earthly sins, every fashion of earthly works might pass away and fall, and by no means rise again to its former state. In that day, that is, in the day of judgment, the Lord will visit upon the host, or upon the adornment, of heaven on high, so that he may judge not only earthly but also heavenly things. And what the adornment or host of heaven is, let us learn from the writing of Moses: Beware lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon, the stars and all the adornment of heaven, you be deceived and worship them (Deut 4:19). And the Lord will visit, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, the host and army of heaven as one sick and in need of the knife and cautery, according to this: I will visit their sins with a rod, and their iniquities with scourges (Ps 88 [89]:33). For in what follows too we read: My sword has been made drunk in heaven (below, Isa 34:5); and in Job: The stars are not clean in his sight. And: Against his angels he has found something perverse (Job 25:5). He will visit also upon the kings and princes of the earth, the rulers of this darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Of these princes, who preside over the various provinces, it is written also in Daniel: The prince of the kingdom of the Persians came out to meet me, and the prince of the kingdom of the Medes, and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks (Dan 10). These princes, then, who did not keep their rank, the Lord will gather in the day of judgment, bound together as in one bundle, and will cast them into the pit of hell, so that in them too may be fulfilled what is written of the impious: He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the ditch which he made (Ps 7:16). And they will be shut up in prison, according to what the Lord says: Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). But what follows, And after many days they will be visited, seems to applaud my friends who grant repentance to the devil and the demons, in that after long times they are visited by the Lord. But let them consider that the divine Scripture did not say openly, They will be visited by the Lord, or, they will be visited by the angels, but absolutely, they will be visited. From this ambiguity of the word both remedy and correction can be understood: that after the righteous have received their rewards, those are visited in perpetual punishments. Yet it must be known that human frailty cannot know the judgment of God, nor pass sentence on the greatness and measure of the punishments, which has been left to the Lord's decision. Then the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, according to what the Apostle says: For the creation itself groans and travails (Rom 8:22), seeing that men who enjoyed its light have done nothing worthy of the goodness of God, who makes his sun rise upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matt 5): as if a steward and bailiff, when the master comes, were to see the household subjected to various torments and not having fulfilled his precepts at all. Of this same passage the Savior teaches more fully in the Gospel: The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be moved, when the sign of the Son of man has appeared in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth have beaten their breasts, and have seen the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven in power and much glory (Matt 24:29, 30). We have learned of the overthrow of the earth, the visitation of the host of heaven, the gathering of the kings and princes into one bundle, and their thrusting down into the pit, and the keeping of the prison, and the visitation of those shut up after a long time, the blushing of the moon and the confusion of the sun. After all these things the Lord of hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in the heavenly Jerusalem, of which it is written also in the Epistle to the Hebrews: And in the sight of his elders he will be glorified (Heb 12). Such an elder was Abraham, who died in a good old age and was gathered to his fathers (Gen 25). Such were the elders whom Moses too is commanded to choose, whom he knows to be elders (Num 11): for the gray hair of a man is his wisdom (Wis 4:8); who imitate the Ancient of days, whose hair is described as white, so that length of age may be shown (Dan 7:9). This can also be understood of the ecclesiastical rank, if only they do not destroy the dignity by their works.

25:1ff.

O Lord, you are my God: I will exalt you, I will confess to your name, for you have done wonders, ancient faithful designs: amen. For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. Because of this a strong people will praise you, the city of mighty nations will fear you. For you have become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation, a hope from the whirlwind, a shade from the heat: for the spirit of the mighty is like a whirlwind driving against a wall. Like heat in thirst, you will bring low the tumult of strangers; and as with scorching heat under a cloud, you will make the offshoot of the strong wither. LXX: O Lord my God, I will glorify you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, an ancient true counsel, so be it. For you have made cities a heap, strong cities, that their foundations might fall. The cities of the impious will not be built for ever. Therefore the people of the poor will bless you, and the cities of men who suffer iniquity will bless you. For you have been a helper to every lowly city, and a protection to those who are sad because of want; you will deliver them from most wicked men: a shade of the thirsty, and the spirit of men who suffer iniquity, like faint-hearted men thirsting in Zion, from the impious men to whom you have delivered us. The exposition of this place is twofold. The Jews think it is the voice of the saints and of the believing people, when God has done against the whole world the things said above, and the prophecies of all the prophets have been fulfilled; and the overthrown city they interpret as Rome, which is to be utterly destroyed; and the strong people, which praises the Lord, and to which the Lord has become strength in its tribulation and distress, they refer to Israel, which has been freed from the persecution of the nations as from most burning heat and thirst. But others, both better and more correctly, understand it as said in the person of the prophet, giving thanks to the Father for the passion of the Lord Savior, because he has done wonders and has fulfilled his ancient designs in truth, when those standing at the right hand will hear: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt 25:34). Understanding this, Paul too said: As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless (Eph 1:4); and, desiring that what he prophesies should come to pass, he adds the Hebrew word AMEN (אמן), for which the Seventy translated so be it. And the Lord in the Gospel often uses this word: Amen, amen, that is, truly, truly I say to you (John 6:54). And why he praises and confesses to the name of the Lord, and what these wonders are, and the ancient designs which he showed true in deed, follows: For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. The once strong city is understood as Jerusalem, which has become the house of strangers; of whom the Savior says in the psalm: Strange children have lied to me, strange children have grown old and have limped in their paths (Ps 17 [18]:46). This city, when it has been destroyed, will never be built for ever, so that the dreams of a thousand-year kingdom and of a golden and jeweled Jerusalem may be laid to rest. And when Jerusalem has been destroyed for its impiety, a strong people will praise the Lord. And who the strong people is, the following verse shows: The city of mighty nations will fear you. While those blaspheme, the people of the nations will fear you. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). And a strong people will praise you, and the city of mighty nations will fear you, that is, the Church gathered from the nations. For you have become strength to the poor, to your Christ, of whom we read also in the Psalms: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And in Zechariah, according to the Hebrew truth, the poor man, that is, EBION (אביון), is described as sitting upon the colt of an ass (Zech 9). Strength to the needy, in the tribulation of his passion, a hope from the whirlwind of the cross, and a shade from the heat, when he said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit (Luke 23:46). For as when the wind is dashed against a wall and passes by, so the whirlwind of the blaspheming Jews could not harm him. And to use another comparison: as an offshoot is scorched by most grievous heat and droops, so you will make the tumult and clamor of the strangers, that is, of those who have become strangers to you, wither and perish. According to the Seventy translators, I could not find in this place, I do not say the sense, but the order and sequence of the words. And for that place where we have translated, like heat in thirst, for which in the Hebrew is written BASAION (בציון), which among them means pathless place or thirst: why they turned pathless place and in thirst into in Zion, the error is plain, from the likeness of the words SAION and SION (Both ציון), since it is marked with the same letters.

25:6, 8

And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a feast of fat things, a feast of the vintage: of fat things full of marrow, of a vintage refined from the lees. And he will cast down on this mountain the face of the bond that was bound upon all peoples, and the web that he wove over all nations. And he will cast down death for ever, and the Lord God will take away the tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth: for the Lord has spoken. LXX: And the Lord Sabaoth will make for all nations upon this mountain: they will drink gladness, they will drink wine. They will be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Deliver all these things to the nations, for this counsel is upon all nations: death, prevailing, has devoured. And again: The Lord God has taken away every tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he has taken away from all the earth. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken. For what we have rendered, the face of the bond that was bound upon all peoples, Aquila translated, the face of darkness upon all peoples. And whereas Aquila said darkness twice, Theodotion named darkness once, the rest alike. For this Symmachus translated, the face of the Ruler who rules over all peoples. And what the Seventy meant to say for this place, Deliver all these things to the nations, is plain to the reader: that they set down not the words of Scripture but their own sense, because all the mysteries of the Law and of the Temple were to be transferred to the Churches of the nations. After the passion of the Lord, then, when he has freed him from thirst and heat and whirlwind, the Lord will make, not at all for the people of the Jews, but for all nations, on Mount Zion a fat feast, burnt offerings full of marrow, and the wine of a vintage refined from the lees, so that he may cast down and cause to be swallowed up the face of death and of the bond by which all peoples were bound; and he will break the net of death, and the web that had caught all nations. And according to the Apostle, death will be swallowed up for ever (1 Cor 15). And the Lord will take away the tear from every face, when, death being overcome, the kingdom of Christ has come, and the reproach of the human race, which had been made to the image of the Creator, has escaped the slavery of the devil and of death. Nor is it surprising if according to Symmachus death is called a ruler, since the blessed Apostle said: Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned, in the likeness of the transgression of Adam (Rom 5:14). The Ruler of all peoples, or the face of darkness upon all peoples, and the web that was woven over all nations, some wish to be understood as the Antichrist, who is to be consumed on the Mount of Olives, as we also said on the last vision of Daniel. According to the Seventy, a feast of gladness is prepared for all nations on Mount Zion, in which they will drink the wine which the Lord promised that he would drink with his saints in the kingdom of his Father (Matt 26 and Luke 22); and they will be anointed with ointment, so that, reborn in Christ, they may be made a new people; whence it is said: Deliver all these things to the nations, which Israel once celebrated in type and image. For this is the counsel of the Lord, that all things should be transferred to the nations, because death has been swallowed up (1 Cor 15), and every tear wiped away, and the reproach of the whole earth blotted out, as the rule of Christ succeeds.

25:9ff.

And they will say in that day: Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord, we have waited patiently for him; we will exult and be glad in his salvation. For the hand of the Lord will rest on this mountain; and Moab will be threshed under him as straw is crushed in the wagon. And he will stretch out his hands under him, as a swimmer stretches them out to swim, and his glory will be brought low with the dashing of his hands. And the fortifications of your lofty walls will fall, and will be brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust. When death has been swallowed up for ever, the people of God which has been freed from the hand of death will say to the Lord: Behold, this is our God, whom the unbelieving thought only a man; and we have waited for him, that is, we have believed his words, that he will fulfill his promises, and he will save us. Therefore, snatched by his help from the jaws of death, we will exult and be glad in him; and his hand and his power will rest on this mountain, of which we read above: When the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of his elders (Isa 24:23). And Moab, which means from the father, will be crushed as straw is wont to be crushed by the wagon. He speaks according to the custom of Palestine and of many provinces of the East, which, for lack of meadows and hay, prepare straw for the feeding of animals. Now there are iron-shod carts, with wheels turning in the middle in the manner of saws, which crush the stubble and break it up into straw. As, then, straw is crushed by iron-shod wagons, so Moab will be crushed under him, whether under the power of God or in himself, so that nothing whole remains in him. And as one who swims is wont to stretch out his whole body, so he will be dashed from his power to the ground, and in falling will make a noise. And all the fortifications of his lofty men, or of his walls, as is contained in the Hebrew, will fall and be brought low, and will be pulled down to the ground, broken to the dust. So the prophetic discourse, although it weaves its prophecy generally about the consummation of the world, yet, so as not to seem to neglect present things entirely, names Moab, which was an enemy of Israel, so much so that it made them commit fornication with the Midianites and be consecrated to the idol Baal-peor, which means Priapus; against which Jeremiah speaks: Chemosh will go forth into captivity, his priests and his princes together (Jer 48:7); and again: Moab will be confounded in Chemosh, as the house of Israel was confounded in Bethel (ibid., 13), and other things like these. And from one idol and the demon who presided over this idol, he indicates that all the adverse powers are to be brought low and led down into Tartarus, and crushed like dust. But if this is how it will be, where is the repentance of the devil?

26:1

In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. LXX: In that day they will sing this song in the land of Judea: Behold a strong city, and our salvation will set a wall and a surrounding wall. When Moab has been brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust, and all enemies laid beneath the feet of Christ, then this song will be sung in the land of Judah, or Judea, each of which means confession: so that, as we have understood Zion and Jerusalem as the heavenly city, so we may also understand the region of this city as the heavenly confession. Indeed, the saints, unwilling to sing the song of Judea in a foreign land, say: How shall we sing a song to the Lord in a foreign land? (Ps 136 [137]:4). I think that this is the song which in another place too the saints are commanded: Sing to the Lord a new song (Ps 95 [96]:1). And this song will be what follows: The city of our strength, the Savior (Matt 5). Which is this city? The one which, set on a mountain, cannot be hid. Of which it is written also in another place: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4); and again: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:2). The founder of this city is he of whom the Father speaks: he has built my city; nay rather, the city of our strength is the Savior, that is, Jesus. And a wall and an outer wall will be set in it: the wall of good works, and the outer wall of right faith, so that it may be enclosed by a double fortification. For it is not enough to have the wall of faith, unless faith itself is confirmed by good works. This wall and this outer wall, or surrounding wall, is built of living stones, which, according to the prophet, are rolled upon the earth. For what we have rendered, outer wall, Symmachus translated bulwark: so that the walls themselves are girded with fortifications, and with rampart and ditch and other walls, which in the building of camps they are accustomed to call breastworks.

26:2, 4

Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, keeping the truth. The old error has gone; you will keep peace: peace, because we have hoped in you. You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages. LXX: Open the gates, let the people enter which keeps righteousness, and keeps the truth, laying hold of the truth, and keeping peace: peace, because they have hoped in you, O Lord, for ever. This whole song, which the saints are to sing in the land of confession and praise, suddenly changes persons, and is woven as if by question and answer. The people of God had said: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. The Lord answered, or rather commanded, not those who had said this, but the angels who presided over the gates of the Lord's city, that they should open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter through them, keeping the truth, or, as is said in the Hebrew, EMMUNIM (אמונים), which in our language is rendered faiths, in the plural number, not the singular. Which are the gates that are opened by the angels, so that there may enter, not the people of the Jews, which has been cast off, but the righteous nation, which from faith has received the name of the faithful? Surely those of which the holy man speaks: Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered them, I will confess to the Lord (Ps 117 [118]:19). But no one will be able to enter these gates except one who has been freed from the gates of death, as the Psalmist said: You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Ps 9:15). For when we have been snatched from the gates of death, then we shall be able to sing all the praises of the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion. And as I consider the gates of death to be sins, of which it is said to Peter: The gates of hell shall not prevail against you (Matt 16:18), so I consider the gates of righteousness to be all the works of the virtues; and he who has entered them will find one gate, of which it is said: This is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter by it (Ps 117 [118]:20). And as through many pearls one comes to the one pearl, so through many ways and gates we come to him who says that he is the way and the gate, through which we enter to the Father. After the word of God, the people answered in Hebrew JESER SAMUCH (יצרסמך), which Aquila and Symmachus translated alike, πλᾶσμα ἐπηρεισμένον, that is, our error has been taken away, or our thought has been made firm, which before wavered between you and the idols, so that we are by no means carried about by every wind of doctrine, but believe with our whole mind in you, the Lord Savior. For this, so that the sense might be made plainer, we translated, the old error has gone. And because our thought has been made firm, therefore you will keep for us the peace which you promised to the Apostles, saying: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14:27); and not once only but a second time, so that the recompense which is promised with a double word may be secure, according to what the Apostle too said: Rejoice, again I say rejoice (Phil 4:4). And this he obtains of whom it is said in Leviticus: Man, man, of the children of Israel (Lev 17); and in the book of Numbers: Man, man, whose wife has defiled his bed (Num 5:12): so that the double man and the double husband may obtain a double peace. And we merit peace, they say, because we trust in you with our whole mind. After the words of the people and the answer of the Lord, and again the voice of the people, the Prophet speaks to the believers: You have hoped, or hope in the Lord, for everlasting ages, and the rest that follows. According to the Seventy, he enters the gates of the Lord who keeps righteousness in good works, and keeps or embraces the truth in the truth of faith, so that through good works and faith he may come to the peace which surpasses all understanding, and may merit to receive that peace; because he has believed in God, who is the eternal rewarder of good works (Phil 4). Hence also in another place it is written: You have desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you (Sir 1:33).

26:5-6

In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever: for he will bow down those who dwell on high; he will bring low the lofty city, he will bring it low even to the ground; he will pull it down even to the dust. The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy. LXX: O great eternal God, who have brought low and pulled down those who dwell on high, you will destroy strong cities, and will bring them down even to the pavement, and the feet of the meek and the lowly will trample them. These things too the Prophet speaks, who answered from that place where he had said above, Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages; and he joins to it what we have now set forth: In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever, and the rest. For the Lord God, the strong one, the Hebrew has three names, IA (יה) and ADONAI (יהוה) and SUR (צור), of which one signifies invisible, another ineffable, another mighty; the first of them is placed as the last syllable in ALLELUIA (הללו יה). And let the diligent reader observe this, that we sometimes divide the text in setting out a testimony, because the edition of the Seventy produces one sense, and the translation rendered word for word from the Hebrew another. The Prophet says, then: Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages: in the Lord God, the strong one, for ever, whose help is everlasting. For he will bow down those who dwell on high, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; those who boasted that they had Abraham as their father, and said in insult of the Lord: We were not born of fornication (John 8:41). He will bring low the lofty city: as the Jews think, Rome; as we prove to be more correct, Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to it, and at the last killed the son of the householder, so that, the heir being slain, the inheritance might perish (Luke 13). Nor is it called a city, which in Hebrew is said IR (עיר), but CARIA (כריה), which Aquila translated πολίχνην, which we can call either little city or hamlet or small town; and Jerusalem is frequently called by this name in the Scriptures. And he did well to set down a double humbling, He will bring low, he will bring it low: first under the Babylonians, when the temple was destroyed; the second time under Titus and Vespasian, whose ruin remains until the end. The foot will trample it, and he repeats and joins the feet of the poor, without doubt of Christ, of whom we have said above too: He has become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation. The steps of the needy, namely of the Apostles, who, imitating the poverty of the Lord, obtained also the privilege of his power; who, not being received, shook off upon it the dust of their feet. And because it is said in the words of the Savior, Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), we can refer this not only to men but also to the adverse powers. According to the Seventy, the Prophet sings praises to God because he brings low all the proud, and razes the fortifications of all cities to the ground, and the feet of the saints, the meek and the lowly trample them.

26:7, 9

The path of the righteous is straight, straight is the track of the righteous for walking; and in the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have waited for you; your name and your memorial are in the desire of the soul: my soul has desired you in the night. LXX: The way of the righteous is straight, the way of the righteous has been made straight, and prepared. For the way of the Lord is judgment; we have hoped in your name, and in the remembrance which our soul desires. The Prophet is still speaking of Christ, of whom he had said above: The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor. The path of this righteous one, then, is straight, or, to coin a new word, straightnesses, which the Greeks call εὐθύτητας, and which we can call more in the Latin manner equities; and in Hebrew they are called MESSARIM (משרים). In the one path of Christ, then, all righteousnesses are found; and for that reason he trod and wore it with his own foot, so that whoever wishes to walk along it may walk with an unstumbling course. In this path of the Lord's judgments the saints have waited for him, and have hoped in him, because hope does not confound. And they have had his name and memorial in the desire of their soul, saying: My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times (Ps 118 [119]:20); and again: My soul desires, and has fainted for your salvation (ibid. 81). And he who has the name of the Lord in his desire desires nothing else. And this must be noted, that the desire for the Lord is not in the flesh but in the soul, according to what we read in another psalm: My soul has thirsted for God, the strong, the living (Ps 41 [42]:2). For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal 5). For these are opposed to one another, so that we do not do the things we wish. And what follows, In the night, according to the Seventy is joined to the following passage, according to the Hebrew to the former one. And he can say, My soul has desired you in the night, who says confidently with the Psalmist: Every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with tears (Ps 6:7). Night and darkness can also be taken for tribulation and distress. Hence in another psalm too the Prophet sings of the security of the righteous: The sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6), that is, neither in prosperity nor in adversity will you ever be moved from your place.

But also with my spirit within my breast, from the morning I will watch for you. LXX: From the night my spirit rises early to you, O God: for your judgments are a light upon the earth. We wish both to follow the Hebrew and not to pass over the common edition entirely, and by this necessity of things we are compelled to seek different understandings in a different order and wording. So what is said, from the night, is, according to the Seventy, as we said, the beginning of this passage; according to the Hebrew, the end of the preceding one; although even according to the Seventy it can be taken at the end of the preceding testimony, so that the sense is: My soul desires you in the night; and afterwards it begins: in the morning my spirit rises to you, O God. And it rises in the morning for this reason, because your precepts are a light upon the earth. For, keeping your commandments, and illumined by the light of those of which it is said, The precept of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9), I cannot sleep, but desiring you at all times, I rise to you with my spirit. And this must be observed, that while still placed in the night we desire the Lord with the soul; but after our spirit within our breast has moved itself toward God with the whole mind, let us watch for him in the morning: and, to speak more plainly, night and desire are joined to the soul, but morning and watching to the spirit. Further, he watches for God with the spirit within his breast who can say: Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord (Ps 129 [130]:1).

26:10

When you have done your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. Let us have mercy on the impious, and he will not learn righteousness; in the land of the saints he has done wickedly, and he will not see the glory of the Lord. LXX: Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth. For the impious has ceased, and he will not learn righteousness upon the earth; he will not do truth; let the impious be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew, and when we have chosen to express the sense of the Prophet, then let us pass to the Seventy translators. As long as you do not exercise your judgments upon the earth, and neither repay good to the good nor evil to the evil, your righteousness, O Lord God, is unknown on the earth. But when on the day of judgment you have rendered to each what he deserves, according to the quality of his works, then your righteousness will be known in the world, which before seemed unjust among the unbelieving, so that one of the saints too said: But my feet were almost moved, my steps had well-nigh slipped: for I was zealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners (Ps 72 [73]:2). To which the Lord answered: Let us have mercy on the impious; which all, except the Seventy, translated alike. And the sense is: rather let the impious obtain mercy, and learn my clemency, while he too is saved. And again, to the Lord as he speaks, the Prophet answered in the person of human impatience: And he will not learn righteousness. And the sense is: and how will he be able to know your righteousness, if he has experienced only clemency? And he gives the reasons why he wishes him to learn the righteousness of God: because he has acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and has fought continually against your saints, he ought to feel torments. And again the Lord, tempering the sentence, says: And let him not see, or he will not see the glory of the Lord. And the sense is: it is enough for him, in place of all punishment, that he will not see me reigning with my saints in my majesty. Some wish the impious one, that is, RESA (רשע), to be understood as the devil, of whom it is written in the ninth psalm: You have rebuked the nations, and the impious has perished; you have blotted out their name for ever and for ever and ever. The swords of the enemy have failed unto the end, and their cities you have destroyed (Ps 9:6). But let us take the impious generally either for the sinner or for one who does not have the worship of God. According to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth are commanded to learn righteousness. For every man seems righteous to himself; but God knows the hearts of all, who will render to each according to his works (Prov 21). And in another place of the same book it is said: There are ways of a man which seem straight; but their ends look into the depth of hell (Prov 14:12). Hence we ought to learn righteousness, and not trust in our own judgment. For there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl 7); not because he is righteous, but because he seems to himself to be righteous. But if Christ has been made for us by God wisdom and righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1), those who are commanded to know righteousness are commanded this: to learn and know Christ. And I command you, he says, to learn righteousness for this reason, because the impious has been taken away, and his kingdom destroyed, who, as long as he reigned on the earth, could neither know righteousness nor do truth; of which it is written elsewhere that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). And because the impious does not do truth on the earth, he will be taken away: for he does not deserve to see the Lord reigning.

26:11

O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see: let them see, and let the zeal of the people be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies. LXX: O Lord, your arm is lofty, and they did not know; but knowing they will be confounded: zeal will seize the untaught people, and now fire will eat the adversaries. What he had said above, and he will not see the glory of the Lord, can be understood thus: You ask, O Prophet, that I should not have mercy on the impious, lest, if I have had mercy on him, he who has acted wickedly in the land of the saints should begin not to know righteousness; I answer you: will he then not see the glory of the Lord? Will he then not behold my triumphs, he who rather ought to see me reigning, so that he may know how great a good he lacks? And this is to be read more pointedly, with the voice of one asking a question. To which the Prophet answered: O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and be stretched out to strike, so that the impious may not see you, and may not enjoy the light of your glory, not even for repentance. To whom the Lord answered: Let them rather see and be confounded, either the zeal of the people or those zealous for the people, and let fire devour and consume your adversaries, that is, those of the people of the saints. And it is the fire of repentance, which tortures their hearts because they have lost such a Lord. This can also be understood of the Jews, who did not know Christ, the arm of the Lord, and when they have seen and recognized him whom they had fastened to the gibbet, will be confounded. Then the untaught people, not knowing the law of God, will be roused by the goads of zeal, when it sees that the nations have succeeded to its place, and burns with the fire of regret, or with the pain of punishment, when it hears that which is written: Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41).

26:12

O Lord, you will give us peace: for you have wrought all our works for us. LXX: O Lord our God, give us peace: for you have rendered all things to us. It must be noted that after he has rendered to us our works, he is going to give peace, and how they set out the reasons why they ask for peace. For they say that for all the works which they have wrought upon the earth they have endured torments, and that it is just that after punishments and tortures they should obtain mercy. Or otherwise: Because the consummation of the world has come, and all that you spoke through the Prophets has been fulfilled in deed, and you have rendered all that you promised, grant us peace, which surpasses all understanding.

26:13

O Lord our God, lords have possessed us without you: only in you may we remember your name. LXX: Lord our God, possess us: O Lord, besides you we know no other, we call upon your name. For this reason we seek mercy and peace, which is to be granted after all things, because lords have possessed us without you, namely the idols, or the demons who sit by the idols; and we ask nothing else but that, after very many errors, we may be worthy to remember your name. According to the Seventy, those who said, Lord God, possess us, pray for this, that after peace has been restored to them they may become the possession of God. This indeed we read also of Wisdom, which according to the Hebrew speaks in Proverbs: God possessed me, the beginning of his ways (Prov 8:22), although some copies wrongly have creature for possession. Then it follows: But before all the hills he begot me. For how can begetting be fitted to a creature, when it rather suits possession? It is written in Deuteronomy: Is not he your father, who possessed you, and made you, and created you? (Deut 32:6). And this must be considered, that he did not say, the Lord, or God, possessed you, and made you, and created you; but father, so that the clemency of the name might soften the severity of the power. And what follows, O Lord, besides you we know no other, does not exclude the Son, but joins him to the Father; for he did not say "We know no other," but "Besides you we know no other." And since the Son says, I am in the Father and the Father in me, we do not know the Son outside the Father (John 14:10), because we know him in the Father. And indeed we name his name too, saying in the Lord's Prayer: Our Father, who art in heaven (Matt 6:9).

26:14

Let the dying not live; let the giants not rise again. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have destroyed all memory of them. LXX: For the dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up. Therefore you have brought on, and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs. Symmachus, in his manner, more plainly: The dead will not give life; the giants will not raise up. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have utterly destroyed all memory of them. Let us speak first according to the Seventy. The question seems difficult, how the dead do not see life. It is solved thus: they do not see life so long as they are dead. As if we were to say, a blind man does not see the light so long as he is blind; but if he has recovered his health, he will look upon the light: so too he who is dead in iniquity and sins cannot live before he is given life by righteousness and the virtues, through him who says, I am the life (John 14). Hence God is also called the God of the living, not of the dead (Matt 22). For the soul that sins, it shall die (Ezek 18:4). We read in the Epistle written to the Hebrews: Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works (Heb 6:1). But if sins are called dead works, why should not, on the contrary, the virtues be called living works? And what follows, Nor will physicians raise them up, its sense is plain: the fables of the poets are condemned, who boast that Virbius was raised up by Aesculapius. And this is to be said not only of the dead, but of every infirmity: that without the mercy of God the art of healing avails nothing. But how? Unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it: unless the Lord guards the city, he has watched in vain who guards it (Ps 126 [127]:1, 2). So unless the Lord has cured the sickness, the physicians labor in vain who desire to heal the sick. Unless the Lord has guarded health, they guard it in vain who even publish precepts for guarding health in their own books; and one must always learn, not only in the health of the body but also in that of the soul: Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your sicknesses (Ps 102 [103]:1, 3). Further, those who persist dead in sin, and can recover the health of the soul by no art of medicine, will be utterly destroyed and taken away by the Lord, and whatever is strong in them, which is called the male, will be wholly removed. Hence Pharaoh too does not wish to kill the female sex, which is frail in itself and can easily perish, but every male, which, if it has grown up and come to manly age, is killed with difficulty (Exod 1). According to Symmachus, the dead will not give life, because, being dead in sin, they cannot give life to others, nor is praise seemly in the mouth of a sinner. And the giants, that is, RAPHAIM (רפאים), will not raise up others, they who themselves, according to the book of Genesis, are called the falling. And the Lord visits them, so that all memory both of the dead and of the giants may be blotted out. For he alone it is who raises the dead, of whom it is said: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he will (John 5:21). We can call the dead the images of dead men, and the giants the demons who sit by their images. Nor should it trouble us why the Seventy translated male and the other translators memory, since among the Hebrews both are written with the same three letters, ZAI (ז), and CHAPH (כ), and RES (ר). But when we say memorial, it is read ZACHAR; when male, ZOCHOR. And they think that Saul was deceived by this ambiguity of the word when he fought against Amalek and killed every male of them (1 Sam 15). For when God commanded that he should blot out all memory of Amalek under heaven, he, for memory, led astray not so much by error as by the desire for plunder, interpreted males, not knowing that saying of the Apostle: Do not err, God is not mocked (Gal 6:7).

26:15

You have been indulgent to the nation, O Lord, you have been indulgent to the nation. Have you been glorified? You have removed far all the ends of the earth. LXX: Add evils to them, O Lord, add evils to the glorious of the earth: you have made far off all the ends of the earth. The evils which the Seventy put twice are not found in the Hebrew; but because he had said above, Therefore you have brought on and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs, following the same sense they added of their own, evils: so that those who are glorious on the earth may be crushed by double evils. Further, according to the Hebrews the sense is far otherwise, and in agreement with the earlier discussion. The Lord had said: Let us have mercy on the impious. The Prophet had answered: And where is your righteousness? especially since he has wrought such great evils against your saints. To which the Lord: And he will not see, he says, the glory of the Lord. Again the Prophet: Let your hand be exalted to strike, and let them not see your glory, which they do not deserve to behold. To which the Lord: Let them see rather and be confounded. Again the Prophet: O Lord, give us peace, and possess us, who remember your name. But let the impious and the proud not live, nor rise again in glory, but crush all memory of them. And he gives the reasons why he desires them to perish: You have been indulgent to the nation, O Lord, you have been indulgent to the nation; have you been glorified? And the sense is: You have often had mercy on the nations, that is, on the human race, and have exercised toward them an incredible clemency; have they known you? Have they glorified your name? Have they not, on the contrary, withdrawn far from you? For security breeds negligence, and negligence contempt.

26:16

O Lord, in distress they have sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching was to them. LXX: O Lord, in tribulation I remembered you; in small tribulation your teaching was to us. Because, being indulgent, you have often been despised and not glorified, but on the contrary all have withdrawn from the knowledge of you, therefore, O Lord, strike them, so that in distress they may seek you, and in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching may be to them: when so great a weight of evils presses upon them that they do not even dare to cry out confidently, but swallow their pain in silence. According to the Seventy, the Prophet remembers the Lord in tribulation, according to what is said in the psalm: Out of tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a broad place (Ps 117 [118]:5). And in another place: To the Lord I cried when I was troubled, and he heard me (Ps 119 [120]:1). Hence the Apostle says: We are troubled, but not distressed; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken (2 Cor 4:8). And in another place: The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us (Rom 8:18). But if a small tribulation teaches, and amends, and corrects, how much more a great one, when we are reminded of our condition and remember the power of God!

26:17-18

As a woman who has conceived, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in pain in her pangs: so have we become before your face, O Lord. We have conceived, and as it were travailed, and have brought forth spirit. LXX: And as a woman in travail, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in her pain: so have we become ÷ to your beloved ⁚ because of fear of you, O Lord; we have received in the womb, and have travailed, and have brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which we have made upon the earth. As a woman drawing near to the birth is compelled by pain to cry out, so we seek you in distress, and before the face of the dread of you we have conceived, and travailed, and brought forth, not children of the flesh, but of the spirit: so that we may believe in you with our whole mind, and learn through torments him whom we did not perceive through benefits. What the Seventy added, so have we become to your beloved, for which the others translated, so have we become before your face, O Lord, is to be marked beforehand with an obelus. But we can take the beloved of the Lord as Christ, for fear of whom we conceive, and travail, and bring forth, and make the spirit of salvation upon the earth. An apostolic man can say this too, when he instructs the peoples and imitates the apostle Paul: My little children, with whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). Or is it to be doubted that the apostle Paul made the spirit of salvation upon the earth, who preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum (Rom 15), and as a wise architect laid the foundation, besides which no one can lay another, which is Christ Jesus (1 Cor 3)? Whether, then, we read, because of fear of you, O Lord, we have received in the womb, or according to the Hebrew, before your face, O Lord, we have conceived, and have received in the womb, both pertain to this: that from the fear and remembrance of the Lord we conceive the word of God, and our heart is illumined as we say: The light of your countenance has been signed upon us, O Lord (Ps 4:7). And, show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps 79 [80]:4).

Salvations we have not wrought on the earth; therefore the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. LXX: We shall not fall, but the inhabitants of the earth will fall. A different translation must needs have a different sense too. According to the Hebrew this is said: Because we have done nothing worthy of your mercy, therefore the impious have not fallen, but to this day prevail and possess the earth. But the Seventy assert this: that while the saints make the spirit of salvation upon the earth, those who are inhabitants of the earth fall; although between world, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל) and in Greek οἰκουμένη, and earth there is much difference. Whoever, then, have given themselves to dwelling on the earth, and have been grounded with a fixed root in earthly works, will fall; and they will not fall who sit in the world and rest in the Church, which is the dwelling place of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

26:19

Let your dead live, let my slain rise again: awake and give praise, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is a dew of lights, and the land of the giants you will pull down to ruin. LXX: The dead will rise again, and they will rise again from the tombs, and those who are in the earth will rejoice. For your dew is their healing, but the land of the impious will fall. While the saints travail and bring forth the spirit, and the inhabitants of the earth fall, because they have not wrought salvations on the earth, those whom the Apostle calls the dead in Christ, and who have been slain for the name of the Lord, will rise again in glory (1 Thess 4). And because their death is sleep, they are said, not, as according to the Seventy, to rise again, but to awaken and to wake up. Hence Lazarus too, who was to be awakened, is called sleeping by the Lord (John 11). All the martyrs, then, and the holy men who shed their blood for Christ, and whose whole life was a martyrdom, will rise again and awaken, and will praise God their Creator, they who now dwell in the dust, of whom it is written in Daniel: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise again, some to everlasting life, and some to reproach and everlasting confusion (Dan 12:2). And in John the Evangelist we read: The hour will come, and now is, when those who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28, 29). For the dew of the Lord, surpassing, as in the fables of the poets, all the Paeonian herbs, will give life to the bodies of the dead. And as, when seeds have been cast into the earth, the dew little by little makes the plants grow and come to the fruits of their kind, so the dew of the Lord, which is put for mercy, will be a dew of very many lights, which in Hebrew is called OROTH (אורות). But the land, that is, the bodies of the Raphaim, namely of the giants and the impious, the Lord will pull down into everlasting punishments. Indeed, for RAPHAIM (רפאים) the Seventy alone translated the impious. And because we read above, The dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up, for which Aquila and Symmachus translated Raphaim and giants, we ask what the cause of the error is, that for the Hebrew RAPHAIM some put giants, others physicians. If the Hebrew word RAPHAIM has VAU following its first letter RES, it is read ROPHAIM (רופאים) and signifies physicians; but if it is written without the letter VAU, it is read RAPHAIM, and is translated giants. And at the same time, because he had said above, The dead will not see life, so as to show more plainly that it was not said there of those dead by the law of nature and the separation of soul and body, but of those who are dead in sin, he now on the contrary says to God: Your dead will live, who have been slain for your sake; who are not called dead absolutely, as the Seventy translated, but, according to the Hebrew, where it is said JEJU METHECA (יהיו מתיך), your dead.

Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your doors upon you: hide yourself a little for a moment, until the indignation passes. For behold, the Lord will come forth from his place, to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him; and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer cover its slain. LXX: Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door: hide yourself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes. For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer hide the slain. Above he had said of the saints, The dead will rise again, and those who are in the tombs will rise again; for the dew from you is their healing; and on the contrary of the impious, but the land of the impious will fall. Now he speaks to the saints: because resurrection has been promised to you, until the wrath of God rages against sinners and the impious, enter into your tombs and hide yourselves, for it is a short time until the indignation of God passes. For indeed the Lord comes forth from his place, because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, and the most clement father is compelled to strike his negligent children, and in a manner to be changed from his own judgment, so that he may visit and bring his wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, of whom it is said in Hosea: Cursing and lying and adultery and theft have been poured out upon the inhabitants of the earth (Hos 4:2). And in the Apocalypse we read three times, Woe upon the inhabitants of the earth (Rev 8:13). But the righteous, although they are seen on the earth, yet their citizenship is in the heavens; they can say, I am a stranger on the earth, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were (Ps 38 [39]:13), and they enjoy the dwelling of the Most High, of whom the holy man speaks: He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven (Ps 90 [91]:1). Then the earth will disclose its blood, of which God speaks to Cain: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand (Gen 4:10, 11). This can also be understood of the Martyrs, who shed their blood for Christ and cry out beneath the altar of God: How long, O Lord, do you not avenge our blood on those who dwell upon the earth? (Rev 6:10). Of them Moses too says in the Song: The blood of his sons will be vindicated and avenged, and he will repay vengeance to his enemies (Deut 32:43). This blood the earth which had received it will disclose, and it will by no means cover the slain of the Lord, but will bring them out into public view for the condemnation of those who killed the Martyrs. Let this be understood of the simple resurrection. But according to the anagogy, the people of God is commanded to enter into its chambers, or storerooms, for ταμεῖα means both: to shut, according to the precept of the Gospel, the door of its chamber (Matt 6), and to say with the Prophet: Set a guard, O Lord, on my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips (Ps 140 [141]:3); and to hide itself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes, so that it does nothing for the sake of glory, but enjoys the good of conscience and awaits God alone as judge. And the storerooms which are to be shut and hidden by those who have become rich in works and words are prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice, so that the left hand may not know what the right hand does, so that we may enjoy the riches of the Law and the Prophets and the Gospel. And that all the days of our life are short and very small, Jacob, exceeding a hundred years, says: Small and very evil are my days (Gen 47:9). And the wrath of the Lord that is to pass is that which those store up for themselves who are unwilling to do penance; after it has passed, the storerooms will by no means be shut any longer, but what is written will be fulfilled: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and secret that will not be made manifest (Luke 8:17). And what follows, For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring his wrath, signifies this: that the wrath of God begins from the saints, or that all his vengeance is just and holy, not coming down from disturbance of mind, as is usual among men, but from zeal to correct. And I consider the earth of the inhabitants to be that of which it is written: Let the earth hear the words of my mouth (Deut 32:1). And: Give ear, O earth (Isa 1:2). And again: Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord (Jer 22:29). For as those who dwell on the earth, so those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8). And earth in this place signifies the soul that lives carnally. And it will disclose its blood, if it has caused anyone to stumble, and deserves to hear with Cain: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood (Gen 4:10, 11). All blood, then, will be required on the day of judgment, nor will the earth hide its blood; and the slain whom it has killed, whether willingly or through negligence, it will bring out into the open.

27:1

In that day the Lord will visit with his hard and great and strong sword upon Leviathan the bar serpent, and upon Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the whale that is in the sea. LXX: In that day God will bring the holy and great and strong sword upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. The Hebrews hand down that the devil, that is, the slanderer, which is a Greek name, is called in Hebrew SATAN (שטן), that is, adversary. Hence in Zechariah too it is said: Satan, that is, the adversary, stood at his right hand to oppose him (Zech 3:1). And he is also called BELIAL (בליעל), that is, apostate, transgressor, and without yoke. Hence the Apostle too: What fellowship, he says, has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor 6:15). And wherever the Seventy put sons of pestilence, in the Hebrew is written sons of Belial. Hence also that which is sung in the psalm about the mystery of the Savior, The son of iniquity shall not proceed to harm him (Ps 88 [89]:23), in the Hebrew is said the son of Belial. And he is called by other names too, as is written in another psalm: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon (Ps 90 [91]:13). This dragon is properly called in the Hebrew language LEVIATHAN (לויתן). He is the great whale of whom it is told in mystical language in Job that he is to be caught by Christ: Who is going to catch the great whale (Job 40:20); for there too Leviathan is put for whale; and again: But you will draw the dragon with a hook, you will put a halter about his nostrils; and immediately: This is the beginning of the Lord's creation, which was made to be mocked by his angels. And in the psalm: This is the great and wide sea: there are creeping things without number, small animals with great. This dragon which you have formed to mock him (Ps 103 [104]:25, 26). Of him John too writes in the Apocalypse: There was a battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them in heaven (Rev 12:7ff.). And: The great dragon was cast out, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who makes the whole world go astray; and he was cast down to the earth, and his angels with him; and there it is said: The accuser of our brethren has been cast out, who accused them before our God (ibid., 12:10). And it must be noted that in the psalm and in Job the dragon, that is, Leviathan, is said to have been made for this purpose, that he might be mocked by the angels. Hence also the Apostles receive power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy (Luke 10). Because, then, from the place where it is written, Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth and will lay it bare (above, Isa 24:1), or, according to the Seventy, Behold, the Lord will destroy the world and will make it desolate, up to the present passage, judgment has been foretold against the world at the consummation of the world, and the last enemy, death, will be destroyed (1 Cor 15): therefore the final sentence is against the devil, that the holy and great and strong sword be brought upon him, or, according to the Hebrew and the other translators, the hard sword. For it is not said CADESA (קדשה), as the Seventy thought, which, if it were so, would signify holy; but CASA (קשה), which is properly translated hard. Hence also Kish, the father of Saul, is interpreted hard. And the holy, or hard, sword, on account of the sense of him who suffers it, some of our writers understand as the Word of God, of which the Apostle says: For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb 4:12). Hence in another place too we read that a two-edged sword goes out of the mouth of the Savior (Rev 19). And when at the end of the world the holy, or hard, and great and strong sword has been brought against Leviathan, who at the beginning of Genesis is called the most cunning serpent above all the beasts (Gen 3:1) that were on the earth, he will flee who was never accustomed to flee, not knowing that which is written: Whither shall I go from your spirit, or whither shall I flee from your face? (Ps 138 [139]:7). A certain poet in his Gigantomachy jested finely about Enceladus: Whither do you flee, Enceladus? Whatever shores you reach, you will always be under God. And this Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, is called in the Hebrew BARI (ברי), which Aquila translated bar, Symmachus shutting in, Theodotion mighty. I think he is called bar, or the one who shuts, because he has shut many in his prison and subjected them to his own power; and he has nothing straight in him, and for that reason is called twisting, nor can he imitate the rod of the Lord, of which it is written: A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom (Ps 44 [45]). Him the Lord will slay with the breath of his mouth (2 Thess 2), him who was once the inhabitant of the sea, of its salty and bitter waves. Let those who say that the devil will do penance and obtain pardon explain to us how they take what is written: And he will slay the dragon that is in the sea, or the whale. For in the second place in the present passage he is not called Leviathan in the Hebrew, but THANNIN (תנין), which properly means whale. Hence the Hebrews suppose that Leviathan dwells under the earth and in the ether, but Thanniim in the sea; which is a Jewish fable. And what is said at the end of this passage, in that day, Eusebius joins to the former chapter, lest the following prophecy be fitted to this time. But the Hebrews and the other expositors join it to the following, which we are now about to set forth.

27:2-3

In that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him. I the Lord, who keep it, will suddenly give it to drink: lest perhaps it be visited, I keep it night and day. LXX: In that day the good vineyard is his desire, that he may be its prince. I am a strong city, a city which is besieged: in vain will I give it drink. For they will be taken by night, and by day the wall will fall. The Hebrew in this place differs much from the edition of the Seventy; therefore let us discuss the particulars as we have set them out. The vineyard of which Isaiah speaks above, A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place: how it ought to be understood, let us learn from his own teaching: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:1); of which it is sung in the psalm: You brought a vine out of Egypt, and so on (Ps 79 [80]:9). To this vineyard too he gives the cup of purest wine to drink through Jeremiah (Jer 25). For when he had sent him to give drink to all the nations, and the Prophet had willingly offered himself for this office, he is commanded first to make Jerusalem drunk. Hence he says: You have deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived (Jer 20:7). Jerusalem, then, will drink, and an unmixed draught is given it to drink, so that it may learn lamentation and weeping. And the Lord says that he has guarded it for a long time and has given it a place for repentance, and because it would not be converted, it is to be made drunk suddenly. For he says that he has done this by days and by nights, so that it might always be kept by his help. But the Seventy call the same vineyard beautiful, in which were the Law and the Prophets, the priesthood and the high priesthood, and the knowledge of God, as Scripture says: God is known in Judea, his name is great in Israel (Ps 75 [76]:1). Others think that, according to their edition, it pertains to the Church, than which nothing is more beautiful, and of which it has been said: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:3): which is the princess of her mother, and says in the Song of Songs: The sons of my mother have fought against me (Song 1:5). And she says: I am a firm city, a city which is besieged. And he did well to say is besieged, not is taken by storm. And immediately he adds concerning the Synagogue, which has been turned from head into tail: In vain do I give it the drink of my teachings, for it will be taken in the darkness of its error. And because it did not receive the open light, its wall has fallen by day, that is, all that it thought its help; and there will be none of the adversaries who does not take it, which we ought to understand of the adverse powers.

27:4-5

Indignation is not in me: who will make me a thorn and a brier in battle? I will march upon it; I will burn it up together. Or rather shall I hold fast my strength? It will make peace for me, peace it will make for me. LXX: There is none that has not laid hold of it. Who will set me as keeper of stubble in a field? Because of this adversary I have driven it back. Therefore the Lord has done all that he arranged: I have been burned; its inhabitants will say, we will make peace with him, we will make peace with him. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: I, who by days and nights have always preserved my vineyard, lest the boar out of the wood should lay it waste, lest the beasts should devour it, have I no indignation, and do I not know how to strike the sinner, and to render to each what he deserves? Where Aquila put thorn and brier, in the Hebrew is written SAMIR (שמיר) and SAITH (ושית), which signify adamant and places full of brambles. Hence he says: Who will teach me to be hard, and to overcome my clemency, and to advance savage in battle and contest, so that I may march upon the vineyard which I kept before, and burn that which I had hedged with my wall? Or rather will my strength bring this about, that I defer my wrath, and save by the clemency of the Gospel those who were by no means saved by the authority of the Law? And according to the Hebrew it is to be read ἐμφατικῶς: Who will make me hard and cruel, so that I overcome my nature? For this indeed is signified by the desert and by the thorns: that I should crush, as in battle, and burn that which I have always guarded with my diligence. Or rather shall I hold fast my strength, which without doubt is Christ, and of which we read, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), so that it may make peace for me and reconcile the world? According to the Seventy, this is the sense, if we take it in the person of the Church: I am a firm city, a city surrounded by many enemies, I who in vain gave cups to my enemy the Synagogue. For it will be taken by night, and its wall will fall, and there will be none of the adverse powers which does not lay hold of it. Again I will speak: What does it profit me to guard her, who has stubble in her, not grain, who is so uncultivated that she is full of briers and thorns, whom I wished to save? But because she deals with me as an enemy, I have withdrawn from her. And the Apostles, born in me and from me, said: It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). Therefore the Lord will do what he threatened, so that all in her burn, surrounded by Roman fire. Or certainly they burn with vices and sins, so that they cannot quench the burning darts of the devil. For all are adulterers, their hearts like an oven. And those who formerly dwelt in her, after they have cried out, The city is taken and burned, will leave her, and, reconciling the world to God, will say: Let us make peace with him, let us make peace with him, that is, with Christ, always writing in their Epistles: Grace be with you and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord (1 Cor 1:3). Of whom we read in this same Prophet: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings of peace! (Isa 52:7). Some refer this place to the Churches: that they are indeed guarded by God, but many in them bear no fruit; and for that reason they are set on fire by the burning zeal of a good teacher, so that they cry out and confess their error, and afterwards make peace with God, being truly called sons of Jacob.

27:6

Those who come forth from the root of Jacob, Israel will blossom and bud, and they will fill the face of the world with seed. LXX: Those who come are the sons of Jacob: Israel will bud and blossom, and its fruit will fill the world. After the Apostles, preaching the Gospel in the whole world, have said, We will make peace with Christ, we will make peace with him, those who were of the seed of Jacob on high, and have attained to the apostolic dignity, will be called sons of Jacob. Then Israel will bud and blossom, seeing that the whole world has been filled with the teaching of its sons and has borne most abundant fruits, which while it remained in Judea it had not borne.

27:7

Has he struck him according to the stroke of him who struck him? Or as he killed his slain, so was he killed? This place is understood in two ways: either against Jerusalem, so as to say that it was not struck by God as it itself struck Christ and his Apostles; or against the multitude of the nations, in that, while they persecuted and shed Christian blood, the Apostles and apostolic men nonetheless took care of their salvation and reconciled them to God.

27:8

In measure against measure, when it has been cast off, you will judge it. LXX: Quarreling and reproaching, he will send them away. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: As Jerusalem did, so will it receive, and according to the measure with which it measured, it will be measured back to it. And it will receive the measure heaped up when the time of judgment has come and God has cast it off. According to the Seventy, what is said depends on what precedes. For Israel will not be struck as it struck, nor killed as it killed: Israel, which quarreled against the Apostles, and reproached its teachers, and commanded them not to speak in the name of Christ. Therefore the Lord will cast them off and drive them out of his flock.

He has meditated in his hard spirit through the day of heat. LXX: Was it not you who meditated with a hard spirit to kill them, with a spirit of fury? According to the Hebrew this is said: with the measure with which it measured, Jerusalem will receive; therefore God in his hard and vehement spirit has meditated, or spoken, against it in the day of heat, that is, in the time of persecution, when the day of indignation and punishments is more burning. According to the Seventy, it is said to Jerusalem itself, or to Israel: Was it not you who, in your most hard and cruel spirit, and in the fury of your blasphemies, desired to kill the Apostles and teachers of the Lord?

27:9

Therefore by these things iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and this is all the fruit, that his sin may be taken away: because he has made all the stones of the altar like stones of ash dashed to pieces; the groves and the shrines will not stand. LXX: Therefore the iniquity of Jacob will be taken away, and this will be his blessing, when I have taken away his sin, when he has made all the stones of the altars crushed like ash ground small, and their trees will not endure, nor the idols. He gives the reasons why, after the Jews have laid hands on the Lord, they may obtain pardon if they are willing to do penance, so that the prayer of the Savior may be fulfilled: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34). Therefore, he says, iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and its sin will be taken away, so that it may merit the blessing of God, which had called down a curse upon itself, saying: His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt 27:25); because through the Apostles of the stock of Israel the Gospel will be sown in the whole world, and idolatry will be destroyed, and the altars will be ground down to dust, the groves will be cut down, the shrines will fall, and the knowledge of the one God under the mystery of the Trinity will be preached.

27:10

For the fortified city will be desolate; the beautiful one will be left, and abandoned as a desert. There the calf will feed, and there he will lie down and consume its topmost shoots. LXX: Their idols will be cut down like a grove, and the flock dwelling far off will be abandoned like a forsaken flock, and it will be for a long time for pasture, and there the flocks will rest, and after a long time there will not be in it anything green, because it has been dried up. Jerusalem, the city once firm and fortified, because it did not receive the son of the householder, but said, Come, let us kill him, for this is the heir, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt 21:38), will be desolate. And she who was once beautiful, of whom it is said in Ezekiel too, You ate fine flour and honey and oil, and you became exceedingly beautiful (Ezek 16:13), and in whom dwelt he of whom it is written, Beautiful in form above the sons of men (Ps 44 [45]:3), will be left and abandoned as a desert, as the Lord says to the Apostles: Arise, let us go hence (John 14:31). There the calf will feed, the Roman army, of which it is said in another place under the name of the boar: The boar out of the wood will lay it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it (Ps 79 [80]:14). And there he will lie down and consume its topmost shoots, under the metaphor of a vineyard and its shoots, so that nothing green, nothing of the tendrils, remains in it, but the enemy consumes all. According to the Seventy, because they did not receive the good shepherd, therefore they will be like a forsaken flock, and will lie open to the bites of the beasts; and nothing green will remain in them, because drought will possess all things.

27:11

In the drought of its harvest the women coming and teaching it will be crushed. For it is not a wise people: therefore he who made it will not have mercy on it, and he who formed it will not spare it. LXX: Women coming from the spectacle, come: for it is not a people having understanding; therefore he who made them will not have mercy on them, and he who formed them will not spare. What is said, In the drought of its harvest they will be crushed, for which the Seventy translated, there will not be in it anything green, because it has dried up, according to the Hebrew is coupled with what follows, according to the Seventy with the preceding sense. Let us speak first, then, according to the Hebrew. When the time of the drought and the harvest of Jerusalem, and, to speak more openly, of its devastation, has come, the throng of the synagogues will run together from the whole world to lament Jerusalem and console her evils. Or he is speaking openly of the women who, with bared breasts, strike their arms till they bleed; and the prophecy of the Lord will be fulfilled: Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but lament over yourselves and over your children (Luke 23:28). And it is a great unhappiness for the people to learn songs of lamentation from women; just as it was a reproach to the people of Israel when, in the book of Judges (Judg 4), the Lord wrought salvation by the hand of the woman Deborah, and at the time of the approaching captivity, while the men were silent, the woman Huldah prophesied (2 Kgs 22). But for this reason the women will be crushed by the long journey, worn out by weakness, hunger and squalor, and they will teach the wretched people, because it is not a wise people, nor has it understood its Creator, who, neglected and despised by them, will not have mercy on his handiwork and will not spare his creature. According to the Seventy, it is said of Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, and the rest of the women, who first saw the Lord rising again, and held his feet, and merited to hear from him: Do not fear: go, tell my brethren to go into Galilee, and there they will see me (Matt 28:10).
