LXX: O Lord, have mercy on us, for we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has come to perdition, but our salvation is in the time of tribulation: because of the voice of fear the peoples were astonished at the fear of you, and the nations were scattered. But now your spoils will be gathered, small and great: as if someone were gathering locusts, so will they mock you: holy is God who dwells on high. Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness; they will be handed over in the law; in treasures is our salvation: wisdom has come, and discipline, and piety from the Lord; these are the treasures of righteousness. The Hebrews think that the preceding section, in which we read: Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? and the rest to the end, was spoken against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians: that after he had overthrown the cities of the ten tribes, which were called Israel, and had also taken the cities of Judea, except Jerusalem, he himself would be overcome, and his army would be destroyed when the Angel struck. Hence they contend that the things contained in the present section are now spoken in the person of the people giving thanks to God and saying: O Lord, have mercy on us, we have waited for you: that he himself was the arm and the strength of the people hemmed in by the siege, in the morning time, and their salvation in need and distress. For at the voice of the Angel, which Symmachus rendered just as it is written in the Hebrew, AMUN (המון), and whom the Hebrews hold to be Gabriel and to have the etymology of people, the Assyrian fled, and at the exaltation of God the nations that were with him were scattered this way and that. As they fled, the spoils were gathered by the Jews, as a multitude of young locusts and of locusts is usually gathered when they have been heaped up in ditches. In their victory the Lord was magnified, and Zion was filled with judgment and righteousness, and the faith of the besieged people was proven; and they had all their riches in wisdom, and in the knowledge of God and the fear of the Lord, who alone was their treasure. These things they may say according to the history, striving by every means to overthrow the mysteries of Christ and of his Apostles. But we, after the blessedness of the Apostles, of whom it was said above (cf. Isa 32:20): Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread, and after the lamentation and wailing of those who persecuted them, of whom it is said in what follows: Woe to those who make you wretched; but no one makes you wretched: and as a moth in a garment, so will they be worn away, prove that these things are spoken in the person of the same Apostles and of all believers. And the sense is: Lord, we have hoped in your help, and we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has perished for ever, and our salvation has appeared in the time of tribulation. For when you gave help, the whole multitude of the nations was scattered, and became a prey and a mockery to the victors. And this came about because the holy Lord dwells on high, and Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness, of which it was written above: Judgment and righteousness will rest in the desert. This, then, is Zion, which before was called the desert; and whoever dwells in her, to him will be handed over the law of the Gospel, in whose treasure is our salvation, and the wisdom of believers, and discipline and piety, or faith, which properly belongs to Christians, and the fear of the Lord, in which the treasures of wisdom are contained.

33:7ff.

Behold, those who see will cry outside: the Angels of peace will weep bitterly. The ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the path has ceased, the covenant has been made void, he has cast off the cities, he has not regarded men. The earth has mourned and languished, Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf, and Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. Now I will rise up, says the Lord: now I will be exalted, now I will be lifted up. You will conceive burning heat, you will bring forth stubble; your spirit, like fire, will devour you. And the peoples will be like ashes from a burning: thorns gathered together will be burned with fire. The Hebrew word ARELLAM (אראלם), for which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated I will appear to them, dividing the last syllable and reading ARE LAHEM (ארא להם), the Hebrews think signifies Angels, and that this is a prophecy, after the calling of the nations and the riches of the Church, of the overthrow of the Temple: that the Angels will weep, no longer dwelling within, but going outside; and those who before were messengers of peace will weep bitterly. Or the Apostles themselves, who had been sent to announce peace to Jerusalem, to which the Lord said: If you too had known the things that belong to your peace (Luke 19:42), and to whom the Lord appeared, to strengthen them by his sight, will weep for Jerusalem, because it did not receive their preaching, because the ways are laid waste, and the one who passed along the righteous path has ceased, according to what is said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemnity (Lam 1:4). The covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has also been made void: He has cast off the cities of Judea: he has not regarded men, who by their own fault chose to be beasts. The earth has mourned and languished for those who dwelt in the land (Gen 15 and 22). Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf: without doubt it signifies the Temple, of which we read in Zechariah: Open your gates, O Lebanon, that fire may devour your cedars (Zech 11:1). Or Jerusalem, which in Ezekiel is called Lebanon, when the Prophet says: A great eagle with great wings, which has the design of entering into Lebanon (Ezek 17:3); which the divine word afterward interprets: when, it says, Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem; plainly explaining the Eagle as the king of Babylon, and Lebanon as Jerusalem. Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. For Bashan, the LXX translated Galilee, the province in place of one place of the province. Sharon, moreover, is the name of the whole region around Joppa and Lydda, in which very broad and fertile plains stretch out. Bashan too is a region beyond the Jordan, which the two and a half tribes possessed, and which means most fruitful and fat (Deut 3); and Carmel, of which we spoke above. The once fertile places of Judea, then, will be turned into a wilderness, by which it is shown μεταφορικῶς that all the opulence of the Jews is to be exchanged for want and poverty. Since, then, they would not receive the word of the Apostles, Lebanon is confounded, and Sharon is turned into a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. Therefore the Lord says that he will rise up, either from his very great patience, or from the underworld, and will be exalted among the nations, and lifted up on the cross. And he turns in apostrophe to the Jews themselves: You will conceive burning heat, and you will bring forth stubble, and your spirit will kindle a fire for you, so that the devouring flame may consume what was conceived and brought forth. And the peoples of the Jews, he says, will be like ashes from a burning, showing the greatness of their misfortune by the remnants of the embers. For their thorns, which have been gathered together by the multitude of their sins, will be devoured by the burning; which most refer to the last captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem. Others affirm that it will come about more fully and perfectly at the time of judgment.

33:13ff.

Hear, you who are far off, what I have done, and you who are near, know my strength. The sinners in Zion are terrified, trembling has seized the hypocrites. Who of you can dwell with devouring fire? Who of you will dwell with everlasting burnings? He who walks in acts of righteousness, and speaks truths, who casts away avarice from calumny, and shakes his hands free of every bribe, who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil. He will dwell on high; fortresses of rocks are his height: bread has been given him, his waters are faithful. His eyes will see the king in his beauty: they will behold the land from afar. Your heart will meditate fear. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? You will not see the imprudent people, the people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue, in which there is no wisdom. LXX: Those who are far off will hear what they have done: those who draw near will know my strength. The lawless who were in Zion have departed; trembling will seize the impious. Who will announce to you that fire is burning? Who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness, and speaks the right way, and hates impiety and iniquity, and shakes his hands free of gifts, and stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and shuts his eyes so that they may not see iniquity, he will dwell in a lofty cave of a very strong rock. Bread will be given him, and his water will be faithful: your eyes will see the king with glory, they will see the land from afar; your soul will meditate fear. Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? Where is he who numbers those who nourish both the small and the great people? To whom he did not give counsel: nor did he know his deep voice, so that the despised people did not hear, and there is no understanding for the one who hears. Since the ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the paths has ceased, the covenant with the people of the Jews has been made void, God has cast off their cities and has not counted them among men; therefore you who are far off, hear what I have done, and draw near, that you may know my strength. The sinners, or the impious, who were in Zion are terrified, or have departed, and trembling has seized the hypocrites, to whom the Lord said in the Gospel: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14)! Who of you can dwell with him who is a devouring fire? Who will dwell with everlasting burnings? Or according to the LXX: Who will announce to you that the eternal fire is burning, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels? Who, then, will be able to dwell with God, or to announce the punishments to come? Everyone who is such as the prophetic word describes: who walks in many acts of righteousness, and loves acts of righteousness not once but always, and speaks truths not on one occasion but continually; who casts away avarice, which is the mother of calumny. For money is not heaped up for one man except with another's loss and harm. And he shakes his hands free of every bribe; for bribes blind the eyes even of the wise. He stops his ears lest he hear the judgment of blood. All iniquity and oppression and injustice is a judgment of blood: and though one does not kill with the sword, yet he slays by his will. And he shuts his eyes lest he see evil. Happy the conscience that neither hears nor beholds evil. He, then, who is such will dwell on high, that is, in the kingdom of heaven, or in a lofty cave of a very strong rock, in Christ Jesus: the rock that followed the people of Israel, that they might drink from it and be protected by its strength. Bread will be given him, and his waters are faithful: which the fables of the Gentiles understand as ambrosia and nectar. But we shall interpret the bread and the most faithful waters as the law of God. He, then, who is such will behold Christ the king in his brightness, of whom it is said above (cf. Isa 32:1): Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule in judgment. And his eyes will see from afar the land which they had long desired, the land of the meek and gentle, of which it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the land (Matt 5:4); or, set in heaven, they will look down on earthly things. Your heart will meditate fear: so that when you have attained all things, you may say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor 15:9). For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? (Prov 9:1). Where, he says, are the scribes and Pharisees, who, weighing the words of the Law in the balance, deceived the unhappy people? whom the Scripture now calls little ones: little in sense, little in understanding. And when the eyes of the believer have beheld the king in his majesty, and his heart has meditated fear, then he will not see the imprudent people, the people of the Jews, or of the philosophers and orators of the world, who applaud themselves for secular learning and eloquence, of whom he now says: A people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue; whose whole adornment is in words, who have only the leaves and the shade of speech, and do not possess the fruit of truth. Then there follows: In which there is no wisdom; of whom it is also said in another place: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor 1:19). Why? Because God has made foolish the wisdom of this world.

33:20ff.

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a wealthy habitation: a tabernacle that can by no means be moved, nor will its pegs be taken away for ever, and none of its cords will be broken. For only there is our Lord magnificent: a place of rivers, streams very broad and open; no ship with oars will pass through it, nor will a great trireme cross it. For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us. Your cords are loosened, and will not hold: so will your mast be, that you cannot spread out the ensign. Then the spoils of many preys will be divided: the lame will seize the plunder. Nor will the neighbor say, I am faint: the people that dwells in it, iniquity will be taken away from it. LXX: Behold Zion, the city, our salvation: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich city, tabernacles that will not be moved: nor will the stakes of its tabernacle be taken away for ever, and its cords will not be torn apart: for the name of the Lord is great to you: your place will be rivers and streams very broad and spacious: no ship driven by oars will go in through it: for my God is great: the Lord will not pass me by, our judge, the Lord our prince, the Lord our king, the Lord himself will save us. Your cords are broken because they did not hold: your mast is bent, so that it lets the sails go: it will not raise the ensign until it is given over to devastation. Many lame, therefore, will take spoils: and they will not say, I shall labor; the people that dwells in them, their sin will be forgiven them. O righteous one, to whom it was said above: your heart will meditate fear; and, the imprudent people you will not see; and who had heard before, your eyes will see the king in his beauty: look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity, see the Church of Christ, in which is the true solemnity: your eyes will behold the vision of peace, and riches beyond hope, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, and the tabernacle that can by no means be moved. For the former tabernacle, which the people of the Jews had, was moved and taken away. Nor will its pegs be moved for ever, and all its cords will be firm; so that the Lord dwells in it, which is the place of all the rivers and running streams, through which no one of the opposing side will be able to sail: nor a great trireme, which is interpreted as the devil, will be able to cross it: because the Lord himself is our judge, and prince, and king, and Savior, and under his protection we shall fear the snares of no one. These things are said of Zion, the city of our solemnity, and of Jerusalem, the richest habitation, which the Lord himself will surround and fortify with his rivers. But now he speaks to the earthly Jerusalem: that the cords of its tabernacle are loosened, and could not hold up the tent, and its mast, on which the most beautiful sails once hung, has fallen with its ropes broken, so that it is useless not only for sailing but also for an ensign. And after their ship has been broken up and the tabernacle scattered, so that the cords are torn apart on both sides, the plunder will be divided among the victors: who will be so weak in their own strength that they are called lame; and nonetheless, since the wrath of God gives them strength, they will feel no weakness, nor will they say: I have labored. For whoever is among them, iniquity and sin will be taken away from him, because he has carried out the will of God.

34:1ff.

Come near, you nations, and hear, and you peoples, attend: let the earth hear, and its fullness, the world and all its offspring. For the indignation of the Lord is upon all the nations, and his fury upon all their host: he has slain them and given them over to slaughter. Their slain will be cast out, and from their corpses a stench will rise: the mountains will melt with their blood. And all the host of the heavens will waste away: the heavens will be rolled back (or folded together) like a book: and all their host will fall away, as a leaf falls from the vine and from the fig tree, for my sword has been made drunk in heaven. Behold, it will come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my slaughter, to judgment. The sword of the Lord is filled with blood, it is fattened with fat: with the blood of lambs and goats, with the blood of rams full of marrow; for the Lord has a victim in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. And the unicorns will come down with them, and the bulls with the mighty. Their land will be made drunk with their blood, and their ground with the fat of the fat ones. After the overthrow of Jerusalem and the shipwreck of the once most solid ship, and the plundering of all its furnishings, it speaks of the destruction of all the nations, and of the consummation of the world, which is on the future day of judgment. Hence all the nations and peoples, the earth and its fullness, the world and all its offspring, both the places that are inhabited and those that are uninhabitable through excess of cold and of heat, are commanded to hear, and to learn with all trembling of mind what is to come. For the indignation of the Lord is described as coming not upon the one nation of Judea alone, and upon the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Egyptians, the Moabites and the Ammonites and the Philistines, but against all the nations, and upon all their host, or, as the LXX translated, their number, to slay them and to make the stench of rotting bodies rise on high, signifying the sins of all the nations; so that the mountains are filled with their gore and filth and blood: all the lofty powers and the Angels who presided over the several nations; and all the host or strength of the heavens wastes away: the heavens are rolled back, or folded together, like a book, and all their host and army, and, as the LXX translated, the stars will fall away, in the likeness of leaves which, as the cold draws near, fall withered and shrivelled from the vine and the fig tree. Which indeed the Savior also says in the Gospel: The stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be moved, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven (Matt 24:29, 30). And this must be considered, that he does not say that the heavens perish, but that they are rolled back, or folded together, like a book: so that after all sins have been laid open and read through, the heavens which before were open are folded together, so that the offenses of many are no longer written in them. Of books of this kind Daniel speaks in his volume: The judgment sat, and the books were opened (Dan 7:10), in which the works of each had been written down. Most think that the stars fall according to the Apocalypse of John (Rev 6 and 8), and according to what is written elsewhere: All the stars, burning, will be dissolved, and heaven and earth will pass away (Luke 10:2). For the form of this world passes away. Some think that this is said of the stars that glitter in the heaven, so that the whole is shown in the part: namely, that through the ruin of the stars the destruction of the heavens too is shown (1 Cor 7). Others, however, think that those stars will fall of which the Apostle Paul also writes: Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph 6:12). Nor is it surprising if the demons who dwell in the air are called heavenly, since the Scripture also names the birds of heaven, which certainly fly not in heaven but in the air. For Satan too transforms himself into an Angel of light (2 Cor 11), pretending to be a star. And the Savior saw him falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10). And tropologically it is said of him as of a great star: How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning? (Isa 14:12). All these things will come about because his sword has been made drunk in heaven: the punishment and sentence and vengeance upon sinners which is pronounced by the Lord. This sword and blade is sharpened against the impious in Ezekiel (Ezek 21), and, when very many have been slain, is commanded to go back into its sheath. And when it has been made drunk and filled in heaven, that is, in the air, which by the usage of the Scriptures is called heaven, then it will come down to Idumea too, that is, to earthly things: so that after the punishment of the demons the souls of men too may be judged. For Idumea in our language means earthly. And it is filled with blood and fattened with the fat of lambs and goats, and of rams full of marrow, and of bulls: so as to signify that princes and people alike are to be punished. For the Lord has a victim in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. Of this Bozrah and Idumea the same Prophet also testifies in what follows (cf. Isa 63:1), saying: Who is this who comes from Edom, with his garments red from Bozrah? And some think that, because Bosor means flesh, the torments of all in the flesh are shown by the Lord's victim in Bozrah: they fall into a pious error. For in the present place it is written not with the letter SIN, which is set in BOSOR (בשר), that is, flesh, but with SADE, and it is called BOSRA (בצרה), which according to Joshua and Jeremiah is found not in Edom, that is, Idumea, but in the land of Moab (Jer 48). And Bosra in our language means fortified and surrounded, or strengthened: to teach that the world has been made firm by the will of the Lord, according to what is sung in the psalm: He has founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers (Ps 23 [24]:2); and of the firmness of the earth it is said in the person of God: I have made firm its pillars (Ps 74 [75]:3). And when the Lord's victim has been in Bozrah, and his slaughter in Idumea, the unicorns will come down with the mighty bulls, namely the kings and princes of the earth; and all things will be filled with slaughter and blood, and with the fat of those once rich and mighty. By these words, which, after the manner of human speech, strike terror into the hearers, torments are shown against all princes and mighty men, and against peoples and small ones. By Bosra, that is, fortified and strengthened, and by Edom, or Dumah, and Idumea, the teachers of the Jews want Rome to be understood, and all the things contained in the following section to be said of it.

34:8ff.

For it is the day of the Lord's vengeance, the year of the recompenses of the judgment of Zion. And its torrents will be turned into pitch, and its ground into sulphur: and its land will become burning pitch. Night and day it will not be quenched, for ever: its smoke will go up: from generation to generation it will be desolate; for ages of ages there will be none passing through it. And the pelican and the hedgehog will possess it, and the ibis and the raven will dwell in it, and the measuring line will be stretched over it, to bring it to nothing, and the plummet unto desolation. Its nobles will not be there: they will rather call upon the king, and all its princes will be as nothing. And thorns will spring up in its house and nettles, and the thornbush in its fortresses: and it will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches. And demons will meet with onocentaurs, and the hairy one will cry out one to another: there will lie down the lamia, and will find rest for herself. There the hedgehog has had its hole, and has reared its young, and has dug round about, and cherished them in its shade: thither the kites have gathered, one to another. Search diligently in the book of the Lord, and read: not one of them was missing, one did not seek the other: for what proceeds from my mouth, he has commanded, and his spirit, he himself has gathered them. And he himself has cast the lot for them and his hand has divided it to them by measure; they will possess it for ever: from generation to generation they will dwell in it. The Hebrews, as we said above, contend that these things were prophesied of the Roman empire, and that the devastation of a once most powerful kingdom is foretold in vengeance for Zion; and most of our writers think that this, according to the letter, is also written in the Apocalypse of John. But we, from what is said, the day of the Lord's vengeance, the year of the recompenses of the judgment of Zion, judge this to be the year of which the Savior himself speaks: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives, and to the blind that they may see, to call the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompense for our God: to comfort all who mourn, and to give glory to those who lament for Zion (Luke 4:18, 19; Isa 61:1-3); and of which it was said above: Wealthy women, rise (Isa 32:9), and remember the days of the year in grief with hope; and therefore we judge that after the general consummation of the whole world the Scripture returns to Jerusalem, to which it was speaking at that time, and describes its devastation at full length: namely, that after the time of the Roman siege has come, all things will be filled with pitch and sulphur and burning flames, and its smoke will remain for ever, and the pelican and the hedgehog and the ibis and the raven will dwell there, animals which are accustomed to dwell in desert places; and that this will come about because the line and the plummet of the Lord, that is, his sentence, cannot be changed. Its nobles, that is, the Apostles and the believers, will not be there, nor will they be joined to the number of the lost, but will rather call upon Christ the king. But all its princes, namely the scribes and Pharisees, will be brought to nothing, and in the once most adorned houses thorns and nettles and the thornbush will spring up. And it will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches, which are themselves also signs of utter desolation. And there will meet one another in it, according to the LXX, various phantoms of demons, or, as all the others translated according to the Hebrew, SIIM (ציים) and IIM (איים), onocentaurs and hairy ones and the lamia, which the fables of the Gentiles and the fictions of the poets describe. The hedgehog too rears its young there, and has a most secure lodging: thither the kites are gathered, a most rapacious bird, which in Hebrew is called DAJOTH (דיות), or, as the LXX translated, stags, of which we shall speak below. Among these things the Prophet speaks to his hearers: O men who hear me speaking, what I announce as to come will all be fulfilled in deed. For they are written in the book of the Lord, and his sentence is fixed, and not even one will be void. For what proceeds from my mouth, he has commanded; that is, I indeed speak, but the words are the Lord's, and by his spirit whatever has been said will be accomplished. By his decree and measure each thing will be fulfilled, and they will not abandon their order unto everlasting generations. Let these things be said according to the Hebrew and the historical explanation. But those who follow tropology affirm that, once the people of the Jews has been driven out, idolaters and those who serve various superstitions will dwell in Jerusalem under the names of beasts and monsters; and that these are the pelicans and hedgehogs, the ibis and the raven, the dragons and ostriches, and the onocentaurs, and the demons, and the hairy ones, and the lamia, which in Hebrew is called LILITH (לילית), and was translated lamia by Symmachus alone, and which some of the Hebrews suspect to be ἐριννὴν, that is, a fury. And indeed, if we consider that colonies brought from various nations were settled in Jerusalem, and that according to the rite of their own provinces the several households worshipped the monstrous forms of their own demons, we shall affirm that all these dwelt in Jerusalem. And what the LXX translated: There the stags met one another, and saw one another's faces: they passed by in number, not one of them perished, nor did one seek the other. For the Lord commanded them, and his spirit gathered them: and he himself gave them lots, and his hand will divide for them, that they may feed for ever, and possess it from generation to generation, and rest in it: this we shall interpret allegorically, to teach that the stags, that is, the Apostles and all holy teachers, of whom it is written: As the stag longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God (Ps 41 [42]:1); and elsewhere: The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags (Ps 28 [29]:9); and again: Let the stag of friendship and the foal of your graces speak with you (Prov 5); and in Job: But you have watched the months of the stags, and you will bring forth their young (Job 39:2); and in the Song of Songs it is said: My kinsman is like a roe, or a young stag upon the mountains of spices (Song 2:9); met one another in Jerusalem and saw each other's faces, and passed through it and left it, and went on to various provinces, because the Lord commanded them: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19); and that his spirit gathered them, and gave them lots and divided them, so that one went to the Indians, another to the Spains, another to Illyricum, another to Greece, and each rested in the province of his own Gospel and teaching. What we have said is prophesied of Jerusalem, and what the Jews suspect is said of the Roman empire, some refer to the whole world, so as not to seem to disagree with what precedes.

35:1-2

The desert and the pathless land will be glad, and the wilderness will exult, and will flower like the lily. Budding, it will bud forth, and will exult, joyful and praising. The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the Lord, and the beauty of our God. LXX: Rejoice, thirsty desert, and let the wilderness exult, and let it flower like the lily. The deserts of the Jordan will flower and exult: the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the honor of Carmel: and my people will see the glory of the Lord, and the height of our God. Since Jerusalem has been turned into pitch, and its everlasting smoke has gone up, and the pelican and the hedgehog, the ibis and the raven, dragons and ostriches, demons and onocentaurs, the lamia and the hairy ones dwell in it, and the sentence of the Lord has been fulfilled upon it: Your house will be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35): therefore she who before had been deserted, of whom it is said in the psalm: The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh. The voice of the Lord preparing the stags; and he will lay bare the thickets of the forests (Ps 28 [29]:8, 9), will be changed into an abundance of all things; and, as the stags fight, the beasts which formerly possessed all the forests of the nations will be driven out of them, so that what is said in this same Prophet may be fulfilled: Rejoice, barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry, you who do not travail; for more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa 54:1). She who before was thirsty, or pathless, not having life-giving waters, and through whom the Lord did not walk, will now flower into a lily, or, as Aquila expressed it more significantly, καλύκωσις, which we can call a swelling rose whose petals have not yet opened. And she will flower, so as to declare with the Apostle: We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place (2 Cor 2:15); and that saying of the Song of Songs: Flowers have appeared in the land: the mandrakes have given their fragrance (Song 7:12, 13). And what is set down in the LXX, and the deserts of the Jordan will exult, is indeed not found in the Hebrew; but we can say that by the river Jordan John's baptism of repentance is shown, which the Lord sealed and confirmed by his own washing. And since this is said figuratively of the wilderness, which refers to the nations, and in which John was, the Jordan can fittingly be joined to it, so that through the desert of the nations we may come to the baptism of the Savior. And what follows, the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the beauty of Carmel and Sharon, we must take according to the earlier explanation, in which we said that by Lebanon the Temple or Jerusalem is understood, as Zechariah says: Open your gates, O Lebanon (Zech 11:1); and Ezekiel: A great eagle with great wings, full of talons, which has the design of entering into Lebanon and Carmel (Ezek 17:3); and that Carmel signifies the former people, of which it was said above: And the desert will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest (Isa 32:15); and that Sharon has the same meaning, since the Scripture says: Sharon has become like a desert. All the brightness, then, the worship of God, and the knowledge of circumcision, and the most fruitful and level places, which are called Sharon, for which Symmachus translated plains, will be given to the once deserted Church, and its inhabitants will see the glory of the Lord, and the beauty, or height, of our God.

35:3-4

Strengthen the slackened hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to the faint-hearted (or to the fearful), Be strengthened, and do not fear; behold, your God will bring the vengeance of recompense: God himself will come and will save you (or, as the LXX translated, us). Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped (or will hear). Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened, for waters have broken out in the desert, and torrents in the wilderness, and what was dry ground will become a pool (or marshes), and the thirsty land springs of water. In the lairs in which dragons dwelt before, the green of reed and rush will spring up (for which the LXX translated: There will be the gladness of birds, and folds of flocks). And there will be a path there, and a way (or a clean way), and it will be called the holy way; the polluted will not pass through it. And this will be for us a straight way, so that fools may not go astray in it (or, as the LXX translated, nor will there be an unclean way there, but those who have been scattered will pass through it, and will not go astray). There will be no lion there, he says, and no evil beast will go up by it, nor will one be found there, but those who have been set free will walk in it. And the redeemed of the Lord will return, and will come to Zion with praise, and everlasting gladness will be upon their head. They will obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning will flee away. We have mingled both editions, lest, by setting out each one, the size of the books be stretched, which already exceeds the measure of brevity. The Apostles, of whom it was said above: They will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God, are commanded to strengthen the hands that had grown slack among the nations, and to make firm the feeble knees; so that those who before could not do the work of God with slackened hands, and had a withered right hand, may stretch it out to good works; and those who long limped among idols with various errors may walk with firm step upon the truth; and that, strengthening the faint-hearted or timid by faith in the Lord, they may make them not fear, and the fear of the one God may drive out the fears of all error. And the cause of their security and constancy is that Christ is to come, to whom the Father has given all judgment, and he will render to each according to his works (John 5). He himself will come and will save you, you to whom it is said, Do not fear; or us, so that the Apostles may say that salvation is common to them with the believers. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened. And although this was fulfilled by the greatness of signs, when the Lord said to the disciples of John who had been sent to him: Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise again, the poor have the gospel preached to them (Luke 7:22); yet it is fulfilled daily among the nations, when those who before were blind, and stumbled against wood and stones, behold the light of truth. And those who with deaf ears could not hear the words of the Scriptures now rejoice at the precepts of God; when those who before were lame, and did not keep the right way, leap like stags, imitating their teachers; and the tongue of the dumb is opened, whose mouths Satan had shut, so that they could not confess the one Lord. And for this reason the eyes will be opened, the ears will hear, the lame will leap, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened: because in the once deserted Church the waters of saving baptism have broken out, or burst forth, and torrents and streams in the wilderness, namely the various spiritual graces; and what was dry ground has been turned into a pool and marshes, so that it is not only free from the burning of thirst, but is navigable and well watered, and has very many springs, which the stag longs for, and of which whoever has drunk can bless the Lord, according to what is written: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). In the lairs of the Gentile souls, in which dragons dwelt before, there will be the reed and the rush, with which the faith of the Lord may be written, and on which limbs once weary may rest; or there will be the gladness of birds, and folds of flocks: so that they may take the wings of a dove, and, leaving lowly things, hasten to the heights, and be able to say with the Psalmist: The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing: in a place of pasture, there he has set me: beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up. There will be a path there, and a most clean way, which will be called holy, and which says of itself: I am the way (John 14:6), through which he who is polluted will not be able to pass. Hence it is also said in the psalm: Blessed are the undefiled in the way (Ps 118 [119]:1). And this way, that is, our God, will be for us so straight and level and plain that it has no error: and fools and the senseless may be able to walk in it, to whom Wisdom speaks in Proverbs: If anyone is a little one, let him come to me. And to the unwise she said: Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Leave childishness, and live, and walk in the ways of prudence (Prov 9:4-6). For God has chosen the foolish things of the world (1 Cor 1): the prince of which fools speaks in the psalm: O God, you know my foolishness. And the foolishness of God is wiser than men (Ps 68 [69]:6). Hence the LXX translated: And those who had been scattered (1 Cor 2), and separated from the fellowship of the Lord, will by no means go astray. There follows: There will be no lion there: our adversary the devil, who goes about roaring, seeking how he may enter the sheepfold of the Lord (1 Pet 5). And the evil beasts, his attendants, will not go up by it. For the track of a serpent cannot be found upon a rock. But those will walk in it who have been set free from the chains of sins, and redeemed by the blood of the Savior, and have repented, and have come to Zion, of which we have often spoken: You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22); lest after the Jewish fashion we seek a golden Zion and a jewelled Jerusalem, which, according to the prophecy of Daniel, has been dissolved into everlasting ashes (Dan 9). And the everlasting gladness of those who praise the Lord will be upon their head, so that after they have conquered the world they may be able to say with the Apostle and with the Prophet: I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness (2 Tim 4:7, 8); and, O Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us (Ps 5:13). Then, as joy and gladness take their place, sorrow and groaning will flee away, when he comes out of Zion who will deliver. All these things we, following the apostle Paul, interpret of the first coming of the Savior: but the Jews, and our Judaizers, refer them to the second, on the strength of a single little verse, They will return and come to Zion with praise, longing for the blood of victims, and the servitude of all the nations, and the beauty of wives.

Book Eleven

It is difficult, nay impossible, to please everyone: and there is not as great a diversity of faces as there is of opinions. In my explanation of the twelve prophets I seemed to some longer than I ought to have been; and for this reason in my short Commentaries on Daniel I aimed at brevity, except in the last and the second-to-last vision, in which, because of the greatness of their obscurity, I had to stretch out my discourse: and especially in the exposition of the seven and the sixty-two and the one weeks, in discussing which I briefly gathered what Africanus, the writer on chronology, what Origen and Eusebius of Caesarea, Clement too, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, and Apollinaris of Laodicea, Hippolytus, the Hebrews and Tertullian thought, leaving it to the reader's judgment which of the many he should choose. So what I did out of modesty in judging, and out of respect for those who were going to read, may perhaps not please some, who desire to know not the opinions of the ancients but my own view. To them the answer is easy: that I did not wish to accept one in such a way as to seem to condemn the others. And certainly, if men so great and so learned displease fastidious readers, what would they have done with me, who, for the slenderness of my little talent, lie open to the bites of the envious? But if I have named the aforesaid men masters of the Church, let them understand that I do not approve the faith of all of them, who certainly contradict one another, but that I spoke so to distinguish them from Josephus and Porphyry, who have disputed a great deal on this question. And if, in expounding the statue and the discrepancy of its feet and toes, I interpreted the iron and the clay of the Roman kingdom, which Scripture foretells as strong at first and then weak, let them impute it not to me but to the Prophet. For princes are not to be flattered in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected; nor is a general discussion an injury to one person. And while this was being guarded against by the kind zeal of my friends, it was suddenly removed by the judgment of God, so that both my friends' zeal for me and the snares of my rivals might be shown. But of this elsewhere: now let us carry out what we have begun. The eleventh book on Isaiah, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, because it is going to discuss a great part of history, will be easier at the beginning, up to two thirds of it; the rest must be dictated in a like manner: and brevity must be so pursued that no loss is done to understanding.

36:1ff.

And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And the king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to king Hezekiah with a heavy hand, and he stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, in the way of the fuller's field. And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder; and Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust? Or with what counsel and strength are you planning to rebel? In whom do you have confidence, that you have withdrawn from me? Behold, you are trusting in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt: on which if a man leans, it will enter into his hand and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if you answer me, We trust in the Lord our God, is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has taken away, and has said to Judah and Jerusalem: You shall worship before this altar? And now deliver yourself to my lord the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, and you will not be able on your part to furnish riders for them. And how will you withstand the face of the judge of a single place, one of the lesser servants of my lord? But if you trust in Egypt, and in chariots, and in horsemen: and now, have I come up without the Lord against this land to destroy it? The Lord said to me: Go up against this land, and destroy it. The history is plain and needs no interpretation; and these same things are related, written more fully, in the volumes of Kings and of Chronicles: that in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign. He was twenty-five years old, it says, when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, and he did what was good before the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. And a little after: He hoped in the Lord God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him: he clung to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps, and he did his commandments which the Lord had commanded Moses: whence also the Lord was with him, and in all things to which he went forth he conducted himself wisely (2 Kgs 18:2, 7). And he rebelled against the king of the Assyrians and did not serve him: in the sixth year of whose reign Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians took Samaria and the ten tribes which were called Israel, and carried them away to the Assyrians, and settled them in Halah and in Habor, the rivers of Gozan, in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17 and 18). And after seven years, that is, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians entered Judea and besieged its fortified cities, wishing to take them. And when he was besieging Lachish, Hezekiah sent messengers to him, saying: I have sinned; withdraw from me, and whatever you lay upon me I will bear. And when he had paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold at the king's command, having broken off the doors of the Temple of the Lord and stripped off its plates, which he himself had fastened on, the king of the Assyrians sent Tartan and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a strong hand to Jerusalem: and when they had gone up, they came to Jerusalem and stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, which is in the way of the fuller's field, and called the king to them. And there went out to them Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the overseer of the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder; and Rabshakeh said to them: Speak to Hezekiah: Thus said the great king, the king of the Assyrians, and the rest that is contained in the history. In this the arrogance of Rabshakeh is to be considered: that, like some opposing power, he imitates the custom of the Prophets, so that what they are accustomed to put in their prologues, Thus says the Lord, to show the authority and greatness of the speaker, this man now said: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians. And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was overseer of the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder. This is the Eliakim son of Hilkiah of whom we read above, in the Vision of the valley of Zion (cf. Isa 22:20, 21): I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and give your power into his hand, and he shall be as a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah, and the rest. Now these things are said to Shebna, who before him was overseer of the Temple, of whom it is written in the same vision: Go and enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna the overseer of the Temple (ibid., 15); and the Hebrews relate that he, terrified by Rabshakeh's threats, surrendered to the Assyrians and betrayed the lower part of Jerusalem to the enemy, so that, apart from the citadel of Zion and the Temple, nothing else remained that the Assyrian did not hold. Hence those err who think that the Shebna who now goes out with Eliakim and Joah to Rabshakeh is the same as the one above. For there Shebna is set down as overseer of the Temple, who is said to be destined for capture by the Assyrians; but here Shebna is a scribe, that is, γραμματεὶς, which in Hebrew is called SOPHER סופר, and he is ὁμώνυμος with the former. As for Rabshakeh, who spoke in the Hebrew tongue, the Jews suppose him to have been a son of the prophet Isaiah, who was himself also a traitor; and that the other son of Isaiah, who was left, was called Jasub, which in our language means left. Others, again, think that he was a Samaritan, and that for this reason he knew the Hebrew speech and blasphemed the Lord so boldly and impiously. Let us then consider the words of Rabshakeh; and first, what he says: You are trusting in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt, is false: for no history relates that Hezekiah sent to the Egyptians and asked for Pharaoh's help. And what he adds: If you answer me, We trust in the Lord our God, is true. But again he joins a lie to the truth: that Hezekiah had taken away His high places and altars. For he had done this not against God but for God, so that, idolatry and the old error being destroyed, he might command God to be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his Temple was; although we read that by a very bad custom the people sacrificed victims to God on the mountains and hills, even when the altar had already been built. And his promising two thousand horses, wishing to show the fewness of the besieged, for which Hezekiah could not furnish riders, does not come from the weakness of the people of the Jews, as if it lacked the skill of riding, but from the observance of the commandments of God, who through Moses had commanded concerning the king of Israel: He shall not multiply horses for himself, and he shall not have very many wives (Deut 17:16, 17). But if, he says, you cannot withstand me, the servant of Sennacherib, who am the least of his servants, how will you withstand the so great might of the king? And to what he had said, If you answer me, We trust in the Lord God, he replied cunningly and shrewdly that he had come not by his own will but by the Lord's commands: The Lord said to me: Go up against this land and destroy it. And the argument is: certainly I could not have come here without the Lord's will. But since I have come and taken many cities, and only part of Jerusalem remains untouched, it is clear that I came by his will. I have read in someone's Commentary that this Sennacherib is the same who also took Samaria, which is altogether false. For the sacred history relates that first Pul king of the Assyrians, under Menahem king of Israel, laid waste the ten tribes; second, that Tiglath-pileser came to Samaria under Pekah son of Remaliah of Israel; third, that Shalmaneser under Hoshea king of Israel took all Samaria (2 Kgs 15, 17); fourth, that it was Sargon who stormed Ashdod (Isa 20); fifth, Esarhaddon, who, when Israel had been carried away, sent the Samaritans into the land of Judea as guards (2 Kgs 17); sixth, Sennacherib, who under Hezekiah king of Judah, having taken Lachish and the other cities of Judea, besieged Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18). Others, however, think that one and the same king is called by many names.

36:11ff.

And Eliakim and Shebna and Joah said to Rabshakeh: Speak to your servants in the Syrian tongue, for we understand it: do not speak to us in the Jewish tongue in the ears of the people who are on the wall. And Rabshakeh said to them: Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their feet with you? And Rabshakeh stood and cried out with a loud voice in the Jewish tongue, and said: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians. Thus says the king: Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to rescue you; and let not Hezekiah give you confidence in the Lord, saying: The Lord will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of the Assyrians. The accusation of Rabshakeh is a testimony to Hezekiah: that when all the cities of Judea had been taken he trusted in the Lord and said to the people: Do not fear, nor be afraid of the king of the Assyrians and of all the multitude that is with him; for there are many more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh; with us is the Lord our God, who is our helper and fights for us. And the people, it says, were strengthened by such words of Hezekiah king of Judah. Hence Rabshakeh wishes to destroy what the other had built up, and he speaks to the people: Let not Hezekiah deceive you; and let him not give you confidence in the Lord God. And the humble entreaty of Eliakim and Shebna and Joah, Speak to your servants in the Syrian tongue, for we understand it; and do not speak to us in the Jewish tongue in the ears of the people who are on the wall, has this sense: What need is there for the people to be stirred by false terrors, and for you to boast of a vain strength? Speak a language which the people do not understand. For we have knowledge of your language, and we know the Syrian speech, which is common to both. To which Rabshakeh arrogantly: Has, he says, my lord sent me to your lord and to you, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall? And again, increasing the terror with a threat, that they may eat, he says, their own dung, and drink the urine of their feet with you? By this he shows that they will be taken by hunger and want and thirst. And at the same time he joins enticement to fear, so that those whom he had not conquered by terror he might deceive by promises and persuasion, saying, in the words of the king of the Assyrians:

36:16, 18

Make a blessing with me, and come out to me, and eat each one of his vine, and each one of his fig tree, and drink each one the water of his cistern: until I come and take you away to a land that is like your land: a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. Let not Hezekiah trouble you, saying: The Lord will deliver us. Have the gods of the nations delivered each one his land from the hand of the king of the Assyrians? For which in the volume of Kings one reads: Do with me what is profitable, and come out to me (2 Kgs 18:31). So the sense is the same. Do, he says, what may benefit you and turn to your blessing. Or he says this: Bless the Assyrian king and praise him, and confess him your lord, so that you may obtain rewards; and until I return from Egypt, or, having taken Libnah, come back, dwell in your city and enjoy your goods. But afterward I will come and transfer you to a land which is like your land, of grain, wine and olives. And he does not say the name of the region, because he could not find one equal to the land of promise; but he promises a likeness. For this is what each one desires: the land in which he was born. Some think that Media was promised them, which had a likeness to the land of Judea both in situation and in its crops. And what he adds:

36:19ff.

Where is the God of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the God of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who is there among all the gods of these lands that has rescued his land out of my hand, that the Lord should rescue Jerusalem out of my hand? And they were silent and answered him not a word. For the king had commanded them, saying: Do not answer him. This shows that Samaria served all these gods, and was taken for that reason. But if, he says, with so many gods presiding, we easily overcame the ten tribes, how much more easily shall we conquer you, nay, Jerusalem alone, with one God as its guardian? And all the people kept silent and answered him nothing; for they had received the king's command not to answer him. Truly righteous was Hezekiah, doing all things faithfully and everything with counsel. And he had commanded that the blaspheming Assyrian not be answered for this reason: lest he provoke him to greater blasphemies. Hence it is written: Do not kindle the coals of the sinner (Sir 8:13); and in the psalm we read: When the sinner stood against me, I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silent from good things (Ps 38 [39]:2-3); and again: Set, O Lord, a guard to my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips: incline not my heart to words of malice (Ps 140 [141]:3).

37:1ff.

And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came in to Hezekiah with their garments torn, and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh. And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah had heard, he tore his garments, and was covered with sackcloth, and went into the house of God. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos, and they said to him: Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation and of rebuke and of blasphemy, for the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth. If by any means the Lord your God may hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of the Assyrians his master sent to blaspheme the living God and to reproach him with words which the Lord your God has heard. Lift up therefore a prayer for the remnant that is found. And the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah; and Isaiah said to them: Thus shall you say to your master: Thus says the Lord: Do not be afraid before the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me. Behold, I will give him a spirit, and he shall hear a report, and shall return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land. Leaving aside what is plain, let us discuss only those things in which a hidden sense lies. They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming. The king himself also tears his garments, because he believed it was owing to his own sins and the people's that Rabshakeh had come up to the gate of Jerusalem and had spoken such things against the Lord. Hence the high priest, because he believed the Savior had blasphemed, tore his garments (Matt 26); and Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians offered them the worship due to God, tore their garments (Acts 14). In place of royal attire, then, he was covered with sackcloth; and going from the palace to the Temple, he sent Eliakim the high priest, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos. In this the humility and prudence of the king is to be considered. He himself goes to the Temple; the princes of the people and the elders of the priests, covered not with priestly stoles but with haircloth, he sent to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos. For which in the volume of Kings one reads: He himself was covered with sackcloth and entered the house of the Lord, and he sent Eliakim the overseer of the house, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amos (2 Kgs 19:1, 2). Here, because Isaiah was writing the history about himself, he did not call himself a Prophet but the son of a Prophet; there, however, because the writer of the history was another, he writes that he himself was a Prophet. This we read also of Matthew the Evangelist: that Matthew himself called himself a publican (Matt 9), while the other Evangelists were silent about the name of publican and set down only the apostolic dignity; and that in the pairings of the Apostles he is second in his own list and first in the others'. And they said, it says, to him: Thus says Hezekiah, not 'the king', not swelling with the title of empire: This day is a day of tribulation and of rebuke and of blasphemy: of our tribulation, of God's rebuke, of the enemies' blasphemy. And he sets down the likeness of a woman in labor and in pain, who has come up to the birth and cannot bring forth, nor say: From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived, and have been in pain, and have brought forth the spirit of salvation. There follows: If by any means the Lord your God may hear the words of Rabshakeh (Isa 26:18 LXX). For we do not dare to call the Lord of all our Lord, since through his anger we suffer so much; but we call him your Lord. And we have this confidence of vengeance: that the living God is blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols. And they have reproached with words which the Lord your God has heard. Lift up therefore a prayer, our prayer, which lies prostrate: not for the whole people, which has already perished, but for the remnant, which is besieged. And when the servants of king Hezekiah had come to Isaiah: again he was silent about the name of Prophet, in order to keep the humility he had begun. And Isaiah anticipated them: for by the same spirit by which he knew things to come, he had heard the king too, though absent; and he tells them what they should answer to their master, humbled in this confidence of conscience. Say, he says, to your master, who is your lord; for my Lord says this: Do not fear the words with which not you but I have been blasphemed. Nor do I tell all that I am going to do to the king of the Assyrians, lest I seem to boast of my power; but only that a spirit is to be given him, not of God but an adverse one. And having heard a report, let him return to his own land and fall in it by the sword: so that Hezekiah might hear both things he desired together, that he was to be freed from siege and danger, and that the hostile and angry king would die in his own land. If anyone asks why in a book of Prophecy the history written in the volumes of Kings and Chronicles seems to be mixed in, let him consider that prophecy is coupled with the history, as much concerning the liberation of the city as concerning the destruction of the Assyrian, and the turning back of the sun by ten hours, and the prolonging of life by a space of fifteen years, which belongs both to prophecy and to history.

37:8ff.

And Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah: for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish. And he heard concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, people saying: He has come out to fight against you. And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying: Thus shall you say to Hezekiah king of Judah, speaking: Let not your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, saying: Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Behold, you have heard all that the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands which they overthrew, and will you be able to be delivered? Have the gods of the nations rescued them, whom my fathers overthrew, Gozan and Haran, and Rezeph, and the sons of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Ana and Ava? In the same words and with the same sense it is written in the volume of Kings and of Chronicles that Rabshakeh, according to the will of the Lord, abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and went on to his master, who, as he had learned, was going to attack Libnah, Lachish having been either abandoned or taken. Sennacherib himself too, hearing that Tirhakah king of the Ethiopians was bringing war against him, went to meet him as he came, and nonetheless sends messengers and letters to Hezekiah, so that those whom he had not yet taken by force he might terrify by words. And just as he had said to the people, Let not Hezekiah deceive you (2 Kgs 18:29), so he speaks the same blasphemy to the king: Let not your God deceive you (2 Kgs 19:10). And he sets out the examples of his forefathers: that just as their gods could not deliver the other lands out of their hands, so neither would Jerusalem be delivered. In the enumeration of the other nations he sets down ANA (הנע) and AVA (ועוה), which the Seventy ran together, saying anavegava; and the conjunction and, that is, vau, between the two nations Ana and Ava, they set down in the Hebrew tongue, so that to the ignorant it seems one nation or city. We pass quickly over the plain things in order to dwell on the doubtful ones. That Sennacherib king of the Assyrians fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium, and that, when the mounds had already been built to take the city, Tirhakah king of the Ethiopians came to its help, and that in one night near Jerusalem one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell by pestilence, is related by Herodotus, and most fully by Berosus, the writer of Chaldean history, whose credibility must be sought from their own books.

37:14ff.

And Hezekiah took the books from the hand of the messengers and read them; and he went up into the house of the Lord and spread them out before the Lord, and prayed to the Lord, saying: O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, who sit upon the Cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth: for you made heaven and earth. Incline, O Lord, your ear and hear; open, O Lord, your eyes and see, and hear all the words of Sennacherib which he sent to blaspheme the living God. For truly, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have made desolate the lands and their regions, and have given their gods to the fire: for they were not gods, but works of men's hands, wood and stones; and they broke them in pieces. And now, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, and let all the kingdoms of the earth know that you alone are God. Against the blasphemies of king Sennacherib Hezekiah seized his accustomed weapons. And again he goes to the Temple and spreads out his letters before the Lord. Before, he had been silent: for, terrified by fear of the Lord, he did not dare to open his mouth in the Temple or to pour out free prayers to God. But now, because he had already heard Isaiah saying: Do not be afraid before the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me, and the rest, he boldly entreats the Lord and asserts that God alone is living; whereas the idols we understand as images of the dead. And what he adds: For truly, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have made desolate the lands and their regions, and have given their gods to the fire: for they were not gods, but works of men's hands, wood and stones; and they broke them in pieces, is proved by many histories, which write that the kings of the Persians came into Greece and overthrew and plundered the temples of the Greeks. And he asks for vengeance, so that through his occasion all kingdoms may know that he alone is God, who can deliver his own from danger.

37:21ff.

And Isaiah son of Amos sent to Hezekiah, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: As to what you have asked me concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, this is the word which the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; behind you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached, and whom have you blasphemed, and against whom have you raised your voice and lifted up the height of your eyes? Against the Holy One of Israel? By the hand of your servants you have reproached the Lord and have said: With the multitude of my chariots I have gone up to the height of the mountains, the ridges of Lebanon, and I will cut down its lofty cedars and its choice fir trees, and I will enter the height of its summit, the forest of its Carmel. I dug, and drank water, and dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the embankments. Because Hezekiah had entreated the Lord so boldly and did not send to Isaiah as he had sent before, the Prophet himself does not go to him, but sends messengers to tell him in the words of God: Concerning Sennacherib, against whom you pray, this is the Lord's sentence: The virgin of Zion and daughter of Jerusalem (who is called virgin and daughter for this reason, that while all the nations worship the images of dead men, she alone preserves the chastity of the religion of God and the worship of the one Godhead) has mocked you and despised you; and she who, lest she provoke you to greater blasphemy, had not answered you when you were present, has shaken her head behind you as you go away, sure of vengeance, secure about punishment. And she has said this: Not against me, but against the Lord you have been proud; and not you yourself, but through your servants, so that the arrogance of the blasphemer might be the greater. For you said that with the multitude of your chariots you would climb the height of the mountains and the ridges of Lebanon, and cut down its lofty cedars and fir trees. This we ought to take either μεταφορικῶς of all the nations and their princes, or of Jerusalem, which is what Lebanon means, so that we refer its cedars and firs to all its powerful and noble men, and the height of its summit and the forest of Carmel to the Temple. For he himself had said above: Have you not heard what the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands which they overthrew? Therefore neither will you be able to be delivered. And what he adds: I dug and drank water, and dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the embankments, can be understood according to the history: that because of the multitude of his army he dried up all the streams, so that he was compelled to dig wells for himself; according to the metaphor: that he laid waste with his army all the peoples, who are sometimes described under the name of waters. For which the Seventy alone translated: and I have set a bridge, and I have made desolate the waters, and every gathering of waters: that is, that no nation was impassable to him, but he trod with his foot upon all the waters of the peoples.

37:26ff.

Have you not heard what I did to it long ago? From the days of old I formed it, and now I have brought them, and it has come to be for the uprooting of the hills that fight together, and of fortified cities. Their inhabitants, with shortened hand, trembled and were confounded: they became like the hay of the field, and the grass of the pasture, and the herb of the housetops, which withered before it ripened. Your dwelling, and your going out, and your coming in I have known, and your madness against me, when you raged against me. Your pride has come up into my ears; I will therefore put a ring in your nostrils, and a bridle in your lips, and I will lead you back by the way by which you came. These things are to be understood as spoken in the person of God against the words of the Assyrian: that the Lord answered his blasphemy thus: Do you not know that these things which you have done, you did by my will, and that I foretold them as to come, and commanded that they be done through you? So what I decreed long ago has been fulfilled in its time: that the hills, that is, the princes who formerly fought among themselves, and the most fortified cities, when I drew back my hand and did not furnish my accustomed help, should be uprooted and tremble and perish, and be compared not to the olive and the vine and fruitful trees, but to hay and grass and the herbs of the housetops, which are a hindrance to the crops and wither before they come to maturity. So I knew beforehand your sitting, and your going out, and your coming in, and I spoke of the madness with which you were going to rage against me, through the Prophets as they prophesied (above, on Isa 14:13): through whom I had long ago known that you would say: I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High. So your fury and your pride have reached my ears, and I will by no means bear with you any longer, so that you may understand that what you were able to do, you were able to do not by your own strength but by my decision. For the impious nations and the unfruitful trees deserved to be cut down and to fall through you, as through my axe and saw. So I will put a ring, or a muzzle, in your nostrils, to bind fast your blaspheming mouth, so that you may by no means dare to speak such things any more; and I will put a bridle on your lips, to tame your ferocity and lead you back to the Assyrians. This figure Scripture also uses in the Psalms against the impious: With bridle and muzzle bind fast the jaws of those who do not draw near to you (Ps 31 [32]:9).

37:30ff.

But this shall be a sign to you: Eat this year what springs up of itself, and in the second year feed on fruits; but in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And what has been saved of the house of Judah, and what is left, shall send down root downward and bear fruit upward: for out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and salvation from mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this. All these things the Prophet speaks to Hezekiah through messengers: what Sennacherib said, what the Lord answered him. Now he addresses his speech to the king himself, lest perhaps he doubt that the things spoken will come. And it was for this reason above all that the Prophets had credit for their words among the people: because they told not only of things that were to come many ages later, but also of things to be fulfilled at once and after no great space of time; and that within two years both the Assyrian king would perish and security would be restored to the city of Jerusalem. This, he says, will be the sign of the things to come that I foretell: that this year you will eat what springs up of itself; or, according to the Seventy, what you sowed before. And in the second year, according to Symmachus, feed on fruits; or, according to the same Seventy, on what has sprouted from the former crops and from seed falling to the ground. But in the third year, the Assyrian now put to flight and the siege lifted, sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruits. For the remnant of this small city, which is now walled in by a hostile army and does not believe it will escape, will receive such abundance and happiness in all things that, like a tree founded on a deep root, they will be filled with the thickest fruits. For out of Jerusalem and out of mount Zion a remnant shall go forth and fill the land of Judea, not by its own merit but by the mercy of God, nay by the zeal with which he was jealous for his people against the impious.

37:33-34

Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of the Assyrians: He shall not enter this city, and he shall not shoot an arrow there, nor shall a shield seize it, and he shall not cast up a mound around it. By the way by which he shall come, by it he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord; and I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant. He returns to his subject, and after the hope of things to come he shakes off the present fear. For there was not as much gladness over the things he had promised would come long afterward as there was anxiety about those that were imminent. And when he says that the Assyrian will withdraw, and will not raise a shield against Jerusalem nor shoot darts, nor is the city to be walled in with siege works and a mound, and that the adversary will return by the way he came, and the city will be freed from the present siege, and at the end adds: for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant, this signifies that they are preserved not by their own merit but by God's clemency, nay by the memory of their father David. In this they are reminded both of their own negligence and of his faith and righteousness: that God so loves righteousness that he protects even the descendants of holy men, not by their own merit but by the virtue of their forefathers.

37:36ff.

And the Angel of God went out and struck in the camp of the Assyrians one hundred and eighty-five thousand; and they arose in the morning, and behold, all were corpses of the dead. And Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went out and departed and returned, and dwelt in Nineveh. And it came to pass, while he was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons struck him with the sword; and they fled into the land of Ararat; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place. One hundred and eighty-five thousand of the bravest men are slain by one Angel in one night, and without wounds on the slain a cruel death runs through them, driving the souls out of the bodies by the will of God. Concerning which one reads in Chronicles: And the Lord sent an Angel, who struck every strong man and warrior and the commander of the army of the king of the Assyrians; and he returned with disgrace to his own land (2 Chr 32:21). He was preserved for this reason, that he might know the power of God and restrain his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness of that majesty which a little before he had despised. As for what he added, And they arose in the morning, let us take it either of the Israelites or of the rest of his army: although it is written in the volume of Kings that when the king himself had risen at daybreak, he saw all the bodies of the dead (2 Kgs 19). Pharaoh too is preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt, so as to perish last: which this man also suffered. For when he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his god, as though bringing back a victory over his enemies, and was entering the shrine of his idol triumphant and giving thanks, the despiser of the true God is slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity: and he perishes not by the Angel's sword, which would have been a fate shared with many, but by the parricide of his sons.
