And when they had fled into the land of Ararat, which is understood as Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded to his father's place, who, as Scripture testifies, sent inhabitants to Samaria, so that the land should not remain uncultivated. Ararat is a level region in Armenia, through which the Araxes flows, of incredible fertility, at the roots of mount Taurus, which extends as far as there. So the Ark too, in which Noah was delivered with his children when the Flood ceased, was carried not to the mountains of Armenia in general, which is called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overhang the plains of Ararat.

38:1ff.

In those days Hezekiah was sick unto death; and Isaiah son of Amos, the Prophet, came in to him and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live. And Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, and prayed to the Lord, and said: I beseech you, O Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes: and Hezekiah wept with a great weeping. Whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives (Prov 3). Lest the heart of Hezekiah be lifted up after his incredible triumphs and the victory won out of the midst of captivity, he is visited with infirmity of body and hears that he is going to die, so that, turning to the Lord, he may bend his sentence. This indeed we read also in the prophet Jonah, and in the threats against David, which are said to be coming and were not done: not because God changes his sentence, but because he calls mankind to the knowledge of himself. For the Lord repents over evils. And Hezekiah turned his face to the wall because he could not go to the Temple: to the wall of the Temple, that is, next to which Solomon had built the palace. Or simply to the wall, lest he seem to display his tears to those sitting by. Or certainly, according to Jeremiah, to his heart; who calls CIR (קיר), that is, wall, the heart: so that he entreated the Lord with his whole mind. And he says: I beseech you, O Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes. And hearing that he is going to die, he does not pray for life and many years, but leaves to God's judgment what he wishes to grant. For he knew that Solomon had pleased God for this reason, that he did not ask for more years of life; but as one about to go to the Lord, he recounts his works, how he walked before him in truth and with a perfect heart. Happy the conscience that in time of affliction remembers its good works: For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). And what of its being written elsewhere: Who shall boast that he has a pure heart (Prov 20:9)? This is solved thus: perfection of heart is ascribed to him here because he destroyed the idols, overturned the vessels of the temple of Baal, broke the bronze serpent in pieces, and did the other things which Scripture records. And he wept with a great weeping because of the Lord's promise to David, which he saw would perish in his death. For at that time Hezekiah had no sons; for after his death Manasseh began to reign in Judea when he was twelve years old. From which it is clear that Manasseh was begotten after the third year of the life granted to him. So all this weeping is because he despaired that the Christ would be born of his seed. Others assert that even holy men are terrified by death, because of the uncertainty of judgment and their ignorance of God's sentence as to what abode they will have. And at the same time the question of fate is solved, and of the chains of necessity and of causes: that the day of death is by no means fixed beforehand for each person, but that by the will of God and by causes unknown to mortals one either lives or dies; especially since the necessity of death, once set, is here postponed, and we have read that very many were raised up after death.

38:4ff.

And the word of the Lord came to Isaiah, saying: Go and say to Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add to your days fifteen years, and I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I will protect it. And this shall be a sign to you from the Lord, that the Lord will do this word which he has spoken: Behold, I will make the shadow of the lines, by which it had gone down on the dial of Ahaz in the sun, go back ten lines: and the sun went back ten lines by the steps by which it had gone down. Here, as in a prophecy, the history is related in reversed order, which in the volume of Kings is read in better sequence. While Hezekiah was weeping with a great weeping, before Isaiah had gone out of the middle part of the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: Go back and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: I have heard your prayer and seen your tear: Behold, I have healed you. And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: What will be the sign that the Lord will heal me (2 Kgs 20:4 and 5)? To him the Prophet answered: This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do the word which he has spoken: Do you wish the shadow to advance so many lines, or to go back as many steps? And Hezekiah said to him: It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines, and I do not wish this to be done; but that it go back ten steps. And when, at Isaiah's calling upon the power of the Lord, the sign had been accomplished, Isaiah commanded that a lump of fresh figs be brought: and when they had brought it and laid it upon his wound, he was cured. The Prophet returns to the king at the Lord's command, so that he who had struck might himself heal; and Hezekiah is called the leader of his people, and son of David, whose works he followed, for he had done what was right according to all that David his father did: and his prayer is heard and his tears are seen, because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, and had wept with a great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his eyes. Fifteen years are added to his life, which he had not asked for, and besides, the security of the kingdom during his lifetime is promised. But if, as some think, to live in the body is a condemnation, and, according to what is said: Return, my soul, to your rest (Ps 114 [116]:7), and in another place: Bring my soul out of prison (Ps 141 [142]:8), death is to be desired, that we may be freed from prison: how does the Lord now grant it as a benefit that one who was about to be freed should live yet fifteen years in prison? And a sign is given, that the sun should go back ten steps, which we, following Symmachus, have rendered as lines and dial; for he understood the steps as lines, to make the sense clearer to readers. Or else the steps had been built by mechanical art in such a way that the shadow, descending through each one, marked off the spaces of the hours. This sign was a type both of the present time and of the future: that as the sun went back to its beginning, so Hezekiah's life too returned to years already unwoven; and that for us, who live in the hebdomad and the ogdoad, the spaces of life are prolonged through the resurrection of Christ. The guides to the holy Places in this province are accustomed to show, within the enclosure of the Temple, the steps of the house of Hezekiah, or of Ahaz, down which the sun descended. But I will never believe that the house, I do not say of Ahaz, who was an impious king, but of any righteous king whatever, was in the Temple of God: since Solomon is said, among other things, to have offended God for this reason, that he built Millo on high, from which, walking in the tower of his palace, he used to look down on the court of the Temple (1 Kgs 9).

38:9

The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick and had recovered from his infirmity. LXX: The prayer of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he was sick and rose up from his infirmity. I wonder how the Seventy alone put prayer for writing, since prayer is called THEPHELLATH (תפלת), and not MACHTHAB (מכתב), which is what is written in the present place; otherwise prayer would fittingly be said if it concerned the present time and not the past. For it is clear that after his health was restored, rising from his infirmity, he wrote these things down; from which it follows that it is not a prayer but a thanksgiving for the benefit he had received.

38:10ff.

I said: In the half of my days I shall go to the gates of hell: I sought the remainder of my years. I said: I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living: I shall not behold man any more, and the dweller of rest. My generation has ceased: it is taken away and rolled up from me like a shepherds' tent. My life is cut off as by a weaver: while I was yet beginning, he cut me off: from morning to evening you will make an end of me. I hoped until morning: like a lion, so he has broken all my bones. From morning to evening you will make an end of me. LXX: I said: In the height of my days I shall go to the gates of hell: I will leave the remaining years. I said: I shall by no means any more see the salvation of God in the land of the living, nor shall I see man any more with the inhabitants: I have failed from my kindred. It has gone out and departed from me, as one takes down a tent who had pitched it: like a web my spirit has departed, when it is cut off by the weaver. In that day I was given up until morning: like a lion, so he has broken all my bones. From day to night I was given up. He relates what he thought silently in the time of pressing distress and imminent sickness. I said, he says, in my heart, in the half of my days, or, as Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated, in the infirmity and silence of my days; for which the Seventy translated height, because of the likeness of a letter, reading RAME (רמי) for DAME (דמי): although some have rendered DAME as blood, so that the sense is, In the blood of my days, when my blood and my death were being sought. So in despair I said: I shall go to the gates of hell, either by the common law of nature, or those gates from which the Psalmist sings that he was freed: You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may announce all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Ps 9:15). These I think are the gates of hell which do not prevail against Peter (Matt 16), because he slept in the fullness of his days. The saints fill up their days, as Abraham did, who died full of days in a good old age (Gen 25). But sinners and the impious die in the half of their days, of whom the Psalmist also speaks: Men of blood and deceitful men shall not live out half their days (Ps 54 [55]:25). For they do not fulfill the works of virtue, nor are they eager to amend their faults by penance. Hence in the middle of life's course and in the darkness of their errors they will be led to Tartarus. I sought, he says, the remainder of my years, thinking that he would live no longer. I said: I shall not see the Lord, the Lord in the land of the living. For Lord and Lord, IA (יה) is set twice in the Hebrew, which sounds in the last syllable of ALLELUIA (הללויה); for which the Seventy translated: I shall by no means any more see the salvation of God in the land of the living. Of which it is written in another place: I will please the Lord in the region of the living (Ps 114 [116]:9). And again: I will please the Lord in the light of the living (Ps 55 [56]:9). The region of the Saints, then, is the very one that is called the light of the living. For he is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matt 22). And this is all that he fears: that, led down to hell, he may by no means deserve to behold the salvation of God. There follows: I shall not behold man any more, and the dweller of rest. This we had formerly joined to the following verse because of the ambiguity of the word; for the Hebrew word HOLED, if it is read or written ELED (חלד), means rest; if EDEL (חדל), it means setting. So he fears that he may not dwell in rest with the saints and the men of God, that he may not see the Lord in the land of the living, that his generation may be dissolved like a tent, that like a web it may be cut off at the very beginning of the light, and that the Christ may by no means arise from his seed. And that our body is called a tent the Apostle too teaches, saying: We who are in this tent groan, being burdened (2 Cor 5:4). From morning, he says, to evening you will make an end of me: I hoped until morning: which Job too says he endured in his distress and in the torments of his body (Job 4), when in the day he awaited the night, and in darkness looked for the light, thinking that with the change of the times his torments could change. That this is true he knows who burns with high fevers, whose inner fire, like a lion, consumes all his bones, and who, for the greatness of his pain, does not think he will live any longer.

38:15

Like the young of a swallow, so will I cry: I will meditate like a dove: my eyes are worn thin looking upward. O Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me: what shall I say, or what will he answer me, since he himself has done it? LXX: Like a swallow, so will I cry; like a dove, so will I meditate. For my eyes have failed with looking to the height of heaven, to the Lord, who has rescued me and taken away the pain of my soul, and he himself has done it. Imminent death and the pressing pain of sickness, like a lion, were breaking all the bones of my body; but I, like the swallow and the dove, joined days and nights with weeping and groaning; and from God alone, who could help, with my eyes lifted on high, I awaited aid. And I said to him: I suffer more than my deserts require; but even if I have erred in anything, I will turn to the better; do you answer for me: For it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom 9:16). And again he turns back into himself: What shall I say, or what shall I plead against you, my maker? Or what will he answer me, who himself has done what he willed? Whatever he has decreed, then, must be endured. For young of a swallow, or swallow, as the Seventy translated, in the Hebrew is written SUS AGOR (סוס עגור), which Aquila translated the horse Agor; Theodotion, SIS AGUR (סיס עגור); for the middle vowel-letter, if vau is put between two Samec, is read sus and means horse; if jod, it is read sis and is called swallow. Symmachus translated thus: Like a shut-in swallow, so will I sing. This word agor is also read in Jeremiah, where it is written: The kite in heaven has known its time: the turtledove and the swallow and the stork have kept their times (Jer 8:7).

38:16ff.

I will reckon up all my years in the bitterness of my soul. O Lord, if one lives thus, and if in such things is the life of my spirit, you will rebuke me and you will give me life. Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter. But you have rescued my soul, that it should not perish: you have cast all my sins behind your back. For hell will not confess to you, nor will death praise you: those who go down into the pit will not await your truth. The living, the living, he will confess to you, as I also do today. The father will make your truth known to the children. O Lord, save me, and we will sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord. LXX: O Lord, concerning it, it was announced to you: and you have raised up my spirit, and, having comforted me, you have given me life. Behold, in peace is my bitterness: for you have delivered my soul, that it should not perish, and you have cast all my sins behind me. For in hell they will not praise you, nor will the dead bless you. Nor will those who are in hell hope for your mercy: the living will bless you, as I also do. For from today I will make sons, who will announce your righteousness, O Lord of my salvation, and I will not cease blessing you with the psaltery all the days of my life before the house of God. Nothing belonging to mortals is long-lasting, and all the happiness of the world is lost even while it is held. For when the time of tribulation has come, all that is past is no help to the one who endures it. Hence the foolish opinion of Epicurus, who asserts that present evils are softened by the remembrance of past goods. So Hezekiah says that he reckons up all the years of his reign, and of his past happiness, as he thought it, in his present bitterness. And because he is now secure and no longer suffers what he relates, he philosophizes on the human state and says: O Lord, if one lives thus: if we have been born in such a condition, you have rebuked me, but you have given me life, and you have granted peace, the Assyrian being put to flight; but my peace was more bitter to me than all bitterness, because, when tranquillity was restored to the peoples and the city was secure, I alone entered the threshold of death. But you have rescued my soul, that it should not perish, either for the present life or for the future. For you have cast all my sins behind your back, lest I should look upon them in sadness, but that I might contemplate your mercy. For hell and death will not confess, nor will they praise you, according to what is written: But in hell who will confess to you (Ps 6:6)? And confession in this place is taken not for penance but for glory and praise, as we read also in the Gospel: I will confess to you, O Lord, Father of heaven and earth (Matt 11:25). Those who go down into the pit, he says, will not await your truth: better than mercy in the Seventy. For he who is in hell does not await the truth of judgment but the mercy of God: especially since the Savior descended into hell to free the prisoners from the lower world. For pit the same translators more plainly rendered hell. The living, the living, he will confess to you, as I also do today. Here too confession is put for praise. For he does not confess his crimes, but gives thanks to God: and praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sir 15). And while hell and death do not confess nor praise God, on the contrary life and the living glorify the Lord. And what follows: The father will make your truth known to the children, signifies what is said in Deuteronomy: Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you (Deut 32:7), so that through the successions and each generation the clemency of God may be proclaimed to posterity. For which the Seventy set: For from today I will make sons, who will announce your righteousness. And the causal conjunction joins what follows to what precedes: namely, that the living, and he himself living, bless God for this reason, that from this day he would make sons who would announce his truth, which certainly was not in his own power. For those children were not promised him through the Prophet; only the present life was granted. Especially since he begot a most impious son, Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with blood from gate to gate, and did not bless but cursed God, persecuting his saints. We can therefore say this according to the Seventy: that he did not say I will make sons, but παιδία, which we understand either as little ones, or boys, or little infants, and descendants, so that from the fact that he himself obtained mercy, all posterity to come, knowing this, might praise his incredible clemency. Save me then, O Lord; and all of us who believe in you and have been delivered by your help will sing to you in the Temple all the days of our life.

38:21-22

And Isaiah commanded that they take a lump of figs and plaster it upon the wound, and he would be healed. And Hezekiah said: What will be the sign that I shall go up into the house of the Lord? This is to be read before the prayer of Hezekiah, or Writing, which we have now interpreted: for the plaster was laid on the wound, and the sign of future health was asked by him, before he gave thanks to the Lord, which he is said to have done when healed. The Hebrews say that the word SIIN (שחין), which the Seventy passed over, means ulcer, not wound. For Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion also translated ἕλκος, by which they wish the royal disease to be understood, to which whatever is sweet, whether taken as food or applied to the body, is thought to be contrary. So, that the power of God might be shown, health was restored through things harmful and contrary. Others suppose SIIN to be not ulcer but abscess: when the swelling body is filled with ripened and putrefying pus. And according to the art of physicians, all matter is drawn out to the surface of the skin by dried and pounded figs: and hence a medicine established by use and experience is not to be despised, since God too made this one. So the prayer and thanksgiving is written up to this point. As for the sign that was given, the earlier order of the history has narrated it.

39:1ff.

At that time Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick and had recovered. And Hezekiah was glad over them, and showed them the storehouse of spices, and of silver, and of gold, and of perfumes, and of the best ointment, and all the storerooms of his furnishings, and all that was found in his treasuries: there was not a word that Hezekiah did not show them in his house and in all his dominion. Above we read that in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them, and afterward besieged Lachish, passed on to Libnah, and sent part of his army to Jerusalem; and that, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army had been slain by the Angel, he himself fled to Nineveh and was killed by his sons in the shrine of his god, and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place; that Hezekiah fell sick and recovered his health at the Prophet's message; that an incredible sign was done, so that the sun went back by the space of ten hours toward its rising, and the day became almost double. Now we read that at that time, that is, in the same year in which all these things were done, Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah; not Esarhaddon, who had succeeded his father Sennacherib in the kingdom among the Assyrians, about whose death or life Scripture is silent. From which it is clear that the kingdom of the Assyrians was then one thing, and that of the Babylonians another. Indeed, the Assyrians took Samaria, that is, the ten tribes; but Judah and Jerusalem, we read, were taken later by the Chaldeans, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar. And because among them there is the observation of the heavenly bodies, and the course of the stars is known by long practice and exercise, as is shown also at the Lord's nativity, they understood that the sun had gone back and the spaces of the day had been doubled, in the service of him whom they thought the only God. And when they inquired into the causes and reason of this miracle, as the report flew through all the nations, they learned that because of the sickness of the king of Judah even the course of the brightest sign had been changed. That this is not my opinion but the faith of holy Scripture, the words of Chronicles testify, which say after other things: This is Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and turned them down to the west of the city of David. In all his works he accomplished prosperously what he wished; but in the embassy of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had happened on the earth, God left him, that he might be tested, and that all that was in his heart might be made known (2 Chr 32:30, 31). And he was left to temptation for this reason, because after so great a victory, and the sun's going back, and the congratulation of a most powerful kingdom, his heart was lifted up. Indeed, in the same volume it is written: Many brought victims and sacrifices to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah: and he was exalted before all the nations. In those days he was sick unto death, and he prayed to the Lord; and he heard him and gave him a sign; but he did not make return according to the benefits he had received: for his heart was lifted up, and there was wrath against him, and against Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chr 32:23, 24). And again holy Scripture says that the lifting up of his heart was softened by penance, adding: And afterward he was humbled because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah. He was glad, then, at the coming of the envoys of Merodach, whom the Hebrews suppose to have been the father of Nebuchadnezzar, and at the offering of gifts and the congratulation on his recovery. And he showed them, according to the Seventy, the house NECHOTHA (נכתה), for which Symmachus translated of his spices; and the treasuries of silver, and of gold, and of perfumes, and of the best ointment, which in the Hebrew is written of good oil; and all the treasuries of the vessels of his gaza, or, as is read there, of his vessels. Now in the language of the Persians riches are called gaza; nor is it a Hebrew word, but a Barbarian one. There was not, he says, a word (which according to Hebrew usage is frequently taken for thing) that he did not show them in his house and in all his dominion. Hence the most just wrath of God, because he showed not only his own treasures and those of the palace but also those of the Temple, which certainly was within his dominion, and from whose doors he had already earlier taken the plates of gold.

39:3ff.

Then Isaiah the Prophet came in to king Hezekiah and said to him: What did these men say, and from where did they come to you? And Hezekiah said: From a far country they came to me, from Babylon. And he said: What did they see in your house? And Hezekiah said: They saw all that is in my house: there was not a word, or thing, that I did not show them in my treasuries. And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: Hear the word of the Lord of hosts. Behold, the day will come, and all that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up until this day, shall be carried away to Babylon: nothing shall be left, said the Lord. And of your sons who shall come forth from you, whom you shall beget, they shall take away: and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: Good is the word of the Lord which he has spoken. And he said: Only let there be peace and truth in my days. The Hebrews relate that Hezekiah fell sick for this reason, because after the unheard-of victory of the Jews and the destruction of the Assyrian king he did not sing praises to the Lord, as Moses sang when Pharaoh was drowned (Exod 15), and Deborah when Sisera was killed (Judg 4), and Hannah when Samuel was born (1 Sam 2); and that hence he was reminded of his frailty. And again, after the health of his body and the greatness of the sign, another occasion of pride was offered him, which, as a prudent man and a worshiper of God, he ought to have avoided; nor ought he to have shown to foreigners his riches, which he possessed by God's gift. From which, according to the laws of tropology too, we learn that pearls are not to be cast before swine, nor what is holy given to dogs (Matt 7). For he who is of a faithful spirit hides matters; and whoever does not do this, all his strength is unnerved, and his posterity perishes, and, its manly vigor lost, is reduced to womanly softness (Prov 11:13-15). So Isaiah goes in to the king and, as though not knowing, inquires: What did these men say, and from where did they come? He asks two things: what they said, and from where they came. The king answered one, passing over the other, which is to be read with ἐμφάσει and a lifted brow: From a far country they came to me, from Babylon: meaning that the farther the land from which they came, the more glorious is he on whose account they came. And they came, he says, to me, when he ought to have said: they came to glorify God for the greatness of the sign; from Babylon, which is the most powerful city in the whole world. And again Isaiah: What, he says, did they see in your house? And he answered with part of the truth: that they saw everything in his house, and there was nothing that he did not show them in his treasuries. But he is silent about the other thing, for which he feared offense: that he showed them all that he had in his dominion; no doubt the furnishings of the Temple as well. For these reasons Isaiah pronounces the sentence in the word of God: Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: The time will come when all these things which are in your house, acquired not by your labor but by your fathers', will be carried over to Babylon, and of your seed eunuchs will be made in the royal court. From this the Hebrews hold that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who were of the royal seed, were made eunuchs; that they were in the service of king Nebuchadnezzar there is no doubt. So Hezekiah said: Good is the word of the Lord which he has spoken. In this he is reproached by the Hebrews for not imitating the goodness of Moses, who spoke to the Lord: Either forgive them this offense; or if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written (Exod 32:32). Hence the apostle Paul too wishes to be anathema from Christ for his brethren who are Israelites (Rom 9); and they say that for this reason Hezekiah was not approved by the words of God, who in what follows says: Comfort, comfort, O my people, says your God, so that those for whom he had not prayed might be comforted by the Lord's clemency.

40:1ff.

Comfort, comfort, O my people, says your God: Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call to her; for her evil is fulfilled, her iniquity is forgiven. She has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins. LXX: Comfort, comfort my people, says God; ÷ O priests ⁚ speak to the heart of Jerusalem: comfort her: for her humiliation is filled up. Her sin is loosed, for she has received from the hand of the Lord double her sins. According to the other translators, others are commanded to comfort the people of God and Jerusalem alike; according to the Hebrew, the people itself is commanded to comfort, and to speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and to call to her. To speak to the heart of Jerusalem is an idiom of the Scriptures. For he who speaks to one who mourns, and comforts with soothing words, is said to speak to the heart. Let Shechem son of Hamor teach us, who, after he had violated Dinah, spoke to her heart and comforted her (Gen 34). And wherever you find anything similar, it has this sense. And the cause of the comfort is the remission of sins; and the cause of the remission, that she has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins. For he who knows the will of his Lord and sins will be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12). And everyone who has the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, whom the Savior promised to the Apostles, saying: I will ask my Father, and he will give you another comforter, to be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth (John 14:16); and again: But when the comforter, the Holy Spirit, has come, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things (ibid., 26); and again: When the comforter has come, whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me (John 15:26); and: It is to your advantage that I go: for if I do not go away, the comforter will not come to you (John 16:7); he is a comforter, and he is now commanded to comfort the people of God. Hence the Apostle Paul too said to the believers: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our tribulation, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any tribulation, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God: for as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our comfort also will abound (2 Cor 1:1-6); and again: And our hope for you is firm: knowing that as you are partakers of the sufferings, so you will be also of the comfort (2 Cor 1:7). But who this people is that is comforted through the Apostles and churchmen, not Israel and Jacob and Judah, as Scripture records in other places, but the people of God, the prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion: for I will come and dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord. And many nations shall flee to the Lord in that day, and shall be his people, and they shall dwell in the midst of you, and they shall know that the Lord almighty has sent me to you (Zech 2:10, 11). By this testimony it is clearly shown that very many nations are to be turned into the people of God. And these things the Lord says, sent by the Lord whose name is Almighty. And this is to be noted, that our sins are not loosed unless we have received them from the hand of the Lord. Nor is it the same for sins to be loosed and to be forgiven. For he to whom they are forgiven does not need loosing, as he hears in the Gospel: Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you (Matt 9:2). But he for whom they are loosed, for him they are loosed for this reason, that they have been purged and paid off through punishments. According to the history, Jerusalem received from the hand of the Lord double her sins: once from the Babylonians, the second time from the Romans. And what is added by the Seventy, O priests, is to be marked beforehand with an obelus.

40:3ff.

The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight in the wilderness the paths of our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low: and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough ways plain; and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh together shall see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken. LXX: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord: make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough ways plains. And the glory of the Lord shall appear, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God, for the Lord has spoken. Mindful of this voice, the Scribes and Pharisees and the princes of the Jews, when they heard that John was preaching in the wilderness a baptism of penance and teaching the people, send men to ask him whether he was the Christ, or Elijah, or the Prophet; and when he had answered that he was none of these, they ask again: Tell us then, who are you? that we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say of yourself? And he answered: I am the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord; as Isaiah the Prophet said (John 1:22, 23). In this it is to be noticed that the straight ways of the Lord and the paths of our God, the filling of the valleys, and the lowering of the mountains and hills, and the correction of the crooked, and the level plains made of rough places and rocks, and the glory of the Lord and the salvation of our God, are proclaimed not in Jerusalem but in the wilderness of the Church and in the deserted multitude of the nations, of which we read above (cf. Isa 35:1): Rejoice, thirsting desert: let the wilderness exult and flower like the lily. For this multitude was deserted of the knowledge of God, and was held by idols: low in confession, lifted up in pride, rough and intractable in savagery. But after the glory of the Lord appeared, and all flesh saw the salvation of God, all things were suddenly changed and the way of the Lord prepared, so that the glory of God appeared in the wilderness: when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, and the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained on him; and the voice of the Father thundering from above was heard: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear him (Matt 3:17). And all flesh saw the salvation of God. It was called flesh for this reason, that before it did not have the Holy Spirit. Of it the Lord also says: My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh (Gen 6:3). But that flesh will see the salvation of God of which the same Lord spoke through Joel: I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy (Joel 2:28). This was cried out not only at that time by John, who, as the forerunner and precursor of the Word of God, is rightly called a voice (Matt 3); but to this day in the desert of the Gentiles the teachers of the Churches cry out: that we should make straight ways and paths for God in our hearts, and be filled with virtues, and be bowed down by humility; that we should change the crooked into straight and turn the rough into smooth: and so deserve to see the glory of the Lord and the salvation of God.

40:6ff.

The voice of one saying: Cry. And I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass is withered, the flower has fallen; because the spirit of God has blown upon it: truly the people is grass. The grass is withered, the flower has fallen; but the word of our Lord shall stand for ever. LXX: The voice of one saying: Cry: and I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen ※ because the spirit of God has blown upon it ※ truly the people is grass ※ the grass is withered, the flower has fallen ⁚ but the word of our God abides for ever: What is marked with asterisks, because the spirit of God has blown upon it: truly the people is grass: the grass has dried up, the flower has fallen, has been added from the Hebrew and the edition of Theodotion. From which it is clear that it was either passed over by the Seventy or gradually lost by the fault of copyists, since both the former and the following verse end in flower. Above we read, the Prophet saying: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: Behold, here am I, send me; and he said: Go and say to this people: With the ear you shall hear and not understand: and seeing you shall see and not see, and the rest. Having suffered hard things for that preaching, now, when the Lord's voice says Cry, fearing the like, he asks what he ought to cry; and beginning from the general, All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass, he comes to the particular, so as to say none the less of the people: Truly the people is grass. And indeed, if anyone looks at the frailty of the flesh, how from moment to moment we grow and decline and do not remain in the same state, and how the very time in which we speak, dictate and write flies away from the portion of our life, he will not hesitate to call flesh grass, and its glory like the flower of grass, or the meadows of the fields. He who was lately an infant is suddenly a boy; he who was a boy, suddenly a young man; and up to old age he is changed by imperceptible stages; and he perceives himself an old man before he wonders that he is no longer young. A beautiful woman who drew flocks of young men after her is shrunk with a furrowed brow; and she who before was an object of love is afterward one of disgust. This the distinguished orator among the Greeks also writes: that the beauty of the body either fails with time or is consumed by sickness. So the flesh has withered and its beauty has fallen, because the spirit of the fury and sentence of God has blown upon it (to return from the general discussion to the order of Scripture): the flesh of him who bears the image of the earthly and serves vices and luxury; and it is grass and a passing flower. But he who has and keeps the image of the heavenly, he is the flesh that sees the salvation of the Lord, that is renewed daily unto knowledge according to the image of the Creator, and, receiving an incorruptible and immortal body, changes its glory, not its nature. But the word of our Lord, and those who are joined to the word, abide for ever.

40:9ff.

Go up on a high mountain, O woman who brings good tidings to Zion: lift up your voice with strength, O woman who brings good tidings to Jerusalem: lift it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God: behold, the Lord God will come in strength, and his arm shall rule. Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. Like a shepherd he will feed his flock: in his arm he will gather the lambs, and in his bosom he will lift them up: he himself will carry the ewes with young. LXX: Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion: lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem: lift it up, do not fear: say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God, behold the Lord God will come with power, and his arm with dominion: behold, his reward is with him, and his work in his sight. Like a shepherd he will feed his people, and in his arm he will gather the lambs: and he will comfort those that are with young. The choir of the Apostles is commanded to climb the heights for the preaching to all flesh which is to see the salvation of God, and, being about to speak of great things, to abide on the heights. Moreover, the Hebrew and the other translators put it in the feminine gender, so as to say: O woman who brings good tidings to Zion, and O woman who brings good tidings to Jerusalem. In the Greek this word is ambiguous, so that we can take it either of her who announces or of her to whom it is announced. Whether, then, Zion and Jerusalem announce the word of God and the salvation of the Lord, For out of Zion has gone forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa 2:3), or it is announced to them through the Apostles, they must climb the heights and pass over to the mountains. And in a wonderful way, although Zion itself is a mountain, as Scripture says, Mount Zion, in which you have dwelt (Ps 73 [74]:2), she is commanded to ascend another, higher mountain, by which the prince of Tyre was wounded. And because there were to be many things opposed to the teaching of the Apostles, and they were to be led and set before governors and tribunals, there is joined: lift it up, do not fear: say to the cities of Judah, that is, to the Synagogues and peoples of the Jews, of whom the Lord said: I have not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And the apostle Paul: To you, he says, the word of God had to be announced first (Acts 13:46). And what is it that they are commanded to say? Behold your God, whom you were always expecting: Behold, the Lord God will come in strength, whom you despised when he came in humility. And his strength will rule, who before had taken the form of a servant, made obedient to the Father unto death (Phil 2). Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him (Isa 40 and 62). According to what he himself says in the Gospel: For the Son of man is to come in the glory of his Father, and he will render to each according to his work (Matt 16:27). Like a shepherd he will feed his flock. He who afterward is to come in majesty first takes the form of a shepherd, and says of himself: I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and mine know me, and I lay down my life for my sheep (John 10:14, 15). Of him the Father speaks in Zechariah: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zech 13:7). In his arm, he says, he will gather the lambs; not the bulls and rams and he-goats and great sheep, whom he threatens through Ezekiel (Ezek 34) because they feed on the milk and are clothed with the wool and crush the weak of the flock, but the lambs, still tender and of an unformed infancy in Christ, who have lately been reborn in baptism, of whom the Lord himself spoke to Peter: Feed my lambs (John 21:15). Hence also in the same Ezekiel it is written: I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, my servant David; and he shall be their shepherd, and I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst. I the Lord have spoken, and I will make with David a covenant of peace (Ezek 34:23-25). In this it is to be considered that, long after the time of David, the gluttonous shepherds being rejected, he says he will raise up our Lord, who is of the stock of David, to gather the lambs and cherish them in his bosom, and himself to carry on his shoulder the young of the sheep, or the ewes with young; as we read in the Gospel that he carried back to the fold on his shoulders the sheep that had strayed and stayed behind from its accustomed flock (Luke 15). We can call the ewes with young the Apostles and apostolic men and all the teachers of the Church, who are in labor with the salvation of very many, and say with the Apostle: My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). The Hebrews assert, and there is no doubt about this matter among them, that the Holy Spirit is called in their tongue by the feminine gender, that is, RUA CODSA (רוח קדשה). And what is said in Psalm 67 (68): The Lord will give the word to those who bring good tidings with great power, they understand thus: The Lord will give the word to those women who bring good tidings with great power (Ps 122 [123]:3): namely, to those souls which have obtained the Holy Spirit. And also the verse: As the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress: they interpret the soul as the maidservant and the Holy Spirit as the mistress. But also in the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes read, the Lord says: just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me. No one ought to be scandalized in this matter, that spirit is said among the Hebrews in the feminine gender, while in our language it is called in the masculine gender, and in the Greek speech in the neuter. For in the Godhead there is no sex. And therefore in the three principal languages in which the title of the Lord's passion was written, it is called by three genders, so that we may know that what is diverse is of no gender.

40:12ff.

Who has measured the waters in his fist, and weighed heaven with his palm? Who has poised the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a weight, and the hills in a balance? Who has helped the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him? With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him the path of righteousness, and schooled him in knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding? Behold, the nations are like a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the tipping of a balance: behold, the islands are like a little dust. And Lebanon is not enough for burning, and its beasts will not be enough for a burnt offering. All the nations are before him as if they were not, and they are counted to him as nothing and void. LXX: Who has measured the water with his hand, and heaven with his palm, and all the earth with his fist? Who has set the mountains in a weight, and the rocks in a balance? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who was his counselor? Who taught him, whose counsel did he receive, and who instructed him? Or who showed him judgment, and who showed him the way of understanding? If all the nations are counted like a drop of a bucket, and as the tipping of a balance, they are counted also as spittle. Lebanon is not enough for burning, and all the four-footed beasts are not enough for a burnt offering, and all the nations are as nothing, and are counted to him as nothing. Lest anyone should think the calling of the nations difficult, and that all flesh should see the salvation of God, that those who bring good tidings to Zion should be commanded to climb a high mountain, and that the Lord himself should come in strength and render to each according to his work, and like a shepherd cherish the lambs in his bosom and himself carry the ewes with young, his greatness is described: that nothing is impossible to him; and that he who founded all things and is the Creator of all can accomplish also these things, which are small in comparison with those. In calling it fist and palm, he uses the words and measures of human custom, so that we may learn the power of God through our words. Where the Seventy translated: Who has measured the water with his hand? or, as we rendered: Who has measured the waters in his fist? Aquila translated: Who has measured the waters with his smallest finger? For this is what λιχὰς means: that, namely, not with the whole hand but with the little finger, which is commonly called the taster, the whole vastness of the waters is weighed; while σπιθαμὴ, that is, the palm, signifies the hand stretched out from the thumb to the tip of the last finger. But if we close the hand, it becomes a fist: so that through the palm and the fist we may know the outstretched heavens and the globe of the earth. For fist, which the Seventy translated in the grasping of the earth, in the Hebrew is written SALIS (שליש), which Symmachus translated τρίτον, Aquila τρίσωμον: and we, to make it plainer, rendered it three fingers; namely, that he weighed the mass of the earth and the heights of the mountains and hills as if with three little fingers and with the small tipping of a balance: by which the majesty of God and the power of the Creator is shown. Who, he says, has helped the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him? etc. For which Symmachus translated: Who has prepared the spirit of the Lord, and who has shown him the man of his counsel? With whom did he take counsel, and who gave him understanding, and taught him the way of judgment, and instructed him in knowledge, and showed him the road of prudence? By this he shows more plainly that the spirit was prepared, or established, the one of whom one reads in the Apostle: Now the Lord is the Spirit. And: Upon whom the Spirit of God rested, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and the rest. Who says in what follows: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me: because he has anointed me (Isa 61:1). For he himself is the spirit of the Lord and the man of his counsel, in whom dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2). With him he took counsel, of whom we spoke above (cf. Isa 9:6): Wonderful, Counselor. And in Proverbs it is written: God founded the earth by wisdom, and prepared the heavens by understanding (Prov 3:19). Moreover, the Seventy, who said: Who has known the mind of the Lord, and who was his counselor? wish it to be understood that the mind and reason and sense of God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, is he of whom it is sung in the Psalms: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth (Ps 32 [33]:6). All the nations that did not know their Creator, or the whole race of mortals, are in comparison with God like a drop of a bucket, and like the tipping of a balance, which with a light weight inclines to one side. And just as, if a small drop flows from a bucket, it is disregarded by the one who carries it, so the whole multitude of the nations, compared with the heavenly ministries and the multitude of the Angels, is counted as nothing. The islands too are counted as spittle, or, as Symmachus and Theodotion have it, setting down the Hebrew word itself, as DOC (דק), which falls off: for which Aquila translated λεπτὸν βαλλόμενον. And the Hebrews say that this word signifies the finest dust, which, snatched up by the wind, is often thrown into the eyes and is felt rather than seen. The tiniest and almost invisible particles of dust, then, are called by this word: what perhaps Democritus with his Epicurus calls atoms. And there are many words which are read in the Greek just as they are set down in the Hebrew, because of the difficulty of translating, and because of the poverty of both the Greek and the Latin speech in comparison with the Hebrew language. And at the same time, to draw men away little by little from idolatry, he takes away the ceremonies of victims, and teaches that all the wood of Lebanon and the herds that graze on it could not suffice for his burnt offerings. But if all the nations are in his sight as if they were not, and are counted as nothing and void (and among all the nations is Israel too), then Israel too is as if it were not, and is counted as nothing and void. This we say so that its pride may be broken, and they may know that they are like the other nations.

40:18ff.

To whom then have you likened God, or what image will you set up for him? Has the smith cast a graven image, or has the goldsmith shaped it with gold, and the silversmith with plates of silver? The wise craftsman has chosen strong and incorruptible wood: and he will seek how to set up an idol that will not be moved. Having described the greatness of God and shown his power in part, the nations and islands being counted as a drop of a bucket and the tipping of a balance, and as dust, and the ceremonies of victims being rejected, he teaches in what follows why all the nations are as nothing in his sight and are counted as void: To whom have you likened God, or what image will you set up for him, who is spirit, and is in all things, and runs everywhere, and holds the earth as in his fist? And at the same time he mocks the folly of the nations, that a craftsman or bronze-smith, or goldsmith or silversmith, should make a god for themselves, and fasten it together with plates and nails and set it firmly, lest it be pushed over by the blasts of the winds. And what he added: the wise craftsman has chosen strong and incorruptible wood, in the Hebrew is said AMSUCHAN (המסכן); which is a kind of incorruptible wood from which idols are especially made. He says these things so that, idols being rejected, he may prepare the way for the teaching of the Gospel, and all crooked things may be directed into straight; the valleys exalted and the hills brought low; and the glory of the Lord revealed, so that all flesh may see the salvation of God. According to tropology we can say that the chiefs of the heretics are rebuked, who fashion various idols from their own heart: whether by the charm of eloquence, which silver signifies; or by the splendor of gold, which is referred to the understanding; or by incorruptible wood, which are the baser doctrines: and these are thought perpetual by those who fashion them, and are strengthened by the dialectical art, so that they may not be moved and fall, but stand on a solid root.

40:21ff.

Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not understood the foundations of the earth? He who sits upon the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts; who stretches out the heavens like nothing, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in; who makes the searchers of secrets as though they were not; he has made the judges of the earth as void. Indeed, their stock was neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth: suddenly he blew upon them and they withered, and the whirlwind will carry them off like stubble. And to whom have you likened me and made me equal? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things: who brings out their host by number, and calls them all by name. Because of the greatness of his might and strength and power, not one was left behind. LXX: Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not known the foundations of the earth? He who holds the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants as locusts; who has set up the heaven as a vault, and stretched it out as a tent to dwell in; who makes princes reign as nothing, and has made the earth as nothing. For they shall not be planted, nor sown, nor shall their root be made firm in the earth. He blew upon them, and they were dried up, and the tempest will take them up like stubble. Now therefore to whom have you likened me? Shall I be made equal to them? said the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has shown all these things. He who brings out his array by number, he will call them all by name, from much glory and in the strength of might: nothing is hidden from you. From the beginning, he says, I taught you by the natural law, and afterward through Moses I testified by the written Law that idols were nothing, and that the Creator of the world was himself God, who had founded so great a mass of earth upon the seas and set it upon the rivers, so that the heaviest element hangs over thin waters at the will of God, who like a king sits upon the circle of the earth: from which some contend that it is like a point and a globe; and its inhabitants are like locusts. For if we consider the various nations in the whole world, from Ocean to Ocean, that is, from the Indian sea to the British, and from the Atlantic to the frozen North, where the waters congeal and beautiful amber grows solid, we see the whole race of men in between dwelling like locusts. Why then is earth and ashes proud? Since the heaven, or rather, to use the authority of the Scriptures, the heavens, are stretched out like a vault; or, as it stands in the Hebrew, like DOC, of which we spoke above, for which the Seventy there translated spittle: and the one word they rendered now spittle, now vault, that is, arch; and since he stretches out their so great breadth above like a tent and a pavilion, so as to cover men like a roof and make them dwell as in a most spacious house: why should we wonder if the small bodies of men are counted like locusts and tiny creatures? Again, those who in this place too contend that the heaven hangs over the earth as a ἡμικύκλιον, and that the heaven is in the likeness of a sphere, misuse the word vault, as though the middle part of a sphere covered the earth: whereas in the Hebrew we have read not vault but DOC, that is, the finest dust. For which the spittle that is spat upon the ground, and is mixed with dust, and perishes, shows that the whole greatness of bodies is to be counted as nothing. And he who stretched out the heavens and spread them out, so that either the multitudes of Angels might dwell above or men might abide beneath, and made, as it were, a great house for rational creatures, he himself according to the character of the times appoints princes, or searchers of secrets, so that they are as though they were not; and he has made the judges of the earth as void. For which the Seventy translated: and has made the earth as nothing; since also at the beginning of Genesis, where it is written: But the earth was invisible and unformed (Gen 1:2), the others translated: But the earth was void and nothing. How many kings Greek and Barbarian and Roman history recounts! Where is that countless army of Xerxes? Where the multitude of Israel in the desert? Where the incredible power of kings? Why should I speak of ancient things? Present examples teach us that princes are as nothing, and that the judges of the earth are counted as void. These princes and judges of the earth (or, as others suspect, of heaven) were neither sown nor planted nor made firm with a solid root, and suddenly, at God's command, they are carried off and perish, as stubble is snatched away by whirlwind and tempest; according to what is written: And I passed by, and he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:36). Since, then, so great is the power and majesty of the Creator, to what likeness do you compare God? And do you not rather understand the maker from the greatness of his creatures? If you do not believe words, at least believe your eyes; and from the service of the heavens and of all the elements consider the power of the Lord. Who brings out their host by number, that is, of the heavens; and calls them all by name: understand, the stars. Of which it is also sung in the Psalms: Who numbers the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by name (Ps 146 [147]:4). Or let us interpret the host of heaven as the Angels and all the armies of the heavens, of whom Daniel also speaks: Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten times a hundred thousand stood before him (Dan 7:10). Hence he is also called the Lord Sabaoth, which in our language is said the Lord of the army and of hosts, or of powers. And he brings out the host of the heavens by number, so that the sun and the moon and the other stars, which Abraham could not number, are numbered by him and serve in the office assigned them (Gen 15): while the sun completes the same course of heaven in one year, Lucifer and Vesper in two years, the moon in each month, and all the stars accomplish it in fixed times; and some of them are called wandering, and we perceive their unequal motions with the eyes, not the mind, and we do not so much understand as wonder. For the greatness of God's might makes all things serve in their order. Or, according to the Seventy, because of the multitude of his glory and the power of his strength, nothing can be hidden from him: but by the majesty of the Creator he knows the ways and reasons and courses of all things.

Book Twelve

No writer is so unskilled that he does not find a reader like himself; and far the greater part are those who turn over Milesian tales than those who turn over the books of Plato. For in the one there is play and amusement, in the other difficulty and sweat mixed with toil. Indeed, Tullius himself, who translated it, confesses that he does not understand the Timaeus, which discusses the harmony of the world and the course and numbers of the stars; but the Testament of Grunnius Corocotta the Piglet is chanted in the schools by troops of cackling boys. So let our Luscius Lanuvinus too enjoy his witnesses, or rather his partisans, and let him win by numbers, since perhaps he wins by talent. For me the testimony of a few suffices, and I am content with the praise of friends, who, in seeking out my little works, slip through love for me and through zeal for the Scriptures. And I think there will be some who will contend that this very thing, that I address my discourse to you, Eustochium, lies open to detraction, not considering that Huldah and Anna and Deborah prophesied while men were silent, and that in the service of Christ it is not the difference of sexes that counts, but of minds. The twelfth book of explanations on Isaiah, then, will have this beginning.

40:27ff.

Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment will pass away from my God ? Do you not know, or have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord who created the ends of the earth, will not fail, nor will he labor, nor is there any searching out of his wisdom. He gives strength to the weary, and to those who have no might he multiplies strength. Boys will fail and will labor, and young men will fall in weakness. But those who hope in the Lord will change their strength, they will take on wings like the eagle, they will run and not labor, they will walk and not fail. LXX: For do not say, Jacob, and why have you spoken, Israel: My way is hidden from God, and my God has taken away my judgment and has departed? And now do you not know, and have you not heard? The eternal God, the God who created the ends of the earth, will not hunger, nor will he labor, nor is there any finding out of his understanding. He gives strength to the hungry, and sorrow to those who do not grieve. For young men will hunger, and youths will labor, and the chosen will be weak. But those who wait for God will change their strength. They will take on wings like eagles; they will run and not labor; they will go on and not hunger. Since the greatness of Almighty God is so great that nothing escapes him, and all things are governed by his will, why do you say, Jacob, that is, the two tribes which were called Judah, and speak, Israel, the other ten tribes in Samaria, you who have already been led captive to the Assyrians: My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment will pass away from my God? And the sense is: You say, earthly things do not concern God, nor does he consider what each one of us does; hence we too are unjustly oppressed by our enemies, and, according to Habakkuk, we are destroyed like beasts and fishes, without any ruler (Hab 1). To them God answered: Do you not know, and have the words of the preceding Scriptures not taught you? or, according to the Seventy, are you ignorant, because you have not heard, that the eternal God and Creator of all, the Lord, knows all things, holds all things together, and orders all things by his majesty? Nor does he ever fail or labor, so that he should not understand your judgment, and your ways should be hidden from him. Nor is there, he says, any searching out of his wisdom; from which place I think that saying of the Apostle was taken: Incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways (Rom 11:33); or, as the Seventy translated, he will not hunger, and he will not labor. For where there is food, there is often hunger, if you take the food away; and where there is hunger, there is also labor. But since these things are not in God, why do you attach human passions to him? Rather, he himself gives strength to the hungry and the weary, and to those who seem to be as nothing in the world he multiplies power and might; or, according to the Seventy, he gives sorrow to those who do not grieve; for there is a sadness that leads to death, and there is a sadness that leads to life. Hence to those who have an impenitent heart he gives sadness, so that they may understand their sins. And because many rejoice in the health of the body, and think youth and boyhood to be perpetual, he adds and says that the flowering age quickly falls, and robust bodies wither. But those who have their trust not in their own strength but in God, and always await his mercy, change their strength and go from strength to strength, and take on wings like the eagle, and hear: Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's (Ps 102 [103]:5); they run to the Lord and do not labor in their desire for him; they walk and never fail. We have often said that the old age of eagles grows green again by the changing of their feathers, and that they alone can look at the radiance of the sun and gaze with flashing eyes upon the splendor of its rays, and that by this test they prove their young, whether they are true-born. So too the saints grow young again, and, having put on an immortal body, do not feel the labor of mortals, but are caught up in the clouds to meet Christ, and, according to the Seventy, never hunger, because they have the Lord present as their food.

41:1ff.

Let the islands be silent before me, and let the nations change their strength; let them approach, and then let them speak; let us draw near together to judgment. Who raised up the Righteous One from the East, called him to follow him? He will give the nations before him, and he will hold kings. He will give them as dust to his sword, as stubble swept off by the wind to his bow. He will pursue them; he will pass on in peace; the path will not appear in his feet. Who has wrought and done these things, calling the generations from the beginning? I the Lord, I am the first and the last. The islands saw and were afraid; the ends of the earth were astounded; they drew near and came. Each will help his neighbor, and will say to his brother Be strong. The coppersmith strengthened the one who was forging at that time, striking with the hammer, saying, It is good for gluing; and he strengthened it with nails, so that it should not be moved. LXX: Be renewed toward me, you islands, for the princes will change their strength; let them draw near and speak together; then let them declare judgment. Who raised up righteousness from the East, called it to his feet, and it will go? He will give before the nations, and will cast kings into amazement, and will give their swords into the earth, and their bows like stubble cast away; and he will pursue them; the way of his feet will pass over in peace. Who has wrought and done these things? He will call it, he who calls it from the beginning of the generations. I God am first, and for the things that are to come I am. The nations saw and were afraid; the ends of the earth were astounded and drew near; they came together, each judging to help his neighbor and his brother; and he will say: The craftsman and coppersmith has prevailed, striking with the hammer, at the same time drawing out; at one time indeed he says, The soldering is good. They strengthened them; they will fix them with nails; and they will not be moved. The nations, that is, the islands, which are beaten by the false and bitter waves of this world, are bidden to listen and to close their mouths, and to know what was said to Israel: Hear, Israel, and be silent; and to change their strength, lest through their former weakness they be unable to hear the word of God, so that they may first approach the Lord, and not be content with their own salvation, but teach others what they have learned, and dispute with the Lord whether the God of all has kept what is just. And he so questions them and challenges them to answer, as to teach by questioning what they do not know: Who raised up the righteous one from the East, or righteousness? For he is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the nations, who called Christ the Lord, the Savior, who was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1); in whom, according to the same Apostle, the righteousness of God is revealed (ibid.). And he called him to follow him in all things and to do the works of the Father, and to fulfill that which he says: O God, I have willed to do your will (Ps 39 [40]:9). In his sight kings and nations will bow their necks, and to his sword and arrows the adverse powers will be made subject like stubble and dust. He will pursue them, namely the kings and princes of the several nations; and he will pass through in peace, calling all to peace, so that they may be reconciled to God. The path will not appear in his feet, that is, he will not feel the labor of the way, nor any weariness of human weakness, but will drink of the brook in the way, and therefore will lift up his head (Ps 109 [110]). Who, he says, has wrought and done these things? Who raised up the righteous one, or righteousness? Who delivered nations and kings to him? Who subjected all things to his sword and bow? Surely he who from the beginning of the world foretold that these things would come, who is the Founder of all. And because he had said, with the feeling of one inquiring, Who raised up the righteous one from the East, and so on, while all were silent he answered himself: I am the Lord, I am the first and the last. It is he who speaks also in the Apocalypse of John: I am the alpha and the ω, the beginning and the end (Rev 1:8; and 22:13). The islands saw, that is, the nations, or the Churches gathered from the nations, which endure the storms of this world; and they feared the Lord: For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). All the ends of the lands trembled at the words of the Apostles, drawing near and coming together to the Gospel of Christ. And when they saw that they themselves were saved, they fulfilled in deed what they had heard above: let them approach, and then let them speak, so that they helped their neighbors and wished to strengthen their brothers in the Lord, and said to them: Depart from idols, despise the ancient images of demons, which a human hand fashioned, which were produced by the beating hammer, which were joined with glue, which were made fast with nails so that they should not be moved, and which, when they stand, cannot walk. What we have interpreted of the person of Christ, and the calling of the nations, and the preaching of the Gospel, and the condemnation of idols, some refer to Cyrus king of the Persians: that God raised him up from the East against the Babylonians and made him obey his command, laying many nations low before him and subjecting all things to his sword and bow; and they refer what follows to his person, namely that their idols, made by human effort and called into being by the coppersmith's art, did not profit the Babylonians. Some of the Hebrews think it is said of Abraham, who was called righteous from the East, that is, from the Chaldeans, because he alone was found righteous; and he followed him, going out of his native land into a land he did not know; and God delivered into his hand the kings who had come against Sodom and Gomorrah, and before his sword and bow made them like stubble and dust; and he pursued them and returned in peace, and did not feel the course of the long journey; and this he did not by his own strength but by the mercy of the Lord, who from the beginning knew that these things would come. Saw, he says, the islands, that is, the nations round about, and were terrified by his power: and the ends of the earth: namely Shem the son of Noah, who at the furthest time of the lands had escaped from the Flood with his father and his brothers, and had been preserved until that time (Gen 14). Him they want to be understood as Melchizedek, and that he came to meet Abraham as he returned from the battle, and received him, and blessed him, and strengthened him with the blessings of God; and that he is the coppersmith who forged Abraham and with the hammer of his art brought him out into better things, and said to him: It is good that you be glued to the fear of the Lord and joined to him. And he strengthened him, or made him solid, with the nails of the Lord's precepts, so that he should not be moved but should abide in his fear,

41:8ff.

And you, Israel my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham my friend. In whom I took hold of you from the ends of the earth, and called you from its far places, and said to you: You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not cast you off. Do not fear, for I am with you; do not turn aside, for I am your God; I have strengthened you and have helped you and the right hand of my righteous one has upheld you. Behold, all who fight against you will be confounded and will blush; they will be as though they were not; and the men who contradict you will perish. You will seek them and will not find them; the men who rebel against you will be as though they were not; and the men who war against you, as a thing consumed. For I the Lord your God have taken hold of your hand, saying to you: Do not fear, I have helped you. Do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead out of Israel. I have helped you, says the Lord, and your redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sawing teeth. You will thresh the mountains and crush them, and you will make the hills like dust. You will winnow them, and the wind will carry them off, and the whirlwind will scatter them; and you will exult in the Lord, you will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. LXX: But you, Israel my child, Jacob whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham whom I loved, whom I took up from the ends of the earth, and from its heights I called you, and said to you: You are my child; I have chosen you and have not forsaken you. Do not fear, for I am with you, lest you go astray; for I am your God, who have strengthened you, and I have helped you, and have made you firm with my righteous right hand. Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and will blush; for they will be as though they were not; and all your enemies will perish. You will seek them and will not find them, the men who will rage against you. For they will be as though they were not, and those who fight against you will not be. For I am the Lord your God, who hold your right hand, who say to you: Do not fear, Jacob, little Israel. I have helped you, says God, I who redeem you, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I have made you like the new wheels of a threshing wagon, in the manner of saws; and you will thresh the mountains and crush the hills, and you will make them like dust and winnow them, and the wind will carry them off, and the tempest will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the Lord and in the holy ones of Israel. That there is a fleshly Jacob and Israel and a spiritual one, the Apostle Paul teaches: Behold Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor 10). From this we understand that there is also another according to the spirit; and to the fleshly Israel it is said: If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. To them also it is said above (cf. Isa 40:27): Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed away from my God? Now, on the contrary, God speaks to the spiritual Israel, which received the coming of its Lord, which he calls first servant, then chosen, and finally the seed of Abraham. For first we received the spirit of bondage in fear (Rom 8); and afterward, being chosen, we are joined in friendship with God. So after the calling of the nations, when the islands saw and feared, the ends of the earth were astounded, drew near and came, the remnant according to the election of grace is called, of whom the Gospel also writes: These twelve Jesus chose, whom he also named Apostles (Luke 6); who, after the bondage of the Law as tutor, were chosen in the Gospel, and were found worthy to be the seed of Abraham the friend of God. For in him he took hold of them from the end of the earth, and from its far-off borders he called Israel out of all the nations, gathering first the people of the Jews, of whom the Apostle Paul also says: It was necessary that the word be preached first to you; but since you turn us away, we go to the nations (Acts 13:46). To you, therefore, who are both my servant and my chosen one, who are to preach among the nations and to suffer very many persecutions, I say: Do not fear, for I am with you, to whom I speak in the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt 28:20). Do not go astray, nor turn aside from the truth, nor deceive yourself with a false persuasion that by your own strength, unskilled and naked, you will penetrate the forest of the nations and call the fiercest peoples to gentleness. It is I who have strengthened you and have helped you; and the right hand of my righteous one has upheld you, or protected you, that is, of the Lord the Savior; or my right hand, as the Seventy translated. For behold, your adversaries, the people of the Jews, and all who fight against you, and your persecutors, will be turned into nothing, and you will seek your adversaries and will not find them. And the reason is given why he does not find his adversaries: Because they will be as though they were not. These adversaries are said to rage against the Apostles, or, according to the Hebrew, to be consumed. And for this reason you ought not to fear, because I have taken hold of your hand, I who say to you: Do not fear, I have helped you; do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead out of Israel, or, as the Seventy have it, very few out of Israel. What we have set down, I have helped you: do not fear, worm Jacob, is not found in the Seventy.
