And he who restores Jerusalem and destroys Babylon also says to Cyrus, king of the Persians, who first destroyed Babylon and the Chaldeans: You are my shepherd, or, as the Seventy translated, that he should be wise. The cause of this difference is plain. For if we read the Hebrew word ROI with the letter RES (רעי), it is understood as my shepherd; if with DALETH (דעי), as knowing or my understanding one; and the likeness of these letters is distinguished by a small stroke, and for this reason they are often confused. It is written at the beginning of Ezra that at the edict of Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, the captivity of the people of Israel was loosed, and those who wished to return were sent back to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest. For the Lord inspired him to do his will and to fulfill his commands. And significantly he added, who say to Jerusalem: You will be built; and to the Temple: You will be founded. For under Cyrus it was ordered that Jerusalem and the Temple be built, but while he lived only the foundations of the Temple were laid. For the rest, under Darius, in his second year, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, the Temple began to be built.

45:1ff.

Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have taken hold of, to subdue nations before his face, and I will turn the backs of kings, and I will open doors before him, and the gates will not be shut. I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth; I will break the gates of bronze, and I will shatter the bars of iron. And I will give you hidden treasures and the secrets of hidden places, that you may know that I am the Lord, who call your name, the God of Israel. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I have also called you by your name; I have likened you, and you have not known me. I am the Lord, and there is none besides; apart from me there is no God; I girded you, and you have not known me; that they may know, those who are from the rising of the sun and those who are from the west, that besides me there is none. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I form light and create darkness; I make peace and create evil. I am the Lord who does all these things. I know that in this passage very many, not only of the Latins but of the Greeks, err badly, thinking that it is written: Thus says the Lord to my anointed, the Lord; so that it may be understood according to what we read elsewhere: The Lord rained from the Lord (Gen 19:24); and: The Lord said to my Lord (Ps 109 [110]:1). For it says not κυρίῳ, which means Lord, but Cyrus, who in Hebrew is called CHORES (כרש), the king of the Persians, who overcame Babylon and the Chaldeans; and, joined with the Medes, he is read of above as the driver of a two-horse chariot, that is, of the camel and the ass. He was called Christ, that is, the anointed of the Lord, because this was the mark of royal power among the Hebrews; so that, as among us the diadem and the purple are given to emperors alone, so among the Hebrews those who were to reign were anointed with ointment. Hence Saul too is called the Lord's anointed (1 Sam 6). And in the Psalms we read: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no harm to my prophets (Ps 104 [105]:15). His right hand he took hold of and held, so that no one could resist his strength. Let us read Xenophon's history of the elder Cyrus in eight books, and we shall see the prophecy of Isaiah fulfilled. For what city was not opened to him? What city did not bow beneath him the backs of its kings? What walls, before impregnable, were not overthrown by his siege? Hence God makes an apostrophe to Cyrus himself: I have given you the treasures and the hidden wealth of all the cities, so that you, who before worshiped idols, might perceive the one God through his benefits, especially since you know that your name was foretold long before you were born. Josephus too relates this in the eleventh book of the Jewish Antiquities: that Cyrus read that Isaiah had prophesied of him by his very name, and that for this reason he loved the Jews very much as God's intimates. And these things, he says, I have granted you for the sake of Jacob my servant, and Israel my chosen, and I have called you by your name, as I called Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and foretold you long before, as I did Isaac and Josiah: lest you should be thought to be that Christ to whom you have been likened, and whose type and image you went before. But you have not known me, that is, you have worshiped images, not God. I girded you with strength; I made you victor over many nations, and you have not known your helper. In this place I cannot sufficiently marvel at the folly of readers, that they refer these things to Christ, through whom the world was reconciled to God. I, he says, am the Lord, and there is none besides apart from me. For besides my Word and Reason, and my power and wisdom, which is in me, there is no other God. And I have done these things so that the whole world, from the East and the West, may acknowledge that there is no other God besides me. I am the Lord, and there is no other. For the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, who says in the Gospel: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). And in the volume of Ezra it is set down that Cyrus wrote to all the nations that there is no God but the God of Israel alone. Or it is to be understood thus: that the release of the captives and God's clemency toward his people made God better known to all the nations. I, then, who gave you strength, and am the only God, myself make things contrary to one another, light and darkness, that is, day and night; peace and evil, that is, leisure and war; by which he signifies both that he was angry with his people, when it endured the darkness of captivity and the evils of bondage, and again that he had mercy on it, when, sent back to their homeland, they received peace and joy. For as darkness is contrary to light, so war is contrary to peace. Hence let the heresy be confounded which thinks God the founder of evils; since here evil is set not as the contrary of good, but for affliction and war, according to what is written in the Gospel: Sufficient for the day is its own evil (Matt 6:34). According to tropology we can say these things also of the churchman, to whom God has given speech and wisdom, so that by his disputation he may overturn all the sects contrary to the truth, as holy Scripture records of Stephen too (Acts 6), that no one could resist his wisdom; and so that he may subject kings, that is, the patriarchs of the several heresies, to his power, and may open and break what before seemed shut fast by the art of dialectic, and may bring into the open the secrets of the heretics, overcoming and refuting them, so that they may come to know the secrets of Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2). Such a man God calls by his own name, because he is the defender of his child Jacob and of his chosen Israel. Him he takes up and likens to his own word; and he must beware lest he think that what he speaks is his own, but must refer all to the glory of the giver, lest he too deserve to hear: I girded you, and you have not known me. For when, equipped with the armor of the Apostle, he has taught all that there is no other God but one, who is the God of Jacob and Israel, Marcion will be confounded, who understands two gods, one good and the other just, one the founder of things invisible, the other of things visible; of whom the former makes light, the latter darkness, the one peace, the other evil: whereas the one and the same God has founded both according to the diversity of merits.

Book Thirteen

Many mishaps overwhelm those who sail. If the wind blows more violently, the storm is a cause of fear. If a gentler breeze ruffles the back of the element that lies beneath, they dread the ambushes of pirates. And so it comes about that souls entrusted to fragile timber either fear danger or endure it; and of these each is heavier than the other: either to fear death perpetually, or to endure what you have feared. This I see happening to me as I sail on the sea of Isaiah. For while the sails were spread on an unhindered course, and the keel glided on, furrowing the plains of the deep, with the sailors' hands at ease, a sudden whirlwind of sickness arose, and with such great masses of waves and the crash of billows dashing against one another resounding, it so terrified the fearful hearts of my friends that they were compelled to say: Master, save us, we are perishing (Matt 8:25). Therefore, Eustochium, unique example in the whole world of nobility and of virginity, let not the apple of your eye be silent; cry out in your heart: Abba, Father (Rom 8:15). And say with the Psalmist: Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord (Ps 43 [44]:23)? so that, by your prayers and Christ's mercy, I may complete the work enjoined on me on Isaiah. For already the thirteenth book of the Explanations is being forged, and it has not yet come to its end. And meanwhile, until the merciful and compassionate Lord, patient and of many mercies (Ps 85 [86] and 144 [145]), restores my former health, I have dictated this little preface in hurried speech, so that what is in hand may be copied out on sheets, and the full correction be reserved to the reader's judgment.

45:8

Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one: let the earth be opened, and let it bud forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together: I the Lord have created him. LXX: Let the heaven rejoice from above, and let the clouds sprinkle righteousness: let the earth bud forth, and let mercy spring up, and let it bud forth righteousness together: I am the Lord who created you. The interpretation of this passage is twofold. For some think that it clings to what was said above, and that, when King Cyrus sets the captives free, heaven and earth rejoice: μετωνυμικῶς, that is to say, those who dwell in heaven and on earth. Others separate it from what precedes and want it to be the proper beginning of this chapter, and a prophecy of the Lord's coming: that command is given to the clouds, of which it is written above (cf. Isa 5:6): I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it, that is, upon the vineyard of Israel; and to which the truth of God reaches, that they should rain upon the world the righteous one, or righteousness; and that the earth should be opened and bud forth the Savior. Of it is sung in the Psalms: Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven (Ps 84 [85]:12); or, according to the Seventy: The earth has budded forth mercy and righteousness alike, so that sinners may obtain mercy and the righteous their rewards. And as for what follows: I the Lord have created him, or, I am the Lord who created you, he will not be scandalized at the word 'creature' who has read that he is a worm and a servant, and that he sprang from the earth.

45:9ff.

Woe to him who contradicts his maker: a potsherd of the Samian earth. Does the clay say to its potter, What are you making? and, Your work is without hands? Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? and to a woman, What are you bringing to birth? Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, his fashioner: Ask me about things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands give charge to me. I made the earth, and I created man upon it: my hands stretched out the heavens, and I gave command to all their host. I have raised him up to righteousness, and I will direct all his ways. He will build my city, and he will let my captivity go, not for a price nor for gifts, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: What better have I made than the potter's clay? Will the ploughman plough the earth? Will the clay say to the potter, What are you making? because you do not work and have no hands? Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? and to a mother, What are you bringing to birth? For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who made the things to come: Ask me about my sons, and concerning the works of my hands give charge to me. I made the earth, and man upon it. I with my hand made firm the heaven: I gave command to all the stars. I raised him up with righteousness as king: all his ways are straight. He will build my city, and will turn back the captivity of my people: not with a price nor with gifts, said the Lord God Sabaoth. Those who wish to refer what is said to the person of Cyrus interpret this passage thus: When I promise great things, that for the sake of my people's return to Judea I will lay all kingdoms beneath Cyrus, woe to him who is unbelieving and does not think that the things I say will come, as if clay and a broken potsherd should cavil at its potter, why it was made, or why it was made so; and a work should speak against the hands of its craftsman; and a son should cavil at his father and mother, why he was poured out onto the earth by the law of nature. Since therefore I, the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, have fashioned Cyrus, and he was begotten at my command, it is superfluous for you to doubt about things to come; rather you ought to know that I dispose of my sons, the people of Israel, and of the work of my hands, not at your discretion but by my will: so that I, who formerly created darkness and evil for them, now grant light and peace. For I am God, who did not create the earth for emptiness, that it should be deserted and squalid, but that men should dwell in it. I stretched out, or made firm, the heavens, that they might be the dwelling place of the angels. And I distinguished them with the variety of the stars, and commanded each in what order to run, and to complete the different spans of days and months and years. I, then, who made heaven and earth, what great thing is it if I have created one king to keep my commands, and if I direct all his ways? For he will order that my city Jerusalem be built, and that the captives return to Judea. Not for a price, nor for gifts, but because of my will, says the Lord God of hosts. But one who refers the understanding so begun to Christ frames the words of his explanation thus: Woe to those who contradict God and do not think that Christ will come; as if clay and a potsherd from among potsherds should contradict its potter. Woe to him who says to the Almighty Father, Why do you beget a Son? and to the woman, holy Mary, What are you bringing to birth? Of whom the Apostle too writes (Gal 4): That Christ was made of a woman, and made under the law. These things, then, says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, who fashioned the Savior in the virginal womb, saying through Gabriel: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35): and the holy thing that will be born in you will be called the Son of God: let the potsherd question me and search out the secrets of things to come. And let it instruct me how I ought to regenerate the adopted sons who are to believe in my Son. The evangelist John too says: As many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God (John 1:12). But if I made the earth to be inhabited by men, and stretched out the heavens above, and adorned them with the variety of the stars, so that worshipers of God might dwell on the earth, what wonder is it if I have sent my Son, a righteous king, into the world, or raised him up from the underworld, all of whose ways are straight? For he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth (1 Pet 2:22). He it is who is to build my city upon the rock, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail (Matt 16); and which, set on a mountain, cannot be hidden (ibid., 5); and to let go free all who were formerly bound with demonic chains, not for a price nor for gifts: for we have been saved freely, the Apostles hearing and doing: Freely you have received, freely give (Matt 10:8). Some refer these things to Zerubbabel, who led the captives out of Babylon, and built the city, and constructed the temple, while Haggai and Zechariah prophesied and said: The hands of Zerubbabel have founded this house, and his hands will complete it (Zech 4:9). But we say more rightly and more truly that neither did Cyrus build the city, which was constructed afterwards under Nehemiah, nor were all his ways made straight, he to whom it was said above: I took you and girded you, and you did not know me; and that all that is said exceeds the station of Zerubbabel, who was under the nod and power of the Medes and Persians. For Zerubbabel neither constructed the city, nor let the captivity go, nor can he be called king who, living under other kings, lacked this name. But what the Seventy mean, who at the beginning of this chapter translated: What better have I made than the potter's clay? Will he who ploughs plough the earth? I am not able to know: unless perhaps I follow the edition of Theodotion, who put in place of this: Woe to him who contends against his maker, ploughing those who plough the earth: namely, that he wounds the hearts of mortals unto penitence, and, after the manner of furrows, breaks them up and overturns them. But this too is a frivolous interpretation. Further, that God, our Creator and maker, is called a potter, the apostle Paul too says in the Epistle to the Romans: Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: Why have you made me thus? Has not the potter power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom 9:20)? And in Jeremiah it is written at greater length, who relates, after other things: I went down into the potter's house, and behold, he was making a work on the wheel, and the vessel that he was making was spoiled in his hands. And again he made from the same clay another vessel, as it pleased in his sight. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not, like this potter, make you, house of Israel, says the Lord? Behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hands, house of Israel (Jer 18:3, 4). And what is written: I gave command to all the stars, has given some an occasion to hold that the stars are rational and have soul and sense. For, they say, he would not command any but beings who understand: not remembering that it is written in Jonah: The Lord commanded the scorching wind (Jonah 4:8). And again: He commanded the morning worm (ibid., 7). And that in the Gospel the Savior rebuked the winds and the sea (Luke 8), in which it is plain that there is neither sense nor reason.

45:14ff.

Thus says the Lord: The labor of Egypt, and the merchandise of Ethiopia, and the Sabaim, men of stature, will pass over to you, and will be yours: they will walk behind you, they will go bound in manacles: and they will worship you, and make supplication to you: only in you is God, and there is no God apart from you. Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior. They are confounded and have blushed, all of them: together the makers of errors have gone off into confusion. Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation: you will not be confounded, and you will not blush, for ever and ever. LXX: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and of the Sabaim: lofty men will pass over to you, and they will be your servants, and they will follow you bound in manacles, and they will pass over to you, and will worship you, and will pray in you: because God is in you, and there is no God apart from you. For you are God, and we did not know it: the God of Israel, the Savior: let all his adversaries be confounded and blush, and let them walk in confusion. ÷ Be renewed unto me, islands ⁚ Israel is saved by the Lord with an eternal salvation: they will not be confounded nor blush for ever. In this passage too, those who follow the history say that Egypt, and the Ethiopians, and the nations of the Sabaim, which are beyond Ethiopia, served Cyrus, and that the furthest nations were subjected to him; and that from his wondrous victory they understood that the Lord was in him, and that there was no other God besides him who dwelt in him. But how what follows: Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior, can fit the person of Cyrus, I do not understand. Unless perhaps they use the edition of Theodotion, who translated: In you is the strong one, and there is no other God besides him: therefore you are the strong, hidden God of Israel, the Savior. Whithersoever they turn, they will not be able to escape the snares of the truth. For grant that God is in Cyrus, and that there is no other God besides him who is in Cyrus: how will it be fitting to say to the person of Cyrus, Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior? Therefore the God in whom God is, is more rightly and more truly understood as our Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). He is called a hidden God because of the mystery of the body he assumed, and the God of Israel, Savior, which means Jesus. For he, according to the angel Gabriel, will save his people (Luke 1). They are confounded and have blushed, all together, namely the Scribes and Pharisees. And the makers of error have gone off into confusion, who spread a lie through the whole world, saying that he had been stolen away by the Apostles (Matt 28). But Israel, saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation, is understood as the choir of the Apostles, and those who believed through the Apostles. Hence it is said to them: You will not be confounded nor will you blush, not only in the present age but also in the one to come. That Egypt, and the Ethiopians, and the Sabaim, lofty and exalted men, served him, no one doubts, since one sees the world subjected to him, and perceives that, under the name of a few nations which dwell at the furthest ends of the earth, all the hinges of the heavens and all the shores of the earth are to believe in him. Hence it is beautifully said, as to men laboring in the error of idolatry, that the labor of Egypt ceases. For no nation was so given over to idolatry, and venerated such innumerable monstrosities, as Egypt, of which we read above (Isa 19:1): Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt will melt in its midst. Further, what is added in the Seventy: Be renewed unto me, islands, we can expound thus: we may say that the Churches gathered from the nations are renewed in Christ, and are called islands because they endure the rage and the storms of persecutors, and, founded upon the rock, are shaken by no mass of whirlwinds. The Hebrews strive with foolish contention to assert that, up to the place where we read: Only in you is God, and there is no God apart from you, it is said either to Jerusalem or to Cyrus; but that what follows: Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior, is suddenly an apostrophe made to the almighty God; though it is plain even to fools that the texture of the discourse is one, and that a sense which is joined together in the very order and reasoning of the narration cannot be divided.

45:18ff.

For thus says the Lord, who creates the heavens, God himself who forms the earth and makes it, he himself its fashioner: he did not create it in vain; that it might be inhabited he formed it: I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob: Seek me in vain. I am the Lord who speaks righteousness, who declares right things. Gather together, and come, and draw near together, you who have been saved from among the nations: they have not known, who lift up the wood of their graven image, and pray to a god that does not save. Declare, and come, and take counsel together: who has caused this to be heard from the beginning, has foretold it from that time? Is it not I the Lord, and there is no God besides me? A righteous God and one who saves, there is none besides me. Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is no other. By myself have I sworn: the word of righteousness will go forth from my mouth, and will not return: for to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear. Therefore he will say in the Lord: Mine are righteousnesses and dominion: to him they will come, and all who resist him will be confounded. In the Lord all the seed of Israel will be justified and will be praised: LXX: Thus says the Lord who made the heaven: this God who showed the earth and made it, he himself prepared it: he did not make it for emptiness, but formed it to be inhabited. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob, Seek vanity: I am the Lord who speak righteousness, I declare truth. Gather together and come, and take counsel together, you who are being saved from the nations; they have not known, who carry the wood of their graven image: they pray to gods that do not save. If they declare, let them draw near, that they may know together who has made these things heard from the beginning; then it was declared to you. Am I not the Lord God, and there is no other besides me: a righteous one and a savior, there is none besides me. Be converted to me, and you will be saved from the ends of the earth. I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear: unless righteousness shall go forth from my mouth: my words will not be turned back, for to me every knee will bend, and every tongue will swear and will confess to God, saying: Righteousness and glory will come to him, and all who separate themselves from the Lord will be confounded: all the seed of the sons of Israel will be justified and will be glorified in God. Having called Egypt, and Ethiopia, and the Sabaim, lofty men, by which the salvation of all the barbarian nations and the conversion of the whole world to God is shown, God shows his righteousness: that he is the Lord not of the Jews only, but also of the nations. For he, the maker of heaven and earth, is equally the God of all, and he created the earth for no other reason than to be the dwelling place of men, who should worship and understand their Creator, and despise all idols. For on Mount Sinai too, from its lofty summit, he spoke these things in the hearing of the peoples: You shall have no strange gods besides me, nor shall you make yourself an idol (Exod 20:3, 4). But it is better that we believe this was said of the preaching of the Gospel: for Moses spoke in a hidden wilderness to one people only. But the sound of the Apostles went out into the whole world, and their words reached to the ends of the earth (Ps 18 [19]). I did not say, he says, to the seed of Jacob, Seek me in vain. For I promised them the kingdoms of heaven, and I spoke to them first: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And therefore I spoke righteousness and declared right things, or truth, so that, leaving behind the images and ceremonies of the Law, they might follow the truth of the Gospel. But because they would not believe, and judged themselves unworthy of salvation, therefore I say to the nations: Gather together from the whole world; and come and draw near to me together, you who have been saved from among the nations. By this he shows that not all the nations will believe at once, but gradually and in parts. Finally he rebukes those who remained in their former error, saying: They have not known, who lift up the wood of their graven image, and pray to a god that does not save. And the sense is: They did not understand my words, weighed down by the burden of their idols, and hoping in those in whom there is no salvation. Hence the Apostles are commanded to proclaim the truth in season and out of season (2 Tim 4), and to enter on counsel for the salvation of the nations. And this, that is, that very many from the nations should be gathered and come and be saved, God spoke from the beginning, and the mouths of all the Prophets sang it, who spoke by the word of the Lord, besides whom there is no other. For the Son is God not apart from him, but in him. And beautifully he joins: A righteous God, not of one nation at all, but of the whole world, to which he says: Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth; fulfilling what the Father promised the Son: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8). And he swears by himself that the sentence of his mouth, and the word he has once uttered concerning the salvation of the nations, will by no means be made void; but that the promise of him who said above: Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth, will be fulfilled in deed. And he swears, according to the Apostle (Heb 6), so that through two immovable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have firm consolation; but he also swears this: that, idols abandoned, every knee should bow to him, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue of mortals should swear by him (Phil 2). In this the Christian people is plainly signified. For it is the custom of the Church to bend the knee to Christ: which the Jews, displaying the pride of their mind, do not do at all. And every tongue too of all the barbarian nations confesses God, not in synagogues but in the Churches of Christ. And every tongue that confesses Christ will speak in the Lord, and will say: Mine are righteousnesses, and mine is the dominion, not the Jewish people's. To him all the nations will come, and those who formerly resisted his Gospel will be confounded; and all the seed of Israel will be justified and praised, whose preaching and most fertile sowing has borne the richest fruits throughout the whole world. Or, according to the Seventy, every tongue that swears by and confesses God will say that the righteousness and glory of the whole world comes to him, and that the Jews, who separate themselves from him, are confounded. But those who have sprung from the stock of the sons of Israel, and who have sprouted from the seed of the Apostles, and have believed in Christ, may they have righteousness and everlasting glory.

46:1-2

Bel is broken, Nebo is crushed: their idols are made over to beasts and cattle, your burdens with heavy weight even to weariness. They have wasted away and are crushed together: they could not save the one who carried them, and their soul shall go into captivity. LXX: Bel has fallen, Dagon is crushed: their graven images are made into beasts and cattle; you carry them bound together like a burden for one who labors, and faints, and hungers, and has no strength besides, who will not be able to save from war: but they themselves have been led captive. After the calling of the nations, and the election of believers from Israel, he testifies that the idols have collapsed. Bel has fallen, has fallen, or is broken: whom the Greeks call Belus, the Latins Saturn. So great was his worship among the ancients that they sacrificed to him not only human victims, captives and mortals of low birth, but even their own children. Nebo, too, is itself an idol, which means prophecy and divination, which he signifies fell silent throughout the whole world after the truth of the Gospel. Or, according to the Seventy, Dagon, which, however, is not found in the Hebrew. And it is the idol of Ascalon, of Gaza and of the other cities of the Philistines. And he passes from the particular to the general: Their idols are made over to beasts and cattle. Not that the idols of the Gentiles were exposed as prey to beasts and cattle: but that the religion of the nations consists in images of beasts and of brute animals, which above all in Egypt were consecrated to divine worship. Of which Virgil says (Aen. 8.698): Monsters of gods of every kind, and barking Anubis.

For most of their towns too have names from beasts and cattle: κυνῶν from dog, λέων from lion; θμοῦϊς, in the Egyptian tongue, from the he-goat; λύκων from wolf; to say nothing of the dreadful and horrible onion, and the noise of the puffed-up belly, which is the religion of Pelusium. These idols, he says, which cannot save those who carry them, are nothing else but burdens for the priests, weighing them down even to weariness. And when captivity comes, they are the first to be led captive, for the value of the metals of which they are made, and they cannot set free their own soul, or that of those who carry them. Not that dumb idols, which are without sensation, have a soul and some sense of pain; but that soul and members are spoken of καταχρηστικῶς in things that are without sense and members. Otherwise, too, we read in Proverbs: In the hand of the tongue are death and life. Or else this must be said: that the heaviest burden among the nations was the error of idolatry, which weighed its worshipers down to the earth, and could not save them, and made their souls captives of the devil and of demons.

46:1, 3ff.

Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, who are carried from my womb, who are borne from my matrix. Even to old age I myself, and even to gray hairs I will carry you: I have made, and I will bear: I will carry, and I will save. To whom have you likened me, and made me equal, and compared me, and made me like? You who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh silver on the scales, hiring a goldsmith to make a god: and they fall down and worship. They carry it on their shoulders, bearing it and setting it in its place, and it will stand, and will not move from its place. But when they cry to it, it will not hear: it will not save them from tribulation. LXX: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of Israel, who are carried from the womb, and are instructed from a little child even to old age. I am, and until you grow old I am: I sustain you: I have made, and I will carry: I will take you up, and I will save you. To whom have you likened me? See, consider, you who err and lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver on the scales, and hire a goldsmith: they have made the works of their hands, and bowing down they have worshiped: they carry it on their shoulders, and go. But if they set it in its place, it stays, and will not move: and whoever cries to it, it will not hear him, and will not deliver him from evils. He by no means calls him Jacob, nor Israel, which itself, we explained above, is said in reproach of the people when it is without the addition of servant, and child, and chosen: but, much more meanly, house of Jacob, and remnant of Israel, because of the nearness of flesh and blood, and as it were the dregs of the remnant of Israel. And he teaches them that they were carried by God out of Egypt like children and sucklings, as it were from a mother's womb and the matrix of one with child. Not that the ineffable and incomprehensible majesty of God has either a womb or a matrix, or feet and hands and the other members of the body; but that we may learn God's affection through our own words. Otherwise, in Psalm 109 (110) too, this same thing is sung in the person of God. For in the place where the Seventy translated, from the womb before the morning star I begot you, the Hebrew has written MEREHEM מרחם, which means from the matrix. But in the present passage it is written not only from the womb and from the matrix, that is, MEBETEN מבטן and MEREHEM מרחם, but MENNI מני, a preposition which signifies from my womb, or from my matrix. And the sense is: I who begot you from infancy, and bore you in my womb and matrix, will myself protect you even to old age, not mine but yours; so as to teach them that they are to be saved by the divine mercy. For the Creator of all spares his creature, and the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John 10). But he who is a hireling, whose own the sheep are not, flees when he sees the wolf. Since, then, I made and begot children, I will bear them and I myself will carry them. According to the Seventy, who said: Who are carried from the womb, and are instructed from infancy even to old age, this signifies that they meditate on the law of God day and night in vain, having no knowledge of God, but venerating images of men and beasts: so much so that they need prophetic rebuke, through which God speaks to them: To whom have you likened me, and made me equal? and the rest: that they lavished gold and silver, and, hiring a sculptor, made idols, and worshiped the works of their own hands, which are carried on shoulders, and, fixed and set firm, cannot move themselves, nor profit those by whom they are worshiped. We pass quickly over what is plain, so that by the mercy of Christ we may unlock what is closed.

46:8ff.

Remember this, and be grounded, and return, transgressors, to heart. Recall the former age, for I am God, and there is no God beyond, nor is there any like me. Declaring from the start the last things, and from the beginning things not yet done, saying: My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done. Calling a bird from the East, and from a far land the man of my will; and I have spoken, and I will bring it about; I have created, and I will do it. LXX: Remember these things, and groan: repent, you who err. Return in heart, and remember the former things from of old; for I am God, and there is no other besides me. I who declare beforehand the last things before they happen and are fulfilled, and I have said, all my will shall stand, and all that I have planned I will do. I who call a bird from the East, and from a far land, those concerning whom I have planned: I have spoken, and I have brought it about: I have created and I have done it. Because I myself begot you, I myself carried you, and from infancy even to old age you are saved not by your merit but by my compassion: forsake the idols you have made, and return to the worship of the one God. Repent, groan for the error that held you; nay, be grounded, lest the sudden whirlwind of idolatry overturn you again: and return to heart, that is, to your mind, you who, venerating images, dashed yourselves like madmen against wood and stones. Consider from the beginning of the world that there is no God besides me, and that no other could know things to come, except me, who announce through the Prophets what I am going to do: so that, when I have fulfilled what was foretold, I may prove my divinity by divination. For I now say that the mystery which in times past was unknown to all generations, or rather my counsel, will stand; so that, when you see it brought to pass, you may know no God but him who knew that these things would be, nay, commanded them to be done. I am he who calls a bird from the East: as the Hebrews think, Cyrus king of the Persians, or Darius prince of the Medes; and from a far land the man of my will, to fulfill all my will against Babylon and the Chaldeans. Or, as we prove to be true, the Lord Savior, of whom Balaam too prophesies: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man out of Israel (Num 24:17), whose name is the East (Zech 6), whom the Magi coming from the East worshiped. For he it is who speaks in the Psalms: O God, I have willed to do your will (Ps 39 [40]:9), of whom the Father spoke: and he proved his pledge by deed. In place of what we have rendered from the Hebrew, the man of my will, the Seventy put, those concerning whom I have planned. According to them, then, by the birds called from the East we can understand the ministries of the angels, which run to and fro through the whole world at the Lord's command; who are ministering spirits, and are sent for the salvation of believers. Of whom it is also sung in the psalm: You who make your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire (Ps 103 [104]:4).

46:12-13

Hear me, you hard of heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness near: it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not delay: I will give salvation in Zion, and in Israel my glory. LXX: Hear me, you who have lost heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought near my righteousness, and the salvation that is from me I will not make to tarry. I have given salvation in Zion, and to Israel glory. Those to whom he had said above: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, and again: Return, transgressors, to heart, even now he calls, according to the Hebrew, hard of heart because of their unbelief, and, according to the Seventy, men who have lost heart and mind. Following this, the most learned man Stephen the martyr, worthy of his name, says in the assembly of the Jews: Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did (Acts 7:51). These, then, are far from the righteousness of God, because they did not believe in it; which God, in his clemency, made to be near, and wishes by no means to tarry or to be far off in coming to the earth. For he has given Zion his salvation, and Israel his glory. Let this be said of the prophecy of things to come, and of the coming of the Lord Savior. But according to the history, salvation is given to Zion, and glory to Israel, because God made his righteousness to be near, so that he called a bird from the East, and from a far land the man of his will, to avenge the wrongs of Israel and of overthrown Jerusalem, and, with the Medes and Persians victorious, to destroy Babylon and the Chaldeans, as the following words of the Prophet testify.

47:1ff.

Go down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon: sit on the ground, there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for no more shall you be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, and grind meal: lay bare your shame, uncover your shoulder, reveal your legs, pass over the rivers. Your disgrace shall be revealed, and your reproach shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and no man shall withstand me. LXX: Go down, sit upon the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for no more at all shall you be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, grind meal. Reveal your covering, lay bare your gray hairs, uncover your shins, pass over the rivers: your disgrace shall be revealed, your reproaches shall appear. What is just I will take from you, no more at all will I hand you over to men. As in Ezekiel the adornment of Tyre, which is given over to trading, is set forth under the figure of a ship and all its equipment (Ezek 26), and the king of Egypt, because of the abundance of waters, is called a dragon, and his scales, and the rush and papyrus and little fishes are described, and the likeness of harlots and of a brothel bears witness to Jerusalem's fornication with idols: so in the present passage the servitude of Babylon is shown under the person of a captive woman who was once a queen: and she is told to come down from the pride of her kingdom and sit in the dust. And she is called a virgin and a daughter: either because all of us men are God's creation, and Babylon is not, as the heretics hold, of a damnable nature; or because of the luxury and adornment of a city once most powerful, which, when she had grown old and was near her setting, boasted that she was a little virgin and a girl. Although from what is written according to the Seventy, daughter of Babylon, some interpret it not of Babylon itself but of the city of Rome, which in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 14) and in the Epistle of Peter (1 Pet 5) is specifically called Babylon, and they maintain that all that is now said to Babylon fits its ruin, against which the bird and the righteousness of God are to be called: so that, after Zion, that is, the Church, has been saved, she may perish for ever. It is said, then, to Babylon, queen and daughter of the Chaldeans (for she was founded by the Chaldeans), that she will no more at all be called soft and tender and overflowing with delights, she who was carried in the hands of all the nations, so that she scarcely pressed the soles of her feet to the ground: and she is commanded to take the millstone and grind meal, which is a sign of harsh captivity and the utmost servitude; so that she who was once a queen afterwards serves at the work of grinding meal. But because there follows: Lay bare your shame, the millstone too is understood figuratively by the Hebrews, namely that, after the manner of a harlot, she lies open to the lust of the victors. And what is written in the book of Judges about Samson (Judg 16), that he was condemned by the Philistines to the mill, they wish to signify this: that, being the strongest of men, he was compelled, for the sake of offspring, to do this with foreign women. In the place where we have translated, lay bare your shame, for which the Seventy translated, reveal your covering, Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, SAMTHECH (צמתך); Aquila SEMMATHECH; Symmachus τὸ σιωπηλόν σου: which we can express as your silent part, because it ought to be kept silent for modesty. This indeed we also read in the Song of Songs, where the beauty of the bride is described: at the end he adds: Apart from your silent part (Song 4): the translators being unwilling to render a word which in holy Scripture would sound shameful. And rightly he uses immodest names against Babylon (though there is nothing shameful in calling a member of the human body by its own name), she who is commanded to bare her breasts, and to uncover her legs and thighs, and to go into captivity, and to have her disgrace seen, and to lie open to everlasting reproach. And the Lord says he has done this to take vengeance on her who oppressed his people, and that he will hear no intercessor on her behalf who might try to soften the Lord's anger by coming before him. And he means the angel who presides over the Babylonian nation, who says with the other angels: We have cared for Babylon, and she is not healed. And as for what the Seventy translated, what is just I will take from you, no more at all will I hand you over to men, Babylon is understood: or certainly, that which is just, and taken away from Babylon. The Stoics argue that many things shameful in reality are, by the depraved custom of men, decent in words, such as parricide, adultery, homicide, incest, and other things like these. And again, that things decent in reality seem shameful in their names, such as begetting children, relieving the swelling of the belly by breaking wind, easing the bowels of excrement, loosing the bladder by pouring out urine: and finally, that we cannot, as from ruta we say rutula, so make a ὑποκοριστικὸν of menta. Therefore SEMMATHEC (צמתך), which Aquila put, as we have said, is the name for the private parts of a woman. Its etymology among them sounds your thirsty one; so as to show the insatiable lust of Babylon.

47:4ff.

Our Redeemer, the Lord of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel. Sit silent, and go into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans; for no more shall you be called mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people, I defiled my inheritance, and I gave them into your hand: you showed them no mercies. Upon the old man you made your yoke exceedingly heavy, and you said, For ever I shall be mistress: you did not lay these things to heart, nor did you remember your latter end. LXX: He who delivered you has said, the Lord Sabaoth, his name is the Holy One of Israel. Sit pierced with grief, enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans: no more at all shall you be called the strength of the kingdom: I was angry against my people, I defiled my inheritance. I gave them into your hand, but you gave them no mercy: on the old man you made the yoke exceedingly heavy, and you said, For ever I shall be mistress: you did not understand these things in your heart, nor did you remember the last things. According to the Seventy, the first verse is joined to what precedes, so that the sense is: And these things will he do who delivered you, the Lord Sabaoth, his name is the Holy One of Israel. But according to the Hebrew, the Prophet speaks in the person of the people, saying that the Lord of hosts, whose name is the Holy One of Israel, has done these things against Babylon. And again the discourse is directed to Babylon itself. Sit silent, or pierced with grief, and remember your crimes. Enter into darkness: because for confusion and disgrace you cannot bear the light: no more at all shall you be called mistress, not of one kingdom, nor even of all kingdoms. And at the same time, because a hidden question arose, why God should be angry against the Chaldeans whom he himself had sent to take Israel, he answered that, being angry against his people, he had wished to chastise them, not to destroy them; to scourge them, not to kill them. But they had given free rein to their own cruelty, and had laid on more stripes than God's vengeance demanded: and it is a great sign of Babylonian cruelty that they did not spare even old men, whose age is venerable even among enemies. And this too is a sign of pride, that, deceived by present prosperity, she did not consider the uncertainties of the future. We ought therefore always, in prosperity, to beware of what is to come, and not to oppress those handed over to us, who are being instructed for this purpose, that they may become better.

47:8ff.

And now hear these things, you delicate one, who dwell confidently, who say in your heart: I am, and there is none besides me any more: I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know barrenness. And these two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day, barrenness and widowhood: all things have come upon you, because of the multitude of your sorceries, and because of the hardness of your enchanters, exceedingly. And you trusted in your wickedness, and you said: There is none who sees me: your wisdom and your knowledge, these have deceived you, and you said in your heart: I am, and besides me there is no other. Evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its rising, and calamity shall rush upon you which you shall not be able to expiate, misery shall come upon you suddenly which you shall not know. Two things will come upon Babylon together, barrenness and widowhood, so that she has neither sons, that is, peoples subject to her, nor a husband, whom we can understand as the king: which she suddenly endured while she did not expect them. For she could not suppose that the Persians, of no strength before, would, in the reign of Cyrus, overcome her and subject her to their power. What you have suffered, he says, is not only because of your pride and the abundance of all wealth and your delights, but also because of the multitude of your sorceries, and of your enchanters, in whom you trusted. And evil shall come upon you which you did not know before, and whose rising you did not know. Or, as the Seventy translated: Destruction shall come upon you, and you shall not know it: a pit, and you shall fall into it: so that you who were preparing the evil of captivity for all the nations may yourself fall into the pit that you prepared. What is plain we pass over in brief speech.

47:12ff.

Stand with your enchanters, and with the multitude of your sorceries, in which you have labored from your youth, if perhaps anything may profit you, or if you can become stronger. You have failed in the multitude of your counsels: let the augurs of the heaven stand and save you, who gazed at the stars and reckoned the months, that from them they might announce to you things to come. Behold, they have become as stubble, fire has burned them: they shall not deliver their souls from the hand of the flame: there are no coals to warm them, nor a hearth to sit by: so have they become to you, all those things in which you had labored: your traders from your youth have gone astray, each in his own way: there is none to save you. LXX: Stand now in your enchantments and in your many sorceries, which you learned from your youth, if they can profit you: and you have labored in your counsels: let the astrologers of the heaven, who gaze at the stars, stand and save you: let them announce to you what is to come upon you. Behold, they shall all be burned as brushwood in the fire: and they shall not rescue their soul from the flame; because you have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them. These shall be a help to you. You have labored in your exchange from your youth: man has gone astray in himself: but for you there shall be no salvation. That Babylon and all Chaldea pursued the arts of enchanters and augurs, and soothsayers and Gazarenes, whom we call haruspices, is proved by the reading of Daniel the Prophet, who records that the kings of Babylon did everything on their counsel. And in place of what we have translated, following Symmachus and Theodotion: Let the augurs of the heaven stand and save you, the Seventy translated more plainly, Let the astrologers of the heaven stand and save you; who are commonly called mathematicians, and think that human affairs are ruled by the course of the stars and the motion of the heavenly bodies. Hence the Magi too came from the East, saying they had seen the Lord's star, either from the knowledge of their art, or from the prophecy of Balaam, their own Prophet, who had said in Numbers: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man from Israel (Num 24:17). Let these, then, who reckon the months and count up the years, and, weighing the moments of the hours, promise knowledge of the future, tell you what the Lord has planned against you; and, since they are silent about what is to come, the Prophet answered: Behold, they have become as stubble, fire has devoured them; so that those who promised salvation to others did not know their own punishments: and there is no doubt that, when the city was burning, the devouring flame consumed its inhabitants. And what follows: There are no coals to warm them, nor a hearth to sit by, the Hebrews explain thus: They have no knowledge of warmth, nor an enlightening sense that could dispel their darkness and drive out the cold of error. For which the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated: You have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them: these shall be a help to you; unless perhaps we can say this, that fire and burning are much more useful to Babylon than the magi and Gazarenes, the astrologers and enchanters, were. For the one calls them to repentance through penalties and punishments; the others lead them through error to pride. All her labor and her traders, whom we understand as the magi, achieved this: that each went astray in his own way; and, himself lost, could not offer salvation to another. Let us ask those who assert that there are different natures whether Babylon is of an evil nature or a good one. If they say of an evil one, which there is no doubt they will answer, how is she called to repentance, and told: Sit pierced with grief, enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans? And then, after the enumeration of her sins and crimes: You have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them: these shall be a help to you? And what is meant by what is added according to the same Seventy: You have labored in exchange from your youth? What is this exchange? Surely from good to evil. From which it is plain that men are good by nature, and become evil by will. Finally it is added: Man has gone astray in himself, not by nature, but by the choice of the mind.

48:1ff.

Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come forth from the waters of Judah: who swore in the name of the Lord, and make mention of the God of Israel, not in truth nor in righteousness. For they are called after the holy city: and upon the Lord of Israel they are established: the Lord of hosts is his name. These things I foretold would come upon the Chaldeans and Babylonians, and what I have spoken through my Prophets must be fulfilled in deed. But you, house of Jacob, and you who are called by the name of Israel, and who have come forth from the water of Judah, and the rest that follows, hear more attentively what I am about to say. And it is to be noted that he by no means calls them Jacob, but the house of Jacob; nor Israel, since they are falsely called by this name, not having the work of the name. And from the waters, he says, of Judah you have come forth, σεμνοτερῶς calling it waters in place of seed, so as to show that they are by no means sons of the virtues of the Patriarchs, but of their flesh. And rightly he called them the waters of Judah, because that tribe alone was still then remaining in the land of Judea; and at that time the royal seed of David was being preserved. Who, he says, swore in the name of the Lord, not that you might honor the Lord; but that, having taken up his name, you might do him wrong, while you want him to be the witness of your lie, and you rest in the holy city, and lean upon the Lord of Israel; so that you may boast that you are inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, and have the privilege of the Lord Sabaoth, while you take up the empty names of Jacob, of Israel and of the holy city, and of the almighty God.

48:3-4ff.

The former things I declared from of old, and they went forth from my mouth, and I made them heard: suddenly I worked, and they came to pass. For I knew that you are hard, and your neck is a sinew of iron, and your brow is bronze. I foretold it to you from of old: before they came, I made it known to you, lest perhaps you should say: My idols have done these things, and my graven images and my molten images have commanded them. What you have heard, see it all: but you have not declared it. I have made you hear new things from that time: and things kept in store which you do not know: they are created now, and not from of old: and before the day, and you did not hear them, lest perhaps you should say: Behold, I knew them. You have neither heard, nor known, nor from of old was your ear opened: for I know that you will deal very treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb. For my name's sake I will put my fury far off: and with my praise I will bridle you, lest you perish. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver: I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty. For my own sake, for my own sake I will do it, that I be not blasphemed: and my glory I will not give to another. LXX: The former things I declared still: and they went forth from my mouth: and it was made heard: suddenly I did them, and they came to pass, I know that you are hard: and your neck is a sinew of iron, and your brow is bronze: and I declared it to you long ago, before they came upon you. I made it heard to you: lest perhaps you should say that idols have done it for me, that graven and molten images have commanded me. You have heard all things, and you have not known: but I have made you hear new things, those which are now to be. And you did not say, They are being done now, and not long ago: and not in former days. Do not say either, I knew them: you neither know, nor understand, nor from the beginning did I open your ears. For I know that you will deal very treacherously: and you will be called wicked even from the womb. For my name's sake I will show you my fury: and I will bring my glorious things upon you, that I may not kill you. Behold, I have sold you, not for silver: but I have rescued you from the furnace of poverty: for my own sake I will do it, because my name is profaned: and my glory I will not give to another. I foretell to you that the Babylonians are to be overcome by the Medes and Persians, and I will suddenly do what I have threatened, lest, when the things foretold have come, you should think they happened either by the nod of the gods you worship or by chance. Nor do I boast of knowledge of the future, but I speak because of your unbelief, you whose heart I knew from the beginning to be unbelieving, and your neck of iron, and your brow of bronze. Behold, you have heard all the things that are to come, and yet you hide the truth in silence. Nor do I recount the past things by which my power has often been proved: how I led the people out of Egypt, drowned the Egyptians in the Red Sea, handed over the land of promise, subjugated various nations to you. But I announce the new things that I am going to do against Babylon, so that the shameless lie of your mouth may be refuted, you who claim to know what you do not know. For from the beginning you have been a transgressor of my commandments; and God called you a transgressor from the womb, when, set free from Egypt, you were, as it were, conceived in my womb, and brought up, and instructed. You longed for the ox's head of Egypt, saying: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Not for your merit, then, but by my mercy I have put off my fury, lest you should perish utterly, and for the praise of my name I will bridle you, so that, like a beast of burden and a horse in bridles, you may follow me against your will. Behold, I have refined you, that is, I have tested you, as silver is smelted. Or, I wished to test you not in riches but in the furnace of poverty. From this it is shown that most men are tempted both by riches and by poverty, if they either badly abuse the former or by no means bear want with virtue. For my own sake, then, I will do it, lest my name be blasphemed among the nations, and they think that you were overcome not by my anger but by the help of their idols. And what he adds, my glory I will not give to another, signifies this: lest the idols be thought to have crushed the people of God. Or certainly, when he says, I will not give to another, he shows that he has already given it to another; for 'to another' is said to distinguish it from the former. Most of our writers, to touch briefly on a few things according to the Seventy Translators, hold that the coming of Christ is prophesied: that he comes suddenly, unhoped for, and shows his presence to a most hard people, whose ears God never opened, because its heart had grown fat, and it heard heavily with its ears. And that, as soon as the Lord was poured forth from the virginal womb, it was called transgressor and wicked, seeking to kill him. And as for what he joins: For my name's sake I will show you my fury, and my glorious things I will bring upon you, he draws on the sense of the Apostle, or rather the apostle Paul (Rom 1) takes his testimony from this passage, that the wrath of God is revealed to terrify those who sin, and afterwards glory is offered to those who have turned: Behold, he says, I have sold you, not for money, but I have sold you in your sins, and I have rescued you from the furnace of poverty. For which reason Solomon too (Prov 30) does not wish to have riches or poverty, but asks only for necessaries, lest either by the former his heart be lifted up into pride, or in the latter he be compelled to do what he does not wish and, pressed by want, to blaspheme God. Hence the Apostle too says: Having food and clothing, he says, let us be content with these (1 Tim 6:8).

48:12-13ff.

Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call. I myself, I am the first, and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens: I called them, and they will stand together. Gather together, all of you, and hear: who among them has declared these things? The Lord has loved him: he will do his will in Babylon, and his arm upon the Chaldeans. I, I have spoken and called him: I have brought him, and his way is made straight. Draw near to me, and hear these things: not from the beginning have I spoken in secret: from the time before it came to be, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit. LXX: Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am the first, and I am for ever: and my hand founded the earth, and my right hand made firm the heaven. I will call them, and they will stand together: and all will be gathered, and will hear: Who has announced these things to them? Loving you, I have done your will upon Babylon: to take away the seed of the Chaldeans. I have spoken and I have called. I have brought him and have made his way prosper. Bring them to me, and hear these things: Not from the beginning have I spoken in secret: when it was being done, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit. To those to whom he had already said before: Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come forth from the waters of Judah, he now speaks: Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. For many are called, and few chosen (Matt 22). Hence he names them not chosen, because they had not yet received the Savior; but called. I am, he says, α and ω, the first and the last, who live, and was dead (Rev 22); so that you may refer life to the first, and the last to him who died. Who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father; he humbled himself even to death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). My hand founded the earth. Hence in Proverbs too he says: God by his wisdom founded the earth, and his right hand measured (Prov 3:19), or made firm the heavens, or the heaven, as the Seventy translated. And he calls the heavens, that they may obey his command and tell forth his glory. But if the heavens obey the will of the Lord and run in their order, why does earth and ashes glory (Sir 10), and not know its own frailty? Gather together, all of you, and hear: either heavens, or the whole creation, or the whole multitude of Israel. What are the things they are bidden to hear? That the Lord has loved him: there is no doubt that he means Cyrus and Darius, who did the will of the Lord against Babylon, and exercised his arm upon the Chaldeans. And he himself spoke and called him by his name, and brought him, and his way was made straight, so that none dared to resist his might. Hence he summons them to draw near and hear, and, as the Lord foretells it, to know that the king of the Persians and Medes will come, to overthrow Babylon and destroy the Chaldeans. And to announce these things, the Prophet says that he has been sent by the Lord and by his spirit. This is according to the Hebrews and their opinion. But according to Symmachus, who translated: Who has announced these things to him? whom the Lord has loved, who does his will in Babylon: and according to the Seventy, to take away the seed of the Chaldeans, it is referred to the person of the Lord: who is truly beloved by the Father, and who did all the will of the Father, and who overthrew in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of this world, all the seed of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as demons. He himself spoke, and heard the Son, and brought him, who says to believers: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28). And hear these things which from the beginning I have spoken in secret, that is, through the riddles and mysteries of the Prophets, which had been unknown to all past generations. When all things were being made by the Father, he himself was with him, who rejoiced with him, who even now says: I, who was always with the Father, and in the Father, and was never without the Father, even now speak (John 14): and according to the frailty of the flesh I assumed, I say that the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit: and in one short verse the mystery of the Trinity is shown to us.

48:17-18ff.

Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the Lord your God, who teach you profitable things, who guide you in the way in which you walk. Would that you had heeded my commandments; your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the whirlpools of the sea. And your seed would have been like the sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles: they would not have perished, and his name would not have been worn away from before my face. Since he has promised Israel things to come, he gives the reasons why he afflicted them before: if they avoid these, they will by no means suffer the like. If, he says, you had heeded my commandments, as the Seventy translated: or certainly, with the feeling of one who wishes, would that you had heeded my commandments: if you had done them, your peace would have been like rivers, and your righteousness like the whirlpools of the sea: signifying abundance and plenty of all things. And as for what follows: and your seed would have been like the sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles: it seems indeed to hold good in the people of the Jews, who to this present day sprout sons and grandsons like little worms; but how is this to be taken as a promise, when they have neither peace nor righteousness? For either he is angry with them, or appeased. If angry, how is his seed multiplied daily? If appeased, how are they in servitude, and do not possess peace and righteousness? From this it is plain that he now speaks of the Apostolic seed, of which we also read above (cf. Isa 1): Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom. Since this is by no means seen fulfilled at that time, it is fulfilled in the coming of Christ: and the seed of Israel remains before his face.

48:20-22

Go forth from Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans: declare it with a voice of exultation, make this heard, carry it to the end of the earth, and say: The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob. They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out; he brought forth water from the rock for them, and he split the rock, and the waters flowed. There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord. Those who understood the place above, where it is written: I, I have spoken, and called him: I have brought him, and his way is made straight, of Cyrus and Darius, refer these things too to his times, when the people went forth from Babylon, and fled from the Chaldeans, and was redeemed by the Lord its God. This also that is said: They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out, he brought forth water from the rock for them; and he split the rock, and the waters flowed, although they cannot show it fulfilled according to the history (for under Zerubbabel and Ezra they did not come through a desert, nor did a split rock furnish them waters, as is related to have happened to those going out of Egypt), they nevertheless maintain was fulfilled hyperbolically, in the likeness of the former happiness, when they came into Judea through the desert of the nations, and were set free from captivity. And so that we may know, they say, that it was prophesied not of Christ but of Cyrus, there is joined: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord: and the sense is: Perfect happiness will not be except under Christ, which is reserved for the last time. But those who, more truly and more rightly, refer these things to the Savior's coming (cf. below, Isa 61:1), of which it is said: He has sent me to announce good news to the poor, to preach release to the captives (Luke 4:18, 19), understand it to be an exhortation of those who announce the Gospel of the Lord Savior himself, that we should go forth from Babylon, that is, from the confusion of this world, and flee the Chaldeans, of whom it has often been spoken. For the Lord redeemed his servant Jacob with his most precious blood, and led him through the desert of the world, and split water from the rock. Concerning which the Apostle too says: And the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). And the divine word is split, and divided into many parts, so that what we cannot receive whole we may take in parts. And lest this preaching should be thought to be spoken to all the seed of Jacob, and not only to those who were to believe through the Apostles, there is added and joined: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord: that is, to those who remained in their former error; who did not deserve to drink from the rock. Whose side, to speak in a new way, wounded by the lance, flowed with water and blood (John 19), consecrating for us baptism and martyrdom.

49:1ff.

Hear, islands, and give heed, peoples from afar: the Lord called me from the womb, from the belly of my mother he remembered my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword: in the shadow of his hand he protected me. And he made me like a chosen arrow: in his quiver he hid me; and he said to me: You are my servant, Israel, for in you I will glory. And I said: I have labored in vain, without cause and vainly I have spent my strength: therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God. LXX: Hear me, islands, and give heed, nations. After a long time it shall stand, says the Lord. From the belly he called me, and from the womb of my mother he called my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword, and under the protection of his hand he hid me. He made me like a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me. And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel: and in you I will be glorified. And I said, I have labored without cause, in vain, and I have given my strength for nothing. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my labor before my God. I know that both these things and those further on that we are going to speak of belong to the knowledge or understanding of a single chapter, and that all must be taken in the person of Christ. But I did not wish, by setting everything out together, to burden the reader's mind, and to confound by its magnitude what can more easily be said in parts. Hence I have also set down both editions, so that what seems obscure in the one may be unlocked by the reading of the other. After the calling of the remnant of Israel, then, and the casting off of the people that remained in unbelief, of whom he had said: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord (Isa 48:22), he passes over to the Churches gathered from the nations, and speaks to them under the name of islands. These lie open to the ambushes of persecutors as to the waves of the sea, and, with shipwreck raging on every side, are beaten rather than moved. And lest anyone think that our exposition is forced, and that what is said belongs not to the nations but to the Synagogues of the Jewish people, there follows: And give heed, peoples, or nations, from afar, that is, from the furthest ends of the earth. Or, as the Seventy translated, after a long time it shall stand, that is, not at this time in which they are spoken; but they will come to pass after many times. The Lord, he says, called me from the womb, and from the belly of my mother he remembered my name. Which for the present seems obscure to the hearers, but afterwards will become known to all the nations, when Gabriel will have said to Joseph of the virgin birth: And you shall call his name Jesus: for he will save his people (Matt 1:21). He also made his mouth like a sharp sword, so that with the spirit of his mouth he may slay the wicked one. Of which sword he himself also speaks in the Gospel: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword, separating the evil from the good: For I came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (Matt 10:34, 35). And in the shadow, he says, of his hand he protected me, so that the lowliness of the flesh might be covered by the power of the divinity, as the angel announced to the Virgin: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35). He made me, he says, like a chosen arrow, in his quiver he hid me. When he says, a chosen arrow, he shows that God has very many arrows, but not chosen ones: which arrows are the Prophets and the Apostles, who run through the whole world. Of whom it is sung in another place too: Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty; peoples will fall beneath you (Ps 44 [45]:6); and again: The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals (Ps 119 [120]:4). But Christ, out of many arrows and very many sons, is the one chosen arrow, and the Only-begotten Son: whom he hid in his quiver, that is, in a human body, so that the fullness of the divinity might dwell in him bodily. And rare is the faith of believers: to whom it is also said above (Isa 45:15): You are a hidden God, and we did not know it. Receiving a wound from this arrow, the bride too speaks in the Song of Songs: I am wounded with love. And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel: for in you I will be glorified (Song 4:9). A servant, because, though he was in the form of God, he deigned to take the form of a servant (Phil 2), and Israel, because he was born of the seed of the Jews. And, what can be understood of no other of the servants, there is joined: For in you I will glory. For he himself also says in the Gospel, Father, glorify your name (John 12:28). He it is who in the psalm says to the Son: Arise, my glory, and arise, psaltery and harp (Ps 56 [57]:9), that is, the choir of all the virtues. And when the Father said to me these things that I have related, I answered him: How are you glorified in me, Father, since I have labored in vain, and could not call back to you a great part of the Jewish people? And all these things are said to show the free will of man. For it is God's to call, and ours to believe: nor, if we do not believe, is God at once powerless; but he leaves his power to our choice, so that the will of the righteous may obtain its reward. Since, then, they would not believe in you through me, my judgment is with you, that I have done all things that I ought to have done for them, saying in the Gospel: I have glorified you on the earth, having completed the work which you gave me to do (John 17:4); and again: I have manifested your name to men. And my work, or my labor and pain (for this is what πόνος signifies), is in your sight. For in the Gospel too he wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19), and in the psalm, because of the multitude of unbelievers, he says that in a certain way he suffered in vain: What profit is there in my blood, while I go down to corruption (Ps 29 [30]:10)? And according to the Hebrew, hanging on the cross, he says: Far from my salvation are the words of my lamentations (Ps 21 [22]:1).

49:5-6ff.

And now says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I might bring Jacob back to him, and Israel will not be gathered: and I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and my God has become my strength. And he said: It is a small thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light of the nations; that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth. LXX: And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I might gather Jacob to him, and Israel: I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord, and my God shall be my strength. And he said to me: It is a great thing for you to be called my child, and to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back the dispersion of Israel. Behold, I have set you for a covenant of the race, for a light of the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth. When I said, I have labored in vain, without cause and vainly I have spent my strength, because the Jews would not believe, and my judgment is with the Lord, and my work, which with his help I have fulfilled, is with the Lord: the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, answered me.
