By this he shows that he is called servant who was formed from the womb. He also says in the psalm: From the belly of my mother you are my God (Ps 21 [22]:11). What, then, does the Lord say to him? That he should bring back to him Jacob, who had wandered off, who, having forsaken his Creator, was serving idols. Hence he himself says to the disciples: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:5); and in another place: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). This, then, was the will of the Father: that the wicked vinedressers should receive the Son who was sent, and render the fruits of the vineyard; but they killed him, saying: Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt 21:38); and this is what he now says: And Israel will not be gathered, that is, will not return to the Lord. And I greatly wonder how the common edition has overturned, by a different interpretation, a very strong testimony against the faithlessness of the Jews, saying: I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord: since Theodotion and Symmachus agree with our interpretation. About Aquila, however, I do not wonder, that a man most learned in the Hebrew language, and rendering word for word, has in this place either feigned ignorance or been deceived by the perverse exposition of the Pharisees, since he chose to translate, and Israel will be gathered to him, that is, to God. For the Hebrew word LO in this place is not written with LAMED and VAV (לו), which, if it were, would signify to him or to that one, but with LAMED and ALEPH (לא), which properly sounds not. Since, then, Jacob was not brought back to God, nor Israel gathered, therefore, since they did not believe, the Son says: I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord. For in me the whole world has believed: and my God has become my strength, who also comforted me in my sadness over the casting off of my people; and said to me: It is a small thing if you serve me to raise up the tribes of Jacob, which fell through their own fault; and to turn back the dregs, or remnant, of Israel. For this is what the Hebrew word NESURE (נצורי) sounds. For in their place I have given you as a light of all the nations, to illumine the whole world, and to make my salvation, through which all are saved, reach to the ends of the earth. And what is read in the Seventy, I shall be gathered, and glorified before the Lord, can be understood thus: that the Lord has been gathered together with the believers. And as for what follows: He said to me: It is a great thing for you to be called my child, let us refer 'great' to the man and to the child, who is small in comparison with God.

49:7

Thus says the Lord, the redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to the contemptible soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of lords. Kings shall see, and princes shall rise up, and they shall worship for the Lord's sake, for he is faithful: and the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you. LXX: Thus says the Lord who delivered you, the God of Israel. Sanctify him who despises his own soul, who is an abomination to the nations, who is the servant of princes. Kings shall see him, and princes shall rise up, and they shall worship him for the Lord's sake: for the Holy One of Israel is faithful, and he has chosen you. In place of what we have said: to the contemptible soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of lords, Theodotion translated: to him who despises his soul, who is an abomination to the nation, who is the servant of princes: which plainly fits the person of Christ. For he, the good shepherd, laid down his soul for his sheep (John 10), and despised it, he who is an abomination to the nation of the Jews, who curse him three times every day in their synagogues under the name of the Nazarenes. He was the servant of princes, and so humble that he stood before Annas and Caiaphas, and was sent to Pilate and Herod to be crucified. With this interpretation Aquila agreed, and in part the Seventy, although they changed and weakened the sense in this, that for nation they translated nations, and for servant servants. Others, however, think that this is said to the nation of the Jews, which despised its own soul, and is an abomination to the whole world, and serves princes, of whom it is written: Who devour my people as they eat bread (Ps 13 [14]:4). But the interpretation concerning Christ is better. What, then, does the Father, once the redeemer and the Holy One of Israel, say to the Son? Kings shall see, and princes shall rise up, and they shall worship, when he comes in the glory of the Father with his angels, and sits on the throne of his glory, judging the living and the dead: then all will worship him for the sake of the Lord his Father, who chose him. Or it is to be understood thus: Kings, whose heart is in the hand of God, and the princes of the Church of God, will worship you: for the Lord is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you. And all these things he refers to him who despised his own soul, who is abhorred by the nation, who is the servant of princes.

49:8ff.

Thus says the Lord: In a pleasing time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. And I have kept you, and given you as a covenant of the people, that you might raise up the land, and possess the scattered inheritances: that you might say to those who are bound: Go forth; and to those who are in darkness: Be revealed. In the ways they shall feed, and in all the plains shall be their pastures. They shall not hunger nor thirst, and the heat and the sun shall not strike them: for he who has compassion on them shall rule them, and shall give them drink at the springs of waters. And I will make all my mountains a way, and my paths shall be raised up. Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, those from the North and the sea, and these from the land of the South. Praise, O heavens, and exult, O earth: shout praise for joy, O mountains, for the Lord has comforted his people, and will have mercy on his poor. LXX: Thus says the Lord: In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. And I have formed you, and given you as a covenant of the nations, that you might establish the land, and possess the deserted inheritances. And that you might say to those who are in bonds, Go forth, and to those who are in darkness, Be revealed: in all the ways they shall feed, and in all the paths shall be their pastures. They shall not hunger nor thirst, nor shall the heat nor the sun strike them; but he who has mercy on them shall comfort them, and shall lead them by the springs of waters. And I will make every mountain a way, and every path a pasture for them. Behold, these shall come from afar, these from the North and the sea: and others from the land of the Persians. Rejoice, O heavens, and let the earth exult, let the mountains break forth into gladness: for God has had mercy on his people, and has comforted the lowly of his people. The Apostle Paul used this testimony in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: In an acceptable time I have heard you: and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time, etc. (2 Cor 6:2). If, then, the vessel of election refers what is said to the understanding of the first coming, let us too follow the footsteps of his exposition, and, like little children, press our letters upon the lines our teacher has traced. The pleasing and acceptable time, and the day of salvation, is the passion and resurrection of the Savior, when he prayed on the cross: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matt 27:46)? And he kept him, or formed him, when death had been overcome, and gave him as a covenant of the people of the Jews, that is, of those among them who were willing to believe: that he might raise up the land, which lay in the errors of idolatry, and possess the scattered, or deserted, inheritances, which did not have God as their inhabitant, and might say to those who were in bonds, Go forth, those who were held fast by the bonds of sins, since each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5); and to those who were in darkness, Be revealed: those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, and could not see the light. And after they have been converted, and have beheld the clear light of Christ, they shall feed in the ways and in the paths of the holy Scriptures, and shall say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture there he has set me: he has brought me up beside the waters of refreshment (Ps 22 [23]:2). And he who has been fed and nourished in such ways and paths shall neither hunger nor thirst, nor feel the heat of the sun: and in him what is written will be fulfilled: The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6). So that he feels neither the adversities nor the prosperities of this world. Since the Lord is merciful and compassionate, he himself will comfort them and rule them, and lead them to the springs of waters. Or, he will give them drink at the springs, of which it is written: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). And in another place: Draw waters from the springs of the Savior (Isa 12:3). These springs are in the Old Testament and the New. And all the stumbling-blocks that could hinder the steps of believers the Lord will turn into level ground for them, and he will bring low the high places and raise up the low, that they may have a level and open road. And who these are for whom the way is prepared, he sets out more plainly: Behold, these shall come from afar: and behold, those from the North and the sea, and these from the land of the South. Showing the four regions of the world, East and North, West and South, he put afar for the East: for the southern region, in the Hebrew is read SINIM (סינים), which the Seventy translated of the Persians. The rest expressed it as it is read in the Hebrew, sinim, which we have translated from the South: suspecting this, that Mount Sinai is situated in the southern part, according to the Prophet Habakkuk: God will come from the South, and the holy one from Mount Paran, shady and thick (Hab 3). But if by sinim, as the Seventy translated, we understand the Persians, who are situated toward the East, we shall be able to refer what is said above, Behold, these shall come from afar, to the South. And the heavens and the earth are commanded, either the powers that dwell in heaven and on earth, or angels and men, to sing together the praises of God. And those who are set on the height of the virtues are to testify to the gladness of their mind with jubilation and exultation. For the Lord has comforted his people, those of the Jews who were willing to believe. And he has had mercy on his poor and lowly ones: or on all his people, who were called to him from East and West, North and South, having neither Law nor Prophets nor spiritual riches, but, deserted, poor and lowly, lay subject to all the demons.

49:14ff.

And Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me. Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity on the son of her womb? And if she should forget, I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on my hands: your walls are always before my eyes. Your builders have come: and those who destroyed you and scattered you shall go forth from you. Lift up your eyes round about, and see, all these are gathered together, they have come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them about you like a bride, for your deserts and your solitudes, and the land of your ruin, shall now be too narrow for the inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up shall be chased far away. Still they shall say in your ears, the sons of your barrenness: The place is too narrow for me, make room for me to dwell. And you shall say in your heart: Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and not bearing, carried away and captive: and who has brought these up? I was left destitute and alone: and these, where were they? LXX: But Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me. Will a woman forget her little one, so as not to have pity on the offspring of her womb? But if a woman should forget even these, yet I will not forget you, says the Lord. Behold, upon my hands I have painted your walls: and you are always before me. And quickly you shall be built by those by whom you had been destroyed: and those who scattered you shall go forth from you. Lift up your eyes round about, and see: all these are gathered together, they have come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them about you like a bride's necklace: for your deserts, and the places that were scattered, and those that fell down. Now you shall be straitened because of the inhabitants: and those who had humbled you shall be far from you. For your sons, whom you lost, shall say in your ears: The place is too narrow for me: make me a place to dwell. And you shall say in your heart: Who has begotten these for me? But I was childless and a widow, and who has brought these up for me? I was left alone, and these, where were they? We have often recalled that Jerusalem and Zion are to be understood in four ways in the holy Scriptures. In one way, according to the Jews, the city over which the Lord laments in the Gospel: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets, and stone those who are sent to you (Matt 23:37). And in another place: When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near (Luke 21:20). Second, it is the congregation of the Saints, who, set in the peace of the Lord and on the watchtower of the virtues, are rightly called Zion, of which it is said: Its foundations are on the holy mountains: the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:1). For neither were the foundations of the Jewish Zion, which we see destroyed, loved by the Lord, nor could what is loved by the Lord be destroyed. Third, the multitude of the Angels, Dominions and Powers, and all that is appointed to the ministry of God, is called Jerusalem. Of this Jerusalem the Apostle too was speaking: But the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all (Gal 4:26). And in another place: But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22). Fourth, that is called Jerusalem which the Jews, and our own Judaizers, following the Apocalypse of John, which they do not understand, think is to be set down from heaven, golden and jeweled (Rev 21), whose bounds and boundless breadth they think are described also in the last part of Ezekiel. Since these things are so, we must now consider more carefully which of the four Zions has said: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me. And there is no doubt that it is the congregation of the Saints, which formerly was among the Jews and has been forsaken by the Lord, that recalls these things, and complains with a tearful voice that it has been deserted and left destitute of the Lord's help. To it God answered, using a likeness from nature: If it can happen that a mother forgets her infant, and is not moved by pity toward the offspring of her own womb, then I too will forget you. I will say something more: even if she should forget, overcoming the laws of nature by hardness of mind, yet I will not forget my creature, and I will always hold the souls of the Saints in my heart. For know, you who think yourself utterly forsaken, that you are engraved and painted on my hands, and that your walls remain continually before my eyes. From this we learn that Jerusalem is by no means to be sought in the region of Palestine, which is the worst of the whole province, and rough with rocky mountains, and suffers a dearth of water, so that it uses the rains of heaven, and consoles the scarcity of springs by the construction of cisterns; but in the hands of God, to whom it is said: Your builders have hastened. Or, according to the Seventy: Quickly you shall be built by those by whom you had been destroyed. For destroyed by the Jews, it was built by the Jews. Deserted because of the guilt of the Scribes and Pharisees, it was gathered together at the preaching of the Apostles of Christ, both from the Jews and from the nations. There follows: And those who destroyed you and scattered you shall go forth from you: the most wicked teachers; so that you may by no means follow the commandments and traditions of men (Matt 15), but the law of God. And she is told to lift up her eyes round about, and see the sons who had been gathered to her. Of whom the Lord too spoke: Lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are already white for harvest (John 4:35). And to make us secure: As I live, says the Lord (which, according to the Old Testament, is said by the custom of swearing), you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them about you, as a bride puts a necklace about herself. Happy is he who is of such merit and such virtue that he is called an ornament of the Church. I think, moreover, that these signify the various spiritual graces by which the bride's array is adorned. Of her too it is sung in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety (Ps 44 [45]:10). For what had before been deserted, and had fallen into solitudes and ruins, will, at the coming of the Gospel of Christ, be restored, and will have so great a multitude of inhabitants that it cannot hold them. Provided only that the persecutors be chased far away, or those of whom we spoke above: Those who destroyed you and scattered you shall go forth from you. And the sons of your barrenness, whom you thought you had utterly lost, and by them to have been widowed, shall say in your ears: The place is too narrow for me in the synagogues, make room for me in the Churches, to dwell more widely, so that I may not be crushed by the blasphemies of the Jews, so that your breadth may hold the whole world together with me. But you, unable to utter with your mouth the greatness of your joy, will ponder silently in your heart, and will say: Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and a widow, deserted and captive among the people of the Jews; I had ceased to have sons; for a long time I had not given birth. After Haggai and Zechariah and Malachi I had seen no other Prophets until John the Baptist; and how is it that I, who had been alone and destitute of a husband's help, have now begun to have so many sons? And so that we may know that Zion is built from both peoples upon the rock and foundation of Christ, Paul says to believers: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone. (Eph 2:20.) From this it is plain that the one foundation of the Apostles and Prophets is our Lord Jesus Christ.

49:22-23

Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and to the peoples I will raise up my standard: and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses. With face bowed to the ground they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet: and you shall know that I am the Lord, in whom those who wait for him shall not be confounded. LXX: Thus said the Lord God: Behold, I raise my hand over the nations, and over the islands I will lift up my standard, and they shall bring your sons in their bosom, and carry your daughters on their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers: and princesses your nurses: on the face of the earth they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, and those who wait for me shall not be confounded. To what the Church had said: I was barren and captive, who has begotten these for me? I was left destitute and alone, and these, where were they? the Lord answered: Do you wonder why these things have come about? You will by no means wonder when you hear that I have lifted up my hand to the nations. Of this hand the Saint too says: You have formed me, and laid your hand upon me (Ps 138 [139]:4). And the Savior himself: No one can snatch out of my Father's hand (John 10:29). And the Apostle Peter: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation (1 Pet 5:6). This hand lifted up to the nations is the very one of which this same Prophet speaks here: There shall be the root of Jesse, who shall rise up to be the prince of the nations: in him the nations shall hope (Isa 11:10). And not only will he lift up his hand to the nations; but he will also raise up his standard among the peoples. There is no doubt that this is the banner of the cross, so that what is written may be fulfilled: The earth is full of his praises. And again: In all the earth his name is wonderful (Ps 8:1). Then they shall bring the sons of Zion in their arms, or in their bosom, and carry her daughters upon their shoulders. Such too was Lazarus, and all the saints who rest in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16), and the souls of believers, to whom Paul the Apostle said: I gave you milk to drink (1 Cor 3:2). And elsewhere: My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). And in another place: As a nurse cherishes her children: so, longing for you, we desire to impart to you not only the Gospel of Christ, but also our own souls (1 Thess 2:8). Otherwise it is ridiculous, in the Jewish manner, for full-grown sons and daughters to be carried in arms and on shoulders. But the kings who are foster fathers, and the queens and princesses who are nurses, plainly point to the Apostles and to Apostolic men: such as Abraham too was, to whom it is said: You are a king from God among us (Gen 23:6); and whose heart is in the hand of God (Prov 21): who say to believers: As newborn babes, rational and without guile, desire milk (1 Pet 2:2). The princess also, that is, ἄρχουσα, which is the sound of Sarah's name, and the queens, or the queen, of whom it is sung in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, nourishes Christ's little ones daily, and leads them to perfect age: and every age, sex and rank will worship Zion for the sake of him who dwells in her. For if Christ is the head of the Church, the head is worshiped in the body. And if it is said to certain people: Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet (not that the footstool is to be worshiped; but that the majesty of his feet is indicated), why should not the Church be worshiped, which embraces the whole body of Christ, so that what is written in Zephaniah may be fulfilled: They shall worship him, each from his own place: all the islands of the nations (Zeph 2:11), so that they by no means come to Jerusalem three times a year in the Jewish manner, but, worshiping the Lord in their own place, possess Jerusalem. And as for what follows: and they shall lick the dust of your feet, this signifies that kings and princes, whatever of earthly work has clung to the feet of the Church, wipe and lick it away by their word. Hence the Apostles too are commanded to shake off the dust of their feet. And it is said to Peter that he who has once been washed needs only to wash his feet. (Matt 10; John 13). Through all these things the Church learns that there is no other Lord besides him, and those who have waited for him will possess eternal glory.

49:24ff.

Shall the prey be taken from the strong? or can what has been captured by the mighty be safe? For thus says the Lord: Indeed even the captivity shall be taken from the strong: and what has been carried off by the mighty shall be saved. But those who have judged you, I will judge: and your sons I will save. And I will feed your enemies with their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with new wine: and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who saves you, and your redeemer, the strong one of Jacob. LXX: Shall anyone take spoils from a giant? And if anyone leads a captive away unjustly, he shall be saved. Thus says the Lord: If anyone captures a giant, he shall take spoils, and he who takes from the strong shall be saved. But I will judge my judgment. And I will rescue my sons, and those who afflicted you shall eat their own flesh, and shall drink their own blood like new wine, and shall be drunk: and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who rescued you, and the help of the strength of Jacob. Our Lord and Savior, who had spoken earlier through Isaiah, himself repeats the same sense in the Gospel: how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his house (Mark 3)? The strong man and giant is the devil, who had subjugated all the nations to his rule, daring to say to the Savior: All these things have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matt 4:9). For the world lies in the evil one (1 John 5), and none of the righteous could conquer him: nor, according to Amos, take the prey from the lion's mouth (Amos 3). The question having been set, then, that no one could conquer the strong man and the giant, nor save what had been seized by him, the Lord answered that all would be accomplished by his coming: namely, that the nations formerly captured would be taken from the giant, and all his furniture and his whole household be divided among the Apostles. So is fulfilled what is written: The king of the powers of the beloved, and to the beauty of the house to divide the spoils. For he it is who, ascending on high, led captivity captive, he gave gifts among men (Ps 67 [68]:13, 19; Eph 4): that is, those who had formerly been taken captive unto death he received unto life. Hence Symmachus translated more plainly: But even the captivity of the strong one shall be taken away, and the plunder of the terrible one shall be safe. He wishes the strong and terrible one to be understood as the devil, who has been overcome by the power of the Lord. Therefore the Lord, judging those who had oppressed Zion, or judging her judgment, will set free her sons who had been captured by the giant, and will save them, and he will feed the adverse powers with their own flesh, and make them drunk as with new wine, so that they may be glutted not by the slaughter of others but by their own death. And those who are flesh, because they have lost the spirit of God, are to feed on their own flesh. This indeed the Saint also says in the Psalms: When those who afflicted me drew near to eat my flesh (Ps 26 [27]:2). For it is not the spirit, which is incorporeal, that is eaten, but the flesh, which lies open to the bites of fierce beasts. And then Zion will learn, nay, all flesh which will see the salvation of God, that her Redeemer and Savior is he who wrestled with Jacob, or who was the helper of the strength of Jacob: so that in his passion, lifted up on high, he blessed those who crucified him: Father, forgive them: for they do not know what they are doing (Luke 23:34).

50:1

Thus says the Lord: What is this bill of divorce of your mother, with which I put her away? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your crimes I put away your mother. For I came, and there was no man: I called, and there was none to hear. LXX: Thus says the Lord: What kind of bill of divorce of your mother is it, with which I put her away? Or to which creditor and exactor of mine did I sell you? Behold, for your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I put away your mother, for I came, and there was no human being: I called, and there was none to obey. After the calling of the nations, and the kings and princes, the foster fathers and nurses, and the captivity of the one formerly strong and mighty, whose prey has been distributed to the Apostles, and after the madness of the demons, who have been glutted with their own flesh and made drunk with their own blood, when all flesh has known that the Redeemer and the strong one is himself the God of Jacob, he speaks to the people of the Jews concerning Zion, who had said before: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me. Do you think that your mother, the earthly Jerusalem, has been cast off by my harshness, and that I, of an unbending mind, gave her a bill of divorce, and do you not rather understand, what is true, that she withdrew from me by her own fault? For when I said to her: Cease to act wickedly, learn to do good, she would not hear me; but turned against me a shoulder that drew away: hence I said to her sons: Woe to them, for they have withdrawn from me. Manifest are those who have acted wickedly against me. And to her herself: Your departure will instruct you, and your wickedness will rebuke you; and you will know that it is evil for you that you have forsaken me. But perhaps you cannot show a bill of divorce, and some creditor of mine, demanding money, while I had nothing to pay, takes you in compensation for the debt? It is not so: but I will show you why I have forsaken your mother with her sons. Your crimes and sins have sold you to the demons, so that, ensnared by the pleasures of the present age, both you forsook your parent and she her husband. Hence I could no longer keep your adulterous mother, but, as she wished to go, I let her. And that each one is sold by his own sins, since, left to our own choice, we are led by our will either to good or to evil, Paul the apostle also teaches: But I am carnal, sold under sin (Rom 7:14). For he who commits sin is the servant of sin (John 8). And as the avaricious and the robbers are servants of mammon, so every sin lords it over sinners. To whom it is said: Let not sin reign in your mortal body (Rom 6:12). And so that you may know that your mother was not repudiated by me, but withdrew by her own will, after many benefits I took a human body, and spoke no more through the Prophets, but in person. I came, and there was no man, or human being. For all, abandoning the image of man and of a human being, took on the images of beasts and serpents. Hence it is said to Herod because of his malice: Go and tell that fox (Luke 13:32). And to the Pharisees: Brood of vipers (Matt 23:33). And to the lustful: They have become horses mad after females (Jer 5:8). And of the pleasure-lovers: Do not cast your pearls before swine. And to the shameless: Nor give what is holy to dogs (Matt 7:6). And in common of them all: The vision of the four-footed beasts that were in the desert (Isa 30). The Lord therefore came, and did not find a man. For man, when he was in honor, did not understand: he was compared to senseless cattle, and became like them (Ps 48 [49]:13). I called them, he says, as a rational animal, and said: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth (Ps 77 [78]), and my people did not hear my voice. I cried out, and said: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). And in another place: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28). And there was none to hear; hence I said to them in the Gospel: You have neither seen the form of God, nor heard his voice, because you do not have his word abiding in you (John 5:37, 38).

50:2

Is my hand shortened, and made very small, so that it cannot redeem? Or is there no power in me to deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, I will turn the rivers into dry land: the fish shall rot for lack of water, they shall die of thirst. I will clothe the heavens with darkness, and make sackcloth their covering. LXX: Is my hand not able to deliver, or is it not strong enough to rescue? Behold, by my threat I will make the sea a desert, and make the rivers deserts, and their fish shall dry up, because there is no water, and they shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering as haircloth. Against those who thought that the Lord had not been able to free his people from captivity, he sets out a reason and the fullest examples: that he who made the Red Sea passable for his people (Exod 14), dried up the streams of the Jordan, and, when the rivers in Egypt dried up, turned the fish to rottenness (Exod 7), and who for three days in Egypt made a darkness that could be felt, so that the heaven seemed covered as with sackcloth and darkness, could surely also free his people from danger. Or, because he had said above: I came, and there was no human being: I called, and there was none to hear, we can say this: that he who is the performer of such great signs, and makes heaven and earth and the seas serve his nod, could also himself have escaped the cross, as he says in the Gospel: Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would give me at once more than twelve legions of angels (Matt 26:53)? According to the anagogy, at the rebuke of the Lord the sea becomes a desert when all the bitterness of this world is dried up, and the rivers are made desolate, of which the spiritual dragon in Egypt said: The rivers are mine, and I made them (Ezek 29:9). And of which we read in another place: What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers (Jer 2:18)? The fish too, when the net has been cast into the sea, shall rot, those which have been separated from the good fish. And as for what follows: I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and its covering shall be as haircloth, either let us understand by heaven all that is above us, as the birds which are in the air are called heavenly, and the adverse powers, which run to and fro between heaven and earth, are said to be heavenly. Or certainly the heaven is clothed with darkness when it is covered with clouds. According to what is written: Who covers the heaven with clouds, and gives rain to the earth (Ps 146 [147]:8). And in threatening drought God says: I will make the heaven bronze, and the earth iron (Deut 28:23). Not that the nature of the elements is changed, but that by bronze and iron the greatness of the punishments is shown. The philosophers say that the clouds are not raised up more than ten stadia from the earth, and hide the brightness of the sun. It is not, then, the heaven that is wrapped in sackcloth, but, the light of heaven being shut off, the air that is beneath is darkened by the darkness of the cloud. We can interpret the heavens wrapped in darkness and covered with sackcloth thus: that we say all are under sin, and that the saints too need the mercy of God.

Book Fourteen

The Lord who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, who touches the mountains and they shall smoke (Ps 103 [104]), who speaks in the song of Deuteronomy: I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal (Deut 32:39), has with frequent illnesses made my earth too tremble, the earth to which it was said: Earth you are, and into the earth you shall go (Gen 3:19). And when I forget the human condition, he often admonishes me to know that I am a man, and old, and on the very point of dying. Of this it is written: Why does earth and ashes glory (Sir 10:9)? Hence he who had struck me with a sudden sickness healed me with incredible speed, so as to frighten rather than afflict, and to correct rather than scourge. Therefore, knowing to whom all that I live belongs, and that perhaps my falling asleep is put off for this reason, that I may complete the work begun on the Prophets, I give myself wholly to this study; and, set as it were on a watchtower, I contemplate, not without groaning and sorrow, the whirlwinds and shipwrecks of this world, thinking not at all of things present but of things to come, and trembling not at the fame and petty gossip of men but at the judgment of God. And you, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, who helped me with your prayers when I was sick, call down also upon me, now healed, the grace of Christ, that by the same Spirit by which the Prophets sang of things to come I may enter into their cloud and darkness, and know the word of God, which is heard not at all with the ears of the flesh but with those of the heart; and say with the Prophet: The Lord gives me a tongue of discipline, that I may know when I ought to speak. This testimony is the beginning of the fourteenth book on Isaiah, which I now wish to expound.

50:4ff.

The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain by a word him who is weary. He rouses in the morning, in the morning he rouses my ear, that I may hear him as a master. The Lord God has opened my ear: and I do not gainsay; I have not gone backward. I gave my body to those who struck, and my cheeks to those who plucked them. I did not turn away my face from those who rebuked and spat. The Lord God is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: therefore I have set my face like a very hard rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded. LXX: The Lord gives me a tongue of discipline, that I may know when I ought to speak a word. He set me in the morning, he added to me an ear for hearing; and the discipline of the Lord opens my ears. But I do not refuse, nor do I gainsay. I gave my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to blows. But I did not turn away my face from the shame of spittings. And the Lord is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: but I have set my face like a very strong rock, and I shall know that I shall not be confounded. The Jews, separating this little chapter from what goes before, want to refer it to the person of Isaiah: that he says he received from the Lord the word by which to sustain the weary and wandering people and call it back to salvation; and that, after the manner of little children, who are taught in the morning hours, he hears from the Holy Spirit what he should speak; and that he did not gainsay his command, but when the Lord asked, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? he answered him: Here am I, send me (Isa 6:8). And because he had said, Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom: give ear to the Law of our God, you people of Gomorrah (Isa 1:10), he suffered such hard things that he was exposed not only to insulting words but also to the pains of blows. Yet, through his awareness of the God who commanded him, he was not at all terrified; but, according to what is said to Ezekiel, Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and flint I have made your face (Ezek 3:8, 9), he beat down all their assaults. So let those say who strive by every means to overturn the prophecies about Christ and to twist them by a crooked interpretation into a perverse understanding: as if, should these things too have been written of Isaiah, they could take away the other testimonies about Christ, which are so plain that they pour their clear light into the eyes of all. To the person of the Lord, then, with whom the previous book also ended, these things too are to be referred: that according to the dispensation of the body he assumed he was taught, and received a tongue of discipline, that he might know when he ought to speak and when to be silent. Indeed, he who was silent in his passion now speaks through the Apostles and apostolic men in the whole world. And it belongs to great knowledge to give one's fellow servants their food in due season, and to consider the persons of the hearers. Hence the Apostle Paul too speaks to those who did not accept the faith of the Prophets with testimonies from their own authors: as some of your own poets have said: For we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28), meaning Aratus. And again, from the Comic poet: Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor 15:33); and the hexameter verse of Epimenides: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies (Titus 1:12). If these do not keep the order and measure of the meter in translation, it must be known that in Greek they run on metrical feet. And he did this because he had received a tongue of discipline, that he might know when he ought to speak a word. To him an ear was added by grace, which he did not have by nature: so that we may understand that by no means are the ears of the body to be taken here, but those of the mind, of which the Lord also spoke in the Gospel: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8). This discipline and instruction opened his ears, that he might pass on the knowledge of the Father even to us; he who did not gainsay him, but became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). So that he set his body, or his back, to the blows; and scourges cut the breast that held God, and he did not turn his cheeks away from the slaps. That he endured this from the servant of the chief of the Priests is not in doubt, so that the crowds of the Jews too mocked him, vying with one another. Struck and spat upon, he did not blush, but was led as a lamb to the sacrifice; and as a sheep before its shearer he did not open his mouth. And that the Son, according to the mystery of the body he took up, heard from the Father what he should speak, we learn more fully in the Gospel, in which he himself says: And the Father who sent me has given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. And again: As I hear, so I judge (John 8:28; 5:30).

50:8-9

Near is he who justifies me: who gainsays me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord God is my helper: who is he that will condemn me? Behold, they shall all be worn away like a garment, the moth shall eat them. LXX: He who is near justifies me: who is he that is judged with me, let him resist me together? And who is he that enters into judgment against me? Let him draw near to me. Behold, the Lord is my helper, who will afflict me? Behold, all of you shall grow old like a garment, and like a moth it shall eat you. If anyone, he says, thinks that I was justly given over to the cross and had committed some sin, let him resist me. Who is he that is judged with me, so that he may be overcome not by the power of my majesty but by reason? Now a man is judged with the Lord not by the authority of one who reigns but by comparison of virtues: as the Apostles also judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Ninevites and the queen of Sheba judge the people of the Jews. In this sense it is said to Jerusalem: Sodom is justified by you (Ezek 16:52). Since, then, no one can be justified in the presence of the Lord, all shall grow old like a garment (Ps 101 [102]). And what grows old is near to perishing. And like a moth, he says, it shall eat them: namely the conscience of sins, and jealousy over the nations that have been saved. Of this it is said at the end of this volume: Their worm shall not die. And in Micah, against the perverse princes: I will take away their goods like a moth that eats them up, and walks upon the rule in the day of watching (Mic 7:4 LXX). And in Proverbs: An understanding heart is a moth of the bones (Prov 14:30 LXX). For moth in the present place Symmachus translated rust, Aquila worm.

50:10-11

Who among you fears the Lord, hearing the voice of his servant? He who has walked in darkness and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God. LXX: Who is there among you that fears the Lord, let him hearken to the voice of his child: those who walk in darkness have no light. Trust in the name of the Lord, and lean upon God. You scourged me, you spat upon my face: yet I call my persecutors to repentance. For I do not will the death of the sinful people, but only that it turn back and live (Ezek 33). And I say: who is there among you that fears the Lord and hears the voice of the servant, or child, that is, of his Son? Of these the one belongs to the flesh he assumed, the other to his nature. Nor let us think it a small thing to fear the Lord, according to what is said in Proverbs: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). For perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love. But here fear is put for timidity, and εὐλαβείᾳ, of which we also read elsewhere: Blessed is he who fears all things (Prov 28:14), on account of εὐλάβειαν, that is, on account of timidity: those whom people commonly call God-fearing in the religion of God. For the Lord protects their path, and guards the way of the God-fearing. Of this fear it is written: The fear of the Lord surpasses all things. And elsewhere: There is no want for those who fear him (Sir 25:14; Ps 33 [34]:10). Indeed, it is only after many steps of virtue that one arrives at such fear of the Lord. For the divine word speaks in the person of a master and father, instructing a disciple and a son: If you call upon wisdom, and give your voice to understanding, and if you seek her like money, and search her out like treasures: then you shall understand the fear of the Lord, and find the knowledge of God (Prov 2:3). This is the fear that keeps the souls of the saints whole, chaste and pure, of which it is said: The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever. To it the divine oracles exhort us: Fear the Lord, and give him glory (Rev 14:7). Let him, then, who so fears the Lord hear the voice of his servant, or child, who walked in darkness, and there was no light for him; who had no form nor glory, but in the likeness of sinful flesh took the form of a servant, that he might overcome sin in the flesh. Of him it is said that he should hope in the name of the Lord and lean upon his God, so that whatever belongs to human frailty he may strengthen and sustain by the divine majesty. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy it is said of sinners, who would not obey the voice of his Son, and walk in the darkness of error, and therefore have no light. For it could not be that wisdom should enter into a perverse soul. They neither knew nor understood, and therefore they walk in darkness. For they did not do the works and commandments of the Lord, nor sow righteousness for themselves, nor gather the vintage of the vine, so as to kindle for themselves the light of knowledge. For he who desires wisdom, let him keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to him. Hence it is also said to God: Your precepts are light. And elsewhere: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9). And the ungodly are commanded to trust in the Lord, and, falling through their sins, to lean upon his help and be sustained by it.

50:11

Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled: by my hand this has been done to you; you shall sleep in sorrows. LXX: Behold, all of you kindle a fire and strengthen the flame; walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame that you have kindled; because of me these things have been done to you. You shall sleep in grief. Exhortation profits nothing, nor is there hope of salvation after crimes. All have turned aside, together they have become useless (Ps 13 [14]); all kindle a fire for themselves and strengthen the flame. For they have in themselves hay, wood, stubble, thorns and thistles and darnel, which are to be handed over to the eternal burning. Hence it is also written in Proverbs: In much wood the fire thrives (Prov 25:21). But if a little fire lays hold of great material, how much will a great flame lay waste? It is said also in the Epistle that is ascribed to the Hebrews, of the earth that, bringing forth thorns and thistles, is reprobate and near to a curse, and its end is burning (Heb 6:8). Therefore those who are girded and surrounded with flames, and have strengthened the burning for themselves, are called to salvation, and it is said to them: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled, that in punishments and torments they may learn the power of God and return to salvation. And it signifies the devastation of the Jewish people, by which they were handed over to the Romans, and they bear the yoke of captivity to this day. For by the hand of Christ all these things were done, and they shall sleep in grief and sorrows, because neither through benefits nor through torments would they receive the Son of God. Hence he speaks to them: Go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). This is what the Apostle also says: For wrath has come upon you to the end (1 Thess 2:16). From this little chapter we learn that each one kindles a fire for himself according to the quality of his sin. And just as, of people staying in the same place and, if one may say so, in the same bed, some are healthy while others burn with the heat of fevers, feeling different torments from the diversity of their humors and phlegm: so the fire that is kindled by sinners has its fuel in sins and in iniquity, of which it is written: Iniquity shall burn like a fire, and shall be devoured by burning like dry grass (Isa 9:18).

51:1ff.

Hear me, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and multiplied him. The Lord therefore will comfort Zion, and will comfort all her ruins, and will make her desert like delights, and her wilderness like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise. LXX: Hear, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the strong rock which you hewed out, and to the hole of the pit which you dug. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you, for he was one, and I called him, and blessed him, and loved him, and multiplied him: and now I will comfort you, Zion. And I have comforted all her deserts like a paradise, and the things that are toward the west like the paradise of the Lord: they shall find exultation and gladness in her, confession and the voice of praise. While those who kindled a fire for themselves and made the flames most strong sleep in grief and everlasting sorrow, you who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord (and he means the choir of the Apostles and of those who believed through the Apostles), look to the rock, that is, to Abraham your father, from whom you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out, that is, to Sarah who bore you. And consider this: that when he was a hundred years old and one, and had a barren wife, I multiplied his sons like the stars of heaven, so that their multitude surpassed number. If, then, from one man so many thousands of peoples were born, what great thing is it for me to restore the ruins of Zion, and to change her deserts into a paradise of pleasure, and into the garden of the Lord which God planted in Eden toward the East; and that there should be found in her, in place of the various trees, joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise? The Jews refer this to the times of Zerubbabel, because after the devastation of Babylon Zion was restored, the Temple built, and the ancient religion given back. But just as above (Isa 49:22, 23) it is said to Zion: They shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses; and: Behold, these shall come from afar, and those from the north and the sea, and these from the land of the south; when Zion shall say: The place is too narrow for me: make room for me that I may dwell: things which exclude the meanness of those times, and are not known to have been fulfilled in the earthly Jerusalem: so here too the Lord speaks to those who pursue what is just, according to what is said elsewhere: Seek peace, and pursue it (Ps 33 [34]:15); and again: Pursuing hospitality (Rom 12:13). And they seek the Lord, so that one may infer things present from things former: since far more difficult things have already been done, let them not doubt that these things which are promised will come to pass. Further, according to the Seventy it is said to the pursuers of righteousness that they should look to the most strong rock which they hewed out, and the hole of the pit which they dug, that is, to the Lord the Savior, of whom the Apostle speaks: And the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). And elsewhere it is written: He set my feet upon a rock (Ps 39 [40]:3). And again: On a rock he exalted me. For they pierced his side with a lance, and from it came out blood and water; and they dug his hands and feet, as the Lord the Savior himself says: They dug my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones (Ps 21 [22]:18). We can call the hewn rock the tomb of the Savior, in which he was laid, and, rising from the dead, he begot innumerable sons. And he was called Abraham, that is, father of many nations. Just as Sarah, at first barren, is understood as the Church, which by another name is called Zion, whom the Lord has comforted, and whose deserts he has made like a paradise. For more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband. And what is said, And the things that are toward the West I will make into the paradise of the Lord, or into the garden of God, signifies that on those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death a sudden light has arisen. For paradise, in whose place we rendered delights, the Hebrew has EDEN (עדן), of which it is written at the beginning of Genesis. And this is to be noted, that in Zion, which is compared to the paradise of God, there ought to be nothing else but joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise, so that what the saints will do in heaven with the Angels of God, this they may practice on earth too in the unceasing praise of the Lord.

51:4-5

Attend to me, my people, and my tribe, hear me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall rest for a light of the peoples. Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth: and my arms shall judge the peoples. The islands shall wait for me, and shall wait upon my arm. LXX: Hear me, hear me, my people, and kings, attend to me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations. My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my salvation shall go forth like a light: and in my arm shall the nations hope. The islands shall wait for me, and in my arm they shall hope. Once in the Hebrew it is said, Attend; twice according to the Seventy, hear me, hear me: to teach us that we ought to hear both with the ears of the body and with the sense of the soul. And the multitude of the nations, which is the people of God, is called to listen carefully to what is said; of which Zechariah says: Many nations, he says, shall flee to the Lord, and shall be his people (Zech 2:11). Or, as some will have it, the remnant of believers from Israel is called the people; and the tribe, or nations, are those who believed from the multitude of the nations, as Moses says to the nations in the Song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, you nations, with his people (Deut 32:43). For tribe, as we have translated, Theodotion translated race, Symmachus nation, the Seventy kings. For we are the tribe, and the nation, and the royal and priestly race of the Lord, such as Abraham also was, who was called a king, and the other saints, of whom it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones (Ps 104 [105]:15). What is it that they are bidden to hear? For a law, he says, shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the peoples, or of the nations. Here is shown the spiritual law of the Gospel, which shall go forth from Zion, not that of Moses, which was given of old on Sinai; and my judgment shall go forth for a light of the nations, by which he established and decreed that all nations are to be saved. And lest perhaps we should think that what he promised would come after a long time, he adds: near is my righteous one, or righteousness. For Christ has been made for us by the Father wisdom and redemption (1 Cor 1), holiness and righteousness, and all the names by which virtue is called. And it is beautifully said that righteousness will go forth, so that not one nation only but the whole world may be saved. And that the Son of God, who was sent by the Father, is called Savior, or salvation, which in Hebrew is said Jesus, Simeon declares, holding the child in his arms: Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the nations (Luke 2:29ff.). And as for what follows, And my arms shall judge the peoples, or according to the Seventy, and in my arm shall the nations hope: it signifies either that all are judged by his power, or that all the nations will believe in Christ, who is the arm and strength of God. It is said also in another place: Your arm is with might. Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand exalted (Ps 88 [89]:14). And again: Sing to the Lord a new song: his right hand will save for him, and his holy arm (Ps 97 [98]:1, 2). For the right hand and arm of the Lord is he himself who saved for himself those who were formerly lost, so that none should perish of those whom the Father had given him (John 17). And that the islands are said to be either the souls of the Saints, which in the persecutions of this world have been made solid by a firm faith in God, or the multitude of the Churches from the nations, we have often explained. And just as by the arm of the Lord we can understand the Savior, so by his arms which judge the peoples we can understand all the saints, in whom God will judge the world.

51:6

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath: for the heavens shall melt away like smoke, and the earth shall be worn away like a garment, and its inhabitants shall perish like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. LXX: Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look upon the earth beneath, for heaven has been made firm like smoke. But the earth shall grow old like a garment, and its inhabitants shall die like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). And David sings in the psalm: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed (Ps 101 [102]:26). From this it is shown that the perishing of the heavens signifies not destruction but a change for the better. Of these it is said: There shall be a new heaven and a new earth, which I will make to remain in my sight (Rev 21:2). For if it is written of the saints, We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed (1 Cor 15:51), and in the titles of four psalms we read, For those who shall be changed: how much more is this to be believed of heaven and of the sun and the stars, when the moon shall receive the light of the sun, and the sun shall glow with sevenfold brightness? Hence the whole creation too groans and travails, awaiting the revelation of the sons of God, that it may be changed for the better (Rom 8). And not only the souls of men, which are immortal, but their bodies too are to be changed into a glorified substance. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality (1 Cor 15:53). And since heaven and earth grow old, it follows that the things contained within the circle of heaven, and men, who are the inhabitants of the earth, also die like these: not unto their destruction, but unto the abolishing of their old baseness and the renewal of the glory to come; when the righteous shall shine like the sun (Matt 13:43), and, the past and old things departing, all things shall have been made new. Some take perishing and growing old for abolition and death, according to what we read in the catholic Epistle: The heavens that now are, and the earth, have been reserved for fire by the same word. And again: The elements, burning, shall be dissolved (2 Pet 3:7). This is indeed also the opinion of the philosophers of the world, that all the things we see will perish by fire. Hence the Apostle too: Passes away, he says, the fashion of this world, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (1 Cor 7:32). Something of the kind the apostle John also writes: The world passes away, and its desire (1 John 2:17). And in the Hebrew it is said, The heavens shall melt away like smoke; or, according to Aquila and Symmachus, they shall be ground to nothing, and be crumbled and vanish in the manner of salt; of whom the former said ἡλίσθησαν, the latter ἁλίσουσιν, which plainly draws its etymology from the crumbling and dissolving of salt. In place of this I wonder what the Seventy meant to say, heaven has been made firm like smoke: for if firmness is taken for strength, how is what is firm compared to smoke? Unless perhaps we can say this: that all the firmness and strength and might of the heavens is made equal to the emptiest wind and to smoke, which dissolves into the air, according to Ecclesiastes: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2). And this must be said: if heaven and earth shall perish and grow old, by what consequence should its inhabitants die and perish like these, when we know that souls are everlasting, and that bodies will rise again? From this it is plain that heaven and earth do not perish and are not reduced to nothing, but are changed for the better.

51:7-8

Hear me, you who know what is just, people: my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For as a garment, so shall the worm eat them; and as wool, so shall the moth devour them. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness to generations of generations. LXX: Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, of whom my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt. For like a garment they shall be consumed by time, and like wool they shall be eaten by the moth. But my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation to generations of generations. He who had said above, A law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations, now speaks to the same people, who know his judgment and have his law in their hearts, that they may do all things with judgment, and have the law which the Lord promises through Jeremiah, saying (Jer 31:31ff.): I will establish a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers; but I will establish a covenant, putting my laws in their minds, and upon their heart I will write them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: so that they may live by no means according to the letter but according to the spirit, restoring the natural law in their hearts, of which the Apostle also writes: For when the nations, which do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom 2:14). Of this law it is signified in the psalm: The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted (Ps 36 [37]:30, 31). And because the prophetic spirit knew that many persecutions would come upon believers, he exhorts them to fortitude, nay rather to contempt of those who are going to persecute them. Which the Lord also said in the Gospel: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matt 10:28). And in another place: Rejoice when they speak all evil against you, lying (ibid. 5:11). For as a garment is consumed by the worm, or by time, and as wool is devoured by the moth, so all the reproach of the persecutors will pass away with the persecutors. Hence the Apostles too gloried that they had been counted worthy to suffer insults for the Lord (Acts 5). And they gloried because the salvation and righteousness of the Lord, which had promised them victory and rewards, that is, the Lord and Savior, abides for ever, or in each generation, of the former people and of the later, who received his coming; of whom it is also said above: Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth.

51:9ff.

Arise, arise; put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, in the generations of ages. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty deep, who made the depth of the sea a way, that the freed might pass over? And now those who have been redeemed by the Lord shall return and come into Zion praising; and everlasting gladness shall be upon their heads: they shall hold joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee. LXX: Rise up, rise up ÷ Jerusalem ⁚ and put on the strength of your arm. Rise up as in the beginning of the day, as an everlasting generation. Are you not she who cut down the breadth, who undid the dragon? Are you not she who made the sea a desert, the many waters of the deep; who made the depth of the sea a way of passage for those who had been freed and redeemed? For by the Lord they shall be led back, and shall come into Zion with gladness and everlasting exultation. For on their head praise and gladness shall take hold of them. Sorrow and grief and groaning shall flee. The name Jerusalem, which was added here by the Seventy, is neither found in the Hebrew nor did any of the three Translators put it; hence it is to be marked beforehand with an obelus, and so the following little chapter is to be joined with the sense of the preceding. The Lord had exhorted those who believe in him, saying: Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. And he had promised them, as their help, his salvation and everlasting righteousness, which is none other than Christ, the arm of the Lord, of whom he had said above: And in my arm shall the nations hope. Hence the people speak to the arm of the Lord, and pray for his coming, and implore the promised help, saying: Arise, arise: put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, and exert all your strength, so that you who through many ages delivered your Saints from dangers may protect us too by your strength. For you are he who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon, namely Pharaoh king of Egypt, who in Ezekiel too is called the great dragon (Ezek 29). You dried up the Red Sea, so that through the most mighty waters and the depths of the sea your people might find a way and escape the pursuing Egyptians. You, then, who did these things, now too lead back into Zion those redeemed and freed by your blood, into the heavenly Jerusalem, or into the Church which you have prepared for yourself by your blood: and when they are in it, they shall rejoice with everlasting gladness, and shall say: Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us (Ps 5:13). For they shall have joy and gladness, sorrow and groaning fleeing away. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy, Jerusalem, that is, the sinful soul, is called to put on the strength of her arm, and to take up her former works, as she had been before she fell, when she dwelt in the day and in the light. For you are she, he says, who overcame the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and broke up the dragon, the crooked serpent, of which we also read in the Psalms: You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters (Ps 73 [74]:13). Remember your former strength, that you trod down the sea of this world and made it a desert, and found a way in the midst of the waves. Hence the Apostle Peter too passed over the sea of this world to the Lord, and he who was walking by faith began to sink through unbelief, except that he was held up by the right hand of the Lord. As, then, the former victory was granted with the Lord's help, so also to those who return after repentance and hear, Shall he who falls not rise? says the Lord (Jer 8:4), and, Turn to me, you sons that turn, and I will heal your bruises (ibid. 3), he himself will stretch out his hand, and lead them back into Zion, the watchtower and summit of virtues, with joy and everlasting gladness, and will set praise and gladness upon their head. For the eyes of the wise man are in his head; and they shall have this crown and be protected by this diadem, so that they always rejoice and praise the Lord, because joys have taken the place of sorrow, grief and groaning.

51:12-13

I, I myself will comfort you. Who are you, that you should have feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who shall wither like grass? And you have forgotten God your maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth; and you have been in dread continually all the day at the face of the fury of him who afflicted you and had made ready to destroy. Where now is the fury of the afflicter? He shall come quickly, walking, to open, and he will not kill unto utter destruction, nor shall his bread fail. But I am the Lord your God, who trouble the sea, and its waves swell: the Lord of hosts is my name. I have put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, that you may plant the heavens and found the earth, and say to Zion: You are my people. LXX: I am, I am he who comforts you. Know who you were, and that you feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who have withered like grass; and you have forgotten God your maker, who made heaven and founded the earth; and you feared always, all the days, the face of the fury of him who afflicted you, as he planned to take you away; and now where is the fury of him who afflicts you? For when you have been saved, he shall not stand nor remain ※ and he will not kill unto corruption, and his bread shall not fail ⁚ for I am your God who trouble the sea and make its waves resound. The Lord Sabaoth is my name. I will put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you: by which I set up heaven and founded the earth; and Zion shall say, You are my people. The people of believers had prayed to the arm of the Lord, who himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God, to arise and give them help, so that, with him fighting for the saints, they might possess joy and gladness, sorrow and groaning being put to flight. So either the arm of the Lord or the Lord himself answered: I am, I am; and not at all through the Prophets, but I myself will comfort you: the God of mercies and the Father of all consolation. And I wonder how, when I said above, Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies, you feared the rage of the persecutors, and did not know that they are mortal, who like grass suddenly wither and perish. And surely at the time when you feared them, you forgot the Lord your maker. For if the memory of me had always dwelt in your heart, you would never have feared men, who are to be dissolved into ashes. And whom did you forget? God, who hung the heavens by incredible power, and founded the earth as a stable mass. And you feared your adversaries not for a short while, which could in some measure have been granted you, but continually and all the day, so that, though you had the light of faith, the darkness of dread possessed you, and dread of him who thought you would perish. Where then now is the pride of the persecutors? Where is the worldly power with which they raged against you with rabid mouth? My son will come quickly, walking and trampling your adversaries, to open to you the way of victory; or to unbar the underworld; who will not kill unto utter destruction, but wills to save those who turn. Then too his bread, which, as the Gospel proves, means doctrine, shall never fail, but shall always lie open to those who wish to eat. And at the same time he makes an apostrophe to the Son, whom he promises will come quickly, and whose bread he says is everlasting: that he himself, according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, is his Lord God, who makes the sea troubled and its waves swell, so that the pride of the persecutors is puffed up against his servants, and then, with the Lord's help, grows calm again. And he says that he has put his words in his mouth. For whatever the Son speaks are the words of the Father; and that he protected him in the shadow of his hand; and that he was protected for this reason, that he might plant new heavens and found a new earth, and say to Zion, that is, to the Church: You are my people. Therefore Zion is nothing other than the people of God. Symmachus, in the place where we said, He shall come quickly, walking, to open, and he will not kill unto utter destruction, translated thus: Quickly the underworld shall be opened, and he shall not die unto corruption, Christ being understood, who speaks in the fifteenth psalm: You will not leave my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. In that place too where we, according to the Hebrew and Aquila, rendered, I have put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, that you may plant the heavens, and found the earth, and say to Zion: you are my people, he translated thus: I will put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you, by which I planted heaven and founded the earth, and that I may say to Zion: you are my people. According to the Seventy it is said to every believing soul that, though created in the image and likeness of God, she did not know her own dignity, but feared man and the son of man, who can kill only the body, and did not know that she is immortal, nor say with the Prophet: The Lord is my light and my savior, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid (Ps 26 [27]:1, 2)? And again: The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man may do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies (Ps 117 [118]:6, 7). And what man is, is shown by another verse: In the Lord I will hope: I will not fear what flesh may do to me (Ps 55 [56]:5). Hence it is now said too: You feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who have withered like grass. For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass (Isa 40); and, terrified by the power of the judge, you forgot that he himself was your protector, who made heaven and earth and all the elements we see; or those heavens that bear the image of the heavenly one, and that earth which multiplies the Lord's seed. And what is said above, And he will not kill unto corruption, and his bread shall not fail, was added from Theodotion's edition out of the Hebrew. He troubles the sea and makes its waves resound, he to whom it is also sung in the Psalms: You rule the strength of the sea, and the tossing of its waves you calm (Ps 88 [89]:10). In Jeremiah too it is written: Will you not fear me, says the Lord, and will you not tremble before my face, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting decree which it shall not pass (Jer 5:22)? The seas were troubled when the Lord's dragnet drew out a multitude of fish (Matt 13). And the Lord put his words in the mouth of the believer, and protected him in the shadow of his hand. He also says in the Gospel: When they hand you over, do not think how or what you are to speak; for what you are to speak will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt 10:19, 20). And in another place he says to the righteous man: Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it (Ps 80 [81]:12). And again: Open your mouth to the word of God: For the Lord will give the word to those who preach the good news with great power. Hence God speaks to the inner man of Jeremiah, after he touched his mouth: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth (Jer 1:9). He could sing with the Psalmist: He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God (Ps 39 [40]:4). And who has wrought all these things but the Lord and Savior, who made heaven and earth, and says to Zion, You are my people? Which properly suits the Church gathered from the nations. And in Hosea he promises to believers, saying: I will call not my people, my people; and he shall say to me: You are my God (Hos 2:24).

51:17ff.

Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath: you have drunk to the bottom of the cup of stupor, and have drained it to the dregs. There is none to sustain her, of all the sons whom she has borne; and there is none to take her by the hand, of all the sons whom she has brought up. Two things there are that have befallen you; who shall be grieved over you? devastation and destruction, and famine, and the sword: who shall comfort you? LXX: Rise up, rise up, lift yourself up, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury. For the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of fury, you have drunk off and emptied: and there was none to comfort you of all your sons whom you bore; and there was none to take you by the hand, nor of all your sons whom you raised up. These two things are against you: who shall be grieved with you? ruin and destruction, famine and the sword: who shall comfort you? That Jerusalem and Zion are δυώνυμον I have often taught: of which Zion, which means watchtower, because it is set upon a mountain, is called the citadel; while the rest of the city is called Jerusalem, which was formerly called Jebus and Salem. Her the Prophet now exhorts to arise, she who had earlier fallen by denial, saying in the passion of the Lord: Crucify, crucify such a one: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15); and to do penance, and to feel through the evils of captivity why she offended her Creator. Physicians are accustomed to give to a nauseated stomach a most bitter antidote, which took its name from its taste, so that it may vomit up the harmful humors and be able to pass on into the bowel the food cooked and digested, which the great quantity of phlegm did not allow to be digested. So Jerusalem too, who drank from the cup of the Lord's fury, and from his κόνδυ, which Symmachus translated bowl, and which, according to the book of Genesis, Joseph ordered to be hidden in the sack of his brother Benjamin (Gen 44), is bidden to arise from her drunkenness, because she drank it, and emptied it, and drained it to the dregs: which the three expressed by a single word, Ἐξεστράγγισας. This is the cup of which we read in the Psalms: A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed. And he has poured from this into that; yet its dregs are not emptied out: all the sinners of the earth shall drink (Ps 74 [75]:9, 10). Of it God also speaks to Jeremiah: Take the cup of pure wine from my hand, and you shall make all the nations drink of it, to whom I shall send you.
