And they shall drink and vomit, and go mad before the face of the sword which I shall send among them (Jer 25:15, 16). And when he says that he gave it to drink to the other nations and to Jerusalem and the cities of Judea, he adds: Thus says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk, and vomit, and fall before the face of the sword which I shall send among you (Jer 25:27). And it is to be noted that this cup of the Lord's fury is his sword, which is sent into the midst of sinners. Here a question arises: how, after the drinking, the drunkenness and vomiting and the fall, it is said in Jeremiah that Jerusalem cannot arise, and now he speaks to her through Isaiah: Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem. It is resolved thus: as long as someone drinks the cup, and is drunk, and raves, and vomits, and falls, he cannot arise; for he has not yet drained the cup of the Lord, nor come to the dregs, so as to have drunk it to the bottom. But now he speaks to Jerusalem in the past tense: who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury, and not, who are drinking. And at the same time we must consider that from then on there was no prophet, no Apostle in Judea to comfort her, and take her by the hand, and lift her up as she lay. From this it is plain that these things are said of the time after the last captivity: otherwise, history relates that in Babylon and after Babylon she had Ezekiel and the other Prophets. And as for what he says, Two things there are that have befallen you, or these two things are against you: who shall be grieved over you?, and in place of two he names four, devastation and destruction, famine and the sword: like this is what is sung in the Psalter: Once God has spoken, these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy: for you will render to each according to his works (Ps 61 [62]:12, 13). For there too God speaks once, that he is almighty, and the Prophet hears two things, that his omnipotence prevails on both sides, so that he both grants mercy to the penitent and renders to those who persist in sin the punishments they deserve. In the same way in this other place two things befell Jerusalem, each of which has two parts. For destruction follows ruin, or devastation; and death follows famine and the sword. We can understand these things according to the anagogy also of the sinful soul, which, not wishing to drink the cup of the Lord's fury, says in the psalm: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath (Ps 6:1). But if she has drunk it, it is good for her to feel her punishments, and to hear the Lord saying: When the wrath of my fury has passed, I will heal again. And elsewhere: Shall he who falls not rise again, says the Lord (Jer 8:4)?

51:20

Your sons have been cast out, they have slept at the head of all the ways, like an ensnared oryx: full of the indignation of the Lord, of the rebuke of your God. LXX: Your sons, in want and sleeping at the head of all the ways, like a half-cooked beet, full of the fury of the Lord, and failing from the Lord God. For half-cooked beet the other translators rendered an oryx caught and ensnared, which in Hebrew is called THO (תוא), a kind of beast born in the desert, which is placed among the clean animals in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For this the Seventy supposed the Syriac word thoreth, which means beet. From the name let us pass to the sense. Your sons, like an oryx caught in the snares of the hunters, have slept at the crossroads and in the streets, and, laying their naked limbs upon the naked ground, have shown by their own miseries the indignation of the Lord and the rebuke of their God. Further, according to the Seventy: those who would not have spiritual riches in every word, and knowledge, and good works, but were poor who do not endure threatening, shall by no means dwell in houses that are built of virtues, but at the beginnings of the ways and at their outlets, touching all things and leaving all things. They are rightly said to sleep that sleep of which it is written: They have slept their sleep, and found nothing (Ps 75 [76]:6); with which sleep the king of Assyria lulled them. And they are compared to a half-cooked beet, which is a kind of vegetable most cheap and most fragile. Of such vegetables I think it is said in the Psalms: Do not be jealous of evildoers, nor envy those who work iniquity. For like grass they shall swiftly wither, and like green herbs they shall quickly fall (Ps 36 [37]:1, 2). For it is the food of the sick. He who is once and for all unbelieving is called a raw beet. But he who, content with simple faith, does works of righteousness without reasoning and the truth of doctrines, can be called a cooked beet. Further, he who wavers in the middle between vices and virtues, and approaches the service of God with a double heart, is most rightly called a half-cooked beet; to him too God speaks in the Apocalypse of John: Would that you were either hot or cold: but now, because you are lukewarm, I will vomit you out (Rev 3:15, 16). These, lukewarm and sleeping, are full of the fury of the Lord, and dissolved, or failing, through the Lord God: not that the Lord, who did not make death and does not delight in the destruction of the living, is the cause of their dissolution; but in that those who have sinned under the Law are judged through the Law, which works the wrath of God for those who are its transgressors.

51:21ff.

Therefore hear this, poor little one, and drunk, but not with wine. Thus says your ruler, the Lord, and your God, who fought for his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation: you shall not drink it again any more. And I will put it in the hand of those who humbled you, and said to your soul: Bow down, that we may pass over; and you made your body like the ground, and like a road for those passing over. LXX: Therefore hear, you who are humbled and drunk, but not with wine. Thus says the Lord God who judges his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of my fury: and you shall not drink it again any more: and I will give it into the hands of those who unjustly oppressed you and humbled you; who said to your soul, Bend down that we may pass over; and you made your middle parts level with the ground for those passing outside. O Jerusalem, to whom I said, Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, and do penance, because you have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury and drained it to the dregs; and your sons, who are scattered through the whole world, and led away captive, have lain in the streets and at the heads of the ways: know that you are poor and humbled, and drunk, not with wine, but with the fury of the Lord. Therefore, if you do penance, and, lifted up, arise, you will know that the cup of stupor and of ruin, or according to Symmachus and Theodotion, of tearing and of commotion, is to be taken from your hand; and that you will no more drink the condy, for which in this place too Symmachus translated bowl; but that it is to be handed over to your adversaries, who said to your soul, Bow down, that we may pass over: and when they said it, you bent down of your own will. And you made your body like the ground, or your back; or according to the Seventy, your middle parts and your necks for those passing outside. Let this be said according to the history: that Jerusalem, if she is willing to lift herself up and arise, shall by no means drink the cup of the Lord's fury, nor suffer any more what she endured before. But to come, according to the Seventy, to the spiritual understanding: it is said to the soul humbled by vices and drunk with passions, that she may know that she has the Lord as her judge, and that she will render account for all things. And if she has been turned to better things, the cup of ruin is to be taken from her hands, and the bowl of the Lord's fury, which held punishments, of which Ezekiel also says to Jerusalem: You shall drink the cup of your sister Samaria, deep and wide, that you may be drunk (Ezek 23:32), is to be handed over into the hands of those who had humbled her. There is no doubt that he signifies the adverse powers, which said to her soul: Bow down, that we may pass over. Here it is likewise to be noted that they did not bend her down, nor use force so that she who was formerly upright should be bowed to the ground, but left it to her own choice. And she of her own will laid down her neck, or her back, or her whole body, not inside but outside, for those who trampled her. Something of the kind we also read in the Gospel (Luke 13): that for eighteen years Satan had bent a woman down, whom the Lord raised up to her former stature, so that she could say: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence my help shall come (Ps 120 [121]:1); and: To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1).

52:1

Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion: put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, city of the Holy One: for the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no more pass through you. LXX: Rise up, rise up, ÷ Zion: ⁚ put on your strength, Zion, and put on your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. No more shall the uncircumcised and the unclean pass through you. Here again the name Zion, as above, was added by the Seventy, and therefore it has been transfixed with the spit. To her, then, to whom he had said above (Isa 51:17), Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem, he now says: Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion. And who Zion is, the following verse shows: Put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem. We have said this to prove that Jerusalem and Zion are one city. And she is commanded to put off her garments of mourning and to put on those which she had before she drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of fury. And she is called the city of the sanctuary, for this is what CODES (קדש) signifies, on account of the temple which was built in her; or of the Holy One, on account of the knowledge of God; or holy, because she alone in the whole world had received the law. Hence too, after the resurrection of the Savior, the bodies of the dead appeared in the holy city, which surely, on account of its blasphemy and the hands laid on the Lord, could not be holy (Matt 27). And what is promised, that if she rises after her ruin and puts on her strength and glory, the uncircumcised and unclean shall no more pass through her, signifies what the Apostle Paul also says: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What part has the believer with the unbeliever? What accord has the temple of God with idols (2 Cor 6:14, 15)? All these things too, as we began to explain, are referred to the state of the soul. If through penance she has recovered her former strength, let her be called the dwelling of the Holy One, and become a Temple of God, and let no uncircumcised and unclean λογισμὸς pass through her. Of these it has been said: From my hidden sins cleanse me, O Lord, and from those of others spare your servant. If they have not had dominion over me, then I shall be spotless, and shall be cleansed from the greatest offense (Ps 18 [19]:13, 14). But all the things that are promised to Zion and Jerusalem are not said, as the Jews dream, of her stones and ashes and embers, that she may be restored to her former state; but of the people of Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to it (Matt 23), and at the last laid hands even on the Son of God. That people, falling in the passion of Christ, was raised up in his resurrection, when many thousands of the Jews believed and the remnant was saved. The same we can say of the Church also, which is the vision of peace and the watchtower: if she has fallen into heresy, she is commanded to go out and take up the ornaments of her former faith. And if she has been raised up, the rewards of holiness and continence are promised to her, so that the uncircumcised and the unclean shall by no means pass through her. This can be referred not to the cutting of the flesh and the foreskin, but to the uncleanness or cleanness of works, so that we call uncircumcised and unclean those who serve the pleasure and lust of the body. Indeed, Jeremiah speaks to those circumcised in the flesh, not in the spirit: All the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh; but the sons of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts (Jer 9:26). And the blessed Apostle, disputing of virginity and continence and marriage, threw in, in the midst: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not draw on a foreskin. Was he called in foreskin? Let him not be circumcised (1 Cor 7:18). This seems to me to say in other words: Has he been called without a wife, and believed? let him not take a wife. Or on the contrary: having a wife, has he believed in Christ? let him by no means make a divorce. And he keeps this sense not only in circumcision and foreskin, but in freedom and slavery, so as to call virgins and the continent free, and slaves those who render the debt to a wife. For it is not in our power to draw on a foreskin after circumcision, as those in the book of Maccabees are said to have made foreskins for themselves: which is said of the sons being born, and not of the fathers. Or he who has been called free is rather the slave of Christ (ibid. 7:22), since in the baptism of Christ there is no difference of Jew, pagan, Greek and Barbarian, man and woman, free and slave.

52:2-3

Shake yourself from the dust: arise, sit down, Jerusalem: loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver. LXX: Shake off the dust, and rise up, Jerusalem. Loose the bond of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money. That the Prophet's word is by no means addressed to Jerusalem, that is, to the ruins of her stones, and her ashes and embers, but to the people that dwells in her, and that it is called daughter on account of the effeminacy of its spirit, the following verse shows, in which he says: Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For truly captive is the people of the Jews, which to this day bears the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, and is bound fast by the cords of its sins and blasphemies; which was sold for nothing, and did nothing worthy for which it could be redeemed. To it also it is said above: Behold, for your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I put away your mother. And he gives the reasons why they were sold, why they were cast off: Because, he says, I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none to hear. From this it is plain that they were handed over to error and to demons because they had not heard him crying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28). But those who are willing to believe shall be redeemed, by no means with silver and money, but with the precious blood of Christ, so that they hear through the Apostles: Grace to you and peace (Rom 1:7). For not because of merits, but because of grace and faith in Christ, we have been reconciled to God. It is said also to the soul which, polluted by the filth of vices, had lost the whiteness of her former way of life, that she should shake off, with the Apostles, the dust that has clung to her feet (Matt 10). For it could not be that she who, prostrate, had laid down her neck for those passing outside, and had joined her middle parts to the earth, and had said, My soul is humbled in the dust, my belly cleaves to the earth (Ps 43 [44]:25), should not have taken on the image of the earthly. From this the Apostle calls us back, saying: As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear also the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:49). Hence those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8). Not that the nature of the flesh is condemned, whose maker is God, and in which very many have pleased God and reign with Christ; but that the works of the flesh are rejected, of which the same Apostle speaks: But I am carnal, sold under sin (Rom 7:14). Indeed, to men of this kind he says: But where there is jealousy and rivalry among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man (1 Cor 3:3)? And on the contrary to the saints: But you are not in the flesh, since the Spirit of God dwells in you. The dust, then, is shaken off, of which it is written, Shall the dust confess to you, or declare your truth (Ps 29 [30]:10), so that the bonds of our neck may be loosed, and we may by no means hear, your neck is an iron sinew, but may deserve to hear with the bride: How beautiful are your cheeks, like the turtledove's: your neck like necklaces (Song 1:9). And again: I have put bracelets on your hands, and a necklace on your neck; so that, freed from the heavy burden and receiving back our former ornaments, we may cease to be captives: redeemed by him who came to proclaim release to the captives, and of whom it is written (above, Isa 45:13): He shall build my city, and bring back the captivity of my people, not for a price nor for gifts. With this sense the Apostle Peter also agrees: Knowing that you were redeemed from your vain way of life handed down from your fathers, not with corruptible things, silver and gold, but with the blood of the spotless lamb (1 Pet 1:18).

52:4ff.

For thus says the Lord God: My people went down into Egypt at the beginning, to sojourn there; and Assyria oppressed him without any cause. And now what have I here, says the Lord? For my people has been taken away for nothing: its rulers act unjustly, says the Lord, and continually all the day my name is blasphemed. Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself who spoke, behold, I am here. LXX: For thus says the Lord: My people went down into Egypt formerly, to sojourn there; and they were violently led away to the Assyrians; and now what shall be here, says the Lord? Because my people has been taken away for nothing, wonder, and howl. Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations. Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself who spoke am here. He rebukes the people of the Jews and foretells what is to come: that the people which of its own will went down in Jacob to the Egyptians, and in a time of need and famine sojourned in the land of Goshen (Gen 47), afterwards suffered oppression from the Assyrians, whom it had harmed in nothing, and was carried away in captivity into Babylon (2 Kgs 17:23). Hence he adds: And now what have I here, says the Lord? And the sense is: I have nothing left for which I should remain in this region, from which my people has been taken away for nothing, and sold for its sins, and caught like an oryx in a net, either by the forces of the Romans or by the snares of the devil, in which it is held bound to this day. And that they should suffer these things, their rulers and teachers acted unjustly; who, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, shall howl, according to Aquila, shall weep, when they have been handed over to torments. For they are the ones who stirred up the people against the Savior, so that they cried with one voice: Crucify, crucify such a one (John 19:15). Of them he had already said before: The Lord himself will come with the elders of the people and with its princes. But why have you burned my vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in your houses (Isa 3:14)? Wherefore according to the Seventy he says to them: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations. And it must be known that among the nations is not found in the Hebrew, but simply, my name is continually blasphemed, so that "in your synagogues" is understood: who day and night blaspheme the Savior, and, under the name of Nazarenes, as I have often said, heap curses on the Christians three times a day. While they, then, blaspheme and curse the Lord, his people, of whom much has already been said, that is, the Christian people, shall know the name of him who is to come in the name of the Father. And it shall know it because he himself who formerly spoke through the Prophets will instruct the peoples in person. According to the Seventy, God says to Israel that it went down into Egypt of its own will, as Moses says in Deuteronomy: With seventy souls your fathers went down into Egypt (Deut 10:22); and they were led away captive violently by the Assyrians. Hence it is said to them: And now what are you here? What are you doing in the land of Judea, you who after the murder of the Prophets laid hands on the Son of God? Or else God speaks to the angelic powers and the Angels who presided over the Temple: What are you doing here, why do you not leave the blaspheming people? As Josephus also relates (Antiquities of the Jews, Book 6, ch. 12): when the gates of the Temple were suddenly opened and unbarred of their own accord, gates which many men could scarcely shut, a voice came forth from the inner sanctuary of the Temple, of those saying: Let us pass over from these seats. Here we must consider the exactness of the words: that they did not say, Let us depart, but, Let us pass over, namely to the people of the nations. Hence too the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom, so that all the ceremonies of the Jews were laid open, and at that time was fulfilled what is said in this same Prophet: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many nations, even far off (Isa 2:3, 4). For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps 18 [19]). And in every place incense is offered to God, and a pure sacrifice (Mal 1), since the prophetic word was fulfilled: All the ends of the earth shall remember and return to the Lord: and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight; for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations (Ps 21 [22]:28ff.). Hence it is said to the princes of the Jews: Wonder, and howl, since you are the cause of the people's ruin. Further, according to the anagogy we can say this: that the people of God goes down of its own will into the Egypt of this world when it is a lover of pleasures rather than of God, and does not hear that prophetic word: Woe to those who go down into Egypt for help (Isa 31:1). When it has been beguiled by vices, and has dwelt in a place of waters and rivers, which does not have the dryness of chastity, then it shall be handed over violently to the Assyrians, so that they may rule over it, who afterwards may accuse and convict it in its sin. For they are both enemies and avengers, of whom he speaks to Israel: And now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon; and what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the rivers (Jer 2:18)? He, then, who has gone down into Egypt, and has slipped from the height of Jerusalem to lower places, and going to Jericho, another Egypt, has received many wounds from robbers, to him it is said: And now what have you here? Why do you pretend to be in the land and in the Church of God, you who with eagerness and all desire went down into Egypt, and are possessed by the Assyrians, and have been taken captive; and you ought rather to howl and mourn, because on account of your vices and sins the name of God is blasphemed among the nations? To such it is said in Ezekiel: You have defiled my name among the nations (Ezek 36:20). And as the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel, Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16), so on the contrary, when we have done evil works, the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of us. Therefore he who has the knowledge of the name of God, and is not ignorant that he was created in his image and likeness, will dwell in light. And he will be in the day which Abraham rejoiced to have seen (John 8), of which holy David also speaks: This is the day which the Lord has made, let us exult and rejoice in it (Ps 117 [118]:24). For those who have lit for themselves the light of knowledge, and have the everlasting light which has been promised to believers, The Lord shall be to you an everlasting light (Isa 60:20), walk honestly in the day, and are sons of light and of the day; and they know him who says to Moses, Go, say to the sons of Israel: He who is has sent me (Exod 3:14); and him whom they had known before in the saints they will know to be present to themselves too.

52:7-8

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, and announces good, who proclaims salvation, and says to Zion: There shall reign your God. The voice of your watchmen: they have lifted up their voice; together they shall praise, for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord has turned Zion back. LXX: As an hour upon the mountains, so are the feet of him who brings good news of the hearing of peace, who brings good news of good things: for I will make my salvation heard, saying: Zion, your God shall reign. The voice of those who guard you has been lifted up, and with the voice together they shall rejoice, for eyes shall see to eyes, when the Lord has had mercy on Zion. Consequently, of him who had said above, I myself who spoke, behold, I am here, the Prophet now testifies that he himself preached the Gospel upon the mountains, that is, upon the Apostles, of whom it is written: Draw near to the everlasting mountains (Mic 2:9 LXX); and whose doctrine is the illumination of God. Hence it is said to him in the Psalms: You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains (Ps 75 [76]:5). He announced and proclaimed peace to those who were far off, that is, to the nations, and to those who were near, that is, to the Jews, reconciling the world to God; of him it is sung in the psalm under the name of Solomon: In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon be taken away (Ps 71 [72]:7). And in this same Prophet, of the child who is born and of the son who is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and who shall be called the Angel of great counsel, it is said after the rest (above, Isa 9:7): And of his peace there shall be no end. For he is our peace, who has pacified all things through the blood of his cross, in heaven and on earth; who said to the Apostles: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you (John 14:27). And he announced good things to us, not those which the Philosophers call indifferent, but those which are truly good, which the Father gives to those who ask him, that is, all the graces of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, another Evangelist writes in the same place: How much more will your Father who is in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13)? These are the good things which the Lord promises to believers: Hear me, and you shall eat good things, and your soul shall delight in good things; and he announced to all not only good things but salvation, which he himself gave, who says to Zion, that is, to the Church: There shall reign your God. Hence the Apostle too says to the Saints: Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires (Rom 6:12). And writing of sinners: Death, he says, reigned from Adam to Moses (Rom 5:14). And what follows, The voice of your watchmen, or of your guards, signifies the Apostles, of whom God speaks to the Church in another place too (below, Isa 62:6): Upon your walls I have set guards, who shall never be silent, remembering the Lord, who will lift up their voice, discoursing of lofty things. Hence it is said to them (above, Isa 40:9): Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion. Lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem. These will praise God with one voice, and see with eyes to eyes; which the Apostle says in other words, Face to face (1 Cor 13); when the Saint sings, My eyes are ever toward the Lord (Ps 24 [25]:15), and, To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1). And the Lord will answer him: For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayer (Ps 33 [34]:16). What the Seventy translated, as ὥρα, that is, an hour upon the mountains: so the feet of him who brings good news of the hearing of peace, and the rest, Paul, following the sense of the Hebrew Truth, sets down in the Epistle to the Romans: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, who bring good news of peace (Rom 10:15): wishing the Apostles to be understood, whose feet the Lord washed (John 13), that they might be clean and beautiful for preaching, and might run through the whole world, and in a short time fill the world with the doctrine of Christ. Now ὥρα, that is, hour, according to the Seventy and the ambiguity of the Greek word, signifies either time or beauty. If time, this will fit it: In an opportune time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have been your helper (Isa 49:8). Hence the Apostle adds: Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2). For at the opportune time he shed his blood for all, when all had turned aside, together they had become useless; there was none who did good, there was not even one (Ps 13 [14]): that he might taste death for all, because all had sinned and were in need of the glory of God (Rom 3). But if we refer beauty to what is said in the psalm, Beautiful in form above the sons of men (Ps 44 [45]:3) (for what is more beautiful than that the form of a servant should become the form of God, and sit and reign with Christ in the heavenly places?), ὤρα can, according to the breadth of the Greek language, also be called care and solicitude, according to what the Saint says: You will multiply me in my soul, in your strength (Ps 137 [138]:4). For you will multiply me, in the Greek it says πολυωρήσεις με, that is, you will hold me worthy of much care and solicitude. And elsewhere: According to your height ἐπολυώρησας the sons of men (Ps 11 [12]:9): which in other words is said in Greek, πολλῆς ὤρας, τοῦτ' ἔστι, φροντίδος ἠξίωσας. But these things are superfluous; and the feet of Christ or of the Apostles are rather to be taken as beautiful, as all except the Seventy translated alike, Paul approving their interpretation.

52:9-10

Rejoice and praise together, deserts of Jerusalem, for the Lord has comforted his people: he has redeemed Jerusalem. The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. LXX: Let the deserts of Jerusalem break forth into gladness together, for the Lord has had mercy on her, and has rescued Jerusalem. The Lord will reveal his holy arm in the sight of all the nations. And all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. When the people of the Jews had been led into captivity and the city burned, there was in Jerusalem either a rare inhabitant or none. But after he who formerly spoke in the Prophets, and was in the beginning with God, God the Word, dwelt among us and was made flesh, the deserts of Jerusalem were restored; and he came of whom it is written: He shall build my city, and bring back the captivity of my people: so that she is by no means lamented by Jeremiah, How does the city sit alone that was full of peoples: she has become like a widow, she who was multiplied among the nations (Lam 1:1), but hears David singing: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted (Ps 125 [126]:1, 4). And a little after: We became glad. And so that we may know that these things are by no means said of the people of the Jews, but of all who were to believe in the Lord through the apostles, he sets it down and says: he who comforted her, or had mercy on her, and who rescued or redeemed her, he himself prepared or revealed his holy arm in the sight of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. From this it is plain that, once the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, which had been abandoned by the Jews, was built up through the Apostles, the arm of the Lord is revealed to all the nations, and all the ends of the earth see his salvation. This is understood in two ways. For either the Father reveals his arm to all the nations, or the Son reveals his strength, of which it is written: For power went out from him and healed all (Luke 6:19). And again: I perceived that power went out from me, which healed the woman with the issue of blood (Mark 5:30). And that the Son of God is called the right hand and arm of the Father, there are many testimonies, of which we shall mention a few: Will save for him his right hand, and his holy arm (Ps 97 [98]:2). And elsewhere: In my arm shall the nations hope (Isa 51:5). Of him Jacob says: He shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen 49:10). And Psalm 88 (89): Your arm is with might. With this arm the Lord led the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt. Of this he spoke to the prince of the Apostles: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matt 16:17). And the Apostle Paul of himself (Gal 1:15): When, he says, it pleased God, who separated me from my mother's womb, to reveal his Son in me. And that he joined all the ends of the earth to all the nations who are to see the salvation of God shows what is also said in another place: Turn to me from the ends of the earth, and you shall be saved (Isa 45:22); and through Jeremiah: To you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth (Jer 16:19); and again: All the families of the nations shall remember and turn to the Lord; for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations (Ps 21 [22]:28ff.): so that not only the variety of the individual nations but all the hinges of the world too are foretold as about to believe in Christ; according to what he himself says: But when this Gospel has been preached in the whole world, then shall the end come (Matt 24:14). Others will have the heights and extremities of the earth to be understood as those who, standing not in the middle of the earth but at its extremities, like the rims of wheels, forsake lowly things and hasten to the heights.

52:11, 13

Depart, depart, go out from there, do not touch what is polluted: go out from the midst of her, be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. For you shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you. LXX: Depart, depart, go forth from there, and do not touch what is unclean: go out from the midst of her: be separated, you who carry the vessels of the Lord, for you shall not go out with tumult, nor go with flight: but the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel who gathers you. This too the Jews try to expound thus: Go out from Babylon, and abandon their idols. Go out from the midst of her, and bring back into the temple the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off when Jerusalem was taken (2 Kgs 15), now that Cyrus releases the captives under Zerubbabel and Ezra (Ezra 1); and do not go out of Babylon as you fled out of Egypt before, with tumult and fear, but with peace and with the goodwill of the king of the Persians and Medes, in whom the will of the Lord appeared, who protected and gathered you. Others interpret what we have said of Babylon as said of the Roman kingdom: that all these things are to be fulfilled at the coming of Christ, who is to set them free. But we, having heard above, How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, and, The Lord will reveal his arm in the sight of all the nations, and, all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God, understand this by no means of the Jews, but of the choir of the Apostles and of all the Saints. They are commanded to depart from Jerusalem and to preach the Gospel in the whole world, as the Lord the Savior says: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19): so that they may by no means stay with the blaspheming Jews, for whose slaughter the Roman army was being made ready, but may leave the polluted, and that those who carry the vessels of the Lord may be separated from them and be cleansed. For they are the Temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3), and the vessels of gold and silver of a great house. Such was the Apostle Paul, who is called a vessel of election (Acts 9); for he had prepared himself to be a precious vessel, fit for the ministry of God. Or surely this must be said: that the vessels of the Lord are the spiritual armor of God, of which the Apostle Paul also spoke: Put on the armor of God (Eph 6:11); and he lists it piece by piece: the breastplate of righteousness, and the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which means the word of God. To these he adds the belt of truth, and the feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace. And in another place: Laying aside, then, the works of darkness, let us put on the arms of light (Rom 13:12). There follows: You shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For they departed from Jerusalem not as the vanquished but as victors: so that they who, preaching the Gospel of God daily in the Temple, had brought many thousands of the Jews under the faith of Christ, might subdue the world too to his Gospel. For they had the Lord going before them, to gather them, the God of Israel, that is, to make one flock out of the whole world, so that what the Lord says to the Father in the Gospel might be fulfilled (John 17:21): Grant that, as I and you are one, so these too may be one in us: so that, with the same mind and the same judgment, forsaking the vices that fight one another and are contrary, they might lay hold of the one and only virtue. For vices and passions do not follow one another, as is said of the virtues, in which there are neither ὑπερβολαὶ nor ἐλλείψεις, that is, neither more nor less, but all things are tempered. In the vices, by contrast, all things are contrary: as panic to boldness, superstition to impiety, luxury to thrift.

Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted, and lifted up, and shall be very high. As many were astonished over you, so shall his appearance be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men. He shall sprinkle many nations: over him kings shall shut their mouth: for those to whom it had not been told of him have seen; and those who had not heard have beheld. LXX: Behold, my child shall understand, and shall be exalted, and shall be greatly glorified. As many shall be astonished over you, so shall your appearance be in glory from men, and your glory from the sons of men: so shall many nations marvel over him, and kings shall shut their mouth, for those to whom it has not been announced of him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand. So that no ambiguity may be left to readers as to who it is that said, I who spoke, behold, I am here, and what the holy arm of the Lord is, which has been revealed to all the nations, God the almighty Father teaches plainly: Behold, my servant shall understand, or my child, of the difference between which we have spoken above. And he shall understand not as the Word of God and wisdom, but as servant and child. He, though he was in the form of God, deigned to take the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). Wherefore he exalted him, and gave him the name which is above every name. He speaks in the psalm: I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding (Ps 15 [16]:7); and of him David sings: Who made the heavens in understanding (Ps 135 [136]:5). For he himself is wisdom and understanding, he who as a child advanced in age and wisdom; of whom Peter too speaks: The God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed handed over, and denied before the face of Pilate, when he wished to release him. But you denied the holy and righteous one (Acts 3:13, 14); of whom too we showed that it was written above: I am witness, says the Lord, and the child whom I have chosen: over him very many shall be astonished (Isa 43:10), when they have seen his signs. And hence the wonder will be greater, that his appearance will be without glory among men: not that it signifies ugliness of form, but that he came in humility and poverty. He, though he was rich, became poor for us; and he said to believers: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matt 11:29); of whom Clement too, the apostolic man, who governed the Roman Church after Peter, writes to the Corinthians: The scepter of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, did not come in the boasting of pride, though he could do all things, but in humility. So much so that, when struck by the servant of the priest, he answered: If I have spoken evil, convict me of the sin; but if well, why do you strike me (John 18)? though he had twelve thousand Angels who would obey his nod. He shall sprinkle many nations, cleansing them with his blood and consecrating them in baptism to the service of God. Over him kings shall shut their mouth, and the princes of the world, all of whose wisdom has been overthrown by the preaching of the cross; and those who had not had the Law and the Prophets, and to whom nothing had been announced of him, they themselves shall see and understand. Of them the Savior also speaks: Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed (John 20:29). In comparison with them the hardness of the Jews is reproved, who, seeing and hearing, fulfilled in themselves the prophecy of Isaiah, who says: Hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand: and seeing you shall look, and shall not see. For the heart of this people has been made fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily (Isa 6:9, 10).

53:1ff.

Who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall go up like a sapling before him, and like a root out of a thirsty land: there is no form in him, nor comeliness: and we saw him, and there was no appearance, and we desired him. Despised and the lowest of men, a man of sorrows, and knowing infirmity; and his face was as it were hidden, and despised: whence we did not esteem him. Truly he bore our sicknesses, and our sorrows he carried: and we thought him as it were a leper, and struck by God, and humbled. LXX: Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced as a little child before him, as a root in a thirsty land. There is no form in him nor glory, and we saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness: but his form was without honor, and failing beyond the sons of men. A man in a stroke, and knowing how to bear infirmity, for his face is turned away, despised and not esteemed. He carries our sins, and suffers pain for us, and we esteemed him to be in pain, and in stroke, and in affliction. After the words of the Father, by which he had announced to the world that his Son would come, and before the scandal of the cross, of which he was going to say, His appearance shall be without glory, and his form beyond the sons of men, he had put first the glory of the resurrection, He shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high, so that the glory of the resurrection might go before the humility of the cross: now the choir of the Prophets answers that it has fulfilled its office and, as far as lay in it, has announced to all his arm and power. And in saying, Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?, it signifies how rare believers from among the Jews are. And as for what follows, He shall go up like a sapling before him, for which the Seventy translated, We announced as a little child before him: for sapling Symmachus translated branch, to show the man assumed, who came forth from the virginal womb. Of him he adds: Like a root out of a thirsty land. For thirsty Aquila translated pathless, to show the privilege of virginity: that he was created without any human seed from an earth previously untrodden. This is he of whom we read above too: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall go up from his root (Isa 11:1), so as to signify his birth and his going up in the world. But if he had no form nor glory, but his form was ignoble and failing beyond the sons of men, or, as it stands in the Hebrew, despised and the lowest of men, how is it said in the Psalms: Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty, in your beauty and comeliness (Ps 44 [45]:4)? This is easily resolved. He was despised and ignoble when he hung on the cross and, made a curse for us, bore our sins, and said to the Father: God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matt 27:46)? But he was glorious and comely in appearance when at his passion the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and, as the sun fled, the elements feared an eternal night. Of him the bride too says in the Song of Songs: My kinsman is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands (Song 5:10). White in the fullness and purity of his virtues, ruddy in his passion, of which we shall read later: Who is this who comes up from Edom, tawny are his garments from Bozrah; chosen out of thousands in the resurrection, so that he who was the firstborn of all creation might become the firstborn from the dead. And what he adds, A man in pain, and knowing how to bear infirmity, or a man of sorrows, and knowing infirmity, shows the true body of a man and a true soul, he who, knowing how to bear infirmities, overcame them all by his divinity. And his face was hidden and despised, so that the divine power was concealed by the human body; of whom it was said above: You are a hidden God, and we did not know. He truly bore our sicknesses and sins, and suffers pain for us, not in seeming, that is, τὸ δοκεῖν, as an old and a new heresy suppose; but he was truly crucified. He truly suffered pain, saying in the Gospel: My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38). And: Now my soul is troubled (John 12:27). And we thought him unclean, or in pain, as the Seventy translated; for which Aquila and Symmachus put leprous, Theodotion scourged. This, in other words, by Hebrew idiom is understood as leprosy, according to what is written in the psalm: And the scourge shall not come near your tent (Ps 90 [91]:10). And the sense is: We thought him struck by God for his own sins, he who was humbled for our sake and crucified with robbers. Where Symmachus translated Ἐν ἁφῇ ὄντα, that is, in leprosy, Aquila put ἁφημένον, that is, leprous; which many, not understanding, take to mean abandoned, and others read καθήμενον, that is, sitting. At the beginning of the chapter, in which according to the Seventy it is said, Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed (Rom 10), a testimony which the apostle Paul also uses to the Romans, expounding it of the Lord's passion, Lord is not found in the Hebrew, but was added to make clear the person to whom it is said.

53:5, 7

But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, each one in his own way has turned aside: and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. LXX: But he was wounded for our sins, and was weakened for our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him: by his bruise we have been healed. All like sheep have gone astray, man has gone astray in his own way. And the Lord handed him over for our iniquities, and he, because of affliction, did not open his mouth. We, he says, thought him a man of sorrows, or, according to the Seventy, to be in pain, and struck by God, and bearing his own sins. But he was wounded for our iniquities, saying in the psalm: They dug my hands and feet (Ps 21 [22]:18), so that by his wound he might heal our wounds; and he was bruised, or weakened for our crimes, so that, made a curse for us, he might free us from the curse. For cursed is every man who hangs on a tree (Deut 21; Gal 3). Hence the discipline of our peace is upon him. For what we ought to have endured for our crimes, he suffered for us, pacifying through the blood of his cross both the things that are on earth and the things that are in heaven. For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of partition, dissolving the enmity in his flesh, and by his bruise we have been healed (Eph 2). From this it is plain that, just as his scourged and torn body bore the marks of injury in weals and bruises, so his soul too truly suffered pain for us, lest it be believed that in Christ there was truth in part and falsehood in part (Rom 3). All, he says, like sheep have gone astray, and we have needed the mercy of God, saying in the psalm: I have gone astray like a lost sheep (Ps 118 [119]:176); the sheep which in the parable of the Gospel was carried back on the shoulders of the good and careful Shepherd (Matt 18). And who these sheep are, the following verse shows: Man has gone astray in his own way; or each one has turned aside in his own way, to follow his own error, and, forsaking the right way, to hold differing opinions about the Crucified. The Lord, however, has laid on him the iniquity of us all, or handed him over for our sins, so that what we could not bear through the weakness of our strength, he might carry for us, he who was offered because he himself willed it. For he endured the cross not by necessity but by will, saying in the Gospel: The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it (John 18:11)? And to Peter, who was scandalized at the name of the cross, because he did not know the mystery and trembled with human fear: Get behind me, Satan, you are a scandal to me, for you do not savor the things that are of God, but those that are of men (Matt 16:23). Otherwise, if he had not been offered by his own will, he who could point out and foretell the traitor, and said to the Apostles, All of you will be scandalized in me this night, could have avoided those who had been sent against him; but he went to meet them fearlessly, and offered himself of his own accord, saying: Whom do you seek (John 18:4, 6)? And at once they fell backward; for they could not bear the voice of God present before them. And beautifully he added: And he did not open his mouth. When Pilate said, Do you not speak to me?, he would not answer. Or according to the Seventy: Afflicted, he did not open his mouth. Or according to Symmachus and Theodotion, hearing, he did not open his mouth.

53:7ff.

As a sheep he shall be led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he shall be dumb, and he shall not open his mouth. From distress and from judgment he was taken away. Who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off from the land of the living: for the crime of my people he struck them. And he shall give the ungodly for burial, and the rich man for his death: because he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth. And the Lord willed to bruise him in infirmity. LXX: As a sheep he was led to the sacrifice, and as a lamb dumb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall declare his generation, for his life is taken from the earth? By the iniquities of my people he was led to death; and I will give the worst men for his burial, and the rich for his death. For he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth: and the Lord wills to cleanse him from the stroke. This testimony, when in the Acts of the Apostles the Eunuch of queen Candace was riding in his chariot (Acts 8ff.) and, reading it, did not understand it, he understood when Philip interpreted it of the passion and name of the Savior; and at once, baptized in the blood of the lamb of whom he was reading, he deserved to be called a man, and was sent as an Apostle to the nation of the Ethiopians. He, then, who was offered to Pilate because he himself willed it, and did not answer, so that, condemned, he might mount the gibbet for us, was himself led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he was dumb. For Christ our passover has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5), whom John the Baptist pointed out, saying: Behold the lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). He too is often mentioned in the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist as the lamb that was slain (Rev 5). He speaks of himself in Jeremiah (Jer 11): But I was like an innocent lamb, led to the sacrifice, and I did not know. For though he knew no sin, he was made sin for us (2 Cor 5). And as a lamb, when it is led to the sacrifice, does not resist, so he suffered by his will, that he might destroy him who had the dominion of death (Heb 2), humbling himself unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). This is the lamb in whose figure a lamb was sacrificed, whose blood, smeared on the doorposts, put to flight the destroyer of Egypt (Exod 12); who not only redeemed us with his blood, but also covered us with his wool, so that he might warm with his garment us who were freezing with unbelief, and that we might hear the Apostle saying to us: As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ (Gal 3:27). And in another place: Put on Christ Jesus (Rom 13:14). And as for what follows, From distress and from judgment he was taken away, or as the Seventy translated, in humiliation his judgment was taken away: it signifies either that from tribulation and judgment he ascended victorious to the Father; or that he, the judge of all, did not find the truth of judgment, but without any fault was condemned by the sedition of the Jews and the voice of Pilate. Hence the Prophet marvels that the God of all handed himself over to suffering. Of which Paul speaks: For if they had believed, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). There follows: Who shall declare his generation? This is understood in two ways: for either it is to be taken of his divinity, that it is impossible to know the mysteries of the divine birth, of which he himself speaks in Proverbs, Before all the hills he begot me (Prov 8:25), according to what we read elsewhere, Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor (Rom 11:34)? that is, no one; or of the Virgin's giving birth, that it can be explained only with difficulty. Indeed, when it was said to Mary by the Angel, You shall conceive and bear a son, she answered: How shall this be to me, since I do not know a man? To whom the Angel in turn: The Holy Spirit, he says, shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you (Luke 1:31, 34, 35); so that the mysteries of this birth are told only by the Angel or by the Evangelist. Its narrator is most rare, according to that saying: Who is wise, and he will understand these things? understanding, and he will know them (Hos 14:10)? But if a prudent reader answers in silent thought: And how is it written, No one knows the Son but the Father, and no one knows the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him? and he who knows the Father and the Son can surely also declare the mystery of the generation: let him hear that it is one thing to know and another to utter, because often what we conceive in the mind we cannot unfold in speech. Therefore the saints too can know the mystery of the divine birth in the body by faith rather than tell it. Otherwise the Apostle too, caught up into the third heaven and into paradise, heard words which a human tongue can by no means utter (2 Cor 12). But the Spirit too intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. Of him, then, whose generation either no one or hardly anyone can declare, the life was taken away from the earth, so that he might live not on earth but in heaven. Or he was cut off from the land of the living, so that there might be fulfilled of him what is written in the Apocalypse of John: I am the first and the last: I who was living, and was dead: and behold, I live for ever (Rev 1:18); so that after the life he lived on earth, dead to the earth, he might live in heaven for ever. And what is joined to this, For the crime of my people he struck them, or, according to the Seventy, by the iniquities of my people he was led to death, has a double sense. For either by his death he struck the persecutors and the criminals of his people; or because of the greatness of the sins of the people which he always held as his own peculiar people, he was led to death, so that by his death he might call them back to life. He gave the ungodly for his burial, and the rich man for his death; or the worst men for his burial, and the rich for his death: signifying both peoples, so that in the evil and the worst, who before had no knowledge of God (Rom 9), the multitude of the nations is shown; in the rich, to whom belonged the Testament and the Lawgiving and the Prophets, the Jewish people is pointed out. Therefore the Lord suffered and was buried for this reason, that he might gather to himself a Church from both peoples. Or this must be said: that the Scribes and Pharisees, and Sadducees, the priests and high priests, who formerly reigned among the people and abounded in excessive wealth, God handed over to the Romans after the Lord's passion, and subjected to everlasting servitude. He for whose burial and death the ungodly and the rich were handed over did no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. This can be understood of no man at all, that he sinned neither in deed nor in word, as Scripture says, No one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been of a single day, and, all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned aside in his own way (Job 25), except of him who bore our sins, and suffers pain for us, and was wounded for our iniquities, and afflicted for our crimes, by whose bruise we have been healed. Expounding this testimony about him, Peter the prince of the Apostles also says: For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps; who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; who when he was cursed did not curse, and when he suffered did not threaten (1 Pet 2:21ff.). And the Lord willed to cleanse him from the stroke which he had received when pierced by the soldier's lance. Or to bruise him in infirmity and wound; of which he himself also said: For they persecuted him whom you struck (Ps 68 [69]:27). And through Zechariah God says: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered (Zech 13:7). Therefore his suffering was not of necessity, but of the will of the Father and of his own, he who said to him: O God, to do your will, I have willed it (Ps 39 [40]:9). Of which we also read above: He was offered because he himself willed it.

53:10-11

If he lays down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand. Because there has labored his soul, he shall see, and be satisfied: by his knowledge he himself, the righteous one, shall justify my servants who are many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities. LXX: If you give an offering for sin, your soul shall see a long-lived seed: and the Lord wills to take away his soul from pain, to show him light, and to form understanding; to justify the righteous one who serves many well: and he himself shall bear their sins. According to the Hebrew this is the sense: If he whom the Lord willed to bruise, or to cleanse, lays down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, which he sowed in good ground. Of which it is written in the Gospel: The sower went out to sow; and again: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field (Matt 13:3). And the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand, so that whatever the Father willed may be fulfilled by his powers, as he says to the Father: I have kept in your name those whom you gave me. I have guarded them, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition (John 17:12). And he shall see an everlasting seed, and the will of the Father shall be directed in his hand, because his soul labored for a long time, finding no rest among the Jews, and saying in the Gospel: Foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt 8:20). And in this same Prophet: I have labored, bearing it (Isa 1:14). Because, then, he labored, he shall see the Churches rise up in the whole world, and shall be satisfied with their faith. Indeed, when, hungry and thirsty, he had sat down by the well of Jacob (John 4) at midday under the scorching sun, he would not use the food that had been bought, because he was already satisfied with the faith of the Samaritan woman and of the city of Shechem coming out to him. In this sense he said among the eight beatitudes: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5:6). By his knowledge, that is, by his doctrine, he himself, the righteous one, who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, and the servant of the Father, who had taken the form of a servant and had served the will of the Lord, shall justify many who believe from the whole world. And he himself shall bear their iniquities, which they could not bear, and by whose weight they were crushed. According to the Seventy this is said: O you for whose sins the Son of God was led to death, you who, the worst men and rich in evil, were given for his burial and death: if you are willing to do penance, and to offer for your sins a sacrifice pleasing to God, a contrite spirit, your soul shall see a seed of long time, the Lord the Savior himself. Of whom it is sung in Psalm 88 (89): His seed endures for ever, and his throne like the sun in my sight. And again: I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne like the days of heaven. Which in other words Gabriel says to the Virgin: Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, who shall be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1:31, 32). For the Lord wills to take away from pain the soul of him who had said, My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38), so that the shame of the cross may be tempered by the glory of the resurrection. And to show him light, so that he may see all enlightened through him. And to form with understanding, him being understood, upon whom the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall have come down. And to justify the righteous one, who has served many well; for he came not to be served but to serve (Matt 20), washing away in Peter's feet (John 13) the sins of all the Apostles. He appeared in the flesh, was justified in the spirit. Of him Judas the traitor too confesses: I have sinned, betraying righteous blood (Matt 27:4). And Pilate's wife: Have nothing to do with that righteous man: for I have suffered many things today in dreams because of him. And it is to be noted that he was not justified so that from being unrighteous he might become righteous; but the righteous one is justified, not so that he might begin to be what he was not, but so that what he was might appear to all. This righteous one suffered for the unrighteous, that he might offer us all to God. Of him it is said to the Jews: And you denied the holy and righteous one, and asked that a murderer be granted to you (Acts 3:14). And their sins, he says, he himself bore, as a physician bears the sicknesses of the sick; of him the healthy have no need, but those who are ill (Luke 5).

53:12

Therefore I will allot him very many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong: because he handed over his soul to death, and was reckoned with the wicked: and he bore the sins of many, and prayed for the transgressors. LXX: Therefore he shall possess many, and shall divide the spoils of the strong: because his soul was defiled in death, and he was reckoned with the unrighteous, and he took up the sins of many, and for their iniquities he was handed over. He gives the reasons why after his passion Christ obtains many rewards. Because, he says, he suffered, and did all the things which the preceding discourse described, and himself bore the iniquities of many: therefore I will allot him very many, so that, in place of Jacob, the portion of the Lord, and Israel, the line of his inheritance, they may believe in him, coming from the East and the West, and recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matt 8): when that is fulfilled which is written: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession (Ps 2:8). Of which we also read in this same Prophet: There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who shall rise to rule the nations, in him the nations shall hope (Isa 11:10). These very many were once held by the strong; and under the figure of the ass and the colt they had many masters, to whom the Apostles said: The Lord has need of them (Matt 21:3). These were strong before Christ took up a human body and, having overcome the strong man, plundered his house. So he handed over and divided the prey of the strong to his Apostles, so that Peter, James and John became the princes of the circumcised people, and Paul and Barnabas were sent to the nations, separated in place, not in mind, and stood under one Lord in different battle lines, so that by the victory of both columns they might raise a triumph to the Savior. Hence those who say that the dispensational contention between Peter and Paul (Acts 15) was truly a quarrel and a struggle, so as to satisfy the blaspheming Porphyry, and who assert that the ceremonies of the old Law are to be kept in the Church of Christ by those of the stock of believing Israel, ought also to expect a golden Jerusalem in the thousand years, so as to sacrifice victims and be circumcised, so as to sit on the sabbath, sleep, be filled, get drunk, and rise up to play: a play which offends God. We have said this on account of what is now prophesied: And he shall divide the spoils of the strong (Isa 53:12). According to what is written in another place: When the heavenly one divided kings in it. And again: The king of the hosts of the beloved, and the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils (Ps 67 [68]:13). Indeed, of the apostle Paul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, it is said according to the Hebrew: Benjamin a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall eat, and at evening he shall divide the spoils (Gen 49:27). Of these too we have already spoken before: They shall rejoice in your sight, as those who rejoice at harvest, and as those who divide the spoils (Isa 9:3), dividing among themselves the Churches of Christ in the whole world. Therefore he shall receive very many nations, he who came to proclaim release to the captives, and led captive the captivity formerly held by the devil and the demons, and gave it as a gift to men and to believers, because he handed over his soul to death and was reckoned with the wicked, or unrighteous (1 Cor 9). For if his Apostle became to those who were without law as one without law, though he was not without law but was under the law of Christ, why should not Christ too have been reckoned with the unrighteous, that he might redeem the unrighteous from sin and become all things to all, that he might save all? For he bore our sins in his body (1 Pet 2), fastening them to the wood of the cross, that he might blot out the handwriting which we had made to the devil and his angels, written by the hands of the soul, that is, by its works. Of these the apostle Paul speaks: And you, when you were dead in sins and in the desires of the flesh, he made alive with Christ, forgiving us all sins. And blotting out the handwriting that was against us, which was contrary to us, he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross: despoiling the principalities, he put the powers to shame, triumphing over them confidently (Eph 1:2; Col 2:14, 15). And the unrighteous with whom he was reckoned, the Evangelist Mark understands as the robbers, writing: And they crucified with him two robbers, one on the right, and the other on the left. And the Scripture was fulfilled which says: And he was reckoned with the unrighteous (Mark 15:27). This can also be understood more deeply, as the Lord says of himself: I am reckoned with those who go down into the pit: I have become like a man without help, free among the dead (Ps 87 [88]:4). For he was truly reckoned among sinners and the unrighteous, so that he might go down to the underworld, which in many places of the Scriptures is called the pit, and set free those bound in prison. He was handed over for our sins, and rose again for our justification (Rom 4). And he was of such clemency that he prayed on the cross for the transgressors, nay rather for his persecutors, and said: Father, forgive them: for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34).

Book Fifteen

I know that I have often said, Eustochium, that the Apostles and Evangelists, wherever they set down testimonies from the Old Instrument, were accustomed, if there is no difference between the Hebrew and the Septuagint, to use either their own words or those of the Seventy Translators; but if the sense is one thing in the Hebrew and another in the old edition, they follow the Hebrew rather than the Seventy Translators. In short, just as we have shown that they set down many things from the Hebrew which are not found in the Seventy, so let our rivals show some testimonies taken from the Seventy which are not in the books of the Hebrews, and the dispute is finished. We have said this because the present passage, though it is one in sense, differs in words. With its explanation the fifteenth book on Isaiah begins.

54:1

Praise, O barren one, who do not bear; sing out praise and neigh, you who were not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who had a husband, says the Lord. LXX: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said. Symmachus translated this passage thus: Rejoice, O barren one, who have not borne. Be glad in exultation, and neigh, you who have not been in labor: For more are the sons of the scattered one than of her who was under a husband. From him Theodotion and Aquila do not differ, apart from a few words. After the nativity of the Savior, and the course of His life and mighty works, the passion of the cross, and the glory of the resurrection, when, laying down His soul, He saw a long-lived seed, and in His knowledge He, the righteous one, justified very many, and divided the spoils of the strong, and prayed for the transgressors, giving room for repentance, the Prophet passes to the calling of the nations, and describes in full discourse those who were to believe in Him. This passage the apostle Paul too refers, under the name of Sarah and Isaac, to the Church (Gal 4:27ff.): that the former people, from Mount Sinai and Hagar, is in bondage with her children, but the later one is free, of whom Isaiah says: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband; and immediately: But we, he says, brethren, are sons of the promise according to Isaac. But as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the spirit, so it is now also. But what does the Scripture say? Cast out the bondwoman and her son. For the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman. But we, brethren, are not sons of the bondwoman, but of the free: with which freedom Christ has endowed us (Gal 4:27ff.). If, then, the vessel of election, taking from Isaiah the testimony which we now have in hand, referred it to the sons of the promise, and to the Church gathered from the nations, or from both peoples, which had been deserted and abandoned among the Jews, which had not had God as her husband, nor had received the Law or the Prophets, we are compelled by that very reasoning to follow the footsteps of our predecessor, and to call her the deserted one of whom we read above (cf. Isa 35): Rejoice, O deserted one, and the rest like these. Of her too it is written in Jeremiah, in the person of God: She who bore seven has been made empty, and her soul has fainted. Her sun has set while it was yet midday (Jer 15:9). And in the volume of Samuel: The barren has borne seven, and she who had many sons has been weakened (1 Sam 2:5). And in the Psalms: Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of sons (Ps 112 [113]:9). Now the synagogue is said to have borne seven sons because of the mystery of the week and of the sabbath, to which the former people had been bound. Or else, for seven, many are to be understood, according to an ambiguity of the Hebrew speech, by which both sabbath and many are signified; of this more has been said in the book of Hebrew Questions which we wrote on Genesis. She, then, as long as she had God, the divine word, for her husband and was joined to the Law, bore very many sons to God; but when she received the bill of divorce, and would not answer her husband when he called, she heard: You are your mother's daughter, who have forsaken your husband (Ezek 16:45). And again: You have not called me as Lord, nor as father and guide of your virginity (Jer 3:4): therefore she is lamented in this same Prophet: How has the faithful city become a harlot, Zion, full of judgment: in which righteousness slept in her, but now robbers (Isa 1:21). But this too is to be noted, that when he says: More are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband, the synagogue is not wholly excluded from childbearing, but the multitude of the nations is preferred to her. For she too, in the Apostles and through the Apostles, first bore a people from the Jews. Hence the two chief of the Apostles divided between them the hosts of those who believed in Christ, of the Circumcision and of the Gentiles, so that from both peoples they might build up Jerusalem, formerly deserted and poor. And that the Hebrew has put neighing for gladness signifies the greatness of joy, in the likeness of a horse neighing for victory; of which more is written in Job (Job 39). This passage and the rest that follow the Jews and our own judaizers refer to Jerusalem, which they say is to be restored in a kingdom of a thousand years, and they say she is the same who formerly had a husband and afterward ceased to have one, and that after the divorce she will have many more sons than she had before under a husband. Yet the comparison is plainly set out of two women: of her who had a husband and was put away, and of her who was always deserted and without a husband. Nor is it to be wondered at in the Jews, whose eyes and ears are closed, if they do not see the open truth. Of the Christians I do not know what to say, who, though the Apostle says, which things are allegorical, and refers Sarah and Hagar to the two Testaments, the old and the new, give their hands to the Jews out of desire for earthly pleasures in the thousand years.

54:2-3

Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles: do not spare: make your cords long, and make your stakes firm. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations, and shall inhabit the deserted cities. LXX: Enlarge the place of your tabernacle, and fix the skins of your curtains, do not spare. Lengthen your cords, and strengthen your stakes; yet more to the right, and to the left spread out, and your seed shall possess the nations, and you shall make the deserted cities to be inhabited. To her to whom he had said: Praise, O barren one, who do not bear; break the bonds, by which you were formerly held bound, and cry out in confession of the Lord, you who had no children, it is now commanded, in the likeness of the tabernacle of Moses which he once had (Exod 36) in the desert, that she enlarge her tent and stretch out the skins; and make her cords longer, and drive deep and strengthen the stakes by which every tent is shaped, lest it be scattered by the blasts of the winds. And let her penetrate to the right and to the left, and by no means imitate the narrowness of the Jewish tabernacle, which enclosed a hundred cubits of length and fifty of breadth, nor be shut in by the smallness of the Temple, which had sixty cubits in length and twenty in breadth; but let her not cease to take up room to the right and to the left (Exod 27). And lest we think this is said, according to the frivolous contention of the Hebrews, of Zion, which is to be restored by the Lord to its ancient state, he sets out more plainly what lay hidden: And your seed shall inherit the nations. Of this we read in the Gospel also: He who sows went out to sow (Matt 13:3); and again: Did you not sow good seed in your field (ibid., 27)? This seed will also make the deserted cities to be inhabited, so that Churches of the nations rise up throughout the whole world. Or certainly the seed is to be called that of the Apostles and the remnant of the Jewish people, of which it is said in this same Prophet: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9). And the Apostle: A remnant, he says, has been saved (Rom 11:5). This concerns the greatness of the Churches, which, in place of the one land of Judea, and that a very narrow one, will spread their bounds through the whole world. Let us come to the spiritual understanding. He who is in a tabernacle does not possess a firm and perpetual dwelling; but he always changes places, and hastens on to what lies beyond, saying in the psalm: I will pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle (Ps 41 [42]:5), forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself forward to what is to come, until he attains the prize of the heavenly calling. Of this tabernacle we read in another place also: How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of powers! my soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord (Ps 83 [84]:1). And afterward he adds: Blessed are they who dwell in your house; for ages of ages they shall praise you (ibid., 6). For the end of the tabernacles is the possession of an eternal house, which does not change its foundations, nor is moved from one place into another. For those who are planted in the house of the Lord have first flowered in His courts, so that they may come from flowers to fruit, and may be able to say: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God (Ps 51 [52]:10).
