In short, the holy man, hastening to pass beyond the tabernacles and longing to see the house of God, says that he has one wish, never to go out of the house of God: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps 26 [27]:4). The tabernacle, then, must be enlarged, and the curtains and skins stretched out, and the cords of manifold and varied discourses drawn out further, and the stakes made firm by reason on the right and on the left, so that the seed of the word, that is, of the doctrine of God, may be able to possess the nations, and to make habitable the cities which he received who had doubled the mina. Now the right and the left in the holy Scriptures are taken in a good sense when we understand them both according to the spirit and according to the letter, through the arms of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor 6), so that the humbler understanding may hold to the ordering of life and the examples of our forebears, and the spiritual and sublime one may carry us over from present things to things to come. This is what the Lord also said to the Pharisees when they questioned Him: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matt 22:21): that we should both be subject to the powers of this world, which not unjustly bear the sword for vengeance on those who have done evil, and this is understood as the left; and that we should render to God the things that are God's, so as to fear no one else but Him who has power over both soul and body, and this is taken as the right (Matt 10). Finally, it is said of the wisdom of God, to which nothing precious can be compared, that in her right hand she has length of life and very many years, but in her left riches and glory; so that those riches are to be understood which consist in knowledge in the present and in good works, and the glory which he receives through whose works God is glorified among the nations; while length of life and very many years signify eternal life, which, disregarding present things, hastens toward what is to come.

54:4-5

Do not fear, for you shall not be confounded, nor shall you blush: for you shall not be ashamed, because you shall forget the confusion of your youth, and shall no more remember the reproach of your widowhood. For He who made you shall rule over you, the Lord of hosts is His name: and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of all the earth. LXX: Do not fear, because you have been confounded: nor be confounded, because you have been reproached: for you shall forget the eternal confusion, and of the reproach of your widowhood you shall not be mindful: for the Lord who made you, the Lord Sabaoth is His name: and He who delivered you, the God of Israel, shall be called of all the earth. A question arises: if it is said to the Church gathered from the nations: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear; and: More are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband, meaning that she who afterward bore more sons had not had a husband, and that she who formerly had a husband was turned to barrenness, how is it now said to her who had no husband: You shall no more remember your widowhood, and you shall forget the confusion of your youth? From this the Jews wish it to be understood that all that is said is said to Jerusalem, which, deserted by God, is to be restored by Him again. They will easily be repelled when they are reminded that it is said in the person of the Lord in Zechariah: And I took to myself two rods: the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord: and I fed the flock (Zech 11:7). Of this we have spoken more fully in its place, and now it will be spoken of in part. The two rods are the two peoples, of the nations and of the Jews; of these the first to be called was the throng of the Gentiles, which received the natural law fixed in their hearts, about which Paul, writing to the Romans, argues most forcefully (Rom 1); and nothing is more beautiful than this rod, that every creature should be called equally to the worship of its Creator. But the second, that is, the rod of the people of the Jews, was called Cord: which, after the offense of the nations, is called the portion of the Lord, and Israel the cord of His inheritance (Deut 32). Finally, after Israel was called in Abraham, the Lord says: I took my rod which was called Beauty, and I cut it off, to make void my covenant which I struck with all the nations (Zech 11:10). Therefore at the coming of Christ it is said to the rod that had been cut off: Do not fear, nor blush, nor flood your face with shame. For you shall by no means be confounded any longer, as you had been confounded before, nor shall you be mindful of the confusion of your youth, and you shall not remember your widowhood, through which you were abandoned by God: for your maker Himself shall rule over you, whose name is the Almighty, who reigns not in the one nation of Judea but in the whole world. Finally, there follows: He who had made you has Himself redeemed you with His blood, and He shall be called the God of all the earth: that is to say, of all who dwell on the earth. From this it is plainly evident that this is by no means said to Jerusalem, which never ruled over the whole world, but to the Church of Christ, whose inheritance is the possession of the world.

54:6-7

For the Lord has called you as a woman forsaken and mourning in spirit: and as a wife cast off from her youth, says your God. For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you: and with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while: and with everlasting mercy I have had pity on you, says your redeemer, the Lord. LXX: Not as a woman forsaken and faint-hearted has the Lord called you, nor as a woman who is hated from her youth, says your God. For a little time I left you: and with great mercy I will have pity on you. In a little wrath I turned away my face from you: and with everlasting mercy I will have pity on you: says the Lord who delivered you. Here the friends of the Jews debase the forsaken woman and the wife cast off from her youth, whom the Lord forsook for a moment and for a little while, saying that she is Jerusalem; and that He, hiding His face for a little while, took her up again in everlasting mercies and changed her past grief into joy. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy he says that He did not call her as a forsaken woman and faint-hearted, nor as a wife who had been held in hatred from her youth; but that He left her for a little while and turned away His face for this reason, that He might have pity on her forever. If, then, the Jews and our judaizers say that Israel was forsaken for a little while, so that at the coming of Christ God might have pity on it, and interpret 'a little' by comparison with the whole of eternity, why do they not grant us too to call that a little time during which the nations were forsaken, so that they, cast off in the middle period, who in their youth had been God's, might afterward in their old age obtain eternal mercy? Especially since, in the time of Israel's calling, the throng of the Gentiles was never shut out, but a door of return always lay open to them through the proselytes; so that, as we seem to have been shut out for a little while by their calling, so by their perpetual exclusion a return to God is granted to us. But we have spoken of a perpetual exclusion if they do not repent. Otherwise the apostle Paul says: God has shut up all things under sin, that He may have mercy on all (Gal 3:22). What we have interpreted of the Church gathered from both peoples, and the Jews take of Jerusalem, those who follow tropology alone, and in the most difficult places flee the questions that arise by an excursion of free disputation, refer to the sinful soul, which has been cast off by God, not out of hatred but by dispensation, so that, pressed by the weight of evils, she may return to her former husband, and, having lost her substance, may not despair of the father's clemency (Luke 15). Is it not great mercy to run to meet the returning son, to hold out the ring and the robe and a kiss, and, after the likeness of another parable, to say to the envious brother: Friend, if I am good, why is your eye evil (Matt 20:15)?

54:9-10

As in the days of Noah, so is this to me, to whom I swore that I would no more bring the waters of Noah upon the earth: so I have sworn not to be angry with you and not to rebuke you. For the mountains shall be moved, and the hills shall tremble: but my mercy shall not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace shall not be moved, says the Lord who has compassion on you. LXX: From the water which was under Noah this is to me: as I swore to him at that time that I would by no means any more be angry with the earth over you, nor in threatening you remove the mountains: nor shall your hills be removed. So neither shall my mercy fail, nor shall the covenant of my peace be taken away, says the Lord who is merciful to you. So that the congregation of the saints may believe the mercy of the Lord to be everlasting, and that we were forsaken for a moment and briefly for this reason, that they might be joined in friendship with God by an eternal covenant, he sets forth the examples of the forebears, saying: As, when the whole world was sinning, after all the earth had corrupted the way of the Lord, the flood was brought in, and together with all the authors of sins all sins were blotted out, and in one man, Noah, the human race was preserved; to whom I swore that a flood would by no means be brought on the lands, and my pledge has been kept until now and will never be made void (Gen 8 and 9): so I swear to my Church, which I have redeemed for myself with my blood, that I will by no means be angry with those on whom I have had pity, nor will my clemency be changed by any harshness of rebuke. For the mountains and hills will more easily be moved than my sentence will be changed. In accordance with which He also says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). And this, he says, is my mercy: that the covenant of peace, by which the world has been reconciled to me, is kept not by the merit of those to whom it was given, but by my clemency. According to the Seventy the sense is confused, and everything is so disordered that what is being said can hardly be understood: not that I do not know what a most prudent man has said on this passage, but that it does not satisfy my mind. For he posits a tropological flood, which he interprets of the baptism of the Savior, gathering very many examples, such as this: The Lord makes the flood to be inhabited (Ps 28 [29]:10). And again: The Lord is sweet to those who wait for Him in the day of tribulation: and knowing those who fear Him, in the flood of the journey He makes an end (Nah 1:7, LXX): namely, that He blotted out all sins in baptism, saying in another place: I am, I am He who blots out your iniquities (Isa 43:25). For all had turned aside, together they had become unprofitable (Ps 13 [14]:3). There was none who did mercy or truth, nor was there knowledge of God upon the earth. Cursing and lying and murder and adultery and theft had seized everything, and they had mingled blood with blood. Whence He speaks through the Prophet: Woe is me! for the devout man has perished from the earth. There is none who does right among men; all are judged in my blood. Each afflicts his neighbor with affliction, and they prepare their hands for evil (Mic 7:2, LXX); and the rest like these. Among them is this: No one is clean from filth, not even if his life upon the earth be of one day (Job 14:4). Hence he holds that the Lord made the flood, who according to the apostle Peter was put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit (1 Pet 3), and preached to the spirits set in prison, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, bringing the flood upon the ungodly; after whose pattern water cleanses us, not washing away the filth of the flesh, but as the questioning of a good conscience toward God. And the mountains and hills which are not moved, and in a flood of this kind had been shaken, he wants to be understood as the saints, once the everlasting covenant has been received, who in the former flood had been moved and had left their firmness. He says that the mountains are also the demons and the adverse powers, who saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and, wounded by the dart of love, took for themselves wives of all whom they chose, and lost their former strength; and they will by no means be in this flood (Gen 6). This is what he may have said; its explanation I leave to the reader's judgment.

54:11-12

Poor little one, torn by the tempest, without consolation. Behold, I will lay your stones in order: and I will found you on sapphires: and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of carved stones, and all your borders of desirable stones: All your sons taught by the Lord, and a multitude of peace for your sons, and in righteousness you shall be founded. LXX: Lowly and unstable, without consolation. Behold, I prepare for you the carbuncle as your stone, and sapphire as your foundations: and I will make your battlements jasper, and your gates stones of crystal, and your walls choice stones: and all your sons disciples of God, and great peace shall be for your sons, and in righteousness you shall be built. Where we have said: I will lay your stones in order, in the Hebrew is written BAPHPHUCH (בפך), which all except the Seventy have translated alike: I will lay your stones in stibium, in the likeness of an adorned woman who paints her eyes with stibium, so as to signify the beauty of the city. And where we, following the Seventy, have said jasper, the Hebrew has written CHODCHOD (כדכד), which Symmachus alone translated χαλκηδόνιον. For crystal also, in whose place ECDA (אקדה) is read among the Hebrews, Symmachus and Theodotion put of carving, that is, γλυφῆς, and Aquila τρυπανισμοῦ: a word that conveys the sense of bored and engraved gems. We have spoken of the difference of translation; let us come to the sense. He is still speaking to the Church, formerly lowly and poor, which had neither the Law nor the Prophets nor the word of God; torn by the tempest or unstable, which had endured many whirlwinds of the world and wavered among the various errors of idols; which had no comforter, and in vain spent all her substance on physicians: that He Himself will come, He Himself will descend, and build on earth the heavenly Jerusalem, which in the Apocalypse of John is called the bride and wife of the Lamb, having light like a precious stone, like jasper and crystal, and a great wall, and twelve gates inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel, of which three were on the East, and three on the North, and three on the South, and three on the West (Rev 21); and the wall rested on twelve foundations, its whole building of jasper stone, and the several foundations of the walls had each its own stone: the first jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. Reading this, we cry out and say: O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor (Rom 11:33, 34)? And again: Who is wise, and he will understand these things; understanding, and he will know them (Hos 14:10)? Let them answer, the lovers of the letter alone, which kills, who in the thousand years make ready exquisite foods for gluttony and luxury, whose God is the belly and whose glory is in their shame (Phil 3); who after the second coming of the Savior in glory hope for marriages, and little children of a hundred years, and the outrage of circumcision, and the blood of victims, and a perpetual sabbath; who say with Israel, in a perverse way: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall reign: let them answer what this heavenly Jerusalem is to which it is now said: Behold, I will lay your stones in order; or according to the Seventy: Behold, I prepare for you the carbuncle, your stone: so that the whole city is full of carbuncles, and has sapphire foundations, and battlements of jasper or chalcedony, and gates of crystal or carved in relief, and a wall of precious stones round about; and all her sons have no men as teachers, but God, and are called disciples of God; and there is in her perpetual peace and the building up of righteousness. From this it is clear that under the occasion of righteousness, which is the name of a virtue, we ought to seek the other virtues too for the building up of the Church, and not follow Jewish ravings. For let them explain what it is that is said of wisdom in Proverbs: She is more precious than all the most precious stones (Prov 3:15). For if Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1), it is foolish for Christ to be compared to senseless stones. And again we read of the judgments of God: The judgments of the Lord are right, justified in themselves, desirable above gold and very precious stone (Ps 18 [19]:10, 11). From this it is plain that the stone compared with the other stones is the one of which it is said above in this same Prophet, in the person of God: Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a corner stone, a chosen stone, precious: and he who believes in it shall not be confounded (Isa 28:16). This stone the builders rejected (Ps 117 [118]), namely the Scribes and Pharisees and the chief men of the Jews, and it has become the head of the corner (Matt 21). Of it the Apostle Peter also says in his discourse: To us therefore who believe in the corner stone, precious and chosen, there is honor; but to unbelievers it is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense (1 Pet 2:7, 8). And he too speaks to the chief priests in the Acts of the Apostles: This is the chosen stone, precious, which you despised and rejected (Acts 4:11); which has become the head of the corner, and holds together the two peoples, of the nations and of Israel; which built the city whose builder and maker is God: of which the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: You are God's building. And: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one see how he builds. For no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, Jesus Christ (1 Cor 3:9, 10). And if anyone builds on this foundation gold and precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each one's work will be made manifest. Of this foundation he speaks in another Epistle also: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the corner stone (Eph 2:20); and again: In whom you are all being built as living stones into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices (1 Pet 2:5). Of these stones it is said mystically: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth (Zech 9:16), with which Christ builds the Church upon the rock, saying in the Gospel: Upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt 16:18). He who has deserved to enter this city says joyfully to the Lord: As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of powers, in the city of our God: God has founded it forever (Ps 47 [48]:9). Concerning the founder of this city it is said in another place also: He shall build my city, and shall bring back the captivity of my people (Isa 45:13). As for the nature of the twelve stones and gems, this is not the time to speak, since very many both of the Greeks and of the Latins have written of it. Of these I will name only two: the bishop Epiphanius, a man of holy and venerable memory, who has left us a notable volume of his genius and learning, which he entitled περὶ λίθων; and Pliny the Second, at once orator and philosopher among the Latins, who in his most beautiful work of natural history filled the thirty-seventh book, which is also the last, with a treatment of stones and gems. These twelve stones are written in order in Exodus and in Ezekiel, that is, ἐν τῷ λογείῳ of the high priest, and in the crown and diadem of the prince of Tyre. Let us speak first of Exodus: four rows of stones were woven in (Exod 28). The first row had the sardius, topaz, emerald; the second row, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper; the third row, ligure, agate, amethyst; the fourth row, chrysolite, beryl, onyx, set in gold; and they were inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. In which it is to be noted that the second row of stones is also set down in the present Scripture: carbuncle, sapphire and jasper. For we do not yet hold what is perfect, nor have we come to the first things, because now we see through a mirror in an enigma. Further, in Ezekiel we find it written thus: You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. You were clothed with every first stone: sardius, topaz and emerald, carbuncle and sapphire and jasper, silver also, and gold and ligure, and agate and amethyst, and chrysolite and beryl and onyx; and with gold you filled your treasuries and your storehouses within you. From the day you were created, I set you with the Cherubim on my holy mountain; you were in the midst of the fiery stones, spotless in your days, from the time you were created until your iniquities were found in you (Ezek 28:12ff.). For who is so foolish and of so senseless a mind as to think that the prince of Tyre, whoever he believes him to be, set in the paradise of God, and created among the Cherubim, and dwelling among the fiery stones (which we understand without doubt as the Angels and heavenly Powers), was one adorned with earthly stones and having the likeness and the seal? Of the nature of all the stones, then, and of each one in part, this is not the time to speak; for not everything is always to be said. Now let us discourse only of the carbuncle, the sapphire and the jasper. The carbuncle which is prepared, or laid in order, seems to me the fiery word of doctrine, which, putting to flight the error of darkness, illuminates the hearts of believers. This is the one which one of the Seraphim took, grasped with tongs, to purify the lips of Isaiah (Isa 6); which is born, according to the faith of Genesis, in the land of Havilah, where there is the best gold (Gen 2), and the carbuncle stone and the leek-green. Further, the sapphire, which is placed in the foundations, has the likeness of heaven and of the air above us: and it is such that it can say that line of Aristophanes with Socrates: Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον; which we can turn into the Latin tongue: I tread the air and look down upon the sun (See Suidas under περιφρονεῖν). Or with the apostle Paul: But our conversation is in heaven (Phil 3:20). The Scripture of Ezekiel also records that the place where the throne of God is has the likeness of sapphire, and that the glory of the Lord consists in this color, which bears the image of what is above the heavens. And the battlements of the Lord's city, that is, the ramparts of the walls, are strengthened with jasper: those who can destroy and refute every height that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, and subject falsehood to truth (Ezek 1; 1 Cor 15). He, then, who is most strong in disputing and strengthened by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, he is a battlement of the Church. There are many kinds of jasper: one has the likeness of emerald, which is found at the springs of the river Thermodon, and is called Grammatias, by which they assert that all phantoms are put to flight. Another is greener than the sea, and tinged as if with flowers; they report that this is born on Mount Ida in Phrygia and in its deepest caves. Another, again, is found among the Iberians and the Hyrcanians and by the Caspian Sea, and especially by the lake Neusis. There is also another jasper like snow and the foam of the sea waves, and mildly reddish as though with blood mixed in. We have said this so that we may recognize all the spiritual graces in the battlements of the Church; he who has them puts vain fears to flight, and can say with the bride: My kinsman is white and ruddy (Song 5:10). And the gates of this city are of crystal stone, which is carved in various ways; than this stone nothing is purer. In short, in the most violent frosts of the Alps, and in caves inaccessible to the sun, waters are said to congeal into crystal: to the touch it is stone, to the sight water. By this it is shown that those who are at the doors of the Church ought to be stained by no filth, but to be of the purest faith, and to say with the prophet: From your commandments I have understanding (Ps 118 [119]:104), and to hear this: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). And the walls of the city, or the borders and περίβολος, are built of choice stones, by which we can understand the remaining stones, and that all her sons are taught, or are disciples of God: a testimony the Lord uses in the Gospel of John, saying: No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him, and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me (John 6:44, 45). And shortly after: It is written in the prophets: They shall all be taught by God. He also speaks through Jeremiah: Putting my laws in their minds, and I will write them on their heart; and they shall no more teach each his neighbor and his brother, saying: Know the Lord. For all shall know me, from the least to the greatest. For I will be merciful to their iniquities, and their sins I will not remember (Jer 31:33, 34). And the teaching of the disciples of God has a multitude of peace, which was left to them by the Lord; and the building of the most beautiful city is completed in righteousness, so that He is the God not of one nation but of the whole world, calling to His faith slaves and free, Greeks and Barbarians, rich and poor, noble and lowly, men and women, little children and old men, and all things in the world which seem to be contrary (John 14). We have gone beyond the measure of brevity, which is useful in all that has to be said, since we seek the city of God not, with the Hebrews and our Half-Jews, on earth, but in the heavens: the city which, set on Christ the mountain, cannot be hidden.

54:14

Withdraw far from calumny, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. LXX: Withdraw from the unjust man, and you shall not fear, and trembling shall not come near you. A most beautiful order. He had consoled the poor and lowly one, promising her spiritual graces. Now he teaches what she ought to do if she does not wish to dread the assaults of her adversaries. And the sense is: You do not wish to fear your enemies? Do what I say: Withdraw far from calumny, or from iniquity, for all iniquity and plunder is born of calumny; and you shall not fear, and trembling and terror shall not come near you, so that you fear not men but God, saying with Moses: I am trembling and fearful (Deut 9:19); and with one of Job's friends: Horror and trembling came upon me, and shook my bones greatly (Job 4:14); and with the prophet: At the voice of my prayer trembling entered into my bones (Hab 3:16); and: Upon whom does the Lord rest, but upon the humble and quiet, and him who trembles at His words (Isa 66:2)? But the trembling of the ungodly is another, which is born of the fear of punishment; of it is written: Trembling seized the ungodly (Ps 47 [48]:7).

54:15

Behold, the sojourner shall come who was not with me; he who was once a stranger to you shall be joined to you. LXX: Behold, proselytes shall come to you through me, and they shall be your settlers, and shall flee to you for refuge. These things too the Jews think are said to Jerusalem: that many of the nations will be proselytes and will take up the law of Moses and its ceremonies. We, according to the interpretation we have begun, refer this to the Church, which has been gathered through the apostles from both peoples, which has neither spot nor wrinkle, which is free, and the mother of all believers (Eph 5; Gal 4). To gather these proselytes and strangers the Lord sent His disciples, saying: Teach all nations (Matt 28:19), so that they might flee to the Gospel and take up the new Law, and that those who were once dwellers in idolatry might become settlers of the Church. Of them it is said in the psalms: The Lord makes the blind wise. Or, as is read in the Latin codices: The Lord gives light to the blind, the Lord loves strangers (Ps 145 [146]:8, 9): so that after the blind have received the light of truth, and the foolish have learned wisdom, then, passing over to the Church, they may be loved by the Lord, and hear through the prophet: I will call not my people, my people (Hos 2:24); and when this people enters the Temple of God, jealousy seizes the unlearned people.

54:16-17

Behold, I have created the smith who blows the coals in the fire, and brings forth a vessel for his work: and I have created the slayer to destroy. Every vessel that is fashioned against you shall not prosper: and every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge. This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord: and their righteousness is with me, says the Lord. LXX: Behold, I have created you, not as a coppersmith blowing the coals in the fire and bringing forth a vessel for work. But I have created you not for perdition, to destroy: every vessel that is made against you shall not prosper: and every voice shall rise against you in judgment: you shall overcome them all ÷ and they shall be liable to you in it ⁚ There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord, and you shall be righteous to me, says the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew: If you wish not to fear, and that dread be far from you, do what the preceding discourse has related; for I am He through whom you are to have proselytes. I am He who created the smith who blows the coals in the fire, that is, the devil, the craftsman of all evils, not by necessity of nature but by the choice of his mind; who has kindled fires and will bring forth vessels against you, such as were Simon and Elymas the magicians, who resisted the apostles Peter and Paul (Acts 13). I have created the slayer of those who are going to be unbelievers: not that I am the cause of their perdition, but that the adversary is created for battle, so as to be perdition to the vanquished and a cause of rewards to the victors. And all who have been fashioned against you by the blowing smith shall not prosper, but shall feel both present punishments and those to come. And what before seemed hidden is said more plainly in what follows: And every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge, destroying the wisdom of the wise and rejecting the prudence of the prudent. And all the leaders of the heretics, and the teachers of the Jews, and the philosophers of the world, whom that smith had forged, you will condemn by your judgment; as the Queen of Sheba also condemned the unbelievers, and the Ninevites; and on the contrary Sodom will be justified by comparison with a worse Jerusalem (Matt 12). After this he adds what the rewards to come are, lest they think the contest is in vain and ends with the present death. This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, that is, the kingdom of heaven, and life everlasting, and the repayment of labors, the things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him (1 Cor 2). And if for those who love Him, then also for those who serve Him, who have no other Lord but God. And this is the righteousness of those who are with God, says the Lord: that present tribulation should be compensated by future joy. Further, according to the Seventy this seems to me the sense: I, your Creator, have not made you as the devil, that worst of smiths, forges vessels of iniquity with an unclean spirit and brings them forth to perdition; and he ought to know that vessels of this kind do not have a prosperous course, but are broken in mid-career. What the vessels are he shows in the following words: And every voice that shall rise against you in judgment, you shall overcome them all. The vessels of iniquity have a voice, and this voice rises against the Church when the heretics set their mouth on high and their tongue passes through the earth. And what follows, And they shall be liable to you in it, we have marked beforehand with an obelus, because it seems to have been added not so much by the Seventy as by bad copyists. And when the Church has overcome every voice that rises against her, then those who serve and obey the Lord will have an inheritance, an eternal possession; of which it is said in Jeremiah in other words: There is a reward for your works (Jer 31:16). And the dwellers of the Church will be righteous to the Lord. For everyone who does righteousness is born of God; and to them the Lord says: Be holy, for I am holy (Lev 20:26).

55:1

All you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no money, hasten, buy and eat: come, buy without silver and without any exchange wine and milk. Why do you weigh out silver not for bread, and your labor not for fullness? LXX: You who thirst, go to the water, and as many as have no money, go, buy, and eat, and walk, and buy without money and without price wine and fat. Why do you buy with money, and your labor not for fullness? The Hebrew word OI (הוי), of which I had said above, in the prophecy against Ariel (cf. Isa 29), that it was ambiguous, and signified either the interjection of one calling or woe, set here at the beginning of the passage, is read not with the feeling of one lamenting but of one calling. Since, then, he had said that every vessel fashioned against the Church is to be broken, and that every voice and tongue that had armed itself against the knowledge of God is to be overcome, he summons the believers to the river of God, which is filled with waters, and whose stream gladdens the city of God, that they may drink waters from the fountains of the Savior, who says to the Samaritan woman: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me to drink, you would have asked Him, and He would have given you water. The water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into life eternal (John 4:10, 14). Of these waters He cried out in the Temple: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who drinks of the water that I shall give him, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:37, 38), signifying the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive, and of whom the Prophet sounded forth in mystical speech: My soul has thirsted for the living God (Ps 41 [42]:2); and again: With you is the fountain of life (Ps 35 [36]:10). He Himself spoke of Himself: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold waters (Jer 2:13). These waters the clouds sprinkle, to which the truth of God reaches, as it is written: And the clouds sprinkle righteousness (Isa 45:8, LXX). And the thirsty are commanded by no means to drink the muddy waters of Sihor and the swelling floods of the Assyrians, but to go to the waters of Siloam, which go with silence; and not to fear poverty of speech if perhaps they have no silver (Isa 45; Jer 2), but to hear the Apostle saying: By grace you have been saved (Eph 2:8); and the Lord saying to the disciples: Freely you have received, freely give (Matt 10:8). And in a wonderful manner they buy waters without money; and they do not drink them, but eat them. For He is both water and the bread which came down from heaven (John 6). Therefore what is read in some copies, Buy and drink, was changed by unskilled copyists, who thought it more consistent if the waters were drunk rather than eaten. But there is also a most wicked money, or silver, which the Scripture rejects, saying: Money that is given with deceit shall be reckoned as a potsherd (Prov 26:23, LXX); and in another place: Your silver is reprobate (Jer 6:30). And there is a silver which is compared to the utterances of God: The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances: silver tried in the fire of earth, purified sevenfold (Ps 11 [12]:7). Spurning, then, that silver and those moneys with which we cannot buy the waters of the Lord, let us go to Him who, holding the cup of the Sacrament, said to the disciples: Take and drink; this is my blood, which shall be shed for you for the remission of sins (Matt 26:27, 28). This wine Wisdom too mixed in her bowl, summoning to drink all the foolish of the world and those who do not have the wisdom of the world; and so that we may buy not only wine but also milk, which signifies the innocence of little children: a custom and type which is kept to this day in the Churches of the West, that wine and milk are given to those reborn in Christ. Of this milk Paul also said: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor 3:2). And Peter: As newborn little children, desire the rational milk (1 Pet 2:2). Hence Moses too, understanding the wine and the milk of the passion of Christ, testifies in mystical speech: His eyes are lovely with wine, and his teeth white with milk (Gen 49:12). For milk in the present passage the Seventy translated fat; of which holy David says in the psalm: Let my soul be filled as with fat and fatness (Ps 62 [63]:6); and in another place: He fed them with the fat of wheat, and with honey from the rock He satisfied them (Ps 80 [81]:17). These fats denote nothing other than the mystical flesh, to which the Lord exhorted the disciples, saying: Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in you (John 6:54). Hence also He was betrayed in Gethsemane, which means valley of fat, or most fertile. And at the same time he rebukes those who follow worldly wisdom and the perverse and feigned doctrines of the heretics, and the traditions of the Pharisees, and all knowledge falsely so called which is lifted up against God, and who at great prices and with unceasing labor weigh out silver for a discipline in which there is no bread, and sweat for foods in which there is no fullness. From this it is shown that the wisdom to be pursued is the one which lies not in the leaves and flower of words but in the marrow and fruits of meanings; which does not fly past the ear but refreshes the mind. To learn it we do not cross the seas, nor do we need great expense, but the word is near, in our mouth and in our heart.

55:2-3

Hear, you who hear me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in fatness. Incline your ear, and come to me: hear, and your soul shall live. And I will strike with you an everlasting covenant: the faithful mercies of David. LXX: Hear me, and eat good things, and your soul shall delight in good things. Attend with your ears, and follow my ways: and hear me, and your soul shall live in good things. And I will establish for you an eternal testament, the faithful holy things of David. Lest anyone think that the hearing to which the divine word exhorts those who are to hear is of the flesh and not of the mind, it promises them good things not of the flesh but of the soul. For if, he says, you hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land (Isa 1:19). Or the good: He who says, I am the good shepherd (John 10:11). And your soul shall delight in good things and in fatness. Therefore the good things promised to the soul are not riches, and health of body, and the dignities of the world, which even the philosophers call indifferent, that is, neither good nor evil, and which vary according to the quality of those who use them; but those are to be believed good to which God exhorts us: Turn aside from evil, and do good (Ps 36 [37]:27). But if honesty and the virtues are called the good things of the soul, then evils too are to be taken to be not poverty, and infirmity of body, and low birth, but all the vices, which are truly evil. In short, Abraham did not have good things because he was rich, but because he used his riches well (Gen 13). And Lazarus, who afterward rested in his bosom, did not endure evils because he suffered the torments of diseases together with want; rather, through what were thought evils in the world, he obtained true goods. Hence too that rich man clad in purple received his good things in his lifetime, which were good to him who thought them good (Luke 16); and of Lazarus it is not said, conversely: He received his evil things in his lifetime; but: he received evil things in his lifetime, which seemed evil not to him who suffered them but to others. An example of both is given us by blessed Job, who was overcome neither by the goods nor by the evils of the world, but bore all things with equal firmness of mind (Job 2). Wherefore Solomon prays to God: Give me neither riches nor poverty. But appoint for me what is necessary and sufficient for my living, lest, being full, I become a liar and say: Who sees me? or, being in want, I steal and forswear the name of the Lord (Prov 30:8, 9). And if he prays for this, to have neither riches nor poverty but only the necessaries of living, of which the Apostle also says: Having food and clothing, with these we are content (1 Tim 6), it is clear that riches and want, health and sickness, pleasure and torments, are neither good nor evil, but become good and evil according to the difference of those who bear them. Therefore it is not, as the χιλιαστὰς would have it, abundance of wealth, and dainty foods, and fatness of body, pheasants and stuffed turtledoves, mead, unmixed wine, the beauty of wives, swarms of children, that the Lord promises to the soul, but those delights to which He summons us mystically, saying: Delight, or take your delight in the Lord, and He will give you the petitions of your heart (Ps 36 [37]:4); and elsewhere: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps 26 [27]:13); and in another psalm: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me His holy name; who fills your desire with good things (Ps 102 [103]:1 and 5). Finally he adds: Hear me, and your soul shall live (Isa 55:3). The promise of all good things is life everlasting. If you are willing to hear, and your soul lives forever, I will strike with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David. Of these the same Psalmist sang: The mercies of the Lord I will sing forever. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth (Ps 88 [89]:1, 2). And so that we may know what these mercies are, he shows in the following words: Once I have sworn by my holy one: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun in my sight, and as the full moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven. He is called faithful for this reason, that He has fulfilled His promises. For these the Seventy translated the faithful holy things of David (Acts 13:34), which can be taken as firm and strong; as is this: All His commandments are faithful, confirmed for ever and ever (Ps 110 [111]:8). And in another place: God is faithful, and there is no iniquity in Him (Deut 32:4). And the apostle Paul: If we deny Him, he says, He remains faithful: He cannot deny Himself (2 Tim 2:13). And in another place, writing to Timothy: A faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance (1 Tim 1:15). And this covenant which the Lord promises will not be brief and for one time, as was that of the people of the Jews, but will remain forever, so that the true David may come, and in the Gospel may be fulfilled what was promised in the person of God: I have found David my servant; with holy mercy I have anointed him (Ps 88 [89]:21); whose hand He set in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers. Him, according to Ezekiel, when David had already been asleep for many ages, He calls His servant and shepherd, saying: I will raise up for you one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23).

55:4-5

Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation which you did not know: and nations which have not known you shall run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, because He has glorified you. LXX: Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a prince and commander to the nations: nations which did not know you shall call upon you: and peoples who were ignorant of you shall flee to you for refuge: because of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you. He had summoned the people of the Jews to believe, to incline their ear and receive the everlasting covenant which the Lord had promised to David, and to Abraham and his seed, saying: In your seed the nations shall be blessed (Gen 22:18). The apostle Paul, explaining this: He did not say, he says, in seeds, but, in seed, which is Christ (Gal 3:16). And because He knew that, while they did not believe, the peoples of the nations would believe, He passes over to the nations, and says that He has sent His Son as a witness or testimony of all the nations, to announce His precepts and commandments to the peoples; who says of Himself: This Gospel must be preached in the whole world, for a testimony to all the nations (Matt 24:14). Finally, He refutes the proud Pilate with this word: For this I was born, to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37). Of Him the apostle Paul writes to Timothy: One mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a redemption for all, a testimony in its proper times: in which I have been appointed a herald and an Apostle (1 Tim 2:5). All that is said, then, is to be referred to Him who was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer did not open His mouth. Of Him it is said above: We saw Him, and He had neither form nor comeliness (Isa 53:2); and: He Himself bore our sins, and suffers for us. To Him have fled, or run, those who before did not know Him, saying: Our God is refuge and strength (Ps 45 [46]:1); and again: Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation (Ps 89 [90]:1). Of their faith we read above also: Those to whom it was not preached concerning Him shall see: and those who had not heard shall understand. He is the witness of all that the Father promised and bestowed on the world, whose mystery Paul gathers up in a brief word to the Ephesians: The God, he says, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory (Eph 1:17); of whom it is written now as well: Because of the Lord your God, and the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you, and that with the glory which He had before the world was made. Of it the Prophet also testifies: The glory of God shall appear (Heb 1), He who is the brightness of glory and the form of His substance, when every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of the Father (Phil 2). He answered the Son, when He asked for the glory which He had had before: I have both glorified it, and will glorify it. Of which the apostle John also says: We saw, he says, His glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth (John 12:28; 1:14). Therefore, when he speaks of Him who in the beginning was with God, God the Word, He is called the Father of glory; but when of Him who says in the Gospel, Why do you persecute me, a man who speaks the truth to you (John 8:40)? He is called the God of our Lord Jesus Christ. Not that there is one and another (which is the very bad error of many), but because one and the same Son of God speaks now with the feelings of the glory of His divinity, now with those of our nature, which He deigned to take up.

55:6-7

Seek the Lord while He can be found: call upon Him while He is near. Let the ungodly man forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him, and to our God: for He is abundant in forgiving. LXX: Seek the Lord: and when you have found Him, call upon Him. And after He has drawn near to you, let the ungodly man forsake his ways and the unrighteous man his thoughts and return to the Lord: and he shall obtain mercy: for He will abundantly forgive your sins. Since, then, as we have already said before, you would not receive the everlasting covenant and the faithful mercies of David, which, when you were unwilling to take them up, the throng of the Gentiles took up, I the Prophet warn you, my own people, and solemnly charge you: while there is time, do penance. Turn to Him who now speaks to you through the Prophets, who afterward will speak in person. Seek Him while He can be found, while you are in the body, while room for repentance is given; and seek Him not by place but by faith. How God is to be sought is said more fully in another place: Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek Him in simplicity of heart: for He is found by those who do not tempt Him, and appears to those who are not unbelieving toward Him (Wis 1:1, 2). Hence we too, knowing the word spoken of sinners, Those who withdraw far from you shall perish, let us say to the Lord: Whither shall I go from your spirit, and whither shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there: if I descend into hell, you are present (Ps 138 [139]:7, 8). And let us call upon Him while He is near, lest through our vices and sins He withdraw far away. For He draws near to those who draw near to Him, and joyfully runs to meet the son returning after a long time. Wherefore the holy man sings in the psalm: But for me it is good to cleave to God (Ps 72 [73]:28). And Moses alone drew near to the Lord (Exod 20). And through Jeremiah God says: I am a God who draws near, and not from afar (Jer 23:23): drawing near to those who draw near to me by faith, and withdrawing far from those who depart far from me by unbelief. Because of this it is said to believers: Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. And lest we should think this could suffice, he at once adds: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (Jas 4:8). Of him it had been said above: Your adversary the devil, like a lion, going about, seeks whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith (1 Pet 5:8, 9). Nor is it enough to seek the Lord, and to find Him while it is the time of repentance, and to call upon Him while He is near, unless the ungodly man forsakes his former ways and the old thoughts by which he had turned aside from the Lord. For then we shall return to the Lord, who will have mercy on us, and to the most clement father, who is abundant in mercies and ready to forgive, when we have forsaken our former thoughts and ways, so that afterward we may deserve to hear: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Ps 31 [32]:1).

55:8-9

For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts. LXX: For my thoughts are not as your thoughts: nor are your ways as my ways, says the Lord. But as far as heaven is distant from the earth, so far is my way distant from your ways, and your thoughts from my thought. Do not think, he says, that what I promise is difficult, and let it not seem incredible to you that the ungodly and the unrighteous can be saved, whether the people of the Jews or all those among the nations who did not know God: consider this, that there is a great difference between my counsels and yours, and as great a diversity of will as of nature (Prov 19). For many are the thoughts in the heart of a man, but the counsel of the Lord abides forever. You, as men, often repenting of a promise, have overturned your old will with a new will. For the Lord scatters the counsels of the nations, and rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and makes void the wills of princes (Ps 32 [33]); but the thoughts of His heart are from generation to generation, and whatever He has decreed cannot be changed. Do you wish to know the difference between my counsel and yours? As far as heaven is distant in place from the earth, and the dwelling of the Angels is one thing and that of men another, so far are my thoughts separated from your counsels. For of my thoughts it is said: His judgments are inscrutable, and His ways past finding out (Rom 11:33). But of yours: They devised a counsel which they could not establish (Ps 20 [21]:12). And in another place: Whatever counsel you have entered upon shall be scattered, and whatever you have spoken shall not remain among you (Isa 8:10). Things that are clear need no interpretation; therefore they are touched on briefly rather than discussed.

55:10-11

And as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and will not return thither again; but they soak the earth, and water it, and make it spring up, and give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it. LXX: As if the rain or the snow should come down from heaven, and not return until it soaks the earth, and it bring forth and spring up, and give seed to the sower and bread for eating: so shall my word be which has gone forth from my mouth: it shall not return until it accomplishes what I willed, and I will make its ways and my precepts prosperous. What is said hangs on what went before, and briefly the sense is this: let the people of the nations not be incredulous that after such great crimes the ungodly man is suddenly saved. For my thoughts are not as the thoughts of men, and as far as heaven is distant from the earth, so far are my thoughts separated from the thoughts of men. For I am most clement and abundant in forgiving. Do you wish to receive another likeness also? As the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and will not return thither again, but soak the earth, and water it, and make various seeds sprout, so that from full harvests bread is produced for the use of men: so the word of my promise, which I have once pledged and which has gone forth from my mouth, will not be void, but all will be fulfilled in deed. According to the anagogy the understanding is twofold: the word of the Lord is either He of whom it is written: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1), who will not return to Him empty unless He has done the Father's will, and fulfilled all the things for which He had been embodied, and reconciled the world to God. He is said to proceed from the mouth, and from the womb and belly: not that God has these members, but that we may learn the nature of the Lord through our own words. Or certainly this is to be said, that the word of the Gospel's teaching is called rain, and the showers which the spiritual clouds pour upon the good earth, the clouds to which the truth of God reaches. This rain and these showers Moses promises in the Song of Deuteronomy (Deut 32:1, 2): Let the earth hear the words of my mouth: let my speech be awaited as the rain, and let my words come down as the dew; so that those who have sown in tears may reap in joy (Ps 125 [126]). And let those who have sown in righteousness and in the spirit reap the fruit of life everlasting, and receive the bread of the Gospel's teaching, of which it is written in Proverbs and in Ecclesiastes: Open your eyes, and be filled with bread (Prov 20:13); and again: Cast your bread upon the water, for in the multitude of your days you will find it (Eccl 11:1). For it is not to be believed that those who eat are commanded that, to eat this bread by which bodies are nourished, they must open their eyes and so be filled with the bread which in Habakkuk the poor man eats in secret (Hab 3). Rather, he exhorts us to the bread of the teaching of God, which we cannot eat unless we have opened the eyes of our heart. Of this Paul too often writes to those who are nourished by the words of faith and truth (2 Cor 9). And the teacher is commanded to cast the bread of his teaching upon every water, and to pour spiritual grace upon all, and to know that if he does what has been commanded, he will receive rewards in the last time. And it would seem unjust enough that, while he who gives alms makes for himself friends of the mammon of iniquity, who may receive him into the eternal tabernacles (Luke 16), he who bestows spiritual foods, and gives his fellow servants their rations in due season, should not find them after many ages, which Ecclesiastes calls the multitude of days (Eccl 11).

55:12-13

For you shall go out in gladness, and be led forth in peace. The mountains and the hills shall sing praise before you, and all the trees of the country shall clap their hands. Instead of the saliunca the fir shall come up, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall grow. And the Lord shall be named for an everlasting sign, which shall not be taken away. LXX: In gladness you shall go out, and in joy you shall be led forth. The mountains and the hills shall leap, awaiting you with joy, and all the trees of the field shall applaud with their branches. And instead of the στοιβὴ (that is, the most worthless stalks) the cypress shall come up: and instead of the conyza the myrtle shall come up. And the Lord shall be for a name and for an everlasting sign, and it shall not fail. My word, he says, shall not return empty, but after it has fulfilled all that I willed, and done my will on earth, then it will come to me; and that will be fulfilled which is written: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps 109 [110]:1, 2). For you shall go out in gladness from the blood of idolatry, and you shall be led forth in peace, so that you may hear from the Apostle: Grace to you and peace (Rom 1:7). Or, you shall be led forth in joy, so that after the shadow of the Law you may learn the truth of the Gospel. For the mountains and hills, by which we can understand the Angels and the souls of the Saints, which are called mountains and hills according to the variety of their virtues, will rejoice over those who repent, and will show the gladness of their mind by leaping. This the Lord also says in the Gospel: The Angels in heaven will rejoice over one sinner who does penance (Luke 15:7). All the trees of the field also shall clap with the hand, or with their branches: those which are planted beside the running waters, which shall give their fruit in its season, and their leaf shall not fall off (Ps 1). One such tree spoke in the psalm: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord (Ps 51 [52]:10). Let us ask those who follow the simple history alone and eat the flesh of the lamb boiled whether trees clap with their branches and applaud with the hand, and in what sense that which is said of the rivers is to be taken: The rivers shall clap with the hand (Ps 97 [98]:8). And not only shall the mountains and hills leap and sing, and all the trees of the field which the Lord has blessed clap with their branches and applaud with their hands, but the στοιβή too and the κονύζη, or the saliunca and the nettle, shall be turned into the fir and the myrtle and the cypress. Στοιβή, according to Symmachus and the Seventy, is written in the Hebrew NESUS (נעצוץ), which Aquila and Theodotion interpreted as κονύζην. Now κονύζη is a most worthless and bitter herb, of a very foul smell. And where the Seventy translated κονύζη, the word which in the Hebrew is SARPHOD (סרפד), Symmachus rendered nettle. However the proper sense of the names stands, this is to be said: that evil things are turned into good, and virtues spring up in place of vices, that is, righteousness in place of iniquity, fortitude in place of rashness, temperance in place of luxury, prudence in place of folly. Let us give examples of our forebears: Matthew and Zacchaeus and the publicans were saliunca, and στοιβή, and useless stalks, and κονύζη of bitter taste and most loathsome smell, saying: My scars have rotted and are corrupted, because of my folly (Ps 37 [38]:6). These, suddenly changed into Apostles, became cypress and fir and myrtle, of the best fragrance and needful for various works. Paul too, the persecutor of the Church, when he heard from the Lord, Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard to kick against the goad (Acts 9:4, 5), was a nettle, having the stings of persecution. But when he preached the Gospel in the whole world and could say, We are the good odor of Christ (2 Cor 2:15), he is rightly called a cypress and a myrtle. Harlots and publicans go before the Pharisees into the kingdom of God, and the thief passes from the cross into paradise (Matt 21). Therefore what is said in the Gospel, A good tree cannot bear evil fruits (Luke 6:43; Matt 7:18), by no means refers to a property of nature, as the heretics would have it, but to the choice of the mind. Finally it is added: Either make the tree good, and its fruits good. From this it is clear that each one by his own will makes his soul a good or an evil tree, whose fruits vary. There follows: And the Lord shall be for a name and for an everlasting sign, which shall not fail. To those who have been changed from evil into good the Lord will be for a name and for an eternal sign, so that from His name they are called Christians, and are branded with the brand of His cross. Of this sign Simeon spoke, holding the little child in his arms: This one shall be for the fall and for the rising again of many, and for a sign which shall be spoken against (Luke 2:34); and of it was said above: The Lord shall give you a sign (Isa 7:14); and the holy man sings in the psalm: Make with me, O Lord, a sign for good (Ps 85 [86]:17). And He Himself who is the sign says: When you see, He says, the sign of the Son of Man: a sign which shall not fail, nor be changed by any end, but shall pass from the present way of life into the future.

56:1

Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment, and do righteousness: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. For righteousness the Seventy translated mercy; the rest alike. The prophecy about the nations being ended, which at the coming of the word of God are to be changed from saliunca and nettle into cypress and myrtle, Isaiah speaks to the hearers of that time, that they should do all things that are right and prepare themselves for the coming of the Savior, because He Himself is the righteousness and mercy of God. For if the thoughts of the Saints are judgments, and we ought to have senses trained for discerning good and evil, why should we not at all times keep judgment, so as not to despise the person of the poor man in judgment, nor be frightened by the power of the rich, but judge the great as we judge the small, knowing, according to Moses, that judgment belongs to the Lord, who judges those who judge (Deut 1)? In accordance with which we also read in the psalm: God has stood in the synagogue of gods: and in the midst He judges the gods (Ps 81 [82]:1). To what is now said, Keep judgment, and do righteousness, this is like: Blessed are they who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times (Ps 105 [106]:3), so that they may pursue justly what is just. And yet under the name of righteousness the whole field seems to me to be signified: that he who has done one righteousness is said to have fulfilled all the virtues, which follow one another and cling to each other, so that he who has one has all, and he who lacks one lacks all. Something of the kind the fourteenth psalm also sounds: He who walks without blemish and works righteousness (Ps 14 [15]:2). And elsewhere it is written: Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth (Isa 26:9). And that the Savior, who has been made for us righteousness and holiness and redemption, is Himself the mercy of God (1 Cor 1), the words of the saints testify: And God sent His mercy and His truth (Ps 56 [57]:4).

56:2

Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who lays hold of it: keeping the sabbath, so as not to profane it: keeping his hands, so as not to do any evil. LXX: Blessed is the man who shall do these things, and the man who holds them fast, and keeps the sabbaths, so as not to profane them, and guards his hands, so as not to do iniquity. He who can say with the apostle Paul: When I was a little child, I spoke as a little child; I understood as a little child, I thought as a little child; when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belong to a little child (1 Cor 13:11): he obtains the present blessedness, forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself forward to what is to come, until he attains to the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to the perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ; so that that psalm can be fitted to him: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly (Ps 1:1). This man, then, and son of the inner man, of whom it is said more than once in Leviticus, Man, man (Lev 17:8), is blessed in this, that he first does, and then lays hold of, these things: namely judgment and righteousness and the salvation of the Lord, which is near and is to be revealed to all the nations; so that he not only does what is commanded but holds it with a tight hand; and keeps the sabbath, so as not to profane it. And what the sabbath is which he has commanded to be kept the following verse shows: Keeping his hands, so as not to do any evil. For it profits nothing to sit still on the sabbath, or to sleep, and to gape after feasts; rather, it profits if one, doing good, rests from evil, and keeps a continual sabbath, that is, a rest, from iniquity, and does only those things that pertain to the salvation of the soul, and does not set his hand to any servile work. For he who commits sin is the slave of sin (John 8). But we have been called into freedom, with which freedom Christ has endowed us (Gal 4), so that we may by no means work for the food that perishes; but, cleaving to the Lord, let us say with the Prophet: But for me it is good to cleave to God (Ps 72 [73]:28). Let us become one spirit with Him, and let us fulfill the dedicated sabbaths, lest we be of the six days in which the world was made, to which the Apostles did not belong, to whom the Lord said: If you were of this world, the world would love what is its own. But now you are not of this world, because I have chosen you, and therefore the world hates you (John 15:19).

56:3

And let not the son of the stranger who cleaves to the Lord say: The Lord will divide me from His people with a separation: and let not the eunuch say: Behold, I am a dry tree. LXX: Let not the foreigner who has been joined to the Lord say: Do you think the Lord will separate me from His people? and let not the eunuch say: For I am a dry tree. Those who understand this passage in a lowly way refer what is said to proselytes from the nations and to eunuchs in the literal sense: that both strangers, if they have taken up the law of the Lord and are circumcised, and eunuchs, such as was that eunuch of Queen Candace (Acts 8), who could not be idle even on a journey, and, while he sought an interpreter of his reading, found Christ whom he was seeking, are not strangers to the salvation of God. And this, they say, is said against the Jews, who boast of the nobility of their race, and say that they are sons of Abraham, and think those blessed who have seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem (John 8). But we understand that the same people whom we interpreted above (above, on Isa 55) through the saliunca and the nettle and the κονύζην and the στοιβήν as turned into the fir and the cypress and the myrtle are now summoned to the faith of the Gospel: that they ought not to despair if they cleave to the Lord, nor think themselves separated from the people of God. For all who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ (Gal 3:27). There is neither Jew nor Gentile, Circumcision nor Uncircumcision; to whom it is commanded in the Song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, you nations, with His people, that is, of God, who had as His former people the Jews (Deut 32:43). These, coming from the East and the West, will rest in the bosom of Abraham. This is what John the Baptist also said: And do not say, We have Abraham as our father. For I say to you: God is able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham (Matt 3:9). And as among the proselytes there is no difference, but both men and women are called equally to salvation, so too among the eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven both sexes are included: those who have put to death their members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, until all attain to the perfect man and say with the Apostle: We know no one according to the flesh. And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him no longer (2 Cor 5:16). Therefore by eunuchs are by no means to be understood those whom the fiery poet describes, saying (Lucan, Book 10): And the unhappy youth too, maimed by the steel, and cut away from manhood........ But those of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:12); such were the Apostles too, to whom, when they wondered and said because of the difficulty of the thing, Who then can be saved?, the Savior answered: He who can take it, let him take it. Hence the Apostle too testifies that concerning eunuchs of this kind, that is, concerning virgins, he has no commandment of the Lord, but gives counsel as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord, wishing all to be as himself: For the time, he says, is short: it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none (1 Cor 7:29). For he who has been called free from the bondage and duty of marriage is truly the slave of Christ.

56:4-5

For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: If they keep my sabbaths, and choose the things I have willed, and hold fast my covenant, I will give them in my house and within my walls a place, and a name better than sons and daughters: an everlasting name I will give them, which shall not perish. LXX: Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that I will, and hold fast my testament, I will give them in my house and within my wall a renowned place, better than sons and daughters: an everlasting name I will give them, and it shall not fail. He had set forth two, proselytes and eunuchs. He speaks first of the eunuchs, and gives them precepts for living, and promises them the rewards to come; and after them he comes to the proselytes, promising them also like things. He speaks, then, to the eunuchs, who in despair said, Behold, I am a withered tree (Exod 23), that they should not think themselves subject to the curse spoken to the barren: Cursed is the barren one who does not raise up seed in Israel (Deut 7). If, he says, they keep my sabbaths, and choose out of my precepts those things which I have willed, and not those which I have conceded because of the weakness of the hearers, and hold fast my covenant or testament with all fidelity, I will give them in my house, and in my Temple, and within the walls of my most strongly fortified city, a place, and a name better than sons and daughters, which shall be blotted out by no forgetfulness. Who the eunuchs are we have said above: those who are anxious for the things that are God's; to whom the Wisdom also speaks which is inscribed with the title of Solomon: Blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not known the bed in transgression; she shall have fruit in the visitation of souls. And the eunuch who has not wrought iniquity with his hand, nor devised evil things against the Lord: for the chosen grace of his faith shall be given him, and a most delightful portion in the temple of the Lord (Wis 3:13, 14). This barren woman is fruitful in virginity; this eunuch does violence to the kingdom of heaven and takes it by force. He is a keeper of the sabbaths, so as never to do the works of marriage (1 Cor 7). He has chosen what the Lord willed, so as to offer more than is commanded: so as to consider not the indulgence of His Apostle but his will. He holds fast the everlasting covenant of the Lord, so as not to be free for prayer for a time and then return again to the same thing, but he knows that he will receive in the house of the Lord, which is His Church, the best place. For there are many mansions with the Father (John 14). And he who has been a eunuch and has done all the things that are written will have the best place within His walls, namely, so as to become a tower of the Lord and to stand in the priestly rank, and instead of sons of the flesh to have many spiritual sons. That such a eunuch was the Evangelist John, whom Jesus loved most, the histories of the Church relate: he who reclined on the breast of Jesus (John 13); who, while Peter walked more slowly, ran to the Lord borne up on the wings of virginity (John 20); who, plunging himself into the secrets of the divine nativity, dared to say what all the ages had not known: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: He was in the beginning with God (John 1:2). Away, then, with all the cavilling of the Jews, and let it cease to make itself ridiculous at the opening of the kingdom of heaven to half-men, since chastity lies not in the weakness of the body but in the will of the mind.

56:6-7

And the sons of the stranger who cleave to the Lord, to worship Him and to love His name, so as to be His servants: everyone who keeps the sabbath so as not to profane it, and holds fast my covenant, I will bring them to my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer. LXX: And to the foreigners who have been added to the Lord to serve Him, and to love His name, so as to be His servants ÷ and handmaids ⁚ and all who keep my sabbaths so as not to violate them, and hold fast my testament, I will bring them into my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer. After the eunuchs he passes to the foreigners whom he had named before, and to them also he promises rewards: that if they serve Him, and pass from servitude to the love of His name, they shall be His servants; such as was the Apostle Paul too, who writes at the beginning of his Epistles: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ (Rom 1:1); and Moses, the servant of God (Heb 3). And that and handmaids has been added in the Seventy we have marked beforehand with an obelus. For it cannot be that in spiritual gifts there should be any difference of sex, since in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female, but in Him we are all one (John 17). Of the sabbath and the everlasting covenant we have spoken above. Whoever, then, does these things, God will bring him to His holy mountain and fill him with gladness in His house of prayer. The holy mountain is either the doctrines of truth and the confession of the Trinity, or the Lord Himself, to whom in the last time (according to this same Isaiah and the prophet Micah) very many nations shall flow together (Isa 2; Mic 4). And the house of prayer is the Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, and not the Temple of the Jews, which was confined within the very narrow bounds of the land of Judea.

56:8-9

Their holocausts and their victims shall please me upon my altar: for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples, says the Lord God, who gathers the scattered of Israel: I will yet gather to him his gathered ones. All you beasts of the field, come to devour, all you beasts of the forest. LXX: Their holocausts and victims shall be acceptable upon my altar. For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, says the Lord, who gathers the scattered of Israel: for I will gather to him a congregation. All you wild beasts, come, eat, all you beasts of the forest. The difference between sacrifices and holocausts we learn more fully in Leviticus. Holocausts are those which are burned whole upon the altar; victims and sacrifices are those of which part is offered to the altar and part is given to the priests. It is not to be believed, then, that the sacrifices of the foreigners and the eunuchs are required according to the Jewish rite. But we ought to know this: that the eunuchs offer holocausts, since they consecrate themselves wholly to God; and the foreigners victims, since they are free for prayer for a time; of which God says: The sacrifice of praise has glorified me; and in another place: Offer to God the sacrifice of praise (Ps 49 [50]:14). Of these victims and holocausts the Lord speaks through Hosea: I desire mercy and not sacrifice: the knowledge of God more than holocausts, which are offered upon the altar of the Lord (Hos 6:6); the altar which John in the Apocalypse testifies that he saw in heaven, under which were the souls of the martyrs (Rev 6); from which one of the Seraphim, grasping a coal with tongs, brought it to purify the lips of Isaiah (Isa 6:6). This is the altar, and this the tabernacle, to whose likeness all the things made in Exodus are referred, by which spiritual victims have been offered to God (Exod 38). Otherwise, concerning bodily sacrifices and holocausts, the same God testifies above: To what purpose do I want the multitude of your victims? says the Lord. I am full of the holocaust of rams, and of the fat of lambs, and the blood of bulls and goats I do not want. For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. Not for the one nation of Judea, nor in the one place of Jerusalem and its city, but in the whole world; by no means of bulls and goats and rams, but of prayer. This testimony the Lord made use of when He spoke against those who, under the name of the Holy Spirit, sold the gifts of doves in the Temple, and sat in the chairs of pestilence, and had the tables of the money-changers (Matt 21 and John 2), doing all things for the sake of shameful gain, not knowing what is written: Freely you have received, freely give (Matt 10:8). These things the Lord promised would be, He who gathers the scattered of Israel; to whom the Apostle Peter also writes an Epistle; of whom the Evangelist says: This he did not say of himself, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that He might gather into one the sons of God who were scattered (John 11:51, 52); and that might be fulfilled which was said: The congregation of the peoples shall surround you: for its sake return on high (Ps 7:8). And when the remnant of Israel had been gathered through the Apostles, and those who before had been scattered had been brought into one flock, all the beasts are summoned to come and devour Israel, namely those who would not believe, of whom the Apostle says: For the end shall come upon them (Phil 3). And the Lord in the Gospel: But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its consummation has come (Luke 21:20).
