Or this is to be said: that they were handed over to be devoured by the beasts which the Prophet abhors, saying: Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess to you (Ps 73 [74]:19). Of these beasts, tropologically, which devoured a certain portion of the Lord, we have read above also (cf. Isa 9): Syria from the rising of the sun, and the Greeks from the West, who devour Israel with their whole mouth. And in Jeremiah: Israel is a wandering sheep, the lions have driven it out: first the king of Assyria devoured it, and last the king of Babylon shall break its bones (Jer 50:17). This too can be said: that together with the people of Israel the nations, formerly ravening, are summoned to faith, so that, leaving the forests which slew very many of Absalom's army, they may come to the Church, and eat the heavenly bread, and be filled with the flesh of the Lamb.

56:10, 12

His watchmen are all blind, they have all not known: dumb dogs, not able to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping, and loving dreams. And the most shameless dogs have not known fullness: the shepherds themselves have not known understanding: all have turned aside into their own way, each to his own avarice, from the highest to the last. Come, let us take wine, and be filled with drunkenness, and it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more. LXX: See how they have all been blinded: they have all not known, dumb dogs, they will not be able to bark: dreaming of a bed, loving slumbers. And dogs shameless of soul have not known fullness. And they are evil, not knowing understanding: they have all followed their own ways. Each one alike from its summit. Come and let us take wine, and be drunk, and let tomorrow be such a day, great, exceedingly more ⁚. So that all the beasts of the forest may come and devour those who have been gathered, he says, or so that the throngs of the nations may succeed into the place of the Jews, their watchmen are the cause, namely the Scribes and the Pharisees: because they were all blind and did not know the Lord the Savior, nor would they see the present light. To them the Lord said: Fools and blind, which is greater, the gold, or the altar that sanctifies the gold (Matt 23:17)? and again: Blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel (ibid., 24); and: The blind leading the blind, both fall into the pit (Matt 15:14). And that teachers are called watchmen we have read above also. For in the place where, according to the Seventy, it is said: The voice of your guardians has been lifted up (Isa 52:8), in the Hebrew is written: The voice of your watchmen. Of these was Ezekiel, to whom God says: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel (Ezek 3:17). But those watchmen were not blind; indeed, they were called seers. But these of whom the Prophet now speaks are called not only blind watchmen but also dumb dogs, not able to bark. For those who ought to have guarded the Lord's flock, and driven off the wolves, and barked for the Lord, love dreams and delight in demonic visions. And the sense is: they cannot speak the truth, but all lies. Nor were they content with this end, they who slept in guarding the Lord's flock, and could not bark, and loved their couch, by which the pleasure of the body is indicated; but among their own, shameless of soul, they have not known fullness, they who are never sated with their error; who devour the people of the Lord as a meal of bread, and the houses of widows, and serve gluttony and lust. For they cannot say: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9), nor know what is written: A man's wisdom enlightens his face (Prov 17:24). And they are dumb dogs against the enemies, of whom it is written: Do not give what is holy to the dogs (Matt 7:6). And sleeping dogs, who do not know the precept: Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids (Ps 131 [132]); and again: Watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come (Matt 24:42). And therefore, giving place to the devil, they are most shameless dogs, which are never sated. For they vomit what they have eaten, and return to their vomit (Prov 26). Of them the Apostle Peter also speaks: There has happened to them that true proverb: The dog returned to his vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire (2 Pet 2:22). That these watchmen and dogs are the same as the shepherds the following words show: The shepherds themselves have not known understanding. For the Hebrew word ROIM (רעים), which is written with four letters, res and ain and jod and mem, if it is read roim, means shepherds; if raim, the worst. We have said this to show the causes of the varying interpretation. For all have sought their own things, and not the things that are God's, nor have they walked in the way of the Lord (Phil 2), of which it is written: Seek which is the good way, and walk in it (Jer 6:16). But according to what is read in the volume of Judges: There was no king in Israel; each one did what seemed right to himself (Judg 17:6), and followed his own errors. And what follows: Each to his own avarice, from the highest to the last: come, let us take wine, and be filled with drunkenness, and it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more, is not found in the Seventy Translators, but has been added from the Hebrew and is marked beforehand with shining stars. In short, none of the Church's interpreters has expounded these little verses, but they leap over them and pass them by, as if a pit lay open in the middle of the road. And what he says is this: since, turning aside from the way of the Lord, they have followed their own paths, therefore they burn with avarice from the highest to the last, from the princes to the common people, so that, after they have begun to beat their fellow servants, and to eat and drink with the drunken, they say: Come, let us take wine, and be filled with drunkenness. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more (1 Cor 15:32). This is what he said above: They have not known fullness: they are not sated with past pleasure, but prepare future delights, much greater than those they had enjoyed before. If this is said of the princes of the Jews, because of whom the people of the Lord was devoured by the beasts, let us avoid the examples of the worse; let us not be drunk with wine, in which is luxury, nor be overwhelmed by pleasures; let us not be dumb in speaking and ravening dogs against our adversaries; but let us follow the ways of God rather than our own, and hear the Scripture warning us: Think of the Lord in goodness (Wis 1:1). And again: Understanding is best for those who practice it. And if we have been dogs, let us not despair of salvation, hearing the words of the Canaanite woman saying to the Lord: Yes, Lord, for the little dogs also eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters' table (Matt 15:27). For this reason she obtained mercy, and heard from the Lord: O woman, great is your faith: be it done to you as you will. For she could say with the Prophet: I have run the way of your commandments (Ps 118 [119]:32). And again: Lead me in the right way.

57:1-2

The righteous man has perished, and there is none who reflects on it in his heart: and men of mercy are gathered, for there is none who understands: for the righteous man has been gathered away from the face of malice. Let peace come: let him rest in his bed, who walks in his uprightness. LXX: See how the righteous man has perished, and no one takes it to heart: and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers. For the righteous man has been taken away from the face of iniquity: his burial shall be in peace: it has been taken away from the midst. Because of the blind watchmen and the dumb dogs, who are themselves the shepherds, not knowing understanding, who are not sated with present pleasures but are always preparing themselves for future ones, the righteous man has perished, of whom Pilate's wife says: Have nothing to do with that righteous man (Matt 27:19). And Pilate, having washed his hands: I am innocent, he says, of the blood of this righteous man. Herein it is to be considered that the word of perdition, about which the heretics often raise a cavil, that it signifies destruction and abolition forever, is applied to Christ, whose perdition certainly shows the greatness of the persecution, and not an end of substance. And there is no one, he says, who reflects on it in his heart, or lays it up. For it could not be that the blind and dumb, seeing vain things and loving dreams, and ignorant of understanding and wisdom, should think of the things that are God's. And what follows, And men of mercy, or righteous men, are gathered and taken away, signifies the Apostles, who are slain by the ungodly and gathered by the Lord. And he gives the reasons why the righteous man was slain and taken away, saying: For the righteous man has been gathered away from the face of malice, so that he might not see the evils of the world; or, because of the malice of men, whose sins He Himself bore, He ascended as victor to the Father. And as for what is said according to the Hebrew, Let peace come, let him rest in his bed: let him walk in his uprightness, the sense indeed is clear, but the sequence of the words, which stands in the idiom of its own language, seems disordered in ours. And what he says is this: Let the peace of the Righteous One come, which, ascending to the Father, He left to the Apostles, saying: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you (John 14:27). And when the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, has come, His Apostles will rest in their beds, and their death will rest. By this he shows that the martyrs do not perish but conquer, and rest in an eternal seat. But He Himself whose peace it is, and whose Apostles rest in their beds, walks in His uprightness, ascending as victor to the Father by a straight road. Further, what is read in the Seventy, The righteous man has been taken away from the face of malice, his burial shall be in peace, it has been taken away from the midst, is all referred to Christ, without mingling in the person of the Apostles: His burial is in peace, and has been taken away from the midst. For His flesh did not see corruption, nor did He remain in the sepulcher, He who is free among the dead, as the Angel says to the women: Jesus whom you seek is not here: Come and see the place where the Lord was laid (Matt 28:5, 6). The Jews think that both this and the rest that follow are to be understood either generally of all the righteous, whose blood Manasseh shed, and filled Jerusalem from gate to gate; or else that Isaiah prophesies of his own death, because he was to be sawn by Manasseh with a wooden saw, which is a most certain tradition among them. Hence most of our own writers also refer what is set down in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning the passion of the Saints, They were sawn asunder (Heb 11:37), to the passion of Isaiah.

Book Sixteen

It is an excellent saying of a most eloquent orator: The arts would be happy if only the artists judged them. And lest I seem to take my example only from profane writers, this is surely what the Prophet shows in other words: Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who listen (Sir 25:12). You, my daughter Eustochium, have made me a sharer in that happiness. For when you read the little preface of the previous book, in which I asserted that the Apostles and Evangelists, whether in their own words or in those of the Seventy Translators, set down from the Seventy only those testimonies that agree with the Hebrew, and wholly passed over whatever had been added by others, you at once brought me no small little question: namely, that the Apostle, writing to the Romans, made use of eight verses of the thirteenth psalm which are read in the churches but are not found in the Hebrew: Their throat is an open sepulcher; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips. Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and the way of peace they have not known; there is no fear of God before their eyes (Rom 3:13ff.). When I heard this, as though I had been struck by a most powerful boxer, I began to seethe in silence and to betray the stupor of my mind by the pallor of my face. A Hebrew, I said, of the Hebrews, as to the law a Pharisee, and taught at the feet of Gamaliel, either did not know these things, or abused the ignorance of those who were going to read him (Phil 3:5; Acts 22:3). The one of these belongs to an unlearned man, the other to one cunning in malice, and neither to him who said: Though I be unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge (2 Cor 11:6); and again: in simplicity and sincerity I have announced the word to you (2 Cor 1:12). At last, coming back to myself, I asked for the space of one day, so that my answer might in no way be the product of human wit, but the fruit of constant reading. And so, running through the whole of Scripture in my mind, I noticed that, just as almost the whole Epistle to the Romans is built out of the Old Instrument, so this testimony too has been woven together from the Psalms and Isaiah (Verse 11). For the first two verses, Their throat is an open sepulcher; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully, belong to the fifth psalm (Verse 11). What follows, The poison of asps is under their lips, belongs to the hundred and thirty-ninth psalm (Verse 4). Again, what is said, Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, is taken from the ninth psalm (Verse 29). The three little verses that follow, Their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and the way of peace they have not known, I found in the prophet Isaiah, and I am going to expound them in the sixteenth book of my explanation of him, which I now wish to dictate. The last verse, that is, the eighth, There is no fear of God before their eyes, is at the beginning of the thirty-fifth psalm. Nor should it seem to anyone a discrepancy if what is said in the singular number in its own places is said in the plural by the Apostle, who was writing to many and was drawing many examples together into one sense. I think your question is solved, and that our rule about the translation of the Old Instrument has been shaken rather than moved. And it is not so much that the Apostle took from the thirteenth psalm what is not found in the Hebrew, as that those who did not know the Apostle's art of weaving the Scriptures together sought a fitting place in which to set the testimony he had taken up, since they did not think it had been set down in Scripture without authority. In short, all the Greek commentators who have left us commentaries on the Psalms from their learning mark these little verses with an obelus and pass them by, plainly confessing that they are not found in the Hebrew, nor are they in the Seventy Translators, but in the common edition, which in Greek is called κοινὴ, and which differs throughout the whole world. But now it is time for us to apply ourselves to the work we have begun and to pursue what remains.

57:3-4

But draw near hither, you sons of the sorceress, seed of the adulterer and of the harlot. Against whom have you made sport? Against whom have you opened wide the mouth and thrust out the tongue? LXX: But draw near hither, you lawless sons, seed of adulterers and of a harlot. In what have you made sport? Against whom have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you thrust out your tongue? The righteous man having been taken away, whose burial is in peace, or rather having been taken out of the midst, you who are sons of iniquity, draw near to me and hear what I shall say (John 8). For just as he who commits iniquity is a slave of iniquity, so he who, like Judas the traitor, is a son of perdition, can be called a son of iniquity. Indeed it is written of the Lord the Savior: And the son of iniquity shall not proceed to afflict him (Ps 88 [89]:23). For of iniquity, or of the lawless, which the Seventy translated, Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, ONENA (עננה), which we, following Symmachus, have rendered of the sorceress, because, that is, Jerusalem, who is the mother of those who hear, was always given over to idolatry. Therefore he calls them the seed of the adulterer, or of adulterers (of whom it is said: And they committed adultery with wood and stone [Jer 3:9]), and of a harlot; and without doubt he means the same woman of whom we read above: How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot? (Isa 1:21). Against whom, he says, have you made sport, spitting in his face and plucking his beard; and against whom have you opened wide and opened your mouth, and thrust out your tongue, saying to him: You are a Samaritan and have a demon (John 8:48)? And again: This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons (Matt 12:24). And afterward, at the passion: Crucify, crucify such a one (Luke 23:21). And again: His blood be on us and on our children (Matt 27:25). And elsewhere: Ah, you who destroy the Temple and in three days rebuild it! He saved others; himself he cannot save. Let him come down now from the cross, and we believe him (ibid. 40).

57:4-5

Are you not wicked sons, a lying seed, you who take comfort in gods under every leafy tree, sacrificing little children in the torrents under the overhanging rocks? LXX: Are you not sons of perdition, a lawless seed, you who call upon idols under leafy trees, sacrificing your sons in the valleys in the midst of the rock? You, he says, have done these things which the preceding discourse has related. You who are wicked sons, or sons of perdition, such as was Judas the traitor, who was called the son of perdition (John 17); and a lawless seed, or a lying seed and a seed of falsehood, who delight in gods under every leafy tree, and sacrifice your sons in the torrents (Acts 8). Of this the history of Kings and of Chronicles also tells, that they sacrificed their sons to gods and consecrated them in the fire (2 Kgs 16 and 17). That Ahab king of Israel and Manasseh king of Judah did this is not in doubt; they went on from the murder of their children to the blood of the Prophets. Of this also it says in Hosea: Sacrifice men, he says, for the calves have failed (Hos 13:2); or, as it is written in the Hebrew: Sacrificing men, you adore calves. And in the psalms it is written more fully: They were mingled among the nations and learned their works, and served their graven images, and it became a stumbling block to them. And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and they shed innocent blood, or harmless: the blood of their sons and of their daughters, and they sacrificed to the graven images of Canaan. And the land was stained with bloods, and was polluted in their works (Ps 105 [106]:35ff.). Since, then, the history is plain, that the slayers of Christ are the sons of those who did these things, a question arises against those who will have it that there are different natures, one lost and evil, which cannot be saved, and another good, which cannot perish: how are sons called sons of perdition? For if, as they think, the sons of perdition are of a most evil nature, how was that found which had first been lost? Indeed in the parables of the penitent, both the sheep lost out of a hundred sheep and the drachma that had perished out of ten are recovered, and the lost son is found, of whom the father had said to the elder son: This your brother had perished, and is found; he was dead, and has come to life again (Luke 15:32). For nothing ever perishes unless it was first safe, and nothing ever dies unless it had lived before. Therefore these who are now called sons of perdition, or of iniquity and wickedness, forsook the Lord by their own fault, and from sons of the Lord began to be sons of perdition, as this same Prophet says to them: You have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger (Isa 1:4). We can also take these things, according to tropology, of the heretics, who are sons of perdition and a most evil seed, or a seed of falsehood. For they are liars from the beginning, like the devil, who is its father, who is the father of every lie. These call those whom they have deceived to idols, or to the images of their dogmas, under leafy and shady trees, promising them pleasures and delights, or concealing their impurities. Hence Adam too, after he had sinned, hid himself in paradise under a tree, so as not to be open to the sight of God (Gen 3). Nor is there any doubt that sons of perdition of this kind, and a lawless seed, have very many sons, whomever they have deceived, and that they slay them in deep valleys and in the abyss of impiety under overhanging rocks, which always threaten to fall; and these, because of the diversity of falsehood and the variety of perverse dogmas, are called rocks in the plural. But we have one rock, which always follows the people of God, from which the people of Israel once drank, when it enjoyed the familiar friendship of the Lord.

57:6

In the parts of the torrent is your portion; this is your lot, and to them you have poured out a libation, you have offered a sacrifice. Shall I not be angry over these things? LXX: This is your portion, this is your lot; and to them you have poured out libations, and to these you have prepared victims. Shall I not then be angry over these things? The things said fit the times of Isaiah. For all the mountains, valleys and torrents were full of the worship of demons, of which Jeremiah speaks: that the fathers and sons gather wood and kindle the fire, to make chavonas for the host of heaven, while the women knead and mix fat with fine flour, in order to provoke the Lord to anger (Jer 7). And no one doubts that he means cakes, or little pastries prepared by the hand of an artisan; for that is what chavonas means in our tongue. Of these Moses, speaking in the person of the Lord with a prophetic spirit, sang beforehand in the Canticle of Deuteronomy: They provoked me with strange gods, and with their abominations they stirred me to anger; they sacrificed to demons and not to God (Deut 32:16, 17); and this they did by their own will, because it lies in our choice to choose good or evil. Thus to those who have offered themselves to God by virtues it is said: He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, which he loved (Ps 46 [47]:5). And in another place: The Lord's portion was made his people Jacob, Israel the cord of his inheritance (Deut 32:9). And in the Acts of the Apostles it is related that very many gave themselves to the portion and lot of Paul and Silas. Those, then, who have been the portion and lot of the Lord, like the Levites, will have the Lord as their portion and will be able to say with David: The Lord is my portion (Ps 72 [73]:26). These things we can also take of the person of the heretics. For they, having abandoned the worship of God, venerate the images of their errors, and offer victims to them and pour out libations, doing in secret things that it is shameful even to speak of, and leading captive silly women laden with sins, who are led away by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3). Since, then, the impious do these things in both kinds of impiety, is it not just that the anger of God should be provoked against them?

57:7

Upon a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you went up to sacrifice victims. And behind the door and back of the post you have set your memorial. LXX likewise. That Israel sacrificed victims to the gods of the nations on high mountains and hills, and like a most shameless harlot spread her feet for all the demons, sacred history relates; and there was no place that was not defiled by the filth of idolatry, so much so that they set idols behind the doors of their houses, which they call the household Lares, and poured out the blood of their souls in public as much as in private. With this error and most evil custom of antiquity the cities of many provinces are afflicted; and Rome herself, the mistress of the world, venerates with wax tapers and lamps, in every tenement block and every house, the image of Tutela, whom they call by that name for the protection of their dwellings, so that, as they enter and as they leave their homes, they may be ever reminded of their inveterate error. The heretics too, whose heart is lifted up in pride, and who, despising the humility of the Church, promise themselves lofty things, go up the most lofty mountains of their dogmas, and there prostitute their bed to demons. And because, according to the Prophet, they have turned backward, imitating the wife of Lot (Gen 19), they are changed into a pillar of salt, having the appearance of the Church's seasoning and none of its savor at all; they are cast out of doors, and are good for nothing except to be trodden under the feet of all. Therefore the Lord warns in the Gospel that he who holds the handle of the plow should not look behind him (Luke 9).

57:9

For beside me you have uncovered yourself and received the adulterer; you have enlarged your bed, and you have made a covenant with them; you have loved their couch with open hand; and you adorned yourself for the king with ointment, and you have multiplied your perfumes. You sent your envoys far off, and you were humbled even to hell. LXX: You thought that if you had departed from me you would have something more. You have loved those who sleep with you, and you have multiplied your fornication with them, and you have made many to be far from you, and you have sent envoys beyond your borders, and you were humbled even to hell. Let us discuss the Hebrew first, which in this place differs much from the Seventy. To her of whom he had said above, Upon a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and whom he had rebuked as a harlot, prostituted at the entrance of houses and in dark places behind the doors, so that whoever wished to enter the dwelling might have the pleasure set out before his eyes: this same woman he now rebukes and refutes as an adulterous wife, because, while sleeping with her husband, she secretly received the adulterer, and uncovered the coverlet, or rather enlarged her bed, and made a pact, as though drawing up the instruments of a dowry with the adulterers. He says this to show that they worshiped idols not only in the fields and in houses, but also set up the image of Baal in the Temple, which Ezekiel too says he saw when he had dug through the wall. You have loved, he says, their couch with open hand (Ezek 8), so that you did not blush at your sin, nor desire to hide the shame of your fornication, but sinned with all freedom. And you adorned yourself for the king with ointment, and you have multiplied your idols. And the sense is: You sought various ornaments, so as to entice the adulterers both by sight and by scent. What is said, you adorned yourself for the king with ointment, is understood in two ways: either for God the king, while you adorn yourself with the things that he had given and prostitute yourself to idols; or certainly for the king who is the idol of the Ammonites, who is called Moloch, which in our tongue means king, and whom according to the Seventy we read in other places as Melchom (Zeph 1). And you sent your envoys far off, so that you might have a zeal for fornication not only with the idols of the neighboring nations, but also with those of nations set far away. He means the gods of Babylon and of Egypt. And you were humbled, he says, even to hell: not with the humility that is praised, but with that by which Amnon had humbled his sister Tamar (2 Sam 13). And truly it is a great humiliation, or rather a hurling down even to hell, to be hurled from the light and summit of chastity into the darkness of the brothel, or rather into the abyss of lusts. To her it is said in another place: You shall be brought down even to hell. According to the Seventy, in the things in which they disagree, the sense seems to me this: Did you think, harlot, that if you had departed from me and joined yourself to your lovers, you would find something more? To her God also speaks through Ezekiel: To all harlots wages are given, but you have given wages, and in you this perverse thing has been done (Ezek 16:33). For not only did you receive nothing from your lovers, but you even lost the things you had received from your husband. What follows, You have enlarged your bed, and you have made a covenant with them, is not found in the Seventy. This woman loved those who sleep with her, the blind watchmen and the dumb dogs, who in their sleep see dreams of vanity. And she multiplied her fornication, so as to have intercourse not once with one, but often and with very many. For this reason she made many depart far from her: the Angels who were her guardians, or the holy men who withdrew from the company of such a harlot. This we can also say of the heretics, who, having forsaken God, follow their own errors and think they have something more, when by following falsehoods they have lost the truth, and have multiplied their fornication, not in one dogma but in many, and have made the Angels who preside over the Churches depart from them; who, not content with fornication near at hand, send envoys beyond their borders to the dogmas of the gentiles and the errors of barbarous nations, in order to deceive their hearers with novelty of words.

57:10

In the multitude of your way you have labored, and you did not say: I will rest. You have found the life of your hand; therefore you have not asked me. LXX: In your many journeys you have labored, and you did not say: I will leave off. Strengthened, you have done these things; therefore you have not asked me. He who walks in the one royal way does not labor, the way about which God commanded through Moses: You shall walk in the royal way, and you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left (Deut 5:32). There is one way of truth, which says in the Gospel: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6); and many ways of falsehood, in which Jerusalem is now accused of having walked. God, knowing the difference between these ways, speaks above to those who stray: Your ways are not as my ways (Isa 55:8); and they, confessing to the Lord, say: You have made our ways turn aside from your ways (Ps 43 [44]:19). Having come to know, then, the one royal way, let us see which are the ways to the right and to the left, by which we are forbidden to go. The royal way is the tempered one, having in itself neither more nor less. For example, the straight and royal way is prudence. We turn aside to the right if we are wiser than we ought to be wise, and love cunning instead of prudence; for the serpent was more prudent than all the beasts in paradise (Gen 3), and the sons of darkness are more prudent than the sons of light (Luke 16). And we turn off to the left when we are foolish and are less wise than is needful; of whom it is said: The fool has said in his heart, There is no God (Ps 13 [14]:1). Piety too and true religion is a royal way. He turns aside to the right who is superstitious, and deserves to hear: Be not overly righteous (Eccl 7:17); to the left, he who neglects the worship of God and is numbered among the kids and the he-goats. Liberality too and stewardship is a very great virtue, from which he turns aside to the right who is stingy and does not give what is needful, not only to others but not even to himself; to the left, he who devours his substance with harlots and says with Israel: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die (Isa 22:13). Fortitude also and constancy is a royal way, from which he turns aside to the right who is rash and stubborn, to the left he who is fearful and timid. Hence the holy man, desiring to walk by the straight way, prays: Lead me, Lord, in the straight way (Ps 138 [139]:24). And in another place: Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I should walk, for to you I have lifted up my eyes (Ps 142 [143]:8). Of a way of this kind Scripture also speaks elsewhere: Seek the good way and walk in it, and you shall find purification for your souls (Jer 6:16). Jerusalem, then, was humbled even to hell for this reason, that she labored in many ways and did not say: I will amend my error by repentance; but on the contrary: I will be strengthened in what I have begun, and I will not heed the sentence of him who warns: Turn your foot away from the rough way, and your throat from thirst (Jer 2:25). Then it follows: But she answered, ἀνδρίσομαι, that is, I will act manfully, which is now said with another word: I will be strengthened. And because she has done the things that the preceding discourse related, therefore she has not entreated the Lord, having confidence in her own strength rather than in God. Further, what is set down according to the Hebrew, You have found the life of your hand; therefore you have not asked, has this sense and meaning: Because you have abounded in all things and overflowed with riches, therefore you have neglected the Lord. Such riches Solomon too refuses to have, lest he forget God (Prov 30 and 31). And to Sodom it is said through Ezekiel that because she was filled with bread, she therefore grew proud (Ezek 16). Yet not only riches but poverty too tests a man. Hence it is written above: I have tested you in the furnace of poverty (Isa 48), in which Lazarus too was tested, the poor man who endured want and infirmity together (Luke 16).

57:11

For whom have you been anxious and feared, that you have lied, and have not remembered me, nor thought of me in your heart? For I am silent and as one not seeing, and you have forgotten me. LXX: Whom have you feared and been terrified of, and you have lied to me, and have not remembered me? Nor have you set me in your mind and in your heart. And I, seeing you, will despise you, and you have not feared me. Because, with your barns full, you have confidence in riches and would not ask me, therefore you have feared a great many. For you could not say: The Lord is my helper, and I will look down on my enemies (Ps 117 [118]:7); and again: The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear? (Ps 26 [27]:1). And even if at some time you wished to say this against the conscience of your mind, you lied. For how could you call upon me, you who had no memory of me, and never thought on the precepts of him who says: Honor the Lord, and you shall be strengthened, and apart from him fear no one (Prov 7:1)? For I am he who, according to Symmachus and Aquila, always kept silent about your sins, and passed over with dissimulation whatever crimes you committed, as though I did not see them, so that you might return to me, if not out of fear of me, at least because of my patience; I who question the sons of men not with my eyes but with my eyelids. But you on the contrary have forgotten me, and have deserved to hear: You have forgotten the law of your God, and I will forget your sons (Hos 4:6). And again: They walked perversely against me, and I will walk against them in perverse fury. The mind, which in the Seventy is joined with the heart, is not written in the Hebrew, but has been added as a kind of interpretation of what ought to be understood by the heart in the Scriptures.

57:12

I will declare your righteousness, and your works shall not profit you. When you cry out, let those whom you have gathered deliver you. LXX: I will declare your righteousness and your evils, which shall not profit you. When you cry out, let them rescue you in your tribulation. I who always kept silent, and passed over your sins as though I did not see them, will by no means keep silent any longer, but will say what I already said before: I have kept silent; shall I always keep silent? And I will declare your righteousness and your works. This is to be read as irony, as if someone were to say to a man caught in crimes: See your good works! Therefore, if ever a time of tribulation comes upon you, and you begin to stretch out your hands not to the idols you have worshiped but to heaven, and to implore the help of God, let those hear you and deliver you from danger whom you worshiped in your security. God speaks to the same woman through Jeremiah also: Where are your gods which you had made? Let them rise and save you in the time of your evils (Jer 2:28). Where the Seventy translated, Let them rescue you in your tribulation, and we have said, Let those whom you have gathered deliver you, Symmachus translated: Let your synagogues rescue you. He therefore speaks properly to the Jews, that the crowd of their synagogues will not be able to deliver them in the time of siege.

57:13-14

And the wind shall carry them all away, a breeze shall take them off. But he who has confidence in me shall inherit the land and shall possess my holy mountain. And I will say: Make a way, provide a road, turn aside from the path, take away the stumbling blocks from the way of my people. LXX: For the wind shall take all these away, and the tempest shall carry them off. But those who hope in me shall possess the land and shall obtain my holy mountain by inheritance, and they shall say: Make clean the ways before his face, and take away the stumbling blocks from the way of my people. The Jews assert that these things are prophesied of the Babylonians: that when these have been overcome by the power of God, the people return to Judea and possess Mount Zion, and all the hindrances of the journey are taken away, and they suffer the ambushes of no nation, because the Lord has made the way level for his people. And they contend that these things were fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Ezra. But we, joining what is said to what goes before, assert this: that the wind and the tempest take away all the idols which could not deliver them, and they are like the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth; but that those who have had confidence in the Lord will possess the land of which we shall read in this same Prophet: He will lift you up to the good things of the land. From this it is clear that this land is not below but above, to which the saint will climb as the Lord lifts him up, the land of which we have often spoken: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land (Matt 5:4); and I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps 26 [27]:13). The holy mountain of God is to be understood as that of which the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews speaks: You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to many thousands of Angels, and to the Church of the firstborn who are written in the heavens (Heb 12:22). We can also understand the land and the mountain of the Lord which the saints are going to possess as the holy Scriptures, which the Lord threatens shall be taken away from the Jews, saying: The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits (Matt 21:43), so that they may find in them that mountain of which we read in this same Prophet (Isa 2) and in Micah: In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest (Mic 4:1). And the Lord himself commanded the Apostles and all the teachers of the Church to resolve by their interpretation whatever seemed harsh and difficult, and to provide a way for understanding, and to take all stumbling blocks out of the midst, so that the people of the Lord may understand what it reads without any hindrance and may advance in the fear of God. Of these ways John the Baptist too said: Prepare the ways of the Lord, etc. (Matt 3:3). Where we have put, in the person of God, and I will say, the Seventy put and they shall say: namely those who shall possess the land and obtain the holy mountain of God by inheritance. Nor will they be content with their own salvation, but will also call forth the other peoples to teaching. Symmachus interpreted this place thus: But he who trusts in me shall possess the land, and shall obtain my holy mountain by inheritance, and shall say: Make a straight way, and so on; because he who has possessed the land and the mountain himself instructs the others to prepare a way for the Lord.

57:15

For thus says the high and lofty one who inhabits eternity, and holy is his name: dwelling in the high and holy place, and with the contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble and to revive the heart of the contrite. LXX: Thus says the Most High, who dwells in the heights for ever, Holy among the holy is his name, the Most High resting among the holy, and giving patience to the fainthearted and life to those who are contrite of heart. The prophetic discourse had begun against the people of the Jews, whose teachers he called blind watchmen and dumb dogs and shepherds who know no understanding, and lawless sons, and the seed of adulterers and of a harlot. After this he came to Jerusalem, whom he reproaches for her fornication, because she enlarged her bed for her lovers, and received them with open hand, and adorned herself for all the idols, and sent envoys far off, so as to enjoy foreign lovers too. This rebuke finished, he comes to those who trust in the Lord, to whom he had promised the land and the mountain as a possession, and for whose return he had ordered the road to be prepared: doubtless to the Apostles, at whose preaching men of both peoples believed. Hence he begins with the praises of God, and in the following discourse bears witness to what he has promised concerning the return of his people. For thus says the Lord, high and lofty, who dwells in the heights, and Holy among the Holy, not by place but by the merit of those in whom he dwells, one of whom says in the psalm: I will exalt you, Lord, for you have upheld me (Ps 29 [30]:2); and again: Be exalted, Lord, you who judge the earth (Ps 93 [94]:2). Not that God is lifted up by human words, but, according to what is said elsewhere, The Lord has become my salvation (Ps 117 [118]:21), he becomes high even for the humble. He resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4), so that he may lift them up and dwell in the heights. For the Lord is high, and looks upon the lowly (Ps 137 [138]:6). And in the Gospel the Angels cry out: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace (Luke 2:14). And again in the Psalms: Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights (Ps 148:1). And not only does the high one dwell in the heights, but the holy one also among the holy, he who says in another place: Be holy, for I am holy (Lev 11:44). And just as wisdom does not enter a perverse soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins (Wis 1), so the holy one dwells among the holy; and wherever there is filth, purity cannot dwell, as the saint says to the Lord: But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel (Ps 21 [22]:4). Hence we too dare to say in prayer: Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. And in the second psalm we read: He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall deride them (Ps 2:4). For Christ does not dwell in those who are earthly, but in those who are above the heavens, who tell the glory of the Lord, of whom it is said: May he hear him from his holy heaven (Ps 19 [20]:7). And again: The heaven of heaven is the Lord's (Ps 113 [115]:16). With this sense Moses too, the servant of God, agrees in like words: Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heaven belong to the Lord your God (Deut 10). We must certainly not take this in the Jewish manner, as though God, who is diffused everywhere and by whom all things are contained, were shut in any place and dwelt in heaven alone; rather, let us rightly understand the heights and the heavens as the Saints and the Powers. For he it is who dwells in heaven, of whom it is written in the Gospel: No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven (John 3:13). He rests among the holy and dwells in the humble and in those who are contrite in spirit, of whom it is said: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise (Ps 50 [51]:19). He gives patience to the fainthearted, so that those set in straits may endure tribulation in the hope of things to come. He gives life, namely to those who were dead through sin. Of him it is said: With you is the fountain of life (Ps 35 [36]:10). He it is who says in the Gospel: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6).

57:16

I will not contend for ever, nor will I be angry to the end; for the spirit shall go forth from my face, and I will make the breaths. LXX: I will not take vengeance on you for ever, nor will I always be angry with you. For the spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath. The Lord who dwells in the heights and looks upon the lowly, whose name is holy, and who rests among the holy, who upholds the afflicted and grants life to the oppressed (Ps 112 [113]), has spoken thus: I will not always be angry, nor will I be indignant without end. I strike in order to amend; I kill in order to give life. For I have pity on my creature, and those whom I myself have made I will not allow to perish for ever. My spirit too, which shall go forth from me, or which, according to the Hebrew, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, surrounds all things (for this is what περιειληθήσεται and περιβαλλεῖ signify), is the quickener of all things. And the breath, or in the plural the breaths (for this is what NASAMOTH נשמות means), I have made, of which it is written elsewhere: Every breath, or everything that breathes, praises the Lord (Ps 150:6). Of this spirit and breath it is written at the beginning of Genesis: God breathed in the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Job says something of the kind: The spirit of the Lord which is in my nostrils, and the breath of the Almighty which teaches me (Job 27:3). Since, then, the spirit goes forth from me, and all things are quickened and live by my breath and inspiration, it is not just that those who are upheld by my breath and spirit should perish for ever. Some of our writers say that this is the spirit by which the whole world is breathed upon and governed, and through which all things have knowledge of God; the distinguished poet, writing of it after the Stoics, says (Virgil, Aeneid 6): In the beginning, the heaven and the earth and the watery plains, the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars, a spirit nourishes within; and mind, poured through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body; and so on. Others, however, understand the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning was borne over the waters and gave life to all things; who goes forth from the Father, and because of the fellowship of nature is sent by the Son, who says: It is expedient for you that I go. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you (John 16:7). Of him again he says: When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who goes forth from the Father (John 15:26). Let it scandalize no one if the Spirit is said to go forth from the Father, since the Son too said of himself: I went forth from the Father and have come; for I did not go forth of myself, but he sent me (John 16:28). Of this Spirit he spoke: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you always, the Spirit of truth (John 14:16). This is the Spirit of whom Moses also writes: Who will grant that all the people of the Lord be prophets, and that the Lord give his Spirit upon them? (Num 11:29). And Joel, in the person of God: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (Joel 2:28). And Zechariah: But receive my words and my ordinances, which I command by my Spirit to my servants the Prophets (Zech 1:6). And again: I will pour out upon Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and of mercy (Zech 12:10). And many other things from both Testaments, which it would take long to repeat now. This alone we say, that the same Prophet has spoken of this Spirit and breath together: Thus says the Lord God, who made the heaven; and a little after: Who gives breath to his people that is upon it, and spirit to those who tread on it (Isa 42:5).

57:17ff.

Because of the iniquity of his covetousness I was angry, and I struck him; I hid, and I was indignant; and he walked mourning in the way of his heart. I have seen his ways, and I healed him; and I brought him back, and restored consolations to him and to those who mourn for him. I created the fruit of the lips, peace, peace to him who is far off and to him who is near, said the Lord, and I healed him. But the impious are like the raging sea which cannot rest, and its waves overflow into trampling and mire. There is no peace, said God, for the impious. LXX: Because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I struck him; and I turned my face away from him, and he was grieved and walked sad in his ways. I have seen his ways, and I healed him; and I comforted him, and gave him true consolation, peace to those who are far off and to those who are near, says the Lord, and I will heal them. But those who are lawless shall be tossed like waves, and shall not be able to rest. There is no joy for the impious, says the Lord God. After the casting off of the people of the Jews and of those who refused to believe in the Savior, he had promised those who have confidence in him the land of the meek and the mountain of the saints, and had commanded the Apostles: Make a way for the returning people, and take all stumbling blocks out of the midst. And lest this seem incredible, he sets forth his power: that, being high and great, he can easily grant pardon to the penitent, and that it is just for the Creator to have pity on his creature. Because of this he adds that he was angry and grieved his people, and that he did so because they had sinned and had the covetousness of iniquity, and were not content with one iniquity, but always added sins to sins. And I struck, he says, him for a short while, in order to heal him, and I hid, understood, my face, so that he might long for me the more and say: Show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps 79 [80]:4). And I was indignant; and he, perceiving this, went about sad, saying: All the day I went about sad (Ps 37 [38]:7). And he walked mourning, or turned, in the way of his heart, so as to do penance not before the faces of men but in his heart. Therefore, seeing the ways of his conversion, I healed the wounds with which I had struck him before. And I brought back to me him whom I had first cast out, and restored to him true consolation; for many are the false consolations by which the human race is deceived. Or: I comforted those who mourn for him, saying in the Gospel: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). What follows, I created the fruit of the lips, has this sense: I have fulfilled what I had promised, saying: As I live, says the Lord, I would rather the repentance of the sinner than his death (Ezek 33:11); or: I have granted all that I had promised before. And what is the Lord's promise? My peace I give you; my peace I leave you (John 14:27). And this is what he now says: Peace upon peace; not to one nation only, but to the whole world: namely to those who were far off and to those who were near, that is, first to the nations, and afterward to those of Israel who were willing to believe. Of these the Apostle too says: To you indeed it was necessary that the word of God be preached; but since you judge yourselves unworthy of salvation, behold, we turn to the nations (Acts 13:46). He, writing to the Ephesians and discussing most fully the people of the Circumcision and of the Gentiles, adds: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near in the Blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of partition, dissolving the enmity in his flesh, and so on (Eph 2:13, 14); and again: And coming, he announced peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near (ibid., 17). For through him we both have access in one spirit to the Father: giving peace upon peace to those who had been far off and to those who were near, both those who had not had the Law and the Prophets and those who had received them before, he received them and healed them. But the impious, or lawless, shall be tossed like the raging sea, and shall never be able to rest. Although this can be understood of every impious man, yet it refers properly to the people of the Jews, who cried out with one voice and persevered in their impiety, saying: Crucify, crucify such a one. We have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). As, then, the raging sea cannot rest, but its waves overflow and roll up on the shores and are sucked back again, and breaking upon themselves make a mire that is trampled underfoot, so the impious will be subject to eternal trampling; they have no joy, and they rest in no peace, because they persevere in being impious. Some understand this place specifically of the Savior: that because of the sins of the world he was grieved for a little while, saying: My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38); and that the Father struck him, he who speaks through Zechariah: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered (Zech 13:7); and that he himself said of himself in the sixty-eighth psalm: For they persecuted him whom you struck (Ps 68 [69]:27); and that God turned his face away from him, so that for a little while he took the form of a servant and walked sad, mourning the sins of the people, lamenting and bewailing Jerusalem; and that the Father, who saw his ways, therefore healed him who was free among the dead, and his flesh did not see corruption, so that he who was struck on the cross might be healed in the resurrection. And I comforted him, he says, giving him the whole world in place of the one nation of the Jews. And those who mourn for him, understood, I comforted; and there is no doubt that he means the Apostles. And he fulfilled the fruit of his lips, he who had said to him: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8): peace upon peace, reconciling the world to God, so that he might call both peoples to himself and be healed by the Father. But the impious, of whom we have spoken above, he compares to the sea, which can never rest, but even in the greatest calm rolls with its waves breaking on the shores, and its end is mire and trampling.

58:1

Cry, cease not; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes, and to the house of Jacob their sins. LXX: Cry with strength, and spare not; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to the people their sins, and to the house of Jacob their iniquities. The preceding chapter finished, in which peace is announced to the righteous and no rest to the impious, God commands the prophet Isaiah to cry with strength, and to lift up his voice like a trumpet, and not to fear to tell the sins and crimes of the people of Israel, by no means afraid of death, nor of the threats and abuse of the impious, but rather considering the Lord who commands him. And because they have deaf ears and can scarcely hear, according to Symmachus and Aquila he is to turn his throat into a horn, which in Hebrew is called SOPHAR (שופר), and which they interpreted as κερατίνην, that is, of horn. Above, indeed, where it was said to the Apostles, Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not fear (Isa 40:9), neither horn nor trumpet is taken up, but they are ordered to go up the mountain. Here, however, because those to whom the message must be announced were sinners and lingered below, the Prophet is not ordered to go up onto a mountain, but only to lift up his voice like a trumpet and announce to them the wars to come. Besides, of the day of judgment, when the resurrection of the dead and the last trumpet are spoken of, it is written: For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorrupt; so that, as they are to be judged at the sound of the trumpet, so Israel, dead in sin, may hear his crimes. And at the same time he is called the people of God, so that he may learn what kind of father he has lost, who calls even a sinner his people.

58:2

For they seek me from day to day, and wish to know my ways, as a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God. LXX likewise. This properly fits the Jews, who run every day to the synagogues and meditate on the law of God, desiring to know what Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did, and what the rest of the saints did, and, turning over the books of the Prophets and of Moses by heart, chant the divine commandments. To them this will most rightly be applied: The wicked will seek me and will not find me. For thus it is written: Everyone who seeks finds (Matt 7); whoever does not find is proved to have sought wrongly. For the Lord is found by those who seek him in goodness, and is shown to those who are not unbelieving toward him. Since, then, they have forsaken the righteousness and the judgment of God, by which names Christ is shown, as the psalmist says, O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son (Ps 71 [72]:1), for Christ has become for us redemption, holiness and righteousness (1 Cor 1), in vain do they boast of their knowledge of the law, since the saint glories not in the knowledge of the Scriptures but in works, saying: I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart (Ps 118 [119]:32).

58:3

They ask of me the judgments of righteousness, and they wish to draw near to God. Why have we fasted, and you have not looked? Why have we humbled our souls, and you have not known? Behold, in the day of your fast shall be found your own will, and you have exacted again from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and contentions, and you strike with the fist wickedly. LXX: They now ask of me righteous judgment, and they desire to draw near to God, saying: Why have we fasted, and you have not seen? Why have we humbled our souls, and you have not known? For in the days of your fasts your own wills are found, and you afflict all who are subject to you, fasting for lawsuits and quarrels, and you strike the lowly with your fists. This is another rashness of the Jews: as though in the confidence of a good conscience, they demand righteous judgment and imitate the words of the saints, who say: Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my innocence (Ps 25 [26]:1, 2); and again: Prove me, Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart; and in another place: Judge my cause and redeem me (Ps 118 [119]:154). And they desire to draw near to God, whereas this is not a matter of place but of affection, and not of an idle mind but of laborious work. In short, what it is to draw near to God, Scripture teaches, saying: Seek the Lord; and when he has drawn near to you, let the impious man forsake his ways and the unrighteous man his thoughts. For the Lord draws near to those who draw near to him, and to those who righteously pursue what is righteous and can say: But for me it is good to cling to God (Ps 72 [73]:28). For if Almighty God is the Father of truth and righteousness, whoever is a liar and unrighteous cannot draw near to God, of whom it is written: The malicious shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the unrighteous abide before your eyes (Ps 5:6). Why have we fasted, they say, and you have not looked? Why have we humbled our souls, and you have not known? They accuse the Lord of unrighteousness, because he does not regard their good works, and they press upon God only the hunger of the belly, without the work of the virtues: not eating the foods which God created for the faithful and for those who know the truth, to be taken with thanksgiving, but those of which it is written in Proverbs: For these are fed with the foods of impiety, and are drunk with the wine of iniquity (Prov 4:17). Glutted with feasts of this kind, the Pharisee, among his other words of pride, boasted that he fasted twice in the week (Luke 18); he had not drunk the wine of the vine of Sorek, but of the vine of Sodom, whose wine is the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, and their grape is a grape of gall. Them God rebukes through the Prophet: They eat the sins of my people (Hos 4:8); and again: Why have you kept silent about their impiety, and gathered the vintage of iniquities, and eaten the grain of falsehood? (Hos 10:13). Since, then, they had put a question to God, desiring to know why they had fasted and humbled their souls and God had not looked on them, forgetting the ancient history, why he did not look on the gifts of Cain, who offered rightly but did not divide rightly with his brother (Gen 4), not seeing the charity of God, as Scripture says, You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and your neighbor as yourself (Matt 22:39): therefore God answered that he does not reject fasts but the works done during fasts, saying: In the days of your fasts your own wills are found, so that you do not God's will but your own wills, which Paul, writing to the Ephesians, rejects: According to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of unbelief, among whom we all too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of the thoughts; and we were by nature sons of wrath, as the rest also (Eph 2:2, 3). What follows according to the Seventy, And you goad all who are subject to you, or you afflict, Theodotion and Symmachus translated better, and we have followed them in this place: And you exact again from all your debtors. By this he shows that it is not without danger to dun a poor man who is unable to pay, and not to give back to a debtor shivering with cold the cloak you have taken in place of a pledge, lest his cry come to God. For he who has pity on the poor lends to God (Prov 19); and on the contrary he who duns one who has nothing does violence to God. And that we may know that this is the sense in the present place, we are going to read further on in this same chapter: Loose the bonds of impiety, undo the bundles that weigh down. Doubtless he means bonds of debt. For what does it profit for the face to grow pale with fasts, and to fast for lawsuits and quarrels, when Scripture says, He who loves sins rejoices in quarrels (Prov 17:19)? The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle (2 Tim 2), and imitate him who says: Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matt 11:29), so that the humility be not affected but of the heart, seeking not the glory of men but the conscience of the soul. You fast, he says, and strike the lowly with your fists, and beat them with slaps (1 Tim 3). Hence a bishop must not be a striker. For how can he rein in lust who cannot restrain either his hand or his tongue? Fasts of this kind the Lord rebukes at the beginning of this prophet too, saying: Fasting and idleness, new moons and sabbaths and your other solemnities my soul hates (Isa 1:13). Hence it is commanded through Joel: Sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing (Joel 2:15), so that we may fast from vices, and, by good works and the healing of our sins, our fasts may become holy. Then it follows: Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room, so that in the time of fasting we may be free for prayer, lest our inner man feed on the flesh of the dragon, which was given as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians. And we say these things not as rejecting fasts, through which Daniel too, the man of desires, came to know the future (Dan 9), and the Ninevites appeased the wrath of God (Jonah 3), and Elijah (1 Kgs 19) and Moses (Exod 34), in a hunger of forty days, were filled with the familiar friendship of God, and the Lord himself (Matt 4) fasted as many days in the desert, so as to leave us the solemn days of fasts; but because it does not profit to carry an empty belly and to do other things that displease God. And, to pass over the rest, there are those who disfigure their faces so as to appear to men to be fasting, who, obtaining glory in the present, will be shut out of the kingdom of God, because they have received their reward (Matt 6). Hence the Apostle too says that, even if he hands over his body to martyrdom so as to burn, or to glory (for both are found in the copies), without the charity of God (1 Cor 13), which is in the conscience of the heart, he sheds his blood in vain.

58:4-5

Do not fast as you have until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this such a fast as I have chosen, for a man to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to twist his head round like a ring, and to spread sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord? LXX: Why do you fast to me as today, so that your voice may be heard in clamor? I have not chosen such a fast, and a day for a man to humble his soul. Not even if you bend your neck like a ring and spread under you haircloth and ashes, not even so shall you call it an acceptable fast. Lest he seem to reject the fast which he himself had commanded, he teaches how one should fast; or rather, before teaching what they should pursue, he instructs them in what they ought to avoid. So that your cry, he says, may be heard on high: do not bring a clamor to prayer, praying in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets so as to be seen by men (Matt 6), and lifting up your voice on high, and proclaiming your fasts and works with the Pharisee, who is condemned by the Lord's judgment (Luke 18). For this reason the Lord, rejecting the prayer of the Pharisees, teaches his disciples how they ought to pray (Matt 6): with the chamber of their breast shut, so that they may speak to God alone, who can hear the silence of the heart; that they may cry in their hearts, Abba, Father (Rom 8:15); and that they may not disfigure their faces, but wash them with water and anoint their head with oil. Of this John the Evangelist too writes: And you have an anointing from the holy one (1 John 2:20); when they have been anointed with it, they too become holy. For God does not seek only affliction and the humbling of the soul through injury to the body, that a man should twist his body like a ring, and bow his neck, and go about sad, according to what is said in the Psalms: I am afflicted and bowed down to the end; all the day I went about saddened (Ps 37 [38]:7); nor that one should be clothed in sackcloth and sleep in ashes, as we read of David and of Ahab (2 Sam 3; 1 Kgs 21); but that along with these he should do the things that follow. Otherwise the Apostle too says that he fasted often (2 Cor 6 and 11), and the Lord teaches that his disciples will fast when the bridegroom has been taken from them (Matt 9); and in the Psalms the penitent says: I have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping (Ps 101 [102]:10); And when they were troublesome to me, I put on haircloth (Ps 34 [35]:13). From this we learn that the things the Lord wills must be done first, and the others not passed over.

58:6-7

Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? Loose the bonds of impiety, undo the bundles that weigh down; let those who are broken go free, and break every burden. Break your bread to the hungry, and bring the needy and the wanderers into the house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. LXX: Is not such a fast what I have chosen, says the Lord? But loose every bond of iniquity. Undo the obligations of violent contracts. Let the broken go in release, and tear up every unjust writing. Break your bread to the hungry, and bring the poor without a roof into your house. If you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise those of the household of your seed. After teaching what kind of fast he rejects, he shows what kind he gladly accepts. Loose, he says, the bonds of impiety; undo the bundles that weigh down; or, as the Seventy translated more plainly, the obligations of violent contracts, which our translators, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, that is, συναλλαγμάτων, rendered as exchanges instead of bonds of debt. He means the bundles of papers in which the frauds of moneylenders are contained and by which the poor are oppressed with debt, which in all cities is the chief cause of sedition. Hence the Roman people too occupied the neighboring hills, and hence the New Tables, which the Greeks call χρέων ἀποκοπάς. The Prophet, then, does not command that no one should exact what is owed, especially what he lent justly and justly asks back; otherwise he would be a champion of tribunician sedition. But where the contract is unjust, where the poor are oppressed by fraud, there the bundles of contracts and all the bonds of iniquity must be broken. Or certainly this must be said, since the discourse is about fasts, and a fast involves the affliction and humbling of the soul, while the affliction of the body begs for the pardon of sins: the divine Scripture teaches that we should forgive our debtors, so that the heavenly Father too may forgive us our debts (Mark 11). The old history relates that in the seventh year of release, or in the fiftieth, which is the true Jubilee, all possessions return to their owners, and their former freedom is restored to slaves, and all the debts, which people commonly call contracts, become void (Lev 25 and 27). But if this is commanded in the old Law (Exod 21), how much more in the Gospel, where (Matt 5) all good things are doubled, and we are by no means told to take an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, but to offer the cheek to him who strikes us! And so that we may know that what we said above, You exact again from all your debtors, is written of creditors, something is added more plainly about debtors: Let those who are broken go free, that is, those who are broken by poverty, whom want has afflicted: do not let their children go begging. And break every burden by which they are weighed down. For this the Seventy translated more plainly, and tear up every unjust writing; which Symmachus translated: And break every false contract. But it could happen that someone would say: I have no debtors; what must I do for my fast to be accepted? It follows: Break your bread to the hungry. Not many loaves, lest you plead poverty, but one loaf; and not even the whole of it, but a part of the loaf, which you would have eaten if you were not fasting, so that your fast may not be a gain for your purse but a filling of your soul. And he fittingly added your, lest you make alms out of plunder: For the ransom of a man's soul is his own riches (Prov 13:8); and in another place: Honor the Lord from your righteous labors (Prov 3:9). Surely, if you have no bread, and the multitude of the hungry is very great, give something from which you suffer no loss. A thing in which there is no expense: the poor without a roof bring into your house; or, as it is in the Hebrew, into the house, so that, if you have no house of your own, you may bring them into the little lodging which you hold either on rent or by favor. If you see the naked, cover him. This the Lord too said in the Gospel: He who has two tunics, let him give the other to him who has none (Luke 3:11). For he did not order one tunic to be cut and divided, which many do for the sake of popular favor, but the second not to be kept back; increasing the precepts of righteousness, so that he said that even a cup of cold water held out has its rewards. And do not despise, he says, your own flesh. For every man is our flesh; and according to the Gospel parable of the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and was wounded by robbers, he who did him good is called his neighbor (Luke 10). Or certainly, according to the Seventy, who said, And do not despise those of the household of your seed, let us understand those of the household of the seed as those of whom the Apostle too teaches that alms must be given to all, but above all to those of the household of the faith (Gal 6). For they are our flesh and our seed, who are begotten with us of one parent. To them the Savior also stretched out his hand, saying: These are my mother and my brothers, who do the will of my Father (Mark 3:34, 35). And so that we may know that there is one Lord of both the New and the Old Instrument, the Lord says the same things in the Gospel of those who will stand on the right hand on the day of judgment: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink; I was sick and in prison, and you came to me; a stranger, and you brought me into your house; and naked, and you clothed me (Matt 25:34ff.). And when they say in humility that they have done nothing for the Lord the Savior, he answers: As long as you did it to one of the least of my brothers, you did it to me. According to tropology we can say this: Let him who fasts from all evils, and wishes his fast to be regarded, not only turn away from evil but also do good, so as to loose every bond of iniquity by which the simple among believers have been bound through the frauds of the heretics; and the στραγγαλιὰς, the obligations of violent treatises, which the Prophet too points out in the psalm, saying: But those who turn aside into obligations the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity (Ps 124 [125]:5). For all who are bound with the chains of the heretics turn aside from the Lord, and are like an ox led to the sacrifice; and they choose and exchange falsehood for the truth. Such men, then, who are broken in judgment, let the churchman release and set free; and let him undo and break every writing of the heretics, of whom this same Prophet says: Woe to those who write iniquity; for writers write malice, robbing the judgment of the poor of my people (Isa 10:1, 2), so that they may by no means hold the simple entangled in their snares. And when he has done this, let him break the bread of the Church's doctrine to the hungry, as the Lord too did, giving the broken loaves to the Apostles; he left these to them in seven baskets and twelve hampers, by no means whole as they were held in the Law, but crumbled and broken in the Gospel, so that they might have something to bestow on the poor (Matt 15). Those whom you see not having the warmth of faith, but shivering outside the Church in the cold of unbelief, needy and strangers, bring, he says, into the house of the Church, and cover them with the cloak of incorruption, so that, clothed with the tunic of Christ, they may by no means remain in the tombs, as we read of him who, possessed by a legion of demons, lived naked among the memorials of the dead. And when, he says, you have done this, and your liberality has been laid open to all, do not, in particular, despise those of the household of the faith.

58:8-9

Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your health shall quickly arise, and your righteousness shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you up. Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry, and he will say: Here I am. LXX: Then your morning light shall break forth, and your healings shall quickly arise, and your righteousness shall go before you in your sight, and the glory of God shall surround you. Then you shall cry, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, he will say: Here I am. When you have not done the things which the preceding discourse related, and have done these of which we have now spoken, then your fast will be acceptable, and your morning light will break forth: the sun of righteousness, namely, of whom the prophet Malachi speaks in the person of God the Father: For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing in his wings (Mal 4:2). He who is called the sun there is called the light here. For as the morning light dispels the darkness, so the light of knowledge and truth puts all errors to flight. And your healings, he says, shall quickly arise. For this Aquila, rendering word for word, put: And the scar of your wound shall quickly close over; so that, that is, the wounds of our sins may be closed at the rising of the sun of righteousness, the scar quickly forming over them. Where the Seventy translated τὰ ἰάματά σου, that is, your healings, the Latin translators, led by the likeness of the word ἱμάτια, that is, garments, put that instead. Hence many, deceived by the falseness of the translation, use this testimony to prove the resurrection of the body, wanting the body to be taken as the garment of the soul, which is to arise on the day of resurrection. And your righteousness, he says, shall go before you in your sight (Gen 30:33 LXX), according to what Jacob says: My righteousness will hear me tomorrow; and what is written will be fulfilled: Behold the man and his works. And the glory of the Lord shall surround you, as with a most beautiful garment, so that you may be glorified before God and before men. Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry, and he will say: Here I am, not by voice but by deed, not by an answer but by benefits. This is proved according to the letter in the Gospel too, when the leper said to the Lord, If you will, you can make me clean, and the Lord answered, saying: I will; be clean.

58:10

If you take away the chain from your midst, and cease to stretch out the finger and to speak what does not profit; when you pour out your soul to the hungry, and fill the afflicted soul, then your light shall rise in the darkness, and your darkness shall be as the noonday. LXX: If you take away from you the bond, and the ordination, and the word of murmuring, and give your bread to the hungry from your soul, and satisfy the humbled soul, then your light shall rise in the darkness, and your darkness shall be as the noonday. The Hebrew word MOTA (מוטה), which in Jeremiah is translated iron collar (Jer 28), is read twice in the present chapter. For in the place where, above, according to the Seventy, we said, Undo the obligations of violent exchanges, let us know that for the one word MOTA they put violent contracts, for which Aquila translated error, Symmachus turning aside, Theodotion κλοιὸν, that is, collar. Again, in the present place, where we have rendered, If you take away the chain from your midst, for chain the Seventy translated συνδεσμὸν, that is, binding together, or bond; Aquila, as above, interpreted it error; Symmachus, going over to Theodotion's view, put collar. Let this be said about the variety of interpretation. For the rest, the sense is joined with what precedes thus: The morning light will rise for you, and your healings will quickly arise, and your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will crown you; and he will hear you at once when you entreat him, and will show that he is present. Only on this condition: that to the works mentioned above you also add these, that you take away from yourself the bond and the chain with which your soul is bound.
