As for what is set down above, Why have you made us stray (Isa 63:17)?, in what sense it is to be taken Jeremiah teaches most fully: You have led me astray, O Lord, and I was led astray; you took hold of me, and you prevailed (Jer 20:7). For while you promise me mercy, and like a merciful father you conceal your severity, and like a skilful physician you hide the sharpest knife so as not to frighten the sick man before you heal him, you have made me careless. For this reason God says of Jerusalem too: Behold, I will lead her astray, and I will make her like a desert, and set her like a land without water, and I will speak to her heart; and I will give her possessions from there, and the valley of Achor to open understanding (Hos 2:14, 15). Let us consider the order of each thing: he leads her astray, and makes her deserted and without water, so that she may suffer thirst for the virtues. After she has said, My soul has thirsted for you, how many ways my flesh for you (Ps 62 [63]:2), then he will speak to her heart and console her as she mourns. And he will give her a possession from there, that is, from the repentance and sorrow which works salvation. And the humility of her troubled heart (for this is what the valley of Achor means) opens her understanding, so that she may not be ignorant of her Creator. Our enemies, he says, have trodden down your sanctuary. There is no doubt that he means the Temple, which the victorious Romans trod down. And we have become as in the beginning, before we were called in Abraham, and while we were in Egypt, having no God, nor kings, nor princes, nor Prophets, nor the Law of the commandments of God (Hos 3); all of which was fulfilled after the passion of the Lord, and is being fulfilled today. For since they said, His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt 27:25), an everlasting curse remains, and God does not rule over them, nor is his name called upon them, since they are by no means called the people of God.

64:1ff.

O that you would rend the heavens and come down! At your presence the mountains would flow down. As the burning of fire they would melt away; the waters would burn with fire, so that your name might be made known to your enemies; at your presence the nations would be troubled. When you do wonders, we shall not endure them; you came down, and at your presence the mountains flowed down. LXX: If you open heaven, trembling will seize the mountains because of you; and they will melt as wax melts before the fire, and fire will burn up the adversaries; and your name will be manifest among the adversaries; at your presence the nations will be troubled. When you do glorious things, trembling will seize the mountains because of you. Since our enemies have trodden down your sanctuary, and we have become as in the beginning, when your name was not called upon us, therefore we entreat and say: O that you would rend the heavens and come down, and that you who are always promised would at some time fulfill your promises. This was said at the time when the Savior had not yet come, nor had yet assumed from the virgin's womb, out of our nature and substance, the man whom he would save; so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15). If you did this, they say, and the heavens, or heaven, were opened, at the coming of your majesty the mountains would flow down, or trembling would seize the mountains, and they would be consumed as wax is consumed before the fire. To Ezekiel too the heavens were opened, and he saw a great vision (Ezek 1). And Moses as well, in the blessings of Deuteronomy, prays: May the Lord open to you his good treasure, the heaven, to give you blessing (Deut 28). And in the Gospel (Matt 3) John the Baptist is related to have seen the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit coming down upon the Lord in the form of a dove. The mountains which at the coming of the Lord, of whom it is written, God is a consuming fire (Deut 4:24), will be consumed and melt like wax, are the adverse powers and all who raise themselves up against the knowledge of God. Of them it is sung in the ninety-sixth psalm too: He saw, and the earth was shaken. The mountains melted like wax at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of the whole earth (Ps 96 [97]:4, 5). For if you came down and fulfilled your promises, the waters of the sea would melt away (according to Symmachus), and that fire would consume all their saltness. Of this it is written in another psalm too: As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish; as wax is consumed before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God (Ps 67 [68]:2). And this is to be noted, that when the waters of the sea have been consumed by the divine fire, then the name of the Lord Savior will be made known to his enemies; of whom it is said in the sixty-seventh psalm: The tongue of your dogs, from the enemies, by him; so that him whom they had not perceived through his benefits they may come to know through the overthrow of their city and their own captivity. And at his presence the nations will be troubled, or, as is said more expressively in the Hebrew, will be moved: so that those which before were immovable may come to salvation. And when he has done wonders, and shown in the Gospel the signs which he once showed in Egypt and in the wilderness, they will confess that they cannot bear the glory of his coming, or that trembling has seized the mountains. And beautifully, according to the Hebrew, as though those who above had entreated, O that you would rend the heavens and come down! At your presence the mountains would flow down, had been heard, they afterwards add: You came down: you, the Word, were made flesh and dwelt among us, truly Emmanuel, which means God with us. And therefore at your presence all the mountains flowed down, of which we spoke above. The Hebrews expound this passage thus: The fire will burn up the wicked just as the waters boil with the heat of fire; for by AMASIM (חמסים) they wish to be understood not consumption and melting, as the others translated, but the wicked.

64:4-5

From of old they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears; the eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you. You have met him who rejoices and does righteousness in your ways; they will remember you. LXX: From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides you, and your works, which you will do for those who wait for mercy; for he meets those who do righteousness, and they will remember your ways. A paraphrase of this testimony the apostle Paul, as a Hebrew of the Hebrews, takes from the authentic books in the Epistle which he writes to the Corinthians, not rendering word for word, which he altogether disdains to do, but expressing the truth of the sense, which he uses to support what he wished (1 Cor 2). Let the ravings of the apocrypha, then, fall silent, which on the pretext of this testimony are thrust upon the churches of Christ. Of them it can truly be said that the devil sits in ambush with the rich in the apocrypha, to kill the innocent. And again: He lies in wait in the hidden place like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor (Ps 9 [10]:8). For the Ascension of Isaiah and the Apocalypse of Elijah contain this testimony. And on this pretext, and through many things of this kind, silly women of the Spains, and above all of Lusitania, laden with sins, led away by various desires, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3), were deceived into taking up the monstrosities of Basilides, of Balsamus and Thesaurus, of Barbelo too and Leusibora, and of the remaining names. Of these the apostolic man Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and martyr, writes most carefully, explaining the origins of many heresies, and above all of the Gnostics, who through Mark the Egyptian deceived noble women, first of the Gauls about the Rhône, then of the Spains, mixing pleasure with fables and claiming for their ignorance the name of knowledge (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 1). What the people says in the present passage is this: that they have never come to know, either by ears or by eyes, what God prepares for his saints in the future; that he meets those who do righteousness and remember his ways. Further, according to the Seventy, they say that they have never known any other God besides him who is truly God, nor seen such and so great works of another, which he will do for those who wait for his mercy and do righteousness and remember his ways. And how is it written, No one has ever seen God (John 1:18), and again, No one sees my face and lives (Exod 33:20)? God, then, is by no means set forth in words, nor is he visible to the eyes; but he is seen by those of whom it is written: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8).

64:6

Behold, you are angry, and we have sinned; in them we have always been, and we shall be saved. And we have become as one unclean all of us, all our righteousnesses as the cloth of a menstruous woman. And we have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away. LXX: Behold, you are angry, and we have all sinned; therefore we have gone astray, and we have all become as unclean, all our righteousness as the cloth of a woman who sits apart; and we have fallen away like leaves because of our iniquities; as the wind will carry us away. The order is inverted. It is not because you are angry that we have sinned, but because we have sinned that you are angry. And because we have sinned, you are angry with us, O Lord; therefore we have gone astray and left the right way. Or, according to the Hebrew: we who have always been in sins shall be saved only by your mercy, we who of ourselves are unclean; and whatever righteousness we seem to have is compared to the cloth of a woman who sits apart, or of a menstruous woman. For this Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, EDDIM (עדים), which Symmachus translated κυουσῶν, that is, of women in childbirth; Aquila μαρτυριῶν, that is, of testimonies: when in the first marital union the blood proves a bride a virgin. And we have fallen away, he says, like leaves from the trees, which because of our iniquities are scattered by the blasts of the winds. Here it must be considered that the righteousness which is in the Law is called uncleanness in comparison with the purity of the Gospel. For what was formerly glorified has not been glorified, because of the surpassing glory. Hence the apostle Paul too, who had fulfilled everything according to the righteousness which is in the Law, says that he counted all things as loss, that he might gain Christ (Phil 3), and because of the surpassing knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake he reckons all things as dung, that he may gain Christ and be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which is from the Law, but the righteousness which is from God through the faith of Christ. For there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl 7), if after the truth of the Gospel he wishes to practice the shadows of the Law, and not to pursue justly what is just. Hence, according to the most wise Solomon, every man seems righteous to himself when he lives in the Law; to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: You are those who justify yourselves before men (Luke 16:15). Fleeing this, Paul says: I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this (1 Cor 4:4). But out of sin, the righteousness of God, of which the same Solomon speaks: Understand true righteousness. There is, then, another righteousness which has no truth, and this is the true righteousness, of which again it is said in the Gospel: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5:6); which many prophets and righteous men desired to see, and did not see (John 8). But Abraham saw this righteousness and was glad, by no means following the letter that kills, but the spirit that gives life. Nor is it surprising to say this of men, when even the stars, compared with the righteousness of God, are not clean, and he has found out something perverse in his angels (Job 4:18; 15:15). If anyone, then, after the Gospel of Christ and the coming of the Son of God, observes the ceremonies of the Law, our tutor, let him hear the people confessing that all that righteousness is compared to a most filthy cloth; to which Esther too compares her diadem, which was the badge of royal power, and which she wore by no means willingly but of necessity: You know my necessity, that I detest the sign of my pride, which is upon my head in the days of my display; I abhor it like a menstruous cloth, and I do not wear it in the days of my quiet (Esth 14:16).

64:7

There is none who calls upon your name, who rises up and takes hold of you. You have hidden your face from us, and have dashed us down in the hand of our iniquity. LXX: And there is none who calls upon your name, and who, remembering, lays hold of you. For you have turned away your face from us, and have handed us over because of our iniquities. Because we have fallen away like leaves from the trees, which the wind scatters when they are dried up, therefore no one has been found who would call upon your name, and, rising from the ruin of his iniquities, would lay hold of you or take hold of you, and say with the bride: I have found him whom my soul sought; I will hold him and will not let him go (Song 3:4). The wind is put in the Scriptures in three ways: either for the greatness of temptations, or for perversity of doctrine, or simply for the wind by which the clouds are gathered and the air is driven together into clouds. Of temptations there is that saying of the Gospel: The rivers came, the winds blew, and beat upon that house, and they could not overthrow it, for it had been founded upon rock with a firm mass (Matt 7:27). Of perversity of doctrine: That we may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine in the wickedness of men (Eph 4:14). Of the wind simply: And they could not sail, for the wind was against them (Mark 6:48): not that this too cannot be understood tropologically, but that it only provides a likeness for the present sense. For when the Lord turns his face away from us, we are dashed down in the hand of our iniquity, or we are handed over to temptations because of our sins. From this we learn that iniquity too has hands, and so have all sins, which desire to hold us tightly bound. Hence too death and life are in the hand of the tongue (Prov 18); and the holy man prays: Let not the foot of pride come to me (Ps 35 [36]:12). But we, since the Lord has turned his face away from us, knowing what is written, Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Joel 2:32), let us call upon his name and say: I have made my sin known to you, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my heart (Ps 31 [32]:5). And at once we shall have the Lord answering: I have blotted out your iniquities like a mist, and your sins like a cloud (Isa 44:22); and we shall say: Show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps 79 [80]:4), so that we may by no means be slaves of sin, but your servants. For everyone who commits sin is its slave (John 8).

64:8ff.

And now, O Lord, you are our father, and we are clay; and you are our fashioner, and we are all the works of your hands. Do not be angry, O Lord, exceedingly, and do not remember iniquity any longer. Behold, look: we are all your people. The city of your Holy One has become a desert; Zion has become a desert, Jerusalem desolate. The house of our sanctification and of our glory, where our fathers praised you, has been made a burning of fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruin. Will you hold yourself back over these things, O Lord, will you be silent, and afflict us exceedingly? LXX: And now, O Lord, you are our father; but we are clay, we are all the works of your hands. Do not be angry with us, O Lord, too much, and do not remember our sins in time. And now look, for we are all your people; the city of your Holy One has become a desert, Zion; Jerusalem as a wilderness, for a curse; the house of our sanctuary and glory, which our fathers blessed, has been burned with fire, and all our glorious things have fallen. And over all these things you have held back, O Lord, and you have been silent, and have humbled us exceedingly. If we consider our merits, we must despair. But if we consider your mercy, you who scourge every son whom you receive, we dare to pour out prayers (Heb 12). For you are our father, who deigned to say: Israel is my firstborn son (Exod 4:22). And although we are clay, and the works of your hands, and you are our fashioner, and the vessel cannot answer the potter as to why it was made thus or thus, yet, knowing that we are sons, we dare to say: Do not be angry, O Lord, exceedingly. We do not forbid wrath, nor do we seek any further your patience, through which we have stored up for ourselves wrath on the day of wrath. But this we ask: that you be not angry with us exceedingly, that in the time of vengeance and punishment you do not remember our iniquity, but rather look upon your people, which was once called your people. And have mercy on the city of your sanctuary, in which your name has been called upon. This city is called Zion and Jerusalem, which the rush of the river makes glad, and in which there was once the watchtower of the virtues and the vision of peace (Ps 43 [44]). Your house too, that is, the Temple of our sanctification and glory, in which our fathers praised you, has fallen into ruins and ashes, and has been destroyed by devastating fire; so that no victims are offered in it, no Passover is celebrated, nothing is done of the ceremonies which you commanded to be done; but all our desirable things have been turned into ruins. Since, then, this is how things stand, will you, O Lord, hold back your mercy over these things, and be silent toward the adversaries who blaspheme, and afflict and humble us, not in the usual manner but exceedingly? All this the Jews think was fulfilled in the times of the Assyrians and the Babylonians. But we, in accordance with what follows in the person of the Savior, I appeared to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me (Isa 65:1), refer everything to the time of the Roman victory, which Josephus, the writer of the Jewish history, sets forth in seven volumes, to which he gave the title The Capture of the Jews, that is, περὶ ἁλώσεως. And it is superfluous to discuss in words what lies open to the eyes, since all their desirable things have been turned into ruins, and the Temple, celebrated throughout the whole world, has become the dunghill of the new city, which was called by its founder Aelia, and has passed into a dwelling-place of owls; and in vain they say daily in their synagogues: Over all these things, O Lord, you will hold back, and you will afflict us and humble us exceedingly. We can refer these things to the Church, or to the soul of a holy man, which can rightly be called a watchtower and vision of peace when the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit have dwelt in it. But if, through our fault or that of the people, such a Zion has been forsaken by the Lord, it will at once lie open to the burning of the fiery arrows of the devil; for all who commit adultery, their hearts are like an oven. And when the coolness of chastity has been driven out, the flame of lust will rage in the temple of God, so that whatever in us was formerly glorious and renowned may collapse, be destroyed and perish. And then is fulfilled what is said in the Psalms: They have burned your sanctuary with fire; they have profaned on the earth the tabernacle of your name. This he alone can quench out of whose belly flow rivers of living water.

Book Eighteen

The eighteenth book on Isaiah, or rather the last, is dedicated to your name, O daughter Eustochium, and to that of your holy mother Paula, so that I may now recall with equal remembrance those whom I have looked up to with equal honor: especially since she too, while she lived, often asked for this work together with you, and your brother Pammachius, a most learned man, did not cease, both then and afterwards, to press me with frequent letters; and for me there is one and the same devotion toward friends present and absent, and toward men and women sleeping in Christ, that is, a love of souls, not of bodies. Nor am I unaware how great a diversity of opinions there is among men. I do not speak of the mystery of the Trinity, whose right confession is the ignorance of knowledge, but of the other doctrines of the Church: namely of the Resurrection, of the state of souls and of human flesh, of the Promises of things to come, how they ought to be taken, and in what way the Apocalypse of John is to be understood; for if we take it according to the letter, we must judaize; if we discuss it spiritually, as it was written, we shall seem to go against the opinions of many of the ancients: of the Latins, Tertullian, Victorinus, Lactantius; of the Greeks, to pass over the rest, I shall mention only Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, against whom Dionysius, a most eloquent man, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, writes an elegant book, mocking the fable of the thousand years, and the golden and jeweled Jerusalem on earth, the restoration of the Temple, the blood of victims, the idleness of the sabbath, the outrage of circumcision, marriages, childbirths, the rearing of children, the delights of banquets, and the servitude of all the nations; and again wars, armies and triumphs, and the slaughter of the vanquished, and the death of the sinner a hundred years old. To him Apollinaris replied in two volumes, and not only the men of his own sect but also a very great multitude of ours follow him, in this part at least, so that with a foreboding mind I already see how many people's rage is to be stirred up against me. I do not begrudge them, if they love the earth so much that in the kingdom of Christ they desire earthly things, and after an abundance of food and the gorging of gullet and belly, seek the things that are beneath the belly. Of whom the apostle Paul says: Food, he says, for the belly, and the belly for foods: but God will destroy both it and them (1 Cor 6:13). And: The kingdom of God is not food and drink (Rom 14:17). And the Lord and Savior: You err, he says, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but they will be like the Angels (Matt 22:29, 30). Nor in saying this do I take away the reality of bodies, which I confess will rise incorrupt and immortal, so that they change their glory, not their substance. And so we must walk on the straight path, so as to turn aside neither to the left nor to the right, that is, so as to follow neither the Jewish error nor the heretical. Of these, the one sort, who are of the flesh, love flesh alone; the other, ungrateful for the benefits of God, refuse to have what Christ had both when he was born and when he rose. For when the Apostles thought him a spirit, or, according to the Gospel of the Hebrews which the Nazarenes read, an incorporeal demon, he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and feet, that it is I myself: Handle and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet (Luke 24:38, 39). And again he spoke to Thomas when he doubted: Put your finger here, and see my hands; and stretch out your hand, and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing (John 20:27). Finally, to prove the reality of his body, he is written to have taken food, as he had also ordered food to be given to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom he raised from the dead. And Lazarus, lest his resurrection be thought a phantom, is related to have sat at a banquet with the Savior (Mark 5; and Luke 13; John 12). Not that after the resurrection we shall eat and drink, as our Millenarians would have it, and that immortal and incorrupt bodies must be sustained by earthly nourishment: otherwise, where there is food, diseases follow; where there are diseases, a physician must be called in; where there are physicians, death often follows; and then again a resurrection, and a new way of life all over again; but so that the taking of food might prove the faith of the resurrection. These things we guard against with great care, and we speak with restraint, knowing that we must walk among serpents and scorpions, which bite and strike in secret (Ezek 2). Of whom Ecclesiastes too says: If a serpent, he says, bites in silence, he who disparages in secret has nothing less than it (Eccl 10:11); and his father David: Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against your mother's son you laid a stumbling block. These things you did, and I was silent: you thought, wicked one, that I shall be like you. I will rebuke you, and set it before your face (Ps 49 [50]:20, 21); so that you may be shown to have yourself what you charge against others. But if the length of my explanations on the Prophets displeases anyone, let him hear plainly that I have said far less than the obscurity of the matter demands, and that anyone can make brief little commentaries for himself out of our fullness, which nevertheless will not suffice for a full understanding. For the Prophets do not narrate a simple history and the order of events; but all things are full of riddles, and one thing sounds in the words, another is held in the sense: so that the things you would have reckoned plain, and running on in an unhindered reading, are wrapped again in the obscurities of what follows. But it is time for me to put an end to the prophetic volume, in whose exposition, if I am longer than usual, allowance must be made for its final parts, which I did not wish to divide, lest the number of books be increased.

65:1

They sought me who before did not ask for me: they found, who did not seek me. I said: Behold me, behold me, to a nation that did not call upon my name. LXX: I appeared to those not seeking me: I was found by those who did not ask for me. I said: Behold me, in a nation that did not call upon my name. To the prayer of the people mingled with complaints, in which it had said: Why have you made us err, O Lord, from your way: you have hardened our hearts, so that we did not fear you (Isa 63:17)? there answers, as the Jews would have it, God the Father; as we hold, the Lord and Savior: So far am I from being harsh and cruel, I who prefer the repentance of the sinner to his death, and do not repel repentant sons, provided they have kept the dignity of their name, that I wish to save even strangers (Ezek 33). For those who did not seek me, and could not say: We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the prophets, Jesus (John 1:45), to these very ones I appeared; of whom the Prophet also testified elsewhere: Those to whom nothing was announced concerning him will hear, and those who have not heard will understand (Isa 52:15). But you, who meditate on the law of God day and night, boast in vain of a repentance whose works you do not do. Hence the Evangelists and apostles, always wishing to strengthen the coming of the Lord with testimonies of the Old Testament, said: That what was spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled (Matt 1:22). The centurion was not seeking the Lord, and he heard from the Lord: Not even in Israel have I found such faith (Luke 7:9; Matt 8:10). The Syrophoenician woman did not know the utterances of the Prophets, and she is praised by the voice of the Lord: O woman, great is your faith. The nobleman (John 4), who in Greek is called βασιλικὸς, and whom, from the royal court, we can more correctly render palatine, found healing not only for his son but for his whole house. And what is said according to the Hebrew: They sought me who before did not ask, refers to the same sense: that those who formerly had no knowledge of God afterwards seek the Lord and come to know him by revelation; he who was also revealed to Paul while he was persecuting the Church of believers (Acts 9). And he says to the apostle Peter: Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, for flesh and blood have not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matt 16:17). Him Moses too was seeking when he said to God: If I have found favor with you, show yourself to me openly, that I may see you (Exod 33:13). Looking for the reproach of Christ as greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, while he longed for the recompense of things to come, he contemplated in his mind the invisible God as if he saw him. Of whom it is also read in the Psalms: The hope of all the ends of the earth, and in the sea far off (Ps 64 [65]:6). And in Genesis: He himself shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen 49:10). And what follows: I said: Behold, I am: to a nation that did not call upon my name (Exod 3:14), agrees with that sense: He who is has sent me to you. Who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God, etc. (Phil 2); but, calling forth the nations of the whole world, he made one nation of his name, that of the Christians.

65:2

I have spread out my hands all the day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way not good, after their own thoughts. LXX: I have spread out my hands all the day to an unbelieving and contradicting people, who have not walked in the good way, but after their sins. This which was said above: I appeared to those who did not ask for me: I was found by those who did not seek me, the apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, when he had expounded it of the person of the nations, added: But to Israel he says: I have spread out my hands to an unbelieving and contradicting people (Rom 10:21); a people which, when it was overcome by the benefits of the Lord and saw signs beyond what a man can do, said: This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of the demons (Luke 11:15). And again: You are a Samaritan and have a demon (John 8:48). And again: though you are a man, you make yourself God (John 10:33). And elsewhere: This man is not from God, for he does not keep the sabbath (John 9:16). And many other things, which it would take long to string together. Finally, when he on the cross stretched out his hands to the unbelieving people and said: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34), they on the other side said: Ah! you who destroy the Temple and in three days build it up: let him come down now from the cross, and we believe him. He saved others, himself he cannot save (Matt 27:40). Of him Simeon too, holding the little child in his arms, prophesied: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising of many, and for a sign that will be spoken against (Luke 2:34). At Rome the Jews say to Paul: Concerning this sect it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against (Acts 28:22). We can also take the spread-out hands of the generosity of the giver, in that he denied them nothing when they asked, but at once restored health to the leper who asked (Matt 8), and the man blind from birth received eyes (John 9), and thousands of the people, hungry in the desert, besides children and women, were satisfied (Matt 14). The spread-out hands also signify the mercy of a parent eager to receive his children into his bosom. But they, on the contrary, walked in a way not good, and followed their own thoughts. To them the Lord speaks through the Prophet: Turn your foot away from the rough way (Prov 4:27). For they had loved strangers, and like a harlot had said: I will go after my lovers (Hos 2:5). And leaving the good way, which says in the Gospel: I am the way (John 14:6), they walked on the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and followed their own thoughts; and the Prophet, shunning these, entreats the Lord: From my hidden faults cleanse me, O Lord, and from those of others spare your servant. If they have not ruled over me, then I shall be spotless (Ps 18 [19]:13, 14). And the Apostle teaches that those who did not have the knowledge of God are handed over to a reprobate mind and to evil works, to do the things that are not fitting (Rom 1). But let us say with the voice of the Psalmist: Lead me in the right way (Ps 138 [139]:24).

65:3

A people that provokes me to anger, before my face always: who sacrifice in gardens, and offer sacrifice upon bricks (From Exod 20:4). LXX: This people that embitters me in my sight: they always sacrifice in gardens, and burn incense upon brick ÷ to demons that are not. ⁚ Though the Lord says: You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven, and that is upon the earth. And though through Moses he rebukes those who do so: They provoked me with strange gods, and with their abominations they provoked me to bitterness. They sacrificed to demons, and not to God (Deut 32:16, 17); they, out of a zeal for sinning, as if to irritate and provoke God, not only did what was not lawful, but did it continually and always, sinning in the sight of the Lord, to whose eyes all things lie open, or in his Temple, sacrificing victims to idols. And so that nothing might be lacking to the sacrilege, they sacrificed in gardens and burned frankincense upon bricks, joining luxury to idolatry and pleasure to sacrifices; and instead of the one altar which by the law of God had been built of unhewn stones, they made baked bricks and the turf of the fields bloody with the blood of victims. Let this be said according to the letter: but according to the spiritual understanding, every heretic provokes the Lord to anger, and in the falsity of his doctrines offers unclean sacrifices, by no means firm and lasting forever, but like gardens green for a short time, making provision for the delights of the flesh. To him it is said: All flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen: but the word of the Lord, which is preached in the churches, abides forever (Isa 40:6, 7). Naboth, not wishing such gardens to be made out of his vineyard, poured out his blood to Ahab, that most impious king (1 Kgs 21). For it was not fitting that a father's inheritance should perish, and that, the vines being cut down which bear the fruit that gladdens the heart of man, the herbs of pleasures and vices should spring up in the place of virtues. There is reported a deservedly celebrated and praised saying of the wisest man among the Greeks, who calls all the pleasures of the world, and the pomp and luxury of the world swiftly passing away, the gardens of Adonis. The heretics also sacrifice upon stones, when they strive to make their errors and their studied lies firm by the dialectical art, and to build them up square, and to strengthen them by γραμμικαῖς, as they say, ἀνάγκαις, that is, by dust cut on a brick and marked out with lines. But what is read in the Seventy: to demons that are not, and is not found in the Hebrew, must be taken in this sense: that according to the letter and according to the spirit, neither do demons subsist, since they have already fallen away from God, who truly is, nor do the sects of the heretics, which hold no truth, but pass away and perish like shadows. Hence Esther too speaks to the Lord: Do not hand over your inheritance to those who are not (Esth 14:11). And the saint prays in the psalm: Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart, and be no more (Ps 38 [39]:14). For he who, while he lives in this body, has not obtained pardon of his sins, and so departs from life, perishes to God and ceases to be, although he subsists to himself in punishments.

65:4-5

Who dwell in tombs, and sleep in the shrines of idols: who eat swine's flesh, and profane broth is in their vessels: who say, Depart from me, do not come near me, for you are unclean. LXX: In tombs and in caves they sleep for the sake of dreams: who eat swine's flesh and the broth of victims; all their vessels are profane: who say, Go far from me, do not come near me, for I am clean. There was no sacrilege that the people of Israel left out: not only sacrificing in gardens and kindling frankincense upon bricks, but also sitting, or dwelling, in tombs, and sleeping in the shrines of idols, where they used to lie upon the spread-out skins of victims, so as to learn the future from dreams. This the error of the heathen celebrates to this day in the temple of Aesculapius and in many others, which are nothing else but the tombs of the dead. Nor were they content with this end of impiety, but they also fed on the flesh of swine, which was forbidden by the law, and devoured with greedy throats yesterday's broth, which the Greeks call ἕωλον (Lev 12). Hence both they themselves and their vessels were unclean, and they grew daily to such a pitch of wantonness and pride that whoever was not led by a like error they reckoned unclean, and fled from his touch, as the Samaritans and the Jews do to us, and all the heretics, such as lately sprang up in Gaul under a hot-headed master, who, shunning the basilicas of the Martyrs, flee from us who celebrate prayers there according to custom, as though we were unclean. Yet it is not so much they who do this as the demons dwelling in them, who cannot bear the power and the scourges of the holy ashes. And which of the heretics does not rest in tombs, does not sleep in the caves of his masters? Such was Marcion, and Valentinus, and lately Eunomius, who bore witness to the uncleanness of his mind by his leprous flesh; who, leaving the light of the Holy Spirit and the upper room in which the Apostles stayed, linger in the darkness of the devil and love the caves which Jeremiah condemns in mystical speech: My inheritance has become to me as the cave of a hyena (Jer 12:8), which our people call a beast: an animal that always pursues corpses and lives on the juice and gore of dead bodies. Against these, who dwell in caves, Habakkuk too said with a voice of lament: Woe to him who gives his neighbor a drink of a turbid draught, and makes him drunk, that he may look upon his caves (Hab 2:15). Of these caves the Lord too was speaking: It is written, My Father's house shall be called a house of prayer: but you have made it a den of robbers (Matt 21:13), in which you kill the souls of those you deceive, so that you do not see in them the visions of which the same Savior says: I have multiplied visions, and in the hands of the Prophets I have been likened (Hos 12:10). And another says to him: You spoke, he says, in a vision to your sons (Ps 88 [89]:20); but you believe dreams and phantasms, which the Lord commanded us not to believe. These feed on the flesh of swine, of whom it is said: Do not cast your pearls before swine (Matt 7:6). And they eat profane broth, which is seasoned in their books with heretical art. All their vessels are unclean, that is, both their bodies and their teachings; and they come to such madness that whoever is not like them they detest as one lost.

65:6-7

These shall be a smoke in my fury, a fire burning all the day. Behold, it is written before me: I will not be silent, but I will render and repay into their bosom your iniquities, and the iniquities of your fathers together, says the Lord, who sacrificed upon the mountains and upon the hills, reproached me; and I will measure back their former work into their bosom. LXX: This is the smoke of my fury: a fire burns in it all the days. Behold, it is written in my sight: I will not be silent until I render and repay into their bosom their sins, and those of their fathers, says the Lord: who burned incense upon the mountains and upon the hills, reproached me; I will render their works into their bosom. Because of your works, and the incredible arrogance of your mind, in that, being unclean, you thought the clean unclean, you shall be smoke, a burning fire, which is kindled from my fury. But fury, forgetfulness, anger, repentance we ought to take in God in the same way as feet, hands, eyes, ears and the other members which the incorporeal and invisible God is said to have. Not that he is open to these passions, he who by the gift of his grace extinguishes them in us; but so that through our words we may understand God's disposition toward us. For anger, which is the desire for vengeance, is not defined in God as it is in men; it has its matter in our vices, not in the will of the Lord: for we treasure up for ourselves wrath in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, so that a wise flame may consume our thistles and thorns, and the tares that we have brought in place of God's seed, and also the wood, hay and stubble that we have built upon Paul's foundation (1 Cor 3). Of this perpetual fire we read in the song of Moses too: A fire is kindled from my fury, and it shall burn down to hell below. It shall devour the earth and its produce: it shall burn the foundations of the mountains, and my arrows shall consume them (Deut 32:22). The sense of this testimony is that the fire and vengeance of God always burns for sinners, and pursues them even to the lower world. Such was that rich man too in the Gospel (Luke 16), clothed in purple, who, while Lazarus rested in Abraham's bosom, was tormented with eternal burnings. The same flame will also burn the earth, that is, our flesh, and its produce, that is, the desires of the flesh, and the foundations of the mountains that raise themselves against the knowledge of God. The darts of God will also destroy the mountains themselves, so that, humbled in punishments, they cease to be mountains. Behold, he says, it is written before me. For all our sins lie open to the eyes of God, and are written in those books of which we read in Daniel: Thrones were set, and the books were opened (Dan 7:10). Of which it is said in another place: Let them be written upon the earth (Jer 17:13). And he will by no means keep silent any longer, he who had said before: I have kept silent: shall I always keep silent? says the Lord (Isa 42:14). But he will render to each what he has worked, into his bosom, that is, into the secret place of the heart, so that their own conscience may torment them. Of this the prophet Hosea too prophesies: Their princes shall fall by the sword because of the unruliness of their tongue (Hos 7:16). This is their own detraction in their bosom, which proceeds from the heart of each. Something similar is written in Proverbs: In their own bosom all things are rendered to the wicked (Prov 5:22). This bosom, because of the ruling part of the soul (Greek ἡγεμονικὸν), is called by another name the head: I have given their ways upon their heads (Ezek 9:10). And elsewhere: His sorrow shall be turned upon his head, and upon his crown his iniquity shall come down (Ps 7:17). But there is also a good bosom, which will enjoy the holiness of conscience, of which the Psalmist said: And my prayer shall be turned into my bosom (Ps 34 [35]:13). Bosom is also understood as affection and love toward anyone, as when the word is addressed to a husband: The wife who is in your bosom; and to a parent: They will bring your sons in their bosom (Luke 16). Hence all who have Abraham as their father, and have deserved to be like him in his virtues, rest in his bosom. For we ought not to take as fathers, whose iniquities and sins are now repaid to us, those from whose seed our bodies were born. Otherwise Moses himself, who had said that the sins of the fathers are to be repaid to the sons to the third and fourth generation of those who hate God (Exod 20), interprets his own sentence, saying: The sons shall not die for the sins of the fathers: but each shall die in his own sin (Deut 24:16). Ezekiel approves the same sentence, that that parable is by no means to be spoken: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons are set on edge (Ezek 18:2), but that only his teeth are set on edge who has eaten, and that the sinning soul perishes, and does not pay for another's sins. From this we understand that those are to be taken as fathers, whether in the good sense or in the contrary, to whom each is added when he has departed from this life. Now Israel sacrificed upon the mountains and hills when it set up the golden calves in Bethel and Dan. And it reproached God over his precepts, when it neglected his ceremonies and gave the worship of God to demons: whose works are to be repaid into their bosom (Hos 4). And every heretic who despises the simplicity of the Church sacrifices on the mountains and reproaches God, when he despises his precepts.

65:8

Thus says the Lord: As if a grain is found in a cluster, and it is said: Do not destroy it, for it is a blessing; so will I do for the sake of my servants, that I may not destroy the whole. LXX: Thus says the Lord: As if a grape is found in a cluster, and it is said: Do not touch it, for there is a blessing in it: so will I do for the sake of my servant, that I may not destroy all. The Lord had said that Israel would perish, and that all its sins lay open to his sight, and that he would repay the works of each into their bosom. After this he brings in a likeness and an example by comparison, to teach that each perishes by his own sin, and that, even if the multitude of sinners be very great, one righteous man does not perish through the vice of all. If anyone, he says, in a cluster and bunch of grapes which could not come to ripeness and has borne sour fruit, or has been spoiled by some fault of the air and the soil, finds one grain unharmed, which still has hope of growing larger and coming to its usual ripeness, let him say to another: Do not touch it, but let it be, that it may grow, for it is a blessing of the Lord that, among so great a multitude of grapes, it alone escaped the drought: so, he says, out of the innumerable multitude of the Jews, which has offended God, if I find a few righteous, I will set them free from the destruction of the many. And this I will do for the sake of my servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom the promise was made, or for the sake of those who serve me among very many sinners. Something of the kind we read in Genesis too, when righteous men to free the city from its sin are sought, little by little, from fifty down to ten (Gen 18), and Lot alone, as a righteous man, is snatched out of Sodom with his daughters (Gen 19). Of him it is written in the Catholic Epistle (2 Pet 2) that his soul was tormented as he saw abominations committed, and that he showed the judgment of his soul by the bearing of his body. Enoch too, alone among a very great multitude of sinners, was taken up to God (Gen 5). And Noah with his children the Flood, sent because all flesh was turning away from the service of the Lord, could not destroy (Gen 7). Abraham too was saved from the fire of the Chaldeans by the integrity of his faith (Gen 11). With this sense the words of Jeremiah also agree, spoken in the person of the Lord: As something warm in the desert, I found Israel with those slain by the sword (Jer 38:2 LXX; Vulg. 31:2). For when, he says, the whole world lay lifeless, wounded by the swords of idolatry, I found Israel in Abraham to have the warmth of faith, like a physician who after a battle, among the corpses of the dead, where he perceives that someone still has something of life in his beating veins, applies care to his wounds to restore him to health. For what is written ὡς θερμὸν, that is, as something warm, the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, rendered lupine, and in this most of the Greeks also err. And yet it should be known that in the Hebrew, for warmth, THODA (תודה) is written, which means grace: namely, that Israel was saved by the grace of God, and not by the merit of its own works.

65:9

And I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah one possessing my mountains: and my elect shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there, and the plains shall be folds for flocks, and the valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for my people who have sought me. LXX: And I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah, and it shall inherit my holy mountain, and my elect shall inherit, and my servants shall dwell there, and in the woodland there shall be sheepfolds for flocks, and the valley of Achor for the rest of herds, for my people who have sought me out. Him whom above he called the grain of the cluster, or the grape, or (as many would have it) the bunch, he now calls the seed of Jacob and Judah, who is to possess the mountains, or his mountain. Most understand the seed of Jacob and Judah as Christ, of whom it is said in Genesis: Judah, your brothers shall praise you (Gen 49:8), and the rest. For no one doubts that the Savior was born of the stock of Judah. But others would have the Apostles understood, of whom we have often said: The remnant shall be saved (Isa 1:9). And: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have been as Sodom, and we would have been like Gomorrah (Rom 9:29). These possessed the mountain of the Lord by their awareness of Christ dwelling in them, saying: We have come to Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22). Or his mountains, of which it is sung in the psalms: Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people (Ps 124 [125]:2). And: Its foundations are in the holy mountains (Ps 86 [87]:1). And the elect of the Lord will possess Zion, and his servants will dwell in it. Of whom it is written in the same volume: The seed of Abraham his servants, the sons of Jacob his elect (Ps 104 [105]:6). Whoever, then, is still a seed and has not been formed into a son, he is a servant of the Lord, to whom he says in the Gospel: I know that you are the seed of Abraham, but not yet sons (John 8). For if they were the seed of Abraham, they would surely do the works of Abraham. But he who is a son is also an elect of the Lord. Hence the elect possesses Jerusalem, and the servants dwell in it; and of the difference between sons and servants it is said: You have not received the spirit of slavery again unto fear, but the spirit of adoption (Rom 8:15). And there shall be, he says, plains, or woodlands, as folds for flocks. For plains, SARON (שרון) is put in the Hebrew. The whole region around Lydda, Joppa and Jamnia is suited to pasturing flocks. Of it it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: But the woodlands shall be turned into sheepfolds (Acts 9), according to what is sung in the psalm: The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags, and he will lay bare the woodlands (Ps 28 [29]:9), or the thickets of the forests, so that robbers may cease to lurk there, and beasts and venomous animals, and places once of ambush and blood may pass into churches of the Lord, and flocks may be pastured there by him who laid down his life for his sheep. Of whom it is written: He will shepherd us forever (Ps 47 [48]:15). This voice of the Lord, perfecting the stags and laying bare the thickets of the forests, cries out through John in the desert: Already the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt 3:10). And again: Every valley shall be filled (Luke 3:5); of which it is now also said: and the valley of Achor a resting place for herds, and for rest for my people who have sought me out. Of this valley we also read in the book of Joshua son of Nun that Achan was put to death there, who stole from the accursed thing and from the spoils of Jericho, and was put to death with all his house; and from the fact that he troubled the people, the very place where this happened received the name ACHOR (עכור), that is, of trouble and tumult (Josh 7). The valley of Achor, then, in which there was once a curse and punishment, will be for the rest of herds. Expounding this, Paul says: Is God concerned for oxen (1 Cor 9:9)? or does he not rather speak of us, since he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes on the floor ought to thresh in hope of sharing? Of this valley it is also written mystically in Hosea: I will speak to her heart, without doubt to Jerusalem's; and I will give her possessors from there, and the valley of Achor, to open her understanding (Hos 2:14). For this reason, then, the valley of Achor is handed over as a possession to the herds of the people of God, and the woodlands are turned into folds for flocks: that understanding may be opened, and the truth of the Lord be known.

65:11-12

And you who have forsaken the Lord, and have forgotten my holy mountain; who set a table for fortune, and pour libations upon it: I will number you for the sword, and you shall all fall in the slaughter. LXX: But you who have forsaken me, and have forgotten my holy mountain, and prepare a table for fortune, and fill a drink for the demon: I will hand you over to the sword: you shall all fall slain. In places once wooded and full of trouble, in the places of the Gentiles, there will be folds for the sheep, that is, the Churches of believers from the whole world. But you, O people of Israel, who have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger, who have forgotten his holy mountain, of which we have often spoken, whether the Lord Savior, who is the mountain of mountains and the holy one of all the holy, or Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem: you who do this and that, I will hand over to the sword, so that you may all fall slain together. What the sword is, we shall say later. You set, he says, a table for fortune, and pour libations upon it: or according to the Seventy: You prepare a table for fortune, and fill a cup for the demon, or κέρασμα, which all have likewise translated, that is, a mixed drink. Now there is in all cities, and especially in Egypt and in Alexandria, an old custom of idolatry, that on the last day of the year and of the month which is their last, they set out a table loaded with feasts of every kind, and a cup mixed with honeyed wine, taking an omen of the fertility either of the past year or of the coming one. And this the Israelites did, worshiping the monstrosities of all the images, and they offered not victims upon the altar, but poured out libations upon a table of this kind. And where the Seventy translated to the demon, the Hebrew has MENNI (מני), which Symmachus rendered without me: so that the sense is: You who prepare a table for fortune, and fill a drink without me; to teach that it is done not for him but for the demon. Now the sword by which they are slain is taken for punishment. For not all the people of Israel were handed over to the sword, since we see how many thousands of them are scattered over the whole world; but to punishments and torments, to captivity and the utmost servitude, according to what is said elsewhere: All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword; and in the Song of Deuteronomy: I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour the flesh of the wounded (Deut 32:42). It can hardly be believed that the arrows of the Lord are made drunk with blood, and that his sword is sated with the flesh of the wounded. Job speaks of these arrows, which pierced him at every moment of the hours: The arrows of the Lord are in my body: their fury drinks up my spirit; for when I begin to speak, they goad me (Job 6:4). But according to tropology it must be said that all who desert the Church and forget the holy mountain of God, and give themselves over to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, prepare a table for fortune, believing that nothing is God's concern, but that all things are governed either by the course of the stars or by the changes of fortune: whom Paul rebukes, saying: You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Cor 10:20, 21): for they will be handed over to eternal punishments, so that none of them can escape the slaughter and the ruin.

65:12

Because I called, and you did not answer; I spoke, and you did not hear: but you did evil in my eyes, and what I did not will, you chose. LXX: Because I called you, and you did not hear: I spoke, and you despised, and you did evil in my sight, and what I did not will you chose. You have been handed over to the sword, he says, because you have not only forsaken me and forgotten me and mixed a cup for fortune, but when I was Emmanuel, that is, God with us, of whom John too writes: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (John 1:14), I called you, present among you: Return to me, returning sons (Jer 3:14). And: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28); and you would not answer. I spoke in parables, and did all that I ought to do, and you did not hear me, nay, you even despised me. For I am he who said above as well: I came, and there was no man: I called, and there was none to obey (Isa 50:2). Nor was this impiety enough for you, to despise me when I was present, and to kill the heir sent to you; but you did evil in my sight, and chose what I did not will, and blasphemed the Son of God, so as to ask for yourselves Barabbas the robber, the author of murder and sedition; and you still dare to say: Why have you made us err from your way (Isa 63:17)? For if those who did not know me found me, and those who did not call upon me received me, what torments are you worthy of, who would not receive him who was sent to you and said: I have not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24), but on top of that fastened him to the cross? We must consider what is meant by what he says: And what I did not will you chose; or what the will of the Son of God is, who says in the Gospel: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven: but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven (Matt 7:21). Of which God himself also says: I have willed to do your will (Ps 39 [40]:9). This is the will of which the Lord himself was speaking: I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my wills (Acts 13:22). Hence the saint too prays and says: Teach me to do your will, for you are my God (Ps 142 [143]:10). For all things are lawful, but not all things are expedient. And concerning virgins the Apostle relates that he has no command of the Lord, yet he wishes us to be as he himself is (1 Cor 6). By this he shows that it is by no means the indulgence of the master that is to be followed, but his will (1 Cor 7); and that we ought to choose the things that are expedient, not those that are lawful, as is that concerning second marriage: I wish the younger women to marry, to bear children, to be mothers of families (1 Tim 5:14). And he gives the reasons why he allows this: For already some have turned aside after Satan. Therefore second marriage is not his pure will, since it is cheapened by the comparison with fornication.

65:13-14

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall give praise for exultation of heart, and you shall cry out for sorrow of heart, and for contrition of spirit you shall howl. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall be glad, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall exult in joy, but you shall cry out because of the sorrow of your heart, and because of the contrition of your spirit you shall howl. Not only shall you fall by the sword, you who have forsaken the Lord and done evil in his sight and would not hear him when he was present, but you shall see a great difference between yourselves and the multitude of the nations. For those who will be my servants shall eat and drink, they shall rejoice and give praise for exultation of heart. But you, on the contrary, shall be hungry and thirsty, you shall be put to shame, and for sorrow of heart and contrition of spirit you shall howl. All these things the χιλιασταὶ think are to be fulfilled in the thousand years, believing food and drink to be the kingdom of God, and not understanding what is written: Labor not for the food that perishes, but for the bread of life and truth (John 6:27), and desiring to eat the flesh of Christ and the fruit of the tree of life. Of this the Savior speaks: I am the bread that came down from heaven (John 6:33). And Ecclesiastes: Open your eyes, and be filled with loaves (Prov 20:13). And the Psalmist: I was young, he says, and have not grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread. All the day he is merciful and lends, and his seed shall be for a blessing (Ps 36 [37]:25). Of this bread and spiritual banquet he instructed the disciples: You who have continued with me in my trials shall eat at the table of my Father in the kingdom of heaven (Luke 22:28). But if we take it of simple bread, how shall we be able to explain this: The Lord will not kill the righteous soul with hunger (Prov 10:3). And again: The Lord knows the ways of the spotless, and their inheritance shall be forever. They shall not be put to shame in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be filled (Ps 36 [37]:18, 19). For how many saints die in persecution, worn out by hunger and want; how many righteous men are hungry, while the wicked are distended with surfeit! But the drink is to be taken as that which is drawn from the fountains of Israel; whoever drinks of it will have in himself a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4; Luke 22). This the Savior too promises that he will drink with the Apostles in the kingdom of the Father: it gladdens the heart of man (Ps 103 [104]:14), so that those who drink can say: You have put gladness in my heart (Ps 4:7). Of this food and drink it is said among the eight beatitudes: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5:6). And the mother of the Lord, full of the Holy Spirit, prophesied: He has filled the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53), those who before did not have the food of the Lord: and the rich he has sent away empty, those who were given for his burial, and who spat out him whom the Prophets had promised. Of these the Psalmist sings in another place too: The rich have been in want, and have hungered (Ps 33 [34]:11), that is, the people of the Jews. But those who seek the Lord, that is, the crowd of the Gentiles, shall not lack any good thing. And when those who serve Christ and believe in him have rejoiced and praised God for exultation and joy of heart, then those others will be put to shame, seeing others succeed to their place; and they will cry out for sorrow of heart, fulfilling what is written: There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt 13:50): when the lambs of the nations and of the righteous stand at the right hand, and the goats of the Jews and of the wicked on the left: the one receiving eternal rewards, the other eternal punishments. And the contrition of spirit for sorrow of heart is to be understood of the conscience of sins, according to what is written: Those who err in spirit shall know understanding (Isa 29:24). And: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 50 [51]:19). The spirit is crushed when it has been lifted up; as is written of a king hostile to Israel: The Lord hardened his spirit (2 Kgs 17:14). And of the prince of the Babylonians, when his heart was lifted up and his spirit hardened, so that he said in his pride: This is Babylon, and I have made it (Dan 4:27).

65:15-16

And you shall leave your name for an oath to my elect, and the Lord God shall slay you, and he shall call his servants by another name, in which he who is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in God, amen: and he who swears in the earth shall swear in God, amen. LXX: For you shall leave your name for satiety to my elect. But you the Lord shall slay: and to those who serve me a new name shall be called, which shall be blessed upon the earth: for they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God. For satiety, which in Hebrew is called SABAA (שבועה), the others translated oath; this word has many meanings and varies with the difference of accents. For it is understood as oath, and fullness, and satiety, and many, and seven. Of this we spoke in the book on Genesis, and in this volume (cf. Isa 4), where seven women took hold of one man. Again, where the Seventy translated true, and in the Hebrew it is said AMEN (אמן), Aquila rendered πεπιστωμένως, that is, faithfully. And what he says is this: when others have succeeded to your place, your name will be an oath for my elect, so that they may hold you up as an example of evils and abhor suffering such things, and swear thus: may I not suffer these things which the people of the Jews suffered. Or your name will be for satiety: which is usually said of those whose recollection and memory is hateful, and who have come to the point of satiety and nausea. Or certainly it must be said that they leave their name to the elect of the Lord, so that the crowd of the nations may succeed in their place, and be called sons of Abraham and Israel. Of whom Paul speaks: Peace upon them, and upon the Israel of God (Gal 6:16). For not all who are of the Israelites are Israel, nor are all who are the seed of Abraham sons (Rom 9:7); to whom it is said: If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham (John 8:39). And because they are the seed of Abraham and not sons, of which difference we spoke above, John the Baptist therefore rebukes them, saying: And do not presume to say, We have Abraham as our father: for God is able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham (Matt 3:9). For how can they be his sons who have said to wood and stone, You have begotten me, since, on the contrary, those who are of faith are called sons of Abraham? But you, he says, the Lord shall slay, so that you are by no means called the circumcision, but the concision (Phil 3); so that you lack eternal life, so that you do not have him who says: I am the life (John 14:6). But his servants, he says, he will call by another name, or a new one, which will be celebrated in the whole world. And it will be blessed: so much so that he who has been called by that name is blessed in the Lord, and receives the seal of the true Circumcision, amen: which the Lord often uses in the Gospel to approve what has been said: Amen, amen I say to you (John 5:19). But the new or other name is none other than that which is derived from the name of Christ, so that the people of God is by no means called Jacob, and Judah, and Israel, and Ephraim, and Joseph, but Christian. For whoever swears in the earth will by no means swear by idols and false gods, but by God: and this sentence again is confirmed by the seal of amen. Further, according to the Seventy, who for amen rendered the true God, so that the true God is blessed, and those who swear upon the earth swear by the true God: we do not, according to the error of the Arians, refer this only to the person of God the Father, of whom it is written: That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3), but to the Son, who is himself also true God, as the evangelist John says: The Son of God has come, and has given us understanding, that we may know the true one, and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ (1 John 5:20). This is the true God and eternal life. For if the Savior says of himself: I am the truth (John 14:6), consequently the true God received his name from truth, so that he is by no means called God after the manner of false gods, but after the manner of the true God the Father, and is himself true God. Otherwise, if he is not true, he will be like an idol, which recoils upon the heads of those who deny that Christ is true God. And this is the new name which is written for him on the pebble in the Apocalypse (Chapter 2), which is blessed in the whole world.

65:17-18

For the former distresses have been given over to oblivion, and because they are hidden from my eyes. For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be in memory: and it shall not come up upon the heart: but you shall rejoice and exult forever in the things that I create. LXX: For they shall forget the former tribulation, and it shall not come up upon their heart. For there shall be a new heaven and a new earth: and they shall not remember the former things, and they shall not come upon their heart; but they shall find joy and exultation in it. The cause of the gladness and of the confession of the true God is that an eternal oblivion of the former distresses will follow, so that they will by no means remember the idols and their ancient error, but will pass from darkness to light, so as to enjoy eternal blessedness. For they will forget their former evils, not by a forgetting of memory, but by the succession of good things, according to what is written: In a good day there is forgetfulness of evils (Sir 11:27). And elsewhere: The affliction of an hour brings forgetfulness of delights (ibid. 29): because those placed in distress by no means enjoy in their minds, according to the error of Epicurus, their former pleasures. Though this too may be said: that in the new heaven and in the new earth all memory of the former way of life will be blotted out, lest this very thing be a part of evils, to remember the former distress. Now the new heaven and the new earth those who think that all things we see will perish interpret by the testimony of the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away (Matt 24:35). And by that of the apostle Paul: For the things that are seen are temporal: but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Cor 4:18). But those who consider newness to be a change for the better, and not the destruction of the elements, use this example: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain, and they shall all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed (Ps 101 [102]:26, 27). In this it is clearly shown that perdition and destruction mean not an abolition into nothing, but a change for the better. For neither does what is written in another place: The moon shall shine like the sun, and the sun shall receive sevenfold light (Isa 30:26), signify the destruction of the former things, but a change for the better. That this may be understood, let us set down examples from our own condition: when an infant has grown into a boy, and a boy into a youth, and a youth into a man, and a man into an old man, he by no means perishes through the several ages. For he is the same who was before; but he is changed little by little, and is said to have perished to his former age. Understanding this, the apostle Paul too said: For the fashion of this world passes away (1 Cor 7:31). Let us consider what he said: the fashion passes away, not the substance. Peter too signifies the same thing: This escapes them, willingly: that the heavens were from the beginning, and the earth out of water and through water subsists by the word of God; through which the former world, flooded by the deluge, perished. But the heavens and earth which are now are by the same principle kept for fire (2 Pet 3:5ff.); in what sense this is to be taken, he teaches afterwards: But we see new heavens and a new earth, and his promise (ibid. 13): he did not say, we shall see other heavens and another earth, but the old and ancient ones changed for the better. We can also say this: that those converted from idolatry, having deserted their ancient error, see new heavens and a new earth, by no means reckoning the elements to be gods, nor the things that are born of the earth. Now we confess that heaven and earth are the works of the hands of God: but at that time we venerated servants and the creature with the homage due to God; and David, perceiving this, sings in the psalm: I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers (Ps 8:4): not that at that time, when he said this, he did not see the heavens; but that through the several increases of virtues, and the knowledge of things to come, he sees as new those which he already saw as old. And what is said at the end of this testimony: Which I create, was omitted by the Seventy.

65:19

For behold, I create Jerusalem an exultation, and its people a joy: and I will exult in Jerusalem, and rejoice in my people. LXX: For behold, I make Jerusalem an exultation, and my people a gladness, and I will exult over Jerusalem, and be glad over my people. You ought, he says, to rejoice and exult with everlasting gladness in the creation of new heavens and a new earth, and not to remember the former things at all, lest any sadness should arise in you from the recollection of the old: for I will create not only new heavens and a new earth, but Jerusalem too in exultation, and its people in joy. Without doubt it will be a gladness for the whole earth, so that the city which, when old, was the joy of one nation, when new may be the gladness of all the nations. And so great will be the exultation and gladness of all over the city and people of God, that I too, its founder, will exult and rejoice over Jerusalem and over my people, who shall eat and drink and be glad and exult in it, and who have been called by the new name.

65:20

And there shall no more be heard in it the voice of weeping, and the voice of crying: there shall no longer be an infant of days, and an old man who does not fill out his days. For the child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed. LXX: And there shall no more be heard in it the voice of weeping, and the voice of crying: nor shall there be there any more one untimely and an old man who does not fill out his time. For there shall be an infant a hundred years old, and he who dies a sinner at a hundred shall be accursed. For it will not be fitting that in the city of Jerusalem and in the people of God, which will receive the eternal creation of exultation and joy, the voice of weeping and crying should be heard any more, when sorrow, mourning and groaning have gone away. For contraries cannot exist together. And where there is exultation and joy, which is the fruit of the Holy Spirit, there weeping and lamentation cannot abide, which befits those who mourn and grieve, and above all crying, which Paul expels from the Church of believers, lest, like the Jews, we make a crying instead of judgment (Eph 4). In such a city there will not be different ages: an infant and an old man, small and great, who does not fill out his days; but as sons of the resurrection all will come to the perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, so that no one will lack a span of years nor have more than enough, nor will it be that, while one does not yet have firm strength, another ceases to be what he was and withers in decrepit age; and all will come to the number of a hundred, as Abraham was, who at this age received the promise of his son Isaac (Gen 21). Of the praises of this number there is no need to say much, lest the discussion be superfluous. This only we say: that ten decades have equal sides, and possess the firmness of a square form. In the promises too, for the things we have spent, the Lord promises us them multiplied a hundredfold; and the seed falling on good ground has as its first number of most abundant yield the hundred. Finally Isaac too, sowing one seed of faith, received the works of his labor multiplied by this number. At that time, then, when all will be of one age, both the saint and the sinner will be perfected by a like resurrection, nor will they differ from one another in time; but one will be drawn to rewards, the other to punishments: and the sinner will be accursed in this, that he will suffer eternal punishments in an incorrupt body. That too which we read in the Apocalypse of John (Chapter 20), that after the resurrection small and great are brought into the presence of the judge, signifies differences not of ages but of merits. For he who is small, according to the sentence of Solomon, is worthy of mercy: but the mighty shall mightily suffer torments (Wis 6:7). With this sense the words of the Lord also agree: The servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47). But he who does not know, and has done things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few. The blessed apostle Paul, with Christ speaking in him, expounding the old Scripture, declares the patriarch Abraham to be the father not only of the circumcision but of the uncircumcision (Rom 4), that is, that two peoples were begotten from him; and that the one which had been born according to the flesh, a hundred years old, lies under a perpetual curse because of Christ, who was born of the stock of Abraham, and on whom it laid hands. The Gospels teach this figure (Mark 5), in which it is related that the woman with the issue of blood began to be ill at the time when the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was born, and that when the one was healed the other at once died, within one and the same span of years: that the new people persists in youth, and the old dies in unbelief and is accursed. This we have said according to the Seventy translators, whose edition is spread through the whole world, lest in a most famous passage we should seem to take refuge in the citadel of the Hebrew language. Whether you understand this after the resurrection at the second coming of the Savior, or believe it after baptism in the first resurrection, it is not at odds with the faith of the Church. The Hebrews contend that these things will come to pass before the resurrection in a kingdom of a thousand years upon the earth, and that so long a span of future life is promised that a hundred years are counted as infancy; but that the sinner will die in the hundredth year of his age: namely, so that he may not enjoy the wealth he has gathered, but may know that he is accursed because of his sin. But if it is so, where will be the perfect blessedness, which is violated and corrupted by sin, and where sin is punished by an untimely death?

65:21-22

And they shall build houses, and dwell in them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat their fruits. They shall not build, and another dwell: they shall not plant, and another eat. LXX likewise. Of these houses the prophetic word also makes promise in Psalm 68 (69), saying: For God will save Zion: and the cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell there, and acquire it by inheritance, and the seed of his servants shall possess it: and those who love his name shall dwell in it. All this the Jews take carnally, that Jerusalem and the cities of Judea are to be restored to their former state. But if we grant them this, let them hear that this is promised not only to Jerusalem but also to Sodom, as Ezekiel says: Sodom shall be restored to its ancient state (Ezek 16:55).
